## 1. Purpose, ownership and authoring contract

### 1.1 What this document is

This is the **specification for porting MvcMusicStore's MVC 5 edition from ASP.NET MVC 5 on
System.Web to ASP.NET Core**. It is written to be executed: an engineer holding this document, its
sibling deliverables and repository access should be able to carry out the port without making a
design decision this document declined to make.

Deliverable [12](12-migration-blockers.md) enumerated twenty-two blockers and, for each, named the
successor or recorded that there is none. **This document's job is the next step and a different
one: every one of those twenty-two gets a resolution — a decision, with the target construct named,
the affected sites listed, and the test that proves it.** Section [13](#13-resolution-register--all-22-blockers-of-deliverable-12)
walks all twenty-two and is the audit trail for that claim.

The scope is the **migration source only**. Edition triage is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to
sequence and it selected MVC 5; MVC 4 and MVC 3 are retained read-only as **historical and comparative
references**, and appear here only where their code is evidence about a decision this
document makes — which happens once, in section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command).

**MVC 5 is the sole executable behavioural baseline, and that distinction is load-bearing rather than
terminological.** In this document "behavioural baseline" means *the artifact the suite drives and
compares the port against*, and exactly one edition is that artifact: `LegacyBaselineFixture` drives
**MVC 5** over HTTP (section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)), and **neither MVC 4
nor MVC 3 is driven by the suite at all** — no row of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) issues a
request against either. Calling all three "the behavioural baseline" would advertise three executable
references where there is one, and would imply a cross-edition comparison the suite does not perform.
The reason only MVC 5 can hold the role is that the port derives from MVC 5 and is validated against
it: a difference between the port and MVC 4 or MVC 3 would not be a regression at all, because those
editions' behaviour is not what the port promises to preserve. Per-edition build outcomes — including
whether either of the other two editions can be stood up to be driven — are
[10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s and are not restated here. **The other two editions are
read as evidence; MVC 5 is run.**

### 1.2 What this document is not

It is not an inventory. Where a fact about the current system is already established and owned
elsewhere, this document **cites it and moves to the resolution** rather than re-deriving it. It is
not a schedule: **no implementation effort figure, no delivery duration and no sequence position for the
work** appears anywhere below, because those belong to [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) and
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) and a second statement of them would be a second decision.

**That exclusion is about the delivery of the work and not about time as such, which is worth stating
because a blanket "no figures" claim would be plainly false of the pages that follow.** Operational
periods and retention figures are runtime configuration, they are part of the contracts this document
owns, and they appear throughout: the readiness cache's ten seconds and the genre aggregate's five
minutes (sections [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order),
[8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), the lockout window and the cookie and
security-stamp intervals (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), the submission
token's twenty-four-hour lifetime (section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)), and the legacy-cookie middleware's
retention, which is [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s figure consumed here. None of
those is an estimate, none names a date, and none says how long any of this work takes.

And it is not authorization. See section [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible).

### 1.3 Authoring contract, and the absence of user rules

**`review_rules` returns exactly "No user rules provided."** Verified directly during the production
of this document. There is therefore no project rule to name, summarize or cite, and no rule forcing a
file into scope. That absence is **not** licence to lower the bar; enterprise-standard practice applies
instead, and this document holds itself to four explicit contracts:

1. **Citation contract.** Every claim about the **existing** system carries an inline
   `[<path>:<locator>]` citation at the point of the claim, with a repository-relative path that
   resolves in the checkout. A prescription about the target needs no repository citation — but the
   fact that motivates it almost always does, and where it does, it carries one.
   **The path is written out in full at every citation.** No citation in this document uses a bare
   locator shorthand and none inherits its path from a neighbouring sentence, bullet, table row or
   table column, so any single citation can be checked in isolation without reading what surrounds
   it — the same convention [02 §2](02-dependency-inventory.md) and
   [04 §2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) adopt. The enumeration that establishes it, and the
   locator check that resolves every one of them against this checkout, are in
   [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).
2. **Repository-wide claims carry their reproducing command.** A count or an absence has no single
   line to point at, so its evidence is the command that produces it. Every such command in this
   document was run against this checkout; [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) collects them.
3. **Exact versions only, and version pins are not this document's to state.** Where a version
   matters, [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) and [04 §9.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
   own the pins. This document names the *capability* and cites 04 for the *version*.
4. **One fact, one owner.** Section [1.6](#16-what-this-document-does-not-own) lists what belongs to
   someone else. Where this document needs such a fact, it links to the owner rather than restating
   the value.

Markdown line length follows the corpus convention recorded in [`README.md` § 10 Markdown line-length convention](README.md#10-markdown-line-length-convention).

### 1.4 The no-modification constraint, and the boundary that makes this document possible

The user directed **"Do not make code changes initially"**, and the project's environment setup
instructions independently restate the same gate. **No tracked repository file was created, modified or
deleted in producing this document except the file you are reading** — and that sentence is narrower
than "nothing was written", so the difference is stated rather than glossed.

**Restores and builds were performed against this checkout during the assessment, and they wrote
output into it.** Those runs left **eight gitignored trees** behind — 527 files, 114,310,394 bytes:

```text
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/bin      src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/bin
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/obj      src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/obj
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/bin                              src/MVC4/packages
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/obj                              src/MVC5/packages
```

**All eight were removed and their absence was verified.** None was ever a tracked file and none is in
the checkpoint commit; what they were is ignored output that a status command cannot see. The account
of them belongs to [10 §1.4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md), which owns build hygiene as its
subject and carries the per-tree record; **none of those runs is build evidence**, and MVC 5's build
status remains **blocked pending a Windows verification run**
([10 §3.1](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md),
[10 §5.4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)). This document repeats none of that — what it owes
the reader here is the honest form of its own attestation.

**That is exactly why the acceptance check is four commands rather than one, and why a bare
`git status --porcelain` is not sufficient evidence for it.** All eight trees were ignored on this
checkout, so build and restore output was **invisible** to plain porcelain and to a tracked-file diff
alike: for the whole period they existed, both would have reported a clean tree. An attestation resting
on either was attesting to something it had not looked at.

**Which rule ignored which tree, because the obvious answer is wrong for half of them.** The `bin` and
`obj` trees are matched by `[Bb]in/` [.gitignore:2] and `[Oo]bj/` [.gitignore:1]. The two nested
`packages` trees are matched by **`Packages/` [.gitignore:33]**, not by `packages/*`
[.gitignore:15]: a pattern whose only separator is trailing matches a directory of that name at **any**
depth, whereas a pattern with an interior separator is anchored to the repository root and so cannot
reach `src/MVC4/packages` or `src/MVC5/packages` at all. `Packages/` reaches them only because
`git config core.ignorecase` reports `true` on this checkout, which makes the capitalised pattern match
the lowercase directories — so **on a case-sensitive filesystem nothing in `.gitignore` would ignore
those two trees**, and there they would have been visible to plain porcelain as untracked paths.
[04 §A.6](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns this analysis and states it the same way; the
per-path rule is reproducible with `git check-ignore --no-index -v`, in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility). Neither half of that changes the conclusion for this
checkout: all eight were ignored here, so the two ignore-aware commands are the ones that carry the
claim.

The check therefore runs the two ignore-aware commands beside the two tracked ones, and all four have
to agree:

```bash
git status --porcelain              # -> 0 lines  (no tracked change, no untracked file)
git status --porcelain --ignored    # -> 0 lines  (and no "!!" row: no ignored path exists either)
git clean -ndX                      # -> empty   (nothing ignored is there to be removed)
git diff --name-status ea2552d6eda7c20e9477a512e5c615665618cf35..HEAD
# -> exactly 13 rows, every one an "A", every path under docs/modernization/:
#    01-architecture-overview.md            08-technical-debt-register.md
#    02-dependency-inventory.md             09-security-assessment.md
#    03-modernization-roadmap.md            10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md
#    04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md       11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md
#    05-aspnet-core-migration-approach.md   12-migration-blockers.md
#    06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md    README.md
#    07-effort-risks-sequencing.md
# No M row, no D row, and no path outside docs/modernization/.
```

The first three are read against a clean checkout of the checkpoint commit; the fourth is the one that
survives later commits, which is why it remains the check of record. `git clean -ndX` is listed
because it is the only one of the four that answers the question in the form it is asked — *is any
ignored artifact present* — and it answers it in a dry run that removes nothing.

**This document lives closer to that line than any other in the set, so the line is worth stating
precisely: the prohibition is on *mutating*, not on *planning*.**

Every target artifact named below — `Program.cs`, `appsettings.json`, `ErrorViewModel.cs`,
`Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs`, `Services/ShoppingCartService.cs`, `Data/MusicStoreEntities.cs`,
`Data/ApplicationDbContext.cs`, `Data/Migrations/Catalog/**`, `Data/Migrations/Identity/**`,
`Data/SeedData.cs`, the three `*ViewComponent.cs` classes and their `Default.cshtml` views,
`Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`, `wwwroot/**`, `libman.json`, `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/**` and
`tools/provision-admin/**` — is **content written into this document, not a file created on disk.**
Likewise, every row below whose fate is "Deleted" describes a target state; nothing was deleted.

**This document therefore fails in both directions.** It fails if it reads as authorization to begin
changing code. It fails equally **if it declines to specify a change because it mistook the
prohibition on mutating for a prohibition on planning** — and that second failure is the more likely
one, because it looks like caution. What follows is written as a specification an engineer executes
after approval.

The **registration surface those edges reach** — its name, its signature and what it covers — is this document's and is section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). |
| Per-edition build outcomes, including MVC 5's — **blocked pending a Windows verification run**, on the clean-checkout restore precondition that produced the observed failure | [10 §5.4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md), with the evidence table in [10 §3](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) | Cites. Asserts no build outcome of its own and does not treat MVC 5's application build as established. |

---

## 2. The composition root

### 2.1 Disposition of every current startup and configuration file — twelve files, four fates

Composition in MVC 5 is split across twelve files and two entry points. In the target it is one file
plus a handful of Razor and MSBuild conventions. The table below is the **complete** disposition, and
its column headings matter: *Physical fate* is what happens to the file, *Responsibility* is what
happens to what the file did. Those are different questions, and four distinct answers appear in the
second column.

**"No counterpart" is not the same as "no successor."** A responsibility with a successor moves; a
responsibility with no counterpart **ends**, and the target simply does not have the concern. Both
appear below and each row says which it is.

| Current file | Physical fate | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Global.asax.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11-21] | Deleted | **Moves, per registration** — the five registrations do not share one fate; see [2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate) |
| `Startup.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:4-14] | Deleted | **Moves** — attribute-declared host discovery becomes explicit composition in `Program.cs`; see [2.3](#23-owin-startup-the-abstraction-goes-the-responsibilities-do-not) |
| `App_Start/RouteConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:12-21] | Deleted | **Moves** — one conventional route registration in `Program.cs`; the `.axd` ignore route ends |
| `App_Start/FilterConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/FilterConfig.cs:8-11] | Deleted | **Replaced** — exception-handling middleware plus the global anti-forgery filter of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems) |
| `App_Start/Startup.App.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:14-45] | Deleted | **Splits** — the initializer registration [:16] is replaced by migrations; administrator provisioning [:18-45] **leaves the web application entirely** for `tools/provision-admin` (section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command)) |
| `App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:11-36] | Deleted | **Moves and becomes explicit** — cookie authentication is a framework feature; the policy it silently inherited today is stated in section [6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited). The external sign-in cookie [:20] is **retained in substance**: the Katana registration call ends with `IAppBuilder`, the cookie itself becomes the framework's external scheme, because section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (5) retains the surface it serves. The four commented-out providers [:23-35] **end**, per the same decision |
| `Global.asax` — the markup file [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax:1] | Deleted | **Ends.** The target has no application-declaration file of any kind and nothing reads this one |
| `App_Start/BundleConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/BundleConfig.cs:9-29] | Deleted | **Ends.** No bundler in the target — section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler) |
| `Views/Web.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config] | Deleted | **Splits.** Namespace registration [:14-21] moves to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`; the `BlockViewHandler` mapping [:31-32] **ends** — section [8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports) |
| `Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs:8-15] | Deleted | **Absorbed** into MSBuild properties — [04 §5.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns it |
| `Web.Debug.config` | Deleted | **Ends.** It carries no active transform at all — verified, section [3.2](#32-the-one-active-transform-and-the-two-halves-it-splits-into) |
| `Web.Release.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18] | Deleted | **Re-expressed.** Its one active transform becomes a publish-time Release setting — section [3.2](#32-the-one-active-transform-and-the-two-halves-it-splits-into) |
| `Views/Web.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:1-35] | Deleted | **Splits.** Namespace registration [:14-21] moves to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`; the Razor host and page-base-type section group [:4-23] and the `BlockViewHandler` mapping [:29-34] **end** — section [8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports) |
| `Views/Web.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:1-35] | Deleted | **Splits.** Namespace registration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:14-21] moves to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`; the `BlockViewHandler` mapping [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:31-32] **ends** — section [8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports) |

Two rows in that table are the ones a reader is most likely to compress into the others, so they are
called out. `Startup.App.cs` **splits across a project boundary** — half of it becomes migrations and
half of it leaves the web application to become a separate console tool — which is a stronger statement
than "moves into `Program.cs`". And `Views/Web.config` splits too, with one half having a direct
successor and the other having no counterpart; a plan that deletes the file without noticing the
namespace half loses six `@using` directives that 29 views depend on.

### 2.2 The five `Application_Start` registrations do not share one fate

`public class MvcApplication : System.Web.HttpApplication`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11] runs five registrations in `Application_Start`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:13-21]. Treating the method as one unit is the single most
common way to get this port wrong, because **three different outcomes are present in five lines**.

| Registration | Line in `Global.asax.cs` | Resolution | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AreaRegistration.RegisterAllAreas()` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:15] | **Deleted.** There is no `Areas` folder anywhere in the repository — `git ls-files \| grep -c 'Areas/'` returns `0` — so the call has always been dead scaffolding ([08 §9.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt). Nothing replaces it. | Ends |
| `FilterConfig.RegisterGlobalFilters(GlobalFilters.Filters)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:16] | **Replaced.** Its one filter, `new HandleErrorAttribute()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/FilterConfig.cs:10], becomes **exception-handling middleware** — a pipeline registration, not a filter — and the global filter slot it vacates is taken by the **anti-forgery filter** of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems). Design in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). | Replaced |
| `RouteConfig.RegisterRoutes(RouteTable.Routes)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:17] | **Moves.** The `.axd` ignore route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:14] is **dropped** — the target has no `.axd` handler, so there is nothing to exclude. The single conventional route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:16-20] becomes one conventional route registration with the pattern `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}`, which preserves the whole of the application's URL surface: one route, no areas, no attribute routing, no constraints. | Moves |
| `BundleConfig.RegisterBundles(BundleTable.Bundles)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:18] | **Deleted outright**, under the no-bundler decision of section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler). The five bundle virtual paths cease to exist, which is an approved delta (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)). | Ends |
| `System.Data.Entity.Database.SetInitializer(new SampleData())` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:20] | **Replaced** by explicit migrations plus the guarded seeding command of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks). Note this call is made a **second** time at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:16] — `SetInitializer<TContext>` *sets* rather than *adds*, so only one initialization ever runs ([08 §5.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns the redundancy). Both call sites disappear into one migration path, which is the point. | Replaced |

### 2.3 OWIN startup: the abstraction goes, the responsibilities do not

MVC 5 has a **second** entry point, declared by assembly attribute:
`[assembly: OwinStartupAttribute(typeof(MvcMusicStore.Startup))]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:4]. Its `Configuration(IAppBuilder app)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:9] calls `ConfigureAuth`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:11] and then `ConfigureApp` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:13].

**`IAppBuilder` has no successor type.** Nothing in the target has that shape, so the three method
signatures that take it — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:9],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:14] and
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:11] — cannot be preserved even in principle, and the
`Owin` and `Microsoft.Owin.*` package family goes with it ([04 §8.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
assigns each package its outcome). Attribute-based host discovery goes too: composition in the target is
explicit in the program entry point, so **there is no attribute and no convention to find it by.**

What survives is every *responsibility*: cookie authentication, the database bootstrap decision, and
administrator provisioning. Each is re-expressed rather than translated.

### 2.4 What `Program.cs` contains, in order

Six files collapse into one composition root. Order matters twice over — service registration must
precede use, and middleware order is behaviour, not style — so this is specified as an ordered
sequence rather than a list of ingredients.

**Stage 1 — service registration (the container).** In this order:

1. **Configuration binding.** Options types bound from `IConfiguration` using the options pattern
   (section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)).
2. **The two `DbContext` registrations**, scoped, **both reading the one connection-string key**
   [06 §6.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names — `ConnectionStrings:MusicStore` — and each with
   **its own migrations history table**, with both sets of migrations compiled into **this** assembly
   since neither sets `MigrationsAssembly` (section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables); the project-structural half is
   [04 §12.5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)). **One key, not two**: the two contexts share a single
   database by the decision in section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), and the session cache options and the
   data-protection key context read the same key — so a second key would be a second place for the same
   value to drift, and 06 owns the key's name, its delivery and the authentication mode it carries.
3. **Identity, in one registration.** `AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, IdentityRole>(options => …)`
   followed by `.AddEntityFrameworkStores<ApplicationDbContext>()` and `.AddDefaultTokenProviders()`.
   Every `IdentityOptions` value — password, lockout, sign-in, user — is set in that setup action with
   the explicit values of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). This one call is what
   supplies `UserManager<ApplicationUser>`, `SignInManager<ApplicationUser>` and
   `RoleManager<IdentityRole>` to the constructors of section
   [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces); `.AddRoles<…>()` is
   **not** called additionally, because the two-type overload already registers the role services.
   Role claims are what keep `[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12] working, so the role store is not
   optional here. **Two additions to the same chain, each written exactly once**, because the composition
   root is this document's and the artifacts they register are consumed elsewhere:
   `.AddUserManager<AuditingUserManager>()`, which is the single registration of the audit seam
   [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns — it substitutes the resolved
   `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` so `SignInManager` and every controller go through its overrides, and no
   second user-manager registration exists anywhere; and, **after** this call, the hasher-decorator seam
   whose artifacts [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns and whose registration this composition
   root writes, in **three lines and in this order**:

   ```csharp
   services.AddScoped<PasswordDerivationObservation>();
   services.AddScoped<PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>();          // the inner hasher, by concrete type
   services.AddScoped<IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>(sp =>
       new RehashObservingPasswordHasher(
           sp.GetRequiredService<PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>(),
           sp.GetRequiredService<PasswordDerivationObservation>()));
   ```

   **The middle line is the one that makes the seam constructible, and its absence is not a style
   difference — it is a container that cannot build the object.** The shape an earlier form of this
   document specified,
   `services.AddScoped<IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>, RehashObservingPasswordHasher>()` "wrapping the
   previously registered hasher", **cannot work in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection`**: the
   decorator's own constructor parameter is `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`, which is the service type
   it is *itself* registered as, so resolving it resolves the last descriptor for that service — itself —
   and the resolution recurses until it fails. The container has no descriptor-capturing `Decorate`
   primitive; the library that supplies one is a third-party dependency neither the inventory of
   [02](02-dependency-inventory.md) nor the target package set of
   [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) carries, and this port adds no package to obtain one. So the
   inner hasher is
   made **separately resolvable by its concrete type** — `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` is public, its
   constructor takes `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>`, and the container builds it from the options
   Identity has already registered — and the decorator takes that concrete type. It is the same framework
   hasher Identity would have used, reached by a name the decorator's registration cannot collide with.

   **Why the ordering still matters, for a different reason than the withdrawn one.** `AddIdentity`
   registers its hasher with `TryAddScoped`, so it adds the `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` descriptor
   only if none exists; the factory line above then **appends** a descriptor for the same service, and a
   single-service resolution takes the **last** one. So "after `AddIdentity`" is what makes the decorator
   the resolved hasher — not, as the earlier form had it, what lets it capture a descriptor. Registering
   before `AddIdentity` would leave Identity's `TryAdd` a no-op and the decorator resolved anyway on some
   framework versions and not on others, which is exactly the kind of order-dependence this list exists to
   remove.

   **Four registration lines for the seam, and the number to hold onto is one of each artifact rather than
   a total**: one auditing user manager, one observation object, one inner hasher and one decorator. A
   second `PasswordDerivationObservation` registration or a second user manager gives two objects where the
   contract has one, which is the failure [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s registration row
   guards against; the concrete inner-hasher line is not a second hasher **artifact** — it is the
   framework type the decorator delegates to, given a resolvable name.

   **This is asserted rather than reasoned about, by the coverage assertion, which builds the provider with
   validate-on-build and validate-scopes enabled, resolves `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` from a
   request scope, and exercises the seam concurrently — because a recursive registration of this kind
   throws only when something resolves it, and nothing in a start-up smoke test necessarily does.
4. **The application cookie, configured in exactly one place.** `ConfigureApplicationCookie(options => …)`
   carries the cookie half of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) — name, lifetime,
   sliding expiration, `HttpOnly`, `SecurePolicy`, `SameSite`, `LoginPath`, `LogoutPath`,
   `AccessDeniedPath` and `ReturnUrlParameter`. **There is no second `AddAuthentication().AddCookie(…)`
   call.** Item 3 has already called `AddAuthentication` internally and registered a cookie handler
   under `IdentityConstants.ApplicationScheme`; adding another one would either register a competing
   scheme or overwrite the first handler's options depending on call order — the class of composition
   defect that compiles and then misbehaves.
5. **Data protection**, decided rather than delegated:
   `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()` with
   `.SetApplicationName(...)` taking the **required** `DataProtection:ApplicationName` configuration value,
   validated at startup and never a literal (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables))
   — the key-context decision of section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). The **store's location, protection at
   rest, rotation and slot-isolation policy** remain [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and the
   *requirement* remains [11 §3.2](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)'s; what this document supplies is
   the context, the registration and the migration that creates the table.
6. **The distributed cache, then session.** `AddDistributedSqlServerCache(…)` against the one database
   of section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), then `AddSession(…)` with
   the session options of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). Session stays keyed by
   the constant at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19] (section
   [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)). **The cache registration is load-bearing, not a preference
   between two working options.** `AddSession` registers the session middleware's own services and
   *consumes* `IDistributedCache`; it does **not** register an implementation of it, and no in-memory
   default is supplied on its behalf — that would come from `AddDistributedMemoryCache()`, which this
   application does not call. So with the cache registration removed, `IDistributedCache` is simply
   **unresolved**, and the failure is a dependency-resolution exception the first time the session store
   is constructed rather than a quiet fallback to a per-instance cache. The ordering of the two calls is
   immaterial to the container — registration order does not affect resolution — and they are written in
   this order because it reads in dependency order.
7. **`AddHttpContextAccessor()`.** Stated **explicitly and idempotently**, not because nothing else
   registers it: `AddIdentity` (item 3) already adds `IHttpContextAccessor` as part of its own
   composition, and the accessor's registration uses `TryAddSingleton`, so this call adds nothing when
   Identity is present and is not a duplicate registration. It is written out anyway because the
   dependency is a **first-class requirement of application code**, not a side effect of an authentication
   choice: `ShoppingCartService` resolves the cart id from `IHttpContextAccessor.HttpContext.Session`,
   which is how the `HttpContextBase` parameter at
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:21] stops being a parameter (section
   [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)). Relying on Identity to
   supply it would make the cart badge depend on the authentication stack's internals, so that a change
   to item 3 breaks an anonymous page — a failure at run time rather than at build time, on the first page
   that renders the badge.
8. **Application services** — `ShoppingCartService` scoped
   (section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)).
9. **MVC** — `AddControllersWithViews(options => options.Filters.Add(new AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute()))`.
   That is the **one** global filter: the anti-forgery filter of section
   [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems). Nothing corresponds to `HandleErrorAttribute`, which
   becomes middleware in stage 2.
10. **Anti-forgery options — the header contract *and* the cookie, because configuring only the header
    leaves the cookie on its framework defaults.** `AddAntiforgery(options => { options.HeaderName =
    "RequestVerificationToken"; options.Cookie.Name = ".MvcMusicStore.Antiforgery"; options.Cookie
    .SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always; options.Cookie.HttpOnly = true; options.Cookie.SameSite =
    SameSiteMode.Strict; options.Cookie.IsEssential = true; options.Cookie.Path = "/"; })`. The header
    name is the scripted transport of section
    [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form); the cookie assignments are the
    antiforgery row of the policy table in section
    [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), and **`SecurePolicy` is the one that changes
    behaviour**: its default for this cookie is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, so an application that sets
    `Always` on its authentication and session cookies and says nothing here ships one unmarked cookie
    among three. The coverage assertion requires all three cookies together.
11. **Health checks** — `AddHealthChecks()` with a single registration,
    `AddCheck<CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck>(name: "catalog-db", failureStatus: HealthStatus.Unhealthy, tags: new[] { "ready" }, timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3))`,
    an application-owned `IHealthCheck` rather than the framework's `AddDbContextCheck<T>`. It carries
    the `ready` tag only, so the liveness endpoint of stage 2 runs no dependency check at all, exactly as
    [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) specifies. Net-new capability: the repository has no
    health endpoint of any kind ([11 §3.8](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). **`AddHealthChecks()`,
    `AddCheck<T>()`, the middleware and both endpoint mappings are all shared-framework, so this
    registration adds no package** — and the Entity Framework Core health-check package pinned by
    [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) and explained in
    [04 §10.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) as existing for `AddDbContextCheck<T>` therefore loses
    its only consumer. The manifest is [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, so retiring that pin is
    04's edit and not this document's; what this document owes 04 is the statement that nothing here
    references it any more.

    **Why `AddDbContextCheck<T>` is not used: it is a raw-exception channel, and this document promises
    there are none.** `HealthCheckResult` exposes an `Exception` property and an
    `Unhealthy(string description, Exception? exception, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>? data)`
    overload; `AddDbContextCheck<T>` populates the exception on a failed probe, and the framework's
    health-check service then logs that result **with the exception object**, which puts the provider's
    message — server name, database name, login identity, network detail — into a sink under a category
    this document does not own. That is the same defect as the framework exception-handler log described
    in item 13 below, arriving through a component whose purpose looks unrelated to error reporting.
    Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) lists the category among the channels it
    closes, and this registration is what makes closing it sufficient rather than merely quiet.

    **What the replacement does, precisely.** `CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck` is a scoped service taking
    `MusicStoreEntities`, `IOptions<HealthProbeOptions>`, `ILogger<CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck>` and
    `IHostEnvironment`, and its `CheckHealthAsync(HealthCheckContext, CancellationToken)` does six
    things and nothing else:

    - **It bounds itself explicitly, and the bound is stated in two places on purpose.** A linked source
      — `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(cancellationToken)` with
      `CancelAfter(options.ReadinessBudget)` — caps the probe at **two seconds**, and the probe's own
      `CommandTimeout` is set from the same budget so the wait cannot outlive the token. The
      registration's `timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)` above is a **backstop**, deliberately one second
      longer: the check's own cancellation fires first and produces the sanitized result below, and the
      framework's registration timeout exists only so the endpoint still answers if the check hangs
      before reaching a cancellation point. `HealthProbeOptions.LivenessBudget` is **one second** and is
      the value any liveness-tagged registration must be given; today the liveness endpoint's predicate
      selects no registration at all (stage 2 item 13), so nothing consumes it, and stating it is what
      stops a dependency added to that endpoint later from inheriting no bound. Both budgets are
      configuration with those defaults. An unbounded probe does not fail; it answers **late**, after the
      platform has already decided the instance is not answering, which is the failure mode this
      replaces.
    - **It runs `SELECT 1`, on its own connection, deliberately outside the retrying execution
      strategy.** It takes `Database.GetDbConnection()`, opens it under the linked token, and executes
      `SELECT 1` as a scalar with `CommandTimeout` set to the budget. Going through
      `ExecuteSqlRawAsync` would enter the `EnableRetryOnFailure` strategy of section
      [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — **four attempts and up to three intervening delays
      of up to two seconds each**, by the arithmetic that section states — and a probe that retries is a
      probe that misses its budget. A readiness probe must
      answer *unhealthy* promptly; retrying is the caller's job, and the caller here is the platform.
      `SELECT 1` is also chosen over a query against application data on purpose: the probe must report
      connectivity, not the state of the catalog — which is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
      requirement that the probe be a connectivity check and specifically not the per-request aggregate of
      that document's §6.4.
    - **It answers from a cached result, and every parameter of that cache is
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 4's rather than this document's.** That row fixes
      the cache as **10 seconds, healthy only, per instance, with three invalidations**, and it fixes the
      database frequency that follows from it in row 5 — **at most one `SELECT 1` per 10-second window per
      instance whatever the probe volume**, a ceiling of six per minute per instance against Container Apps'
      `periodSeconds: 10` readiness probe and App Service's roughly one-minute interval, with
      `/healthz/live` contributing zero because it performs no database operation and the release
      pipeline's gate contributing nothing because it is served from the same cache. This document owns
      only the artifact that implements it: a **singleton** `ReadinessResultCache` holding the last outcome
      — the `HealthStatus` and, on a failure, the sanitized failure category — which the scoped check
      consults before opening a connection. Four properties are required and none is optional, because
      each is a row-4 clause and three of them are the ones a plausible implementation gets wrong:
      - **A healthy result is cached for `options.ReadinessCacheTtl`, 10 seconds by default** and
        configuration with that default. It is deliberately **longer** than the two-second readiness
        budget, which costs nothing: a cached answer performs no I/O, so it cannot be the reason a probe
        exceeds its budget.
      - **An unhealthy result is never cached.** Every probe following a failure re-executes the check, so
        a recovered instance is readmitted at the very next probe rather than up to a TTL later — and an
        earlier form of this bullet cached unhealthy results *for the same TTL as healthy ones*, on the
        reasoning that a refusing store should not be hammered. That reasoning is withdrawn: it trades a
        recovery delay on every instance for a load reduction against a store that is already failing, and
        06 row 4 decides it the other way. The re-execution volume is bounded anyway by the probe interval
        and by the two-second budget.
      - **An unhealthy result also replaces any cached healthy value and stores nothing in its place**, and
        **process start begins with no cached value**, so a new instance's first probe always executes a
        real check. Those are row 4's other two invalidations; without the first, an instance that has just
        failed would keep serving a stale `200` for the remainder of a healthy TTL.
      - **Concurrent probes coalesce.** A probe arriving while a check is in flight **awaits that check**
        rather than starting a second, which is what makes row 5's arithmetic a ceiling rather than an
        average.

      The liveness endpoint needs no cache because its predicate selects no registration and it touches
      nothing. A singleton is the correct lifetime precisely because the value being shared is per-process
      rather than per-request — a scoped or per-probe cache would cache nothing — and it is **in-process by
      requirement, never the distributed cache of section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)**, which is
      backed by the very dependency this check is testing.
    - **It returns a sanitized result.** Success is `HealthCheckResult.Healthy()`. Failure is
      `HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(description: $"{category}; trace {traceId}")` — the **single-argument
      description overload**, with **no `exception:` argument and no `data` dictionary** — where
      `category` is one of the **four literals of [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
      shape R4**: **`Timeout`**, **`Unreachable`**, **`Rejected`** or **`Unknown`**. **That vocabulary is
      06's and not this document's**, stated in its register as the one failure-category set it owns rather
      than 05 — every *other* path's categories in this document are 05's, which is why this one is worth
      calling out. An earlier form of this bullet used three locally invented strings,
      `catalog-unreachable`, `catalog-timeout` and `catalog-authentication-refused`; they are **withdrawn**,
      and with them the assumption that three categories suffice. The classification is fixed here because
      06 owns the literals and this document owns the call site:

      | Condition in the check's `catch` or budget | R4 literal |
      | --- | --- |
      | The check's **own** linked token cancelling — the two-second budget elapsing with no answer | **`Timeout`**, and the provider's own command timeout expiring maps here too, since both mean the dependency did not answer in time |
      | A connection-level failure: the connection could not be opened, was refused, was reset, or name resolution failed | **`Unreachable`** |
      | The dependency answered and **declined**: an authentication or authorization refusal, including a managed-identity token the server rejected, and a login that failed for a reason the server stated | **`Rejected`** — this is the literal the withdrawn `catalog-authentication-refused` mapped to, and it is deliberately wider than authentication alone |
      | Any other fault reaching the `catch` — a provider exception that matches none of the above, including a shape a future provider version introduces | **`Unknown`** |

      **`Unknown` is the member the withdrawn three-string set lacked, and its absence was the defect
      rather than an omission of tidiness:** a closed set with no residual member forces a classifier either
      to guess one of the three or to let the fault escape, and both are worse than recording that the fault
      did not classify. **`traceId` is `Activity.Current?.Id`, and where no activity is
      current it is a value the check generates itself** —
      `ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()` — recorded in both the result description and the
      log record below so the two correlate. It is deliberately **not** read from an `HttpContext`:
      `CheckHealthAsync` receives a `HealthCheckContext`, which carries the registration and nothing
      about a request, and a check that reached for `IHttpContextAccessor` would be depending on a
      request that need not exist — the same check is evaluated by the health-check publisher on a timer,
      with no request at all. An activity is normally current for the endpoint-driven case, because the
      hosting layer starts one per request; the generated fallback is what makes the timer-driven case
      correlate too. No provider message, no connection string fragment, no server or database name, and
      no exception type name reaches the result, so nothing raw can reach the response body or the
      framework's own log of that result.
    - **It writes the one record the operator needs, itself, and its fields are 06's closed set rather
      than a locally chosen one.** Exactly one `ILogger` record at **`Warning`** under the application's
      own `MvcMusicStore` category, carrying **the six fields
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 6 fixes for a health-check failure — and no
      seventh**:
      1. the **endpoint literal**, `/healthz/ready`, so a record is attributable to a path without the
         response having to name anything;
      2. the **failure category** — one of the four [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) R4
         literals classified above, `Timeout`, `Unreachable`, `Rejected` or `Unknown`;
      3. the caught exception's **type name**, `GetType().FullName`, plus the **type-name chain of its
         inner exceptions**, types only;
      4. the **stack trace as a string field**;
      5. the **elapsed milliseconds** of the attempt;
      6. the **trace identifier**, which correlates the record with the platform's own probe log.

      Never the message, never an inner message, never `ToString()`, never a provider message, never a
      server, database or connection-string fragment, and never the exception object itself — which is what
      keeps this channel inside the closed-record rule of section
      [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). **This six-field shape is
      [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s record shape R4 exactly, counted the way that
      register counts it** — the sixth field is the envelope's trace identifier, so R4 adds five fields to
      R1 — and it is the health-specific extension of that register's R2 general fault shape, adding the
      endpoint literal and the elapsed milliseconds because a probe record has a path and a budget that an
      arbitrary application fault does not. Where this document earlier carried only three of the six and
      then only the general four-field shape, both forms are withdrawn in favour of R4's. It is
      also why `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks` is pinned to **`None`** in the category
      table of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — that is the category
      `DefaultHealthCheckService` writes a failed check's exception under, and closing it is what makes
      this record the *only* signal a failed probe produces. **The volume is bounded by the readiness cache
      above**, not left to the probe interval: at most one execution, and therefore at most one such
      record, per probe that actually runs — six per minute per instance at the ceiling row 5 states.
    - **It never lets a dependency failure escape as an exception, and exactly one exception may escape
      at all.** Every provider fault, timeout and authentication refusal is caught, classified into one
      of the four R4 literals above and **returned** as an unhealthy result — so no fault of the
      dependency ever reaches the framework as a thrown object. The single exception allowed to propagate
      is an `OperationCanceledException` carrying the **caller's** token, the case where the platform or
      the host abandoned the probe: that is not a statement about the dependency, and swallowing it would
      report a fabricated result for a probe nobody is waiting for. Cancellation from the check's **own**
      linked token — the two-second budget elapsing — is *not* propagated; it is classified as
      **`Timeout`** and returned, which is what distinguishes "the dependency is slow" from "the
      caller left".

      **That one escape cannot reopen a raw-exception channel, and the reason is its content rather than
      its handling.** An `OperationCanceledException` raised from a cancelled token carries the
      framework's fixed cancellation text and no store, server, credential or command detail, so a sink
      that recorded it would learn that a probe was cancelled and nothing more. The channel this
      registration closes is a *provider* exception reaching a log — which is what
      `AddDbContextCheck<T>` produced by attaching one to its result — and that object never exists
      outside this check's `catch`.

    **What the response carries is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) rows 1 to 3's decision,
    and this document's part is the `ResponseWriter` that produces exactly it.** That contract is a fixed
    opaque literal rather than an empty body or a status word, and it is precise enough that a probe
    consumer and a test can both be written against it:

    | Response property | The contract, per [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) rows 1–3 |
    | --- | --- |
    | `/healthz/ready` healthy | **`200`**, body exactly **`ready`** |
    | `/healthz/ready` unhealthy | **`503`**, body exactly **`not-ready`** |
    | `/healthz/live` | **`200`**, body exactly **`live`**. It has no failure body, because a host that cannot answer does not answer |
    | Content type, both paths | **`text/plain; charset=utf-8`** |
    | Cache headers, both paths | **`Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache`**, so no front end, proxy or platform probe ever serves a stale verdict. This is the *response* cache and is not the *result* cache above — row 3 names both precisely because "cached" applied to a health endpoint reads as the first and is meant as the second |
    | What the body may never contain | **No dependency or check name** — not `catalog-db`, not `"database"`, not the context type name; **no server, database, host or connection-string fragment; no trace identifier; no exception type, message or stack; no failure category.** The literals are the whole body: no JSON, no per-check entries, no aggregate status word, no duration, no timestamp |

    **All four response properties are set by one artifact — the shared `ResponseWriter` both endpoint
    mappings are given** — because a body literal written in one place and a cache header added in another
    is how a health response acquires two owners. It is not the security-header middleware of stage 2
    item 2: that middleware sets 06 §10.2's seven-header set, which does not include `Cache-Control`, so
    there is no header both would write and no ordering question between them.

    The framework's default writer is therefore **replaced rather than accepted**: its default emits the
    aggregate status *as text*, which is a status word rather than the fixed literal, and the JSON writers
    that ship for health-check UIs emit per-check entries **by name**, which is precisely what row 2
    forbids. Two earlier forms of this paragraph are withdrawn — one emitted "status and check name", which
    discloses the dependency name; the other emitted **no body at all**, which is not what the coverage assertion requires
    even though it discloses nothing, and a test asserting an empty body would fail an implementation that
    is correct. The failure category, the trace identifier and the elapsed milliseconds live in the log
    record above and reach an operator through the sink, behind its access controls, not through a body
    served on an anonymous path. The coverage assertions require the timeout bound, the exact body literal,
    the content type, the no-store headers, and the absence of any provider text on both the response and
    every retained sink.
12. **Forwarded-headers options, and the host-integrity pair that goes with them.**
    `Configure<ForwardedHeadersOptions>(options => …)` setting **five** members explicitly. **An earlier
    form of this item cleared `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies`** on the reasoning that the platform front
    end is not loopback and the defaults would otherwise ignore the headers. The first half of that is
    true; the conclusion is not, and it is withdrawn — clearing both lists means **every** immediate peer is
    trusted to assert the client address and the scheme, and
    [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) control 2 explicitly requires "the known-proxy or
    known-network restriction of §10.1 in force". An empty trust list is the absence of that restriction,
    not a configuration of it.

    | Member | Value | Why |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `ForwardedHeaders` | `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor \| ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto` | The scheme and the client address, and **nothing else**. `XForwardedHost` is deliberately **absent**, which is [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) control 2 — `X-Forwarded-Host` is the one header that makes `Request.Host` attacker-controlled from outside the front end, and not enabling it is a stronger control than validating it |
    | `ForwardLimit` | **`1`** | Exactly one hop is trusted, because exactly one proxy sits in front of the application on both hosting targets. The framework's default is also 1, and it is set explicitly here because the value is a security property of the topology rather than a default worth inheriting silently: a limit of `null` walks the whole header right-to-left and lets a client-supplied entry become the resolved address |
    | `KnownNetworks` | **Cleared, then populated from the required configuration value `Ingress:TrustedNetworks`** — a non-empty list of CIDR ranges. The primary target's front end reaches the worker over the platform's link-local infrastructure range; a container host's ingress reaches the replica from the environment's infrastructure subnet. The ranges themselves are a deployment input, and [06 §10.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the ingress topology they describe | Populated rather than emptied. The framework's own loopback entries are re-added alongside them, because a sidecar or an in-container probe genuinely is loopback |
    | `KnownProxies` | **Cleared, then populated from `Ingress:TrustedProxies`** where a deployment names individual addresses instead of a range. Either that value or `Ingress:TrustedNetworks` must be non-empty | Same rule, expressed per address. Both may be set; **neither may be left empty**, and that is the check below |
    | `RequireHeaderSymmetry` | **`false`**, deliberately | The platform front end sends `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` with independent cardinality, so requiring symmetry would discard both on ordinary requests. It is stated rather than left at the default so it reads as a decision and not an oversight |

    **Startup fails closed on an empty trust configuration.** An options validator asserts that at least
    one of `Ingress:TrustedNetworks` and `Ingress:TrustedProxies` resolves to a non-empty, parseable value,
    and the application **refuses to start** otherwise. This is the check that makes the difference between
    a configured trust list and the withdrawn clear: an environment that supplies neither would otherwise
    silently trust nothing — the middleware ignores the headers, the application sees `http`, HTTPS
    redirection loops and `Secure` cookies are never sent — or, under the old clearing form, silently trust
    everything. Failing to start converts both into a deployment failure at the moment it can be fixed.

    **Host integrity is the second half, and it is here because it shares the same threat.**
    `AllowedHosts` is set to the application's **real hostnames** — the platform's assigned default
    hostname and any custom domain — **never the template's `*`**, and the default host builder's
    host-filtering middleware then answers **`400`** to a request bearing any other `Host` value. The same
    startup validation rejects a value that is empty or that contains `*` in a non-development environment,
    for the same fail-closed reason. That is [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) control 1, and
    the pair is what closes the class rather than an instance: every absolute URL the application ever
    emits — a redirect, a generated link, a `Location` header — reads `Request.Host`, so the host is
    validated once at the edge of the pipeline instead of at each use.

    **The coverage assertion drives both halves adversarially: a request carrying a hostile `Host` header, and
    a request from an untrusted peer carrying a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`.
13. **The exception record's writer** — `AddExceptionHandler<ErrorRecordExceptionHandler>()`, one
    implementation of `IExceptionHandler`. It exists because the middleware of stage 2 item 3 renders a
    response and the error action deliberately reads no exception
    (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), so **without this registration nothing
    writes the closed record that section promises.** Its `TryHandleAsync` writes the record and
    **returns `false`**, which is the whole trick: returning `false` means "recorded, not handled", so the
    middleware continues to its configured `/Home/Error` path and the generic response is produced by the
    action exactly as specified. It writes **no** response body, sets **no** status code and swallows
    **no** exception. Its content, and the reason it is a separate component rather than a line in the
    action, are in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). Registration order within
    stage 1 does not matter for this one — it is placed last because it is the only registration whose
    subject is another stage's middleware.
14. **Rate limiting** — `AddRateLimiter(options => …)`, a **shared-framework** capability reached through
    the ASP.NET Core framework reference, so **no package is added** and
    [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s manifest is unchanged. It exists because per-account lockout
    does not bound the work an anonymous caller can cause, which is set out in the abuse-model paragraph
    of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **Three
    limiters and one named policy**, all with their limits bound from `RateLimiting:*` configuration — the
    defaults below — validated at startup.

    **The composition is one chained global limiter, and the shape is forced rather than chosen.** The
    two credential controls must **both** apply to the same three actions: a per-source bound on the
    derivation cost, and an aggregate bound that a per-source bound cannot see. Expressing them as two
    **named** policies would silently deliver only one, because
    `RequireRateLimiting`/`[EnableRateLimiting]` attaches an `EnableRateLimitingAttribute` whose
    `PolicyName` selects **exactly one** policy for an endpoint — a second attribute replaces the first
    rather than composing with it, so "two named policies on `Login`" is not a configuration the
    framework has. The framework's composition primitive is
    `PartitionedRateLimiter.CreateChained<HttpContext>(params PartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext>[])`,
    which acquires from every limiter in the array and admits only if all of them admit, and
    `RateLimiterOptions.GlobalLimiter` is typed `PartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext>` — so the chain goes
    there:

    ```
    options.GlobalLimiter = PartitionedRateLimiter.CreateChained(
        perIpCredentialLimiter, aggregateCredentialLimiter, generalLimiter);
    ```

    Each of the three is a `PartitionedRateLimiter.Create<HttpContext, string>` whose partitioner returns
    `RateLimitPartition.GetNoLimiter(...)` for every request it does not govern, so the three compose
    without rationing each other's traffic:

    - **`perIpCredentialLimiter` — the per-source credential bound, keyed on the client address and on
      nothing else.** It governs the three credential-verification endpoints: the `Login` POST, the
      `Register` POST and the change-password POST, selected by a `[CredentialEndpoint]` marker attribute
      read as `context.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<CredentialEndpointAttribute>()` rather than by
      a path string, so a renamed action cannot silently leave the set. For those endpoints it returns
      `RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(clientAddress, …)` with **10 permits per minute per
      partition** and `QueueLimit = 0`, where `clientAddress` is the reconstructed client address defined
      below — **not** the Identity `UserId`, and **not** the submitted user name, for the reasons stated
      with the partition keys. For everything else it returns `GetNoLimiter`. This is the control that
      bounds the fixed derivation cost the service of section
      [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) now spends on **every** attempt, unknown usernames
      included.
    - **`aggregateCredentialLimiter` — the flood bound the per-source limiter cannot see.** Same endpoint
      set, same marker, but **one partition for all of them** — a constant key — with a fixed window of
      **200 permits per minute** and `QueueLimit = 0`. A per-partition limit is blind to a flood spread
      across ten thousand source addresses; this one is not, and its ceiling is set high enough that it
      engages only under an aggregate no real population produces. `GetNoLimiter` everywhere else.
    - **`generalLimiter` — everything the other two do not govern.** A fixed window, **300 permits per
      minute per partition**, `QueueLimit = 0`, so a scripted crawl of the catalog cannot monopolize the
      instance either. It returns `GetNoLimiter` for three sets, each for its own reason: for a
      `[CredentialEndpoint]`, because the 10-per-minute bound already binds and a second budget over the
      same request would only obscure which control refused; for any endpoint already carrying an
      `EnableRateLimitingAttribute`, so an endpoint with a named policy is governed by that policy alone;
      and for the two literals of `HealthPaths`, because rationing a platform health probe reports a
      healthy instance as unhealthy and takes it out of rotation — the same reason item 5 of stage 2
      exempts those paths from HTTPS redirection, and held in the same one place.

    **`"csp-report"` is the one named policy, applied to the violation-report endpoint alone**: a fixed
    window, **20 permits per minute per partition**, `QueueLimit = 0`. It is a named policy rather than a
    reliance on the general limiter for a reason [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states:
    the endpoint is anonymous, browser-driven and outside any user's session, so a report storm from one
    client must not consume a share of the budget that protects the catalog, and the general limiter's
    300-per-minute ceiling is far too generous for a channel whose legitimate volume is a handful of
    reports per deployment. The bound, the accepted media types, the response statuses and the field
    allowlist are **06's**, not restated here. **It is a per-partition bound and therefore a per-instance
    one**, on the same process-local mechanics the block below states: a reporter spread across replicas can
    reach `20 × MaxReplicas` per minute fleet-wide. No derivation is applied to it — unlike the aggregate
    credential bound, 06 states this figure *per partition* rather than as a fleet ceiling, and a
    per-partition figure is per instance by construction.

    **The global limiter runs on every request, including `/csp-report`, and that is why the no-op
    branches are part of the contract rather than an optimization.** The framework evaluates the global
    limiter **first** and the endpoint-specific limiter afterwards, for **every** request that reaches
    `UseRateLimiter` — there is no path the global limiter skips. So the three chained partitioners each
    return `GetNoLimiter` for `/csp-report`, and the named `"csp-report"` policy governs that endpoint
    **alone**: without those branches the report endpoint would be rationed twice, once against a
    catalog-sized budget it has no business consuming and once against its own. The same reasoning is
    what makes the health-path branch above necessary rather than merely tidy.

    **The partition keys differ between the credential limiter and the general limiter, and the difference
    is the point rather than an inconsistency.**

    - **`perIpCredentialLimiter` partitions on the client address, unconditionally — authenticated
      requests included.** The resource it rations is the fixed password-derivation cost of section
      [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), which a request spends whether or not the caller is
      already signed in, and the party driving that cost controls the submitted user name but not the
      address the request arrives from. Keying it on `UserId` for the authenticated case would leave the
      change-password endpoint bounded per session rather than per source, so a caller holding one valid
      session could drive derivations without limit; keying it on the **submitted** user name would be no
      limit at all, because the caller chooses that value, and would additionally make the limiter an
      account oracle. So the credential partition is the address, and the accepted cost is stated rather
      than hidden: a population behind one egress address shares the ten-per-minute credential budget.
      That bound is `RateLimiting:*` configuration, a refusal is a 429 with `Retry-After` rather than an
      account lockout, and the aggregate limiter — not a per-address ceiling — is what a distributed
      flood runs into.
    - **`generalLimiter` partitions on a trusted client identifier, and "trusted" is the load-bearing
      word.** For an **authenticated** request it is the Identity `UserId`, so a signed-in customer
      browsing the catalog is never rationed by whoever shares their egress address; for an **anonymous**
      request it is the client address. The resource here is ordinary throughput rather than a
      cryptographic cost, so the fairness trade goes the other way.

    **Either way the address must be the real one.** It is the client address as reconstructed by
    `UseForwardedHeaders` (stage 2 item 1), which is only meaningful because **stage 1 item 12** populates
    `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` from the required ingress trust configuration and refuses to start
    without it. That matters here more than anywhere else in the pipeline: with an empty trust list the
    middleware ignores `X-Forwarded-For` and **every** anonymous request partitions on the front end's own
    address, collapsing the whole fleet's anonymous traffic into one partition; with the withdrawn
    trust-everything form, any caller could assert a fresh `X-Forwarded-For` per request and hold a
    partition of one each time, which is no limit at all. Partitioning on anything else the caller supplies
    — a header, a cookie — fails the same way, for the same reason the submitted user name is not used.

    **Every permit figure above is a *per-instance* figure, because the built-in limiter's state is
    process-local — and saying so is the difference between a bound and an estimate.**
    `System.Threading.RateLimiting` holds its windows and permit counts in memory in the process that
    created the limiter. There is no shared store, no coordination between replicas and no distributed
    variant in the framework, so a fleet of *n* replicas behind a load balancer admits **up to *n* times**
    any figure written here. That is tolerable for the **per-partition** figures — the ten credential permits
    per address, the general limiter's 300, and the named `"csp-report"` policy's 20 — and **not** tolerable
    for the **aggregate** one, whose whole purpose is to bound a flood spread across many source addresses:
    an aggregate stated as a fleet ceiling and implemented per instance is not a ceiling at all.

    | Requirement | Value |
    | --- | --- |
    | **The replica ceiling is configuration, and startup fails without it** | `RateLimiting:MaxReplicas`, a required positive integer equal to the **maximum** replica count the deployment's autoscale rule permits. The application refuses to start if it is absent, non-positive or unparseable. It is a deployment input for the same reason the ingress trust ranges of stage 1 item 12 are: [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the scaling configuration, and a figure this document invented would silently stop matching it |
    | **The aggregate credential bound is derived from a fleet figure, not written as one** | The figure that means something operationally is the **fleet** ceiling — **200 permits per minute across the whole deployment** — so each instance is configured with `ceiling(200 / MaxReplicas)`. At `MaxReplicas = 1` the instance figure is 200 and nothing changes; at 4 it is 50. **Two consequences of the rounding are stated rather than left to be discovered.** Where `MaxReplicas` does not divide 200 the fleet maximum is the derived figure times the replica count, which **exceeds** 200 by at most `MaxReplicas - 1` — at 3 replicas, `3 × 67 = 201`. The bound is therefore **200 plus at most one permit per replica**, not exactly 200, and rounding **up** is chosen deliberately over rounding down so that no single instance is configured below the fleet share it is expected to serve; an overage of under one percent at any plausible replica count is not what this control exists to prevent. And when the fleet is running **below** its maximum the effective aggregate is proportionally lower than 200, which errs toward refusing rather than admitting — the correct direction for a flood control |
    | **The per-source bounds are per-instance by design, and their fleet effect is stated** | Ten credential permits per minute per address per instance means a caller spread across instances by the load balancer can reach up to `10 × MaxReplicas` per minute. That is accepted: this control bounds a **cost**, the aggregate limiter bounds a **flood**, and account lockout (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) bounds guessing against any one account independently of both. The general limiter's 300 per minute needs no fleet arithmetic at all, because it rations instance throughput and that is what it is written against |
    | **A shared limiter is the alternative, and it is rejected with its reason** | A distributed limiter needs a store touched **before** every request is admitted — the SQL cache of section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) or a new Redis instance — which adds a round trip to every request, makes that store's availability a precondition for serving anything at all, and introduces a fresh failure mode on the hottest path: what the limiter does when its own store is unreachable, where failing open removes the control and failing closed takes the site down. For a bound whose purpose is to blunt abuse rather than meter a paid quota, per-instance accounting with a derived aggregate is the proportionate mechanism. **If an exact fleet-wide quota is ever required, that is a scoped addition with its store named at the time it is approved** — not a silent reinterpretation of these figures |

    **The coverage assertion requires the multi-instance property directly, because no single-instance test can
    observe it.

    **`RejectionStatusCode` is 429** and the `OnRejected` callback sets `Retry-After` from the lease's
    `MetadataName.RetryAfter` — the whole seconds remaining in the window — writes **one** `Information`
    record and returns without invoking the endpoint. The record carries the **limiter identity**, the
    partition kind and the endpoint, and never the submitted user name and never the partition value for
    an anonymous caller beyond a pseudonymous label. **That label's key, its identifier, its rotation and
    its `<keyId>:<HMAC>` grammar are [06 §8.4.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and that section
    is their sole owner** — this document names no key, derives no label and states no rotation period,
    because a pseudonym produced under a second key or a second grammar does not correlate with the records
    every other producer writes, which is the one property a pseudonym exists to have. **The limiter
    identity is
    `context.HttpContext.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<EnableRateLimitingAttribute>()?.PolicyName ?? "global"`**,
    which is exact rather than approximate for one reason: the chain no-ops every endpoint that carries a
    named policy, so a refusal on such an endpoint can only have come from that policy, and a refusal
    anywhere else can only have come from the chain. Which **member** of the chain refused is not
    attributed, because a chained limiter surfaces one lease and the framework does not label it — the
    endpoint plus the retry window is what an operator acts on, and the coverage assertions distinguish
    the per-source bound from the aggregate bound by construction rather than by reading the record.
    Recovery is therefore deterministic and self-service: a fixed window with no queue means a refused
    caller waits out a stated number of seconds rather than being locked out, and nothing an anonymous
    caller does can lock an account it does not own.

**The scheme set this composition produces, stated because it is not visible in the one call that
creates it.** `AddIdentity<TUser, TRole>` registers **four** cookie schemes —
`IdentityConstants.ApplicationScheme`, `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme`,
`IdentityConstants.TwoFactorRememberMeScheme` and `IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme` — and sets
the default authenticate and challenge schemes to the application scheme. Two consequences are
load-bearing:

- **The application scheme carries every session; the external scheme is the retained surface's, and the
  two two-factor schemes are inert rather than removed.** The external-login surface is **retained** and
  re-expressed against the framework's own external-authentication mechanism (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), so `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme` is the scheme
  its challenge and callback use — through `SignInManager.ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties` and
  `GetExternalLoginInfoAsync`, never through a hand-written challenge. **No external provider is
  registered**, exactly as none is registered today
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35], so in a deployment as configured no external
  handshake occurs and no cookie is issued under that scheme; registering a provider later makes the
  scheme live with no further change to the surface, which is the point of mapping it rather than
  deleting it. The two two-factor schemes have no flow at all: nothing challenges or signs into them,
  and they stay registered rather than suppressed, because suppressing them means abandoning
  `AddIdentity` for `AddIdentityCore` and hand-wiring the sign-in manager, the role services and the
  cookie handler in order to remove two registrations that never execute.
- **Sign-in and sign-out go through `SignInManager` only, never through `HttpContext.SignInAsync`.**
  `AddIdentity` sets the default *sign-in* scheme to the **external** cookie rather than the application
  cookie, so a direct `HttpContext.SignInAsync(principal)` would write a short-lived external cookie and
  the user would appear signed out on the next request. `SignInManager` names the application scheme
  explicitly, which is why the sequence in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) is
  expressed in terms of it.

**Stage 2 — the middleware pipeline.** Thirteen registrations, in this order. Order here is behaviour:
every entry is placed where it is because something after it depends on what it does.

1. **`UseForwardedHeaders()`** — **first**, ahead of everything else. The request scheme and the client
   address are read by HTTPS redirection, by HSTS, by secure-cookie emission and by logging, so anything
   registered ahead of it decides on the wrong values. Its options are stage 1 item 12.
2. **The security response headers**, registered here — **before exception handling, before HSTS, before
   HTTPS redirection and before static files** — and applied through `context.Response.OnStarting(...)`
   so the values are written immediately before the first byte, whichever component produced the
   response.
   **Placement is the point, and the intuitive placement is wrong in three separate ways:** after
   `UseStaticFiles()` they would cover controller responses and **not** stylesheets, scripts, fonts or
   images; **after the exception handler they would not cover error responses**, because the handler
   catches the exception below itself and produces the error response from there, so a component
   registered underneath it never sees that response at all; and — the one most easily missed —
   **after `UseHttpsRedirection()` they would not cover the redirect responses that middleware itself
   emits**, which are the very responses an attacker sees first on a plain-HTTP request. A 307 to
   `https://` carrying no `X-Content-Type-Options`, no `Referrer-Policy` and no frame protection is a
   real response to a real client. Registered **first among the response-shaping entries**, the set
   covers **every** response the application emits: controller, static, redirect, status-code page and
