   error page alike, which is what [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §10.2 requires and what
   section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) the coverage assertion requires across all five response kinds.
   **This position is also what makes the callback register exactly once, and the assignment is written
   to be idempotent anyway.** `UseExceptionHandler` and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` **re-execute
   the pipeline below themselves** — they clear the response, rewrite the path and call the remainder of
   the chain again — so a component registered **underneath** them runs a second time for one
   client-visible response and registers a second `OnStarting` callback. That is precisely what the
   earlier below-the-handler placement did, and with an accumulating write it is visible to the client:
   two callbacks each appending `nosniff` produce `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, nosniff`, and a
   duplicated `Content-Security-Policy` is not a stricter policy but two policies the browser
   intersects — the shape that breaks a page nobody changed. Registered **above** the handler this
   middleware is outside the re-executed segment, so it runs once and registers one callback, and the
   response-clearing the handler performs is exactly why the emission is deferred to `OnStarting` rather
   than written eagerly: `Response.Clear()` discards headers already set, and the deferred callback
   re-applies the set to the response the client actually receives.
   Each value is nonetheless written **through the indexer** —
   `context.Response.Headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"` — which **replaces**, and **never**
   through `Headers.Append(...)` or `Headers.Add(...)`, which **accumulate**. The no-duplicate property
   then holds by construction rather than by ordering: any second invocation, from any cause, overwrites
   instead of appending. **The coverage assertion requires it directly: no security header appears with a
   duplicated value on any of the five response kinds, the re-executed error page included.
   **[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §10.2 owns the header set, the exact directive values, the
   `AddServerHeader = false` host option and the report-only-then-enforce discipline for the
   content-security policy**; this document owns the position in the pipeline and the emission mechanism
   above. Two application-side consequences of that policy are specified here because they are code
   changes: the `javascript:` sign-out trigger goes (section
   [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)) and the cart page's inline script becomes a file under the web root
   (section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)).
3. **Exception handling**, branched on the environment:
   `if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage(); } else { app.UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error"); app.UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/Home/Error/{0}"); }`.
   It sits **below the header middleware** for the reason item 2 gives — an error response produced by
   this handler must still carry the header set — and **above everything that can fault**, which is
   everything below it.
   **The condition is `IsDevelopment()`, not "not Production".** Staging, QA, UAT and every other named
   environment get the non-disclosing handler, because a Staging deployment is reachable by people who
   are not developers and the developer exception page renders exception messages, stack frames, source
   snippets, request headers, cookie names and configuration keys to whoever asks. Section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) specifies the error action, the model, the status
   codes, what is logged and what may be disclosed. Status-code pages are registered in the same branch:
   in Development a bare status code is more useful than a rendered page, and in every other environment
   a status-code response must render the generic view **with its own code preserved**.
   **The path form of `UseExceptionHandler` produces a response; it does not produce this document's log
   record.** The framework's own middleware logs the exception itself, under its own category and by
   passing the exception object — so its output carries the provider message, which is a diagnostic rather
   than the actor-enriched closed record section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) specifies, and is **suppressed by that section's
   category and level configuration** rather than left to coexist with it. The error action reads no exception feature,
   so it cannot write the record either. The record is written by the `IExceptionHandler` of stage 1
   item 13, which the middleware invokes before it re-executes the path.
4. **`UseHsts()`, outside Development only, and *configured* rather than merely called** —
   `if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseHsts(); }`. An HSTS header served from a local HTTP
   endpoint pins a developer's browser in a way that is tedious to undo.
   [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the policy **and its numbers** — enabled outside
   development, `max-age` per its **mandatory 1-day → 30-day → 365-day ramp**, `includeSubDomains` set and
   preload not asserted — and this item is its configuration expression, because `UseHsts()` alone silently
   takes the framework's **30-day** default `MaxAge`, which is neither of the ramp's first two values and
   is the one value in this pipeline that would be wrong without anybody writing anything wrong. So stage 1
   also carries `Configure<HstsOptions>(options => …)` setting three members explicitly:
   - **`MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromDays(configuration.GetValue<int>("Hsts:MaxAgeDays"))`** — the value read from
     configuration and **not defaulted in code**. **Whose number this is, stated plainly:**
     [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes the target as
     **`max-age=31536000`** — 365 days — and requires it to be **reached by a ramp**, `Hsts:MaxAgeDays = 1`
     on the first release that enables HSTS, then `30` once the site has been observed serving HTTPS on
     every hostname, then `365`. So the deployed value is **the ramp step the environment is on**, and this
     document neither hard-codes 365 nor supplies a code default that would silently place a first release
     at the target: `Hsts:MaxAgeDays` is a **required** configuration value outside Development, and a
     missing or non-positive one is a start-up failure by the same rule as the trust list of item 12,
     rather than a silent fallback to any figure. **An earlier form of this bullet defaulted to 365 and
     asserted that 06 "publishes no numeric value" so the figure was this document's; both halves are
     withdrawn** — 06 publishes the figure and the ramp, this document reads them, and a code default of
     365 would have made a deployment that forgot the setting land straight on the hardest-to-undo value on
     its first release, which is precisely what the ramp exists to prevent.
   - **`IncludeSubDomains = true`** — 06 §10.1.4's value, stated as the option rather than inferred from
     the header text. Its cost to sibling hostnames is that section's to state and is not restated here.
   - **`Preload = false`, set explicitly** — 06 §10.1.4's value, and the explicit form is what makes a
     future `true` a reviewed change rather than a side effect of someone tidying the configuration; that
     section states what a future `true` would require.
   - **`ExcludedHosts` retains its framework default**, which excludes `localhost` and the loopback
     addresses; the middleware is already off in Development, so this is defence in depth rather than the
     mechanism.

   Registering HSTS *after* the header middleware is deliberate and is not a conflict: `UseHsts` adds
   `Strict-Transport-Security` and the header middleware sets a disjoint set, so neither overwrites the
   other — and it is why the coverage assertion requires that header's **exact value and a cardinality of one**
   rather than merely its presence. The expected value is **the one
   [06 §10.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) check 4 states for the ramp step the environment is
   on**, read from the same `Hsts:MaxAgeDays` value the middleware is configured from so the assertion
   cannot drift from the deployment, with the `preload` token asserted **absent** in every step. Three
   distinct failures are separated by that: a header set that also emitted `Strict-Transport-Security`
   produces two headers and passes a presence check; a `UseHsts()` left unconfigured produces one header at
   the framework's 30-day default, which is a legal-looking value belonging to no ramp step this
   deployment chose; and a `preload` token passes a presence check while asserting something effectively
   irreversible that nobody approved.
5. **`UseHttpsRedirection()`, with the two health paths exempted** —
   `app.UseWhen(context => !HealthPaths.Matches(context.Request.Path), branch => branch.UseHttpsRedirection())`,
   where `HealthPaths` is the single source of the two literals item 13 maps. **The exemption is not
   optional and `.AllowAnonymous()` does not substitute for it.** Anonymous access is an *authorization*
   decision evaluated at the endpoint; this middleware answers **before** routing has selected one, so a
   probe arriving over plain HTTP receives a `307` to `https://` and the health checks never execute. A
   platform or sidecar probe that follows redirects then reports on a **different** request than the one
   it issued, and one that does not follow them reports the instance unhealthy and takes a healthy
   replica out of rotation — the exact failure the anonymous mapping exists to prevent, arriving one
   middleware earlier. Exempting **exactly** two literal paths and nothing else is what keeps the
   exemption from becoming a hole: no prefix match, no wildcard, and every other plain-HTTP request —
   including any path that merely starts with `/healthz` — is still redirected. **Which consumer probes
   over which scheme is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to state, and it states it as
   `1 + 2`: one probe over HTTPS — App Service's health check, which is HTTPS *because* `HTTPS Only` is on
   for the site, so it reaches the instance through the front end and the application sees a
   forwarded-HTTPS request — and two over plain HTTP, Container Apps' internal `httpGet` liveness and
   readiness probes, issued inside the environment straight at the container's target port where no front
   end and no TLS is involved.** The release pipeline's pre-traffic gate is a fourth caller, over HTTPS, and
   is not a platform probe. **The consequence is what scopes this exemption: it exists for the two Container
   Apps internal probes, it is inert on App Service — which needs no exemption and must not be cited as a
   reason for one — and it is present in the same build on both targets so the two do not need two
   builds.** For a consumer arriving over HTTPS the exemption changes nothing at all, because that request
   never enters the redirection branch; the branch predicate is therefore written on the **path** and not
   on the scheme, which is also what keeps the exemption's scope auditable as exactly two literals.
6. **`UseStaticFiles()`**, serving `wwwroot` (section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)).
7. **`UseRouting()`**.
8. **`UseSession()`** — after routing and **before** authentication, because the sign-in path writes the
   cart key into session (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) and the cart badge reads
   it on every page from the layout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26].
9. **The legacy-cookie expiry middleware** — a pass-through middleware that, when a request presents the
   Katana authentication cookie, emits a `Set-Cookie` for that name with an empty value and an expiry in
   the past, then calls the next middleware. **The cookie name is `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie`**: the
   source sets `AuthenticationType = DefaultAuthenticationTypes.ApplicationCookie`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16] and never sets a cookie name, so Katana's
   default applies — its `.AspNet.` prefix followed by that authentication type. **The name alone does
   not identify the cookie, and an expiry that matches only the name does not remove it.** A browser
   identifies a stored cookie by **name, domain and path**, so a `Set-Cookie` differing in any one of the
   three stores a *second* cookie and leaves the first to be presented again on the next request. What
   Katana wrote is knowable exactly, because the source configures **only** the authentication type and
   the login path [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18]: with `CookiePath` unset the
   path is `/`, and with `CookieDomain` unset the cookie is **host-only**, carrying no `Domain` attribute
   at all. The expiry is therefore emitted with **`Path=/` and no `Domain` attribute**, and both halves
   are stated rather than inherited — the framework's `CookieOptions.Path` happens to default to `/`,
   which makes the path right by accident rather than by decision, while **adding** a `Domain` would be an
   active defect, since a domain-scoped deletion does not remove a host-only cookie. `HttpOnly` and
   `Secure` are emitted alongside for consistency with the original; neither participates in the match.
   **Emitting the header is not the same as the cookie being gone**, which is why the coverage assertion in
   section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts on a **follow-up request through a real cookie jar**
   rather than on the header: the second request must carry no `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie` at all. It is
   registered **before `UseAuthentication()`** so the ticket is cleared in the same response in which it
   is first presented and is never handed to a handler that cannot decrypt it; sitting below item 5 costs
   nothing, because a plain-HTTP request carrying the legacy cookie is redirected first and then presents
   the same cookie on the HTTPS request, where the expiry is emitted. The target's own cookie has a
   different name (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so this middleware cannot
   delete a live session, and **the external sign-in cookie is deliberately not handled**:
   `UseExternalSignInCookie` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20] issues
   `.AspNet.ExternalCookie` only during an external-provider handshake, and every provider registration
   is commented out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:22-35], so no browser can be
   holding one. [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s cutover runbook owns the step; this
   is the mechanism that implements it.

   **Its removal has a retention period, and that period is 06's rather than this document's.**
   [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes the middleware's lifetime at **at least fourteen
   days plus one**, measured from the legacy application's stop at [06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
   step 4 — the legacy maximum persistent-cookie lifetime plus a day of clock skew — with removal
   scheduled as a **dated follow-up** ([06 §11.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) rather than as a
   conditional step. **An earlier form of this item said it is removed "once that runbook's verification
   has passed and the window has closed", and that trigger is withdrawn**, for the reason 06 gives and this
   mechanism cannot see: the in-window browser check observes a browser that *visited* during the window,
   while the population this middleware protects is the **dormant** client whose user selected "remember
   me" [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:350] and presents its legacy cookie on a
   first visit that may fall anywhere inside those fourteen days. So the check proves the middleware
   **works**; it is not a licence to remove it. The numeric bound and the follow-up's due date are read
   from 06 and are not restated here.
10. **`UseAuthentication()`** — the call that establishes a principal, and therefore the one every entry
    below it depends on: item 11 partitions on it, item 12 evaluates against it, and the endpoints of
    item 13 authorize against it — including `RecoverCart`, whose `[Authorize]` and whose reading of the
    pending owner both need an established principal (section
    [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)). It sits **after** item 9 for the reason item 9 gives.
11. **`UseRateLimiter()`** — after item 10 and **before** item 12, so the three calls run in the order
    `UseAuthentication()`, `UseRateLimiter()`, `UseAuthorization()`. Both sides of that position are
    requirements rather than taste: it must be **after `UseRouting()`** (item 7) because **both** the
    named policy of stage 1 item 14 **and** the `[CredentialEndpoint]` marker its chained partitioners
    select on are endpoint metadata, invisible before routing has selected an endpoint,
    and **after `UseAuthentication()`** because the partition key for a signed-in caller is their
    Identity `UserId`. Placing it ahead of authorization is the cheaper of the two remaining options: a
    refused request then evaluates no authorization policy either. What the placement concedes is small
    and stated: an anonymous flood still costs one cookie-decrypt attempt per request before it is
    refused, which is cheap and bounded, whereas moving the limiter ahead of authentication would ration
    signed-in users by their shared egress address instead.
12. **`UseAuthorization()`** — after item 10 and never before it. Authorization evaluates a principal;
    authentication is what establishes one. Reversed, every `[Authorize]` in the application sees an
    unauthenticated request, and the whole account, checkout and administration surface challenges users
    who are already signed in.
13. **The endpoints**, in one block:
    - `MapControllerRoute(name: "default", pattern: "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}")` — the
      whole of the URL surface, per section
      [2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate).
    - `MapHealthChecks("/healthz/live", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false })` — no
      dependency check; it answers only whether the process is up.
    - `MapHealthChecks("/healthz/ready", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = registration => registration.Tags.Contains("ready") })`
      — the connectivity probe of stage 1 item 11.
    - `MapPost("/csp-report", …).AllowAnonymous().DisableAntiforgery().RequireRateLimiting("csp-report")`
      — the content-security-policy violation-report endpoint. **It is registered here or the report-only
      header advertises a path that answers 404**, which is the quiet way a report-only rollout produces an
      empty report stream and gets promoted on the strength of it. A route handler rather than a controller
      action, because it takes no model binding, renders no view and belongs to no controller's
      authorization map. Three modifiers, each required and each for a different reason: `.AllowAnonymous()`
      because the reporter is a browser with no session; `.DisableAntiforgery()` because a browser-generated
      report carries no token — recorded as the **second of the two entries** in the anti-forgery opt-out
      register of section [7.1](#71-the-policy), not as a silent exception; and
      `.RequireRateLimiting("csp-report")` because the
      endpoint is anonymous and its body is untrusted input. **The contract itself is
      [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s** — the accepted media types, the size and batch
      bounds, the response statuses, the recorded field allowlist and the promotion-gate tests — and is
      cited rather than restated. What belongs here is the registration, its three modifiers and their
      position in this block. **06 §10.2 places its twelve promotion-gate tests in this document's suite
      and states what each must assert** — an earlier form of this block said the opposite, that they were
      not this suite's tests at all, and that reading is withdrawn; what follows says which instrument
      drives each of them and how they are *counted*, not whether this suite runs them. The division is
      **by instrument, not by ownership**, and it is the one thing a plan can get wrong here silently:
      - **Eleven of the twelve are HTTP-observable and belong to the `WebApplicationFactory` suite**:
        media-type acceptance and rejection, body and batch bounds, malformed bodies, the rate-limit
        partition and its `429`, the anti-forgery exemption and the `405` on `GET`, the recorded field
        allowlist, and the cardinality of records per request. Each is a property of a request and a
        response, which is what that host can drive, and **the closing note of section
        [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is where they are carried** — named in this document's required
        coverage, with 06 §10.2's numbering and contract kept, rather than left as a sentence pointing at
        another document's list, which is how a test set placed in one suite by another goes unwritten.
        They are **not** a numbered parity row there, because the combined executable-scenario total
        already counts 06 §10.2's set in its non-parity term and a row would count these eleven twice.
      - **Browser *enforcement* is not HTTP-observable at all, and the suite must not claim it.** A
        `WebApplicationFactory` client parses no CSP, blocks no script and generates no violation report,
        so it can prove the **header payload** — that exactly one of the enforcing and report-only headers
        is emitted, that its directive set is 06's, that `Reporting-Endpoints` names the same group literal
        as `report-to`, and that `report-uri` names the registered path — and it cannot prove that an agent
        obeyed any of it. The coverage assertion is the payload assertion; the header set's own values are 06's.
      - **06's test 12 and the transport half of its test 10 therefore discharge through 06's
        browser-evidence gate**, its §10.4 browser-matrix review, because they are stated over *agents*:
        that a violation provoked on an agent supporting `report-to` and on one exercising only `report-uri`
        each produce **one** delivery and not two. There is no way to assert per-agent transport selection
        from a test host with no agent, and asserting it there would produce a green suite over an untested
        property — the failure mode this split exists to prevent.

      The registration itself is asserted here regardless, through the anti-forgery opt-out register of
      section [7.1](#71-the-policy), because an endpoint silently absent is indistinguishable from a clean
      report stream.
    - **Both health endpoints are anonymous** — `.AllowAnonymous()` on each — because a probe that
      receives a redirect to a login page is reported as unhealthy, which takes a healthy instance out of
      rotation. **The two paths are exactly `/healthz/live` and `/healthz/ready`**, which are the paths
      [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) configures as the platform health-check path and probe
      targets; the names are a contract between the two documents, not a local choice. They are the same
      two literals item 5 exempts from HTTPS redirection, held in one place so the two registrations
      cannot drift apart.
    - **The probe contract is an application-side requirement stated over both transports, and the
      per-consumer scheme is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s — `1 + 2`: one HTTPS probe
      (App Service's health check, HTTPS because `HTTPS Only` is on) and two plain-HTTP probes (Container
      Apps' internal liveness and readiness), plus the release pipeline's HTTPS gate, which is not a
      platform probe.** That table states which consumer issues which request over which scheme and the
      status each must receive; this document states only what the application must do in either case. A
      request to either path **must answer with the health result — `200` when healthy, `503` when the
      readiness check fails, with the body literal of the contract in stage 1 item 11 — and never a `3xx`,
      over plain HTTP and over HTTPS alike.** Anonymous access and the
      redirection exemption of item 5 are the two halves of the plain-HTTP case and neither alone is
      sufficient: without the exemption the response is a redirect, and without the anonymous mapping it is
      a challenge. **The coverage assertion drives **both** schemes for exactly that reason — an HTTPS-only
      assertion passes an application whose plain-HTTP probe is a `307`, and a plain-HTTP-only assertion
      would leave the scheme any HTTPS consumer uses untested. The two treatments of a stray `307` are
      wrong in opposite directions, which is why `200` is asserted rather than "a success": a platform
      health check reads a redirect as unhealthy and rotates a healthy instance out, while a
      Kubernetes-style `httpGet` probe counts a `3xx` as success and admits an instance whose readiness
      check never ran — 06 states both, and the assertion is what makes the exemption verifiable rather
      than assumed.

**There is deliberately no cart-recovery middleware in this pipeline, and its absence is a decision
rather than an omission.** Completing a pending cart reassignment is a **write**, and a write belongs to
an endpoint: pre-endpoint middleware runs on safe methods, runs before MVC's anti-forgery filter, and —
because the exception handler re-executes the pipeline — runs again while the error page is being
rendered, so a middleware that can fail turns one database fault into a fault on **every** authenticated
request including the one trying to render the error. Recovery is therefore an explicit
`POST /ShoppingCart/RecoverCart` action, `[Authorize]` and inside the global anti-forgery filter, reached
by the conventional route of item 13 like every other action and needing no mapping of its own. Section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) specifies it, and the coverage assertions require both that
it recovers and that its repeated failure is bounded.

**The four requirements [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) places on the application pipeline are
satisfied in this stage, and are listed here so that the two documents describe one pipeline rather than
two:** forwarded-headers handling ahead of anything scheme-dependent (item 1); the security response
header set applied to every response, static assets and error responses included (item 2); the two health
endpoints at the paths 06 polls (item 13); and the legacy-cookie expiry the cutover runbook requires
(item 9). Nothing in 06's list is left to be added elsewhere, and nothing in this stage restates a value
06 owns.

**Migrations are not applied here.** No migration call, no `EnsureCreated`, no seeding and no
provisioning appears in `Program.cs`. Section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) states why
and what replaces it.

---

### 2.5 The health endpoints — the application half of the readiness contract

**The split.** [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the three paths, which probe consumes
each, what each of its five checks asserts, the permission and grant assertions, the response-disclosure
rule, the refresh-and-cache rule with all of its numbers, and every platform-side probe value. **This
document owns three things that are properties of application code rather than of the platform**: the
registration and refresh **shape** that makes those numbers enforceable, the *API-level semantics* of the
migration comparison, and the exemption of pipeline stages 5 and 6 in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). Each is a decision about code that no probe configuration can
express, and each has a wrong answer a platform-side specification cannot rule out.

**Registration shape.** `AddHealthChecks()` with **three tagged registrations**, and
`MapHealthChecks(path, new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = r => r.Tags.Contains(tag) })` per path, so
one registration set serves three endpoints and no endpoint can silently acquire another's checks:

| Registration | Tag | What the registration does when the endpoint is called |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Liveness | `live` | Nothing. It returns healthy, which for this path is the whole contract: the process is answering ([06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids wiring it to any dependency) |
| Startup | `startup` | Returns the verdict of the in-process configuration assertions of [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), evaluated **once** during start and held for the life of the process. Nothing re-evaluates, because none of those values can change without a restart — and the boundary table below states which of those seven checks this endpoint can actually report a failure for, since six of them fail the start instead |
| Readiness | `ready` | Returns the **last completed verdict** of the five checks of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) from memory, performing **no I/O in the request** |

**The readiness registration performs no I/O, and that is the property the whole timing model rests on.**
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) makes the check set a **background refresh** whose result
the handler serves, and publishes every number that goes with it — the refresh interval, the per-operation
bounds, the total refresh budget against the sum of its parts, and the staleness rule that turns a stale
verdict into a 503. **None of those values is restated here**, because a security- or availability-shaped
number with two homes acquires two versions. What this document owns is the **code shape that makes 06's
numbers true rather than aspirational**, and it is four statements:

| Property | The application-side mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| The refresh runs outside the request | A `BackgroundService` registered in stage 1 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) evaluates the check set on 06's interval and publishes an immutable verdict record — status, evaluation timestamp, and the identifiers of **every** check that failed, as an ordered read-only collection rather than a single identifier — into a singleton the readiness registration reads. The collection is what makes [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s "one record per failing check, so a refresh in which two checks fail emits two records" expressible at all: a verdict holding one identifier can only ever produce one record |
| Every operation is individually bounded | Each of 06's per-operation bounds is applied as an explicit **`CommandTimeout` on that command** and a connection timeout in the probe's own connection string, not as one outer cancellation. An outer-only bound would report "the refresh timed out" where 06's log contract requires **each failed check's identifier** |
| The refresh's own total bound is enforced | The evaluation runs under a linked `CancellationToken` cancelled at the total budget the retry arithmetic below pins, and a cancelled evaluation is recorded as a **failed** evaluation rather than as a slow one, so a hung refresh cannot leave the previous verdict looking current. A cancelled evaluation's verdict carries the identifiers of the checks that had already failed plus a `budgetExceeded` marker, so cancellation does not erase the diagnosis the pass had reached |
| Staleness is a property of the read, not of the writer | The registration compares the verdict's timestamp against 06's staleness bound on **every call** and returns unhealthy when it is exceeded, and returns unhealthy when **no** verdict exists yet. Both are read-side checks, so a refresh loop that has died — the case a writer-side check cannot cover — still produces an unready instance |

**The failure record is the application's, and it is specified per check — because the response says
nothing and the log is therefore the only diagnosis.**
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes the response disclosure (a status code and a fixed
opaque body, naming nothing) and requires a `Warning` naming the failed check by identifier, **one record
per failing check**. All five need a record, because all five can fail, so the shape of
each is fixed here. **The cardinality is one record per check the pass actually *evaluated* and found
failing** — never one record per pass, and never a record for a check the pass did not reach — which is
why the algorithm below evaluates the whole set rather than stopping at the first failure, and why the
verdict holds a collection rather than one identifier. Every value below is a **named log-state property**,
never interpolated into the message, for the reason section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) gives:

| Check | What its record names | What it must not contain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C1** | `checkId = "C1"`, the failure kind (connect, login or timeout), the provider's error number where one was returned, and the elapsed milliseconds | The connection string, the server name, the database name and the identity — the connection-validation rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) applies unchanged here, and C1 is the check most likely to tempt an exception dump |
| **C2** | `checkId = "C2"` and **which** of the four flags returned zero, by owner name — `catalog`, `identityStore`, `sessionCache`, `keyRing` — as separate boolean properties, so a query can distinguish "the Identity set was never applied" from "the cache table is missing" | The full statement text, and any object name other than the four this check names |
| **C3** | `checkId = "C3"`, the failing permission as `<object>.<verb>`, and its **expected direction** — a grant that returned 0 and a denial that returned 1 are different incidents and the record says which it was | The identity's own name; the object list is fixed and public, the principal is not needed to act on this |
| **C4** | `checkId = "C4"`, the context whose set failed, the **count** of missing identifiers and the **first** missing identifier — the pair [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires | The whole missing list, which on a badly out-of-date deployment is unbounded |
| **C5** | `checkId = "C5"`, whether the `INSERT` or the `DELETE` failed, and the provider's error number — this is the check that distinguishes a permission from an ability, so the error number is the payload that matters (a full database and a read-only replica look identical without it) | The row key, which carries the instance or replica identifier, and any exception text containing the connection string |

A **successful** evaluation writes nothing at `Warning`; the recovery transition — a failing verdict
becoming healthy — writes one `Information` record naming **every** check that had been failing in the
last failing verdict, so an
incident's end is visible without polling and a two-check incident does not close as a one-check
incident. That, and the single `Information` record
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires for a history row the assembly does not define,
are the only two records a healthy instance produces.

**What each endpoint touches, stated as a boundary because two of the three look like they overlap.**
The three paths answer three different questions and reach three different depths, and the distinction is
what keeps a database incident from restarting healthy processes:

| Endpoint | What it touches | What it never touches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/healthz/live` | Nothing at all. No configuration read, no cached verdict, no dependency | The database, the cache, the key ring, and the readiness verdict — wiring liveness to any of them turns a dependency outage into a restart loop, which [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids |
| `/healthz/startup` | **In-process state only**: the verdict computed once during start, after the options validation of stage 1 item 1 has already passed, plus the deployed migration identifiers read from the **assembly** | **Any outbound call of any kind** — no connection, no history table, no platform service. That bound is [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and it exists because the swap warm-up runs the target slot's settings under the **source** slot's identity |
| `/healthz/ready` | The **cached** verdict of the background refresh, read from memory | Any I/O in the request path, and any application data in the refresh either — C1 to C5 are metadata reads plus one self-removing row in a table the application owns |

**`/healthz/startup` executes no SQL, and that is stated as a flat prohibition because the temptation to
add one is specific and named.** Two of the values the endpoint reports on — the expected server and the
expected database — are exactly the values a release-side gate confirms outside this process: the server
by reading `properties.fullyQualifiedDomainName` from the **control plane** and comparing it against the
expected server, and the database by asserting `DB_NAME()` in the session it has already opened, both per
[06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md). **This endpoint does not do either, in any form.** Its
comparison is
between the **parsed** `DataSource` and `InitialCatalog` of the resolved connection string and the
`Expected:SqlServer` and `Expected:SqlDatabase` members — the fourth check of section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is a string comparison over
`SqlConnectionStringBuilder` fields and opens no connection. So the endpoint's answer means *"this process
is configured for the intended database"*, never *"the intended database answered"*, and the difference is
not a nuance: the warm-up that calls this path runs the target slot's settings under the **source** slot's
identity ([06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), so a connection attempted here would be
attempted as the wrong principal and its failure would mean nothing.

| Question | Who answers it | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is this process configured for the intended server, database and environment? | **`/healthz/startup`**, in-process | Parsed configuration values compared against the `Expected:*` members. **No connection, no command, no outbound call of any kind** |
| Does the intended database answer, hold the four schema owners, and grant this identity what it needs and nothing more? | **`/healthz/ready`**, from the cached verdict of the background refresh | The five checks of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — live SQL, executed **outside** the request by the refresh service, never by the startup path |
| Did the *release* reach the intended server, database and principal? | **The release side**, before traffic and before any write | The server on the **control plane** — the expected server name parsed, required to carry the `database.windows.net` suffix, and compared case-insensitively against the `properties.fullyQualifiedDomainName` the resource itself reports — and then `DB_NAME()` and `USER_NAME()` asserted **in session** against their expected values. That is [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s assertion, re-run by every operator invocation as assertion 1 of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract). It runs under the **deployment** principal, which is the only identity for which the answer is meaningful |

Those three rows are the whole of the division, and no row borrows another's mechanism.

**The startup endpoint's boundary against start-time validation, which is the one place the two contracts
could be read as contradicting each other.** [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists seven
checks (`S1`–`S7`) for that endpoint, and six of them are **also** start-time validators in this document —
so they cannot be observed failing *through* the endpoint, because a process that failed one of them is
not listening. That is not a redundancy and not a contradiction; it is a split between **enforcement** and
**report**, and it is stated here so that neither document is read as promising the other's behaviour:

| [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) check | Enforced by | What the endpoint can report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S1` — the host started and validation passed | The host itself | **The answer is the evidence.** A failed start means no answer at all, which the warm-up reads as a failure and the swap aborts on |
| `S2` — both environment variables present, equal, and equal to the expected name | The environment assertion of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a, applied to the web host as well as to the tools, against `Expected:Environment` | **Nothing it could fail on — a mismatch already prevented the start.** Its observable evidence is therefore a **fail-to-start**, not a 503: the aggregated `OptionsValidationException` naming the member, written unstructured to the container's console stream, which is the record [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A8 **arm 1** reads from the raw console table rather than from a log projection |
| `S3` — the connection's server, database and `User Id` | The connection validator's fourth and third checks of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S4` — no password keyword | The accepted-mode check, over parsed fields rather than a keyword scan | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S5` — the discriminator present and expected | `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator` equality | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S6` — no unresolved `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` value | The standing check on every bound string member | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S7` — the deployed migration identifiers are readable and non-empty | **The endpoint alone.** An assembly with no readable migration set is a packaging defect that does not stop the host from starting, because nothing reads that list during start | **503, with `S7` and the context in the log.** It is the one `S`-check whose failure this endpoint exists to express |

So the honest statement of the endpoint's value is: it converts "the process did not start" into an
unambiguous platform-visible failure, and it independently catches the one packaging defect that starts
cleanly and cannot serve. Both are worth a probe; neither is a re-run of the validation above.

**One failure model, stated once, because the alternative reading is the one an implementer would build
against.** A running endpoint can only report a failure it is running to report, so the set of `S`-checks
whose failure this endpoint expresses is **`S7` and `S7` alone**. The other six are enforced before the
socket is bound, and their failure is observed as a **fail-to-start** — no answer on the probe path, and
the unstructured `OptionsValidationException` on the console stream that A8's arm 1 matches. That is why
the alert has separate arms rather than one predicate over one signal, and why no statement anywhere in
this document should be read as expecting `S1`–`S6` to arrive as a 503 with a `checkId`: they arrive as
silence plus a console record, and both are evidence, but they are not this endpoint's evidence.

**One arithmetic property is this document's, because it is about the registrations rather than about the
checks**: the three registrations are evaluated **concurrently**, not serially —
`DefaultHealthCheckService.CheckHealthAsync` runs each registration in its own task and awaits
`Task.WhenAll` (.NET 8) — so an endpoint's cost is the maximum of the registrations its predicate selects,
never their sum. With each of the three doing an in-memory read, all three endpoints answer in
sub-millisecond time, which is what lets [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) set a two-second
per-probe timeout without that timeout ever being the thing that decides the verdict.

**How the migration comparison is implemented, and why the API matters.**
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s C4 is a **subset test in one direction** — every
identifier the deployed assembly expects must be present, extra rows are not a failure — and that document
states the reasoning and the reads. What this document adds is the two API calls that produce those two
sides, because choosing them wrongly is how the direction gets inverted in code:

| Side of the comparison | Call | What it costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What this assembly expects | `GetMigrations()` — "gets all the migrations that are defined in the configured migrations assembly" | **No I/O at all.** It reads the migrations assembly, so the expectation set is a property of the deployed bytes rather than of anything queryable |
| What the database has | `GetAppliedMigrationsAsync()` — "asynchronously gets all migrations that have been applied to the target database" | **One** read of that context's history table — exactly the read C4 names, under the bound C4 gives it |

`RelationalDatabaseFacadeExtensions`, EF Core, for both. The comparison itself is then in-memory over two
short lists, which is what makes **both** directions available from **one** read per context:

| Difference | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| An assembly migration missing from the history table | **Unhealthy.** This is exactly the set the framework's own `GetPendingMigrationsAsync()` returns — "all migrations that are defined in the assembly but haven't been applied to the target database" (same reference) — so the decision is "that set is empty", and expressing it as a *pending* set rather than as a two-way difference is what makes the direction hard to get wrong. The verdict names the count and the first missing identifier, per [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s log contract |
| A history row the assembly does not define | **Healthy**, with the single `Information` record [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires. This is the direction the second in-memory comparison exists for, and it is the reason the applied set is read rather than only the pending set |

Each context reads **its own** history table, and the two table names are bound once in section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) — which is where
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s C4 takes them from. Two contexts sharing one history
table would make each report the other's migrations as unknown, so the separation of section 4.5 is a
precondition of this check rather than an independent preference.

**The availability argument for the direction is 06's and is not restated**; what belongs here is the
consequence for application code. Because the deployed assembly is one side of the comparison, an instance
answers the question *"is everything **I** need applied"* and cannot answer *"is this database
compatible with me"* — the second needs both revisions' assemblies, which no single instance has. So the
application deliberately implements only the first, and
[06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s release-side comparison owns the second. A probe that
tried to answer the second would have to guess, and a guessing probe removes healthy instances from
rotation.

#### 2.5.1 The instance-verification route, and why it is not a fourth health endpoint

**Where it comes from, and what is being asked of this document.**
[06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines a route, `/healthz/instance`, whose whole
purpose is to make [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s affinity-retirement check provable:
that check has to send requests somewhere and read a worker identity out of the answer, and without such a
route its gate cannot be evaluated at all. That subsection states plainly that it is requiring **two
additions of this document** rather than citing sections that already carry them — the handler, and one
configuration member. This subsection is the first of the two; the `Diagnostics` section of
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) is the second.

**The ownership split, stated first because it is what keeps the two documents from disagreeing.** 06 owns
the path, the single method, both response shapes and their field names, the identifier source, the
four-condition gate and the lifecycle that opens and closes the route. **This document owns the handler's
code, where it is mapped, how each condition is expressed in that code, and the options member's type,
default and validation.** No value 06 fixes is re-decided here, and nothing about the verification
sequence is restated.

| Property | The application-side mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it is mapped** | One `MapGet` among the endpoint mappings of **stage 12** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), in `Program.cs`, with the route path, the session key and the role literal declared as constants on the `public partial class Program` declaration [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) already requires for the test host. **No file and no folder is added anywhere**: `Program.cs` and the options type both fall under the catch-all row of [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map, which delegates the file-by-file contents of `src/MvcMusicStore/` to this document, so that map gains no entry and the project, folder set and project graph are untouched |
| **What it is not** | **Not a health check, and not a fourth health endpoint.** `AddHealthChecks()` keeps the **three** tagged registrations above, this endpoint carries no tag, and no `MapHealthChecks` predicate can select it — so the registration table and the boundary table of this section are unchanged and no platform probe can reach it. It shares the `/healthz/` prefix and nothing else: the three health paths touch no session at all, and this is the only path under that prefix that does ([06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) |
| **How "off" is expressed** | The mapping is **conditional**: the block runs only when the `Diagnostics:InstanceEndpointEnabled` member of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) reads true, so when it is false or absent **the route does not exist** and a request receives **404** rather than a refusal. That is 06's condition 1, and it is also why the endpoint is a `MapGet` rather than an attribute-routed action on a controller: an attribute route is mapped whatever configuration says, so its "off" state could only be a handler returning 404 — a route that exists and confirms its existence on every instance of every environment. [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s V8 asserts the closed state as an authenticated administrator `GET` returning **404 and explicitly not 403**, which only the unmapped form satisfies |
| **The role gate** | `RequireAuthorization` on the endpoint, requiring an authenticated principal in the **`Administrator`** role — the same literal the administration surface's own attribute names [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12], which is 06's condition 3. **No protected diagnostic endpoint exists in this design today**: the three health paths are anonymous by requirement and the report collector of section [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half) is anonymous by necessity. So this is the first, and it borrows the application's one existing role rather than introducing a policy name nothing else uses |
| **Why the refusal is a status code rather than a redirect** | Cookie authentication answers an unauthenticated request with a **302 to `LoginPath`** and a failed policy with a **302 to `AccessDeniedPath`** — the two paths section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) sets. [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s V2a asserts **401 or 403** for the anonymous caller and **403** for the authenticated non-administrator, so an unmodified handler would fail assertions it satisfies in substance, and the gate proof would read as a defect. The resolution is **path-scoped rather than global**: `CookieAuthenticationEvents.OnRedirectToLogin`, which the framework documents as "[i]nvoked when the client needs to be redirected to the sign in url", and its access-denied counterpart, write **401** and **403** for this one path and perform the configured redirect for every other request — so the `/Account/AccessDenied` behaviour section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) specifies is unchanged, and no other endpoint's refusal shape moves |
| **The identifier** | Read from the platform and **never computed, never defaulted**: **`WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID` on App Service** and **`CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME` on Container Apps**, the two variables 06 names, tried in that order because exactly one platform serves at a time and neither sets the other's. **Both absent or empty is the failure shape** — 06's `503` carrying its one `error` field and none of the success fields — and that branch **writes nothing to session**, so a 503 leaves no half-initialized value for a later read to find |
| **Session** | The value lives under a fixed key, `healthz-instance`, which is deliberately **not** the preserved cart key `CartId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so a verification run can neither disturb a cart nor be disturbed by one. It reaches session through the same `AddDistributedSqlServerCache` and `AddSession` registrations and the same **stage 11** `UseSession` placement as every other session access — registration item 6 and pipeline stage 11 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), specified in section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) — which is the point of the check: the round trip is evidence about the shared store only because the route uses the ordinary one. `LoadAsync` is awaited before the first read, on the framework's own guidance for avoiding a synchronous load of a distributed session |
| **Serialization** | 06's field names are already camelCase, so they survive the framework's web-default naming policy unchanged and need **no** `[JsonPropertyName]` attribute and **no** policy change — the annotate-one-model decision of section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) is untouched, and the response the verification parses carries exactly the names 06 publishes |
| **Transport and host filtering** | The path is deliberately **absent** from the `ProbePaths` closed set of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), so HSTS and HTTPS redirection apply to it exactly as to an ordinary page — which is why 06's verification issues `https://` requests. Host filtering applies too, above every application stage, so the request must arrive on a name `Site:Hosts` carries: the operator drives the check at the target's own default hostname, one of the names [06 §8.4.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s union requires that setting to include |
| **Filters and anti-forgery** | It is not an MVC action, so it appears in no filter inventory; and only `GET` is mapped, so section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s policy keeps **exactly the two opt-outs it maps today** — the property 06 relies on when it declines to make the session write a `POST`, and the reason its method behaviour is 06's to state rather than a second decision here |
| **What it logs** | **One `Information` record at start, when the route is mapped**, through the application category section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) holds at `Information` — so an instance carrying an open diagnostic route says so once, in a sink the platform retains, and the record is a fact about configuration rather than about a request. **No per-request record**: a verification issues forty reads, and forty application log records for a one-time diagnostic would be noise in the sink every real incident is read from. The per-request evidence the check actually asserts on is the **response body**, and its corroborating log is the platform's own HTTP log rather than anything this handler writes — [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) reads both, and [06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records that the route's request telemetry is dropped by the `/healthz/*` probe filter while the platform HTTP log keeps it |

**The whole of the code, in two excerpts.** Both are verbatim from one file that **builds with no error and
no warning on the pinned 8.0 SDK** — verified on 8.0.424, inside the band
[04 §3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins, and again under `/warnaserror`. The first sits inside
stage 1 item 4's cookie registration; the second among stage 12's endpoint mappings, with the constants
after the last top-level statement:

```csharp
// Inside stage 1 item 4's AddCookie, after LoginPath and AccessDeniedPath are set:
options.Events.OnRedirectToLogin = context =>
{
    if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(InstanceRoutePath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    context.Response.Redirect(context.RedirectUri);
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};

options.Events.OnRedirectToAccessDenied = context =>
{
    if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(InstanceRoutePath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    context.Response.Redirect(context.RedirectUri);
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};
```

```csharp
// Among the top-level statements of Program.cs, in stage 12 beside the other endpoint mappings:
if (app.Services.GetRequiredService<IOptions<DiagnosticsOptions>>().Value.InstanceEndpointIsEnabled)
{
    app.Logger.LogInformation("Diagnostic instance endpoint mapped at {Path}.", InstanceRoutePath);

    app.MapGet(InstanceRoutePath, async (HttpContext http) =>
    {
        // WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID on App Service, CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME on Container Apps —
        // read from the platform, never computed and never defaulted.
        var instanceId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID");
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(instanceId))
        {
            instanceId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME");
        }

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(instanceId))
        {
            // Neither variable is set: the failure shape, and session is not touched at all.
            return Results.Json(
                new { error = "instance-identifier-unavailable" },
                statusCode: StatusCodes.Status503ServiceUnavailable);
        }

        await http.Session.LoadAsync();
        var sessionValue = http.Session.GetString(InstanceSessionKey);
        var sessionCreated = sessionValue is null;
        if (sessionCreated)
        {
            sessionValue = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
            http.Session.SetString(InstanceSessionKey, sessionValue);
            await http.Session.CommitAsync();
        }

        return Results.Json(new { instanceId, sessionValue, sessionCreated });
    })
    .RequireAuthorization(policy => policy
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .RequireRole(AdministratorRole));
}

// After the last top-level statement, on the same partial Program declaration:
public partial class Program
{
    internal const string InstanceRoutePath = "/healthz/instance";
    internal const string InstanceSessionKey = "healthz-instance";
    internal const string AdministratorRole = "Administrator";
}
```

**Off by default is the security property that makes an instance-identifier route acceptable at all, and it
is stated here rather than left to be inferred from the configuration table.** Three independent things
have to hold before a request can be served: the member is absent from every committed file and its
accessor reads `false` when absent, so a deployment that configures nothing has no route; the platform
setting that would enable it is **never set on a production slot** and is marked slot-scoped so a swap
cannot carry it ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)); and even where it is enabled the caller
must present an `Administrator` principal from inside the operator-network fence
[06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) applies first and removes last. The route's default state
is therefore **absent** rather than merely refusing, and a 404 discloses nothing about whether the
application has such a route at all.

**Neither section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) nor section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) gains a
row, and both omissions are decisions.** §11.7 is exhaustive for **deliberate net-new user-perceptible or
assistive-technology behaviour**; this route is reachable by no user in any environment, is absent unless an
operator enables it for one verification window, and its approval surface is the gate and lifecycle
[06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns — so a row here would put an operator instrument
into a register of user-facing decisions and move a count relied on outside this document
([07 §7.2](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)). §12.4's rows assert behaviour the suite exercises against the
two baselines, and this route is **unmapped in every configuration the suite runs under**: a row asserting
its 404 would assert the absence of an endpoint rather than a behaviour of the application. Its evidence is
V2a's five assertions and V8's negative readback, taken by an operator against a real platform target.

### 2.6 The two hosted services — files, algorithm, timing and containment

Items 14 and 15 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) register two `BackgroundService`
implementations, and [06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names both as the writers of two
mandatory records. A registration and a name are not an implementation, so this subsection is the rest of
it: where the files sit, what each depends on, the algorithm each runs, the timer, the cancellation and
shutdown behaviour, the retry policy, and the containment rule that applies to both.

**Where they sit.** Three new files plus one existing folder, and no addition to
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map is required: that map's catch-all delegates unlisted
content under `src/MvcMusicStore/**` to this document, and `Services/` is the same folder the collector's
sink was placed in by section
[7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half) on the same delegation.

**One further `BackgroundService` exists and is specified elsewhere, named here so this subsection is not
read as the complete roster.** `Services/KeyRingBootstrapService.cs` sits in the same folder under the same
delegation, is registered beside item 15 on the **web host only**, and runs one pass per process start
rather than a loop — so its algorithm belongs with the key store it bootstraps, in section
[4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof).
What it takes from **this** subsection unchanged is the part that is about being a hosted service at all:
the mandatory `await Task.Yield()` before any synchronous work, the off-thread bounded call shape, and the
containment rule below. The two services described here are the two long-lived loops
[06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names as record writers, and that is why the heading
counts two.

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `Services/ReadinessVerdict.cs` | The immutable verdict record — `Status`, `EvaluatedAtUtc`, `FailedCheckIds` as an `IReadOnlyList<string>` (**empty**, never null, when healthy), `NotEvaluatedCheckIds` for the `C1`-short-circuit case, and `BudgetExceeded` — and `IReadinessVerdictHolder`, a one-property interface over it. **`FailedCheckIds` is a collection rather than a single identifier**, and that is a correction: a one-identifier verdict cannot express [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s one-record-per-failing-check cardinality, which the algorithm below now satisfies |
| `Services/ReadinessVerdictHolder.cs` | The **singleton** implementation. One `volatile` reference to a `ReadinessVerdict?`, written whole by the refresh service and read whole by the health registration; no lock, because a whole-reference swap of an immutable record needs none and a lock in a health handler is a place a probe can block |
| `Services/ReadinessRefreshService.cs` | The refresh loop below |
| `Services/KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService.cs` | The heartbeat loop below |

**What each depends on, taken as constructor parameters so both are testable without a host.**

| Service | Dependencies |
| --- | --- |
| `ReadinessRefreshService` | `IReadinessVerdictHolder`; `IServiceScopeFactory` — **not** a `DbContext` and not `IOptions<T>`-scoped state, because a singleton hosted service must not capture a scoped service and every refresh opens its own scope; `ILogger<ReadinessRefreshService>`; `IOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>`; `TimeProvider`, so the interval is testable without waiting for it |
| `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService` | `IKeyManager`; `IDefaultKeyResolver` (see the note below); `IOptions<KeyManagementOptions>`, read for the configured `XmlRepository`'s concrete type; `ILogger<KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService>`; `TimeProvider` |

**The readiness refresh algorithm.** One pass is: open a scope; evaluate
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s C1 to C5 in that order, each under its own
`CommandTimeout` per the bounds table of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract); **evaluate every check
the pass can reach and aggregate their outcomes, with no first-failure short-circuit**; construct a new
`ReadinessVerdict` carrying the identifiers of all of them that failed; publish it into the holder; and —
**on every failing pass, with no de-duplication** — write **one** `ReadinessCheckFailed` record **per
failed check**, each in the per-check shape section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) fixes.

**"No first-failure short-circuit" has exactly one exception and it is 06's own, not a softening of the
rule.** `C1` is a **reachability precondition** rather than a peer of the others:
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) bounds it with "a failure here short-circuits C2–C5 —
there is nothing to ask", and that is literally true, because `C2` to `C5` are statements issued on the
connection `C1` failed to open. So the aggregation rule is stated in two parts and the distinction between
them is the difference between *failed* and *not evaluated*:

| Pass shape | What the verdict carries | How many records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `C1` fails | `["C1"]`. `C2`–`C5` are recorded as **not evaluated**, which is not the same as passing and not the same as failing, and the verdict says so | **One** — for `C1`. A record for a check that was never issued would be a fabricated observation, and A2 would count provisioning or grant failures that nobody had looked for |
| `C1` succeeds and any of `C2`–`C5` fail | Every failing identifier among `C2`–`C5`, in `C2`-to-`C5` order | **One per failing check.** Two failures produce two records, which is [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s stated cardinality and the reason the short-circuit was withdrawn: a pass that stopped at `C2` could never emit the second record that document requires |
| Nothing fails | An empty failed-check collection, and a healthy status | **None** at `Warning` |

**Why the short-circuit was wrong rather than merely suboptimal.** It was justified on the grounds that
"a second failing check adds nothing the first has not already decided", which is true of the *status* and
false of the *diagnosis* — and the diagnosis is the only thing the response discloses nothing about.
`C2` failing and `C3` failing are different incidents with different owners
([06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) sends `C4` to a different owner from the rest), a
release that skipped provisioning fails both, and a document that promises one record per failing check
while specifying an algorithm that can only ever emit one record promises something the code cannot do.
The cost of removing it is bounded and already paid for by the budget arithmetic below: after `C1`
succeeds, `C2` to `C5` are four metadata statements plus one two-statement write whose own timeouts sum to
five seconds in the worst case, so evaluating all four after one has failed cannot push a pass past its
bound.

**Emitting on every failing pass rather than only on the transition is a decision, and suppression is
rejected for a specific reason.** Suppressing the repeat looks like the tidier choice — an outage lasting
an hour writes the same record on every interval — and it would break the alert it feeds:
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A2 fires on a **count of ≥ 1 within its evaluation
window**, grouped by instance and check identifier — **the window is that document's number and is not
restated here** — so a suppressed repeat would let the alert
**auto-resolve after the first window while the instance was still failing**, which is worse than
noisy. The volume is bounded and small: one record per **failing check** per failing pass per instance, at
that document's
refresh period, and the grouping is what makes the repetition readable rather than the emitter's
restraint.

**The heartbeat algorithm, using the public key-management surface.** One pass reads
`IKeyManager.GetAllKeys()` — "returns all keys in the keyring" (`IKeyManager.GetAllKeys`, API reference,
ASP.NET Core 8) — and computes from that one collection every field
[06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires: `keyCount` is its count; the newest key is the
one with the greatest `CreationDate`, and its `CreationDate` and `ExpirationDate` are reported directly
from `IKey`; `newestKeyAgeDays` is the whole days between that creation date and `TimeProvider`'s now;
and `repositoryType` is the **runtime type name** of the `XmlRepository` on the resolved
`KeyManagementOptions`, which is what makes [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A6 a real
comparison rather than a restatement of the intended configuration. One read, one record, no write of any
kind — the heartbeat never creates, revokes or touches a key.

**That read is synchronous, it is database I/O, and where it is issued from decides whether this service
can stop the host from listening. This is a correction: an earlier version of this section had it in the
one place it must not be.** `IKeyManager.GetAllKeys()` is declared
`IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> GetAllKeys()` — no `Task`, no token — and with the EF Core repository of section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) behind it, the call
reads `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` on the calling thread. The framework's own contract for a
`BackgroundService` is explicit about what that costs on the start path: *"No further services are started
until `ExecuteAsync` becomes asynchronous, such as by calling `await`"*, and *"Avoid performing long,
blocking initialization work in `ExecuteAsync`"* (*Background tasks with hosted services in ASP.NET Core*,
ASP.NET Core 8). So an `ExecuteAsync` whose **first** statement is `GetAllKeys()` runs that database read
**inline on the host's start path**, before it has awaited anything — which delays every hosted service
registered after it and, if the key store is slow or unreachable, holds the start open with no cancellation
observed anywhere. That is the exact inversion of the containment rule below, and it is what this shape
prevents:

```text
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    // 1. Yield first, unconditionally, before touching anything.
    await Task.Yield();

    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromHours(6), _timeProvider);
    do
    {
        await EmitOnePassAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false));
}

private async Task EmitOnePassAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    using var bound = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken);
    bound.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
    try
    {
        // 2. The synchronous read runs off the caller's thread, and the wait for it
        //    is bounded and cancellable even though the read itself is neither.
        IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> keys =
            await Task.Run(() => _keyManager.GetAllKeys(), bound.Token)
                      .WaitAsync(bound.Token)
                      .ConfigureAwait(false);
        WriteKeyRingStatusRecord(keys);          // one record, per 06 §7.4
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Shutdown. No record, per the shutdown row below.
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning("keyRingStatusUnavailable: read exceeded its 30s bound");
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning(ex, "keyRingStatusUnavailable");
    }
}
```

**Three properties of that shape, each stated because each is load-bearing rather than idiomatic.**

| Property | Why it is written that way |
| --- | --- |
| **`await Task.Yield()` is the first statement, before the timer and before any read** | It is the one construct guaranteed to suspend: `YieldAwaitable.YieldAwaiter.IsCompleted` is documented as **always `false`**, so the await can never complete synchronously and `StartAsync` for this service always returns at that line. A `PeriodicTimer` first tick or a `Task.Delay` would also yield in practice, but neither is documented as *never* completing synchronously, and this property is the whole point |
| **The read is offloaded with `Task.Run` and the wait is bounded with `WaitAsync` on a linked source** | Two different jobs, which is why both appear. `Task.Run(…, token)` moves the synchronous read **off** the loop's thread, so the loop and the shutdown path are never the thread sitting in provider I/O. `WaitAsync(token)` bounds the **wait** — 30 seconds, or shutdown, whichever comes first — so a hung read cannot make the service unresponsive to `StopAsync`. The token is a `CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken)` with `CancelAfter`, so shutdown and the bound are one token rather than two racing ones |
| **What the bound does *not* do is stated plainly** | Cancelling the wait does **not** abort the read. `GetAllKeys()` takes no token, so a thread blocked inside it stays blocked until the provider's own connection and command timeouts return — which for the EF Core repository are section [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)'s, and they are what actually terminate it. The bound therefore buys **responsiveness of the service**, not termination of the call, and this document does not claim otherwise. One worker thread may remain occupied for the provider's timeout; at one pass every six hours that is bounded and acceptable, and it is preferable to the alternative of that thread being the host's start path |

**`defaultKeyId` is the one field that cannot be computed from the public surface, and taking the
infrastructure API for it is an accepted, recorded exception rather than an oversight.**
[06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires the **default key's identifier**, and the
framework's own selection rule — which key the ring would actually protect with, given activation dates,
expiry and revocations — lives in `IDefaultKeyResolver`, in the
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal` namespace, whose members the API reference
marks as supporting infrastructure and not intended to be used directly from application code. Two
options existed and the second is taken:

| Option | Why not / why yes |
| --- | --- |
| Recompute the selection in this application from `GetAllKeys()` | **Rejected.** It would put a second, independently maintained copy of the framework's eligibility rule in this codebase, and a monitoring field that disagrees with the framework's real choice is worse than no field: A6 and A5 would then be reading this document's opinion of the ring rather than the ring |
| Resolve `IDefaultKeyResolver` and call it, accepting the namespace | **Taken**, with three conditions. It is registered by `AddDataProtection` and resolvable from the container, so **no package reference is added** and [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s pin list is untouched. The call is **confined to two files, and both are named here so an audit has a closed list**: this one, and `Services/KeyRingBootstrapService.cs`, whose single use of the same resolver — asking the framework whether the ring already has a key it would protect with, rather than deciding that itself — is section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof)'s. Two call sites for one question, not a habit; anything else in the application that wants the ring's state reads the record this service emits And it carries a **revalidation obligation**: the framework upgrade of [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s support-window risk must re-check that this type still exists with this shape, and the field's failure mode is defined below so that losing it degrades the record rather than the service |

**If resolution or the call fails, the field is omitted and the record is still emitted**, with one
`Warning` naming `defaultKeyIdUnavailable` and the reason. That ordering matters:
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A4 fires on the **absence** of the whole record, so a
heartbeat that suppressed itself over one missing field would raise an availability alarm about a healthy
key ring.

**Timing, cancellation and shutdown — identical in shape for both, with different periods.**

| Property | `ReadinessRefreshService` | `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First pass | Immediately on start, before the first wait | Immediately on start, **but after `ExecuteAsync` has already yielded** — the `await Task.Yield()` above comes first, then the first `GetAllKeys()` off-thread read, and the record is written when that read returns. That return is also the point [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s "once the ring has resolved" names, because that call is what resolves it. The yield is what makes "immediately on start" mean *concurrently with* the rest of the start rather than *inside* it |
| Period | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s refresh interval. **Not restated here** | **6 hours**, which is [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s figure and is cited rather than re-decided |
| The timer | A `PeriodicTimer` created from `TimeProvider`, awaited with `WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken)`. Chosen over `Task.Delay` in a loop because it does not drift with the duration of the pass, and over `System.Threading.Timer` because it cannot re-enter: a pass that overran its period delays the next tick instead of running twice | The same |
