| Cancellation | The `stoppingToken` is passed into **every awaited call that accepts one** — the scope's database commands and the tick wait — so a shutdown does not wait out a hung database call. **`ILogger` calls are synchronous and take no token**, so the record write is not a cancellation point and is not claimed as one; it is a memory-to-stdout write bounded by the formatter | The same |
| Shutdown | `WaitForNextTickAsync` returns `false` on cancellation and the loop exits. **`OperationCanceledException` raised during a pass while the token is signalled is treated as a clean stop, not an error**, and no verdict or record is written for it — a shutdown must not publish a failing verdict, because on App Service a swap stops instances routinely | The same, and no partial record is emitted |
| What runs at shutdown | Nothing. Neither service holds a resource whose release needs a `StopAsync` override, so neither declares one | The same |

**Retry, with backoff, and it is per pass rather than per loop — and the numbers are pinned here because
an earlier version's did not add up against the budget they ran inside.** A failing pass makes **at most
two attempts**: the initial attempt, then — only for a transient failure — **one** retry after a single
fixed **2-second** delay. A small fixed-step delay rather than an unbounded exponential one, because the
loop itself is the long retry and a pass must finish well inside its own period.

**The arithmetic, in full, because a budget smaller than its own contents is not a budget:**

| Quantity | Value | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Worst-case cost of **one attempt** | **9 seconds** | The sum of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s own per-operation bounds in the case where every one of them reaches its timeout: 3 s connect + 1 s `C1` + 1 s `C2` + 1 s `C3` + 1 s + 1 s (`C4`'s two reads) + 1 s `C5`. It is a *ceiling*, not an expectation — a healthy pass is one round trip plus two small reads |
| Attempts per pass | **At most 2** | This document's retry rule above: the initial attempt plus one transient retry |
| Delay between them | **One 2-second delay** | The same rule. There is no second delay, because there is no third attempt |
| Worst-case cost of a **whole pass** | **9 + 2 + 9 = 20 seconds** | Two attempts at their ceiling with one delay between them |
| The pass's **total budget** | **25 seconds** | The linked `CancellationToken` the whole pass including its retry runs under. It exceeds the 20-second worst case by **5 seconds** of headroom for scope construction, `TimeProvider` scheduling and the record writes, so the budget is never the thing that decides a verdict a bound had already decided |
| Refresh period and staleness bound | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s figures, **not restated here** | 20 seconds of worst-case work must fit inside the refresh period with room to spare, and 25 seconds must remain below the staleness bound, so that a single budget-exceeded pass cannot on its own make an instance stale |

Every earlier figure **in this document** is superseded by that table: there is no third attempt, no
6-second delay, and no 10-second *pass* budget — a 10-second pass budget could not contain even one
attempt's 9-second ceiling plus the 2-second delay, let alone the second attempt, so a transient failure
would have been reported as a budget-exceeded evaluation rather than retried at all.

**And that is not a disagreement with [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), which states a
10-second figure of its own — the two bound different things, and saying so is the whole reconciliation.**
That section's 10 seconds bounds **one evaluation of the five checks**: it is the 9-second sum of its own
per-operation timeouts plus a second of slack, and it is the figure a single attempt must fit inside.
This document's 25 seconds bounds **the pass**, which is up to two such attempts with a delay between
them, and it is the token the retry runs under. Both hold simultaneously and neither needs the other to
move: an attempt that exceeds 10 seconds has failed its own bound and is the retry's trigger, and the pass
that contains two of them plus the delay fits inside 25 either way — **9 + 2 + 9 = 20** against this
document's own ceilings, and **10 + 2 + 10 = 22** against that section's, both under the budget. What
would be a real contradiction, and is not present, is a *pass* budget shorter than the two attempts it is
required to permit.

Two rules bound the retry beyond the arithmetic. The whole pass including its retry runs under the linked
token cancelled at the 25-second budget, so a retry cannot extend
a pass past its bound; and **only transient failures are retried** — for the refresh, the SQL error
numbers the execution strategy of section
[4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)
already treats as transient, and a check that failed **non**-transiently (`C2`'s missing object, `C3`'s
missing grant, `C4`'s absent identifier) is **not** retried at all, because none of those becomes true two
seconds later; for the heartbeat, nothing, because reading an in-memory key ring has no
transient failure mode and a retry there would only hide a configuration fault. After the retry, the
refresh publishes a failing verdict naming every failed check and the heartbeat writes its `Warning`, and
both wait for the next
tick.

**Containment is mandatory, and the reason is a framework default rather than a style preference.**
`HostOptions.BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` **defaults to `StopHost`**, so "if any
`BackgroundService` throws an unhandled exception, the host will crash" — the behaviour
`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` documents (API reference, .NET 8), and the reason the framework
changed the earlier ignore-and-continue default. Neither of these services may rely on that:

- **The body of every pass is wrapped**, so no exception leaves `ExecuteAsync`. A refresh that throws
  publishes a **failing** verdict — which is the correct observable outcome, since an instance whose
  readiness cannot be evaluated is not ready — and a heartbeat that throws writes one `Warning` and waits
  for the next tick.
- **The loop itself is wrapped**, so an exception from the tick wait or from constructing a scope cannot
  escape either. This is the case the per-pass wrapper does not cover and the one that would actually
  take the host down.
- **`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` is left at its default.** Setting it to `Ignore` would be a way
  to get containment without writing it, and it is rejected: it would silently swallow a fault in any
  future hosted service as well, and the containment here is deliberate per service rather than
  host-wide.
- **A monitoring service must never be able to stop the thing it monitors.** A key-ring heartbeat that
  crashed the site because the ring was unreadable would convert an alertable condition into an outage —
  the precise inversion this rule exists to prevent.

**Warm-up behaviour, stated because the first few seconds of a new instance are exactly when a probe
arrives.** Neither service blocks the start, and that is a property of how each one is written rather than
a property of `BackgroundService`. `StartAsync` returns at the first `await`
in `ExecuteAsync` **that actually suspends** — the framework's own wording is that no further service is
started "until `ExecuteAsync` becomes asynchronous, such as by calling `await`" — so a first statement that
completes synchronously, and specifically a synchronous database read, holds the start open. Each service
therefore reaches its first suspension before it touches anything: the heartbeat by the mandatory
`await Task.Yield()` above, and the refresh because its first act is to `await` its own bounded, linked
pass. With that, the host finishes starting and begins listening while the first pass is still
running. The consequences are defined rather than incidental. **Before the refresh's first pass
completes, the holder is empty and `/healthz/ready` answers unhealthy** — the no-verdict rule of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — so a new instance is
never advertised as ready on the strength of never having checked. `/healthz/live` and
`/healthz/startup` answer normally throughout, which is what lets the platform distinguish "starting" from
"broken". And **the heartbeat's startup record is emitted once per process start**, so an instance that is
replaced twice in an hour produces three records rather than one — expected, and the reason
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A4 tests for absence rather than for a count.

**The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)** exercises both: the readiness holder is
asserted empty-then-populated across the first pass, a forced failure inside a pass is asserted to publish
a failing verdict **and leave the host running**, a forced exception in the loop is asserted the same way,
cancellation is asserted to stop both loops without a record or a verdict being written for the
shutdown, **two simultaneously failing checks are asserted to produce two `ReadinessCheckFailed` records
and a verdict carrying both identifiers**, and a forced `C1` failure is asserted to produce **one** record
with `C2`–`C5` marked not evaluated.

---

## 3. Configuration and the one active transform

### 3.1 Configuration: `Web.config` becomes `appsettings.json` read through `IConfiguration`

**The configuration surface is seven groups, not two, and the two that are routinely overlooked are
the two that carry runtime behaviour rather than values.** `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config` is 71
lines and every one of its elements needs a disposition:

| Group | Locator | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `configSections` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:7-10] | The `entityFramework` section declaration, naming `EntityFramework, Version=6.0.0.0` |
| `connectionStrings` | [:11-14] | Two entries |
| `appSettings` | [:15-22] | Six keys |
| `system.web` | [:31-35] | `authentication mode="None"`, `compilation`, `httpRuntime` |
| `system.webServer` | [:36-40] | One module removal |
| `runtime/assemblyBinding` | [:41-60] | **Four binding redirects** |
| `entityFramework` | [:61-70] | **`defaultConnectionFactory` and `providers`** |

`Views/Web.config` is a separate file with its own two responsibilities, dispositioned in section
[8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports). In the target the value-carrying groups become
`appsettings.json` and `appsettings.Development.json`, read through `IConfiguration`, with typed
options classes bound at startup; the behaviour-carrying groups map to code, and the table below gives
each of the seven a target.

**The options pattern is required here rather than merely conventional, and the reason is a specific
line of code.** `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` is read **directly from startup code**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24], via `using System.Configuration;` [:7]. That
is not a configuration *file* problem that a file format solves — it is a startup component reaching
into a static ambient configuration store, which the target has no equivalent of. The two values it
reads are the administrator credential, and section
[10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) removes them from configuration
altogether, so the correct target for [:23-24] is **nothing at all**: no `appsettings` key, no
options class, no environment variable in the web application.

Per-key disposition. Every bare `[:N]` locator below refers to
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config`:

| Current key | Target |
| --- | --- |
| `configSections/entityFramework` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:7-9] | **Deleted.** It exists only so the `entityFramework` element below can be parsed; EF Core has no configuration section and reads no configuration file of its own |
| `connectionStrings/DefaultConnection` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12] | One connection string for one database, supplied by platform configuration — the mechanism and the identity model are [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; the blocker framing is [11 §3.4](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)'s |
| `connectionStrings/MusicStoreEntities` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13] | The **same** connection string; see section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) for why one database and what it trades |
| `DefaultAdminUsername`, `DefaultAdminPassword` [:16-17] | **Removed from source entirely.** Section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command). [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding |
| `webpages:Version`, `webpages:Enabled` [:18-19] | **End.** Web Pages is not part of the target; the same `webpages:Enabled=false` appears redundantly at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:26] and ends with it |
| `ClientValidationEnabled`, `UnobtrusiveJavaScriptEnabled` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:20-21] | **End as configuration keys.** Both behaviours are the target's default and are not switched from `appsettings` |
| `system.web/authentication mode="None"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:32] | **Ends.** The value is an artifact of authentication having been moved to OWIN; the target has no `system.web` |
| `system.webServer/modules remove FormsAuthenticationModule` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:38] | **Ends.** An IIS-integrated-pipeline instruction with no counterpart |
| `compilation targetFramework="4.8"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:33] versus `httpRuntime targetFramework="4.5"` [:34] | **Ends — the concept has no target.** The target has no quirks mode, so there is nothing to carry the value into. The consequence is for the *baseline*, not the port: see below |
| `runtime/assemblyBinding` — four `bindingRedirect` elements for `System.Web.Helpers`, `System.Web.Mvc`, `System.Web.WebPages` and `WebGrease` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:43-58] | **Deleted, all four.** See below: they exist to paper over assembly-version drift that the target's dependency model does not produce |
| `entityFramework/defaultConnectionFactory` — `LocalDbConnectionFactory` with parameter `v11.0` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:62-66] | **Deleted, with no successor and no equivalent fallback.** See below |
| `entityFramework/providers` — `invariantName="System.Data.SqlClient"` mapped to `SqlProviderServices` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:67-69] | **Replaced by provider selection in code:** `AddDbContext<T>(o => o.UseSqlServer(...))` for both contexts (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), supplied by the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer` package that [04 §7](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins |
| `DefaultAdminUsername`, `DefaultAdminPassword` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17] | **Removed from source entirely.** Section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command). [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding |
| `webpages:Version`, `webpages:Enabled` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:18-19] | **End.** Web Pages is not part of the target; the same `webpages:Enabled=false` appears redundantly at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:26] and ends with it |
| `compilation targetFramework="4.8"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:33] versus `httpRuntime targetFramework="4.5"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:34] | **Ends — the concept has no target.** The target has no quirks mode, so there is nothing to carry the value into. The consequence is for the *baseline*, not the port: see below |

**Why all four binding redirects are deleted rather than translated.** Each one maps a range of old
assembly versions onto the single version the project actually ships — for example
`System.Web.Mvc` `1.0.0.0-5.0.0.0` onto `5.0.0.0`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:48-49]. They exist because `packages.config` restore installs each
package independently and performs no unified version resolution across the graph, so an assembly
compiled against an older version of a dependency has to be redirected at load time. The target's
dependency model removes both halves of that problem: `PackageReference` resolves **one** version of
each package for the whole graph (the conversion is [04 §5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s), and
`net8.0` has no assembly-binding-redirect mechanism at all — assembly resolution is driven by the
generated `.deps.json` and a `bindingRedirect` element in a configuration file would be ignored even
if one were written. Two of the four also name assemblies the target does not contain
(`System.Web.Helpers`, `System.Web.WebPages`) and one names a package the target removes (`WebGrease`,
retired with bundling in section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)), so there is
nothing left to redirect.

**Why the EF 6 connection factory has no successor, and what changes when it goes.**
`defaultConnectionFactory` is EF 6's *fallback*: it constructs a connection when a context cannot
resolve a named connection string, and the configured parameter `v11.0`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:64] would make that fallback target a `(LocalDb)\v11.0` instance —
an instance name that appears nowhere in either connection string, both of which name `MSSQLLocalDB`
[:12-13]. In this application the fallback is **inert**, because both contexts resolve a named string:
`MusicStoreEntities` declares no constructor and EF 6 matches the class name to the entry at [:13]
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:5-13], and `ApplicationDbContext` passes
`base("DefaultConnection")` explicitly
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:10-15]. Recording it matters anyway, for one reason:
**EF Core has no ambient fallback of any kind.** A context registered without a configured provider
throws at the first resolution rather than quietly constructing a LocalDB connection, so the class of
misconfiguration this element could mask cannot occur silently in the target — and the explicit
`UseSqlServer` in `AddDbContext` is not an optional convenience but the only thing that configures the
provider.

**The framework-version mismatch is a baseline-integrity problem, and it must be handled before the
baseline is captured rather than diagnosed afterwards.** `httpRuntime targetFramework="4.5"` [:34]
holds 4.5-era compatibility behaviour in force even though the project targets 4.8
([12 F-12-18](12-migration-blockers.md) owns the finding). So the behaviour a reviewer records from
the running MVC 5 application **is 4.5 quirks-mode behaviour**, and the ported application has no
quirks mode at all. The resolution is procedural and belongs to the baseline exercise of section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage): the baseline capture must record that the source
runtime was in 4.5 quirks mode, and any behavioural difference the suite surfaces in request
validation, encoding or a related default must be checked against that setting **before** it is
classified — because the error is available in both directions. A pre-existing configuration artifact
can be misfiled as a port regression, and a real regression can be dismissed as "just the quirks
mode".

### 3.2 The one active transform, and the two halves it splits into

Across the six transform files in the repository there are **fifteen** `xdt:Transform` occurrences and
only **three** of them are outside an XML comment — one per `Web.Release.config`, and all three are
the same line at the same line number:

```text
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
```

The three `Web.Debug.config` files carry **zero** active transforms. Every other occurrence in all six
files is commented-out template text. The verifying command is in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**This one transform splits into two target concerns, and conflating them is the error this section
exists to prevent.**

**Half one — build and publish.** Removing the `debug` attribute from `<compilation>` is what stops
the release deployment compiling with debug semantics. Its target is the **Release build
configuration's own publish behaviour** — the publish step of
[04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s sequence, which owns that invocation and every option on
it — under which optimization and debug-symbol behaviour are properties of the configuration rather than
of a setting anyone writes. It does **not** map to an `appsettings`
key and it does **not** map to an environment variable. There is nothing to write into a configuration
file for it, which is why a reader looking for its successor in `appsettings.json` will not find one
and may wrongly conclude the behaviour was lost.

**Half two — runtime error behaviour.** What `debug="true"` *also* influenced in practice — how much
detail an error response discloses — is in the target a **runtime** decision made in the middleware
pipeline: the developer exception page is registered **only when the environment is Development**, and
the exception-handler middleware handles **every** other environment, Staging included (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), designed in section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). That is governed by the environment the application
runs in, not by the build configuration it was compiled with. **The two are independently settable in
the target and must be set independently** — a Release build can run in a Development environment and
a Debug build in Production, and neither combination should surprise anyone reading this plan.

**One net-new obligation follows from the same six files.** The commented-out examples include a
connection-string substitution that was **never active**, so the repository has no working mechanism
for supplying a secret at deploy time. Providing one is therefore net-new work rather than a migration
of anything, and its mechanism is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s.

### 3.3 The target configuration contract

Section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) says what
happens to each key the application reads **today**. This section says what the ported application
reads **tomorrow** — every section name, every options type, every member with its type, whether it is
required, its default when absent, and what fails the start when it is wrong. It exists because
"configuration moves to `appsettings.json` and the options pattern" is not implementable: a reader
cannot write the file, and a reviewer cannot approve a value that has no name.

**The ownership split, so neither half is stated twice.** This document owns the **contract** — key
paths, types, defaults, validation and precedence. [06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns
the **platform binding**: which key arrives as an App Service application setting, which arrives as a
Key Vault reference, and which are marked slot-scoped so a swap does not repoint an environment
([06 §7.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). 06 refers to these settings **by the key names below**;
it does not restate their types, and this document does not restate its slot scoping.

**The sections, and the type bound to each.** Every options type is bound once, in the registration
surface of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties), and
resolved by constructor injection thereafter. No component reads `IConfiguration` directly — that is the
habit `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24]
represents and the whole reason section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) requires the
options pattern.

| Configuration section | Options type | Consumed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ConnectionStrings` | `ConnectionStringOptions` — one string member, bound from `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` so the value is validated once rather than at each of its three consumers | Both `DbContext` registrations (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), the distributed cache (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)) and the key repository (section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it)) |
| `Identity` | `IdentityPolicyOptions` | The Identity registration, whose values are section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)'s |
| `Authentication:Cookie` | `AuthenticationCookieOptions` | The cookie handler (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) |
| `Session` | `SessionPolicyOptions` | `AddSession` (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)) |
| `Antiforgery` | `AntiforgeryPolicyOptions` | `AntiforgeryOptions` (section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)) |
| `DataProtection` | `DataProtectionSettings` | `SetApplicationName` (section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it)) |
| `SqlIdentity` | `SqlIdentityOptions` | The connection-mode validation above — it is the expected client ID mode **M1** compares against |
| `Expected` | `ExpectedDeploymentOptions` | The connection validation above, the environment assertion of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a, and the application half of [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s startup checks (section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)) |
| `Telemetry` | `TelemetryOptions` | The cart-key pseudonym every cart-scoped log record carries ([06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) |
| `Site` | `SiteOptions` | The report collector's origin check (section [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half)) and the album-art write-path allow-list (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)'s delta 18) |
| `Seeding` | `SeedingOptions` | The seeding guard (section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)) |
| `Diagnostics` | `DiagnosticsOptions` | The conditional endpoint mapping of section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint), and nothing else. It exists because [06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires it, not because anything else in this document needed a `Diagnostics` section |
| `Logging` | bound twice, deliberately: by the **framework's own logging schema**, which does the filtering, and by `LoggingPolicyOptions` as a **validation view** that does no filtering at all | `ILogger`. The keys and their exact values are below; the operational requirement behind each level is [06 §9.2.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, and the sink and its retention are [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s |
| `Kestrel` | the framework's own server schema — **no custom type**, and **Development only** | Kestrel's endpoint binding. The artifact, the exact ports and the developer-certificate prerequisite are [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s; the keys' place in this schema is below |

**Fourteen rows, counted one way so the count is checkable.** **Twelve** of them name a section whose
*whole* binding is an options type this document defines; the other two are bound by a framework schema —
`Logging`, over which this document adds only a validation view, and `Kestrel`, which has no custom type at
all. `Diagnostics` is the newest of the twelve and the only one another deliverable asked for:
[06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires it, its entire content is one optional boolean,
and it changes no validation this section already performs.

**`ConnectionStrings` — one key, and only one.**

| Key | CLR type | Required | Default when absent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` | `string` | **Yes** | **None. An absent value fails the start** |

Both contexts read this **same** key, because both target one database (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); the second EF 6 connection name
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13] is **not** reproduced, so there is no second key for a
deployment to get half-right. The string's **content** — host, database, authentication mode and the
absence of any credential in it — is [06 §6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and is not
restated here. **The committed `appsettings.json` carries no `ConnectionStrings` entry at all**; see the
precedence rules below.

**The string is validated at start, on five properties, and the validation never echoes it.** "Required"
on a connection string means only that some text arrived; the five checks below are what make the arrival
meaningful, and each has a failure this application would otherwise discover later and less clearly. They
run in an `IValidateOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>` — the one-member type that carries the value — under
`ValidateOnStart`, so all five are decided before the first request. Because section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)'s shared half registers this same validated type, they are
also decided inside `tools/provision-admin` before it opens a connection — by way of the **explicit**
`IStartupValidator.Validate()` call that section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) assertion 2 requires, since a
console command that only builds a host has not validated anything. That is why the accepted modes below
are enumerated **per invocation** and not only per environment.

| Check | Rule | Why it is a start-time check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Present** | Non-null and non-whitespace | Without it the failure is the first database touch, which on a warmed deployment may be a real user's request |
| **Parseable** | It constructs a `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnectionStringBuilder` without throwing | A malformed keyword is a typo, and a typo caught at start is a failed deployment rather than a failed checkout. The builder is strict about this: an unrecognised keyword throws `ArgumentException: Keyword not supported`, so the check is real rather than nominal |
| **Authenticates in a mode this invocation may use** | **The row is selected first and the string is checked against that row alone.** The selector is the non-forgeable host-role signal below together with the resolved environment and the presence of the test signal; it yields **exactly one** row of the accepted-mode table, and the parsed builder's `Authentication`, `UserID`, `Password`, `IntegratedSecurity`, `Encrypt` and `TrustServerCertificate` must then satisfy **that** row. Failing it fails the start; there is no fall-through to another row | The dangerous failure here is not a malformed string but a **well-formed one from another path** — a SQL credential this design does not manage, or a mode that authenticates as something other than this environment's identity. Both would work, against the wrong principal, so the refusal has to precede the first use. **Select-then-check rather than search-for-a-match** is what makes that true even when two rows' shapes overlap, which `M1` and `M3` provably do |
| **Names the expected server and database** | The parsed `DataSource` and `InitialCatalog` equal `Expected:SqlServer` and `Expected:SqlDatabase` — compared as **parsed fields**, ordinal case-insensitively, with a leading `tcp:` and a trailing `,1433` normalized away first. **Deployed environments only**: both expected members are absent under `Development` and under the test fixture (below), where the check does not run because there is nothing environment-defined to compare against | A deployment pointed at a neighbouring environment's database is the failure that produces no error at all — it reads and writes successfully, in the wrong place. [06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s pre-traffic gate catches it at swap warm-up; this catches it at start, including on the invocations no swap covers |
| **Carries no unresolved secret reference** | The raw value does not begin with `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` | [06 §8.4.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records the platform mechanic: an unresolvable Key Vault reference is **passed through as that literal string** rather than failing the platform. The check is this document's half of that contract |

**The accepted modes, enumerated — because "the string carries no credential" is not a rule this design
can hold.** The deployed connection **does** carry a `User Id`: it is how a *specific* user-assigned
identity is selected, and [06 §6.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes the exact keyword form.
Development reaches a local instance by integrated security (the `appsettings.Development.json` scoping
table below), and the test fixture reaches a disposable instance of its own. A validator written as
"`UserID` empty, `Password` empty, `IntegratedSecurity` false" would therefore reject the two
configurations that must pass and leave the third undefined. The rule is an explicitly closed set of
four modes instead — **one of which is selected before the string is examined**, by the function stated
immediately after the table — and a string that does not satisfy **the selected one** fails the start,
with no fall-through to any other row:

| Mode | Where it is the accepted mode | `Authentication` | `UserID` | `Password` | `IntegratedSecurity` | Transport |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **M1 — deployed managed identity** | The web host in **every** environment that is not `Development`, on both slots | `ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity` **or** `ActiveDirectoryMSI` — nothing else | **Required**, and equal to `SqlIdentity:ClientId` after both are parsed as `Guid`s | **Must be empty** | **Must be false** | `Encrypt` true and `TrustServerCertificate` false |
| **M2 — local development** | The web host under `Development` only | `NotSpecified` or `ActiveDirectoryDefault` | Empty | **Must be empty** | **Permitted true** — this is the mode M1 forbids, and the only place it is legal | `TrustServerCertificate` true is permitted **only** when `DataSource` is a local instance — `(localdb)\…`, `.`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1` — because a local engine presents a self-signed certificate; against any other host the M1 transport rule applies |
| **M3 — the operator and release invocations** | `tools/provision-admin` and the data-load verbs of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), in any environment | **`ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity` or `ActiveDirectoryMSI`**, with **`ActiveDirectoryWorkloadIdentity`** as the single permitted fallback — the one flow [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) selects for the deployment principal. **`ActiveDirectoryDefault` is rejected here**, because that document prohibits it on the release path: it resolves whichever credential the host happens to offer, which is the opposite of naming a principal | **Required**, and parseable as a `Guid` — it is the **deployment** identity's client ID, not the site's, so it is not compared against `SqlIdentity:ClientId` and is instead confirmed at the database by the `USER_NAME()` assertion of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) | **Must be empty** | **Must be false** | As M1 |
| **M4 — the test fixture** | The in-process test host of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), and nowhere else | `NotSpecified` for the local container, `ActiveDirectoryDefault` for the throwaway managed database — permitted **here only**, because a fixture provisioning its own disposable database is not the release path [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) prohibits it on, and it has no declared principal to name | Permitted for the container | **Permitted for the container only**, and only a credential the fixture generated for that run | Must be false | `TrustServerCertificate` true permitted for the container's self-signed certificate |

**`M1` and `M3` are not distinguishable by the string, and that is a defect in an earlier formulation of
this section rather than a subtlety of it.** Read the two rows: both accept
`ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity`, both require a `UserID` that parses as a `Guid`, both require an empty
`Password`, both require `IntegratedSecurity` false and both require the same transport. `M1` additionally
requires that the `UserID` equal `SqlIdentity:ClientId`; the `M3` row above says of the same member "it is
the **deployment** identity's client ID, not the site's, so it is **not** compared against
`SqlIdentity:ClientId`". So a string carrying a managed-identity authentication, a `Guid` `UserID`, no
password, `Encrypt` true and `TrustServerCertificate` false, alongside a present-and-equal
`SqlIdentity:ClientId`, **satisfies both rows at once**. Under a
validator that searched the table for a matching row, that string had two answers and the table's own
"exactly one row" rule was unsatisfiable — and the consequences run in both directions. The **web** host
could be handed a release-shaped string and admit it under `M3`'s laxer identity rule, so a site would
start authenticating as the **deployment** principal, which holds DDL rights the runtime identity is
deliberately denied. And the **operator** invocation could be admitted under `M1`, whose rule compares the
deployment identity's client ID against `SqlIdentity:ClientId` — a member that names the *site's* identity
— so a correct release either fails for the wrong reason or passes while comparing two unrelated values.

**What the earlier formulation was missing is not a rule but a *fact*: nothing told the validator which
host it was running in.** "Selected by … which host is running" named a discriminator that did not exist.
`IHostEnvironment` supplies the environment and nothing supplies the role, so the validator had only the
string, and the string cannot say. The fix is the same shape as `M4`'s below and is introduced for the same
reason: a **composition-provided signal that no configuration provider can produce.**

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| The signal | `IHostRoleSignal`, an interface **declared** in the application at `Services/IHostRoleSignal.cs` — **the same folder `ITestConnectionModeSignal` is declared in**, under the same [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) map delegation, so **no map row and no new folder is added**. It exposes one member, `HostRole Role { get; }`, over a closed two-value enum: `HostRole.Web` and `HostRole.Operator`. There is no third value and no `Unknown` — an unset role is an absent registration, which is handled below rather than represented |
| Who registers it | **Each composition root, explicitly, and never the shared half.** `Program.cs` registers `HostRole.Web`; `tools/provision-admin/Program.cs` registers `HostRole.Operator`, immediately after its `AddMusicStoreServices` call. It is **deliberately absent from `AddMusicStoreServices`** (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) — a shared registration would have to pick one value, and picking one is exactly the mistake: the shared half is shared precisely because it does not know which host it is composing |
| Why it cannot be forged | It is a **service descriptor**. The configuration system produces keys and values; it cannot add a descriptor to an `IServiceCollection`. A platform application setting, an environment variable, a Key Vault reference, a release-step override and a command-line argument are all equally powerless against it. That is the same argument `M4`'s gate rests on, and it is the only argument available here — **configuration cannot be allowed to select the mode, because configuration is the thing being validated.** A mode selected by a configuration key would let the value under scrutiny nominate the rules it is scrutinised by |
| How the validator reads it | `GetService<IHostRoleSignal>()` on the `IServiceProvider` the one `IValidateOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>` already takes — the same accessor and the same reason as `ITestConnectionModeSignal` below. **Null is a failure, not a default**, and this is where it differs from that signal: a missing test signal is the ordinary deployed case, whereas a missing host-role signal is a **composition defect** in a root this document specifies. It fails the start as `Configuration:HostRole` "no host role was registered by the composition root", named in the aggregated `OptionsValidationException` like every other member. `GetRequiredService` is not used, so the failure arrives as a validation failure the operator can read rather than as a container resolution throw during `Build()` |
| What a **successful** selection leaves behind | One `Information` record, written once per process by the validator, carrying two named log-state properties: `hostRole` (`Web` or `Operator`) and `connectionMode` (`M1`, `M2`, `M3` or `M4`) — **and nothing else**, so the rule that the connection string never reaches a log (below) is untouched. It exists for two reasons: an operator reading a start-up log can see which contract was applied without inferring it, and the two tests below that assert *which row ran* have something to assert on. A validation that succeeds silently is indistinguishable from one that selected the wrong row and happened to pass |

**The selection function, total and single-valued — which is what "exactly one row" now means.** The
triple of role, resolved environment and test-signal presence selects the row; the string is never
consulted in selecting it:

| Host role | Resolved environment | `ITestConnectionModeSignal` | Selected row |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Web` | Anything other than `Development` | Absent | **M1**, and only M1 |
| `Web` | `Development` | Absent | **M2**, and only M2 |
| `Web` | Neither `Production` nor `Staging` | **Present** | **M4**, and only M4 — the fixture's host is a web host, and its own four conditions below still all have to hold |
| `Web` | `Production` or `Staging` | **Present** | **Failure.** The signal has no legitimate presence in either environment, and this is a stronger statement than "M4 is unavailable there": the registration itself is the defect and the start fails naming it |
| `Operator` | Any | Absent | **M3**, and only M3 |
| `Operator` | Any | **Present** | **Failure.** The operator tool is never the fixture's host, so both signals together are a composition defect rather than a combination to resolve |
| Absent | Any | Any | **Failure** — the missing-registration case in the table above |

Two properties follow, and both are the point of doing it this way. **`M1` and `M3` can no longer be
confused**, because a validator that consults one row cannot pick the wrong one from an overlap — the
overlap is still there in the shapes and is now harmless. And **every failure names a row**: "does not
satisfy M3" is a message that tells an operator which contract was applied, where "matches no accepted
mode" told them only that the search failed.

**M4 is bounded by the fixture's own composition rather than by anything the configuration can carry, and
that distinction is the whole of its safety.** An earlier formulation gated the mode on "a marker the
fixture sets on the configuration". That does not hold: a configuration key is exactly what a platform
setting, an environment variable or a release step **can** supply, so a deployed host would have been one
application setting away from selecting the test mode — and the mode that permits an inline password. The
gate is therefore a **service registration, which no configuration provider can produce**:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| The signal | `ITestConnectionModeSignal`, an interface **declared** in the application (`Services/ITestConnectionModeSignal.cs`, inside the folder [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map delegates to this document) and **implemented nowhere in it**. It exposes one member: the closed set of `(DataSource, InitialCatalog)` pairs the fixture provisioned **for this run** |
| Who implements it | The test project alone. `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` holds the only implementation, and the `ProjectReference` edge runs **test → application** ([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so the application cannot name the type even accidentally: the direction of the reference makes it invisible from the side that gets published |
| How it is supplied | The fixture registers it into the service collection through the test host's own configuration hook, **before** the startup validator runs. It is a `services.AddSingleton<ITestConnectionModeSignal>(…)` call in test code — the one channel that is code rather than data |
| The validator rule | The one `IValidateOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>` takes `IServiceProvider` and reads the signal with **`GetService<ITestConnectionModeSignal>()`**, which "returns `null` if there is no service of type `T`" (`ServiceProviderServiceExtensions.GetService`, .NET 8) — deliberately not `GetRequiredService`, whose throw would turn the ordinary deployed case into a startup crash, and deliberately not an unannotated constructor parameter, which the container would require to be registered. **Null — the deployed and developer case — makes M4 unavailable outright**, whatever the string looks like: because the selection function above never reaches M4 without the signal, an M4-shaped string is then checked against the row that *was* selected and fails naming **that** row — `M1` for a deployed web host, `M2` under `Development`, `M3` under the operator role. Non-null admits M4 **only** when all four hold: the parsed `DataSource` **and** `InitialCatalog` appear together in one of the signal's pairs; the `DataSource` is a loopback form (`(localdb)\…`, `.`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) or the throwaway managed database the signal names; any `Password` present is the per-run credential the fixture generated, held in memory and written to no file; and the resolved environment is neither `Production` nor `Staging` |
| The target allow-list | The signal's pairs **are** the allow-list, generated at provision time and different every run, so it cannot be pre-declared, checked into a file or reused. A fixture that provisions a database and forgets to name it in the signal fails the start rather than falling through to M2 — the modes are mutually exclusive rows, not a cascade |

**How it is proven that a normal or deployed builder cannot select M4**, rather than asserted: coverage row
**O10** of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes) enumerates
the published application's service descriptors and asserts **no descriptor for
`ITestConnectionModeSignal` exists**, then builds a host the ordinary way — no fixture involvement — hands
it an M4-shaped connection string, and asserts the start **fails**, naming the row the selection function
chose for that host rather than M4. The
first half catches a future registration added inside the application; the second catches a validator
edit that made the signal optional. Neither can be satisfied by editing configuration, which is the
property the previous marker lacked.

**One validation test per mode, because a closed set of four rows is only closed if each row is exercised
from both sides.** These run against the validator alone — a built host, no database — so they are cheap
enough to be exhaustive, and each names the failure it would otherwise take a deployment to find:

| Test | Given | Asserted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **M1 accepted** | `IHostRoleSignal` registered as `Web`, a non-`Development` environment, `ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity`, `User Id` equal to `SqlIdentity:ClientId`, no password, `Encrypt=True`, `TrustServerCertificate=False`, and all four environment-conditional members present | The start succeeds. Repeated with the `ActiveDirectoryMSI` alias, which parses to a different enum member and must also pass |
| **M1 rejected** | The same, with `SqlIdentity:ClientId` **absent**; and again with it present but **unequal** to the parsed `User Id`; and again with a `Pwd=` keyword added | Each fails the start, naming the member and the rule — **and the message contains neither the connection string nor any password-keyword value** |
| **M2 accepted** | `Development`, `Integrated Security=True`, a local `DataSource`, and **none** of the four environment-conditional members supplied | The start succeeds. This is the test the previous unconditional `[Required]` would have failed, and it is the reason the annotations moved into the validator |
| **M2 rejected** | `Development` with `Integrated Security=True` against a **non-local** `DataSource` and `TrustServerCertificate=True`; and again with `SqlIdentity:ClientId` supplied | Each fails the start — the first on the transport rule, the second because M2 presents no identity of its own |
| **M3 accepted** | Any environment, a generic host built by the operator tool with `IHostRoleSignal` registered as `Operator`, `ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity` with a `Guid` `User Id`, no password, and no `SqlIdentity:ClientId` | The start succeeds and the member's absence is **not** a failure |
| **M3 rejected** | `ActiveDirectoryDefault`; and again with `User Id` absent; and again with a password present — all three under the `Operator` role | Each fails the start. The first is the [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) prohibition, asserted rather than described |
| **M4 accepted** | The fixture's own host, `IHostRoleSignal` registered as `Web`, and `ITestConnectionModeSignal` registered and naming the provisioned pair | The start succeeds, including with the per-run credential present |
| **M4 rejected** | The same string with the test signal **absent**; with it present but naming a **different** pair; and with the resolved environment set to `Production` | Each fails the start. The first two fail against the row the selection function chose instead of M4, naming that row; the third fails on M4's own environment condition. The first is row **O10** above |
| **One string, one row — the overlap is resolved rather than merely acknowledged** | **A single connection string constructed to satisfy `M1` and `M3` simultaneously**: `ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity`, a `Guid` `User Id`, no password, `Integrated Security=False`, `Encrypt=True`, `TrustServerCertificate=False`, with `SqlIdentity:ClientId` present and **equal** to that `User Id`. Presented **twice** — once to a host with `IHostRoleSignal` registered as `Web`, once to a host with it registered as `Operator`, everything else held identical | **Both starts succeed, and each succeeds under exactly one row**: the `Web` host validates it against `M1` and the `Operator` host against `M3`. Asserted on the validator's own record of the row it applied, not on the outcome alone — two passes prove nothing about which rule ran. This is the row that fails if a future edit reintroduces "search the table for a matching row", because a search would have two candidates and no defined answer |
| **An operator-shaped string is refused by the web host** | `IHostRoleSignal` registered as `Web`, a non-`Development` environment, and an otherwise valid M3 string: `ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity`, a `Guid` `User Id` that is **the deployment identity's**, no password, correct transport — and `SqlIdentity:ClientId` present and naming the **site's** identity, so the two `Guid`s differ | The start **fails**, naming `M1` and the unequal-identity rule. This is the finding this table exists to close: without the role signal the string would have been admitted under `M3`, and the site would have opened its connections as the **deployment** principal, which holds the DDL rights section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) keeps away from the runtime identity. Repeated in the other direction — a `Web`-shaped string with `SqlIdentity:ClientId` absent, presented to the `Operator` host — and asserted to pass under `M3`, since M3 does not require that member |
| **No host role registered** | A host built with **neither** signal registered — the composition defect, not a configuration state — and any otherwise valid string | The start fails, naming `Configuration:HostRole` in the aggregated `OptionsValidationException`. Asserted on the message rather than on the exception type, because a `GetRequiredService` throw during `Build()` would also fail the start and would **not** be readable: this row is what distinguishes the two |

**Why the parsed builder rather than a scan of the string, stated because the two are not equivalent.**
Every rule above is expressed over **individual parsed fields**, and that is what makes "no password in
any spelling" enforceable: the builder normalizes the keyword aliases, so `Pwd` surfaces as `Password`,
`Uid` as `UserID`, and both `Trusted_Connection=True` and `Integrated Security=SSPI` as
`IntegratedSecurity = true` — verified against the provider. A substring scan for `Password=` misses all
four. The `Authentication` comparison is against the parsed enum for the same reason, and it accepts
**both** managed-identity members because the documented alias parses to a *different* member
(`ActiveDirectoryMSI`) than the primary spelling (`ActiveDirectoryManagedIdentity`), so a validator
comparing against one alone would reject a form [06 §6.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits.
This is the application-side counterpart of [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s keyword
scan, and where the two could disagree the parsed form governs, because it is the stricter of the two.

**The connection string is never logged, and never appears in an exception message (CWE-532).** The
failure record names the key, the check that failed and — where the check is a comparison — the **field**
whose values differed, together with the expected and actual values of that field only: a server name, a
database name and a client-ID GUID are not credentials ([06 §6.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
says so of the GUID, and [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) already emits the same pair for
its own check, so the two records agree). **What never appears anywhere is the string itself, any
password-keyword value, and any interpolation of the string into a message, an exception, a stack trace or
a diagnostic page** — the validator therefore constructs its messages from named fields and never from the
bound value, and the provider's own exceptions are logged by their type and message rather than by
re-emitting the configuration that produced them.

**What is rejected in every environment, including the two permissive ones.** No mode permits: a
`Password` in any spelling on M1, M2 or M3; a `UserID` holding anything other than the expected client-ID
GUID on M1; a value beginning `@Microsoft.KeyVault(`, which means a reference the platform failed to
resolve ([06 §8.4.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)); an absent or empty `DataSource` or
`InitialCatalog`, which is a string that would connect to whatever the provider's defaults resolve to;
and `TrustServerCertificate=True` against any host that is not the local or containerized instance its
own row names.

**The unresolved-reference check is not specific to this key, and stating it once is what makes it
enforceable.** Any value this section defines can arrive as a Key Vault reference, and the platform's
pass-through behaviour is the same for all of them, so the rule is a **standing obligation on every
validator in this section**: each `IValidateOptions<T>` rejects any bound `string` member whose value
begins with `@Microsoft.KeyVault(`, with the same message shape and the same value suppression as above.
It is one line per validator rather than a separate mechanism, and it is stated here so no later table has
to repeat it — where a table below says a member is validated, this check is part of what that means.

**How every required member below is *declared*, because the obvious declaration cannot detect a missing
key.** This is a mechanism decision and it precedes the values, because getting it wrong makes every
value below unenforceable.

`[Required]` is the reflex answer and it does not work for a value type. The attribute's implementation
rejects **only** `null` and — unless `AllowEmptyStrings` is set — an empty or whitespace string:
`if (value is null) return false; return AllowEmptyStrings || value is not string stringValue ||
!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(stringValue);` (`RequiredAttribute.IsValid`, `System.ComponentModel.Annotations`,
.NET 8). Configuration binding leaves an unsupplied member at its CLR default, and a CLR default is not
null. So a `bool` declared `public bool PasswordRequireDigit { get; set; }` binds to `false` when the key
is absent, `[Required]` passes, and the application starts with digits **not** required — the exact
failure section [6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited) exists to forbid, arriving through
the validation that was supposed to prevent it. The same holds for `int` (`0`), `TimeSpan`
(`TimeSpan.Zero`) and every enum (its zero member — which for `SameSiteMode` is `Unspecified`).

**The rule, applied to every table below:**

| Member's logical type | Declared as | Presence detected by | Range or value constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `string` | `string?` | `[Required]` — correct here, because an absent key really does leave `null` | `[Required]`, plus a per-member rule in `IValidateOptions<T>` where one applies |
| `bool` | **`bool?`** | `[Required]` on the nullable member: an absent key leaves `null`, which the attribute rejects | none — both values are legal, which is precisely why absence must be distinguishable from `false` |
| `int` | **`int?`** | `[Required]` on the nullable member | `[Range]` on the nullable member, which validates the contained value when one is present |
| `TimeSpan` | **`TimeSpan?`** | `[Required]` on the nullable member | A per-member bound in `IValidateOptions<T>`, because `[Range]` has no `TimeSpan` form |
| enum | **`SameSiteMode?`** and equivalents | `[Required]` on the nullable member | An explicit allowed-set check in `IValidateOptions<T>`, because binding an unrecognised name is a bind failure but binding a *legal but unwanted* member is not |

**Nullable declaration is the mechanism; a non-nullable property exposed to the rest of the application is
the outcome.** Each options type exposes the validated value through a non-nullable accessor that the
validator has already guaranteed — so no consumer writes `?? throw`, and no consumer can observe the
nullable form. That is the whole reason the nullability is stated here rather than left to a reader to
infer from "required": it is a property of the options type, not of the key.

**And one member class needs the opposite treatment, because an attribute cannot express a condition and
attaching one anyway makes the condition unreachable.** Some members below are required **only in some
environments or under some connection modes** — the five the safe-default block at the end of this section
names, four conditional on the environment and one on the connection mode. For those, `[Required]` is
**not** declared, and the reason is mechanical rather than stylistic:
`ValidateDataAnnotations()` registers a `DataAnnotationValidateOptions<TOptions>` as one
`IValidateOptions<TOptions>` among the others, and the options factory runs **every** registered validator
and **aggregates** their failures into a single `OptionsValidationException` rather than stopping at the
first (`OptionsFactory<TOptions>.Create`, `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`, .NET 8). So an unconditional
`[Required]` on a conditionally required member fails the start in exactly the environments the condition
was written to permit, and no amount of logic in the environment-aware validator can withdraw a failure
another validator has already reported.

| Member class | Declared as | Where presence is enforced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unconditionally required | The nullable form above, **with** `[Required]` | The data-annotations half. Correct here because the answer does not depend on the environment |
| **Conditionally required** | The same nullable form, **without** `[Required]` and without `[Range]` | **The type's one `IValidateOptions<T>`**, which reads `IHostEnvironment`, the selected connection mode and the sibling members, and reports the failure only when the condition holds. Range and format rules for those members move into the same validator, for the same reason |

**The consequence is a rule with no exceptions: each options type has exactly one `IValidateOptions<T>`,
and for a conditionally required member that validator is the *only* place presence is decided.** A second
validator for the same type would reintroduce the aggregation problem in a form that is harder to see,
because both halves would then be this document's own code.

**`Identity` — `IdentityPolicyOptions`. Every member is required, none has a default, and every value is
stated here.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PasswordMinimumLength` | `int?`, `[Range(8, 128)]` | **12** | `6` (`PasswordOptions.RequiredLength`) | **Deliberate hardening** |
| `PasswordRequireDigit` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` | **Deliberate hardening** relative to the source, which assigns no password validator at all; equal to the target default |
| `PasswordRequireLowercase` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` | **Deliberate hardening**, as above |
| `PasswordRequireUppercase` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` | **Deliberate hardening**, as above |
| `PasswordRequireNonAlphanumeric` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` | **Deliberate hardening**, as above |
| `PasswordRequiredUniqueChars` | `int?`, `[Range(1, 16)]` | **4** | `1` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| `LockoutEnabled` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` (`LockoutOptions.AllowedForNewUsers`) | **Deliberate hardening** — the source has no lockout of any kind |
| `LockoutMaxFailedAccessAttempts` | `int?`, `[Range(3, 20)]` | **5** | `5` | **Preserved** against the target default; hardening against the source, which counts nothing |
| `LockoutDefaultDuration` | `TimeSpan?`, bounded to 1 minute – 24 hours | **`00:15:00`** | `00:05:00` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| `SignInRequireConfirmedAccount` | `bool?` | **`false`** | `false` | **Preserved**, deliberately — section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) records why the hardening is the wrong call here |
| `UserRequireUniqueEmail` | `bool?` | **`false`** | `false` | **Preserved** |
| `UserAllowedUserNameCharacters` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789-._@+`** | the same string | **Preserved**, stated |

**Why the values live here and the labels live in section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled).** A security value and its justification are two different
review objects. The **value** belongs where a reviewer can see it beside its key, its type and its
presence rule — that is this table, and it is the only place any of these numbers appears. The **label and
the reason** belong where the policy is argued, which is section 6.1; that table cites this one for the
number rather than carrying a second copy. The label column above is a one-word pointer at 6.1's
verdict, not a second decision.

**`UserAllowedUserNameCharacters` is load-bearing for the migration, not decoration.** Identity's user
manager validates a username against this set on every write, and the set does not contain a space. The
migrated usernames are the source's own, so section
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) validates every extracted
username against this exact string **before** the load and stops on a violation — a name that loads but
can never be updated afterwards is a defect the load should not create.

**No member has a default, because a default here is precisely the framework-inherited value section
[6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited) exists to forbid.** The two rows section 6.1
deliberately declines to harden — `SignInRequireConfirmedAccount` and `UserRequireUniqueEmail`, both
`false` — are **still required keys**: an explicit `false` is a stated decision, an absent key is an
inherited one, and only the first can be reviewed. That distinction is only expressible because both are
declared `bool?`.

**`Authentication:Cookie` — `AuthenticationCookieOptions`. This section configures the *application*
cookie — the framework's `IdentityConstants.ApplicationScheme`. The other cookies the application issues
are inventoried below it, because "the cookie policy" is not one cookie.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Name` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`.AspNetCore.Identity.Application`** | the same string, but *generated* rather than set: the post-configuration step assigns `".AspNetCore." + Uri.EscapeDataString(schemeName)` when no name is supplied, and the scheme is `Identity.Application` | **Preserved** in value, **stated** in mechanism. Setting the literal means renaming a scheme cannot silently rename a live cookie and sign everyone out |
| `ExpireTimeSpan` | `TimeSpan?`, bounded to 1 hour – 30 days | **`14.00:00:00`** | `TimeSpan.FromDays(14)` | **Preserved** — it equals both the target default and the source middleware's own default, so the ticket lifetime does not change at cutover |
| `SlidingExpiration` | `bool?` | **`true`** | `true` | **Preserved**, stated |
| `PersistentExpireTimeSpan` | `TimeSpan?`, bounded to 1 hour – 30 days | **`14.00:00:00`** | no such option exists — see the wiring below | **Preserved**: the source honours the "remember me" flag [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] and its middleware's persistent cookie expires on the same 14-day ticket window |
| `SameSite` | **`SameSiteMode?`**, restricted to `Lax` or `Strict` | **`Lax`** | `Lax` | **Deliberate hardening** — the source middleware has no such option at all (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)). `Unspecified` and `None` are rejected by the validator rather than merely undocumented |
| `LoginPath` | `string?`, `[Required]`, must begin `/` | **`/Account/Login`** | `/Account/Login` | **Preserved** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:17] |
| `LogoutPath` | `string?`, `[Required]`, must begin `/` | **`/Account/LogOff`** | `/Account/Logout` | **Preserved** — the source's sign-out action is `LogOff` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:300-306], so the framework default would name a route this application does not have |
| `AccessDeniedPath` | `string?`, `[Required]`, must begin `/` | **`/Account/AccessDenied`** | `/Account/AccessDenied` | **Deliberate hardening**, minor: the source redirects a denied authenticated user to the login form (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)). The view is new; section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) owns no change to it because it is not a ported view |

**`PersistentExpireTimeSpan` is wired to a real mechanism, and the mechanism is named because the
framework has no option of that name.** There is no separate persistent-cookie lifetime in
`CookieAuthenticationOptions`. The sign-in handler sets `Properties.ExpiresUtc` to
`IssuedUtc + Options.ExpireTimeSpan` **only when the caller left it unset**, and then, `if
(Properties.IsPersistent)`, copies that value into the response cookie's `Expires` attribute
(`CookieAuthenticationHandler.HandleSignInAsync`, .NET 8). So the value binds to exactly one call site:
the sign-in path passes `new AuthenticationProperties { IsPersistent = <the "remember me" flag>, ExpiresUtc
= TimeProvider.GetUtcNow() + PersistentExpireTimeSpan }`. Two consequences are worth stating: the member
controls the **browser-persistence** window and `ExpireTimeSpan` controls the **ticket** window, so
setting the first longer than the second would produce a cookie the browser keeps and the handler
rejects — which is why the validator requires `PersistentExpireTimeSpan <= ExpireTimeSpan`; and a
non-persistent sign-in passes `IsPersistent = false` and no `ExpiresUtc`, leaving a session cookie whose
ticket window is `ExpireTimeSpan`, exactly as today.

**Every cookie the application can issue, with the one place each is configured.** The list is closed: a
cookie not in it is not issued at all. Three rows are cookies the framework *would* name but this
application never writes, and each says so with the evidence rather than by assertion — they are listed
because an unconfigured cookie that a later change starts writing inherits framework defaults, and two of
those defaults are `SecurePolicy = None`.

| Cookie | Name | Where its attributes are set | `Secure` / `HttpOnly` / `SameSite` / essential |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Application (sign-in) | `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` | `Authentication:Cookie` above | Always / on / `Lax` / essential |
| External sign-in | **`Identity.External`** — the framework sets this one's `Cookie.Name` to the scheme string itself, without the `.AspNetCore.` prefix | Code, on the framework's `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme` options; **no configuration key**, because no provider is registered (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) so the cookie is never written and a key would invite tuning a dead surface. Its `ExpireTimeSpan` stays at the framework's `00:05:00` | Always / on / `Lax` / essential |
| Two-factor | `Identity.TwoFactorUserId` and `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`, by the same scheme-name rule | Code, in the same call as the external cookie's. **Never written**: no two-factor flow exists in the source, none is added, `Identity:*` has no two-factor member and section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) adds no row. Configured anyway, so a future flow starts from these attributes rather than the framework's | Always / on / `Lax` / essential |
| Session | `.AspNetCore.Session` | `Session` below | Always / on / `Lax` / essential |
| Anti-forgery | `.AspNetCore.Antiforgery.MvcMusicStore` | `Antiforgery` below | Always / on / `Strict` / essential |
| Temp-data | `.AspNetCore.Mvc.CookieTempDataProvider` | Code, on `CookieTempDataProviderOptions`; **no configuration key**. The provider **is** registered — MVC's default view services call `TryAddSingleton<ITempDataProvider, CookieTempDataProvider>()`, so the registration is not ours to decline — but **nothing writes `TempData`**, verified by `git grep -n TempData -- 'src/**/*.cs' 'src/**/*.cshtml'` returning nothing, so no cookie is ever written. It is configured regardless because this cookie's framework defaults are the weakest of the set: `SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.None` and `IsEssential = false` | Always / on / `Lax` / essential |
| Consent / policy | none | **Not added.** No cookie-policy consent gate is registered, so no consent cookie exists. Every cookie above is marked essential, which is a factual claim about this application rather than an exemption — the session cookie *is* the cart identity [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19] | n/a |

**Five cookie attributes are deliberately *not* configuration-backed on any cookie: `Secure`, `HttpOnly`,
`IsEssential`, `Path` and `Domain`.** They are set in code — `Secure` to `CookieSecurePolicy.Always`,
`HttpOnly` on, `IsEssential` true, **`Path` to `/` and `Domain` to `null`** — and have **no key**, because
a configurable security attribute is a downgrade that one mistyped application setting can perform, and no
legitimate deployment needs any of them off.

**`Path` and `Domain` are stated rather than left to the framework, and the second of the two is the
decision.** `Path=/` is set explicitly on every cookie in the inventory above so that the scope is a
property of this contract rather than of the request path a cookie happened to be issued from — the
application cookie is issued from `/Account/Login`, the anti-forgery cookie from whatever page rendered
the form, and a path-scoped cookie would then be absent on the pages that need it. **`Domain` is left
`null` deliberately, which produces a host-only cookie**: the browser returns it to the exact host that
set it and to no subdomain. Setting a domain would widen every cookie in the inventory to every
subdomain of it, which this application has no use for — it is served at one host per environment
([06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) and generates no cross-subdomain link (the
`XForwardedHost` row of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) — and widening a session or
authentication cookie's scope for no requirement is the kind of change nobody notices until a
subdomain is delegated. There is a second, concrete reason to fix both values here: the temporary
legacy-cookie stage of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) can only delete a cookie by
matching the `Path` and `Domain` it was issued at, and
[06 §11.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes those as `/` and no domain — so the target's own
cookies are issued at exactly the scope the transition stage is written against. The
local development case is handled by the host rather than by a key: the development server binds an HTTPS
endpoint and uses the development certificate — the artifact and the exact ports are
[04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, and the keys' place in this schema is the `Kestrel` entry
below — so an always-secure cookie is delivered locally too. That is a development-environment
requirement, not a configuration knob.

**`Session` — `SessionPolicyOptions`.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IdleTimeout` | `TimeSpan?`, bounded to 5 minutes – 4 hours | **`00:20:00`** | `TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20)` (`SessionOptions.IdleTimeout`) | **Preserved** — it equals both the target default and the source platform's own 20-minute session window, so an anonymous cart survives exactly as long as it does today |
| `CookieName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`.AspNetCore.Session`** | the same string (`SessionDefaults.CookieName`) | **Preserved** in value, **stated** in mechanism, for the reason the application cookie's `Name` row gives |

**Why the idle timeout is preserved rather than lengthened.** [06 §8.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
requires a session window "at least as long as a realistic shopping session", and 20 minutes satisfies it
for the reason that is easy to miss: **the cart rows are not in session.** Only the cart *key* is
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so an expired anonymous session orphans rows rather
than deleting a cart, which is the same outcome the source produces today and the same one section
[11](#11-the-cutover-decision) accepts at cutover. Lengthening the window would change behaviour, extend
the lifetime of a correlatable identifier and grow the cache table, for no preserved outcome.

**`IOTimeout` is left at the framework's `00:01:00`, and what it actually bounds is narrower than its name
suggests.** An earlier version of this paragraph described it as bounding "an individual cache read or
write", which is not what the option does. It is "the maximum amount of time allowed to load a session
from the store, or to commit it to the store", and the reference adds the qualification that matters:
**"this may only apply to asynchronous operations"** (`SessionOptions.IOTimeout`, API reference, ASP.NET
Core 8). So it bounds the session middleware's **asynchronous load and commit**, not each cache round trip
and not a synchronous property access. Three consequences, and the first is a requirement on application
code rather than on configuration:

| Consequence | What this design does about it |
| --- | --- |
| A synchronous `ISession` access loads the session **implicitly and synchronously** on first use, outside `IOTimeout`'s reach | **Every session access in this application is preceded by an explicit `await session.LoadAsync()`**, which the framework's own guidance requires for exactly this reason ("`ISession.LoadAsync` … must be awaited before `TryGetValue`, `Set` or `Remove`" — *Session and state management in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). It is a **single** call site: cart-id resolution belongs to the service of section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted), so the load is awaited there and nothing else in the application touches `ISession` at all — which is what makes "every access" a checkable statement rather than a hope |
| The **commit** is the other operation the bound covers, and the session middleware performs it asynchronously as the request completes | So the write path is bounded without any further requirement on application code. What the design must **not** do is treat that bound as a health signal. A session write carries the cart **key** and nothing else — the cart rows are in the database (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) — so a commit that exceeds the bound costs an anonymous visitor their key and destroys nothing that was paid for. Whether the database is sick is reported by section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)'s readiness checks, which is the one place that question is answered |
| What bounds the underlying **SQL** call is not this option | It is the provider's own connection and command behaviour against the same database the request is already using, under the resilience settings of section [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them). Setting `IOTimeout` to a hand-chosen value would therefore add a second, unrelated timeout to keep in step with those, which is why the framework's minute is kept |

**The test is the coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**: with the cache pointed at a
target that does not answer, a cart request completes with the load failing inside the bound rather than
hanging, and the request does **not** return a cart populated from a half-loaded session. Asserting a
timeout is only meaningful because the load is explicit — with an implicit synchronous load there is no
awaited operation for the option to bound and the test would be characterising the provider instead.

**Its other four attributes are code-set for the same reason**, and section
[6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) states them: `HttpOnly` on, `SameSite=Lax`, always secure, and
**`IsEssential` true**. The last one is worth its own sentence: the session cookie carries the **cart
identity** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so a consent gate that suppressed it
would empty carts silently rather than degrade a feature — which makes "essential" a factual claim about
this application, not a convenience.

**`Antiforgery` — `AntiforgeryPolicyOptions`.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HeaderName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`RequestVerificationToken`** | `RequestVerificationToken` (`AntiforgeryOptions.HeaderName`) | **Preserved** in value, **stated** in mechanism — the reason is the next paragraph |
