| `CookieName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`.AspNetCore.Antiforgery.MvcMusicStore`** | *derived, not fixed*: when no name is set, the framework assigns `".AspNetCore.Antiforgery." + Base64Url(SHA256(ApplicationDiscriminator)[0..8])` (`AntiforgeryOptionsSetup`, .NET 8) | **Deliberate hardening** of a different kind — see below |

**The cookie name is set because the framework's default one is a function of a value this contract varies
per environment.** The derived default hashes `DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator`, and that member
exists precisely so production and a slot differ (section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it)). Left derived, the anti-forgery
cookie would therefore be **named differently in every environment**, and any change to the discriminator
— a deliberate one, or a slot swap — would rename it, invalidating every in-flight form for reasons no
log would explain. An explicit literal makes the name a constant of the application, decouples it from a
value that is allowed to move, and leaves the discriminator doing only the job section 4.9 gives it.

**Its other four attributes are code-set, and one of them is the reason this cookie is listed in the
inventory above.** `SameSite=Strict`, `HttpOnly` on, `IsEssential` true — all three equal to the
framework's defaults, stated rather than inherited — and **`Secure` always**, which is *not*: this
cookie's framework default is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, the weakest in the set. `FormFieldName` is left
at the framework's `__RequestVerificationToken`, which is byte-for-byte the field name the source's own
`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` emits [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Login.cshtml:13], so the form
transport is preserved without a key.

**The header key exists to state the name once, not to vary it per environment.** Section
[7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form) sets `AntiforgeryOptions.HeaderName` from it
explicitly rather than relying on a framework default, and the **same literal is fixed on the client**
by section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script). So the two move together or cart removal breaks
in the one way that is hardest to see — a rejected POST whose only symptom is a row that does not
disappear. The key is therefore **not** placed in any environment overlay.

**One anti-forgery behaviour is code-set and belongs here because it collides with a header value this
document does not own.** `SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader` is set to **true**. The framework's anti-forgery
emits its own `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` on responses that carry a token, and
[06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) sets that header centrally, for every response, to a
different value. Suppressing the anti-forgery copy leaves **one** owner of the header and no
per-response divergence between a form page and every other page.

**`DataProtection` — `DataProtectionSettings`.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ApplicationDiscriminator` | `string?`, `[Required]`, and validated non-whitespace | **Not stated here, deliberately** — the value differs per environment and is a platform setting, so [06 §8.4.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes it and marks it slot-scoped. This contract owns the key, its type, its required-ness and the failure | *derived*, not fixed: left unset, the framework derives a discriminator from the content-root path ([06 §8.4.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) | **Deliberate hardening**, and the one member in this contract whose absence has no runtime symptom at all |

It is the argument to `SetApplicationName` in section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it), it is what gives each
environment its own ring inside a shared store, and it is **configuration-backed rather than compiled
in** precisely so that a slot can differ from production without a rebuild
([06 §7.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), control 2). A silently absent discriminator is the
worst case in this contract: the application starts, issues cookies against a ring keyed by an inferred
name, and a staging slot may then decrypt production tickets. That is why it is fail-fast rather than
defaulted.

**`SqlIdentity` — `SqlIdentityOptions`. One member, and it is the value mode M1 above compares against.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ClientId` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — a conditionally required member, per the member-class rule above | **Not stated here** — it is one GUID per environment and per slot | **Platform configuration**, `SqlIdentity__ClientId` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), marked slot-scoped so a swap cannot move the staging identity's GUID onto production | All of it in the one `IValidateOptions<SqlIdentityOptions>`, which reads the selected connection mode. **Under M1: required, parseable as a `Guid`, and equal to the connection string's parsed `User Id`.** **Under M2 and M4: required to be absent** — those modes present no identity of their own, so a stray value fails the start rather than being ignored. **Under M3: not required and not compared**, because the identity in play is the *deployment* principal's rather than the site's: its client ID arrives inside the connection string's `User Id`, which the connection validator requires and parses as a `Guid`, and which principal actually connected is then asserted **at the database** by the `USER_NAME()` check of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) assertion 1 — a stronger statement than comparing a GUID against a second locally declared copy of it |

It is not a secret — a client ID names which identity to ask the platform's token endpoint for and
possessing it grants nothing ([06 §6.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) — which is why it may be
named in the failure record of the connection validation above.

**`Expected` — `ExpectedDeploymentOptions`. Four members, every one of them **deployment-supplied
configuration**, and **none of them compiled into the artifact**.**

That last point is the reason this section exists as configuration rather than as constants. The
published output is built once and promoted unchanged ([04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so
an expectation baked into the bytes would make one artifact valid in exactly one environment and destroy
the property the promotion model depends on. Each value below is declared once per environment, in the
same pipeline environment definition that declares [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
`EXPECTED_*` variables, and delivered as a platform setting — so the release-time assertions and the
in-process assertions compare against one declaration rather than two.

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Environment` | `string?`, `[Required]` | The **deployment's** expected environment name — [06 §8.4.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the value, and it is `Production` on both slots of the production site | Platform setting `Expected__Environment` in every deployed environment; the committed Development overlay carries `Development`, which is the only environment whose expectation is committed and the only one the overlay is ever loaded in. For a tool invocation the same value arrives as `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` (section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a) | Non-whitespace; **equal to both `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` and `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT`**, which must themselves be present and agree — the rule section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a states and this key supplies the expected side of |
| `SqlServer` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, per the member-class rule above | The logical server's fully qualified name | Platform setting `Expected__SqlServer`; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_SQL_SERVER` | Non-whitespace, no scheme and no `,`-port suffix; compared against the parsed `DataSource` by the connection check above |
| `SqlDatabase` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, as above | The database name | Platform setting `Expected__SqlDatabase`; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_SQL_DATABASE` | Non-whitespace; compared against the parsed `InitialCatalog` |
| `DataProtectionDiscriminator` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, as above | The discriminator this slot is supposed to be running | Platform setting `Expected__DataProtectionDiscriminator`, supplied **by the release** for the slot being deployed; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_DISCRIMINATOR` | Non-whitespace; **equal to `DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator`**. This comparison is deliberately labelled the **weaker** of the two that exist: both values reach the process as settings on the same site, so it detects a release that supplied one and not the other, and it cannot detect an operator who set both to the same wrong value. [06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s pre-traffic assertion, which compares the site's setting against the pipeline's variable from **outside** the process, is the authority; this is the in-process backstop that also covers the invocations no swap performs |

**`Telemetry` — `TelemetryOptions`. One member, and it is the only secret in this contract.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CartKeyHashSalt` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, per the member-class rule above | **Not stated anywhere, in any document** — one value per environment | A **platform secret**: a slot-scoped App Service application setting or a Key Vault reference resolved by the site's identity ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). **It is never in `appsettings.json`, never in the Development overlay, and never baked into the artifact**; the Development value comes from user secrets, which is the mechanism source 3 of the precedence list exists for | Present and non-whitespace; decodes from base64 to **at least 32 bytes**, because a short salt is a salt an attacker can exhaust; the standing `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` check; and it is **excluded from every log record and every failure message** — a validation failure names the key and the rule it broke and nothing else |

It is consumed in exactly one place: the salted `cartKeyHash` that every cart-scoped record carries
instead of the cart key itself ([06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the hash's
construction and its truncation). The value is **per environment** so that a pseudonym from one
environment cannot be correlated with the same cart's pseudonym in another, and it is a secret for the
reason any keyed pseudonym's key is a secret: with the salt, the identifiers it protects are recoverable
by exhaustion, because the cart key's domain is small — a GUID or a username.

**`Site` — `SiteOptions`. Two members, each existing because a control in another document needs a value
from this one.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Hosts` | **`string?`, `[Required]`** — a **comma-separated scalar**, not an array; the validated collection is a separate `IReadOnlyList<string>` accessor | The host names this application is served at, per environment | The platform setting `Site__Hosts` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), slot-scoped, in every deployed environment; the Development overlay carries `localhost` | Splits on `,`, trims each element, discards empties, and requires **at least one** surviving entry; each entry a syntactically valid DNS host name with **no scheme, no port, no path and no wildcard**; duplicates after case-folding fail rather than being de-duplicated silently; compared ordinal case-insensitively where it is used |
| `PermittedImageOrigins` | **`string?`**, a comma-separated scalar, **no `[Required]`** — legal to omit in every environment, and the exception list at the end of this section counts it | The external image origins the administration write path and the content-security policy both permit | The platform setting `Site__PermittedImageOrigins` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), slot-scoped, **which is its single owner**. It is **not** carried in any committed file: an empty platform value is the fail-closed state and the one [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records today | Splits and trims as above, and an **empty or absent value is legal and reads as the empty list**. Each surviving entry an absolute **`https`** origin — scheme, host and optional port, with no path, query or fragment. `http`, protocol-relative, `data:`, `javascript:` and `file:` entries **fail the start** rather than being filtered at use, so a widened list cannot smuggle a scheme past the write-path validator |

`Hosts` is one key rather than two, and that is worth stating because "the application's hostnames" and
"the CSP's hostnames" sound like different sets. They are not: the report endpoint is **same-origin** —
[06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `Reporting-Endpoints` value is the path
`/csp-report`, not an absolute URL — so the only host set either mechanism needs is the set this
application answers on. It has **two** consumers, and the second is the one an earlier version of this
section left unconnected. The first is the collector's foreign-document check — the rule is
[06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and the endpoint that applies it is section
[7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half)'s: a report whose document
URL names a host outside this list is counted and dropped. The second is **host filtering**, below.

**Both members are comma-separated scalars rather than arrays, and that is a correction rather than a
preference.** The environment-variable provider binds an array only from **indexed** keys — `Site__Hosts__0`,
`Site__Hosts__1` — so a `string[]` member and a platform setting holding `store.example.com,www.example.com`
do not meet: the scalar binds to **no** element of the array, the array stays empty, and a `[Required]`
attribute on a non-null empty array passes. The result is a validated-looking member with nothing in it.
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declares both settings in the **scalar, comma-separated**
form, so this contract takes the value as a scalar and does the splitting itself. Two properties follow.
The delimiter is this document's: it is a `,`, and it is **not** the `;` the framework's own `AllowedHosts`
key uses, because that key is not read at all (below). And the split is **validated rather than tolerant** —
an entry that fails its per-entry rule fails the start, so a mistyped setting is a failed deployment
rather than a silently narrowed policy.

**`Site:PermittedImageOrigins` has exactly one owner, and it is the platform setting.** An earlier version
of this section put the list in the committed `appsettings.json` while
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declared a slot-scoped platform setting of the same name —
two owners for one control, with the committed file losing every time (it sits at precedence layer 1 and
the platform setting at layer 4) and a reviewer reading the wrong one. The platform setting wins on the
merits as well as on precedence: it is slot-scoped, so a staging slot cannot widen production's policy,
which is the property [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) needs and a committed file cannot
provide. The committed files carry no `Site` section at all.

**The validated host list is wired into host filtering, which is the mechanism that makes it enforceable
rather than merely declared.** The default web host **already registers the host-filtering middleware**, at
the very start of the pipeline through an `IStartupFilter`, and fills `HostFilteringOptions.AllowedHosts`
from the `AllowedHosts` configuration key **only when the list is otherwise empty**, falling back to `*` —
allow everything — when that key is absent too (`WebHost.ConfigureWebDefaults`, ASP.NET Core 8 source).
That default is the state this contract must not leave in place, and the wiring is three statements:

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| How the list gets there | `services.AddOptions<HostFilteringOptions>().Configure<IOptions<SiteOptions>>((o, site) => o.AllowedHosts = site.Value.HostList)` — section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 17. The dependency-taking overload is used deliberately: the list is not available at registration time — it is produced by the validated options type, which resolves after the container is built — so a delegate closing over a value read during registration would close over nothing. `Configure` delegates run **before** every `PostConfigure` delegate, and the framework's fallback is a `PostConfigure` that acts only on an empty list, so an explicitly set list is never overwritten and the `*` fallback is unreachable |
| What is **not** used | The `AllowedHosts` configuration key. It is left unset in every file and every environment, so there is exactly one declaration of the host set: `Site__Hosts`. Setting both would be two owners again, with a `;`-delimited spelling beside a `,`-delimited one |
| What a non-matching request gets | The middleware's own response: **400** with no body, and the framework's own record naming the rejected host. The application writes nothing of its own, because the request never reaches any stage of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)'s pipeline — host filtering runs ahead of all of them |
| Whether that record is compatible with the never-record list | **Yes, and it is worth stating rather than assuming.** A `Host` header value is a routing input, not a credential, a session identifier or customer data — none of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s prohibited categories — and the platform's own HTTP log carries the same host on every request anyway ([06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). What the rule does forbid is the application **adding** anything to this path: no record of its own, and specifically nothing carrying the rejected request's cookies, query or body, none of which the application ever sees on it |

**One operational obligation follows and it belongs to the setting's value rather than to this code**: the
list must contain **every** host name that reaches the application, including the platform-assigned default
hostname and whatever host header the platform's own probes present, or a probe is answered with a 400 and
the instance is reported unhealthy. The three probe paths are exempted from HSTS and HTTPS redirection
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 6) but **not** from host filtering, and they
cannot be: the middleware runs before any application-registered stage. The value is
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; the requirement on it is this document's.

**The test is the coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**: a request carrying a `Host`
header on the list is served normally; a request carrying one that is not gets **400** and no body; and the
three probe paths answer only under a listed host. The negative half is the half that matters — with the
framework's `*` fallback in force every one of those requests succeeds, so a positive-only test passes a
configuration that filters nothing.

`PermittedImageOrigins` is the same list twice over by construction, which is the requirement delta 18 of
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) carries: the administration write path validates
`AlbumArtUrl` against it, and if it is ever non-empty the `img-src` origins of
[06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s policy are composed **from this member** rather than
written out a second time. Validation and policy cannot then drift apart, which is the failure a second
copy would eventually produce.

**`Seeding` — `SeedingOptions`. Read by the seeding command; validated everywhere.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Absence | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Enabled` | `bool?` | **`false`** in `appsettings.json`, and in no other committed file — the Development overlay carries no such key, per the file scoping at the end of this section | **Legal, and read as `false`** — the only member in this contract where absence is a decision rather than an omission, because `false` is the fail-closed value | **Deliberate hardening** — the source seeds unconditionally at startup [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/SampleData.cs:9] |
| `AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` | `string?` | **Not committed for any environment.** The seeding invocation supplies it, and section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) states the pattern it must match | **Legal only while `Enabled` is `false`.** Absent with `Enabled` true fails validation | **Deliberate hardening** — no such concept exists in the source |

**Why `Enabled` is `bool?` even though absence is legal.** The nullable declaration is not about
rejecting absence here; it is about distinguishing `false` *supplied* from `false` *assumed*, which is
what lets the validator apply the second rule below without guessing. The accessor the guard reads is a
non-nullable `bool` that is `false` when the member is null.

These are checks 2 and 3 of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) expressed
as keys. Two rules make them a guard rather than a switch. **`Enabled` set to true while the environment
is Production fails the start** — in the web application as well as in the command, because a deployed
configuration that authorizes seeding is itself the misconfiguration section 5.4 is defending against,
and refusing to start is the loud version of that discovery. And **`AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` is
required whenever `Enabled` is true**, a cross-member rule rather than an attribute on one property, so
"enabled with no allow-list" cannot exist.

**`Diagnostics` — `DiagnosticsOptions`. One member, and its absence is its production value.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Absence | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `InstanceEndpointEnabled` | `bool?`, **no `[Required]`** | **Not committed in either file** — no entry in `appsettings.json` and none in the Development overlay. The only place it is ever `true` is the platform setting `Diagnostics__InstanceEndpointEnabled`, set on a staging slot or a non-production revision for the duration of [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s verification and removed by that procedure's own teardown ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) | **Legal, and read as `false`** — the fail-closed value, and with it false the route of section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint) is not mapped at all | **Net-new.** The source has no diagnostic endpoint and no switch of any kind, so there is nothing to preserve or harden |

**The accessor is non-nullable, and the nullable member is not usable as the condition.** As with
`Seeding:Enabled` above, the declaration is `bool?` so that `false` *supplied* and `false` *assumed* remain
distinguishable, and what the endpoint mapping reads is a non-nullable `bool` that is `false` when the
member is null — `InstanceEndpointIsEnabled` in section
[2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint)'s excerpt. Reading
the nullable member directly does not compile: the pinned SDK rejects it with
`error CS0266: Cannot implicitly convert type 'bool?' to 'bool'`, which is worth stating because a mapping
condition is exactly the place the shorter form looks correct.

**One validation rule, and it is the standing one rather than a new kind.** The type carries no
`[Required]` and no cross-member rule — there is no second member for one to relate to — but it is bound
with `ValidateDataAnnotations()` and `ValidateOnStart()` like every other type above, so a **malformed**
value fails the **start**: `ValidateOnStart` forces the options instance to be produced during start, which
is when a value that is not a boolean fails to bind. The distinction that matters operationally is that
*absent* is legal and *unparseable* is not, so a setting typed `Ture` stops the host rather than quietly
leaving the route closed and looking as though the switch had been honoured.

**Why nothing is committed here, when `Seeding:Enabled` commits its `false`.** The two differ in who
supplies the true value and where a wrong one does damage. `Seeding:Enabled` is read by an **operator
command** whose configuration a reviewer inspects, so a committed `false` puts the fail-closed value in the
file that command loads. This member is read only by the web host's endpoint mapping, is supplied by exactly
one platform setting on exactly one non-production deployment unit, and is removed again when the
verification closes — and absence and `false` produce the identical unmapped route, so a committed `false`
would add a third place to look and change nothing.
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s row records the key as platform-supplied and never set on
production; this is the type side of that same fact.

**`Logging` — the framework's schema for the filtering, and `LoggingPolicyOptions` for the assertion.**
The filtering is the framework's: it reads `Logging:LogLevel:<category>` itself, and nothing this document
adds changes that. What is missing without this table is the thing a reviewer needs — **which categories
are named, and at what level, in which environment**. [06 §9.2.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
owns *why* each level is required, and the release-side expected values it asserts are
[06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; this table is the configuration that satisfies them.

| Key | Type | `appsettings.json` — the value every deployed environment gets | `appsettings.Development.json` override | Category it filters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Default` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Everything not matched more specifically |
| `Logging:LogLevel:MvcMusicStore` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | **`Debug`** | The application's own namespace — the root namespace of `src/MvcMusicStore`, so every controller, service and view component |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | **`Information`** | Framework request plumbing |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | **`Information`** | EF Core command text **and parameter values**, which is why the production level is not `Information` |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Key creation, revocation, the repository the stack actually resolved, and a key ring that fails to **load** at startup. **Not** a persistence failure — the table below states exactly what this category does and does not report |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Key-ring resolution and default-key selection. The protector's own *key not found in the key ring* record is `Trace` and does **not** surface at this level |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Sign-in and ticket handling — **and this is the row that reports a cookie the application cannot decrypt**, not the key-management row above |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Identity's own user and password operations |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | none | A rejected token |

**Two of those rows only work because of how the framework selects a rule, and the mechanism is worth
stating because the table looks redundant without it.** `Microsoft.AspNetCore` is at `Warning`, yet four
categories *beneath* it are at `Information`. That is not a contradiction: for each provider the factory
"select[s] rules with longest matching category prefix… If multiple rules are selected, take the last
one" (*Logging in .NET*, .NET 8). So `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` wins over
`Microsoft.AspNetCore` for a data-protection logger, and the four specific rows are what keep the
categories whose failures are otherwise invisible above the framework's noise floor.

**What the data-protection rows do and do not establish — enumerated rather than assumed, because an
earlier version of this table claimed a record the framework does not emit.** The claim removed from the
first row was "a failure to persist a key", and the correction matters operationally rather than
pedantically: that is precisely the record an operator would search for after a key-ring incident, and
searching for a record nothing writes is how a silently non-durable ring survives a review. Each row below
was established by exercising the case on the pinned 8.0 line — a key repository that throws on store, one
that throws on read, a key file deleted between two hosts, and a cookie replayed after its key was gone —
and reading the category, level and event name of every record produced:

| What happens | The record, and the level it is written at | Surfaced by the levels above? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A key is created | `…KeyManagement.XmlKeyManager` / `CreatingKey`, **`Information`** — written **before** the repository is asked to store anything, so its presence says a key was *minted*, not that it was *saved* | Yes |
| The ring cannot be **read**, the absent-table case of section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) | `…KeyManagement.KeyRingProvider` / `ErrorOccurredWhileReadingKeyRing`, **`Error`**, and `…DataProtection.Internal.DataProtectionHostedService` / `KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup`, **`Information`** — both carrying the exception | Yes. This failure is well covered, and it is the one section 4.9 describes |
| The repository **fails to store** a new key | **No named persistence event exists.** What appears is the same generic `ErrorOccurredWhileReadingKeyRing` at `Error`, whose text says *reading* although the operation was a write, and only at the moment the ring is first needed rather than at startup | Partly, and misleadingly |
| The repository is the **wrong one** — keys landing on instance-local storage because the intended registration was not the one in force | **Nothing.** Whichever repository resolved logs an ordinary *success* record for the write it performed, so the healthy-looking case and the ephemeral-key case are indistinguishable from the log | **No** |
| The ring loads successfully at startup | `…DataProtectionHostedService` / `KeyRingWasLoadedOnStartup`, **`Debug`** | **No** — not at a production floor of `Information` |
| No XML encryptor is configured, so keys are stored without an envelope | `…XmlKeyManager` / `NoXMLEncryptorConfiguredKeyMayBePersistedToStorageInUnencryptedForm`, **`Warning`** | Yes — and it is **expected** here, not a defect: section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) records that an explicit repository disables automatic at-rest protection, and [06 §7.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) supplies it with transparent data encryption instead |
| A key **rotates**, or fails to rotate on schedule | **No record of either.** Rotation is a property of key ages, and the framework reports ages nowhere | **No** |
| A cookie cannot be decrypted | `…KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector` / `KeyWasNotFoundInTheKeyRingUnprotectOperationCannotProceed` is **`Trace`**; what actually surfaces is `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies.CookieAuthenticationHandler` / `AuthenticationSchemeNotAuthenticatedWithFailure` at **`Information`**, reading *"Cookies was not authenticated. Failure message: Unprotect ticket failed"* | Yes — through the **authentication** row. The key-management row does not carry it, which is why that row's text was corrected too |

**So the `KeyRingStatus` heartbeat is the sole assurance that key persistence and rotation are working**,
and that is the reason it is a registration in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 15 rather than a remark somewhere: three of the
eight states above produce **no record at all**, a fourth produces a misleading one, and two of the silent
three — a ring persisted to the wrong place, and rotation that has quietly stopped — are exactly the states
an alert has to catch. The heartbeat's fields are chosen to make each of them visible positively: the
repository type actually in use answers the wrong-repository row, and the newest key's age answers the
rotation row. [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the alerting built on it, which is an
alert on the record's **absence** — sound only because the application emits the record unconditionally.
Nothing in this table is a substitute for it, and no level in the table above can be raised to produce one.

**The production values live in the base file, not in a `Production` overlay.** `appsettings.json` carries
the deployed levels and `appsettings.Development.json` relaxes three of them, so a staging slot and
production get the same levels without a third file to keep in step, and no environment can end up
*more* verbose than production by omission. `appsettings.Production.json` is not created — the file set is
the two files this section ends by scoping, and the rule is stated once, in full, where that scoping is.

**It is validated at start, and the validation deliberately does no filtering.** `LoggingPolicyOptions`
binds the same `Logging:LogLevel` section as a `Dictionary<string, LogLevel?>` and asserts five things
under `ValidateOnStart`, then is never read again:

1. **Every one of the nine keys above is present.** A missing key is not a missing value — it is a
   category that silently falls back to `Default`, which for the four `Information` rows means being
   filtered by the `Microsoft.AspNetCore` `Warning` rule instead.
2. **No key is `None`.** A silenced category is an unobservable failure, and the two most tempting to
   silence are the two whose failures are otherwise invisible
   ([06 §9.2.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)).
3. **No key is more restrictive than the value above.** The values are *floors* in that direction: a
   category may not be made quieter than the table, and validation says so rather than trusting a review.
4. **Outside Development, no key may be more verbose than the value above either — the table is
   *exact*, not a minimum.** This is stricter than an earlier version of this list, which made every
   value a minimum and permitted a deployment to relax any category upward, and the relaxation it
   permitted was not hypothetical: raising
   `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` from `Warning` to **`Information`** in a deployed
   environment emits command text **and parameter values** — order rows, addresses, email addresses — into
   a store [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) retains for 90 days, which is CWE-532 performed
   by a configuration edit that no code review sees. A separate check for `Trace` and `Debug` is therefore
   redundant and is folded into this one: outside Development **no** deviation upward is legal, at any
   level, for any category. Development alone may be more verbose, because the three relaxations it needs
   are declared in the table's own override column and no other value may be changed there either.
5. **`Logging:LogLevel` contains no key that is not in the table.** An unlisted category is how a
   relaxation arrives without touching a listed value — `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` at `Information`
   would raise the command category by prefix under the longest-match rule above, without the command
   category's own key changing at all. So the section is a closed set, and adding a category means editing
   this table.

A failure names the key and the two levels — or, for check 5, the unlisted key — and it echoes no log
content, because none has been written yet.

**The levels decide what is written. They do not decide whether it arrives as a record or as a sentence —
and on one of the two hosting targets that difference decides whether the fields are queryable at all.**
[06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) routes the container path's `stdout` and `stderr` to a
Log Analytics workspace, where each line arrives as a **text field**. The default console formatter writes
`Information: MvcMusicStore.Services.ShoppingCartService[0] Order 1043 placed…` — a human sentence, from
which `orderId` is recoverable only by a regular expression that breaks the next time the message template
is edited. So the emission format is part of this contract:

**`AddJsonConsole` is the console formatter, configured explicitly.** Registered as
`builder.Logging.AddJsonConsole(o => { … })`, replacing the default `simple` formatter rather than
supplementing it, so exactly one representation leaves the process:

| `JsonConsoleFormatterOptions` member | Value | Why this value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `JsonWriterOptions.Indented` | **`false`** | **The one option that cannot be wrong.** The formatter writes the object through a `Utf8JsonWriter` constructed with `FormatterOptions.JsonWriterOptions` and then writes a single `Environment.NewLine` (`JsonConsoleFormatter.Write`, .NET 8 source), so indented output would span many lines and the collector would ingest each **line** as a separate record — turning one event into a dozen unparseable fragments |
| `IncludeScopes` | **`true`** | Scopes are written only when it is set: `WriteScopeInformation` begins `if (FormatterOptions.IncludeScopes && scopeProvider != null)` and then emits a `Scopes` array of objects carrying each scope's key/value pairs (same source). This is what carries the hosting scope's request identifier and path onto every record written during a request, without any call site having to pass them |
| `TimestampFormat` | **`"O"`** — the round-trip format | The formatter writes a `Timestamp` property **only if `TimestampFormat` is non-null**, and its default is null (same source), so the default output has no timestamp of its own and relies entirely on the collector's ingestion time. `"O"` is unambiguous and sorts lexically |
| `UseUtcTimestamp` | **`true`** | The formatter chooses `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` over `.Now` on exactly this flag (same source). A container's local time zone is not a fact worth depending on |

**What the record actually contains — stated as the literal payload, because every field this contract
promises has to be reachable from the far end and three of them are not where a reader would expect.**
The record below is a **captured record** from the pinned runtime with exactly the four options above set,
emitted from inside a request; only the identifier values and the request path are substituted for this
document's checkout example. It is shown indented for readability — on the wire it is **one line**, which
is what the `Indented` row above is for.

```json
{
  "Timestamp": "2026-08-29T14:24:00.0391819+00:00",
  "EventId": 0,
  "LogLevel": "Information",
  "Category": "MvcMusicStore.Services.ShoppingCartService",
  "Message": "OrderPlaced: order 1043, trace b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
  "State": {
    "Message": "OrderPlaced: order 1043, trace b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
    "eventName": "OrderPlaced",
    "orderId": 1043,
    "traceId": "b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
    "{OriginalFormat}": "{eventName}: order {orderId}, trace {traceId}"
  },
  "Scopes": [
    {
      "Message": "SpanId:2ce2035e27690aef, TraceId:b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840, ParentId:f5878ff76295d93b",
      "SpanId": "2ce2035e27690aef",
      "TraceId": "b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
      "ParentId": "f5878ff76295d93b"
    },
    { "Message": "ConnectionId:0HNO5R4LID6IK", "ConnectionId": "0HNO5R4LID6IK" },
    {
      "Message": "RequestPath:/Checkout/AddressAndPayment RequestId:0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001",
      "RequestId": "0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001",
      "RequestPath": "/Checkout/AddressAndPayment"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Property | Where it is | What writes it, and what a query has to do with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Timestamp` | Top level | The formatter, **only because `TimestampFormat` is set** — its default is null and the property is then absent altogether (row 3 above). Read directly |
| `EventId` | Top level, **a number** | The formatter, from `logEntry.EventId.Id`. It is **`0` on every record whose call site passes no event id**, which is every record in this application, so it is **not a discriminator** and nothing may key on it |
| `LogLevel`, `Category`, `Message` | Top level, strings | The formatter. `Message` is the **formatted** text, so it is human-readable and not a field set. Read directly; filter on `Category` and `LogLevel`, never parse `Message` |
| `Exception` | Top level, **a string**, present only where an exception was passed | The formatter, from `exception.ToString()` — type, message, inner exceptions and stack trace in **one escaped string**, not a structured object. A query reading `Exception.Message` or `Exception.Type` finds nothing; and because the whole `ToString()` lands in the sink, the exclusion list of [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) applies to exception **messages** as much as to log messages |
| `State` | **Nested object** | The formatter, from the log state: the formatted `Message`, **one property per named placeholder in the message template**, and `{OriginalFormat}` carrying the template itself. **Every field this application contributes is here and nowhere else** |
| `Scopes` | **Array of objects**, present only because `IncludeScopes` is `true` | The framework, not the application — three of them inside a request: an **activity** scope carrying `TraceId`, `SpanId` and `ParentId` (the logging libraries "implicitly create a scope object with `SpanId`, `TraceId`, and `ParentId`", enabled by default through `ActivityTrackingOptions` — *Logging in .NET Core and ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8); Kestrel's `ConnectionId` scope; and the hosting scope carrying `RequestPath` and `RequestId`. A query reaches these only by indexing into the array |

**Three fields a query will look for at the top level and not find — and each one fails by matching
nothing rather than by erroring, which is why this is stated as a shape rather than left to discovery.**

- **`EventId.Name`.** The formatter writes the numeric id only, so a *named* `EventId` puts the name
  nowhere in the payload — verified by emitting `new EventId(4711, "OrderPlacedNamedEventId")` and reading
  back `"EventId": 4711` with the name absent.
- **A top-level `eventName`.** It is a message-template property, so it is at **`State.eventName`**.
- **A top-level `TraceId` or `SpanId`.** Both exist only **inside a `Scopes` element**, and only under two
  conditions: `IncludeScopes` is on, and an `Activity` exists. **A record written outside a request has
  `"Scopes": []`** — verified from a background service, which is exactly where the key-ring heartbeat of
  section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 writes from, so a heartbeat record carries
  no framework-supplied correlation field at all.

**So the rule is one line, and it is the reason every event in this document is specified the way it is:
every field the application contributes is a named log-state property, and it is read from `State`.** That
covers `eventName`, the correlation identifier, and each record's own properties — the audit record of
section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4, the checkout
failure of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), the residual-failure records of
section [4.10.2](#4102-what-retries-do-not-fix), the readiness failures of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract), the key-ring heartbeat
and the transition record of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), and the record of section
[7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half). The event **names**
themselves are [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s.

**The correlation identifier, defined once, because two different values answer to the name "trace
identifier" and they are not interchangeable.** `traceId` carries **`Activity.Current.TraceId`** — the
W3C 32-hex trace id [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires — falling back to
`HttpContext.TraceIdentifier` only where no activity exists, which is a **different shape** entirely
(`0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001`, the connection id and request number, and the value the hosting scope reports
as `RequestId`). Two consequences are load-bearing. The value section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) renders into the error view is **this same value**, so
the identifier a user quotes is the one that finds their record — a view showing `TraceIdentifier` while
the log carried the W3C id would be a support path that never resolves. And each record carries `traceId`
in its **own state** rather than relying on the activity scope, because the scope is absent from every
background and startup record and depends on `IncludeScopes` remaining on.

**Two fields the application deliberately does not contribute, so that the query reads them from the one
place that cannot drift.** [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires the `environment` and
the **slot or revision** on every record and names their source as platform configuration plus the
platform's own enrichment — and that is where they stay. Neither is emitted as a log-state property:
`Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` has no enricher concept, so a fixed per-instance field can reach `State`
only by every call site passing it, and a value repeated at hundreds of call sites is a value that will
disagree with itself. Both are already carried **beside** the record by the collection path — the resource
and host columns of `AppServiceConsoleLogs`, the container-app and revision columns of
`ContainerAppConsoleLogs` — which is a platform fact rather than an application claim, and is the same in
every record whether the application was involved or not.

**And one field that no operational record carries at all: the customer's identity.** This is a standing
rule rather than a property of one event, because the exposure it prevents accumulates rather than
announcing itself — a login name written into a record is a login name in a general-purpose log store that
[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) retains for **90 days** and that every principal with
workspace access can read, which is CWE-532, *Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File*. So **no
record on the ordinary operational stream carries a customer's login name, email address or any other
direct identifier** — not the checkout records, not the cart records, not the error record of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), and not the collector record of section
[7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half). The captured payload above is
the concrete instance: the checkout record carries `orderId` and `traceId` and nothing that names the
person who placed the order.

- **Where a record does have to be attributable to a customer, it carries `cartKeyHash`** — the salted,
  truncated pseudonym [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines, keyed by the
  `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt` entry earlier in this section. For a signed-in visitor the cart key **is**
  the login name, so the hash is a stable per-customer pseudonym that supports the operations an
  investigation actually needs — group one visitor's records together, count how many visitors a fault
  reached — without carrying the name itself. It is also why that entry is a required per-environment
  secret: an unsalted hash over a domain this small is reversible by exhaustion, and one salt shared
  across environments would let a non-production pseudonym identify a production customer.
- **So the checkout record and the cart records are consistent by construction rather than by
  coincidence**, and stating it is the point: they use **one** mechanism, defined once here and once in
  [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), so neither can be hardened without the other
  following. An earlier version of this document interpolated the login name into the checkout record
  while the cart events beside it hashed the same value — the two-authors failure this rule closes.
- **The one exception is a different record on a different path, and naming it is what keeps the rule
  absolute.** The provisioning audit record of section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 carries the
  **target username in clear**, because a record whose entire purpose is to state which account was
  granted an administrator role is useless pseudonymized. It is not an operational record: it is written
  by a one-shot process that never reaches the console channel at all, and its destination is the
  append-only container under a 365-day immutability policy that
  [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns. An administrator account name is an
  administrative fact with a purpose-built home; a customer name is neither, which is why the two live in
  different places deliberately.

**Four prohibitions, because "no PII or secrets in retained telemetry" is a promise and the rules above
are not yet enough to keep it.** [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the exclusion
*list* — what must never reach the sink — and closes with the honest admission that its enforcement is a
review task. A review is not a control, so the four items below are the mechanisms that make the same list
hold without one, and each names the concrete channel it closes.

| # | Prohibition | The channel it closes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **`EnableSensitiveDataLogging` is not called on either `DbContext`, in any environment — including Development.** It is not a Development convenience with a production guard; it is absent from the codebase, so there is no call for an environment condition to get wrong | The option "enable[s] application data to be included in exception messages, and logging" (*DbContextOptionsBuilder.EnableSensitiveDataLogging*, EF Core), which puts parameter values into **both** the command category *and* the message of any provider exception — and an exception message travels through the framework's own unhandled-exception record, where no log-level setting reaches it. Development is included because a developer's connection is to a database that, per section [5.1.1](#511-the-extract-is-pii--how-it-is-held-and-how-it-is-destroyed), can be holding a copy of production PII |
| 2 | **`EnableDetailedErrors` is called only when the environment is Development**, on the same `IsDevelopment()` condition the developer exception page uses (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) — never on a negated Production test | It adds field-level detail to data-reading exceptions, which is a disclosure channel of exactly the shape item 1 closes, and it is the option most often reached for as a substitute once item 1 is forbidden |
| 3 | **No category may be relaxed outside Development, and the category set is closed** — checks 4 and 5 of the validator above, enforced at start | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` at `Information` in a deployed environment, which [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) itself calls "the single largest route by which order data would otherwise arrive in a log store" |
| 4 | **No value the application controls is ever placed in a URL's query string** — not a token, not an identifier of a person, not a cart key, not a configuration value. The application's own query parameters are exactly **three**, enumerated so the rule is checkable rather than aspirational: the error path's `?code={0}` (a status code), `?ReturnUrl=` (a local path, validated as local), and `/Store/Browse?genre=` (a genre name from the catalog's own closed set of fifteen — no person, no secret, and the same value the path of any other route would have carried) | **The platform's HTTP log, which no application setting filters.** `AppServiceHTTPLogs` retains the request query, the referrer and the client address for the 90 days [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) sets, and the auto-instrumented request telemetry retains the URL. Neither passes through `ILogger`, so the only application-side control over them is what the application puts in a URL in the first place. This is the reason the cart's remove call posts its token in a **header** and its id in a **body** (section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)) rather than in a query string |

**What the exception record carries, which is not `exception.ToString()`.** The field table above records
that the formatter writes the whole of `ToString()` — type, message, inner exceptions and stack — into one
string. That is the formatter's behaviour and this document does not replace the formatter, so the control
is on **what is passed to it**:

- **A record the application writes passes no exception object.** It carries three named log-state
  properties instead: **`exceptionType`** (the full type name), **`exceptionStack`**
  (`Exception.StackTrace`, which is the frames of the call stack — method names, and file names and line
  numbers where symbols are present — and carries **no argument values**), and
  **`innerExceptionTypes`** (the chain as an array of type names). The `Exception` top-level property is
  therefore **absent** from every application-written record, and a query for it finds only framework
  records.
- **`Exception.Message` is deliberately the one part left out.** It is the only component of `ToString()`
  that can embed a value — a provider's constraint or parameter text, a validator's rejected input, a
  formatter's argument — and it is the component with the least diagnostic value once the type and the
  stack are present. Where a specific condition genuinely needs describing, it is described by the
  record's own **message template and named properties**, which the field rules above already govern,
  rather than by quoting an exception.
- **The application never throws or wraps an exception whose message embeds request data, a row value or
  a configuration value.** This is the rule that bounds the one channel the two rules above do not reach:
  the framework's own unhandled-exception record, written by the exception-handler middleware, which does
  pass the exception and therefore does emit `ToString()`. With prohibition 1 in force the provider
  cannot put values there either, so what remains in that string is a type, a framework message and a
  stack.
- **`exception.ToString()` is never interpolated into a log message, a view, a response body or a
  header.** Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) already forbids the response half;
  this states the log half, and it is the reason `IExceptionHandlerPathFeature`'s exception is read for
  the record's **type and stack** rather than for its text.

**The fields the application must never place in a record, stated as a list it can be tested against.**
[06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s list is the authority and is not restated; what belongs
here is the application-side form of it, because a rule expressed as "no PII" cannot be asserted and a
named field can. No log-state property, message template argument, scope value or exception field written
by this application carries: a **password**, its hash, or any credential; **any part of a connection
string**; **any configuration value** from the contract in this section; **any cookie value** — the
authentication, session and anti-forgery cookies are all bearer credentials; an **anti-forgery token**;
the **`Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`**; the **raw** cart key or session id, which reach a record only as
`cartKeyHash`; a customer's **login name, email address, full name, postal address or phone number**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]; a **promo code**; or a **request body** or **query
string** in raw form. The one deliberate exception is the provisioning audit record's target username,
which is not written to this channel at all — section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 owns it and its
destination.

**The canary test, because every rule above is only as good as the evidence that it holds.** Coverage row
47 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) plants **two** distinguishable literals — a known secret
value in a configuration member and a known PII value in a seeded order row — then drives the paths that
have historically leaked them: a failed sign-in, a checkout that throws, an unhandled exception in an
action, a deliberate provider failure that produces an exception carrying command context, a readiness
failure, and a request whose route data is malformed. It then asserts that **neither literal appears
anywhere in the captured `stdout` stream** — not in `Message`, not in any `State` property, not in
`Exception`, and not in any `Scopes` element — by searching the raw captured text rather than by inspecting
parsed fields, so a value that arrives inside an unexpected property still fails the row. It is a **canary
rather than a proof**: it demonstrates that the paths it drives are clean, and prohibitions 1 to 4 are what
make that generalize.

**What this half cannot close, and whose it is.** Three retained channels take nothing from `ILogger` and
are unreachable from application code without the in-process telemetry SDK
[04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s pin list deliberately excludes: the platform **HTTP log**'s
query, cookie, referrer, client-address and user fields; the **auto-instrumented** request, dependency and
exception telemetry's URLs, identities and raw exception detail; and the platform's own audit and platform
logs. Prohibition 4 is the whole of what this document can do about the first of them.
**[06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
own the platform-side half** — whether those columns are dropped, redacted or accepted with their
retention stated — and this document states the requirement it places on them: **a field this section
forbids in a record must not be retained beside the record either**, or the exclusion list holds only for
the channel that was easiest to control.

**Where this meets the other document, stated plainly because the two halves have to agree for a single
alert to fire.** [06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the workspace-side extraction — the
parse expression, and the **query-time workspace functions** that project these fields into a normalized
shape. It is deliberately not an ingestion-time transformation: a transformation's output has to match the
built-in table's own predefined schema, so it cannot add columns of its own, and a design that assumed it
could would have produced queries against columns that never appear. Separately,
[06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the event names and the required field set. This
document owns the shape above. The consequence for the query is not a preference: a predicate or a
projection keyed on **`EventId.Name`, on a top-level `eventName`, or on a top-level `TraceId` or
`SpanId`** matches **no record this application emits**, and a filter built from two such tests matches
nothing at all. The fields are at `State.eventName`, `State.traceId` and each record's own `State.*`
properties, with `Scopes` as the framework-supplied fallback for the activity identifiers on
request-scoped records only.

**And one consequence for the operator tool.** Every verb of `provision-admin` — the four of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — runs as a one-shot process
outside App Service, so **nothing auto-instruments it**: its records leave through `stdout`
in exactly the format above and nowhere else. It therefore registers the same formatter with the same
options — it is the one logging decision it shares with the web application — and where its output has
to reach a durable destination, the route is
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, which this document cites rather than designs.

**`Kestrel` — Development only, and it is in this contract solely so that its absence from every deployed
environment is a stated fact rather than an accident.**

| Key | Type | Value | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Kestrel:Endpoints:Http:Url` | `string`, an absolute URL | [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s | `appsettings.Development.json` only |
| `Kestrel:Endpoints:Https:Url` | `string`, an absolute URL | [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s | `appsettings.Development.json` only |

Three properties make this safe to state briefly. **The keys exist only in the Development overlay**, so
no deployed environment loads them — a deployed instance's listening address comes from the platform
([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the container port contract), and a `Kestrel`
section in the base file would fight it. **No `Certificates` section accompanies them**: an endpoint that
names no certificate falls back to `Certificates:Default` or, absent that, to the development certificate
(*Configure endpoints for the ASP.NET Core Kestrel web server*, .NET 8) — the certificate's provisioning
is [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s prerequisite, not a key. And **they are the reason the
always-secure cookie policy above is testable locally**: the HTTPS endpoint is what makes a `Secure`
cookie reach a development browser, which is why the policy needs no development exemption.

**These two keys are also why `launchSettings.json` is not in this contract.** That file is a local
development artifact outside the target file map, and Kestrel reads its own configuration section
regardless of it, so declaring the endpoints here keeps the local HTTPS binding inside a committed file
the map does contain.

**Validation: `AddOptions<T>().Bind(section).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` on every options
type above, plus one `IValidateOptions<T>` per type.** The split between the two halves is not stylistic —
each half can express something the other cannot, and the mechanism paragraph above is why the first half
alone is not sufficient.

| Half | What it checks | Why it cannot be the other half's job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ValidateDataAnnotations()` over the **nullable** members | Presence, via `[Required]` on a member that is genuinely `null` when the key is absent; and a contained value's range, via `[Range]` on the nullable numeric members | It sees one member at a time and knows nothing about the environment or about another member's value |
| `IValidateOptions<T>` | Every rule that needs more than one member, a type `[Range]` does not cover, or the host: the `TimeSpan` bounds; `PersistentExpireTimeSpan <= ExpireTimeSpan`; the `SameSite` allowed-set; a leading `/` on each path; the five connection-string checks and the accepted-mode selection behind the third of them; `SqlIdentity:ClientId` equal to the connection's parsed `User Id`; `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator` equal to `DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator`; the two `Site` members' per-entry host and origin rules; `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`'s decoded length; the members required only outside `Development`; `AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` required when `Enabled` is true; `Enabled` true while the seeding invocation's expected environment is anything other than the non-production name it declares; and the standing `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` check on every string member | An attribute cannot read a sibling property, `IHostEnvironment`, or a parsed form of its own value |

`ValidateOnStart()` is what makes both halves run **before the first request** rather than at first
resolution of the options type ("Options validation runs the first time a `TOptions` instance is created…
To run options validation when the app starts, call `ValidateOnStart`" — *Options pattern in ASP.NET
Core*, .NET 8). Without it, a member that only the checkout path reads would be validated by the first
checkout.

**The rule, stated as a rule rather than as a list of examples: a setting is fail-fast when a wrong or
absent value produces behaviour the application cannot detect at runtime and a user cannot report.**
Every member marked required above meets it. Four consequences are worth naming because each has a
distinct failure signature:

- **`ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` absent** — without `ValidateOnStart` this surfaces as the
  first request to touch a database, which on a deployment with a warm health probe may be a real user's.
- **`DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator` absent** — never surfaces as an error at all. See above.
- **`Seeding:Enabled` true in Production** — surfaces as data loss, once.
- And **any `Identity` member absent** — surfaces as a silently weaker policy than the one section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) had approved.

`ValidateOnStart` is what converts all four from a runtime surprise into a failed start, which the
deployment gate and the health probe of [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) can both see
**before** traffic arrives. A validation failure names the section and the member; it does **not** echo
the value, because the value may be a connection string.

**Safe defaults and conditional requirements — the complete list, counted in one way rather than two.**
An earlier version of this block said "exactly three members are legal to omit unconditionally" and then
qualified one of the three with a condition in the same sentence, which is not a count anybody can check.
The exceptions are therefore sorted by **what the condition is**, and the total is stated once:

| Class | Members | The rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Legal to omit unconditionally** — three members | `Seeding:Enabled`; `Site:PermittedImageOrigins`; `Diagnostics:InstanceEndpointEnabled` | Each read as its fail-closed value: `false` for the first, the **empty** list for the second — no external image origin permitted at all, which is both the safe answer and the state [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records today — and `false` for the third, under which the route of section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint) is not mapped at all. These are the only three members in the contract where absence is a decision rather than an omission |
| **Legal to omit conditionally on another member** — one member | `Seeding:AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` | Legal to omit **only** while `Enabled` is `false`; absent with `Enabled` true fails validation |
| **Required conditionally on the environment** — four members | `Expected:SqlServer`, `Expected:SqlDatabase`, `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator`, `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt` | **Required in every environment that is not `Development` and is not the test fixture**, where each is legal to omit: those two have no environment-declared expectation to compare against and no need of a stable per-environment telemetry salt |
| **Required conditionally on the connection mode** — one member | `SqlIdentity:ClientId` | Required under **M1**, required to be **absent** under **M2** and **M4**, and neither required nor compared under **M3** — the mode table above states each case and why |

**Nine names in total**, and every condition among them is enforced by the type's single
`IValidateOptions<T>` rather than by an attribute, per the member-class rule earlier in this section.
`Antiforgery:HeaderName` is **not** on this list — it is unconditionally required, because a default that
has to match a client literal (section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script)) is a default that can
drift silently. **A conditional requirement is still fail-fast**: absent where its condition holds, each of
the **six** that carry a condition fails the start, while the **three** that carry none are read as their
fail-closed value instead — which is what makes the two classes worth separating rather than counting
together.

**Every other member of every type above has no default, and an absent key fails the start.** Enumerating
the exceptions rather than the rule is deliberate: a reader who wants to know whether a key may be omitted
looks in one place and finds nine names and the condition attached to each. One member defined **outside**
this section carries a default of its own and is counted where it is defined rather than here: the
operator-only `Load:BatchSize` of section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), which no web host binds.

**Precedence, explicitly and completely, because a secret arriving late is the whole mechanism — and
because an omitted provider is a silent override.** The two hosts do **not** have the same source list, and
the difference is a decision this section makes rather than an accident of how each builder is constructed:
the site is built with **`WebApplication.CreateBuilder()`**, parameterless, and
`tools/provision-admin` with `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args)` (section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)). So the site adds **four**
sources and the tool adds **five**, in this order, and **a later source wins**:

1. `appsettings.json` — committed. Non-secret, environment-independent values only.
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json` — committed. Environment-shaped non-secret values.
3. **User secrets** — added **only when the resolved environment is `Development`**, and therefore
   present on a developer machine and in no deployed environment. It exists in this list because it is
   the mechanism that keeps a local credential *out of* the committed Development file, which the file
   scoping at the end of this section forbids from carrying one.
4. **Environment variables** — the layer the platform injects into, including an App Service application
   setting, a connection-string setting, and a **Key Vault reference** resolved by the site's managed
   identity ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)).
5. **Command-line arguments** — **the operator tool only**, added **last** and therefore **outranking
   every other source including the platform's own settings**. The framework documentation is explicit
   about the consequence: "Because the provider is used at the end, it has the highest priority", and
   "configuration values set on the command-line override configuration values set by all of the other
   configuration providers" (*Configuration in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). The tool's own arguments reach it
   through the **closed pre-parse** of section
   [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1b, which runs
   **before** the builder is constructed and rejects every token it does not recognise, so this
   highest-priority provider can contribute only the handful of keys that pre-parse names.

**The site does not have this provider at all, and that is the decision rather than a prohibition on
using it.** An earlier version of this section passed `args` to `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` and relied
on a written rule that nothing would use it. That is not a control: the provider outranks every platform
setting, so anything able to influence the site's command line — a release definition, a container
`command`/`args` override, a start-up script, a debugger profile — could have replaced the
platform-inventoried connection string, the data-protection discriminator, a log level, `Expected:*`, the
environment name or a Key Vault-backed setting, silently and from outside everything that inspects
configuration. Meanwhile the operator tool, which genuinely needs arguments, already has a hard
allow-list parser. The asymmetry is resolved in the direction that removes the channel:

| Host | Builder | Command-line provider | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The site | **`WebApplication.CreateBuilder()`**, no `args` | **Absent** | The builder adds the provider only when it is given a non-empty argument array, so passing nothing removes the provider itself rather than trusting a rule about it. The site needs no arguments: it is started by the platform, not by an operator |
| `tools/provision-admin` | `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args)` | **Present, behind the pre-parse** | A verb and a switch are the tool's whole interface. The pre-parse of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) is what bounds the provider's reach to the mapped keys |

**What the site gives up by not taking `args`, stated so the trade is checkable rather than asserted.**
Three things, and none of them is load-bearing:

- **`--environment` and `--urls` on the site's command line stop working.** Both have platform-native
  equivalents that this design already uses exclusively: `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` for the first
  ([06 §8.4.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) and the platform's own port contract for the second
  ([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), with the Development endpoints coming from the
  `Kestrel` keys above. No release step, container definition or committed file in this plan passes
  either switch.
- **Ad-hoc local overrides on `dotnet run` stop working.** A developer overrides through user secrets or
  `appsettings.Development.json`, which are sources 2 and 3 — reviewable, and the same two a colleague
  reads.
- **Nothing in the test fixture is affected.** `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>` invokes the
  application's entry point **without supplying arguments of its own** and configures the host through
  `ConfigureWebHost`, which is where the in-memory source named at the end of this list is added
  (*Integration tests in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). So the fixture of section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) neither passes nor needs a switch, and an
  earlier claim here that it relied on `dotnet test` argument plumbing was simply wrong: arguments given
  to `dotnet test` reach the test runner, not the application under test.

**The prohibition that remains is narrower and still necessary, because the tool keeps its provider.**
Two things are forbidden:

- **(a) Any secret on the command line, by any process, in any environment.** An argument is visible in
  process listings and recorded in shell and pipeline history — the separate and stronger argument of
  section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1.
- **(b) Any configuration override to the operator tool on a release invocation** — not the connection
  string, not the discriminator, not a log level, not a seeding flag. Configuration reaches it through
  invocation-scoped environment variables ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), and section
  [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) for the two migration channels) and
  through nothing else. The tool's pre-parse enforces this by construction: the only keys its switch
  mapping can produce are the two non-configuration ones named there.
- The reason is not that the channel is weaker in principle but that it is **invisible to the platform's
  own record of configuration**: a value overridden on the command line does not appear in the site's
  application settings, so [06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s pre-traffic assertion and
  every audit of "what is this environment configured with" would both read the wrong answer while the
  process used another. An override that no reviewer can see is the failure mode, and its severity is
  exactly the same whether the value is a secret or a log level. Removing the provider from the site is
  the same argument carried to its conclusion.
- **The two pinned release tools take a credential-free target connection as an argument, and that is
  not an exception being tolerated — it is the only channel either of them has.** A migration bundle
  accepts `--connection`, and omitting it makes the connection compiled into the context decide which
  database receives DDL; `dotnet sql-cache create` takes the connection as its **first positional
  argument** and accepts configuration by no other route at all. Neither is an application host and
  neither reads this contract, so clause (b) above does not reach them — and a rule written as "no
  command line, ever" would have been a rule those two commands cannot obey, which is how a policy stops
  being applied to the host it should bind. What makes the argument safe rather than merely unavoidable
  is four properties [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) states and this document does not
  restate: the value is a declared pipeline variable, it carries no credential because it authenticates
  as a managed identity, it is never echoed into a log or a failure message, and the server and database
  it names are asserted against the expected values before it is used. The invocations themselves are
  [06 §6.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, under the artifact contract of
  [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md).
- **The operator tool's own verb and non-configuration switches are exempt because they are not
  configuration values** — a verb selects which operation runs and `--batch` sizes a loop. Section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) states the closed pre-parse
  that accepts exactly those and rejects everything else, and the namespaced switch mapping that keeps
  the two that *do* become configuration from colliding with any key in this contract.

An **in-memory** source is added after every source above, but only inside the test host — section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) owns it. In the site's list, where there is no
command-line provider, it is the only layer above the environment variables; in the tool's, it is the only
layer that would outrank the command line, and the tool is never run under the test host anyway.

**A nested key arrives from the environment in double-underscore form**: `ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection`,
`DataProtection__ApplicationDiscriminator`, `Identity__PasswordMinimumLength`. The colon separator is not
a legal environment-variable name character on every platform the application will run on, so the
double underscore is the portable form — and it is how both the platform and a one-shot migration or
provisioning invocation supply a nested value without a file. **This is why a Key Vault reference
surfaced as an application setting outranks the committed JSON**: it arrives at layer 4 and the JSON is
layers 1 and 2.

**Precedence is a safety net here, not the mechanism, and the difference matters.** The committed files
contain **no secret and no connection string for any deployed environment**, so in a deployed
