environment there is nothing at a lower layer for the platform's value to override. A design that
relied on ordering to shadow a committed secret would still have committed the secret.

**The administrator credential is not in this contract at all.** Section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) records that the
correct target for the two `appSettings` reads
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24] is *nothing*, and this is where that carries
through: **there is no key, no section, no options member and no member of any type above that holds an
administrator username or password.** The provisioning secret reaches
`tools/provision-admin` through a single-invocation environment variable or an echo-disabled prompt —
section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) owns that channel — and
it appears in no `appsettings` file, in no App Service setting on the web application, and in no options
type. A compromised web process has nothing to read.

**`appsettings.Development.json`, scoped explicitly, because "the developer file" is where secrets
accumulate.**

| May contain | Must never contain |
| --- | --- |
| A **local** connection string carrying no credential — a local instance reached by integrated security, or a container whose credentials arrive through the environment rather than the file | Any secret, any credential, any Key Vault reference value |
| Raised log levels for local diagnosis — the three `Logging:LogLevel` overrides stated above, and no others | Any connection string reaching a deployed database |
| Local values for the `Identity`, `Authentication:Cookie` and `Session` members where a developer needs them to differ | `Seeding:Enabled` — seeding authorization is supplied **per invocation** through the environment, which is check 2 of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks); a committed `true` would authorize every process that believes it is in Development, against whatever database it is pointed at |
| The two `Kestrel:Endpoints` URLs stated above, which exist in this file and nowhere else | `DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator` for any deployed environment |
| Nothing else | A `Kestrel` section in `appsettings.json`, which would bind an endpoint in every deployed environment and fight the platform's own port ([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) |

The file is **committed**, so its content is reviewed like any other source. A developer value that
cannot be committed is not a Development override — it is a secret, and it belongs in the environment of
that developer's own session.

**The file set is exactly two files, and there is no `appsettings.Production.json`.** This is the closing
rule of the section rather than an aside, because it is a fact another deliverable has to be able to rely
on: [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s third rule states that **no command or release step
may require a `Production` overlay**, and cites this section as the place the absence is decided. So it is
decided here, unambiguously and in one direction:

- **`appsettings.json`** and **`appsettings.Development.json`** are the only two files in the set. No
  `appsettings.Production.json`, no `appsettings.Staging.json`, and no per-slot variant — matching
  [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map, which carries those two names and no third.
- **The deployed levels and defaults live in the base file**, which is what makes the absence safe rather
  than an omission: every deployed environment reads `appsettings.json` and gets the production shape,
  and the Development overlay is the only file that relaxes anything.
- **Deployed *values* arrive from platform configuration** ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md))
  at layer 4 of the precedence list below, which is why no file is needed to carry them and why one would
  be a second place for a reviewer to look.
- **Nothing may be built, promoted, copied or asserted on the assumption that such a file exists.** A
  release step that placed one beside an artifact would be placing a file the map does not contain, and a
  step that read one would be reading a source no environment has. The consequence for a generated
  migration artifact specifically — that none of them carries an `appsettings*.json` beside it — is
  [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, for a different reason, and the two rules agree.

---

## 4. Dependency injection and object lifetime

### 4.1 The ten manual instantiation sites constructor injection replaces

Ten sites in the migration source construct a `DbContext` or an Identity manager by hand. They are
enumerated individually because they are not all the same shape and two of them are not in a
controller at all.

| # | Site | What is constructed | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19] | `new UserManager<ApplicationUser>(new UserStore<ApplicationUser>(new ApplicationDbContext()))` — a chained constructor building the entire Identity graph, three objects deep | The chained constructor is deleted; `UserManager` and `SignInManager` are injected. The second, parameter-taking constructor already at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:23-26] is the shape that survives |
| 2 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32] | `new MusicStoreEntities()` — one ad hoc catalog context **inside a method body**, in `MigrateShoppingCart` | Injected catalog context, or the injected `ShoppingCartService` that supersedes this method's body (section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)) |
| 3 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:15] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 4 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:12] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 5 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:10] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 6 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:11] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 7 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:11] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 8 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27] | `new ApplicationDbContext()` at startup | **Leaves the web application.** Resolved from the console tool's host — section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) |
| 9 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:28] | `new UserManager<ApplicationUser>(new UserStore<ApplicationUser>(context))` at startup | As above |
| 10 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:29] | `new RoleManager<IdentityRole>(new RoleStore<IdentityRole>(context))` at startup | As above |

**`AccountController` is the exception in this list, and describing it as "the sixth controller with a
field-initialized context" is wrong.** It has **no** field-initialized catalog context. It holds an
`ApplicationDbContext` only *indirectly*, through the `UserManager` its chained constructor builds
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19], and it creates exactly **one** `MusicStoreEntities` on demand, inside `MigrateShoppingCart`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32]. So dependency injection does two different things to this file: it replaces that single ad hoc
catalog context, and it replaces the hand-built Identity graph with injected managers. The Identity
context remains a **separate registration** either way — it is not folded into the catalog context.

The file also already has the constructor injection needs: `public AccountController(UserManager<ApplicationUser> userManager)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:23-26] exists today and is unused by the framework, because MVC 5 resolves the parameterless one.
The port keeps that shape and deletes the parameterless overload.

### 4.2 What scoped registration actually changes — and what it does not

**Scoped registration gives one instance per context type per request, not one instance overall.**
That sentence is the whole of this section, and it is here because the opposite reading produces a plan
that quietly assumes atomicity it will not have.

After the port there are still **two `DbContext` instances per request** and therefore **two change
trackers** — one for `MusicStoreEntities`, one for `ApplicationDbContext` — and **no automatic unit of
work spanning them**. A `SaveChanges` on one does not enlist the other.

What scoped registration removes is narrower and worth having:

- the hand-rolled construction at all ten sites in section [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces);
- the ad hoc mid-method instance at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32],
  which today means a *second* catalog context exists inside a request that already has none of its
  own — the account controller has no field context, so this instance is created, used and abandoned;
- the consumer-side disposal that becomes wrong (section [4.7](#47-the-dispose-overrides-must-be-removed));
- and the inconsistency where one controller's context is disposed and four others' are not
  ([08 §5.8](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns that as debt).

What it does **not** remove is the two-store boundary. That boundary is a design decision, taken
deliberately in section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), and the
consistency model that makes it safe is section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

### 4.3 The cross-store consistency model

Sign-in writes to the Identity store; cart reassignment writes to the catalog store. And **a database
transaction cannot make an authentication cookie atomic with either of them**, because the cookie is
issued in the HTTP response, outside any transaction and outside the database entirely. So the
ordering has to be designed rather than inherited.

**The current order is the reverse of the safe one, which is the evidence that this needs deciding.**
`SignInAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:346-354] signs out the external
cookie [:348], creates the identity [:349], **registers the sign-in grant** [:350], and only **then**
migrates the cart [:353]. `MigrateShoppingCart` [:30-40] creates its own context [:32], reassigns
ownership through `MigrateCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193], calls
`SaveChanges` [:37] and rewrites the session key [:39]. The action that calls it
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] has no `try`/`catch`, so a failure in the
cart write propagates out of a method that has already granted the sign-in.

**The target sequence, with the API named at each step.** This is the `Login` POST handler in order;
nothing here is optional and the order is the contract.

| Step | Call | What it must and must not do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(model);` | Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:58] |
| 2 | `var user = await userManager.FindByNameAsync(model.UserName);` | A null result takes the **same** failure branch as a wrong password (section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)), so nothing discloses whether the account exists. **A null `user` must not be passed on to step 3** — `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` throws `ArgumentNullException` on a null user, which would make the uniform failure path unreachable for exactly the case it exists for, and answer 500 instead. The null case is handled by step 2a and step 3 is skipped |
| 2a | **Null user only:** `await uniformCost.SpendFullCostAsync(cancellationToken);` — nothing is returned to inspect — then the failure branch of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) | **Fixed work, not an early return.** An early `return View(model)` here is functionally correct and a username-enumeration oracle: it skips the key-derivation function entirely, so an unknown account answers in a fraction of the time a real verification takes and the response time discloses which usernames exist. This step spends **the target derivation cost defined below** so that the unknown-account path costs what the most expensive real path costs. The service is described immediately after this table, because getting it right is not a one-liner: "hash a fixed dummy value" is **not** equivalent work across this application's account population, and the obvious implementation of it does not compile |
| 3 | **Non-null user only:** `var result = await signInManager.CheckPasswordSignInAsync(user, model.Password, lockoutOnFailure: true);` **then, unconditionally, `await uniformCost.TopUpAsync(user.PasswordHash, derivationObservation, cancellationToken);`** — where `derivationObservation` is the scoped observation the hasher decorator below populates, and **never** a flag inferred from `result` | **This is the step that must not issue a cookie, and it is why `PasswordSignInAsync` is not used here.** `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` verifies the password, applies the lockout accounting the policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) enables, and — where the stored hash is in the older format — rehashes and updates the user through `UserManager`. Those are **Identity-store writes, and they are complete when this call returns.** `result.Succeeded == false` takes the failure branch of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **The top-up is what makes this path cost the same as step 2a**: a locked-out account is rejected *before* any derivation and an older-format hash is derived far more cheaply than a current-format one, so both would otherwise answer measurably faster than an ordinary wrong password |
| 4 | `await cartService.MigrateCartAsync(anonymousCartId, user.UserName, cancellationToken)` — **in its own transaction**, in the catalog store, and **only when the session's current cart key passes the three-part provenance test of the isolation rule below** | **Gated, idempotent and keyed on the anonymous cart id, and the gate is a provenance test rather than a shape test.** The value passed as `anonymousCartId` is the session's current key **only if all three of these hold**: it begins with the `anon:` namespace prefix; its remainder is exactly the 32-character lower-case hexadecimal form the issuing service writes; and the session additionally holds the **protected marker** that binds *that* key to *this* session and unprotects to a match. Where **any** of the three fails the step is **skipped, not performed**. **`Guid.TryParse` is explicitly not the gate**, and an earlier form of this row made it one: a shape test is wrong in *both* directions — it rejects every key the target actually issues, because `anon:`-prefixed values do not parse as GUIDs, and it admits the cart of an account whose user name happens to be GUID-shaped. The coverage assertions exist to fail exactly those two mistakes. The write itself is "reassign the rows whose cart id is *this* anonymous id", so a retry finds no rows and cannot double-assign. Retry behaviour is specified in full below rather than as a number. It preserves the source's merge semantics — `MigrateCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193] reassigns rows without combining duplicates of the same album, and this port does not change that |
| 5 | **On success only:** `cartService.AssignSessionCartId(user.UserName)` — an explicit service method that writes the session slot through `IHttpContextAccessor`, so the controller still touches no session directly (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)) | **Omitting this step is a silent, total cart loss, and it is not obvious from reading the migration alone.** `GetCartId` writes the session slot **only when it is empty** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176] and otherwise returns whatever is already there [:179] — so an anonymous visitor's GUID stays in session for the life of that session even after they sign in. With the rows now carrying the username and the session still naming the GUID, **every subsequent cart read returns nothing and the cart renders empty.** The source does this write explicitly at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39] and the port must too |
| 6 | `await signInManager.SignInAsync(user, model.RememberMe);` | **Last.** This is the only step that issues the authentication cookie, and it goes through `SignInManager` rather than `HttpContext.SignInAsync` for the scheme reason in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). If it throws, the handler calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` — undoing step 5, and **only** step 5 — and returns the generic failure, so a session can never name a username while unauthenticated. It does **not** reverse step 4's database write, and it is not meant to: see the invariants below |
| 7 | `if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(returnUrl) && Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)) { return Redirect(returnUrl); } return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");` — the one redirect rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) | Preserves the source's `RedirectToLocal` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:382-392] statement for statement: the same `Url.IsLocalUrl` test [:384] and the same home-page fallback [:390]. **`LocalRedirect(returnUrl)` is deliberately not used**, for the reason in section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **This step also writes the recovery notice** when the recovery cookie of step 4's failure branch is present on the request, which is what re-offers `RecoverCart` to a user who did not take the offer the first time |

**Uniform verification cost — a fixed-work service, not a dummy hash.** The tempting design here is a
`static readonly DummyPasswordHash` field, hashed once at startup, verified against on the unknown-user
path. It fails on two counts, one of them mechanical.

- **It does not compile as described.** A `static readonly` field cannot be initialized from an injected
  instance — `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` is registered per scope by the Identity call of stage 1
  item 3 (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), and a static field initializer has no
  access to any scope. Making the field non-static per controller would recompute a key derivation on
  **every** request that constructs the controller, which is a self-inflicted denial of service on the
  sign-in page.
- **Its constant-work claim is false across this application's population**, which is the more important
  half. This store holds hashes in **two formats at once** after the Identity migration: migrated
  accounts carry the legacy format, whose derivation is roughly a hundredth of the work of the format
  the target hasher produces, and an account is rewritten to the current format only when it next signs
  in successfully (section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)). A lockout, meanwhile,
  short-circuits **before** any derivation at all. So "one dummy derivation" produces three visibly
  different costs — cheap for a migrated account, expensive for a rehashed one, near-zero for a locked
  one — and the response time discloses which of the three a username is.

**The design.** One singleton, `UniformVerificationCost`, with two operations and a stated target:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **The target cost** | **The cost of the most expensive hash format present in the store**, which is the format the configured `PasswordHasherOptions` produces — the migrated legacy format is the cheap one, so the current format is the ceiling and the ceiling is what everything is padded up to. The value is derived from options rather than written down: the service reads `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>` and treats its iteration count as the target |
| **Construction** | A **singleton** taking `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>` — both are process-lifetime, so nothing scoped is captured — which constructs its own `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` and computes **one** reference hash over a cryptographically random 32-byte value in its constructor. The reference value is never persisted, never logged and not a literal. It is computed once per process, on first resolution, and never on a request path |
| **`SpendFullCostAsync`** | Performs one derivation at the target cost against the reference hash and discards the result. This is the unknown-account path, and it is also the fallback whenever no real derivation happened |
| **`TopUpAsync(storedHash, observation)`** | Spends **the difference** between the target cost and the work the real path already did, and it takes that fact as an **observation of the hasher** rather than as an inference from the sign-in result. Where the observation says no derivation ran, the difference is the whole target cost. Where it says one ran, the iteration count the decorator recorded is the work already spent — the legacy format is fixed at its own well-known count and the current format encodes its count — and a top-up derivation is performed over the reference salt for the remaining iterations using the same pseudo-random function. Where the difference is zero or negative — a hash already at or above the target — nothing is spent |
| **Where it runs** | Steps 2a and 3 of the sequence above, and the registration path of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) does **not** use it: `Register` resolves no account and reveals nothing by its timing, which is why step R2 replaces steps 2, 2a and 3 outright |

**Where the "a derivation ran" signal comes from — an observed fact, never an inferred one.** The
signal is produced by `RehashObservingPasswordHasher : IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`, a decorator
registered over the hasher Identity registers, and by nothing else:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Registration** | The three lines in stage 1 item 3 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), placed after `AddIdentity`, and **not** the two-type overload: the decorator is registered by a **factory** that takes the inner hasher from a **separate registration of the concrete `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`**, because a decorator registered as the interface it also depends on resolves itself and the resolution recurses. That item states the mechanism and why the ordering matters; this row states only the lifetime, which is **scoped**, because what it records belongs to one request. The decorator wraps the framework hasher rather than subclassing it, which is the form [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) specifies for the artifact |
| **What it records** | On `VerifyHashedPassword(user, hashedPassword, providedPassword)` it writes, into the scoped `PasswordDerivationObservation`, that a derivation **ran** and the format marker and iteration count it read from `hashedPassword`'s encoded header; then it delegates and returns the inner result unchanged. It also sets **`RehashObserved`** where the inner result was `PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded` |
| **What it never does** | It performs no derivation of its own, changes no result, records no password, no hash and no user name, and takes no branch on what it observed. `HashPassword` is delegated untouched. **It emits nothing** — see the row below |
| **Who reads it, and with what semantics** | Two consumers of **one** scoped object. (1) `TopUpAsync` above reads `DerivationRan`, the format marker and the iteration count on the request path, **before** any store write and **without clearing them** — these three members are 05's, and they are deliberately **not** consume-once, because the top-up must be able to read them again in the same request without a second observation. (2) [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam-1 emitter reads `RehashObserved` and `UserInitiatedCredentialChange`, which **are** consume-once and are read in exactly one place. Nothing else reads or writes any member. Because the two sets are disjoint and only one set is cleared, the two consumers cannot interfere |
| **Who emits, and who owns that decision** | **Not this artifact, and not any code on the sign-in path.** The `ACCT-2002` record carrying `RehashedOnSignIn` is emitted by [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam-1 **artifact 2** — the `AuditingUserManager : UserManager<ApplicationUser>` subclass overriding the `protected virtual UpdateUserAsync(ApplicationUser)` — after `base` returns, and **only** where the returned `IdentityResult.Succeeded` is true, `RehashObserved` is set, and `UserInitiatedCredentialChange` is not. That document owns the seam, its emission condition, its failed-write diagnostic and its registration; this section owns only the composition root that registers the hasher and the scoped observation, and the `TopUpAsync` consumer above. The single registration of `AuditingUserManager` is stage 1 item 3's `AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, IdentityRole>().AddUserManager<AuditingUserManager>()` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so there is **one** user manager type and **one** hasher registration, not one per consumer |
| **Who sets `UserInitiatedCredentialChange`, which is this document's action to write** | The change-password action of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) sets it **before** it calls `ChangePasswordAsync`, because verifying the *current* password of an account still holding a legacy hash makes the hasher report `SuccessRehashNeeded` on a request that is a user action rather than an opportunistic rehash. Without the flag one credential change would produce two `ACCT-2002` records — the action's own and a spurious rehash one — which is the arithmetic section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) states as one change, one record |
| **Rejected form, recorded so the cheaper one is not reintroduced** | Emitting from this decorator, or from the controller reading the observation after `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` returns. Both were an earlier form of this section and both are wrong for one reason: `SuccessRehashNeeded` is the hasher's **advice, returned before persistence is attempted**, and `UserManager.CheckPasswordAsync` then performs the rehash write and **discards the `IdentityResult` it gets back** — so on a run where the store rejected the write, the observation is still set and either form writes an audit record asserting a credential change that never happened. The coverage assertion is the test that fails for both |

**Inferring the signal from `result.IsLockedOut` is wrong in both directions, and each direction is a
real timing channel.** It is worth stating explicitly because the expression reads as obviously correct:

- **True when no derivation ran.** `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` runs `PreSignInCheck` first, and that check
  short-circuits on more than lockout — an account the sign-in options do not permit to sign in returns
  before any verification, and an account whose `PasswordHash` is null fails inside
  `CheckPasswordAsync` **without invoking the hasher at all**. In each of those the result is not
  `LockedOut`, so `!IsLockedOut` is **true**, so the top-up spends only a "difference" against work that
  never happened — and the request answers measurably faster than an ordinary wrong password. The
  null-hash case is not hypothetical here: it is exactly the shape section
  [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
  rejects for the neutralization set, and rejects partly for this reason.
- **False when a derivation did run.** On the attempt that *crosses* the lockout threshold,
  `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` verifies the password — one full derivation — fails, calls
  `AccessFailedAsync`, finds the account now locked and returns `LockedOut`. So `!IsLockedOut` is
  **false**, and the top-up spends the **whole** target cost on top of the derivation already performed:
  that one request costs roughly double every other failure, which is a signature identifying the
  threshold-crossing attempt from the outside. Since the lockout policy of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) admits five failures before locking, that signature is
  reachable by an attacker who simply counts.

**Two honest limits, stated rather than papered over.** Iteration count is a proxy for cost, not cost
itself: fixed overheads, allocation and the store round trip are not iteration-proportional, so this
equalizes the **dominant** term rather than producing identical wall-clock times. And one asymmetry is
deliberate and irreducible: a wrong password against a real account performs the failed-attempt
accounting write that the lockout policy of section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) requires, and an unknown username has nothing to write.
Both are why the acceptance test is a **distribution comparison per population with a stated
tolerance** — **five** populations, rather than one median pair, which can be passed by an
implementation that leaves two of the five distinguishable:

| Population | Why it is its own population |
| --- | --- |
| **Unknown username** | Takes step 2a and never reaches the hasher; the only path with no store write to accompany the derivation |
| **Migrated legacy-format hash** (`V2`) | Its real derivation is roughly a hundredth of the target cost, so it is the population the top-up does the most work for |
| **Current-format hash** (`V3`) | Its real derivation is already at the target, so its top-up is nothing — the control against which the others are compared |
| **Already-locked account** | `PreSignInCheck` short-circuits, so **no** derivation runs and the whole target cost is spent by the top-up |
| **The threshold-crossing attempt** | A derivation **and** the lockout accounting write both happen on one request; it is the population the inferred flag got backwards, so a suite that omits it cannot detect the defect the observation above fixes |

Two fixture requirements make the comparison mean anything, and both follow from framework defaults
rather than from taste:

- **Every sample runs against a freshly provisioned account, or resets `AccessFailedCount` and
  `LockoutEnd` between samples.** Identity's defaults are `MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5`,
  `DefaultLockoutTimeSpan = 00:05:00` and `AllowedForNewUsers = true`, and the policy of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) keeps lockout enabled — so a run of two hundred
  wrong-password samples against **one** account locks it on the fifth and the remaining
  hundred-and-ninety-five measure the **locked-out** path instead of the password path. That is not a
  failed test; it is a test that passes while measuring the wrong thing, in the one place where the whole
  point is which population a timing belongs to. The threshold-crossing population is the exception that
  proves the rule: it is sampled by driving exactly five failures against a fresh account and timing the
  fifth, which is only possible if the fixture provisions accounts per sample.
- **The fixture raises the credential rate limits from configuration.** Two hundred samples against the
  `Login` POST would otherwise be refused from the eleventh, because the per-source credential bound of
  stage 1 item 14 admits ten per minute per address partition, and a fixture drives all its samples from
  one address. The limits are `RateLimiting:*` configuration
  rather than constants precisely so a fixture can widen them; the fixture does that and asserts the
  widening rather than partitioning its way around the limiter, so the samples measure the handler and
  not the limiter.

**The coverage assertion is that test, and it replaces the median-pair clause row 53 used to carry.

**The cart-key isolation rule, and why step 4 is gated rather than unconditional.** Reassigning "the
rows under the session's current cart key" is not safe, because that key is not always an anonymous one.
`GetCartId` writes the **user name** into the session slot for an authenticated caller
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] and a fresh GUID only for an anonymous one
[:172-175], and on any later request it returns whatever the slot already holds [:179]; `MigrateCart`
then reassigns **every** row carrying that value [:184-193]. And both anonymous entry points stay
reachable while already authenticated: `AccountController` carries a class-level `[Authorize]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:15] with `[AllowAnonymous]` on `Login` [:44],
[:54] and on `Register` [:78], [:87], and `[AllowAnonymous]` **permits** an authenticated caller rather
than excluding one. So a caller signed in as A who posts `Login` — or `Register` — for B arrives at step
4 with the slot holding **A's own user name**, and an unconditional reassignment moves **A's cart to
B**. Nothing but A's own session is required for it, and the same shape lets A leave a username-keyed
slot behind for the next anonymous request in that session.

Three rules close it, and all three belong to the cart service rather than to the controller:

- **Migration input must be *proved* to be a server-issued anonymous key, and shape is not a proof.**
  `MigrateCartAsync` is called only when **both** of the tests below pass on the session's current cart
  key. Where either fails, step 4 is **skipped**: no rows are read, none are reassigned, and the sequence
  continues at step 5.

  **Why `Guid.TryParse` alone is insufficient, stated because the opposite is the intuitive reading.** A
  successful parse proves the *shape* of a value, not its *origin* — and a login name of that shape is
  legal in this application. Identity's default `AllowedUserNameCharacters` is
  `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789-._@+`, which admits every hexadecimal
  digit **and** the hyphen, so both `Guid` formats are spellable as user names; the narrower policy of
  section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) still admits letters and digits, so the
  32-character form remains spellable under it too. So "a user name cannot be mistaken for a GUID" is
  false as stated, and an account registered under a GUID-shaped name would have its **own** cart treated
  as an anonymous one and reassigned to whoever signed in next from that session. Two mechanisms close
  it, and both are required:

  - **A namespace no user name can occupy.** Anonymous keys are written as
    `"anon:" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N")` — a fixed prefix, then the 32-character form — and the test
    is the prefix plus a parse of the remainder, never a parse alone. The prefix is chosen for a
    mechanical reason rather than an aesthetic one: **`:` is absent from the framework's default allowed
    set quoted above and from section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)'s narrower set**, so
    no account can ever be created whose name begins `anon:`, and the two value spaces are disjoint by
    construction rather than by convention. `"N"` rather than `"D"` is chosen so the stored value has one
    canonical spelling and no hyphen-form variant to reconcile.
  - **A protected marker binding the key to *this* session.** The session additionally holds a
    data-protection-protected token — `IDataProtector` with a purpose string naming this use — whose
    payload is the anonymous key and the session id, and step 4 verifies it before any row moves. This is
    what makes the rule hold against a value **injected into the session** rather than issued by the
    server: the distributed session store is a database table (section
    [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)), so a session value is not automatically a server-issued one,
    and an unprotectable or mismatched marker fails the test even though the key's shape is perfect.
    The marker is written by the same service method that issues the key, and cleared by
    `ClearSessionCartId()` alongside it, so the two cannot drift apart.

  **Legacy rows carrying the bare form are rewritten, and the rewrite is selected by owner rather than by
  shape — for the same reason the runtime gate is.** The source writes `Guid.NewGuid().ToString()` — the
  hyphenated `"D"` form with no prefix — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172-175] for an
  anonymous cart, and the signed-in user's **name** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167]
  for an owned one, into the same single column. So `Cart.CartId` values arriving from the domain data
  load hold both kinds, and "rewrite every `CartId` that parses as a `Guid`" would rewrite the cart of any
  account whose name is GUID-shaped — the exact collision this rule exists to close, reintroduced as a
  one-off data transformation. The load therefore selects on ownership, using a set the load already has:

  | Class of row | Test | Action |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Anonymous | `CartId` parses as a `Guid` **and** is **not** in the source user-name set, compared upper-invariant as Identity normalizes names | Rewritten to `"anon:" + <32 lower-case hex digits>`: lower-case the value, strip the hyphens, prepend the prefix. Deterministic, so a re-run produces byte-identical output |
  | Owned | `CartId` is in the source user-name set | **Not** rewritten. It is that account's cart, which is what the source writes for a signed-in user, and the prefix belongs to anonymous keys alone |
  | Ambiguous — GUID-shaped **and** in the user-name set | Both tests above are true | Falls under **owned** and is not rewritten, **and** is enumerated in the load report by user name with no cart contents. The ambiguity is pre-existing in the source, which stores both kinds in one column and cannot distinguish them either; the migration inherits it, resolves it in the direction that preserves the account's own items, and reports it rather than silently choosing |

  Three reconciliation assertions close the load, and the third is the one the runtime gate actually
  depends on: the count of rewritten rows equals the count of rows matching the anonymous test; every
  ambiguous row appears in the report; and **every** `CartId` in the loaded table is either in the user-name
  set or begins `anon:` — no third form remains. `CartId` is an unconstrained string with no length
  attribute [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:10], so the five added characters need no schema
  change. Sequencing the rewrite inside the load — after the user-name set exists and before the
  application reads the table — is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to carry as a gated step; the
  transformation, its selection rule and its assertions are stated here because this document owns the
  key format they produce.
- **The slot is cleared before any identity change.** A `Login` or `Register` POST arriving on an
  **already-authenticated** request calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` before step 2, so nothing
  crosses the identity boundary in either direction: the previous identity's key is not migrated, and it
  is not left in place for whoever holds that session next. The previous identity's cart is untouched —
  its rows stay keyed by that user name and reappear when that user signs in again, which is the
  source's own behaviour for a signed-in cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167].
- **Sign-out clears the slot too.** That is section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)'s rule and the third
  side of the same box: without it a username-keyed slot outlives the ticket that justified it.

The first two rules are **approved delta 19** of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) and the third is **approved delta 20**, because the skipped
migration is observable — an authenticated caller who signs in as somebody else no longer carries a cart
across, and an anonymous request after a sign-out no longer sees the signed-out user's items.
**The coverage assertion requires the account-switch isolation on **both** entry points rather than on `Login`
alone, and **The coverage assertion requires the sign-out half. The provenance half needs its own three rows,
because none of the above would fail if the gate were a bare `Guid.TryParse`: **row 100** registers an
account whose user name is a 32-character hexadecimal string, signs it in from a session holding that
same string, and asserts **no** cart row moves; **row 101** writes a perfectly shaped `anon:` key into
the session store without its marker and asserts the same; and **row 102** posts `RecoverCart` with no
authentication and asserts a challenge with no row moved.

**Step 4's retry behaviour, stated as a mechanism rather than a count.** "Up to three attempts" names no
classifier and no execution model, and the wrong reading of it is a `catch`/`retry` loop wrapped around
an explicit transaction, which either replays a half-applied transaction or throws before it retries
anything. **It is also the wrong count**, and the arithmetic is fixed here once for every consumer in
this document: `maxRetryCount` is the number of **retries the strategy performs after the first
attempt**, so `maxRetryCount: 3` is **four attempts in total** — one initial and three replays — and
`maxRetryDelay` caps **each individual delay**, never the sum of them. Six things are fixed:

- **Who classifies a failure as transient: the provider.** `UseSqlServer(…, o =>
  o.EnableRetryOnFailure(maxRetryCount: 3, maxRetryDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), errorNumbersToAdd:
  null))` installs the provider's retrying execution strategy, whose transient set is its own list of
  SQL Server and Azure SQL error numbers plus the timeout and broken-connection cases. **No error number
  is added to it**: widening that set by hand is how a constraint violation becomes something the
  application retries. Anything the strategy does not classify as transient — a unique-index violation, a
  login failure, a permission failure — is **not retried** and takes the failure branch below on its
  first occurrence.
- **What is retried: a delegate, not a statement.** Because step 4 opens an **explicit** transaction, the
  retrying strategy will not silently wrap it — EF Core rejects a user-initiated transaction under a
  retrying strategy unless the transactional block is itself executed through the strategy. So the call
  is `await db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(async ct => { … }, cancellationToken)`,
  and the delegate contains the whole unit: begin transaction, reassign, `SaveChangesAsync`, commit.
- **What the replay boundary implies for the delegate's contents.** A retry re-runs the delegate **from
  the beginning** against a new connection and a new transaction, so its body must be safe to run twice.
  It contains no session write, no cookie write, no `TempData` write, no user-visible outcome and no
  in-memory mutation the caller depends on — steps 5 and 6 are outside it by construction — and the
  reassignment is keyed on the anonymous cart id, so a replay after a commit whose acknowledgement was
  lost finds no rows and completes as a no-op rather than moving rows twice.
- **The change tracker is *not* reset between attempts, so this delegate is written to hold no tracked
  state at all.** This is the hazard "safe to run twice" does not close on its own, because it is not
  about side effects — it is about state the replay silently *inherits*. `ExecuteAsync` re-runs the
  delegate against a new connection and a new transaction, but the `DbContext` and its change tracker are
  the **same instance** across every attempt, and `SaveChangesAsync` marks the entries it accepted
  `Unchanged` when it returns. So the sequence *load the rows, set `CartId`, `SaveChangesAsync` succeeds,
  `CommitAsync` fails transiently* leaves those entries `Unchanged` while the transaction has rolled
  back: the replay's `SaveChangesAsync` finds nothing to send, affects zero rows, commits an empty
  transaction and **reports success having moved nothing.** Step 5 then writes the user name into the
  session, the rows are still under the anonymous key, and the cart renders empty — a silent, total loss
  that raises no exception and that a happy-path test cannot see. Two requirements close it, and both are
  mandatory:
  - **The reassignment is set-based and tracks nothing.** `MigrateCartAsync`'s write is a single
    statement issued inside the delegate's transaction —
    `await db.Carts.Where(c => c.CartId == anonymousCartId).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s
    .SetProperty(c => c.CartId, userName)
    .SetProperty(c => c.ModifiedUtc, nowUtc), ct)` — whose **affected row count is the only outcome the
    delegate reads**. Nothing is materialized, nothing is tracked, and there is therefore no accepted
    state for a replay to inherit: every attempt issues the same `UPDATE` and the first one to commit
    wins, while later attempts match no rows. `ModifiedUtc` is assigned **explicitly in the statement**
    because `ExecuteUpdateAsync` does not pass through `SaveChangesAsync` and so does not run the
    maintenance path the change-tracking group of section
    [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) defines; omitting it would leave the
    column stale on exactly the rows a rollback decision reads
    ([06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). `nowUtc` is captured **once, outside** the
    delegate, so a replay does not move the timestamp and the value is attempt-invariant.
  - **The delegate's first statement is an explicit `db.ChangeTracker.Clear();`, asserted by a test
    rather than assumed.** With the set-based form above there is nothing to clear and the call costs
    nothing — which is the point: it is a **named attempt-state precondition** that survives a later edit
    reintroducing tracked mutation into this delegate, and without it that edit would reintroduce the
    silent loss above with no failing test. Resolving a **fresh `DbContext` per attempt** is the
    equivalent fix and is deliberately **not** chosen: the catalog context is request-scoped and
    constructor-injected (section [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces)),
    and creating a second one inside a retry delegate would leave two catalog contexts live in one
    request for steps 5 through 7 — and for the cart summary the layout renders — to disagree over.
- **Backoff: the strategy's own exponential backoff with jitter, and the worst case is arithmetic rather
  than an impression.** Each delay is drawn below the `maxRetryDelay` ceiling above, so **four attempts
  separated by at most three delays of at most two seconds each** put no more than **six seconds** of
  waiting into the worst case, on top of the attempts' own work. **The two-second ceiling is chosen
  because the ceiling is per-delay and not aggregate**, which is the correction this bullet exists to
  make: at the five seconds an earlier form of it named, the same `maxRetryCount` admits up to fifteen
  seconds of pure delay inside an interactive sign-in — three times the bound that form believed it was
  stating. A longer per-delay ceiling would trade a recoverable cart for an unresponsive login, and the
  failure branch below signs the user in regardless, so waiting longer buys nothing the notice does not
  already deliver.
- **Cancellation is not a transient failure.** The request's token is passed into `ExecuteAsync` and into
  `SaveChangesAsync`; the strategy observes it between attempts and does not retry a cancelled
  operation. An `OperationCanceledException` carrying that token terminates the sequence under rule 4 of
  section [4.10](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once) — the client
  has gone, so there is nobody to sign in and nobody to show a notice to, and steps 5 through 7 do not
  run. A cancellation exception carrying a **foreign** token is not absorbed.

**The coverage assertion requires the two directions that distinguish this from a loop: a retriable failure
injected once completes the reassignment and signs the user in with no notice, and a non-retriable one
takes the failure branch on its first occurrence without a second attempt.

**The failure branch of step 4, and the durable state it leaves.** If cart migration still fails after
its retries — or fails on a non-retriable error — the handler **continues to step 6 and signs the user
in**, skipping step 5, and surfaces a non-blocking notice. A failed sign-in is not recoverable by the
user at all, whereas an unreassigned cart is, which is why the sign-in proceeds. Within that session
nothing is even visibly wrong: step 5 was skipped, so the session still names the anonymous cart id whose
rows still exist, **the user keeps their items**, and a checkout bills them correctly because the order
is written against their user name regardless of the cart's key.

**Leaving the session pointing at those rows is not, however, a recovery mechanism.** The session's idle
timeout is twenty minutes, sliding (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so the
moment it lapses the only link between that browser and those rows is gone and the rows are orphaned —
and the fault that most plausibly caused the failure is a database fault, which is also a **session**
fault, because the session store is that same database (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)).
The recovery link therefore has to survive session expiry and a process restart, and it must not live in
the store that just failed.

**The recovery ticket.** On this branch the handler writes one single-purpose cookie,
`.MvcMusicStore.CartRecovery`, whose payload is **data-protection protected** and carries exactly four
fields — the anonymous cart id, the user name the reassignment is pending for, an absolute expiry, and an
**exhausted-attempt counter** initialized to zero, which the exhausted-retry branch below increments and
re-protects. It is `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, host-only, `Path=/`, with a fixed lifetime of
**seven days** and no sliding renewal. Five properties follow from that shape:

- **It survives what session does not.** Nothing about it is stored server-side, so session expiry, a
  session-store outage and an instance restart all leave it intact; the persisted key ring of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is what lets a different replica read it.
- **It cannot be forged into somebody else's cart.** The payload is protected rather than merely encoded,
  so a caller cannot substitute an anonymous cart id they never held — which an unprotected cookie or a
  client-supplied parameter would allow, an anonymous key being a guessable, unauthenticated string
  whatever its spelling.
- **It is honoured only for the identity it names.** Recovery reassigns only when the authenticated
  principal's user name **equals** the name in the payload; otherwise the ticket is deleted and nothing
  is written.
- **It is the provenance evidence on its own path, and it does not — must not — require a live session
  marker.** This is where the two provenance mechanisms of the isolation rule above divide, and the
  division is deliberate rather than a gap:
  - **In-session migration (step 4)** proves provenance from the session: the `anon:` namespace plus the
    protected session marker bound to *this* session id.
  - **Recovery** proves it from the **ticket**: the payload is protected, so its anonymous cart id was
    written by the server and has not been altered, and it was issued **only** on a branch where the
    session-marker gate had already passed — a ticket cannot exist for a key that never satisfied it.
    Provenance is therefore established once, at issue time, and carried forward cryptographically.

  Requiring the session marker on the recovery path as well would make recovery impossible in exactly the
  cases it exists for: session expiry, a session-store outage and an instance restart all destroy the
  marker, and those are the three conditions the ticket was introduced to survive. So recovery verifies
  the ticket and the caller's identity, and does **not** consult the session marker; the key's namespace
  is still checked, because a ticket naming a non-`anon:` key could only come from a defect and is
  refused rather than trusted.
- **It is single-use and self-clearing.** The cookie is deleted on success, and equally when the payload
  cannot be unprotected, when it has expired, when its user name does not match the caller, when its
  anonymous cart id is not in the `anon:` namespace, and when that id names no rows — so a stale or
  malformed ticket cannot accumulate work.

**Where recovery runs — two places, both of them endpoints, and neither of them middleware.** First, at
the start of the next `Login` or `Register` POST that reaches step 4: the ticket is consumed there, with
the same execution strategy and the same idempotence, before the current session's own migration.
Second, through an **explicit action** — `POST /ShoppingCart/RecoverCart` — reached by the conventional
route of stage 2 item 13 in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order):

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Signature** | `[HttpPost] [Authorize] [RequestSizeLimit(2 * 1024)] public async Task<IActionResult> RecoverCart(CancellationToken cancellationToken)`. It takes no input at all: the anonymous cart id and the pending owner come from the protected cookie, never from the request. Anti-forgery validation arrives from the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) — it is **not** an entry in that section's opt-out register |
| **How it is offered** | A `TempData` notice on the sign-in or registration redirect (the notice mechanism below) renders, in the shared layout, a one-button form posting to this action. The user chooses to recover; nothing recovers on their behalf behind a page they did not submit |
| **Guards, in order** | The cookie must be present; its payload must unprotect; it must be unexpired; its user name must equal the authenticated caller's; its anonymous cart id must be in the `anon:` namespace; and its exhausted-attempt counter must be below three — the ticket's properties above, in the order that fails cheapest first. A failure of any one **deletes the cookie, writes nothing, and redirects to `/ShoppingCart`** with no notice; there is no error page for a stale ticket. The session marker is deliberately **not** among the guards, for the reason the ticket's provenance property gives |
| **The write** | Step 4's reassignment verbatim: keyed on the anonymous cart id, inside `ExecuteAsync` on the catalog context's execution strategy, idempotent under replay. On success step 5's `AssignSessionCartId` runs, the cookie is deleted, and the action redirects to `/ShoppingCart` so the user sees the items they came back for |
| **Where it must not be** | **Not pre-endpoint middleware**, and the three reasons are separate. It would run on **safe methods** — an ordinary authenticated `GET`, a health probe, a violation report — which makes a state change reachable by navigation. It would run **before** MVC's anti-forgery filter, so a `POST` whose token is invalid would have mutated before it was rejected (section [7.1](#71-the-policy)). And `UseExceptionHandler` **re-executes the pipeline**, so a middleware that faults faults again while rendering `/Home/Error` — the recursion section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) exists to prevent, arriving from the one place that section does not look. **Not the cart service's read path** either: the cart badge renders from a view component on every page (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)) and a view component must not write (the coverage assertion) |

Either way the write is the same keyed, idempotent reassignment, so a ticket consumed twice is harmless.

**Recovery has an exhausted-retry branch, and it is the branch that keeps one database fault from
becoming a fault on every request.** A recovery attempt is classified and bounded exactly as step 4 is:
the provider's retrying execution strategy decides what is transient, the same `maxRetryCount: 3` — four
attempts — and the same two-second per-delay `maxRetryDelay` bound the attempts and the backoff, and
cancellation is not a transient failure. **The same attempt-state precondition applies unchanged**, and it
is not optional here either: the reassignment is the same set-based `ExecuteUpdateAsync` statement, the
delegate opens with the same `db.ChangeTracker.Clear();`, and the timestamp is captured once outside it —
so a commit that fails after a successful save replays the write rather than replaying an empty
transaction. What is stated here is what happens when that bound is reached:

- **Transient, retries exhausted.** The cookie is **kept** — the pending reassignment is still pending
  and still recoverable — and the action returns its redirect with a `TempData` notice offering the
  button again. Exactly **one** `Warning` record is written, carrying the failure category, the trace
  identifier and the anonymous cart id, and no provider message (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). Nothing else about the request changes: the user
  stays signed in and every other page still works.
- **Non-transient.** The failure branch on its first occurrence, with the same single record and the
  same notice, and no second attempt.
- **The ticket is not retried indefinitely across requests either, and the boundary is stated as a guard
  rather than as a count.** The payload's fourth field — the exhausted-attempt counter named in the
  ticket's inventory above — is incremented and the payload re-protected on **every** exhausted attempt.
  The guard runs **before** any database work: a post arriving with the counter **already at three** —
  which is the fourth post, the first three having each attempted and exhausted — makes **no further
  reassignment attempt at all**, deletes the cookie, and renders the final notice saying the cart could
  not be restored. So three posts attempt and record, and the fourth deletes without attempting, which is
  exactly the sequence **The coverage assertion drives; stating it as "at three exhausted attempts the cookie
  is deleted" is the ambiguity that lets an implementation delete on the third post and fail that row.
  The counter lives inside the protected payload rather than in a separate cookie or in session so that
  it cannot be reset by the caller and cannot be lost by the store whose failure is being counted.
  The rows are then abandoned anonymous rows, which is the pre-existing ceiling stated below rather
  than a new one.
- **No path leaves a persistent per-request fault.** Because recovery is an endpoint the user posts to,
  a failing recovery affects **that** request and no other, and the error page — which posts nothing —
  cannot re-enter it. **The coverage assertion requires exactly this: recovery made to fail on every attempt,
  with the ordinary pages and `/Home/Error` still answering normally throughout.

Nothing in the failure text names an exception, a store or a connection detail, under the
permitted-content rule of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types).

**The notice mechanism is named, because "a non-blocking notice" does not survive a redirect by itself.**
The branch ends in step 7's redirect, so the message is written to **`TempData`**: read once, on the next
request, and gone afterwards — it survives **exactly one** redirect and no more. It uses the framework's
default **cookie-backed** `TempData` provider rather than a session-backed one, deliberately, because the
failure being reported may be a fault in the very store a session-backed provider would write to, which
would lose the notice for exactly the request that needs it. The text names no exception detail and no
store detail, under the permitted-content rule of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types).

**The notice is also what carries the recovery offer, and the ticket outlives it deliberately.** The
notice renders the one-button form that posts to `RecoverCart`, so the offer is present on exactly the
page the user lands on after the failed sign-in. Because `TempData` survives one redirect and the
protected cookie survives seven days, the two are not the same lifetime and the difference is handled
rather than ignored: **step 7 writes the notice whenever the recovery cookie is present on a successful
sign-in or registration**, not only on the request that created the ticket. So a user who ignored the
offer is offered it again the next time they sign in, and no request outside that path — no `GET`, no
probe, no error page — is asked to do anything about it.

**The durable state on this branch is therefore:** rows under the anonymous id, a protected recovery
ticket naming those rows and their pending owner, the user signed in, one notice shown offering
`RecoverCart`, and a deterministic point at which the reassignment completes. Past the ticket's expiry the rows are
unreachable anonymous rows — indistinguishable from an abandoned anonymous cart, which the source
already leaves behind whenever an anonymous session lapses
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176] — so the ceiling on this failure mode is the
pre-existing one rather than a worse one. **The coverage assertion requires recovery **after the session has
expired** and **after a restart**, which is the pair the session-only story failed.

**The invariants this achieves, stated so a reviewer can check them — and the one that does *not* hold,
stated because a looser version of it would be false.**

Two invariants hold, and they are the ones worth having:

- **Cart rows are reassigned only after the credentials have been verified and the Identity-side writes
  committed.** Step 4 cannot run unless step 3 returned `Succeeded`, so a caller who fails
  authentication — wrong password, unknown account, locked out — never causes a catalog write of any
  kind.
- **A session never names a username unless a cookie was issued for that username.** Step 5 is the only
  writer of that session value, it runs only after step 4 succeeds, and step 6's compensation removes it
  if the cookie is not issued. This is the security-relevant one: without the compensation an
  unauthenticated request in that session would resolve `GetCartId` to the username
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] and read and modify that user's cart.

**What does not hold, and is not claimed: "no cart row ever carries a username unless a sign-in
completed."** If step 6 throws, steps 4 and 5 have already run, the rows already carry the username, and
**`ClearSessionCartId()` does not move them back** — nothing in this sequence does. That residual state
is accepted deliberately, for three reasons:

- **It is not readable by anyone else.** The rows are keyed by the username, and the only session value
  that resolves to a username is the one step 5 writes and step 6's compensation removes. An anonymous
  visitor's key is a fresh prefixed anonymous key, issued where the source issues a bare GUID
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176], and the `anon:` namespace **cannot** be
  occupied by a login name for the character-set reason given with the isolation rule above — so no other
  visitor, and not the same visitor while anonymous, can reach those rows.
- **Nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated.** At the next successful sign-in, step 4 finds no rows
  under the new anonymous id (there are none to move) and step 5 points the session at the username, so
  the same items reappear exactly once. Because step 4 is keyed on the anonymous id, the second run
  cannot double-assign.
- **A compensating reassignment would add a failure mode rather than remove one.** Writing the rows back
  to the anonymous id is itself a database write that can fail, leaving the identical state plus a
  second error to handle; and the realistic cause of a throw at step 6 is a data-protection key-ring
  fault (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), which says nothing
  about the catalog store and would not be repaired by touching it.

The converse case — a signed-in user whose rows did **not** move, from the step 4 failure branch above —
is likewise permitted deliberately, because it is the recoverable direction, and the recovery ticket of
that branch is what makes "recoverable" a mechanism rather than a hope.

A third invariant holds because of the isolation rule, and it is the one the reachability of `Login` and
`Register` while authenticated would otherwise break: **no cart row is ever reassigned from one account
to another.** Every path that moves cart rows requires provenance evidence for the key it is moving, and
there are exactly two admissible forms: step 4 requires the `anon:` namespace **plus** a valid protected
session marker bound to the current session, and recovery requires a valid protected **ticket** whose
payload names both an `anon:` key and the authenticated caller — issued, as the ticket's properties state,
only where the session-marker form had already held. Neither form can be satisfied by a value that names
an account's cart, **including an account whose own name is GUID-shaped**, because an account name cannot
begin `anon:` under either character-set policy. A GUID-shaped user name is therefore no longer a way in
on either path.

**All six failure paths need tests** (the coverage assertions): cart migration failing
after its retries must still produce a successful sign-in **with the notice and with the items still
visible**; an Identity-side failure must produce **no** cart reassignment and **no** cookie; recovery
must complete after the session has expired and after a restart; a non-retriable failure must not be
retried; and recovery failing on **every** attempt must bound itself and leave every other request
working.

**The `Register` POST is the same sequence, and the source is why — not an analogy.** It is easy to read
registration as account creation followed by a redirect, and that reading is wrong here. `Register`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:89-104] calls **the same private helper `Login`
calls** — `await SignInAsync(user, isPersistent: false)` [:97] against
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] — and that helper is the whole orchestration:
external-cookie sign-out [:348], identity creation [:349], the sign-in grant [:350] and **then**
`MigrateShoppingCart` [:353] with its own context, its `SaveChanges` [:37] and its session-key rewrite
[:39]. So registration today issues a cookie, reassigns the anonymous cart and rewrites the session
slot, in exactly the order `Login` does — **including the reversal this section exists to correct.** A
port that gives the safe sequence to `Login` alone reintroduces the original defect on the other
anonymous entry point, and it does so where it is *most* likely to bite: registering is the one moment a
visitor is guaranteed to have been anonymous a request ago, so a pre-registration cart is the normal case
rather than an edge one.

`Register` therefore runs **steps 4 through 7 of the table above, unchanged**, with its own first two
steps in front of them. The differences are only the ones the source's own signature forces:

| Step | Call | How it differs from the `Login` sequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | `if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(model);` | **No difference.** Step 1, and the registration-path counterpart named by the input-bounds rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) — the bound is enforced here, before `CreateAsync` and before any insert |
| R2 | `var result = await userManager.CreateAsync(user, model.Password);` | **Replaces steps 2, 2a and 3.** There is no account to resolve, so no enumeration-timing problem and no dummy-hash step; there is no stored hash to verify or rehash, and no lockout accounting to apply. Identity hashes the password inside this call. `result.Succeeded == false` redisplays the form with the per-error messages the source's `AddErrors` produces [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:102], [:356-362], and — being an Identity validation outcome rather than a credential outcome — it is the `ACCT-2001` event at its `ValidationFailed` outcome, never an `AUTH-1002` one. **This is the step whose writes must be committed before R3**, exactly as step 3 is |
| R3 | Step 4 verbatim: `await cartService.MigrateCartAsync(anonymousCartId, user.UserName, cancellationToken)`, own transaction, keyed on the anonymous cart id, gated on **step 4's three-part provenance test** — the `anon:` namespace prefix, the 32-character lower-case hexadecimal remainder, and a matching protected session marker — and executed through the retrying execution strategy specified for step 4 | **No difference, and not optional.** The source performs it [:353] and the anonymous cart it moves is the items the visitor added before registering. Both of step 4's guards apply unchanged, and **that provenance gate — not a GUID shape test** — is what stops an **already-authenticated** caller registering a second account and carrying their own cart into it: an authenticated session's cart key is the account's user name, which cannot begin `anon:` under either character-set policy and for which no session marker was ever issued, so the gate fails on two counts rather than relying on the name not looking like a GUID — `Register` is `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:78], [:87] on an otherwise `[Authorize]` controller [:15], so that request is reachable. Its failure branch is step 4's failure branch verbatim: skip R4, continue to R5, write the `TempData` notice, and leave the rows under the anonymous id with a protected recovery ticket naming them |
| R4 | Step 5 verbatim: `cartService.AssignSessionCartId(user.UserName)` | **No difference.** Omitting it loses the cart silently for the same reason step 5 gives — the ported `GetCartId` equivalent will not overwrite a session slot that already holds the anonymous key, exactly as the source will not overwrite one holding its bare GUID [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-179] |
| R5 | `await signInManager.SignInAsync(user, isPersistent: false);` | **Last, and always non-persistent.** The source passes `isPersistent: false` [:97] and `RegisterViewModel` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:46-58] carries no remember-me property, so there is no user input to honour and none is introduced. Step 6's compensation applies unchanged: if this throws, `ClearSessionCartId()` undoes R4 and only R4 |
| R6 | `return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");` | **Unconditional, and no `returnUrl` test.** `Register` POST declares no return-URL parameter [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:89] and the source redirects straight to the home page [:98], so the redirect rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) has no input to validate here and `Url.IsLocalUrl` is **not** added — adding a parameter the source does not accept would widen the anonymous surface for no requirement |

Both invariants above hold on this path for the same reasons: R3 cannot run unless R2 succeeded, and R4
is still the only writer of the session's username value with R5's compensation removing it. **Coverage
The coverage assertion requires the continuity** — an anonymous cart built before registration is still the registrant's
cart afterwards — because the failure it guards is silent: registration succeeds, the user is signed in,
and the cart is simply empty.

**Merging the two contexts into one was considered and is not taken.** It would collapse this ordering
problem into a single `SaveChanges` and would be the simpler design on that axis alone. It is rejected
because `ApplicationDbContext : IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser>`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:10-16] is a framework-shaped context whose model the
Identity packages own, and merging the six catalog `DbSet` properties
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] into it entangles the catalog model with
Identity's schema versioning — every future Identity package upgrade would then arrive as a migration
against the catalog. The ordering above is five lines of explicit code; the merge is a permanent
coupling. **The ordering is cheaper than the coupling, so the boundary stays.** Note also that the
merge would not have removed the cookie problem, which is not a database problem at all.

### 4.4 What "the cart" is coupled to — and what it is not

Stated here because sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) both depend on it.

`Order.Username` is a plain string [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18], compared against
`User.Identity.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73]. The cart's
`CartId` is likewise a plain string, holding either the signed-in user's name or a generated GUID
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180] — a single value space shared by two kinds of
identifier, which is the property section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s `anon:` prefix
separates in the target. **Neither references the Identity primary
key, and there is no foreign key between the catalog store and the credential store in either
direction.** The two stores are coupled **only by convention** — a string that happens to match a login
name.

That fact carries three consequences used later: it is why one database is an operational choice rather
than a relational necessity ([4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); it is why
**usernames** rather than user ids are the invariant of the Identity data migration
([5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)); and it is why signed-in
carts survive cutover while anonymous ones do not ([11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)).

### 4.5 Two contexts, two migration sets, two history tables

**Neither context's current configuration convention survives.**

`MusicStoreEntities : DbContext` declares six `DbSet` properties, **no constructor and no
`OnModelCreating`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:5-13]. EF 6 resolves its
connection string by matching the **class name** against a `connectionStrings` entry, and there is one
named `MusicStoreEntities` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13]. The coupling between the class and
its database is a name, expressed nowhere in the code — which is why this is the dangerous half: the
class compiles in the target, instantiates in the target, and simply does not know where its database
is. There is no line for a reviewer to notice, because the thing that stops meaning something is the
**absence** of a constructor.

`ApplicationDbContext : IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser>` passes the name explicitly,
`: base("DefaultConnection")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:12-13], matching the
entry at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12]. This half announces itself — the base overload does
not exist in the target, so it fails to compile. ([12 F-12-19](12-migration-blockers.md) owns the
as-is finding and its two opposite failure modes.)

**Resolution.** Both contexts get an **explicit `DbContextOptions<T>` constructor** and an explicit
container registration, scoped, with the connection supplied from configuration. `MusicStoreEntities`
additionally gains an `OnModelCreating` override, because EF 6 inferred its **entire** mapping by
convention and there is no reason to expect two ORM generations' conventions to agree facet by facet.

**All six entities are mapped explicitly, and every facet is settled against the extracted schema of
section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) rather than against a
convention.** Naming a subset would be worse than naming none, because the unnamed entity is the one
nobody checks: `Artist` and `Order` are as convention-mapped as the other four, and `Artist` is the
smallest and therefore the easiest to assume is fine.

| Entity | Facets that must be stated explicitly rather than inferred |
| --- | --- |
| `Album` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs] | Key `AlbumId` [:10]; `Price` **precision and scale** [:24]; `Title` and `AlbumArtUrl` **length**, where the annotated 160 and 1024 [:17], [:27] are validation attributes and the *column* length is whatever the database holds; **Unicode versus ANSI** on both strings; nullability on every column; the two relationships and their **delete behaviour** [:30-31]; any index on `GenreId` or `ArtistId` |
| `Artist` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs] | Key `ArtistId` [:10]; `Name` length, Unicode and nullability [:11] — **the file carries no annotation at all**, so every one of its column facets exists only in the database and nowhere in the source |
| `Genre` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs] | Key `GenreId` [:7]; `Name` and `Description` length, Unicode and nullability [:8-9], again unannotated; the `Albums` collection [:10], which is **not** `virtual` and therefore never lazy-loaded (section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)) |
| `Cart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs] | Key `RecordId` — the one explicit `[Key]` [:8-9]; `CartId` **length and Unicode**, unannotated [:10] and load-bearing, since it is the cart's whole identity — and because an unfaceted `string` maps to `nvarchar(max)`, which **cannot be an index key column**, this mapping must give it the **explicit bounded length** section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 1 requires before the unique index can exist at all; `DateCreated` **column type and precision** [:14-15]; the `Album` relationship and its delete behaviour [:17]; and the **`rowversion` concurrency token** section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) adds, mapped `IsRowVersion()` and recorded as a deliberate net-new column |
