| `Order` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs] | Key `OrderId` [:12]; `Total` precision and scale [:63-64]; `OrderDate` column type and precision [:14-15]; `Username` length and Unicode [:17-18] — unannotated, and the string the entire ownership check compares [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73], so this mapping must give it the same **explicit bounded length** section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 1 requires of `Cart.CartId`, on the same evidence gate, rather than leaving the model's ownership key as `nvarchar(max)`; the **eight** annotated string lengths [:22], [:27], [:31], [:35], [:39], [:44], [:48], [:52] confirmed against the columns rather than assumed to have produced them, and `Email` [:56-61], which carries a regular expression and **no** length at all so its column length is knowable only from the database; the `OrderDetails` collection [:66] |
| `OrderDetail` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/OrderDetail.cs] | Key `OrderDetailId` [:5]; `UnitPrice` precision and scale [:9]; both relationships and their delete behaviour [:11-12]; any index on `OrderId` or `AlbumId` |

**And across all six, uniformly**: table and column names as the database actually spells them, every
column's **nullability**, every **default constraint**, every **check constraint**, every **index** with
its ordered key columns and uniqueness, and every relationship's **referential action** — that is, the
full output of the extraction of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction), facet for facet. **The acceptance
condition is section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3's: the DDL
generated from this mapping and the extracted schema differ in nothing that is not explained and
recorded as a deliberate change.** "Zero unexplained differences" is the bar, and this table is the
work that meets it — not a convention, and not an assumption that a `[StringLength]` attribute
describes the column it validates.

**One entity-level decision that is not a facet: concurrency on the album update.** The administration
edit marks the whole entity modified — `db.Entry(album).State = EntityState.Modified`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:91] — and **no concurrency token exists on
`Album` in any edition** ([09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md) owns the current-state finding, F-09-27,
including the partial-post and posted-key consequences). The target must therefore *choose*, because
porting the line unchanged into EF Core silently keeps a choice nobody made.

**Decided: last-write-wins is preserved, explicitly and with its consequence stated.** Two
administrators editing the same album concurrently means the later write wins in full and the earlier
one is lost without notice — which is exactly today's behaviour, so this is a **preserved contract**
rather than a new exposure, and the actor set is small and already fully privileged
([09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md) rates the pairing Medium on that basis). Adding a `rowversion`
token would be the better design in a system with concurrent editors; here it would be a schema
addition beyond the extracted baseline, a new column to map, a new failure mode to surface in the view
and a conflict-resolution interaction to design — for a surface with one privileged actor. **If it is
ever wanted**, the shape is fixed here so it is not re-argued: a `rowversion` column added as an
**additive migration in a later release** under the compatibility rule of section
[5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), mapped `IsRowVersion()` on `Album`, with the update path
catching the concurrency exception, re-reading current values and redisplaying the form with a conflict
message — and a test asserting that the second of two concurrent edits is rejected rather than applied.
**Scope note, so the decision is not read as more than it is:** F-09-27's other half — that both
administration actions bind the `Album` entity itself, so a partial post blanks the omitted columns —
is an input-shape question rather than a concurrency one, and [09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md)
remains its owner. Choosing last-write-wins does not address it and is not offered as doing so.

**The two contexts remain separate.** [12 §7.3](12-migration-blockers.md) records this as 05's
decision; it is taken, for the reason in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

**Both target one database.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the hosting and
provisioning; the *reason* belongs here, and it must be stated accurately because the obvious
justification is false. **It is not a foreign key between them — there is none** (section
[4.4](#44-what-the-cart-is-coupled-to--and-what-it-is-not)). Consolidation therefore removes an
**operational** dependency, not a relational one — and that distinction is this document's contribution,
because it is a property of the context and entity design.

**The trade itself — everything gained and everything given up — is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.5's,
and is not restated here.** It is a hosting consequence, it is enumerated there in full, and a partial
copy in this document would read downstream as a second and smaller assessment of the same decision.
A reader weighing whether to reverse the consolidation reads §6.5; a reader asking *why the reason is
not a foreign key* reads this section.

**Each context owns a separate migrations folder and a distinct migrations history table** —
`Data/Migrations/Catalog/**` and `Data/Migrations/Identity/**`, with two differently-named history
tables, configured per context in its `AddDbContext` registration. **The decision is fixed and is not
reopened here; what follows is why, on grounds that hold.**

**One thing a shared history table does *not* do, stated so it is not offered as the reason.** Pending
migrations are computed **per context, from the migrations discovered for that context** — the ones the
generator attributes to it, which in this design are the ones in its own folder and namespace — so rows
recording identifiers that context does not own are **not reported as pending to it**, and a shared
table would not by itself make either context's tooling report the other's work as outstanding. The
separation rests on the two consequences below instead.

- **Migration identifiers can collide, and a collision is silent in the worse direction.** A migration
  identifier is a timestamp prefix plus the name given at creation, and both sets are generated by the
  same tool by developers working to the same conventions — so two contexts each acquiring an
  `InitialCreate`, or each acquiring a same-named migration created in the same second, produce the
  **same identifier**. In one shared table that identifier is the primary key: the second application
  either fails on the key, or — if the row is already there — leaves the second context believing its
  own migration is **already applied** and skipping it, which is a schema that was never created and no
  error anywhere. Two tables make the collision impossible rather than unlikely.
- **A row cannot be attributed to a context, and attribution is what release and rollback need.** A
  shared table records identifiers with nothing saying which context applied them, so "what is the
  catalog schema's current state" is not answerable from the table, and neither a per-context rollback
  target nor an audit of who applied what can be reconstructed from it. With one table per context, each
  context's state is **independently and correctly readable**, which is the property the release process
  is built on.

**Verification that each context's bundle targets its own history table, and that each context reports
its own migration state after a release, is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s** — it owns the
release-side mechanism and the two context-specific bundles, so it owns the check that they landed
against the tables this section separates.

**Two folders in the one web project, not two migrations assemblies.** The distinction matters because
the two are easy to conflate and only one of them is true here: both migration sets live in the single
application project the target map fixes ([04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), in separate
folders under separate namespaces, and **no separate migrations assembly and no separate migrations
project exists**. What separates them is the folder, the namespace and the history table — nothing
about assembly boundaries. Every design-time and release invocation is therefore **context-qualified**,
naming the context explicitly rather than relying on a single-context default that does not apply here;
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the release-side mechanism and the fact that there are
**two** context-specific bundles rather than one.

**The data-protection key table belongs to the Identity context, and this is where that is placed.**
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §7.2 fixes the key ring's location, its protect-at-rest
behaviour, its rotation policy and its slot and revision isolation, and explicitly leaves **which
context owns the migration** to this document, because this document owns the context design. The
placement:

- **`ApplicationDbContext` additionally implements `IDataProtectionKeyContext`** and declares a
  `DbSet<DataProtectionKey>` for the key rows. The Identity context rather than the catalog one,
  because the key ring is authentication-adjacent state and because `ApplicationDbContext` is already
  the framework-shaped context whose model framework packages contribute to — the same reasoning that
  keeps the catalog model out of it in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), read in
  the other direction.
- **The table is `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`**, created by the **Identity context's migration set** in a
  dedicated final migration named `AddDataProtectionKeys`, and recorded in the **Identity context's
  history table**. It is therefore step 4 of the ordering in section
  [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and needs no separate DDL artifact, no third context and
  no third migration set — the two-context, two-set, two-history-table shape above is unchanged.
- **Runtime registration is `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()`**, in
  the service registration of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) step 5. The
  application **reads and writes** key rows and does not create the table, which is what keeps it
  inside the grants [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.6 allows it.
- **Why a dedicated final migration rather than folding it into the initial one.** The Identity
  baseline migration is diffed against the extracted source schema (section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)), and the key table
  exists in no source schema at all. Keeping it in its own migration keeps the baseline diff honest —
  the key table is a **deliberate net-new object**, recorded as one, rather than an unexplained
  difference in a diff that is required to have none.

### 4.6 Lazy loading — a resolution per site, not a policy

EF 6 populates navigation properties on demand through proxies. The target does not: an unloaded
reference navigation is `null`. The code that depends on this **compiles identically under both**, so
nothing announces the change.

**The decision is explicit eager loading or projection at each query site — not a lazy-loading proxy
package.** Two reasons: the affected set is small and fully enumerated below, so explicit loading is
*verifiable* in a way a global proxy behaviour is not; and a proxy package would re-create the exact
property that makes this blocker silent — a query whose loading behaviour is invisible at the call
site.

"Use eager loading" is a policy, not a plan. [12 F-12-15](12-migration-blockers.md) enumerated
**nine** sites in **three categories that need opposite treatment**. Each gets its own resolution.

**Why exactly these sites and no others.** EF 6 lazy loading requires the navigation to be `virtual`.
`Album.Genre` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:30], `Album.Artist` [:31],
`Album.OrderDetails` [:32] and `Cart.Album` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:17] are `virtual`;
`Genre.Albums` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:10] is **not**, which is why the genre-browse
page had to eager-load and is therefore unaffected.

**Category (a) — client-side dereference after materialization. Six sites; every one is a definite
break. Resolution: eager-load or project at the query.**

| # | Query | Dereference | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a1 | `storeDB.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:38] | `@Model.Genre.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:16], `@Model.Artist.Name` [:20] | Replace `Find` with a filtered single-result query carrying **`Include(a => a.Genre)` and `Include(a => a.Artist)`**. `Find` cannot take an `Include`, so the method call changes, not just its arguments |
| a2 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:32] | `model.Artist.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Details.cshtml:18], `model.Genre.Name` [:26] | Same change as a1. Note the sibling **list** action at [:22] already uses the typed `Include(a => a.Genre).Include(a => a.Artist)` and ports unchanged — which is why the admin list page is absent from this table and the admin detail page is in it |
| a3 | `storeDB.Carts.Single(item => item.RecordId == id).Album.Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:61-62] | `.Album.Title` on the same expression [:62] | **Project instead of loading**: select the title directly in the query, so no navigation is dereferenced client-side at all. This also fixes the unscoped read that [09 §6.2](09-security-assessment.md) records, because the projection carries the cart-id predicate |
| a4 | `GetCartItems()` — `ToList()` with no `Include` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-101] | `.Select(a => a.Album.Title)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-92] | The cart-summary path gets its **own projection query** returning count and titles, rather than materializing `Cart` entities and walking navigations. This is the highest-reach site: it renders from the shared layout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26], so a failure is **every page**, not one page |
| a5 | `GetCartItems()` via the cart view model [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:17-24] | `item.Album.Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:64], `@item.Album.Price` [:68] | The cart-page query carries **`Include(c => c.Album)`**. This is the one site where the view genuinely needs the entity graph, so `Include` rather than projection |
| a6 | `GetCartItems()` inside order creation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:129] | `orderTotal += (item.Count * item.Album.Price)` [:145] | **The financial one.** Resolution: compute the running total from `album.Price` — the album the same loop **already loads explicitly** at [:134] and already uses for `UnitPrice` at [:140] — instead of from the lazy navigation at [:145]. One loop, two ways of reaching the same price, and only one of them survives; the surviving one is already in the file. Acceptance is an order-total assertion in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) |

**Category (b) — navigation read inside a server-translated query. One site. Resolution: verify the
translation; do *not* add an `Include`.** `GetTotal` composes
`select (int?)cartItems.Count * cartItems.Album.Price` over the `DbSet` and calls `.Sum()` on the
resulting queryable [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:119-122]. The navigation is read
inside an expression the provider translates to SQL, so **no lazy load ever occurs** and the target
translates it too. Adding an `Include` here would load entities the query does not need and would be a
regression in the name of a fix. The required work is a **test that the query translates and returns
the same total**, not a code change. Listing this alongside category (a) would send the port to the
wrong fix, which is why the category exists.

**Category (c) — collection aggregates inside an `OrderByDescending`. Two sites, and they are two
*different* aggregates, which is why they get two different checks rather than one shared verdict.
Resolution: verify the translation and the result of each, and rewrite to a translatable form if either
fails.** The genre menu orders by a **nested `Sum`** — a `Sum` over each genre's albums of a `Sum` over
each album's order-detail quantities
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] — while the home page orders by a
**single-level `Count`**, `a.OrderDetails.Count()`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:29-32]. Calling both "the nested aggregate" is
what produces the wrong check at one of them, as the table below shows.

**What each runtime actually does with an expression like this, because the usual framing of it is
wrong.** It is often said that EF 6 quietly evaluates in memory whatever it cannot translate, so a
query that "worked" starts throwing on EF Core. That is a **category error**, and a plan built on it
looks for the wrong failure:

- **EF 6 does not partially client-evaluate a translated query.** A LINQ-to-Entities expression it
  cannot translate **fails**, at execution, with `NotSupportedException`. There is no silent fallback
  to substitute for it.
- **Silent partial client evaluation was EF Core's behaviour, in 1.x and 2.x only**, and it was removed
  in **EF Core 3.0** — "LINQ queries are no longer evaluated on the client" is that release's
  highest-impact documented breaking change. From 3.0 onwards, including the target, an untranslatable
  expression outside the final projection **throws `InvalidOperationException`**.
- So **both** runtimes fail loudly rather than falling back, and the migration risk is therefore **not**
  "it used to run in memory". What the source shows statically about the aggregate at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] is its shape: a nested `Sum` over a
  collection navigation inside a collection navigation, composed on the `DbSet` and ordered by — a form
  within EF 6's documented LINQ-to-Entities translation surface, with nothing in it (no local method
  call, no unmapped member) that would put it outside. **Whether it executes is not established by
  reading the source**, and this document asserts no runtime outcome: the source's actual behaviour on
  this page is recorded by the baseline capture of section
  [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage), and the per-edition build and run status is
  [10 §3.1](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s.

**The risk that is real is the SQL and the result, not the fallback — and it is not the same risk at the
two sites.** Both are correlated aggregates the provider evaluates in a subquery beneath an `ORDER BY`,
so both can differ in *shape* between the two providers: subquery versus lateral join, and whether the
aggregate is computed once or recomputed for the projection. What is **not** common to them is the
empty-collection behaviour, and that is the half a single shared verdict gets wrong:

| Site | Aggregate | Empty-collection behaviour | What its check has to establish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Genre menu** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] | Nested `Sum` — over `Genre.Albums`, of a `Sum` over `Album.OrderDetails` | **Real, at both levels. SQL `SUM` over no rows yields `NULL`, not `0`.** A genre with no albums and an album with no order details each produce a null the provider must turn into the `int` the expression is typed as — both `Sum` overloads here are over non-nullable `int`, so the null has nowhere to go in the CLR type. The outcomes available to a provider are a coalesce in the generated SQL, a substitution on materialization, or a materialization failure, and each provider decides for itself | Whether the query returns a row **at all** for a genre with no albums, and **where such a genre sorts**. SQL Server treats `NULL` as lowest, so it sorts **last** under `OrderByDescending` — the same position a provider that coalesces to `0` puts it in, which is why the two are indistinguishable without the assertion and why a genre silently *missing* from the menu is the failure to look for |
| **Home top six** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:29-32] | Single-level `Count` over `Album.OrderDetails` | **None. SQL `COUNT` over no rows yields `0`.** There is no null to propagate, no coalesce to get wrong and no materialization question, so the behaviour above **does not apply here** and a check written to look for it establishes nothing | Whether the **same six albums come back in the same order** as the baseline. The exposure here is **tie ordering**, not nulls: `OrderByDescending` over a count with **no tie-breaking key**, followed by `Take(count)` [:30-31], leaves the relative order of equal-count albums undefined, so a differently shaped subquery may return a different — and equally correct — sixth album whenever the sixth and seventh are tied |

**They also do not run with the same frequency, which is what decides where the caching
[08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) records as separate performance debt is worth adding.** The
genre menu renders from the shared layout
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:25], like site a4, so it executes on **every page
the layout renders**. The top-six query does not: `GetTopSellingAlbums` is a private method whose only
caller is `HomeController.Index` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:18,24], so it
executes on **the home page only**. Both are worth caching; only one of them is a cost on every request.

So the required work is stated as observation rather than repair: **inspect the generated SQL for both
sites once**, and assert the rendered result against the baseline for the case each site is actually
exposed to — the **empty-collection ordering** for the genre menu, with a fixture carrying a genre that
has no albums and an album with no order details, and the **six albums and their order** for the home
page, with a fixture whose order-detail counts are distinct so the expected result is determinate rather
than tie-dependent. The coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) carry the two, one
each, and neither is written as the other's. If a site does not translate, rewrite it as an explicit
grouped projection over `OrderDetails`; that is the contingency, not the expectation.

**One favourable detail that reduces the work.** The **string-based** `Include("Albums")`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:30] **remains valid** in the target, even
though the typed lambda form is the convention. It may be modernized for consistency; it does not have
to be.

### 4.7 The `Dispose` overrides must be removed

Two overrides in the migration source dispose objects the code currently constructs and therefore
currently owns:

| Override | Object disposed | Constructed at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:125-128] | `MusicStoreEntities` | field initializer [:15] |
| [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:324-331] | `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` | chained constructor [:19] |

([12 F-12-20](12-migration-blockers.md) records four across all three editions; the two above are the
migration source's.)

Today each is correct — the controller creates the object, so the controller disposes it, and the
account controller is even careful about it, null-guarding and nulling the field [:326-330].

**Resolution: delete both overrides.** There is no replacement construct; container-owned lifetimes
need no disposal from the consumer. **The reason this is a required step rather than a tidy-up is that
leaving them compiles.** `Dispose(bool)` still exists on the target's controller base class, so there
is no signature error and no warning, and the ownership violation is therefore invisible: the
container owns what it created, and a consumer disposing an injected instance is reaching outside its
own lifetime.

**What that violation does not license is a predicted crash, and the plausible version of this claim is
wrong.** The framework releases the controller — and so calls `Dispose` — **after** result execution,
and `DbContext.Dispose` is **idempotent**, so on today's call graph the disposal is a no-op and no
`ObjectDisposedException` follows. The defect is that the code asserts an ownership it does not have,
and whether that is observable is a property of the current call graph rather than of the design: the
moment any second consumer in the same scope holds the same instance — a view component, a service, a
filter, an action executing after the controller is released — the override disposes an object still in
use. [12 F-12-20](12-migration-blockers.md) states the same correction, and it is why the removal is
justified on ownership grounds rather than on a failure nobody has observed.

The account controller carries the sharper version, because its `UserManager` is one of three objects
its chained constructor builds [:19]. Once the container supplies all three, an override disposing the
middle one reaches an object other consumers may still hold. That override is deleted along with the
constructor, in the wholesale rewrite of section [9.2](#92-the-four-groups).

### 4.8 The service layer, and the two patterns deliberately not adopted

**`ShoppingCart` stops being a model and becomes a service.** Its business logic is real:
`CreateOrder` computes the order total, writes `OrderDetail` rows, sets `order.Total` and empties the
cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:125-158], and `MigrateCart` reassigns cart
ownership on sign-in [:184-193]. That is the one place in the application where business logic sits in
a model, so it is the one place worth extracting — to `Services/ShoppingCartService.cs`, registered
scoped, taking the catalog context and the HTTP context accessor by injection.

Three changes travel with the move:

1. **`HttpContextBase` becomes the framework's context type.** The class takes it as an explicit
   parameter [:21] and reads session through it [:161-180]; it never touches a static ambient context.
   That is the favourable finding of [12 P-12-01](12-migration-blockers.md) — `HttpContext.Current`
   appears nowhere in the repository — and it is why this move is a signature change rather than an
   architectural excavation.
2. **The dead `Controller` overload is dropped.**
   `public static ShoppingCart GetCart(MusicStoreEntities db, Controller controller)` [:29-32] takes a
   `System.Web.Mvc.Controller`, a type with no target equivalent — and it is **provably unreferenced**.
   All six call sites use the `HttpContextBase` overload [:21]:
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:35],
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:17], [:41], [:58], [:89] and
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:47]. **Deleting it has zero call-site
   impact**, which is materially cheaper than porting it ([12 P-12-02](12-migration-blockers.md)).
3. **The static factory pair collapses.** With the service injected and the cart id resolved from the
   accessor, `GetCart` stops being a static factory taking a context and becomes ordinary instance
   state.

**The order-creation path is rewritten, not relocated — it carries two defects that a move would carry
with it.** `CreateOrder` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:125-158] is the application's
only financial write, and it is the one method where "port it as it stands" is the wrong instruction.

**Defect one: an album lookup per cart line, and a price read that depends on lazy loading.** The loop
at [:132] calls `_db.Albums.Find(item.AlbumId)` at [:134] — a lookup per cart line, since
`GetCartItems` returns `Cart` entities with no album data [:98-101] — so an *n*-line cart issues **up to
*n*** album lookups on top of the cart read, fewer when a line repeats an album the context is already
tracking. It then reads the price a second time at [:145] through the `item.Album` navigation (site a6
of section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)).

**What that second read is, precisely, because the difference decides the fix.** `Find` returns a
**tracked** entity, and relationship fixup therefore populates `item.Album` with **that same tracked
instance** — so `UnitPrice` at [:140] and the running total at [:145] read **one object in memory**, not
two fresh database reads, and they **cannot** disagree with each other however the underlying row
changes mid-order. **Nor does the access break in the target.** The `Find` for that same item runs at
[:134] before the read at [:145] within the same iteration, and relationship fixup is a change-tracker
behaviour rather than a lazy-loading one, so `item.Album` is populated under EF Core as it is under EF 6.
This site is therefore **not** one of the silent-correctness breaks: what is real about it is the
**lookup-per-line query cost** and the **unguarded dereference of the `Find` result** at [:140], and both
are removed by the same resolution:

- **One query for every value the order needs, including its own delete keys**, before the loop: a
  projection over the cart rows, cart-id-scoped, returning **`(RecordId, AlbumId, Count, Price)` and the
  row's concurrency token** per line. The loop then reads from that result and performs **no** further
  database access, so the per-line lookups disappear and no navigation is dereferenced client-side at
  all. `UnitPrice` and the running total continue to be computed from **one value**, which is the
  preserved property rather than a new one.
- **`RecordId` and the token are in the projection because the deletion is keyed on them.** A projection
  of `(AlbumId, Count, Price)` alone carries no key, so the only ways to delete afterwards are to
  re-query the rows — which the round-trip claim below forbids — or to attach constructed stubs, which
  makes the delete a change-tracker operation over entities the projection never materialized. **Neither
  is used.** The deletion is a **set-based delete over exactly the `(RecordId, token)` pairs the
  projection returned**, per requirement 7 of section
  [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity): no attach, no second `SELECT`,
  and no `CartId`-scoped predicate that could take a row this transaction never read.
- **A missing album is validated rather than dereferenced — a defensive check, and stated as one.**
  Today `album.Price` at [:140] would throw a null reference if the album row were gone, and the
  administration delete removes an album without consulting the carts that hold it
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116-122]. **Whether that delete can
  actually leave an orphaned cart line is not established from the source code**: it depends on whether
  the real schema carries a foreign key from `Cart` to `Album` and on that constraint's referential
  action, which only the authoritative extraction of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 settles — a `NO ACTION` rule
  would make the delete fail instead, and a cascade would remove the cart lines with it. The validation
  is therefore required as a **defensive** measure pending that extraction, not as the remedy for a
  demonstrated data state: the projected line count must equal the cart line count, and a discrepancy
  fails the checkout with a message naming the unavailable item rather than throwing. **If the extraction
  shows the shortfall is impossible, the check stays** — it costs one comparison and it is the difference
  between a handled message and a null reference in the application's only financial write.
- **Acceptance is a bounded *read* count, a *stated* write-round-trip count, and an unchanged total — and
  the write count is not independent of cart size.** The read side is fixed: **exactly one** query
  resolves the cart lines and every price the order needs, issued **before** the loop, and the loop
  issues **no** database access. One is a reduction from two, not a restatement of today: the source
  reads the cart rows in `GetCartItems` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:129], [:98-101]
  and then reads them **again** in `EmptyCart`, whose deferred `Where` is enumerated by the `foreach`
  that removes them [:89-91]. The target deletes the rows it already read and **must not re-query them**.
  The write side must not be claimed fixed, because it is not. The unit of work contains **one
  order insert, *n* order-detail inserts and the removal of *n* cart lines** for an *n*-line cart
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:136-152], [:87-96]. Two things shape how many round
  trips that becomes, and **an earlier formulation of this document got the second one wrong**:
  - **The cart removal is one statement, not *n*.** Section
    [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 7 makes it a
    **single set-based delete** over the projected `(RecordId, token)` pairs, which is a command in its
    own right rather than *n* tracked deletions inside `SaveChanges`.
  - **The order insert and its detail inserts cannot share a command batch.** `SaveChanges` batches
    commands into fewer round trips, and the SQL Server provider caps a batch at `MaxBatchSize` — a
    **provider default of 42** unless the registration of section
    [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) sets one. But batching is bounded by **dependency**
    before it is bounded by size: each `OrderDetail` carries the order's **generated** `OrderId` as the
    value that relates it to the order (defect two below), so that value has to come **back** from the
    database before the dependent rows can be sent. The provider therefore splits the batch at that
    dependency regardless of `MaxBatchSize`, and the write is **at least two command batches for every
    cart, including a one-line cart**.
  - **The consequence for acceptance: `ceil((2n + 1) / MaxBatchSize)` is withdrawn.** It is not merely
    imprecise, it is wrong at the smallest input — it predicts one round trip for a one-line cart where
    the dependency forces two — and it counts *n* deletions that no longer exist as tracked commands.
    Nothing replaces it with another formula, because the exact number is a property of **the pinned
    provider's batching implementation**, not of arithmetic this document can perform.

  Acceptance is therefore three assertions, in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage):
  - **One SELECT for the whole write path and zero SELECT statements issued from inside the loop**,
    asserted by **counted statements** rather than by elapsed time — a per-line query is invisible in
    every functional assertion and cheap enough not to show up as latency on a small cart.
  - **A DML round-trip count that is measured against the pinned provider and then asserted as a
    recorded number.** The suite counts the statements the pinned provider version of
    [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) actually issues for a given cart size and `MaxBatchSize`, and
    that observed number becomes the assertion — so a later provider change that alters batching **fails
    the test** instead of quietly satisfying a formula. Three cases are required: a **one-line** cart,
    whose count must be **at least two** and is the case the withdrawn formula got wrong; a cart wholly
    inside one batch; and a cart sized **one line past** the boundary `MaxBatchSize` implies, whose count
    must be **strictly greater** than the case below it. That last pair is what distinguishes provider
    batching from a loop that saves per iteration, and the recorded numbers are stated in the test
    rather than here, because this document cannot observe them without running the application — which
    section [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible)
    forbids.
  - **The financial result unchanged**: `order.Total` and every `OrderDetail.UnitPrice` and `Quantity`
    match what the source produces for the same cart, to the cent.

**Defect two: the detail rows depend on key-generation timing that the target does not promise.**
`CheckoutController` adds the order and calls `CreateOrder` **before** any save
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44], [:48], [:51], so `order.OrderId` at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:139]
is still the unsaved default when it is copied into each `OrderDetail` — and because the detail sets
`OrderId` as a **scalar** and never sets the `Order` navigation, the rows are related to their order only
by a value that has not been generated yet. It works today because EF 6 fixes the relationship up during
`SaveChanges`; relying on that is relying on an implementation behaviour rather than on a stated
relationship, and it is silent when it is wrong. **Resolution: relate the detail to the order through
the aggregate** — construct each `OrderDetail` with its `Order` navigation set, or add it to the order's
`OrderDetails` collection [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:66] — so the relationship is declared
and the provider assigns the generated key to both sides. That removes the *ordering* defect; it does
**not** by itself make the unit atomic, which the next paragraph settles.

**The write is one explicit transaction, and the execution strategy owns it. This supersedes an earlier
formulation of this section, which offered the aggregate navigation and an explicit transaction as
alternatives and preferred the implicit one.** That preference cannot hold, and the reason is specific
rather than stylistic: the deletion of the cart lines is a **set-based, token-matched delete** over the
projected `(RecordId, token)` pairs (requirement 7 of section
[4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)), which executes as **its own
command** and therefore **outside** whatever implicit transaction `SaveChangesAsync` opens for the order
and its details. Two commands in two implicit transactions cannot commit or roll back together, so the
preferred path could not deliver the atomicity the whole paragraph claimed for it. The requirement is
therefore:

- **`strategy.ExecuteAsync` wrapping `BeginTransactionAsync`, in that order.** The context's execution
  strategy is obtained first and the transaction is opened **inside** the delegate it executes, so the
  strategy owns the retry boundary and can re-run the **whole** unit — projection, order insert, detail
  inserts, token-matched delete, commit — safely. Opening the transaction outside the strategy is the
  shape that makes the provider refuse to retry and throw instead (section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)), so the nesting order is part of
  the requirement rather than an implementation detail.
- **The aggregate navigation is still used inside that transaction**, because it is what makes the
  generated key reach the detail rows without a second `SaveChanges`. The two resolutions are therefore
  **complementary and both required**, not alternatives: the navigation fixes how the detail rows obtain
  the key, and the transaction fixes what commits together.
- **Everything the unit touches commits or rolls back once**: the order row, its detail rows, and the
  cart lines the projection read. Today's single `SaveChanges`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:51] achieves that incidentally for the rows
  it happens to track; the target achieves it deliberately for a set that includes a command
  `SaveChanges` does not carry.
- **The durable operation id and the `verifySucceeded` callback of section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) are mandatory on this path**, not
  optional as they were when the implicit-transaction alternative was preferred. A retried transaction is
  re-executable; that is not the same as correct, because the first attempt may already have committed.

**The token pairs need a transport, and an unbounded one is not a design.** The delete predicate has to
carry *n* `(RecordId, token)` pairs for an *n*-line cart, and neither an interpolated list nor an
unbounded parameter list is acceptable — the first violates the parameterization rule of section
[4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 2, and the second hits
the provider's parameter limit at a cart size nobody has bounded. So the carrier is specified:

- **Preferred: a table-valued parameter.** A single parameter carrying the pair set, joined against
  `Cart` in one statement. It is one round trip regardless of cart size, every value is a parameter, and
  the type it requires is a **deliberate net-new object** created by the pre-load catalog migration stage
  of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and recorded in the diff of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 with the other four.
- **Permitted alternative: a chunked parameterized `VALUES` list, at a stated bound.**
  `Checkout:DeleteChunkSize`, **default 200**, owner **Engineering**, options-bound and startup-validated
  with the values of section [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access). The
  projection is chunked at that size and **every chunk is issued inside the one transaction above**, so a
  cart larger than one chunk is still one atomic unit. The bound exists because the provider caps
  parameters per command; 200 pairs is two parameters per pair inside that cap with room to spare, and
  the number is Engineering's to revise against the pinned provider rather than a value this document
  measured.
- **The affected set is validated exactly, and the validation is the gate.** The **sum** of the affected
  counts across every chunk must equal **the projected line count** — not "at least", not "approximately".
  Fewer means a row changed underneath, which is requirement 7's stale-projection retry. **More** means
  the carrier or the predicate is wrong — a duplicated pair, a widened join — and the unit **aborts and
  rolls back** rather than committing an order whose cart deletion it cannot account for.

**Empty and stale submissions are rejected before anything is written, and the two are separated because
they have different causes.** This is the requirement that stops the most consequential failure available
to a concurrent checkout:

- **Empty.** If the projection returns **no line**, the submission is rejected with a handled message and
  **no order is created**. Without this rule, the loser of two distinct concurrent submissions — or the
  retry of a unit whose first attempt committed and emptied the cart — re-runs the projection against an
  emptied cart and creates an **order with no lines and a zero total**, which is one of the two
  undetectable states section [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)
  analyses. The operation id makes a *retry* unable to insert a second order; this rule is what stops a
  genuinely second *submission* inserting an empty one.
- **Stale.** If the projection returns lines but the token-matched delete's affected count falls short,
  the submission is not rejected — it is **retried from a fresh projection** under requirement 7, bounded
  by `Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries`, because the customer's late addition belongs **in** the order. A
  shortfall is contention, not an invalid submission, and conflating the two would either reject a valid
  purchase or accept a stale one.
- **Coverage** is section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) rows 10, 10a and 19a case (b): the
  unknown-commit-outcome case, two distinct concurrent submissions, and the concurrent add between the
  projection and the delete.

**This one is verified against a real SQL Server, not an in-memory provider.** Key generation,
identity-value assignment and relationship fixup are precisely the behaviours an in-memory provider
models differently, so a test that passes there proves nothing about the case at hand — which is why the
fixture of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) provisions a real
engine. The assertion is that a multi-line order's detail rows all carry the order's **generated**
`OrderId`, and that the confirmation number the redirect returns
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54] is that same value.

**Two patterns are deliberately not adopted, and the reasons are specific to this application rather
than general.**

**No repository abstraction over EF Core.** `DbContext` is already a unit of work and `DbSet<T>` is
already a queryable collection; the domain has six entities
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] and there is exactly one data source and no
outbound service dependency ([11 §4.3](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). A repository layer would add
indirection with no test seam `DbContext` does not already provide — and the suite of section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) is HTTP-level black-box, so it does not need one.
The one place a genuine seam is wanted is the cart's business logic, and that is what
`ShoppingCartService` is.

**No uniform service layer across the six controllers.** Five of the six are thin: they query, build a
view model and return a view. `HomeController` is 34 physical lines
([08 §3.1](08-technical-debt-register.md)). Wrapping each in a service would produce five pass-through
classes and one real one. The real one is extracted; the pass-throughs are not written.

### 4.11 Result-set bounds and per-request query cost

Two query-shape problems survive the lazy-loading resolutions of section
[4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy) untouched, because neither is a
lazy-loading problem: **two list endpoints materialize their whole table**, and **two components query
on every page of the application**. [08 §5.3](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns the first as recorded
debt and [08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) the second; this section owns the target query shape,
because that is a property of the port.

**"Add paging" is not a plan either.** Paging without a total order returns overlapping and skipped
rows across pages, and paging without a decided page size and a decided projection is three unfinished
decisions wearing one name. Both endpoints are therefore specified completely.

| | **Genre browse** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:18] | **Administration album list** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:22-24] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **As-is** | `storeDB.Genres.ToList()` — the entire genre table, no ordering, no bound | `db.Albums.Include(a => a.Genre).Include(a => a.Artist).OrderBy(a => a.Price).ToList()` — the entire album table with two joins |
| **Stable ordering** | **`Name`, then `GenreId`.** There is no ordering at all today, so the rendered order is whatever the provider returns; ordering by `Name` makes the list deterministic *and* alphabetical, which is what a browse list of genres wants, and `GenreId` is the tiebreaker that makes the order **total** | **`Price`, then `AlbumId`.** `Price` is preserved as the primary sort because it is the shipped order [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:23] and administrators may rely on it — but it is **not unique**, so paging on it alone reorders ties between requests and drops or duplicates rows at page boundaries. `AlbumId` is the unique tiebreaker |
| **Projected fields** | `GenreId` and `Name` only. The view renders the name and a link built from it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Index.cshtml:13] and reads nothing else — notably not `Description` or the `Albums` collection | `AlbumId`, `Title`, `Price`, `Genre.Name`, `Artist.Name` — exactly the five values the table renders [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Index.cshtml:45-59]. Projecting them **removes both `Include` calls**: the joins remain in the SQL, the entity graph does not come back over the wire |
| **Mechanism** | Server-side `Skip`/`Take` over the ordered, projected query, with the page number bound from the query string and validated, plus a scalar `CountAsync` for the total | The same. Not client-side paging, and not a `ToList()` followed by an in-memory `Take` — both of which read the whole table and defeat the point |
| **Page size** | Configuration-bound, one key per list under a paging options section, **defaulting to 25** | Configuration-bound, **defaulting to 25** |
| **Acceptance** | The response contains at most one page of genres regardless of table size; the query count is **two** (page and total); the count text still reports the **total**, not the page — see below | At most one page of albums; query count **two**; the rendered columns and their truncation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Index.cshtml:48], [:51] are unchanged; the three per-row action links resolve to the same album ids [:57-59] |

**Who owns the page size, stated because it is the row most likely to be assumed.** The *mechanism*,
the *ordering* and the *projection* are this document's — they are correctness properties. The **value**
is a product decision: 25 is the default this document specifies so that the port is complete and not
waiting on a meeting, and **Product** is the approval owner for changing it. It is configuration rather
than a constant precisely so that changing it is not a code change.

**One consequence that a paging change quietly breaks.** The genre view renders "Select from
`@Model.Count()` genres" [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Index.cshtml:8] — a count of the
materialized collection, which under paging would report the page size and read as a shrinking catalog.
The total from the scalar count query is carried on the view model and rendered there instead, so the
sentence keeps meaning what it says. This is the reason the query count is two rather than one.

**The every-page pair, and the budget it is held to.** The shared layout renders exactly two child
actions [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:25-26], so `GenreMenu` and `CartSummary`
run on every rendered page — and only those two. `HomeController.GetTopSellingAlbums` does **not**
(section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy) category (c)).

**`CartSummary` is the worse of the two, and it is worse in three separate ways.** The action
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:86-98] materializes every `Cart` row the
visitor owns, because `GetCartItems` ends in `ToList()`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-101]; it then projects titles through the lazy
`Album` navigation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-93]; and it
**enumerates that deferred sequence twice** — once for `Count()` [:95] and again for `Distinct()`
[:96]. The first enumeration is what triggers one album lookup per cart line; the second walks the whole
sequence again. And the titles are unbounded: they are joined into a `title` attribute on the layout's
cart link [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:4], so a visitor with a large
cart adds their entire cart's text to **every page they load**.

**Resolution: title rendering is kept and bounded, and the component is held to one round trip.**
Removing the tooltip would be the cheaper fix and is rejected — it is a visible feature, and section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) exists for deltas that are worth their cost, which its
removal is not. Instead:

- **One cart-id-scoped query, projected, no entities materialized and no navigation dereferenced
  client-side**, returning the row count and the bounded distinct title list. The sequence is enumerated
  **once**.
- **The count keeps its current meaning exactly.** Today's badge is `Count()` over the projected title
  sequence [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:95] — the number of **cart
  rows**, not the sum of their quantities, which is a different number that `GetCount` computes
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:103-112] and the cart page uses. The port must not
  quietly switch the badge to the summed quantity while "improving" the query; the row count is the
  preserved contract.
- **The titles are capped at ten**, ordered and distinct as today
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:93], [:96], with the tooltip indicating
  that more items exist when the cap is reached. Ten bounds the per-page payload contribution to a
  constant regardless of cart size, which is the property being bought, and the cap is approved delta 17
  (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)).
- **Acceptance: exactly one database round trip per rendered page for this component**, asserted for a
  cart with more lines than the cap, and a payload contribution that does not grow with cart size.
  Should the projected form not translate to a single statement — the count and the capped title list
  are two aggregates over the same rows, which is the case worth checking rather than assuming — the
  fallback is **two** explicitly bounded queries and the asserted number becomes two; either way the
  number is **fixed and independent of cart size**, and the generated SQL is inspected once, on the same
  rule category (c) applies to its aggregates.

**`GenreMenu` is bounded already and is left bounded; its cost is the aggregate, and the acceptance
criteria for the cache that removes it are this document's.** It takes nine
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52], so its payload is fixed; its cost is the
nested aggregate, whose translation is category (c)'s subject and whose per-page repetition is the
caching case [08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) records as debt.

**[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the caching mechanism and this document does not
restate or re-decide it** — the store, the one global versioned key, the absolute expiration window, the
post-commit stamp bump, per-key single-flight and the failure fallback are all specified there.
**What this document owns is the query-shape requirement and the acceptance criteria**, because a
per-request round-trip count is a property of the port:

- **When the component is not served from the cache it issues exactly one query**, and its generated SQL
  is inspected once, on the same rule category (c) applies to its aggregate.
- **Acceptance is four criteria, and all four are required:**
  1. **Exactly one database read on a cold miss under N concurrent requests** against one instance — not
     N. This is the criterion the single-flight requirement exists to satisfy, and the only one that
     distinguishes a cold start from a stampede against the nested aggregate.
  2. **Zero database reads on a warm hit.**
  3. **Exactly one database read after the absolute expiration window elapses**, and none before it.
  4. **Exactly one database read after each invalidation event** — the committed-write paths
     [08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) enumerates, including the administrator album edit that
     moves an album's `GenreId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:86-92] and
     so reclassifies historical order quantities.
- **A no-cache implementation fails these criteria, and stating them is what makes that true.** Serving
  the aggregate from the database on every render passes every functional assertion in section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) — the menu still shows the right nine genres — while failing criteria 2,
  3 and 4 outright and criterion 1 under concurrency. So the criteria are asserted on **measured
  database reads**, the count of round trips the component issues, and never on response content: content
  cannot tell a cached render from an uncached one.

### 4.12 Resiliency, timeouts, cancellation and async data access

The current data access has none of these properties and does not need them: it runs synchronously
against a database file attached by a **local** instance under integrated security
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13], where a transient network fault is not a category of event
that occurs at all. **Against Azure SQL it is a routine one** — the service reconfigures, throttles and
fails over as a matter of normal operation — so a policy that is unnecessary today is mandatory in the
target, and it is set explicitly rather than left at provider defaults.

**Transient-fault handling.** Both `AddDbContext` registrations (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) configure the SQL Server provider's execution strategy with
**`EnableRetryOnFailure`**, and its parameters are stated rather than defaulted: a
`maxRetryCount` of **5**, a `maxRetryDelay` bounded by `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds`, and the provider's
default set of transient error numbers.

**`maxRetryCount` is a count of *retries*, not of attempts, and an earlier statement of this paragraph
called it five attempts. That was wrong and is corrected here, because the envelope depends on it.** The
provider performs the initial execution and then **up to `maxRetryCount` further executions**, so a
value of 5 permits **five retries — six executions in total**. The worst-case wall-clock envelope **one
command** can therefore occupy is:

| Term | Bound | Contributes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executions of that one command | `1 + Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` = **6** | Each bounded by `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds` = **30 s** → **180 s** |
| Waits between those executions | `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` = **5** | Each bounded by `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds` → **5 × that value** |

**That envelope is per command, and an earlier revision of this section called it the bound on "a single
request". The figure is right and the label was wrong, which matters because the two differ by more than
an order of magnitude.** An execution strategy retries **the operation it wraps**, so the arithmetic above
bounds **one** command's transient-retry budget. A checkout is not one command: section
[4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) specifies a projection, an
order-and-details save, one or more token-matched delete chunks, a commit and — on an unknown outcome —
a `verifySucceeded` lookup, **and** an outer stale-projection restart bounded by
`Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries`. Each of those commands carries its **own** per-command envelope, and the
outer restart multiplies the whole set. A per-command bound validated against the platform request timeout
therefore does not bound the request, and the deliberate consequence is stated below rather than left to
be inferred.

- **`Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount`, default 5, owner Engineering** — five retries, six executions.
- **`Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds`, default 5, owner Engineering.** This default is **lower than the
  provider's own 30-second maximum delay deliberately.** At 30 seconds the arithmetic above gives
  `180 + 5 × 30` = **330 seconds** for a single command, which is longer than a hosted request is
  plausibly allowed to run and would leave the request terminated by the platform mid-retry — the caller
  receiving a platform error rather than the handled failure this section exists to produce. At 5 seconds
  it gives `180 + 25` = **at most 205 seconds per command**. **Neither figure is compared against an
  assumed platform bound here**: [06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires the selected
  host's actual request timeout to be **read from the platform and recorded**, and the startup validation
  below is what turns this reduction from a judgement into a checked constraint.
- **The per-command envelope is a startup-validated constraint, not a comment.**
  `1 + Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` multiplied
  by `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds`, plus `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` multiplied by `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds`,
  must be **strictly less** than the platform request timeout
  [06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records for the selected host. The comparison is
  performed by the options validation of section
  [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) against a
  configured `Data:PlatformRequestTimeoutSeconds`, and **startup fails** if it does not hold — so a
  later increase to any one of the three values cannot silently produce a command the platform kills.
  **Owner: Engineering for the three values, [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) for the platform
  bound they are validated against.**

**The total unit-of-work deadline, which is the bound the request actually has. Owner: Engineering, with
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owning the platform bound it is validated against.** The
per-command envelope cannot be composed into a request bound by tightening it, because the composition is
a **product** and not a sum: the nested worst case is
`(1 + Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries)` outer attempts × the number of commands in one attempt × the
per-command envelope, which at the defaults above is `4 × 5 × 205 s` = **4,100 seconds** — twenty times
any plausible request timeout. **No assignment of the three per-command values fixes that**, because
reducing them far enough to make the product fit would leave a single command unable to survive one
transient fault, which is the entire purpose of the policy. The requirement is therefore a second,
outermost bound:

- **`Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds`, default 60, owner Engineering.** A **wall-clock deadline for the
  whole logical operation**, established once when the unit of work is entered and **not** reset by any
  retry, restart or command boundary inside it.
- **It is enforced by a linked cancellation source, so it covers every term of the product.** A
  `CancellationTokenSource` is created for the unit, bounded by this value, **linked** to the request's
  own token under the cancellation rules stated later in this section, and its token is the one every
  read, every pre-commit command, every inter-retry wait and
  every outer concurrency restart observes. The **commit boundary alone remains detached**, exactly as
  rule 2 below states and for the reason it states: cancelling a commit does not undo it. So the deadline
  bounds the whole unit **except** the bounded commit itself, and the residual is
  `Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds + Data:CommitTimeoutSeconds` — which is the figure the platform
  comparison below uses, rather than the deadline alone.
- **Expiry is a handled failure, not a dropped request.** The unit is cancelled, the explicit transaction
  rolls back, the caller receives the same handled message as retry exhaustion, and the event is logged
  with the operation id so an operator can distinguish a deadline expiry from a concurrency exhaustion.
  Where the outcome of a commit already in flight is unknown at expiry, it is settled by the
  `verifySucceeded` path (rule 3 below) and **never** reported as a failure on the strength of the
  deadline having passed.
- **Startup validates the full nested product against this deadline and the deadline against the
  platform.** The options validation of section
  [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) computes the
  product above from the configured values and applies **four** checks; every one whose condition is
  stated as a requirement must hold or **startup fails**:

| # | Check | Why it fails startup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds` is present and positive | An absent deadline leaves the nested product as the only bound, and the product exceeds any request timeout. It is the mechanism, so it cannot be optional |
| 2 | `Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds + Data:CommitTimeoutSeconds` is **strictly less** than `Data:PlatformRequestTimeoutSeconds` | Otherwise the platform kills the request before the deadline can produce a handled failure, which is the outcome the whole section exists to prevent. The commit term is included because it is the one interval the deadline deliberately does not cover |
| 3 | The computed nested product and the deadline are both **reported**, and the **smaller of the two is recorded as the binding bound**, together with the **effective** retry budget the deadline leaves | **An earlier revision of this row called the *larger* of the two the binding bound, which is arithmetically wrong and is corrected here.** Two bounds applied to one interval bind at their **minimum**: the deadline cancels the unit at 60 seconds whatever the retry policy would have permitted, so the effective worst case is `min(product, deadline)` and at the defaults that is the **deadline**. The report exists because the deadline truncating the product also truncates each command's retry budget — a 30-second command timeout and a 5-second delay fit **two** executions into a 60-second deadline, not the six `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` implies — and an operator who is not told that believes they have five retries when they have one |
| 4 | `Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds` is **strictly greater** than `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds` | A deadline that cannot admit even a **single** command execution cancels the unit part-way through its first command, so no command ever reaches its own timeout and the resiliency policy above becomes unreachable configuration rather than a policy. This is the check that catches the misconfiguration check 3 only reports: shortening the deadline far enough silently disables retrying altogether, and there is no value of the three per-command settings that repairs it |

  **Checks 3 and 4 are a pair, and neither replaces the other.** Check 3 makes the relationship between
  the two bounds **explicit at the moment either one changes** — an operator who raises the retry count
  sees the product move, sees that the deadline still binds, and sees how many retries actually fit —
  while check 4 is the one that **fails** when that truncation has gone far enough to remove the
  resiliency the policy claims. Reporting without the failing check would let a deadline of five seconds
  ship as a log line; failing without the report would leave every intermediate value silently changing
  the effective retry count.

**Ownership**: the policy and its values are this document's, because they are a property of the context
registration; [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the platform behaviour the policy exists to
absorb, and [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) owns the risk if the values prove wrong under load. No
claim is made here about how often a retry will actually be needed; the envelope is an arithmetic bound
on the configured values, not a measurement.

**Retrying and explicit transactions do not compose, and this is the trap.** An execution strategy
retries the *operation it wraps*; a user-initiated transaction spans several operations, so the strategy
refuses to retry inside one and throws instead. That matters here because section
[4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) **requires** an explicit
transaction for the order write — it is no longer one of two options there — and section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) uses one for the cart merge. **The resolution in both cases
is the nesting order**: the strategy is obtained first and the transaction is opened *inside* the
delegate it executes, never the reverse:

| Operation | Retry-safe? | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any single `SaveChangesAsync` or query — every read path in the application | **Yes**, by the strategy itself | Nothing further to do. `SaveChanges` is already atomic in its own implicit transaction |
| The order write — **one explicit transaction, mandatory** (section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)) | **Not implicitly, and re-executability alone is not sufficient** | **The explicit transaction is not optional here, and an earlier revision of this row said the implicit alternative \"avoids the explicit transaction altogether and is preferred for exactly this reason\". That is withdrawn**: the token-matched cart delete of section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 7 is its **own command**, so it cannot share the implicit transaction `SaveChangesAsync` opens, and no implicit-only shape can commit the order, its details and that delete as one unit. The rule is therefore the nesting order: `strategy.ExecuteAsync` is entered **first** and `BeginTransactionAsync` is called **inside** its delegate, so the strategy owns the retry boundary and re-runs the whole unit. Re-executability still does not make the retry *correct*, for the reason the paragraph below this table states, so the path additionally requires the **durable operation id and the `verifySucceeded` commit-verification callback** specified there — both mandatory rather than conditional. The aggregate navigation is retained **inside** that transaction because it is what propagates the generated key to the detail rows; it is complementary to the transaction, not an alternative to it |
| The cart merge inside sign-in (sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) | **Not implicitly**, and it is already specified as retried | Invoked through the execution strategy, and **idempotent by construction rather than by re-reading**: the merge is an upsert against the unique index of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), keyed on the anonymous cart id, so an attempt that committed unobserved makes the next attempt a no-op or an update — never a duplicate. That is what makes it the one write in the application that needs **no** operation id: its own key **is** the invariant. **This survives the relative-update requirement of section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity), and the reason is specific**: a relative `Count = Count + @n` is not idempotent on its own, but the merge **consumes** the source row — under `UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK` inside its own transaction, per requirement 5 of that section — in the same transaction as the increment it contributes, so a committed-but-unacknowledged attempt leaves nothing for the retry to add, and the exact affected count that requirement asserts is what establishes that rather than assuming it. The alias row is an insert-if-absent on `SourceCartId`, and requirement 6 makes it the row two concurrent merges of one source **serialize on**, so it is idempotent for the same reason |
| The cart quantity statements — add and remove (section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) | **Yes, by the strategy — and mechanised rather than accepted, which reverses an earlier position in this table** | Each is a single token-conditional statement in its own implicit transaction, so the strategy retries it. **A relative update is not idempotent, so a commit whose acknowledgement is lost could be applied twice.** An earlier revision of this row accepted that as a bounded, *visible* exposure, on the ground that **the response renders the committed value**. **That acceptance is withdrawn**, because the premise fails in exactly the case it was invoked for: the fault that triggers the replay is the same fault class that loses the **final** acknowledgement, and when that happens no response is rendered at all, so nothing displays the committed value and the over-count is invisible to the only party who could reverse it. Section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 4 therefore specifies a **durable cart-mutation operation ledger** written in the mutation's own transaction: a replay is detected by primary key and becomes a **no-op returning the committed result**, and an unknown outcome is settled by **reading the ledger** through the same `verifySucceeded` callback the order write uses. **The alternative remains rejected**: an absolute read-modify-write *is* retry-idempotent, but it loses an acknowledged add under ordinary concurrency with no fault at all, silently and unboundedly. **Owner: Engineering** |
| The data-migration executor, section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) | **Its own contract, and deliberately not the strategy's** | It owns one transaction per table and reports a **resumable** failure at the last committed table boundary. An execution strategy retrying a table load silently would defeat the checkpoint, which is the artifact an operator actually reasons about; so the tool's retry semantics are the checkpoint and a re-invocation, not an automatic retry |
| The seed command, section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) | **Its own contract** | One transaction across the three catalog tables, and **no retry at all**: a failed seed exits `4` with the transaction rolled back and is simply re-run, which is safe because the target is non-production by construction |

**A retry after an *unknown* commit outcome is the case the table above cannot solve by re-execution,
and the order write is where it bites.** A transient fault can arrive **after** the commit was sent and
**before** its acknowledgement returns, so the first attempt **may already have committed**. A delegate
that merely re-reads the cart and rewrites derived rows then produces one of two wrong outcomes on its
second run: a **second order** for the same submission, or — if the committed first attempt already
emptied the cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:87-96], [:154] — an **order with no
lines and a zero total**. Neither is detectable afterwards from the data, and the customer has one
confirmation number [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54] either way. The
requirement is therefore two mechanisms rather than a stronger delegate:

- **A durable operation id, generated by the application and constrained by a unique index.** A single
  identifier is generated **once per checkout submission, before the first attempt** — by the
  application, not by the database, and **not regenerated per attempt** — carried in the unit of work
  and persisted on the `Order` row in a dedicated column that the target model declares and the catalog
  migration creates with a **unique** index. A second insert of the same logical order therefore
  **cannot commit**: the constraint rejects it. The column is a deliberate net-new object, recorded as
  one in the schema diff of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 exactly as the key table of
  section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) is, and it is `null` for every
  migrated historical order, so the index is filtered to exclude nulls.
- **Commit verification, not inference.** The transaction is invoked through the execution strategy's
  overload that takes a **`verifySucceeded`** callback, and that callback looks the operation id up. If
  the row is present the first attempt committed, and the strategy reports **success with the existing
  order** rather than retrying; if it is absent nothing committed and the retry proceeds from the start.
  **The unknown outcome is settled by evidence in the database, never by assumption.**

**Scope, so this is not read as request de-duplication.** The operation id makes **the retry** of one
submission idempotent. A visitor who submits the checkout form twice is making two submissions and gets
two orders — which is today's behaviour and is preserved. **Acceptance**: with a fault injected between
the commit and its acknowledgement, the checkout produces **exactly one** order, with its lines and its
total intact, and returns the confirmation number of that order — asserted in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 10 against the real engine of section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), because an in-memory provider has no
commit to interrupt. **Owner: Engineering**, with [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) owning the risk if
the mechanism is descoped.

**Timeouts are bounded on both axes, because an unbounded one is a request that never returns — and
each bound is a named key with a default and an owner rather than an adjective.** The **command
timeout** is set on each context registration, to a value that fails a request faster than the
platform's own request timeout would, so a slow query surfaces as a handled error with a log entry
rather than as a dropped connection with nothing to read.

| Configuration key | Applies to | Default | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds` | Both `AddDbContext` registrations in the web application | **30** | **Engineering**; must remain below the platform request timeout, which [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns |
| `Data:CommitTimeoutSeconds` | The bounded internal commit boundary defined below | **15** | **Engineering** |
| `Data:UnitOfWorkDeadlineSeconds` | The **total** unit-of-work deadline defined above — every command, wait, transaction and outer concurrency restart of one logical operation, the detached commit boundary excepted | **60** | **Engineering**; validated against `Data:PlatformRequestTimeoutSeconds`, which [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns |
| `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` | Both registrations' execution strategy | **5** — five **retries**, six executions | **Engineering**; [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) owns the risk if it proves wrong under load |
| `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds` | Both registrations' execution strategy | **5**, reduced from the provider's 30-second maximum for the envelope reason stated above | **Engineering** |
| `Data:PlatformRequestTimeoutSeconds` | The startup envelope validation above; not passed to the provider | **No default** — supplied from the platform value [06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records, and startup fails if it is absent | **[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)** owns the value; **Engineering** owns the validation |
| `Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries` | The order write's stale-projection retry, section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 7 | **3** | **Engineering** |
| `Cart:MaxMutationRetries` | The cart mutation's contention retry — the re-take-the-decision path of section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 2, and the merge's rollback-and-retry fallback in requirement 5 | **3** | **Engineering** |
| `Checkout:DeleteChunkSize` | The chunked-`VALUES` alternative to the table-valued carrier, section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted); unused when the table-valued carrier is chosen | **200** | **Engineering**; revised against the pinned provider's parameter limit, not against a figure measured here |
