| `Cart:MaxQuantityPerLine` | The business maximum in the bound predicate of section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 3, resolved with the extracted column maximum into one effective bound | **No default** — mandatory, and startup fails if it is absent or non-positive | **Product** owns the value; **Engineering** owns the enforcement |
| `MigrateData:CommandTimeoutSeconds` | `tools/migrate-data`, every sub-command of section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) | **3600** | **Operations**, on the data owner's advice — a table load legitimately outruns any web request |
| `SeedSampleData:CommandTimeoutSeconds` | `tools/seed-sample-data`, section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) | **600** | **Operations** |

Every one of those is bound through the options pattern of section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration), so a value
changes without a code change, and each is **validated at startup** — a non-positive value fails the
host rather than silently meaning "no timeout". **The connection timeout** must be bounded for the same
reason; it is the connection string's `Connect Timeout` keyword, whose content
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns, and this document's requirement on it is that it be
**present and no greater than `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds`** — an unbounded connect attempt inside a
bounded command budget makes the command bound unenforceable.

**Cancellation is propagated to reads and pre-commit work, and detached across the commit.** The two
halves are stated as separate requirements because a single "propagate the request token to every EF
call" cannot coexist with "a commit in flight is never aborted" — the token would abort it. The
boundary between them is therefore explicit:

1. **Every read and every pre-commit call receives the request's `CancellationToken`** — or, inside a
   unit of work, the **linked** token of the total unit-of-work deadline above, which carries the
   request's cancellation as well as the deadline's. Actions accept the request token as a parameter,
   controllers and view components pass it into `ShoppingCartService` and into EF Core, and no such call
   site substitutes `CancellationToken.None`. A client that disconnects mid-request therefore stops
   costing a database round trip, which matters most for the two every-page components of section
   [4.9](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost).
2. **The commit runs inside a bounded internal commit boundary with the request token detached.** The
   `SaveChangesAsync` or transaction commit that closes a unit of work is passed a token from a source
   created **for that commit alone** and bounded by `Data:CommitTimeoutSeconds` — **not** linked to the
   request token. A client disconnect therefore cannot abort a commit in flight, because cancelling a
   commit does not undo it: it only removes the caller's knowledge of whether it happened, which is the
   exact state the operation id above exists to resolve. The boundary is bounded rather than infinite so
   that a hung commit still ends.
3. **An outcome left unknown by that boundary is settled by the verify path**, never guessed and never
   logged as a success. For the order write that is the `verifySucceeded` lookup; for the cart merge it
   is the upsert's own key.

**Data access is asynchronous throughout the web application.** Today it is entirely synchronous —
`ToList`, `Find`, `Single`, `Sum` and `SaveChanges` with no asynchronous counterpart anywhere in the
data paths [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-122],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:18], [:30-31], [:38]; what asynchrony MVC 5 does
have is entirely Identity-facing ([01 §5.5](01-architecture-overview.md) owns the posture) — which
blocks a request thread for the duration of every round trip. Against a network database that is the difference between
a thread pool that absorbs a latency spike and one that starves during it. The target policy:

- **Every EF Core I/O call in the web application is the asynchronous form** — `ToListAsync`,
  `SingleOrDefaultAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `CountAsync`, `SumAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync` — with the
  request token passed, and the enclosing action, view-component and service method asynchronous with it.
- **No synchronous-over-asynchronous bridging.** `.Result` and `.Wait()` appear **nowhere in any
  edition** today — `git grep -n -E '\.Result\b|\.Wait\(\)' -- 'src/*.cs'` returns nothing (Appendix A)
  — so there is no sync-over-async debt to unwind and none is introduced; a call chain that cannot be
  made asynchronous end to end is a design problem to fix rather than to bridge.
- **`async void` is not used for any of it.** The one occurrence in the repository is the provisioning
  path section [10.1](#101-what-it-is-today) retires, and its unobservable-failure property is the
  reason.
- **The one-time tooling is explicitly exempt.** `tools/migrate-data`, `tools/seed-sample-data` and
  `tools/provision-admin` are single-purpose console programs with one caller and no thread-pool
  pressure to relieve; synchronous data access there is simpler to reason about and to fail cleanly,
  and the exemption is stated so that a reviewer does not read it as an oversight.

### 4.13 The cart is one concurrency domain, keyed by cart identity

**Four different code paths write the same `Cart` rows, and specifying each one as individually safe is
not the same as making them safe against each other.** Sections
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and
[4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) each fix one writer — the
merge, and the order write — and each is correct in isolation. This section is the missing half: the
four writers are **one concurrency domain, keyed by cart identity**, and the requirements below are
stated once here so that no writer is designed against a different rule.

**The four writers, and the interleaving each one loses data to.** Every shape below is the source's,
verified at its line:

| Writer | What it does today | The interleaving that loses data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Add** — `AddToCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:34-58] | Resolves the row with `SingleOrDefault` on `(CartId, AlbumId)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:37-39], then inserts [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:44-52] or increments the loaded entity's `Count` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:57]; the caller commits [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:45] | **A lost increment.** Two adds read `Count = 1`, both compute 2, both write 2. The customer added two copies and one was acknowledged and discarded. The unique index of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) does not help: both writers update the **same existing row**, so no constraint is violated |
| **Remove** — `RemoveFromCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:61-85] | Resolves with `Single` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:64-66], then decrements the loaded entity [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:74] or removes the row [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:79] | The same lost update in the other direction, and — because the resolution is `Single` — a **concurrent loser throws** rather than reporting an already-removed line |
| **Merge** — `MigrateCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193] | Enumerates the anonymous cart's rows and rewrites `CartId` on each [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:190] | **A stranded row under a dead key.** A request that resolved the anonymous GUID *before* the merge enumerated the cart writes to that GUID afterwards, and nothing reads that GUID again — the row exists, is acknowledged to the customer, and is invisible to its owner |
| **Checkout** — `CreateOrder` plus `EmptyCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:125-158], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:87-96], committed once [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44-51] | Reads the cart lines [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:129], derives `OrderDetail` rows and the order total from them, then deletes whatever the deferred `Where` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:89] re-enumerates | **A silently deleted purchase.** An add that commits *after* the projection but *before* the delete is acknowledged to the customer, is not in the order, and is then deleted with the rest of the cart. One transaction does not help: the delete is scoped by `CartId`, so it takes rows the transaction never read |

**The unique index and the principal-derived key were both necessary and neither is sufficient.** The
index of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) prevents a duplicate **pair**; it does
not serialize two updates of one row. The key derivation in that same section stops an unauthenticated
request resolving another identity's cart; it does not redirect a request that resolved the *old*
anonymous key. Both remaining holes are closed below, and every requirement here is a **target-state
requirement with a named owner**, not a description of the source.

**Seven requirements follow, in the order they depend on each other**: the concurrency token (1), the
single token-conditional statement that every mutation becomes (2), the quantity bound that statement
carries (3), the durable ledger that makes a replayed mutation a no-op (4), the merge's locked
consumption of its source rows (5), the handoff that keeps a retired cart id resolvable and re-resolves
every writer (6), and the checkout's keyed, token-matched delete (7).

**Requirement 1 — `Cart` carries a `rowversion` concurrency token. Owner: Engineering, with the data
owner approving the added column.** Mapped `IsRowVersion()` on the entity, created by the **pre-load**
catalog migration of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) so that it exists before any
row is loaded, and recorded as a **deliberate net-new object** in the schema diff of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 on exactly the same terms as the
operation-id column of section
[4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access).

**This is the opposite decision from `Album`'s, and the difference is the actor and the loss.** Section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) deliberately preserves last-write-wins on
the album update, because there the actors are two privileged administrators overwriting each other's
edit of the same field, that is the source's behaviour, and the loss is recoverable by re-editing.
Here the losers are two customers, the lost value is a purchase quantity nobody can reconstruct, and
the two writers are concurrent by design rather than by coincidence.

**Requirement 2 — every cart mutation is one token-conditional statement, and its affected-row count is
the outcome. Owner: Engineering.** No cart write is a load, a mutation and a `SaveChanges`, and **none is
a test followed by a second statement that acts on the first one's result**. Every mutation is **one**
statement whose `WHERE` predicate carries the row's key, **the concurrency token the request read**, and
— wherever it raises a quantity — the bound predicate of requirement 3. Its **affected-row count is
asserted to be exactly 1**, and that assertion is the mechanism rather than a diagnostic: a count of 1
means the row this request read is the row it changed, and nothing weaker has to be inferred.

**The two-statement remove is withdrawn, and it is withdrawn because it was the race rather than because
it was untidy.** An earlier revision of this requirement tested `Count > 1` with a guarded relative
update and then, **if that affected no row**, issued a *separate* delete keyed on `(RecordId, CartId)`
alone. An add landing between those two statements raises the count from 1 to 2 and is then **erased by a
delete that never looked at the token** — an acknowledged purchase quantity destroyed, silently, by the
application's own remove path. There is therefore **no "then delete" step anywhere in this contract.**

**The three statement shapes, and there are only three:**

| Mutation | The one statement | Its predicate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Add**, and a merge contribution into a line that already exists | Insert when the line is absent; on the unique-index violation on `(CartId, AlbumId)` (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) take the **relative update** path, `SET Count = Count + @n OUTPUT inserted.Count` | `CartId = @c AND AlbumId = @a AND RowVersion = @t`, **and** the bound conjunct of requirement 3 |
| **Remove, decrement** — selected when the freshly read `Count` is greater than 1 | `SET Count = Count - 1 OUTPUT inserted.Count` | `RecordId = @r AND CartId = @c AND RowVersion = @t` |
| **Remove, delete** — selected when the freshly read `Count` is exactly 1 | `DELETE` | `RecordId = @r AND CartId = @c AND RowVersion = @t` |

**The decrement and the delete are alternatives selected from a value, never a test followed by an
unguarded action.** The remove path performs **one** keyed read returning `(Count, RowVersion)`, chooses
its statement from that `Count`, and conditions that statement on that `RowVersion`. If the row moved
underneath, the statement affects nothing and **the decision is re-taken on the fresh value** rather than
a second statement being issued regardless of what the first one found.

**A count of zero is attributed rather than retried blindly, and the attribution is one keyed read.**
Zero affected rows means the predicate no longer matches. That has exactly three causes, and they carry
different responses because they are different events:

| What the attributing read finds | The cause | The response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No row** | Another writer removed the line | **Remove**: terminal, and shaped as a success — the caller receives the JSON of section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) reporting an already-removed line, which is the one failure path that changes (below). **Add**: the insert path is re-entered once, because the line it meant to increment no longer exists |
| **A row whose `Count` makes the requested delta violate the bound** | **Bound failure** — requirement 3 | **Terminal rejection, and explicitly not a retry**: a bound evaluated against a committed value cannot be satisfied by re-issuing the same request. The caller receives a validation-shaped rejection naming the configured limit, nothing is written, and this is a **different outcome from contention** by design |
| **A row whose token differs while the bound is satisfied** | **Contention** — another writer changed the row between the read and the statement | **Re-take the decrement-versus-delete decision on the fresh `Count`, re-issue with the fresh token**, bounded by `Cart:MaxMutationRetries` |

- **`Cart:MaxMutationRetries`, default 3, owner Engineering.** Bound through the options pattern of
  section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) and
  validated at startup with the values of section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access). On exhaustion the mutation fails
  **deterministically**: nothing is written, the caller receives a handled message asking them to retry,
  and the failure is logged with the cart key and the album id. A cart contended past that bound is
  reported rather than looped over.
- **An affected count greater than 1 is a defect, not a tolerated outcome.** Every predicate above is
  keyed on a unique key — `RecordId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:8-9], or the unique
  `(CartId, AlbumId)` pair section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) requires — so two or more
  is unrepresentable. If it is ever observed the unit of work aborts and rolls back rather than reporting
  a number it cannot account for.
- **The relative update now compares the token, and an earlier revision of this section said it should
  not. The reversal is recorded here rather than left as two positions in one document.** That earlier
  reasoning was that comparing a token on a commutative increment fails on contention for no benefit,
  since the statement reads no value into the client. Two things make it wrong under this contract: the
  increment is **no longer unconditional**, because requirement 3 puts a bound conjunct into the same
  `WHERE`, so a zero-affected result has to be attributable to *which* conjunct failed and a token-free
  predicate cannot separate a bound failure from a vanished row; and the ledger of requirement 4 needs
  "the row I read is the row I changed" to be a fact rather than an inference. The cost is one extra
  round trip **under contention only**, bounded above, and the committed outcome after the retry is
  identical to the uncontended one.
- **The token still advances on every update of the row**, including a set-based one, which is what lets
  the keyed, token-matched checkout delete of requirement 7 detect that an acknowledged increment landed
  after its projection was taken.

**`ItemCount` on the wire comes from the statement itself, and the mechanism is named because the
set-based update API does not return values.** EF Core's `ExecuteUpdate`/`ExecuteUpdateAsync` returns an
**affected-row count and nothing else**, so the decrement is issued as a **parameterized
`UPDATE … SET Count = Count - 1 OUTPUT inserted.Count WHERE …` through the context's SQL-query API**,
which returns the committed value in the same round trip; the wire contract's `ItemCount` (section
[8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy)) is that value and never a second read.
The statement is the **sole** writer of that quantity, so its returned value and the stored value cannot
diverge. If a project standard forbids authored SQL outright, the permitted fallback is
`ExecuteUpdateAsync` followed by a keyed read **inside the same transaction**, and its weakness is stated
rather than hidden: the read returns *a* committed value, not provably the value this statement produced,
so the first form is preferred.

**Authored SQL is more than one site under this contract, so it is enumerated exactly rather than
claimed to be singular. This corrects an earlier statement of this requirement**, which called the
quantity statement "the only place in the ported application where SQL text is authored at all" — a claim
the checkout delete of requirement 7 and the merge consumption of requirement 5 both falsify. The
complete set for the **ported web application** is three sites:

| Authored-SQL site | Specified by |
| --- | --- |
| The three cart mutation statements above — the relative update, the decrement and the delete | Requirement 2 |
| The merge's source consumption — the locking enumeration and the token-conditional deletion of each consumed source row — and the alias row's lock take | Requirements 5 and 6 |
| The checkout's token-matched delete and the bounded carrier that transports its `(RecordId, token)` pairs | Requirement 7 and section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) |

**One rule governs all three without exception: every value is a parameter.** No cart id, record id,
album id, quantity, token or configured bound is interpolated into SQL text at any site under any
circumstance. The one-time tooling of section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) authors SQL of its
own — the identity-insert mechanics of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 and the collation-scoped preflight
of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) — and is held to
the same rule; it is listed apart because it is not deployed with the web application.

**One failure path changes and no successful one does**: the concurrent loser of a remove receives the
JSON shape reporting an already-removed line where today it receives an unhandled exception from `Single`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:64-66]. That is a difference from an unspecified
behaviour rather than from a contract, so it is recorded here and asserted by section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 19a rather than added to section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).

**Requirement 3 — the quantity bound is enforced inside the statement and by a `CHECK` constraint, never
by a client-side precheck. Owner: Engineering for the mechanism, Product for the business maximum, the
data owner for the constraint and for the failure artifact.**

**The client-side checked precomputation is withdrawn as the mechanism, because it is not where the
arithmetic happens.** An earlier revision of this section computed the merged sum in a widened `checked`
context **in the application** before writing. That is necessary and it is not sufficient, on three
counts: the ordinary add path carried **no bound predicate at all**, since the source increments without
any ceiling [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:57] and a client-side merge check does not
cover it; a concurrent update of the destination row can invalidate a precheck between the check and the
write, because nothing holds the row across that gap; and the arithmetic that actually executes is the
engine's — `Count = Count + @n` over an `int` column — which **wraps inside SQL Server before any
post-value can be inspected**, so a widened check in the client never sees the value it exists to guard.
The bound therefore moves into the statement and into the schema.

- **Widened arithmetic in the statement's own predicate.** Every statement that raises a quantity carries
  `AND CAST(Count AS bigint) + CAST(@n AS bigint) <= @effectiveMaxQuantity` as a conjunct of the same
  `WHERE` that carries the key and the token. **The cast is on the stored column**, so the addition is
  performed in `bigint` and cannot wrap at `int` — which is precisely the hole a client-side check leaves
  open. And because the predicate is evaluated inside the statement that writes, **no concurrent update
  can invalidate it**: there is no interval between the check and the write in which to invalidate it.
- **`@effectiveMaxQuantity` is one value resolved from two bounds, so one predicate enforces both.** It
  is the **lesser** of the business maximum `Cart:MaxQuantityPerLine` and the largest value the
  **extracted** target column can hold (section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1, which is where the column's real
  type comes from rather than from the CLR type). It is resolved once at startup and validated there. Two
  bounds enforced by two predicates would be two things to get wrong; two bounds resolved into one value
  is one.
- **A named `CHECK` constraint carries the invariant that configuration must not be able to weaken.**
  `CK_Cart_Count_Positive`, `CHECK (Count >= 1)`, created by the **pre-load** catalog migration stage of
  section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and recorded as a deliberate net-new object in the
  diff of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 on the same terms
  as the token. It is the backstop that makes an overflow **unstorable** rather than merely unlikely: an
  `int` wrap produces a negative value, and a negative value cannot be committed to this column by any
  statement, from any code path, present or future. A quantity of zero is equally unrepresentable, which
  is what makes requirement 2's decrement-versus-delete choice **total** — there is no third state in
  which a line exists holding nothing.
- **The upper bound stays in the predicate and deliberately not in the constraint.**
  `Cart:MaxQuantityPerLine` is Product's to set and is configuration-bound so that changing it is not a
  code change; a `CHECK` constraint carrying it would turn every change to a business number into a
  schema migration applied by the deployment principal. So the split is stated: the **constraint** holds
  what can never legitimately vary, and the **predicate** holds what Product owns.
- **`Cart:MaxQuantityPerLine` is mandatory and has no default. Owner: Product for the value, Engineering
  for the enforcement.** The source imposes no maximum at all
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:57], so there is no existing value to preserve and no
  measurement in this document from which to derive one; a figure asserted here would be a business rule
  invented by an engineering deliverable. **The requirement is that the bound exist, be configured and be
  enforced.** It is bound and validated at startup with the rest of the options (section
  [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)), and an absent
  or non-positive value **fails startup** rather than falling back to an unbounded line. The approval this
  document asks of Product is the number, not whether the bound exists — an engineering deliverable may
  decline to invent a business number, and it may not leave a validated input unsupplied. It is owned by
  Product on the same basis as the page size of section
  [4.9](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost).
- **Bound failure and contention are different outcomes with different responses**, per requirement 2's
  attribution table, and conflating them is a specific defect rather than an imprecision: retrying a
  bound failure would burn the retry budget and then report a **contention** failure for a business-rule
  violation, while treating contention as a bound failure would reject a write that was always going to
  succeed. A bound failure is terminal and names the limit; contention is re-taken on the fresh value.
- **In the sign-in merge, an over-bound contribution fails that line and nothing else.** The merge is
  abandoned **for that line**, the sign-in still completes with the non-blocking notice of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), **both source rows are left intact** so nothing is lost,
  and the affected `(username, album id, both source counts)` triple is written to a controlled artifact
  under section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s controls — it names a user, so it is personal
  data and carries those controls without exception.
- **In the load's merge transformation an over-bound sum is blocking.** In the many-to-one resolution of
  historical duplicate pairs that section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) orders and section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) executes, the transformation **stops, nothing is merged**, and
  the data owner decides the resolution before it is re-run. The asymmetry with the sign-in path is
  deliberate: a live visitor's sign-in must not be blocked by one cart line, and a migration must not
  silently carry a value nobody has approved.

**Requirement 4 — every cart mutation carries a durable operation id, and an unknown outcome is settled
by reading the ledger rather than by re-executing. Owner: Engineering.**

**The previously accepted exposure is withdrawn, and the withdrawal is stated plainly because the
document argued for it at length.** Section
[4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s retry-safety table recorded the
relative update's non-idempotence as a *bounded, visible, deliberately accepted* exposure, resting on
three reasons of which exactly one was load-bearing: **the response renders the committed value**, so the
stored and displayed quantities could not diverge and the customer could reverse an over-count they could
see. **That premise fails in exactly the case the exposure exists for.** The replay is triggered by a
transient fault arriving between a commit and its acknowledgement; if the **final** acknowledgement is
also lost — the same fault class, one round trip later — then **no response is rendered at all**, nothing
displays the committed value, and the over-count is invisible to the only party who could have reversed
it. An exposure whose acceptance rests on a property that the failure itself removes is not an accepted
exposure; it is an unhandled case. It is therefore mechanised, on the same pattern as the order write.

- **`dbo.CartMutationOperation`, a durable ledger with the operation id as its primary key.** Columns:
  `OperationId` (the key), `CartId`, `AlbumId`, `RecordId` (null until an insert path assigns one),
  `Delta`, `Outcome`, `ResultCount` and `CreatedUtc`. It is a deliberate net-new object, created by the
  **pre-load** catalog migration stage of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) alongside
  the token and the `CHECK` constraint, and recorded in the diff of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 as one.
- **The identifier is generated once per submission by the application, not per attempt and not by the
  database** — the same rule as the order write's operation id, for the same reason: an identifier
  regenerated on retry identifies nothing.
- **The ledger row is written inside the same transaction as the mutation**, so a committed mutation and
  its ledger row cannot disagree. This is the whole mechanism; a ledger written in a second transaction
  would be exactly as useless as no ledger.
- **A replay is detected and becomes a no-op that returns the recorded result.** A mutation whose
  `OperationId` is already present does not re-apply the delta: it returns `ResultCount` from the ledger,
  so the caller receives the value that was actually committed. The primary key is what makes that exact
  rather than heuristic.
- **An unknown outcome is settled by reading the ledger before responding, never by assuming and never
  by re-executing.** The transaction is invoked through the execution strategy's overload that takes a
  **`verifySucceeded`** callback (section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)), and that callback looks up this
  operation id. Present → the attempt committed, and the strategy reports success with the recorded
  result. Absent → nothing committed, and the retry proceeds. **Cart mutations therefore stay inside
  automatic retry rather than being excluded from it**, which is the better of the two available
  resolutions: excluding them would leave a transient fault surfacing as a failed add that may or may not
  have landed, which is the same unknown state moved onto the customer.
- **Scope, so this is not read as request de-duplication.** The operation id makes **the retry** of one
  submission idempotent. A visitor who clicks add twice is making two submissions and gets two
  increments, which is today's behaviour and is preserved.
- **Retention and classification.** A ledger row holds a `CartId`, which for a signed-in visitor **is**
  their login name, so it is application data of the same class as `Order.Username`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18], sits under the runtime grants
  [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines, and is **not** a reconciliation artifact — it
  does not fall under section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s artifact controls. It is retained
  for at least the **total unit-of-work deadline** of section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) — the longest interval in which a
  retry of the same submission can still arrive — and is swept by the same bounded, batched cleanup path
  as the alias rows of requirement 6, whose schedule is strictly the longer of the two.

**Requirement 5 — the merge consumes its source rows under a lock it holds to commit, and asserts an
exact affected count. Owner: Engineering.**

**The defect this closes is that the merge read a contribution it later deleted, with nothing holding the
row in between.** Section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) specifies the merge as summing the
source row's `Count` into the destination and then deleting the source row. Under the provider's default
isolation the read takes no lasting lock, so two failures are reachable: a mutation of the source row
between the read and the delete is **discarded without trace**, because the count that was summed is not
the count that was deleted; and two concurrent merges of the same anonymous cart can each read the same
contribution and each add it, **double-counting** it. Neither is visible in any row count afterwards.

- **The source enumeration takes `UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK` inside the merge's own transaction.** The rows the
  merge summed cannot be changed or removed by another writer before it commits, and a second merge of
  the same source blocks rather than reading the same contribution. This is the preferred form because it
  converts contention into a **bounded wait** rather than a bounded retry.
- **The permitted alternative is rowversion-conditional consumption, with its weakness stated.** Where a
  project standard forbids table hints, the merge carries each source row's token from the enumeration
  and deletes it with `WHERE RecordId = @r AND RowVersion = @t`, asserting that the **affected count
  equals the number of source rows it summed**. Any shortfall means a source row changed underneath, so
  the **whole merge rolls back** and is retried from a fresh enumeration, bounded by
  `Cart:MaxMutationRetries`. It is the fallback rather than the default because it retries where the lock
  form waits, and a busy anonymous cart can exhaust the bound.
- **Exact affected counts, asserted at every statement.** Each consumed source row: exactly 1. Each
  destination contribution: exactly 1, through requirement 2's upsert. A partial merge is therefore not a
  state this contract can reach — anything other than the exact expected count rolls the transaction back.
- **The merge is idempotent on the alias row, which is what stops two concurrent merges contributing
  twice.** The alias row of requirement 6 is inserted **inside the merge transaction** with
  `SourceCartId` as its primary key, so two concurrent *first* merges of one source serialize on that
  insert: the loser fails on the unique key, rolls back and re-resolves, by which time the winner has
  consumed the source rows and there is nothing left to contribute. A **later** merge — the
  re-resolution of requirement 6, absorbing a row that arrived after the first merge enumerated the cart
  — finds the alias row already present and takes it `WITH (UPDLOCK)` for the duration of its
  transaction, which serializes it against any other merge for that source on the same key. Both paths
  therefore serialize on one row, and the contribution can be applied exactly once.
- **Coverage** is section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 19a case (a) for the concurrent-add
  interleaving and row 19b for the two-concurrent-merges case.

**Requirement 6 — the handoff is discoverable, indexed by destination, and re-resolved immediately
before every write. Owner: Engineering, with operations owning the expiry job.**

**The defect this closes is that the alias, as an earlier revision specified it, could not be found by
anything that needed it.** `dbo.CartAlias` was keyed by `SourceCartId` and was therefore queryable only
**by** a source id — while section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s key derivation returns
the **principal** for an authenticated request and **reads no session at all**, and the anonymous session
entry is cleared once the reassignment commits. So no later request could present the source id, nothing
could look the alias up, and the row was unreachable in exactly the situation it existed for. A request
that had already resolved the pre-merge key **before** the merge committed bypassed resolution
altogether. **Three fixes, and all three are required together** — any one of them alone leaves a
reachable hole:

- **(a) A scoped handoff slot, retained until the merge is *verified* rather than merely attempted.**
  The source cart id is written to a dedicated session entry, **`CartHandoffSourceId`**, distinct from
  the anonymous cart-id entry section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) governs, **before** the merge
  begins. It is cleared **only** after the merge's own verification passes — no rows remaining under the
  source id, the alias row present, and its state recorded as verified — and **never** on the strength of
  the merge having been attempted. The anonymous cart-id entry is still cleared exactly as section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) states, and that clearing stays deliberately not
  load-bearing; discoverability is carried by the handoff entry instead. The entry holds a **GUID and
  never a username**, so section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s key-derivation boundary
  is unchanged by it.
- **(b) A destination-indexed alias, so a principal with no session is still recoverable.** `CartAlias`
  carries a **non-unique index on `(DestinationCartId, CreatedUtc)`** in addition to its `SourceCartId`
  primary key. That is what makes a **session-free, server-side sweep** expressible: for a given
  authenticated principal, enumerate the alias rows whose `DestinationCartId` is that principal and whose
  state is not verified, and complete each one. The sweep runs at **every sign-in**, as part of the merge
  step, and **on demand** from the operator report of unverified aliases. It deliberately does **not**
  run on every request: an unverified alias is produced only by a merge that failed part-way, which is
  rare and already observable, so a per-request sweep would buy a query on every page for a state that a
  sign-in-time sweep and a report already resolve.
- **(c) Every writer re-resolves the effective cart key immediately before its DML.** A request that
  resolved its cart key early — before a merge committed — must not write under the stale key. Resolution
  is performed **again**, from the principal or the session as section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) specifies and then through the alias, **in the same
  service call that issues the statement**, and the statement's parameters take the re-resolved value.
  No cart key is cached across an `await` boundary and then used in a write. **Reads may use the earlier
  resolution and writes may not**, and the asymmetry is deliberate: a stale read renders a momentarily
  empty cart, which the next request corrects, while a stale write **strands a row** under a key nothing
  will ever resolve again — which is the loss this whole requirement exists to prevent.

**The alias table is mapped, created and accessed explicitly, because a table nothing declares is a
table nothing creates.** `CartAlias` is an entity type in `MusicStoreEntities` (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), mapped in `OnModelCreating` with
`SourceCartId` as its key, `DestinationCartId` and `CreatedUtc` as its other columns, a **state column**
carrying the verified-versus-unverified fact requirement 5 and fix (a) both read, and the index of fix
(b). Both id columns carry the **bounded length** section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) requires of `Cart.CartId`, for the same reason — an
`nvarchar(max)` column cannot be an index key column. It is created by the **pre-load** catalog migration
stage of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), which therefore carries **four**
deliberate net-new objects: the `Cart` concurrency token, the `CK_Cart_Count_Positive` constraint, the
`CartMutationOperation` ledger and this table, each recorded in the diff of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 as a deliberate schema change — and
a **fifth** if section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)'s
preferred table-valued carrier is chosen over its chunked alternative, since that carrier's table type is
created by the same stage and recorded on the same terms.
Ordinary reads and inserts go through the context; the lock take of requirement 5 is one of the authored
statements requirement 2 enumerates.

Resolution consults the alias under two rules that are both load-bearing:

- **The alias is followed only for an authenticated request whose principal equals
  `DestinationCartId`.** An **anonymous** request presenting an aliased GUID is **not** redirected: it
  receives a fresh anonymous cart, which is precisely the access boundary section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) requires and section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 19's fourth failure path asserts. A leaked or guessed GUID
  therefore yields nothing, because following the alias requires already being the identity it points
  at.
- **Resolving through an alias re-runs the merge for any rows still under the source id**, which is a
  no-op in the common case and is what absorbs a write that landed after the merge enumerated the cart.
  The merge serializes on the alias row and asserts exact affected counts (requirement 5), so this
  cannot double-count; it is the same operation reaching a row that arrived late.

**Alias retention and removal.** An alias row is retained for **at least the session idle timeout**
[06 §8.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes, because that is the longest a browser can still
present the pre-merge GUID. It is then removed by **the same cleanup path that expires session rows** —
the bounded, batched backstop delete [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) specifies, extended
to cover this table **and the mutation ledger of requirement 4**: **one scheduled job over three tables,
not three jobs of one shape.** The requirement is stated that way deliberately, because three jobs with
one shape are three things to schedule, monitor and get wrong, and the three tables share both their
expiry rule and their reason for existing. The job is batched so that it cannot hold a long-lived lock on
the cart path. **An unverified alias row is never swept while it is unverified**: it is reported to
operations instead, because sweeping it would silently discard the one record that says a merge did not
finish. The table holds a login name against a GUID, so it is application data of the same class as
`Order.Username` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18], sits under the runtime grants
[06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines, and is **not** a reconciliation artifact — it
does not fall under section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s artifact controls.

**Coverage** is section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 19a case (c) for the post-clear stale request
and row 19c for the already-resolved stale writer.

**Requirement 7 — checkout deletes only the rows it read, matched on `RecordId` and the token, inside the
one transaction the execution strategy owns. Owner: Engineering.** The pre-loop projection of section
[4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) carries each line's
`RecordId` **and its token value**, and the deletion is a set-based delete over exactly those
`(RecordId, token)` pairs. **The delete is not a statement issued beside `SaveChanges`**: section
[4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) places the order insert, the
detail inserts and this delete inside **one explicit transaction owned by the execution strategy**, and
that section owns both the transaction and the bounded carrier that transports the pairs. This
requirement owns the keying, the affected-count rule and the retry. Then:

- **If the delete affects fewer rows than the projection returned, a write landed between the two**, so
  the projection the order was derived from is stale. The **whole unit of work is retried from the
  projection**, under the **same durable operation id** of section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) — the unique index on that column
  is what makes a retry unable to produce a second order — and the retry recomputes the details and
  the total from the cart as it now stands. The customer's late addition is therefore **in the order**,
  which is the outcome they were already told they had.
- **If it affects *more* rows than the projection returned, the unit of work aborts rather than
  committing.** The carrier of section
  [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) is validated on the **exact**
  affected set — the affected count equals the projected line count, no more and no fewer — so a carrier
  that duplicated a pair or a predicate that widened is a failure and not a silent success.
- **The retry is bounded and its exhaustion is handled.** `Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries`, default
  **3**, owner **Engineering**, bound through the options pattern of section
  [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) and validated
  at startup alongside the values of section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access). This bound is **independent of
  the provider's transient-fault retry** in that section and composes with it: a concurrency retry
  restarts the unit of work from the projection, where a transient-fault retry re-executes an
  operation. On exhaustion the checkout fails with a handled message asking the customer to resubmit,
  and because the transaction rolled back, **no order exists and no cart row was deleted** — so neither
  of the two undetectable states section
  [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) analyses can arise here either.
- **A retry that finds the cart empty does not create an order.** Section
  [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) requires the submission to be
  rejected when the projection returns no line, which is what stops the loser of two distinct concurrent
  checkouts producing a **zero-line second order**. That rejection is stated there, with the empty and the
  stale cases separated, because it is a property of the whole write path rather than of the delete.
- **`EmptyCart`'s `CartId`-scoped delete [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:87-96] is not
  ported.** It is the mechanism by which an unread row is destroyed, and replacing it with the keyed,
  token-matched delete above is what closes the hole rather than narrowing it.

**What this section does not claim.** It does not claim a serialized cart. Two customers' carts are
independent and nothing here couples them, and two writers on **one** cart are made *correct* rather
than *ordered* — an add and a remove arriving together still commit in whichever order the engine
chooses, and both orderings produce an outcome the customer's own two actions can account for. The
property bought is that **no acknowledged write is silently discarded**, and it is bought at each of the
four writers rather than by a lock nobody holds.

**It does now claim that a quantity cannot be applied twice, and that is a change from an earlier
position in this document rather than a restatement of it.** Section
[4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s retry-safety table previously
recorded a residual exposure on the relative update — a transient fault arriving between a commit and its
acknowledgement applying one increment twice, bounded by the configured retry count, and **accepted**
because the page rendered the committed value. **Requirement 4 withdraws that acceptance and mechanises
the case**, for the reason stated there: when the final acknowledgement is also lost the page renders
nothing, so the property the acceptance rested on is exactly the property the failure removes. With the
ledger in place a replayed mutation is a **no-op returning the committed result**, so the committed effect
of one submission is **one application** — which is what the source does when no fault occurs, and is
therefore a **preserved contract rather than an approved delta** (section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) records that reasoning explicitly, because the table there
claims completeness). The alternative that was rejected in favour of the accepted exposure — an absolute
read-modify-write — remains rejected for the original reason: it loses an acknowledged add under ordinary
concurrency with no fault at all, silently and without bound. **No latency or throughput claim is made
for any of it**; the cost is one extra column in each predicate, one ledger row per mutation, one lock
take on the merge path, and one attributing read on the contended path only.

**Coverage.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) rows 19a, 19b, 19c, 19d and 19e carry what this
section exists for: the four interleavings and the merge's accumulation bound (19a), two concurrent merges
of one source cart (19b), the already-resolved stale writer and the session-free handoff sweep (19c), the
replay and unknown-outcome fault-injection cases of requirement 4 (19d), and the two **distinguishable**
outcomes of requirements 2 and 3 — a bound rejection naming the limit and a contention exhaustion — in
19e.

### 4.14 The duplicate-`Genre` browse contract

**This document is the sole owner of this contract, and it is stated here in full.**
[08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) measures the source behaviour, records the severity and the
remediation direction, and delegates the resolution here rather than authoring a second contract; it adds
no delta row and no coverage row of its own and does not assume one is already present. What the browse
path does in the presence of duplicate genre names is a migration-and-interface decision, so it is one
contract with one home, and everything a reader needs to implement it — the branch mechanics, the
migration stage the schema change belongs to, the routing form, the approval owners and the test cases —
is below.

**The measured facts it rests on, cited once.**

- `Browse` filters on a **non-key** predicate reached from an unvalidated query-string value:
  `storeDB.Genres.Include("Albums").Single(g => g.Name == genre)`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:27-34].
- `Genre.Name` carries **no key, no unique constraint and no annotation of any kind**
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:8]; the entity's key is `GenreId` [:7].
- **Both internal link forms are built from the name rather than the id** — the genre list
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Index.cshtml:13] and the every-page menu
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/GenreMenu.cshtml:9-11] — and the browse view is bound to exactly one
  genre [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:1].
- **The migration deliberately preserves duplicate names.** The duplicate-detection rule of section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) names `Genre.Name` among the four candidate natural keys the load
  does **not** reject on: duplicates there are counted, enumerated in a controlled artifact and carried
  into the target as they stand, because rejecting on an undeclared natural key would reject legitimate
  historical rows. So the browse path has to be correct **in the presence of** duplicates rather than
  correct once someone assumes there are none.
- **Exactly one write path to `Genres` exists in the source, and it is the seed**
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/SampleData.cs:822], inserting the 15 seeded rows [:805-819]. No
  controller or service writes to the table: `git grep -nE 'Genres\.(Add|Remove|Attach)' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cs'`
  returns that one line and nothing else.

**Part 1 — the contract is non-lossy unconditionally, under both branches below.** The migration
**merges no `Genre` row, deletes no `Genre` row and renames no `Genre` value**, and neither does the port.
Four dispositions are therefore not available to any implementer of this contract, and not one of them is
non-lossy:

| Disposition | Why it is excluded |
| --- | --- |
| **Merge** two same-named genres into one | Removes a catalog row the source holds, and silently reassigns the albums of one genre to another — a data change dressed as a routing fix |
| **Delete** one of them | The same loss, without even the reassignment |
| **Rename** one of them | Rewrites a value visitors read and that **both** internal link forms are built from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Index.cshtml:13], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/GenreMenu.cshtml:9-11], so every external link to the renamed genre stops resolving |
| **Break the tie by assigning a distinct name** | A rename by another word, with the additional property that the assigned value is invented by the migration rather than approved by anyone |

**First-match-wins remains explicitly rejected**, and the rejection belongs to this contract even though
[08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) keeps the reasoning. `First` or `FirstOrDefault` over an
unordered non-key predicate returns whichever row the provider happens to return first, which makes the
other row **permanently unreachable** through the only URL that names it — with no exception, nothing in
the data to indicate it happened, and nothing recorded anywhere. **Adding an `OrderBy` does not rescue
it**: a deterministic choice of one row is still a permanently unreachable other row, so determinism
converts a silent intermittent loss into a silent permanent one and fixes nothing that matters.

**Part 2 — the zero-match case is answered identically in both branches**: an unknown genre name returns
**`NotFound()`**, never an unhandled exception. That is the operator substitution
[08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) states as the remediation direction, and it closes the zero-row
case **only** — which is precisely why the multiple-row case needs the branches below rather than the same
substitution applied more confidently.

**Part 3 — the branch is selected by the extraction, and neither branch is preferred.** The selecting
question is: **does the source hold two `Genre` rows whose `Name` values are equal under the equality
semantics the target column carries?** Both halves of that question are *results* rather than premises,
and this document asserts neither:

- **The source side** is the schema extraction of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 together with a preflight grouping
  over `Genre.Name`, whose output is the enumerated duplicate report section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) already requires for this column. **The preflight is
  length-aware for the same reason section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)'s collision preflight is**:
  SQL's `=` ignores trailing blanks on the character types regardless of collation, so `'Rock'` and
  `'Rock '` group together, and the report carries each value's `DATALENGTH` alongside it so a human can
  see **why** two visibly different names grouped.
- **The target side** is the collation the target `Genre.Name` column actually carries, established by
  **target-side introspection of `sys.columns.collation_name`** after catalog stage 1 is applied — the
  same mechanism and the same reasoning as section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration): a collation is a
  *configured or verified* property, never an inherited one anybody may assume.
- **The decision is re-verified immediately before branch (a)'s index migration is applied**, because
  creating a unique index is exactly the operation that fails late — or folds two rows into one group —
  when the equality semantics underneath it were assumed rather than read.

| Property | **Branch (a)** — the verified duplicate set is **empty** | **Branch (b)** — the verified duplicate set is **not empty** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Schema** | A **unique index on `Genre.Name`**, created by an `AddGenreNameUniqueIndex` migration in the **post-transform catalog stage** section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) names — after the load, so it is never created over data that violates it, and after the collation verification above | **No unique index on `Genre.Name`.** The `AddGenreNameUniqueIndex` migration is **not** applied, and nothing else about the schema changes. Asserting uniqueness here is the lossy change part 1 excludes |
| **Query and dispatch** | `SingleOrDefaultAsync(g => g.Name == genre)`, with `NotFound()` on null. The multiple-row case becomes **unrepresentable**, which is what makes `SingleOrDefault` an honest operator at this site rather than a rename of the throw | A **bounded list query**: the name predicate, ordered by `GenreId` for a total order, projecting `GenreId`, `Name` and `Description`, bounded by the **same configured page size** as the genre list of section [4.9](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost) — no new configuration key, and a duplicate group larger than one page is paged by that same mechanism. Dispatch on the match count: **0** → `NotFound()`; **1** → the browse page exactly as today, with the album list eager-loaded for that one match; **more than 1** → the disambiguation listing |
| **Routing and links** | **Unchanged.** `/Store/Browse?genre=<name>` remains the only form, and both internal link sites are untouched | The **canonical** form becomes id-keyed — a `genreId` parameter on the same action — and both internal link sites emit it. **The legacy name form keeps working**: `/Store/Browse?genre=<name>` still resolves (one match → the browse page, several → the listing, none → 404), so no external link or bookmark breaks. Supplying **both** parameters is a **400**, because silently preferring one of a mismatched pair hides the link defect that produced it |
| **Views** | **Unchanged.** `Browse.cshtml` keeps its single-genre model [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:1] | `Browse.cshtml` keeps its single-genre model unchanged, and **one additive view** renders the listing. Nothing existing is rewritten |
| **Approved delta** | **None.** A valid name behaves identically, and an unknown name returning 404 where the source raised an unhandled exception is the defect resolution [08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns rather than a change of contract | **A conditional approved delta**, recorded in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), **owned by Product *and* the data owner**: Product for the visitor-visible chooser and the link-form change, the data owner for the decision to retain the duplicates rather than resolve them. Two owners because neither can approve the other's half |
| **Coverage** | **No new row.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 1a** covers this branch: its zero-match assertion is unconditional, and its second half additionally asserts **this branch's index** — existence, uniqueness over the column, and the collation read rather than assumed | **Its own row**, section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 1b**, which is explicitly conditional on this branch: the multi-match listing with both genres present and separately reachable by id, the legacy name URL still resolving, the id-keyed canonical links, the mismatched-pair 400, and **no `Genre` row absent afterwards** |
| **Lineage and reconciliation impact** | **None**, and this is worth stating rather than assuming. No `Genre` row is added, removed or changed, so the removed set in the keyed-set rule of section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) stays **empty** for `Genre` and that section's projection row for `Genre` — every column carried unchanged, no transform, no target-only field — stays true. The index is a schema object created after reconciliation and changes no compared value | **None**, for the same reasons. The duplicates are carried as they stand, so nothing about the comparison changes; the difference between the branches is entirely in the schema and the interface |

**One property of branch (a) that is a benefit rather than a delta.** The only write path to `Genres` is
the seed [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/SampleData.cs:822], whose target equivalent is the guarded
non-production routine of section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) and which therefore never runs in a production
release path. With the unique index in place, a **second** seeding run against a non-production database
that already holds those rows **fails loudly** instead of quietly duplicating the catalog. No production
behaviour changes, because no production write path exists to change.

**Part 4 — the branch decision is recorded, not remembered.** The branch taken, the duplicate report it
rests on, the collation introspection result, and the run id under which both were produced are written
as an artifact under section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s controls. A reader six months later
can therefore establish **which branch shipped and on what evidence** without re-deriving it, and a
release that believes it is on branch (a) cannot apply the index without the artifact that says so.

**Part 5 — what this contract deliberately does not decide.** Whether the duplicates are ever *resolved
in the data* afterwards. If Data ever takes that decision it is a **data change** with its own approval,
lineage and reconciliation — not a port change — and only then does branch (a)'s index become available,
authored as the two-release tightening section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) requires
rather than bolted onto the port. This document does not schedule that work and states no preference for
it; [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) places any such workstream if it is ever approved.

### 4.15 Query failure contracts — the complete branch census

Every query in the migration source that can fail on ordinary user input is listed here with **the
contract it gets in the target**. This is a separate exercise from section
[4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy): that section asks *what a query loads*,
this one asks *what happens when it finds nothing, or finds too much*. A site can appear in both.

**The census is ten sites: four input-reachable `.Single` calls and six `Albums.Find` calls.** It was
built by reading every query in the migration source, not by pattern-matching one method name, because
the two shapes fail differently — `.Single` throws on **zero** rows *and* on **more than one**, while
`Find` returns `null` and defers the failure to whatever dereferences it. Counting only one of them
understates the work; treating them as one problem produces the wrong fix for half of the sites.
[08 §5.4](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns the same census as **debt**; this section owns its
**target contracts**.

**Four input-reachable `.Single` calls.**

| # | Site | Reached by | Today | Target contract |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | `Genres.Include("Albums").Single(g => g.Name == genre)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:30-31] | `?genre=` on `/Store/Browse`, unvalidated | An unknown genre name **throws**, and so does a duplicate one. With no live `<customErrors>` in any edition, that is an unhandled 500 | `Genres.Include(g => g.Albums).Where(g => g.Name == genre).Take(2).ToListAsync()`, then **three branches**: **zero rows → `NotFound()`** (an unknown genre is a client error, not a server fault); **exactly one → the view, as today**; **two → a data-integrity failure**, logged at `Error` with the genre name and the two ids, and rethrown so the exception middleware answers **500**. `Take(2)` is deliberate: it distinguishes "one" from "more than one" without materializing every duplicate |
| S2 | `Albums.Single(album => album.AlbumId == id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:37-38] | The route id on `AddToCart` | An unknown id **throws** after nothing has been written | `FirstOrDefaultAsync(a => a.AlbumId == id)`; **null → `NotFound()` and nothing is written** — no cart row is added, no `SaveChangesAsync` is reached. The action is a POST in the target (section [7.3](#73-problem-two--one-state-changing-action-is-a-get-which-no-policy-can-cover)), so this is the first write-path branch a probe reaches |
| S3 | `Carts.Single(item => item.RecordId == id).Album.Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:61-62] | The posted `id` on `RemoveFromCart` | **Two defects in one expression.** It throws on an unknown `RecordId`, and it is **not scoped to the caller's cart** — any authenticated or anonymous caller can name any `RecordId` in the table and have its album title returned to them | One **cart-scoped projection**: `Carts.Where(c => c.RecordId == id && c.CartId == cartId).Select(c => c.Album.Title).FirstOrDefaultAsync()`. **Null → 404 with a JSON body carrying no detail and no state change.** The predicate is the fix for both defects: a foreign row is indistinguishable from an absent one, which is the correct answer to "may I delete this?" |
| S4 | `_db.Carts.Single(cart => cart.CartId == ShoppingCartId && cart.RecordId == id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:64] | The same posted `id`, inside the service | Correctly **cart-scoped** already, but it **throws** when the row is absent — and the `if (cartItem != null)` guard immediately below it [:70] is therefore **unreachable code**: `.Single` never returns `null`, so the guard's false branch cannot execute | `FirstOrDefaultAsync` on the **same** predicate. Null returns a not-found outcome from the service rather than throwing; the controller maps it to S3's contract. **This is what makes the guard at [:70] reachable** — it is not dead code to delete but a branch the source author wrote and the query shape disabled |

**`SingleOrDefault` is not the fix, and this is the single most likely wrong turn in this section.**
`SingleOrDefault` still throws when a second row exists; it converts only the zero-row case. Applied to
S1 it would turn the unknown-genre 500 into a `null` — which the view then dereferences — while leaving
the duplicate-genre case as an unhandled exception whose message ("Sequence contains more than one
element") names neither the genre nor the table. **Zero rows and duplicate rows are two different
contracts with two different owners**: zero rows is a client error answered with 404, duplicates are a
catalog defect answered with a log record and a 500. [08 §5.4](08-technical-debt-register.md) records
the same correction on the debt side.

**Six `Albums.Find` calls.**

| # | Site | Today | Target contract |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F1 | `storeDB.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:38] | Returns `null` for an unknown id, and `View(album)` renders a view that dereferences `@Model.Genre.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:16] — so an unknown album id is a **500 from inside the view** | `Albums.Include(a => a.Genre).Include(a => a.Artist).FirstOrDefaultAsync(a => a.AlbumId == id)`; **null → `NotFound()`**. The `Include`s are lazy-loading site a1 (section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)); the null check is this section's. One query serves both |
| F2 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:32] — `Details` | Null-checked, returns `HttpNotFound()` [:35] | `FirstOrDefaultAsync` with the `Include`s of site a2, **null → `NotFound()`**. Behaviour preserved; only the API name changes |
| F3 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:73] — `Edit` (GET) | Null-checked, returns `HttpNotFound()` [:76] | `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, **null → `NotFound()` before the select lists are built**. Behaviour preserved |
| F4 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:105] — `Delete` (GET) | Null-checked, returns `HttpNotFound()` [:108] | `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, **null → `NotFound()`**. Behaviour preserved |
| F5 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:119] — `DeleteConfirmed` | **Not null-checked.** The result goes straight into `db.Albums.Remove(album)` [:120], so a POST naming a deleted id throws inside `Remove` and answers **500** — the one write action in the controller with no guard | `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, **null → `NotFound()` returned *before* `Remove` is called**, with no `SaveChangesAsync`. This is a change to the source's behaviour and it is the correct one: the same request is already a 404 on the GET at F4, so the POST answering 500 is an inconsistency, not a contract |
| F6 | `_db.Albums.Find(item.AlbumId)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:134] — inside `CreateOrder` | Null would be dereferenced at `album.Price` [:140], inside the checkout's bare `catch` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62], which discards the exception, redisplays the form with no message and **logs nothing** | A cart row referencing a missing album is a **data-integrity failure**: logged at `Error` with the cart record id and album id, the **explicit transaction of section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) rolled back**, **no order persisted**, and a generic error surfaced on the checkout form. The relational constraint makes it improbable — which is exactly why it must fail loudly rather than silently produce a short order |

**One site is already correct and is listed so the census is complete rather than selective.**
`_db.Carts.SingleOrDefault(c => c.CartId == ShoppingCartId && c.AlbumId == album.AlbumId)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:37-39] is genuinely guarded at [:41] and its duplicate
case is prevented by the cart's own key discipline. It ports unchanged apart from becoming
`SingleOrDefaultAsync`.

**What every branch above has in common, stated once instead of per row.** A request that a client can
issue must never produce an unhandled exception; a state that only the data can be in may. So client
input resolves to **404**, and a broken invariant resolves to **a log record at `Error` plus a 500**.
The three status corrections this produces — unknown genre, unknown public album id and the absent cart
row, each a 500 today — are listed as approved delta 15 in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) rather than left as unannounced improvements. **Every
branch in this section has a test in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**; a contract with no test
is a comment.

### 4.16 Asynchronous data access and cancellation — the convention, stated once

Every query and write named in this document is asynchronous and cancellable. The convention is stated
here so the individual contracts — sections
[4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census),
[8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) and
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) — can name an `…Async` API without
re-arguing it each time.

**Where the source starts.** The migration source's async surface is real but confined to one file: the
27 C# files under `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/` contain **9** `async` occurrences, **22** `await`
expressions and **7** `Task<…>` signatures, and every one of them except a single `async void`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] is in `AccountController.cs`. The catalog, cart,
checkout and administration paths are **entirely synchronous** — `Single`, `Find`, `ToList` and
`SaveChanges`, with no `Task` anywhere. There is also **no sync-over-async debt to unwind**: `.Result`,
`.Wait()` and `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` do not appear in any of the 27 files. The commands are in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**The convention, in six rules.**

| # | Rule | Why it is a rule rather than a preference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **An action that touches the database is `async` and returns `Task<IActionResult>`.** An action that touches nothing stays synchronous — `HomeController.Error` (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) is the only one | A synchronous EF Core call blocks a thread-pool thread for the duration of the round trip. Under Kestrel that thread is the request's, and blocking it is the mechanism behind thread-pool starvation |
| 2 | **Every EF Core query and write uses the `…Async` API:** `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `SingleOrDefaultAsync`, `AnyAsync`, `CountAsync`, `SumAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`, `BeginTransactionAsync`, `CommitAsync`, `RollbackAsync`, and the execution strategy's `ExecuteAsync` and `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` | The synchronous overloads exist and compile, so a copied query silently keeps blocking. Naming the API in every contract in this document is what makes the omission visible in review |
| 3 | **Every such action declares a `CancellationToken` parameter**, which MVC binds from `HttpContext.RequestAborted` with no attribute and no registration, **and passes it into every EF Core call in the handler** | A token accepted and not passed on is worse than no token: it looks like cancellation is honoured and nothing is cancelled |
| 4 | **`OperationCanceledException` is not an error — and it is not an outcome either.** Where a handler catches it, the catch is **filtered on the request token** and its body has exactly two statements: record the cancellation, then **`throw;`**. `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)` — the filter is part of the rule, because an `OperationCanceledException` carrying *any other* token is a genuine fault and must keep travelling as one. It is not logged at `Error`, not mapped to a 500 and not mapped to a view; the checkout table in section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) states it for the one handler where it matters | A client that closes the tab produces this exception, so treating it as a fault fills the log with noise. But **an `async Task<IActionResult>` action must still terminate**, and the two obvious terminations are both wrong: returning a view or a status code writes a response to a client that has gone and reports success for work that did not finish, and returning nothing does not compile. **Rethrowing is the terminal behaviour**: the framework recognises a cancelled request, abandons the response rather than inventing one, and — because the exception-handler middleware treats a cancelled request as an abort rather than a fault — no 500 and no error page is produced. The record made on the way out is why the catch exists at all |
| 5 | **View components use `InvokeAsync` returning `Task<IViewComponentResult>` and take the token from `HttpContext.RequestAborted`**, because a component receives no bound parameters from model binding | **All three components query** (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), and the rule reaches all three for the same reason at very different frequencies. The two **layout** components — the genre menu and the cart summary — run wherever the shared layout renders, which is every page, so they are the highest-frequency database callers in the application. `RemoveAccountListViewComponent` runs only on the authorized `Manage` view and reads the Identity store, so it is rare rather than exempt |
| 6 | **No `async void` anywhere, and no synchronous EF Core call in any request path.** The one `async void` in the source is the provisioning method [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21], retired by section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) | An unhandled exception in an `async void` method has no caller to propagate to. That is the specific defect that makes today's provisioning failure invisible |

**Cancellation is safe here because the one multi-statement write is transactional — with one honest
exception, which is not a cancellation problem.** A token cancelled **before or during** the checkout
write aborts the in-flight command and disposes the transaction without committing, so the outcome is
the same as any other failure on that path: nothing persisted, per section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract). A token cancelled **during the commit
itself** is the one case where the client's outcome and the database's can differ — the server may have
committed and the acknowledgement may not have arrived — and that is **exactly the indeterminate commit
of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract), which is settled there by the
submission key rather than by anything in this convention.** Cancellation is one way to reach it, a
dropped connection is another, and the resolution is the same for both. No handler in this application
performs two independent *un*transacted writes that a cancellation could split, which is why rule 3 can
be applied without exception rather than case by case.

**How this convention is checked, since it is the one contract in this document with no coverage row of
its own.** It is a **code-shape** rule, not an observable response, so section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) cannot assert it: a synchronous `SaveChanges` and an asynchronous one
return the same bytes to the client. It is enforced at review, against the six rules above, and the
review is mechanical — the prohibited forms are grep-able (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter`,
`async void`, and any EF Core terminal operator without the `Async` suffix), so a reviewer checks a list
rather than forming a judgement. Rule 4 is the one exception with an observable consequence, and it is
**covered directly**: The coverage assertion cancels the checkout write at three points — before the save,
during the save and during the commit — and asserts the terminal behaviour and the state at each, while
The coverage assertion requires that only a genuine persistence failure produces the user-facing error.

**Two places the request token deliberately does not reach.** The Identity data migration and the
domain data load (section [5](#5-schema-lifecycle-and-the-two-data-migrations)) run outside a request
and take their own token from the hosting process. `tools/provision-admin`
(section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)) passes
`CancellationToken.None` to **every** Identity call it makes — the **four** operations of that section's
property 3 in the provisioning verb, and the **two** of property 3a in revoke mode: each is a single
short call, and an interrupted run is repaired by the per-operation idempotence that section already
requires, so threading a token through it would add a failure mode rather than remove one.

---

### 4.9 The data-protection key store — `ApplicationDbContext` owns it

[06 §7.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires a persisted key ring in `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`,
created by a migration under the deployment principal, and says in as many words that **which context
owns that migration is this document's to place**. Section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) defines two contexts and, until this
section, assigned it to neither — which left a platform requirement with no code behind it. It is
assigned here.

**The decision: `ApplicationDbContext` is the key store.**
