| Element | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Context | `ApplicationDbContext` — additionally implements `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.EntityFrameworkCore.IDataProtectionKeyContext` |
| The interface member | `DbSet<DataProtectionKey> DataProtectionKeys` — the one property the interface requires, mapped to the table below |
| Table | `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`, the name [06 §7.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes. This document does not choose it and does not vary it |
| Created by | A **migration in `Data/Migrations/Identity/`** — the last migration in that set — recorded in **`__EFMigrationsHistory_Identity`** |
| Applied by | The deployment principal, **during step 3** of [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s order and of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)'s — the same executor invocation that applies the rest of the Identity set, because this migration is that set's tail. **Step 4 verifies the table exists; it does not create it** |
| Registration | `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>().SetApplicationName(<`DataProtection:ApplicationDiscriminator`>)` — the discriminator being the configuration-backed value of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), not a literal |
| Read and written by | The runtime identity, with the data-only grants of [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — **`SELECT` and `INSERT` only**, for the reason in the next paragraph |

**The store is append-only, and that fixes the runtime's grants exactly rather than approximately.** The
repository this registration installs has **two** operations and no others:
`EntityFrameworkCoreXmlRepository<TContext>.GetAllElements()` enumerates
`context.DataProtectionKeys.AsNoTracking()` — a read — and `StoreElement(element, friendlyName)` does
`context.DataProtectionKeys.Add(newKey)` followed by `SaveChanges()`, which is an **insert of a new row**
(`EntityFrameworkCoreXmlRepository<TContext>`, ASP.NET Core 8 source). There is no update path and no
delete path in the type at all. **A revocation is an insert too**, not an edit of the row it revokes:
the key manager builds a new `<revocation>` element and persists it through the same `StoreElement`
(`XmlKeyManager.RevokeAllKeys` and `RevokeSingleKey`, ASP.NET Core 8 source), so the ring's history is
accumulated rather than rewritten.

**So the runtime identity needs `SELECT` and `INSERT` on this table and does not need `UPDATE` or
`DELETE`** — a grant this document can state as a consequence of the code rather than as a
least-privilege aspiration. [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) grants exactly those two and
denies the other two, and [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s check C3 asserts the denial
positively; the two documents agree, and this paragraph is why.

**What happens if the table is absent, verified — because the intuitive answer is wrong in a way that
would misplace a control.** An **explicitly configured** `PersistKeysToDbContext` does **not** quietly
substitute an in-memory ring: ephemeral keys exist only where an application asks for them explicitly, and
this one asks for the database. What actually happens has two stages, and only the second is a failure the
user sees:

- **Start-up does not fail.** The framework preloads the ring in a hosted service, inside a `try`/`catch`
  whose comment states the intent exactly — "This should be non-fatal, so swallow, log, and allow server
  startup to continue. The `KeyRingProvider` may be able to try again on the first request" — logging
  `KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup` and returning (`DataProtectionHostedService.StartAsync`, ASP.NET Core 8
  source). So the process starts, binds its port and looks healthy.
- **The first request that protects or unprotects anything throws.** The repository read hits a table that
  does not exist and the provider's exception propagates — in practice on the first rendered form, because
  an anti-forgery token is data-protected, and on the first sign-in for the same reason. The visible result
  is a 500, not a subtly non-durable cookie.

**Two consequences follow, and they are why the verification lives where it does.** The good one: a missing
table is loud rather than silent, so there is no state in which the application appears to work and cookies
quietly stop surviving a restart. The one that needs a control: **the application's own start-up will not
catch it**, which is exactly why the table's existence is asserted before traffic — by step 4 of
[06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and by readiness check C2 of
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — rather than by trusting the process to have failed. A
readiness contract that assumed a start-up crash would let the first customer discover this.

**One property of choosing an explicit repository, stated because it is a trade and not a free
improvement.** "If the developer overrides the rules outlined above and points the Data Protection system
at a specific key repository, automatic encryption of keys at rest is disabled" (*Data Protection key
management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). **What that costs here is less than it sounds, and
saying so precisely matters**: on the App Service default path the same source states keys "aren't
protected at rest" anyway, so this registration forfeits automatic protection that path never provided —
the automatic mechanism applies to the user-profile path, where Windows encrypts with DPAPI. Either way
**at-rest protection becomes an explicit decision rather than an inherited one**, and that decision is
[06 §7.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and is not restated here. The registration in the table
above is what makes it a decision, which is why the consequence is named at the point that causes it.

**Why `ApplicationDbContext` and not `MusicStoreEntities`.** The key ring protects **authentication
cookies and anti-forgery tokens** — the identity and security domain, not the catalog domain. The
Identity context is already that domain's context, so the key table lands beside the tables it protects
tickets for, under one migration set, one history table and one set of grants. Putting it in the catalog
context would give the catalog code path a schema-level stake in cookie key material and would separate
the key table from the credential tables it is operationally paired with — during a restore, during a
slot-scoped repoint, and in the backup that covers both.

**The tension a careful reader will notice, and its reconciliation.** AAP §0.3.2 lists **four schema
owners** — the session cache, the catalog migrations, the Identity migrations and the data-protection key
table — while AAP §0.3.1's and §0.4.1's frozen future map contains exactly **two** contexts and exactly
**two** migration folders. Both are true at once, and conflating them is what would invent a third
context:

- **Conceptually the key table is its own schema owner.** It is not part of either domain model, no
  entity references it, and its lifecycle is the framework's rather than the application's.
- **Physically it is created by the last migration of the Identity set**, so it needs **no third
  `DbContext`, no third migrations folder and no third history table**, and the frozen map stands
  unaltered.
- **So it is a distinct schema owner and not a distinct execution step**, and that is the distinction the
  order in [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) turns on: the table is **created during step
  3**, by the same invocation that applies the rest of the Identity set, and **step 4 asserts that it
  exists** before the data steps proceed. Nothing in steps 1 to 3 needs a key; step 5's Identity data
  migration does, because its acceptance test signs an account in and a sign-in issues a cookie against
  the ring (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)).
- **The consequence is the failure mode a separate creating step would have had, removed:** if a release
  applies the Identity set at all, the key table is created, so there is no state in which steps 1 to 3
  succeeded and the ring's table is absent. Step 4 exists to catch the remaining case — a set applied
  from an assembly that predates this migration — and it catches it by verification rather than by
  creating something the migration set should have.

**Two consequences for the context's own definition**, both of which belong to section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)'s resolution rather than to a separate
design. `ApplicationDbContext` gains the interface and the `DbSet`, so its model contains one framework
entity beyond Identity's own; and its `OnModelCreating` calls the base implementation before any
catalog-independent configuration, exactly as the Identity base type requires.

**Everything operational about the ring is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and is not
restated here**: the store's location and its rationale (§7.2), protection at rest (§7.3), rotation
(§7.4), and isolation between deployment slots and Container Apps revisions (§7.5), including the
slot-scoped marking of the discriminator setting this section consumes. This document's contribution is
exactly the three lines of code that make those decisions real — the interface, the migration's home, and
the registration call.

**And the reason none of it is optional — stated from what the platform default actually does, not from an
assumption that it does nothing.** The framework "attempts to detect its operational environment and
handle key configuration on its own", and on the primary hosting target it does something quite specific:
"If the app is hosted in Azure Apps, keys are persisted to the `%HOME%\ASP.NET\DataProtection-Keys`
folder. This folder is backed by network storage and is synchronized across all machines hosting the app.
Keys aren't protected at rest. The `DataProtection-Keys` folder supplies the key ring to all instances of
an app in a single deployment slot. Separate deployment slots, such as Staging and Production, don't share
a key ring" (*Data Protection key management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). Three things follow,
and the first is the one a "keys are per-instance" reading gets wrong:

- **Multi-instance sharing is not what the database store buys on App Service** — the default share
  already synchronizes the ring across instances of one slot. Saying otherwise would justify the right
  control with the wrong reason.
- **What it does buy there is at-rest protection and slot-swap survival.** The default ring is not
  protected at rest, and it is *slot-scoped*: the same source states that after a swap "any app using Data
  Protection won't be able to decrypt stored data using the key ring inside the previous slot", which
  "leads to users being logged out". [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s release model swaps slots,
  so on the default ring every deployment would sign every user out — and it names a SQL store among the
  external providers that make key rings slot-independent.
- **On the container path the default is not durable at all.** The same source directs that "when hosting
  in a Docker container, keys should be persisted in a folder that's a Docker volume ... or in an external
  provider", so under the secondary option of [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) an unconfigured
  ring dies with the replica. The database store is the one choice that is correct on both targets, which
  is why it is not conditional on which one is chosen.

Either way the pairing with session holds: the distributed session of section
[6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) would be undermined by a ring that a swap or a replica replacement
invalidates — the two controls only work together. The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts exactly
that pairing: a cookie issued by one instance accepted by another, and a cookie issued before a restart
accepted after it.

#### 4.9.1 An empty ring needs a leader — the key-ring bootstrap, and why polling readiness is not a proof

**One state is reached deliberately and repeatedly by this design, and the framework's own behaviour in it
is safe but not *single*.** [06 §6.7.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s recovery sequence deletes
every row of `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` at step **K2** and restarts every instance at step **K3**, so every
instance comes up against an **empty** ring. The framework handles that: with automatic generation left at
its default, a system whose default key is missing generates a new one with immediate activation. What it
does not do is nominate one instance to be the one that generates it. There is **no leader** in that
mechanism — each process independently observes a ring with no default key and each independently creates
one — so with *n* instances the honest expectation is *n* keys, arriving in whatever order the restarts
complete. Step **K4** asserts **exactly one row**, and nothing in the platform's contract makes that
assertion true.

**And polling readiness cannot supply what is missing, which is stated plainly because the earlier
formulation of K4 opened with exactly that.** One request to `/healthz/ready` establishes nothing about
the ring, for three independent reasons and each one alone is sufficient:

| Why | Where the property comes from |
| --- | --- |
| The endpoint performs **no I/O in the request at all** — it returns the last completed verdict from memory | Section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)'s no-I/O rule, which is [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s |
| **None of `C1`–`C5` reads the key ring or protects anything.** `C2` checks that `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` *exists* and `C3` checks that the identity *may* `SELECT` and `INSERT` on it; neither reads a key, and no check calls `Protect` | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s check definitions |
| A probe request is **load-balanced**, so even if it did protect something it would exercise **one** instance's ring and say nothing about the others | The platform's own routing; it is the same property that makes the cross-instance half of the postcondition below necessary rather than redundant |

So a 200 from that path is compatible with an empty ring, with one key, and with five. **Readiness polling
is not a fresh-ring proof and this document does not treat it as one.**

**The application-side mechanism: one leader, one key, by construction.** A third hosted service,
`Services/KeyRingBootstrapService.cs`, sits in the same `Services/` folder as the other three and under the
same [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) catch-all delegation section
[2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) records, so **no map row, no new
folder, no new project and no new operator verb is introduced.** It is registered on the **web host only**,
beside item 15 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) and **not** in the shared
registration half, so `provision-admin` never runs it. Its pass runs **once per process start** and never
again:

```text
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    await Task.Yield();                            // never block the start; see 2.6

    using var bound = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken);
    bound.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));
    try
    {
        // Its own session, because sp_getapplock with @LockOwner = 'Session' holds the
        // lock on the connection that took it. Never the context's connection.
        await using var lockSession = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await lockSession.OpenAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);

        int rc = await AcquireAppLockAsync(lockSession, bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
        if (rc != 0 && rc != 1)                    // -1 timeout, or another instance holds it
        {
            _logger.LogInformation("keyRingBootstrap outcome=notLeader returnCode={Rc}", rc);
            return;
        }
        try
        {
            IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> keys = await Task.Run(
                () => _keyManager.GetAllKeys(), bound.Token)
                .WaitAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);

            DateTimeOffset now = _timeProvider.GetUtcNow();
            if (_defaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy(now, keys).DefaultKey is not null)
            {
                _logger.LogInformation("keyRingBootstrap outcome=alreadyPresent");
                return;                            // idempotent: nothing to create
            }
            IKey created = await Task.Run(
                () => _keyManager.CreateNewKey(now, now + _rotationPeriod), bound.Token)
                .WaitAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
            _logger.LogInformation("keyRingBootstrap outcome=created keyId={KeyId}",
                                   created.KeyId);
        }
        finally
        {
            await ReleaseAppLockAsync(lockSession, CancellationToken.None)
                .ConfigureAwait(false);
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Shutdown during bootstrap. Nothing recorded, nothing created.
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning(ex, "keyRingBootstrap outcome=failed");   // fail-soft; see below
    }
}
```

`AcquireAppLockAsync` and `ReleaseAppLockAsync` are two `DbCommand` invocations of
`sp_getapplock` and `sp_releaseapplock` on that same connection, each with a
`ParameterDirection.ReturnValue` parameter, which is how the procedure's return code is read —
`ExecuteNonQueryAsync` returns a row count and not the procedure's value. `_defaultKeyResolver` is the
same `IDefaultKeyResolver` the heartbeat resolves for `defaultKeyId`, whose acceptance terms and
revalidation obligation are stated once in section
[2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) and are not re-argued here:
`DefaultKeyResolution.DefaultKey` being non-null is the framework's **own** answer to "does this ring
already have a key it would protect with", which is exactly the question the bootstrap must not answer for
itself.

**Three type facts are recorded here rather than left implicit, because they are the kind that fails at
the first compile rather than at review, and each was checked against the shipped 8.0 assembly rather than
recalled.** First, `IKeyManager` and `IKey` are in
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement`, with `GetAllKeys()` returning
`IReadOnlyCollection<IKey>` and `CreateNewKey(DateTimeOffset, DateTimeOffset)` returning `IKey` — which is
why the two `Task.Run` results above are typed the way they are. Second, `IDefaultKeyResolver` is **not**
in that namespace: it is public, but it sits one level deeper, in
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal`, so this file carries a **second `using`**
for that namespace and a file that imports only the first will not compile. Third,
`DefaultKeyResolution` is a **struct** in that same namespace whose `DefaultKey`, `FallbackKey` and
`ShouldGenerateNewKey` are **fields rather than properties** — which is why the sketch reads
`.DefaultKey` off the returned value directly and does not null-check the resolution itself.

Whether taking that namespace is acceptable at all, and what re-checking it costs on a framework move, is
section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)'s decision and its
option table; this section adds only the second call site to the closed list that subsection keeps, and
inherits the revalidation obligation unchanged.

**Six properties of that, each of which is the reason a line is there.**

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The lock is the existing one's mechanism on its own resource name** | `sp_getapplock` with `@LockMode = 'Exclusive'`, `@LockOwner = 'Session'` and a **15-second** `@LockTimeout`, released by `sp_releaseapplock` in a `finally` on the same connection — the contract [06 §6.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes for the release lock, including its return-code handling: `0` and `1` are *acquired*, and every negative value is *not acquired*. The **resource name is `MvcMusicStore-KeyRingBootstrap`, deliberately not the release lock's**, so a starting instance can never contend with a release in flight or delay one. The platform requires only membership of the `public` database role to call either procedure, so the runtime identity needs no additional grant for the lock itself |
| **Exactly one key, because the create is inside the lock and is preceded by a re-read** | Every instance takes the same path: acquire, re-read the ring, create only if the framework's own resolver reports no default key, release. The instance that wins creates one key; the instances that queue behind it re-read a ring that now *has* a default and create nothing; instances whose 15 seconds elapse do nothing at all and say so. `n` instances therefore produce **one** row rather than *n*, which is what makes K4's "exactly one row" an assertion instead of a hope |
| **The write is one the runtime identity is already granted** | `CreateNewKey` is an `INSERT` into `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`, and `SELECT` plus `INSERT` on that table are exactly the two verbs [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `C3` asserts the runtime identity holds — while `UPDATE` stays denied. So the bootstrap needs **no privilege this design did not already give it**, and it cannot rotate or rewrite an existing key even if it were wrong |
| **It cannot block the start, and it cannot stop the host** | `await Task.Yield()` first, both synchronous key-management calls offloaded and bounded exactly as section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) requires of the heartbeat, and the whole body wrapped so nothing escapes `ExecuteAsync` into `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior`'s `StopHost` default |
| **It is fail-soft, deliberately, and that is consistent with this section rather than a weakening of it** | A failure to acquire the lock, to read or to create writes one record and returns; it never fails the start and never makes the instance unready. This section's failure model for the key store is unchanged: **readiness and the release-side assertions are the controls**, not a refusal to start. What the bootstrap changes is only *how many* keys a recovery produces — the framework's own on-demand generation remains the fallback if the bootstrap did nothing, so the worst case is the behaviour that existed before it, not an outage |
| **It is `once per process`, not a loop** | There is no timer and no second pass: the method returns, and the service is finished. Rotation is the framework's and [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; the heartbeat observes it. A bootstrap that ran periodically would be a second rotation mechanism competing with the first |

**The postcondition, and why it is retry-tolerant rather than immediate.** The bootstrap runs *after* its
instance has yielded and after its own scope and connection are open, so it completes at some point shortly
**after** the process starts answering — and instances restarted by
[06 §6.7.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s K3 do not restart simultaneously. The assertion is
therefore a **bounded poll**, and both halves must hold:

| Half | Assertion | Why the poll |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The ring is fresh, and singular** | `SELECT Id, FriendlyName FROM dbo.DataProtectionKeys` returns **exactly one row**, and that row's `Id` is **absent from K1's captured inventory** — the two assertions K4 already states, now backed by a mechanism that makes the first one deterministic | The leader may not have reached its create the instant the first instance answers a request. Poll every **5 seconds** for up to **2 minutes**; more than one row at any point is an immediate failure rather than something to wait out, because the lock should have made it impossible and a second row means the bootstrap did not run |
| **Every running instance is using it** | Each instance's `KeyRingStatus` record reports `defaultKeyId` equal to that identifier — **one record per running instance**, which is the cardinality [06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes for that record | The record is emitted once per process start and reaches the workspace through a channel with a documented ingestion delay ([06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s arithmetic), so an immediate read is a read of an empty window rather than of a failure. Poll on the same bound, and require the instance **count** to match the platform's current count rather than accepting the first record that arrives |

A postcondition that does not hold within the bound is a **failed recovery** and the route stops — the
outcome [06 §6.7.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) already defines for K5, applied to the same
sequence's earlier step. **06 owns the runbook step, its evidence record and its failure action; this
subsection owns only the application mechanism that makes the step's assertions achievable**, and coverage
row 25 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is where the mechanism itself is exercised.

### 4.10 Azure SQL connection resilience — bounded retries, and the transactions that must wrap them

**The source has no retry behaviour of any kind, because it never needed one.** Both connection strings
attach a local file [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13], where a connection either works or the
machine is broken. Azure SQL is different in a way that is not a tuning detail: it drops connections
during service-initiated failover, reconfiguration and throttling, and the resulting exception looks
exactly like a real failure to code that does not distinguish them. **A port that carries the source's
silence forward converts routine platform maintenance into failed checkouts.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
states the platform requirement; the **code contract** is this document's, because it changes how the
explicit transaction of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and the checkout write are
written.

**Retries, with stated bounds rather than "enable retries".** Both registrations of section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) configure the SQL Server provider
identically:

| Setting | Value | Why this value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retry enabled | `EnableRetryOnFailure(...)` on **both** contexts | A retry policy on one context leaves the other's writes unprotected, and the cross-store sequence of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) spans both |
| Maximum retry count | **6** | Covers a failover window without unbounded accumulation. The seventh failure is a real failure and is surfaced |
| Maximum delay between retries | **5 seconds** | The cap is **multiplied by the retry count**, so it is the term that dominates the budget below. At 30 seconds — the value an earlier formulation of this table carried — the delays alone reach three minutes and no request the user is waiting on can contain them. At 5 seconds the six delays total 30 seconds, which still absorbs a service-initiated failover's reconnection window |
| Transient error list | **The provider's own, unextended** — no `errorNumbersToAdd` | Adding an error number classifies a failure as retryable on this application's authority rather than the provider's. Nothing here warrants that |
| Command timeout | **10 seconds**, set on both contexts via `UseSqlServer(o => o.CommandTimeout(10))` | Every command this application issues is a single-row write or a bounded read; 10 seconds is two to three orders of magnitude above expected latency, and it replaces the provider's own 30-second default, which is too long once the retry count multiplies it. The arithmetic is below |
| Per-attempt bound | **15 seconds**, as a linked `CancellationToken` passed into the retried delegate | A command timeout bounds one command; the retried unit contains several. Without a bound on the *unit*, the worst case is (commands × command timeout) per attempt, which is not a number this document can state, because it depends on how EF batches. Bounding the attempt makes the budget below closed rather than approximate |

**The budget, with the arithmetic shown, because a retry policy that can outlive the request it serves
converts a handled failure into a killed one.** Two bounds sit outside the retry policy and the retry
policy must fit inside both:

| Term | Value | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Attempts | **7** — the first plus six retries | The retry count above |
| Worst case per attempt | **15 s** | The per-attempt bound above |
| Worst case total in attempts | 7 × 15 s = **105 s** | |
| Worst case total in delays | 6 × 5 s = **30 s** | Six retries at the capped maximum delay. Using the cap rather than the strategy's actual exponential backoff is deliberate: the cap is an upper bound the provider guarantees, and a budget built on the backoff *formula* would move if the provider's defaults did |
| **Worst-case wall-clock of the retried unit** | **135 s** | 105 + 30 |
| **The application's own request timeout** | **150 s** | An explicit `RequestTimeoutPolicy` — .NET 8's request-timeout middleware, `AddRequestTimeouts` with a `DefaultPolicy` and `UseRequestTimeouts` registered **after** `UseRouting` as its documentation requires (*Request timeouts middleware in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). Strictly greater than 135 s, so the retry policy always completes or fails on its own terms rather than being cut off mid-attempt |
| **The platform's request timeout** | **~240 s on the primary target**, published by [06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) as a platform-fixed limit — this document states only the requirement it places on it: it must exceed **150 s**, which that value does | A platform limit is a hosting fact, not an application one, so the number is 06's and the *ordering* is this document's contract: 135 s < 150 s < the platform's limit. Because the platform's limit is documented as not configurable, the application's own policy is the term that moves: were the platform limit ever below 150 s, the policy value would move down to sit inside it and the retry bounds would move with it. The ordering is the contract, not the three numbers |

**Why an application-level request timeout at all, when the terms above already add up.** Because they
add up only for the retried unit. A request also opens a connection, renders a view and may touch the
distributed cache, and the timeout middleware is what makes the *whole* request bounded by a number this
document states rather than by whichever platform limit happens to be lower.

**What the caller actually receives when it fires, corrected, because the mechanism is not the one an
exception-shaped reading suggests.** An earlier version of this paragraph said the exception handler of
section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 turns the timeout into the generic error page.
It does not, and it cannot: **the request-timeout middleware produces a status code rather than throwing**,
so there is no exception for `UseExceptionHandler` to catch. The full path, in order:

| Step | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. The timeout fires | The middleware cancels the request's cancellation token, and — where the response has not already started — sets the response status to `RequestTimeoutPolicy.TimeoutStatusCode`, which "defaults to 504" (API reference, .NET 8). **`WriteTimeoutResponse` is deliberately left unset**, so no body is written; a delegate there would be a second, hand-maintained error renderer competing with the one the application already has |
| 2. Nothing catches it, because nothing threw | An endpoint that observes the cancellation and returns, and an endpoint whose `OperationCanceledException` the middleware recognises as its own timeout, both end in the same place: a **504 with an empty body**. Stage 2's exception handler is not in the path |
| 3. Stage 3 renders it | `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/Home/Error", "?code={0}")` is what turns a bare status code into a page, so the caller receives `/Home/Error`'s view rendered for **`?code=504`** — the same endpoint, the same generic text and the same trace identifier as every other status-code response, which is the whole reason there is one error endpoint rather than a family of them |
| 4. The re-execution is method-preserving, so a timed-out `POST` re-enters as a tokenless `POST` | Which the global anti-forgery filter would reject with a 400, replacing a 504 with a misleading validation failure. That is exactly the case the **first** of section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s two published opt-outs exists for: `/Home/Error` carries `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]`, and it is rendering-only, so the exemption costs nothing (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) |
| 5. The error page does not render inside the window that just expired | Stage 3 sits **above** stage 8 in the pipeline order of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), so re-execution begins only after the timeout middleware has completed and unwound its scope. The error endpoint also reads nothing from the request beyond the path, query and status code, so it does not depend on the state of any cancellation token either way |

**One consequence for the record, because it changes what a query for these will find.** The framework
record for a timed-out request is the **status-code** path's, not an exception record — nothing threw — so
a search for exceptions will not surface it and the 504 status is what identifies it;
[06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns what is collected and section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) owns the named log-state shape any record this application
writes must take. **The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)** asserts the whole chain with a
policy set short by the fixture: a 504 status, `/Home/Error`'s rendered view with a trace identifier, the
same outcome for a `POST`, and specifically **not** a 400 and **not** an empty body.

**The interaction that bites, and it is not optional to handle.** With a retrying execution strategy in
place, **a user-initiated transaction throws** — the strategy refuses to retry a block it cannot re-run
in full, and it says so rather than silently retrying half of it. So every explicit transaction must be
wrapped:

```text
var strategy = context.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy();
await strategy.ExecuteAsync(async () =>
{
    await using var tx = await context.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
    …                                  // the whole unit of work
    await tx.CommitAsync();
});
```

**The transaction is begun *inside* the delegate**, not outside it. Outside, a retry would resume a
transaction the failed connection already destroyed; inside, a retry re-runs the whole unit against a new
connection, which is the only form that is correct.

That shape is the **general** one, and the cart migration uses it as written. **The checkout write uses
`ExecuteInTransactionAsync` with a verification predicate instead**, because re-running its delegate after
an *unknown* commit outcome can create a second order — section
[4.10.1](#4101-the-checkout-write-needs-an-idempotency-key-because-the-transaction-rolled-back-is-an-assumption)
owns that case and the mechanism that closes it.

**Two sites in this document are affected, and both are named** so neither is discovered at runtime:

- **The cart-migration transaction** of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 2.
- **The checkout write** — the sequence that adds the order, writes its detail rows, empties the cart and
  saves [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44-51] — which is the financial one and
  therefore the one where a half-applied retry would be worst.

**The delegate must be idempotent**, because it can run more than once. For the cart migration that is
already a requirement rather than a new one: step 4 of section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) makes it idempotent and **keyed on the anonymous cart id**
precisely so a retry cannot double-assign rows, and the execution strategy is the mechanism that turns
that requirement into a live one.

#### 4.10.1 The checkout write needs an idempotency key, because "the transaction rolled back" is an assumption

**The reasoning that says the transaction makes the checkout idempotent is wrong, and it is wrong in the
one case that matters.** A retried attempt does start from a rolled-back state — *when the transaction
was in fact rolled back*. It is not always: "if the connection is dropped while the transaction is being
committed the resulting state of the transaction is unknown", and "by default, the execution strategy
will retry the operation as if the transaction was rolled back, but if it's not the case this will result
in an exception if the new database state is incompatible or could lead to data corruption"
(*Connection resiliency*, EF Core). For this application the second branch is the live one: the order's
key is **store-generated**, so re-running the delegate inserts a **second order with a new `OrderId`**,
writes its detail rows again, and reports success. Nothing in the existing coverage would see it —
The coverage assertion requires that an order's `Total` equals the sum of *its* detail rows, and **both** orders
satisfy that.

**The resolution is a client-generated idempotency key on the order, verified when the commit outcome is
unknown.** Three parts, and each is required:

| Part | Specification |
| --- | --- |
| **The key** | `Order.IdempotencyKey`, a **`Guid`**, non-nullable, with a **unique index**. It is generated **once, in the action, before the execution strategy is invoked**, so every attempt of the retried delegate carries the same value. Generating it inside the delegate would produce a fresh value per attempt and defeat the whole mechanism |
| **The verification** | `strategy.ExecuteInTransactionAsync(context, operation: …, verifySucceeded: …)` rather than `strategy.ExecuteAsync(…)`. The method "begins and commits a transaction and also accepts a function in the `verifySucceeded` parameter that is invoked when a transient error occurs during the transaction commit" (same reference), and the predicate here is `context.Orders.AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(o => o.IdempotencyKey == key, ct)` — so an unknown outcome is **resolved by asking the database** instead of assumed |
| **The unique index** | The backstop. If the verification path is ever wrong — a predicate against the wrong column, a context without an execution strategy, a future edit — a second insert with the same key **fails at the database** rather than creating a second order. A correctness mechanism whose only enforcement is application code is one edit away from not existing |

**Why the key lives on the order rather than in a separate transaction-tracking table.** EF Core's own
guidance offers both: a state-verification predicate against the written row, and a per-transaction id in
its own table for the case where "you need to use store-generated keys" (same reference). The separate
table is the more general mechanism and it costs a second write, a cleanup delete and a table that grows
if either fails. The key on the order is **narrower and self-cleaning**: there is exactly one such write
in this application, the key is written by the same insert it protects, and it survives as a durable fact
about that order rather than as bookkeeping to be deleted. AAP §0.4.1 maps `Models/Order.cs` and the
`Data/` model configuration — it maps the **entity**, not its column list — so this addition sits inside
the mapped file rather than adding one.

**Four mechanical properties, because each is a place this goes wrong quietly.**

1. **`SaveChangesAsync` is called with `acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false` inside the delegate**, and
   `ChangeTracker.AcceptAllChanges()` is called after the strategy returns. EF Core's own note gives the
   reason: it avoids marking the entities `Unchanged` before the commit is known, which "allows to retry
   the same operation if the commit fails and the transaction is rolled back" (same reference).
2. **The verifying context must itself have a retrying execution strategy**, because "the connection is
   likely to fail again during verification if it failed during transaction commit" (same reference). Both
   registrations of section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) enable retry, so
   the verification runs on a resilient connection — but it is a property of the design rather than an
   accident, and a future single-purpose context created for this path would have to keep it.
3. **When verification says the order exists, the request completes as a success**, re-reading that order
   by its key to obtain the store-generated `OrderId` the confirmation redirect needs. It does **not**
   re-run the delegate, so the cart is not emptied twice and no detail row is written twice.
4. **The scope is the retry, not the user.** This key defends the one case the execution strategy
   creates — a retry after an unknown commit outcome. It does **not** deduplicate a user who submits the
   checkout form twice, because each request generates its own key. That is the source's behaviour today
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44-51] and it is **preserved**, deliberately:
   changing it would need a token carried in the form, which is an interface change and therefore an
   approval-owned delta rather than a correctness fix. Section
   [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) does not carry one, so this document does not invent one.

The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts the invariant that matters — **exactly
one** order after a lost commit acknowledgement — and the coverage assertion continues to assert the arithmetic
one, which is a different property and never was this one.

#### 4.10.2 What retries do not fix

**Stated so the guarantee is not overstated.** They cover transient failures of EF Core operations, and
nothing else:

- **A failure after the strategy returned but before the response reached the client** is still a failure
  the caller sees. The write happened; the user is told it did not. The idempotency key of section
  [4.10.1](#4101-the-checkout-write-needs-an-idempotency-key-because-the-transaction-rolled-back-is-an-assumption)
  closes the *retry* case, not this one: no server-side mechanism can make a response that never arrived
  arrive. This is why the cart-migration path has an explicit non-blocking-notice branch (section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 5) rather than a retry loop, and why the checkout's
  redisplay path must not be read as proof that nothing was written.
- **A non-transient failure** — a permission error, a schema mismatch, an exhausted database — is retried
  zero times by the provider's own classification and surfaces immediately, which is the wanted
  behaviour.
- **The distributed cache and the key repository do not share these contexts' execution strategy.** They
  are separate components with their own connection handling, so a transient failure there surfaces as a
  failed request rather than as a retried one. That is a recorded limit, and it is one more reason the
  health probe of [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) exists.

---

## 5. Schema lifecycle and the two data migrations

### 5.1 Domain data migration starts with schema extraction

**An EF Core initial migration creates empty tables. It moves no rows.** That sentence needs saying
because "generate the initial migration" reads like the data step and is not it.

Worse, **the generated migration cannot be trusted to match the database the data is actually in.** A
migration generated from the ported model may differ from the real EF 6 schema in column type,
precision and length, nullability, identity and key definition, delete rule, default value and index —
and none of those differences produces a build error or a startup error. They produce wrong data, or a
failed insert, at the first write. **And there is nothing in the repository to compare against:**
MVC 5 ships no schema script at all, and MVC 4's two copies are byte-identical and not runnable as
written ([12 F-12-22](12-migration-blockers.md) owns both facts; [04 §13.1](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
carries the instruction that neither may be used as a baseline).

**Therefore the domain-data workstream begins with extraction, and the diff is a gate.** In order:

1. **Authoritative schema extraction from `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/MvcMusicStore.mdf`.** A
   `sys.columns`, `sys.indexes`, `sys.key_constraints` and `sys.foreign_keys` interrogation of the
   attached database, producing a written schema record for all six catalog tables. This can only be
   done on a supported Windows and LocalDB runtime, because that is the only place the file attaches
   ([10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) owns the toolchain). **It must be done against a
   copy outside the checkout** — attaching the tracked `.mdf` and `.ldf` causes the engine to write to
   them, which would dirty the working tree.
2. **Map every extracted object to the EF Core model**, and express the result in
   `MusicStoreEntities.OnModelCreating` (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)).
3. **Generate the initial catalog migration and diff its DDL against the extracted schema. The diff must
   report zero differences — not zero *unexplained* differences — before any data is loaded.** The rule
   is absolute and it is one rule, because the alternative is the one this step cannot survive: **there
   is no annotation under which a difference is admitted.** "Expected difference, see section X" is
   precisely the label a genuine discrepancy is waved through under, and a single sanctioned exception
   converts the gate from a comparison into a judgement call for every later reader. A reported
   difference therefore has exactly **two** dispositions and no third: it is **corrected in the model**,
   so that the baseline reproduces the source; or — where it is an intended target-state change rather
   than a modelling error — the model is written to the **source's** shape for the baseline and the
   intended change **ships as a named subsequent migration** in the post-load group below, never inside
   the baseline. This is the gate; a data load against an unverified schema is the failure this whole
   section exists to prevent.
4. **Back up the source, then extract the data.** The source `.mdf` is preserved unmodified as the
   rollback position.
5. **Apply the baseline migration to the target database**, then **load in dependency order**:
   **genres and artists** (no dependencies), then **albums** (referencing both), then **carts**
   (referencing albums), then **orders**, then **order details** (referencing orders and albums).
   Identity-column behaviour must be handled explicitly at load time so that existing key values are
   preserved — `Cart.RecordId`, `Order.OrderId` and `OrderDetail.OrderDetailId` are referenced by
   other rows and by nothing else, but `Order.OrderId` is also the **confirmation number** the
   application shows the customer [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54],
   so renumbering orders would change a value users have already been given.
   **The load converts timestamps as it goes**: `Order.OrderDate` and `Cart.DateCreated` are rewritten
   from the required `LegacySourceTimeZone` parameter into UTC, and the load **fails closed** if that
   parameter is absent or unresolvable — section
   [8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) owns the rule, coverage
   The coverage assertions require it.
6. **Reconcile.** Row count **per table**, before and after. And **financial totals per order** —
   `Order.Total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] compared against the sum of its
   `OrderDetail.UnitPrice * Quantity` rows, computed on the source and on the target and required to
   match to the cent. Reconciliation failure blocks cutover.
7. **Protect the data in transit and at rest.** The order tables carry name, postal address, phone
   number and email address [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61], so the extract is PII: it
   travels only over an encrypted connection, is held only in an encrypted location, is access-logged,
   and is destroyed on a stated schedule after reconciliation passes. [09 §6.8](09-security-assessment.md)
   owns the standing PII finding.
8. **Define how rows written between extraction and cutover are handled.** Under the single-cutover
   decision of section [11](#11-the-cutover-decision) the answer is a **drain**: the legacy
   application is drained before the final extract, so the window is closed rather than
   reconciled. Any trickle-load design is therefore explicitly **not** built; if the cutover approach
   were ever revisited, this step would have to be re-answered.
9. **State the rollback position and the closing acceptance criteria.** Rollback is: the source
   database is unmodified, the legacy application is redeployable, and the target database is
   discarded. Acceptance is: the schema diff passed, every per-table row count matches, every order
   total matches, and the coverage of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) passes against the loaded
   data.

**Three groups of schema changes are deliberately held back until after that acceptance, and they are the
only ones.** The first is the checkout submission key, immediately below. The second is the
change-tracking pair that [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires in order to decide a
rollback, specified at the end of this sub-section. The third is the **timestamp column type** of section
[8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display), specified with the second
because it ships in the same deployment step. **All three are held back for the same reason — step 3's
rule admits no annotated exception — and stating them as a closed set of three is what makes that rule
enforceable**: a fourth intended difference is not permitted to appear as an annotation on the diff, it
has to appear here.

**One clarification the closed set needs, because it is the way a fourth member gets in by accident: a
bound on an input model is not a schema difference.** The checkout input model's `[StringLength(254)]` on
`Email` and `[StringLength(16)]` on `PromoCode` (section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)) and the administration models' copied
attributes (section [8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target))
constrain what the application **accepts**; they are not `HasMaxLength` calls on an entity and they change
no column. So they are absent from this set by construction rather than by omission — and the corollary
binds: a validation bound may **not** be paired with a narrower column "for alignment" in the baseline
model, because that pairing is exactly a fourth intended difference wearing an annotation. Section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) records that `Order.Email` therefore keeps the
source's `nvarchar(max)` width, and that narrowing it would require a fourth named post-load migration
with an overlength precheck rather than a note on the diff. The checkout submission key of section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) needs a nullable `SubmissionId` column on
`Orders` and a unique index over it filtered to `WHERE [SubmissionId] IS NOT NULL`. Neither is in the
initial migration, and the reason is step 3: the value of the diff gate comes entirely from the initial
migration being a **pure reproduction** of the extracted schema, so that every difference it reports is a
real one. Introducing the column there would put a known, intended difference into the one comparison
whose whole job is to surface unintended ones — and "expected difference" is exactly the annotation under
which a genuine discrepancy gets waved through. It therefore ships as a **second catalog migration**,
applied after the load and after reconciliation, against which the diff has nothing to say. Every
migrated order carries `NULL` in the new column, which is what the index filter accommodates.

**The second group is the change-tracking pair, and it exists so that a rollback decision rests on
evidence rather than on a probe.** [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) decides whether a
rollback is still available by detecting whether any customer write has been accepted since traffic was
admitted, and it establishes that counting rows cannot answer that question: a successful password change
leaves the account count unchanged, and a quantity-only cart update leaves both the row count and the key
set unchanged. Detection therefore needs per-row evidence, and this document owns the schema, so the
columns are specified here rather than assumed there. Every tracked table gains a database-maintained
`rowversion` column and a `ModifiedUtc` `datetime2` column, **and is made system-versioned** — the third
mechanism, without which the first two cannot see a deletion at all. **Which tables those are is
[06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to state and it states them**: the catalog context's six
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] and the tables the Identity context owns, with
the session cache table, `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` and `dbo.SecurityAuditLog` **excluded** — the first two
as platform state, the third because it is already append-only under an explicit `DENY UPDATE, DELETE`
([06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) and so has no update or delete to capture. That list is
06's and this document does not widen it. This document owns what the requirement takes of the schema and
the model, and there are **four** parts to it.

**It is two migrations, one per context, and it cannot be one.** The columns span both contexts, and each
context owns a separate migrations folder and a distinct history table (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)) — so a single *catalog* migration carrying
`ALTER TABLE` statements against `AspNetUsers` would place Identity DDL in the catalog history, leave the
Identity model's snapshot disagreeing with the database, and make the next Identity migration generate
those same columns a second time. What ships is therefore **`AddChangeTracking` in
`Data/Migrations/Catalog/`** covering the six catalog tables and **`AddChangeTracking` in
`Data/Migrations/Identity/`** covering the Identity tables, each generated from and validated against its
own model snapshot. Both are applied in the same post-load deployment step as `AddCheckoutSubmissionId`
and after it — after the load and after reconciliation, for the same diff-gate reason the first group is
held back — in the sequence [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns.

**The mapping is authored per context, in each context's `OnModelCreating`, and the `rowversion` half takes
three explicit calls rather than one convenient one.** There is no shared base class and no cross-context
convention to lean on, so each context configures its own entities: `ModifiedUtc` as a required
`datetime2`, and a `byte[] RowVersion` property configured with **`.HasColumnType("rowversion")`,
`.ValueGeneratedOnAddOrUpdate()` and `.IsConcurrencyToken(false)`** — the call pair
[06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names, plus the column type that pair leaves
undetermined.

**The third call is why the first is necessary, and this is the one place the shorthand's absence has a
consequence worth writing down.** `.IsRowVersion()` sets store generation *and* concurrency-token
semantics together, and 06 wants only the first half — but SQL Server's provider convention selects the
`rowversion` store type for a `byte[]` property *because* that property is a concurrency token generated on
add or update. Turning the token off therefore also turns off the convention that chose the type, and a
property left with `.ValueGeneratedOnAddOrUpdate()` alone maps to `varbinary(max)`: a column with no engine
maintenance behind it, which never moves, and whose failure mode is that every detection query reports **no
writes** — the one failure this evidence cannot tolerate, because it is silent and it reads as good news.
The type is therefore stated rather than inferred. Two further properties follow from the configuration and
need no extra calls: EF Core's before-save and after-save behaviour for a store-generated,
non-concurrency-token property is `Ignore`, so no insert or update ever sends a value the engine owns; and
because the property is not a concurrency token it never enters an `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause, which is what
keeps last-write-wins intact. The property is declared with a private setter so no application code can
assign it even by mistake.

The two contexts' configurations are deliberately parallel rather than shared, because the alternative — a
common `DbContext` base type introduced solely to hold two property configurations — couples the catalog and
Identity models for the rest of the port's life to save eight lines.

**The maintenance path is per context too, and `ModifiedUtc` is where that matters.** `rowversion` needs
no application involvement at all; `ModifiedUtc` does, and a save path that maintains it in one context
and not the other yields exactly the half-complete evidence [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
says the determination cannot rest on. **Both** contexts therefore override `SaveChangesAsync` — and
`SaveChanges`, so a synchronous call cannot bypass it — to stamp `ModifiedUtc = DateTime.UtcNow` on every
entry whose state is `Added` or `Modified` and whose entity type declares the property. Two consequences
are stated rather than left to be discovered: a write issued through `ExecuteUpdateAsync` **does not pass
through this path** and must set the column in its own statement, which is why the cart reassignment of
section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) assigns it explicitly; and the checkout write path's
single save (section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) step 8) picks the column up
for the order, its details and nothing else, because the cart rows it touches are `Deleted` rather than
`Modified`.

Two properties of the column pair are decisions rather than details. The first is the one the mapping above
implements: `rowversion` is **deliberately not** a concurrency token, because `IsRowVersion()`'s token half
would make every one of these tables optimistically concurrent, turning a second concurrent edit into a
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` — a behaviour change in a port whose baseline is last-write-wins, and one no
approved delta covers. And applying the migration *after* the load is sound
rather than merely convenient, because `ALTER TABLE … ADD rowversion` stamps every existing row at alter
time: every migrated row therefore carries a value strictly below the `MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION()` watermark
[06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records when traffic is admitted, which is exactly the
comparison the rollback regimes make. `ModifiedUtc` is written by the application on every update under
the rule of section [8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display), and
corroborates `rowversion` rather than replacing it — a row version moves on any write, including one a
trigger or a tool made, while `ModifiedUtc` says when the application last wrote.

**The fourth part is system versioning, and it exists because the column pair is blind to exactly one class
of write — the one that removes the row it would have been recorded on.** A `rowversion` and a
`ModifiedUtc` live *on* a row, so a `DELETE` takes both away with it. A signed-in customer who removes the
last line from their cart therefore leaves **no current row, no advanced version and no timestamp**; the
cart surface emits no audit class either — [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) defines none for it and
this document does not extend that catalog — so on the columns alone that removal is indistinguishable from
a cart nobody touched. [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s determination is required to see
it, so the schema carries the mechanism that makes it visible: **each tracked table is a SQL Server
temporal table**, and the engine retains the prior state of every updated row and the **full final state of
every deleted row** in a bound history table. Five parts of that are this document's to state.

| | What ships |
|---|---|
| **Authoring** | `ToTable(tb => tb.IsTemporal(…))` on every tracked entity in that context's `OnModelCreating`, and the resulting DDL is carried **inside the same `AddChangeTracking` migration** in that context's set. So versioning adds **no migration target and no invocation**: the census of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) is unchanged at three or four post-load targets and 06's three invocations. It is authored as a migration rather than as operator DDL for the reason [06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s first operational consequence gives |
| **Naming — 06 defers this to "05's convention", so here it is** | History table `<EntityTable>History` in a dedicated **`history`** schema, one per tracked table; period columns named `PeriodStart` and `PeriodEnd`, mapped as **shadow properties** so they never appear on an entity type and no view or projection can pick them up by accident. The schema is the only departure from EF Core's default, which would put `<EntityTable>History` beside the current table in `dbo`: a separate schema keeps `dbo` legible next to the session cache, key-ring and audit tables that are **not** versioned, and it turns the grant rule below into one schema-level statement instead of one per table |
| **Retention** | An explicit `HISTORY_RETENTION_PERIOD`, set to the PITR retention window [06 §6.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns — **the value is not restated here**, because it is the data owner's at approval and 06 is where it is read. It is applied by a raw-SQL statement **inside the same migration**, because EF Core's temporal mapping models the versioning and the history table but not the retention period, and a migration that calls only `IsTemporal()` leaves retention infinite. One implementation precondition rides with it: retention cleanup requires the history table to carry a clustered index whose leading column is the period-end column, which is what the engine creates when the migration materializes the bound history table — the migration must not replace that index with one of its own |
| **Grants** | **No grant is issued to the runtime principal on the `history` schema.** [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `app_runtime` grants name the current tables only, and ordinary DML on a system-versioned table needs no permission on its history table — so the application keeps working and cannot read the history it is generating. The history rows carry the same fields the current rows do, which makes them personal data on the Identity side; [06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records that consequence and its retention and access treatment, and this document does not restate it |
| **Ordering** | Versioning is enabled in the **same post-load step as the columns**, and that is a precondition of the determination rather than a convenience: [06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) step 8 asserts **zero rows in every history table** at the moment the watermark is taken, and enabling versioning before the load would have filled them with the load's own writes and the Identity data migration's own — so the emptiness assertion, which is what makes any later history row evidence on its own, would simply not be available |

**How the removal of a final cart line is detected, stated as the query rather than as a property.** Two
facts turn it into an existence check with no clock and no arithmetic in it: the history tables are empty
when the watermark is taken, and the engine writes a history row for **every** update and **every** delete
on a tracked table. So "has any tracked row been written since traffic was admitted" is answered per table
by `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM history.<T>History)`, and the removal of a customer's last cart line is caught by
the `history.CartsHistory` row carrying that row's full final state — its `RecordId`, `CartId`, `AlbumId`,
`Count` and `DateCreated` — at a moment when the current `Carts` table holds nothing for that cart at all.

**Why the watermark alone cannot do it, stated because it is the trap an implementer walks into.** The
`rowversion` value retained in a history row is the value the row carried **before** it was deleted. A cart
row written by the domain load and deleted after admission therefore retains a value **strictly below**
`MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION()`, so a scan that applied the watermark comparison to history rows would classify
that deletion as pre-admission and report no write — the same silent false negative the pair produces on
its own. The determination therefore rests on history **existence**, not on the retained version value;
`PeriodEnd`, which the engine sets to the deleting transaction's UTC start, is available where a
*classification* is wanted — a history row whose key has no matching current row is a delete rather than an
update — but the classification table in [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is where each
class is assigned, and this document owns only that the mechanism exists and answers that query.

**One property the pair does not have, which closes a gap this document flags elsewhere.** System
versioning is engine-maintained, so it captures writes that never pass through a `SaveChanges` override at
all: the set-based `ExecuteUpdateAsync` of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — which is
why that statement assigns `ModifiedUtc` explicitly — any future `ExecuteDeleteAsync`, and any write a tool
or an operator makes. `ModifiedUtc` can be forgotten by a code path; a history row cannot.

**The third group is the timestamp column type, and it is held back for exactly the reason step 3 admits
no annotation.** `Order.OrderDate` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:15] and `Cart.DateCreated`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:14-15] are declared bare — no `HasColumnType`, no fluent
configuration, and the source context declares no `OnModelCreating` at all (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); `Cart.DateCreated`'s
`[DataType(DataType.DateTime)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:14] is a *display* annotation and
maps nothing — so EF 6's default mapping for a non-nullable `DateTime` on SQL Server governs and the
extracted schema is **expected to show `datetime`**. EF Core's default for the same property is
`datetime2`, which is the type section
[8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) requires. Both cannot be true
of the baseline, and an earlier form of these two sections resolved that by letting the difference through
the gate as an annotated deliberate change — which is the one disposition step 3 now refuses. So:

- **The baseline maps the source's type.** Both properties carry an explicit `.HasColumnType("datetime")`
  in the baseline model, so the initial migration reproduces the extracted type and the diff reports
  nothing at all.
- **The move to `datetime2` ships as a named catalog migration, `AlterTimestampColumnTypes`**, applied
  in the same post-load deployment step as the two groups above and **last** within it, once
  reconciliation has passed.
  The `.HasColumnType("datetime")` calls are removed from the model in the same change, so the final
  model is the target model and the alteration is the diff between two migrations rather than an
  exception to one.
- **Being last has one consequence worth stating, because it alters a table that is by then
  system-versioned.** `AddChangeTracking` precedes this migration, so both `Orders` and `Carts` already
  carry system versioning and a bound history table when the `ALTER COLUMN` arrives. The requirement is
  that the change land on **both** sides: a current table and its history table must remain
  union-compatible, so `OrderDate` and `DateCreated` end as `datetime2` in the history tables as well.
  Whether that arrives as an alteration the engine propagates to the history table itself or inside the
  suspend-and-re-enable pair EF Core's SQL Server generator emits around alterations of a temporal table
  ([06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s first operational consequence), the pass criterion
  is the same and is asserted rather than assumed: both types equal, versioning back `ON`, and the history
  rows written before the alteration still readable. A one-sided alteration announces itself as a failed
  re-enable, which is why the assertion is worth making at all.
- **Nothing is lost by loading before altering.** `datetime`'s resolution is what the source rows already
  carry, and step 5 writes converted values of exactly that provenance, so the alteration widens a column
  over rows no wider than it. Every value the *target* writes arrives after the alteration, because this
  step precedes traffic admission.
- **The conditional is resolved by extraction, not left open.** If step 1 shows the columns are already
  `datetime2` — which nothing in the source suggests — the baseline maps them as `datetime2`, this
  migration is **not generated**, and the **catalog** post-load set is two migrations rather than three:
  the census of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) then stands at **three** post-load
  targets across the two contexts rather than four, with the catalog head at `AddChangeTracking`, and the
  paragraph above about altering a versioned table does not arise. Either way the decision is made by step
  1's output before the baseline is generated, and neither branch puts a difference through the gate.

#### 5.1.1 The extract is PII — how it is held, and how it is destroyed

**"Encrypted and access-logged" is a property, not a procedure, and an extract with no procedure is the
copy nobody deletes.** Step 4 produces a file — or a set of files — containing every customer's name,
street address, city, state, postal code, country, phone number and email address, joined to what they
bought and what they paid [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]. It is the most sensitive
artifact this entire migration creates, it exists for hours or days, and it is created by a workstream
rather than by a system with a retention policy. So the handling is specified here.

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it is held** | In **one** location: a dedicated container in the migration workstream's own storage account, created for this migration and used for nothing else, with **no public access**, and **not** on an operator's workstation, not in the repository, not in a pipeline artifact, and not in the checkout — AAP §0.11.5 makes a dirty working tree a release failure, and a PII file inside it would be one of the worst forms of that |
| **Encrypted at rest** | Service-side encryption is not optional and is not the control: 256-bit AES "is enabled for all storage accounts and can't be disabled" (*Azure Storage encryption for data at rest*), and it is transparent to any principal holding data-plane read access — which is exactly the failure this handling has to survive. The controls are therefore the ones section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read) sets on a **dedicated account**: **infrastructure encryption** for a second, independently keyed layer; a **customer-managed key**, which is what makes destruction a key purge rather than a search for copies; **no shared-key access**, so every access is an attributable identity; and a **private-only network path**, which is what makes "not on an operator's workstation" a route that does not exist rather than an instruction |
| **Encrypted in transit** | Every hop: the extraction connection to the source, the upload, the download, and the load's connection to the target, all TLS — the two database connections carrying `Encrypt=True` with `TrustServerCertificate=False`, per the mode table of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), and the storage account configured **HTTPS-only with a minimum TLS version of 1.2**. No hop copies through an unencrypted intermediate, which specifically rules out an SMB share and an emailed archive. The private-endpoint path of section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read) is what keeps every one of those hops off the public internet in the first place, so a TLS misconfiguration on one of them is a defect rather than a disclosure |
| **Under whose identity** | Written by the **extraction principal** and read by the **load principal** — **two distinct user-assigned managed identities**, named, attached and scoped in the identity block of section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read), and **neither of them the deployment principal** that executes the load's SQL. The application's runtime managed identity has **no** access to this container and is never granted any: the running application has no reason to read a copy of its own database, and a grant that exists is a grant that gets used |
| **Who may read it** | A **named** set of people, recorded before the extract is taken, each with the reason they are on it, and no group membership standing in for a name. The set is scoped to the migration and is removed when the extract is destroyed, not when the migration ends |
| **How access is audited** | Storage read-access logging enabled on the container **before** the first write, and reviewed as part of the closing acceptance of step 9 — so "who read this" is answerable rather than asserted. An extract whose container has no logging enabled is not taken. **The log is retained 365 days**, outliving the extract by a wide margin: it is an audit record rather than operational exhaust, which is the class [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) gives that number to, and its whole value is being producible months after the container is gone |
| **Cleanup on success** | The extract and every derived file — the checkpoint file of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), any intermediate transform output, any local copy made during troubleshooting — are deleted **within 7 days of reconciliation passing**, and **both containers** and the account are deleted with them |
| **Cleanup on failure** | The **same deadline, from the same clock**. This is the row that matters: a failed or abandoned migration is exactly the case where an extract survives, because nobody is left running the procedure that would delete it. The deadline therefore runs from **extraction**, not from success — 7 days from reconciliation passing **or 30 days from extraction, whichever comes first** — and a migration still in flight at 30 days re-extracts rather than extending |
| **Proof of deletion** | A recorded artifact, not an assertion: the deletion operation's own log entries for the container and the account, plus a post-deletion listing showing both absent, captured into the migration's run record with the date and the person who performed it — **and the key-destruction record, the vault deletion and purge records, and the immutable copy of the access log** that section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read)'s destruction rows fix. The **key destruction** is the piece that does not depend on having found every copy inside the account, and it is immediate; the **vault purge** is the piece that cannot be immediate, because purge protection is mandatory on a vault holding a Storage customer-managed key and it blocks a purge until the retention interval expires. The immutable log copy is the piece that outlives the account it describes. Step 9's acceptance criteria do not close without the same-day items, and the run record does not close without the purge record |

**What this section deliberately does not decide.** It bounds the **temporary extract** and nothing else.
The **standing** retention decision — how long the application itself keeps order PII, which is a policy
question about live data — belongs to the **data owner** through
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s approval gate, and [09 §6.8](09-security-assessment.md) carries the
finding that no such policy exists today. This document does not invent a legal retention period,
because inventing one would let a reader believe the question had been answered.

##### 5.1.1.1 The protection, named — the account, the key, the network path, and the grants that gate a read

**"Password-protected or key-encrypted" is two options, and an option is not a specification.** A
protection that names no mechanism has no access rule, no audit record and no way of being destroyed on
purpose, which is the property the cleanup rows above actually rest on. So the whole of it is fixed here,
once, for **every file this migration puts in that account** — the extract, the
checkpoint file of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), any
row-level extract a troubleshooting step produces, and the verified source backups
[06 §6.7.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) takes, which hold the same PII and come under this
handling from the moment they leave the legacy host.

**And one reason the protection cannot be applied by the database engine, which is where a reader would
look for it first.** `BACKUP … WITH ENCRYPTION` and transparent data encryption are both listed as
**Enterprise and Standard only** — "Encryption for backups" and "Transparent data encryption (TDE)" are
**No** for Web, Express with Advanced Services and Express (*Editions and supported features of SQL
Server 2022*) — and LocalDB "is a lightweight version of Express edition". The legacy source is LocalDB,
so the engine cannot encrypt its own backup, and every artifact it produces is plaintext at the moment it
is written. That is not a gap to be closed inside SQL Server; it is the reason the protection is applied
at the moment the file leaves the host.

**The mechanism is entirely platform-side, and the in-process alternative is rejected on a constraint this
plan already fixed.** An earlier version of this subsection specified **Azure Storage client-side
encryption v2** — envelope encryption performed by the operator utility, with a Key Vault-held wrapping
key — and closed by noting that its package references "belong to [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s
table as an approval-time addition". That closing note is the defect. AAP §0.5.2 fixes the pin list and
states the principle in its own words: secrets arrive as **App Service Key Vault references**, "so no Key
