passes a count-and-total check: two orders' `Username` values swapped, so both customers see the
other's history; a `Genre` renamed or two genres' ids exchanged during a keyed load; an address or
email altered anywhere in the PII columns [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]; a set of
role assignments redistributed among the same number of users. So the acceptance evidence is stronger:

- **Deterministic keyed set comparison, stated so that it is true of every table including `Cart`.** For
  every migrated table:

  > the **source primary-key set** equals the **union of the target primary-key set and the removed-key
  > set recorded in this run's lineage**, and those two sets are **disjoint** — with the missing and extra
  > members named when it does not hold.

  **The union form is the rule and not an exception to it, which is a correction to an earlier statement
  of this bullet.** That earlier statement required plain source-to-target set equality "for every
  migrated table" and left the many-to-one `Cart` case as a qualification recorded in the merge
  sub-section above, several hundred lines away. A reader implementing the rule as written would have
  produced a comparison that **fails a correct `Cart` migration** — the target's key set is legitimately
  smaller after the merge — and, worse, the natural fix for that failure is to relax the `Cart` comparison,
  which would then **pass a transformation that dropped a row it should have summed**. So the rule carries
  the lineage term for every table. **For every table other than `Cart` the lineage removed set is empty**
  and the rule reduces to the plain set equality it always was; for `Cart` after the merge transformation
  it is not empty, and the same single rule still holds. The lineage-specific `Count` and `DateCreated`
  checks the merge sub-section states are **additional** to this rule, not a substitute for it.
  Under the preserve-all-keys decision of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) both sides are compared directly; had a key
  map been used it would run over the mapped values, which is one of the reasons the map is an artifact
  rather than a scratch variable.
- **Per-field digests, over a declared projection rather than over "the row".** For every migrated row, an
  **HMAC-SHA256 digest over its canonicalized field values**, using the **typed, length-prefixed, UTF-8
  canonical serialization** and the **logical-run key held in the approved secret store** that the rerun
  mechanics above define — the same serialization and
  the same key, so a digest written by the load verifies in the `reconcile` pass that runs later and after
  any restart between them. Rows are compared by key and digest. A field that changed value changes the
  digest; a row that moved to another owner changes the digest.
- **The projection is declared per class, because "the row" is not the same set of fields on both sides.**
  A digest computed over every target column and compared against a digest computed over every source
  column **cannot match for any class that gains a column**, and the target gains columns in six places.
  Left undeclared, the implementer resolves that by whichever expedient comes first — dropping the new
  columns from the comparison silently, or comparing digests that can never be equal — and the first of
  those leaves a net-new column asserted by nothing at all. So every migrated class declares its fields in
  three buckets, and the digest is computed over the **carried** and **transformed** buckets only, with the
  **target-only** bucket asserted separately against its defined origin:

| Class | Carried unchanged — in the digest | Transformed — in the digest, with the transform named | Target-only — **not** in the digest, asserted against its defined origin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Genre` | `GenreId`, `Name`, `Description` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:7-9] | None | None |
| `Artist` | `ArtistId`, `Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:10-11] | None | None |
| `Album` | `AlbumId`, `GenreId`, `ArtistId`, `Title`, `Price`, `AlbumArtUrl` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:10-19] | None | None |
| `Cart` | `RecordId`, `CartId`, `AlbumId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:8-11] | **`Count` and `DateCreated` for merge survivors only** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:12-13]: the summed `Count` and the earliest `DateCreated` of the group, both taken from the lineage record. For every non-survivor row both are carried unchanged | **The `rowversion` concurrency token** (section [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 1). **Origin: assigned by the engine on insert.** Asserted as **present and non-null on every loaded row**, and never compared to a source value — there is no source value, and its bytes are meaningless outside the target database |
| `Order` | `OrderId`, `OrderDate`, `Username`, `Total` and every PII column [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:12-64] — the PII columns **by digest only**, per the artifact rule below | None | **`OperationId`** (section [4.10](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)). **Origin: `null` for every migrated historical order**, which is why its unique index is filtered to exclude nulls. Asserted as **null on every loaded row** — a non-null value on a migrated order would mean the load invented a submission identity |
| `OrderDetail` | `OrderDetailId`, `OrderId`, `AlbumId`, `Quantity`, `UnitPrice` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/OrderDetail.cs:5-9] | None | None |
| Identity user | The user id and `UserName`, and `PasswordHash`, `Email` and `PhoneNumber` where the source holds them — the hash **by digest only** | None | **`NormalizedUserName`** and **`NormalizedEmail`** — **origin: the normalizer applied to the carried value**, asserted by recomputing the normalizer over the carried value and comparing, which is a *derivation* check rather than a source comparison. **`ConcurrencyStamp`** and **`SecurityStamp`** — **origin: generated per account by the load**, asserted as present, non-null and **distinct across accounts**. **`EmailConfirmed`, `PhoneNumberConfirmed`, `TwoFactorEnabled`, `LockoutEnabled`, `LockoutEnd`, `AccessFailedCount`** — **origin: the documented defaults section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) fixes**, asserted as **equal to those defaults on every loaded account**, which is what makes a default a checked fact rather than an assumption |
| Identity role, and each carried child class | The keys and names the class carries, per section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) | None | **`ConcurrencyStamp`** on the role, on the same terms as the user's |

  **Two properties make this table a specification rather than a list.** Every target-only field has a
  **named origin and a stated assertion**, so none is left merely absent from the comparison; and the
  buckets are **exhaustive per class** — a column that appears in neither the source nor any bucket is a
  column the diff gate of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 has not accounted for, which is a
  failure of that gate rather than something reconciliation should paper over. **The facets of every
  target-only column remain gated on the extraction of step 1 and the Identity extraction of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)**; this table fixes what is
  compared and what is asserted, not what type or length anything is.
- **Why a keyed digest rather than a plain hash.** A key **scoped to one logical run** means the
  artifacts are useless outside that run, so a digest file that leaks cannot be used to confirm a guessed
  value in a PII or hash column — which a plain hash of a low-entropy field, an email address or a
  password hash, would permit. The key is scoped to the run and **not** to the process: those are
  different properties, and only the first is a confidentiality control.
- **The financial comparison stays**, as the one domain-specific invariant worth asserting twice:
  `Order.Total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] against the sum of its
  `OrderDetail.UnitPrice * Quantity` rows, on source and target, matching to the cent.
- **Usernames are personal data, they appear in these artifacts in the clear, and the controls are
  applied on that basis rather than the claim being avoided.** The keyed sets this section requires are
  keyed **on the username** — the username set, the `(username, role name)` pair set, the child-class
  affected-username sets of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) — and the whole point of a
  keyed comparison is that it **names the missing or extra member**. A reconciliation artifact that
  named nobody would not be a reconciliation artifact. So the statement is the accurate one:
  **reconciliation output contains usernames and role names in the clear, and it is classified and
  handled as personal data** under the controls tabulated below — encrypted in transit and at rest,
  least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only for the run, destroyed on the named schedule
  with an owner. [09](09-security-assessment.md) owns the standing PII finding.
- **What the artifacts still never contain**, which is a narrower and therefore keepable claim: **no
  password hash, no security stamp, and none of the order tables' PII columns**
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] — name, postal address, phone number, email address —
  in any log, report or file. Values in those categories are compared by **digest only**, which is what
  the per-field digest above is for.
- **Pseudonymous references were considered as the alternative and are not taken.** Replacing each
  username with an HMAC reference and holding the reverse lookup in a separately controlled store would
  keep the artifacts free of identifiers, and it was rejected for two reasons: the lookup store is
  itself a username-to-token mapping under the same classification, so the personal data is relocated
  rather than removed; and a mismatch that a human has to resolve — *this* account is missing, *that*
  role assignment moved — is resolved by reading a name, so every real use of the artifact would
  dereference the lookup and reassemble exactly the data the pseudonymisation was meant to avoid. **If a
  data-protection requirement ever mandates pseudonymisation, it is an approved change with the data
  owner and [09](09-security-assessment.md)'s owner as approvers**, and it carries the lookup store's
  own controls with it.
- **Any mismatch blocks cutover.** Exit `5`. It is explained and corrected, or the migration is rolled
  back to the position section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9
  states. It is not waived.

#### Controls on the sensitive artifacts, applied to both migrations equally

Section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 7 states the controls on
the domain extract because the order tables are PII. **The Identity side's artifacts are at least as
sensitive and get the same controls or stronger** — an asymmetry here would be the most consequential
kind of oversight, since the credential store is the one dataset whose compromise is not recoverable by
re-running anything.

| Artifact | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| The Identity extract and schema record | Encrypted transport and encrypted storage; least-privileged access, **access-logged**; held only for the run; destroyed on the stated schedule after acceptance |
| The normalized-username and role-name collision reports | The same, **plus redaction**: they name the colliding accounts by the identifier a human needs to resolve them and carry no hash, no stamp and no email body content beyond that identifier |
| Per-account hash verification | **Digest comparison, never raw values.** The comparison establishes that source and target hold the same hash without either side's artifact containing one; the successful sign-in of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 18 is the functional proof |
| The reconciliation artifacts — keyed sets, mismatch reports, duplicate reports | The same controls as the extract, **and for a stronger reason than digest sensitivity: they name usernames and role names in the clear**, because a keyed comparison that names no member cannot be resolved by a human. They are classified and handled as **personal data**: encrypted in transit and at rest, least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only for the run, destroyed on the named schedule. They carry no password hash, no security stamp and none of the order tables' PII columns [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] |
| The checkpoint table `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` | The same controls; it holds run ids, store names, source fingerprints, table names, counts and digests rather than row values. **It is retained past acceptance**, because the post-load cleanup of [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) verifies the manifest against it. **The table is permanent**; `close-run` deletes only the closing run's rows |
| The run-source table `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource` | **Retained after closure with the parent row**, and on the same basis: it holds a store name, a source server and database name, a fingerprint, a schema digest and two timestamps — **no data row values, no usernames and no hashes** — so it is operational metadata under the log-retention policy [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes rather than under this schedule. Retaining it is what keeps a closed run's per-store provenance answerable |
| The member table `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` | **The strongest controls in this table, because it is the one tool-owned table that holds source values.** Its `SourceNaturalKey` column carries a username for every Identity member, so the table is classified and handled as **personal data**: encrypted in transit and at rest, least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only until `close-run`, which **deletes the closing run's rows** from this permanent table and verifies the deletion. It carries **no password hash, no security stamp and none of the order tables' PII columns** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] — the natural key of a catalog or order member is a key value, not an address |
| The run descriptor `dbo.__DataMigrationRun` | **Retained after closure, deliberately** — it carries run ids, fingerprints, digests, server and database names, the operator name and the lifecycle timestamps, and **no data row values, usernames or hashes**, so it is operational metadata held under the log-retention policy [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes rather than under this schedule. It is the record that makes closure checkable; see the run-lifecycle sub-section below |
| The `(CartId, AlbumId)` merge lineage records | The same controls as the duplicate report they resolve. They are retained until the post-load cleanup has completed, because the cleanup's permitted delete set is enumerated from them, and they are destroyed with the manifest at run closure |
| The logical-run digest key | Held in the approved secret store, labelled with the run id and source fingerprint, **retained until the last artifact it authenticates has been destroyed** and then destroyed as the final step of the run — verified by a failed retrieval and stamped as `KeyDestroyedUtc` on the descriptor |
| Every artifact, at the end | **A named destruction schedule with an owner**, and destruction verified rather than assumed — an extract that outlives the migration is a credential store nobody is watching ([09 §6.9](09-security-assessment.md) records what happens when one is left in place) |

#### The run lifecycle: opening, acceptance and closure

**Four classes of evidence deliberately outlive acceptance, and an earlier revision of this section said
three. The count was wrong and the omitted class was the consequential one.** Acceptance (section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9, executed by `accept-run`) closes
the *migration*; the *run* closes later, once the post-load cleanup of
[06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) has completed and the retention of the reconciliation
artifacts has expired. What survives acceptance until then is:

| # | Retained class | Why it must survive acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The sealed manifest** | The post-load cleanup runs **after** acceptance and consumes it. A manifest destroyed at acceptance leaves the cleanup with no authenticated statement of what it is permitted to delete |
| 2 | **The lineage** — the run's `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` rows **and** the `(CartId, AlbumId)` merge lineage records | **This is the class the earlier count omitted.** The cleanup's permitted delete set is *enumerated* from the lineage rather than re-derived (the merge sub-section above), so destroying it at acceptance would leave the cleanup either unable to run or forced to recompute a set — which is the one thing the exactness requirement forbids. It is also what makes a post-acceptance question about a specific migrated row answerable at all |
| 3 | **The run's `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` rows** | The manifest gates [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists verify the manifest **against** them, so they are an input to the same cleanup |
| 4 | **The logical-run verification key** | It authenticates all three of the above. Destroying it first would convert the controlled cleanup into an unauthenticated delete, which is the correction the rerun mechanics above already record |

**One owner and one schedule for all four, so they cannot drift apart.** The **data owner** approves the
retention period for the whole set and **operations** performs the destruction on that schedule; the four
are destroyed by **one** invocation of `close-run` in the order below rather than by four independently
scheduled jobs. The reason is the same reason the cart cleanup of section
[4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 6 is one job over three
tables: four schedules of one shape are four things to get wrong, and here getting one wrong destroys the
evidence that authenticates another.

**`close-run` does five things in this order, and the order is the requirement:**

1. **Confirm** that the cleanup completed and that every manifest gate
   [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists passed. Closure is not permitted before this —
   exit `2`, nothing written or destroyed.
2. **Destroy the sealed manifest**, verifying the destruction.
3. **Delete this run's lineage** — its `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` rows and its merge lineage records —
   verifying the deletion by re-reading for rows with this `RunId` and finding none.
4. **Delete this run's `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` rows**, verified the same way.
5. **Destroy the logical-run verification key last**, verify the destruction by a retrieval that fails,
   and **stamp `KeyDestroyedUtc`, `ClosedUtc` and `State = Closed` on the parent row**. The key is last so
   that every destruction in steps 2 to 4 happens while the evidence being destroyed is still
   authenticable, which is what makes each of those verifications meaningful rather than a delete followed
   by a hope.

**The four run tables are permanent database objects, and no step in this contract ever drops one. This
corrects an earlier statement of step 3, which dropped `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` outright.**
`dbo.__DataMigrationRun`, `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource`, `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` and
`dbo.__DataMigrationMember` are created once, by the first `extract-schema --begin-run` that finds them
absent, and thereafter persist. Dropping a table would have destroyed **every** run's state rather than
the closing run's: the retained parent and run-source rows of previously closed runs, and — for a table a
later run recreates — the object identity a resume validates against. **`close-run` deletes rows scoped by
`RunId` and nothing else**, which is why steps 3 and 4 are deletions with verification rather than drops.
The two tables whose rows are *not* deleted at closure — the parent and its run-source rows — are retained
for the reason the controls table gives: they hold no data row values, no usernames from the migrated data
and no hashes, so they are operational metadata under the log-retention policy
[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes. Retaining them is what makes closure **checkable**:
a parent row with no `ClosedUtc` is an unclosed run and is reported as one, whereas a deleted parent row
would make an unclosed run and a closed one look identical — which is precisely the failure this
sub-section exists to prevent.

**Opening a run blocks on any *unclosed* run, not on any unaccepted one, and the difference is a real
window.** `extract-schema --begin-run` refuses — exit `2`, nothing written — when the target carries a
parent row whose `ClosedUtc` is null, whatever its `State`. An earlier revision gated on acceptance
instead, which left the whole interval between `accept-run` and `close-run` open: a second run could be
begun while the first run's manifest, lineage, checkpoint rows and verification key were all still live,
and both runs would then be writing member and checkpoint rows into the same tables while one of them was
mid-cleanup against a set enumerated from lineage the other was adding to. **Overlapping runs are
deliberately unsupported**, and the reason is not that they are hard to implement: the clean-target
precondition, the exact-set seal and the enumerate-don't-recompute cleanup rule are all statements about
**the** load of **a** target, and every one of them would need re-deriving per run against a target two
runs were writing. A release that needs a second run runs `close-run` on the first, which is a step with a
contract rather than a judgement call.

**These controls are gate conditions, not advice.** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) places the
workstream gates, and this document's requirement is that the data-movement gates it places cannot be
passed without them — the extract encrypted and access-logged, the reports redacted, the comparison
digest-based, **the username-bearing reconciliation artifacts classified and handled as personal
data**, and the destruction scheduled with an owner named.

---

### 5.7 The data migration is an artifact, not a procedure

**Everything sections [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) and
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) specify is stated as a
sequence of steps, and a sequence of steps has nothing a test can invoke.** That is the defect this
subsection closes. Read the two sections back as an implementer would: extract the schema, diff it,
back up, load in dependency order, reconcile per table, reconcile order totals to the cent, scan for
duplicate normalized user names before the first write, retain the source, roll back on failure. Nine
obligations, every one of them checkable — and **no named thing that performs them**. The consequences are
three, and they compound:

- **The gates are unenforceable.** "The diff must pass before any data is loaded" is a rule about the
  *order of two operations*. With no artifact owning both, nothing can refuse the second because the
  first did not pass; the rule reduces to a person remembering it.
- **The suite cannot exercise them.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is required to prove the
  nine obligations above, and a test can only invoke something that exists. A fixture that *pre-populates*
  the target database proves the assertions run — it proves nothing whatever about the migration,
  because the migration was not what put the rows there.
- **The thing that runs in production is not the thing that was tested.** A migration performed by hand,
  or by a script written on the day, is a different artifact from whatever the tests exercised. That is
  the failure this document has already rejected twice — for administrator provisioning (section
  [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command)) and for seeding (section
  [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)) — and the reasoning is identical here.

**Resolution: one production artifact, `tools/migrate-data`, and the tests invoke that same artifact.**
A `net8.0` console project, `tools/migrate-data/MigrateData.csproj` with `tools/migrate-data/Program.cs`,
carrying its own committed lockfile, restored in locked mode like every other project
([04 §6.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the mechanism and the pins). It is **not deployed with
the web application** — the same separation, and for the same reason, as
`tools/provision-admin` (section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command)): an
artifact that can rewrite the whole dataset has no business inside a process that serves anonymous
requests. It is **run by the deployment principal from the release pipeline**;
[06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns that principal and the identity model, and this
document does not restate them.

**Six modes, because the gates are only enforceable if the artifact owns both sides of each one.**

| Mode | What it does | What it refuses to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extract` | Performs step 1 of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) — the `sys.columns`, `sys.indexes`, `sys.key_constraints` and `sys.foreign_keys` interrogation — against a **copy** of the source outside the checkout, and writes the schema record, the data extract and a manifest into **one immutable, identified directory**, exactly as the handoff contract below fixes | Write to the source. The source is the rollback position and is opened read-only. It also refuses to write into an `<extract-id>` directory that already exists — an extract is created once and never amended |
| `schema-diff` | Generates the DDL the migration set would apply, compares it to the extracted record object by object, and emits a **machine-readable** difference report plus a pass/fail verdict. A difference is `pass` only if it carries a recorded reason. The verdict it records names the `extract-id` it was computed over | Pass silently on an unexplained difference; and **run at all** without a named extract whose every manifest digest verifies |
| `load` | Loads **one scope** — `--scope catalog` applies the catalog context's baseline migration set and loads genres and artists, then albums, then carts, then each order with its own detail rows, in the dependency order section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 fixes, preserving existing key values; `--scope identity` applies the Identity context's set and performs the Identity load of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration), including the pre-write user-name collision scan. Each group's commit writes its own row in the **load journal** below, in that same transaction, and the **receipt** is derived from the journal after the commit | **Run at all unless a `schema-diff` verdict of `pass` exists for the named `extract-id`.** This is the gate, made mechanical: the check is on the artifact's own recorded input, not on a person's memory, and it is keyed on an identifier rather than on "the same extract" — which nothing could previously have checked. It also refuses to write a single row when the user-name collision scan finds a duplicate normalized value; the scan completes **before the first insert of the run**, per section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration). **And it refuses to run at all without `--scope`** — there is no "both", for the reason below |
| `reconcile` | Reconciles **one scope**: `--scope catalog` per-table row counts source against target for the six catalog tables, and per-order `Total` against the sum of its detail rows, to the cent; `--scope identity` Identity account, role, assignment and per-provider linked-login counts, and the administrator's membership by name. Emits a **machine-readable** report and a pass/fail verdict for that scope | Report `pass` on any mismatch; report at all without both datasets available; run against an extract whose digests do not verify — the source-side counts are read from the extract, so a mutated extract would reconcile against fiction; and run without `--scope` |
| `dry-run` | Rehearses **one scope**'s run: every check that scope's `load` performs — the diff over the objects it touches, the collision scan where the scope is `identity`, and the load's own validation — over a named extract, and **writes nothing** to either dataset. The verdicts it emits are the verdicts the real run would emit | Write. It is the mode that makes the sequence rehearsable against a real target before anything is committed to it. It writes **no journal row and no receipt**, because both record a consumed extract and a rehearsal consumes nothing. It also refuses to run without `--scope`, so that a rehearsal is a rehearsal of something specific |
| `seed` | Invokes the **non-production seeding routine** of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) — `Data/SeedData.cs` — behind that section's three fail-closed checks, and emits the same machine-readable report shape naming each check's outcome | **Write anything at all unless all three checks pass**, and run in the production release path. It is a mode of *this* artifact rather than a third executable for the reason the whole subsection gives: a seeding routine invoked one way by a developer and another way by a test is two artifacts |

**`load`, `reconcile` and `dry-run` are scoped, and `--scope` is mandatory rather than defaulted, because
the two stores are migrated at different times and gated separately.** One invocation that moved both the
catalog and the Identity data would be unusable by the sequence that has to run it:
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) migrates the **domain data first and reconciles it**, and migrates
**Identity afterwards and reconciles that**, as two workstreams with two exit gates. A single unscoped
`load` would write both halves before the first gate could examine either, so the domain gate would be
closing over a target that already carried migrated credentials, and a rollback of the Identity half would
have to unpick rows the domain gate had already accepted.

| Property of the switch | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The values are a closed set of exactly two** | `catalog` and `identity`. An unrecognized value exits `2`, as an unrecognized mode does. There is deliberately **no `both`**: a caller that wants both runs the mode twice, `catalog` first, which is the order [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) sequences and the order the data requires — an Identity load reconciles nothing about orders, and an order's `Username` is a denormalized string rather than a foreign key (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)), so neither scope depends on the other's rows |
| **It is mandatory, and absence is `2`** | `load`, `reconcile` and `dry-run` **exit `2` and write nothing when `--scope` is absent**. No default, for the reason every other switch here has none: a defaulted scope is how an operator who meant to migrate the catalog migrates credentials, and it is how a test asserts a gate that ran over something else. Present on `extract`, `schema-diff` or `seed`, it also exits `2` — those three are whole-extract or no-extract operations and an unrecognized combination is refused rather than ignored |
| **Every artifact it produces is per scope** | The journal rows below carry the scope; the derived receipt is **`load-receipt.<scope>.json`**; and `reconcile`'s report is `reconcile-report.<scope>.json`. Two scopes therefore leave two independent records, which is what lets each of [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s two gates cite its own evidence rather than both citing one file whose contents describe two operations |
| **Each scope is independently resumable and independently reversible** | A `catalog` load interrupted part-way is resumed from the catalog journal without touching Identity, and an Identity load abandoned entirely leaves the reconciled catalog exactly as its gate accepted it. That is the property the single-invocation design cannot offer at any price |

**The load journal — the progress record is a SQL table, and the file is derived from it.** "Each group's
transaction writes its own progress record" is only true if the record is written **by that transaction**,
and a file cannot be: a process that commits a group and then dies before writing a file has committed rows
no file describes, and a process that writes the file first and dies before the commit has a file
describing rows that do not exist. Neither state is recoverable by inspection, because a target row count
is explainable by a prior load, by a seed or by a partially applied group. So the record lives **in the
target database, written in the same transaction as the group it describes**:

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | A table the tool owns, `dbo.MigrationLoadJournal`, created by `load` in its own transaction before the first group if absent — not by either context's migration set, because it is the tool's bookkeeping and not part of the application's schema. It is **not** the migrations-history table, which records applied migrations rather than committed data groups |
| **What each row carries** | The `extract-id`; the extract's `manifest.json` digest; the **scope**; the entity group's identifier from the dependency order; the group's committed row count; and the UTC commit time. One row per committed group per scope |
| **Why atomicity holds** | The row is inserted **inside the group's own transaction**, so the row and the rows it describes commit together or roll back together. A journal that names a group is a journal whose group is present, and there is no window in which either exists without the other. This is the property a filesystem receipt cannot have at any ordering |
| **The receipt is derived, and is a convenience** | After each group commits, `load` writes `<report-dir>/load-receipt.<scope>.json` from the journal's current contents — the `extract-id`, the manifest digest, the scope, the UTC start time and the ordered list of committed groups. It exists so that a pipeline step and a human reading an artifact directory can see what happened without a database connection. **It is never read to decide anything**: it may be absent, stale by one group, or unwritable, and none of those changes what a resume does |
| **The resume reads the journal** | A re-run of `load` for a scope reads `dbo.MigrationLoadJournal` filtered to that scope, and resumes after the last group it names. If the journal's `extract-id` or manifest digest for that scope disagrees with the extract this invocation was given, it exits `2` and writes nothing, rather than mixing two extracts' rows into one target. `reconcile` reads the journal too, so a reconciliation always knows which extract that scope was loaded from |
| **Its scope of visibility is the database** | The journal is in the target database, so its scope **is** the target database: two runs against two databases cannot see each other's journals, and no run can be confused by another's progress. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 64's crash cases each acquire their own database under section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s acquisition gate for exactly that reason — a shared journal would make one case's committed groups another case's starting state |
| **What a `1` guarantees about it** | A verdict failure writes **no journal row and no receipt**, which is the same guarantee the exit-code table already states about rows: a refusal before any write leaves nothing to resume from |

**The handoff between modes is a named immutable artifact, not "the same extract".** This is the mechanism
the gates rest on, and without it they are unenforceable in a way that is easy to miss: `load` refuses
without a `pass` verdict "for the same extract", but if the extract is a location that anything may
overwrite, then a `pass` computed over one schema authorizes a load over another, and **the gate passes
while proving nothing**. Nothing errors; the diff was genuinely green, over inputs that are no longer
there. So the extract is addressed by identity and verified by digest.

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The directory** | `extract` writes into **`<report-dir>/extract/<extract-id>/`** and nowhere else. `<extract-id>` is generated by the invocation — a UTC timestamp to the second plus a random suffix, so two extracts taken in the same second cannot collide — and it is **echoed to standard output on its own line and recorded in the extract's own report**, which is how a caller learns the value it must pass to every later mode. The directory is created by that invocation; a pre-existing `<extract-id>` directory is a precondition failure, not an overwrite |
| **Its contents** | Three things, fixed: **`schema.json`** — the schema record of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1, every column, index, key and foreign key of the six catalog tables and of the Identity tables; **`data/`** — the extracted rows, one file per entity group in the dependency order step 5 fixes; and **`manifest.json`** |
| **The manifest** | Carries the `extract-id`; the UTC extraction time; the source-copy identification (server, database name, and the copy's own provenance, never a credential); the culture, time zone and collation literals of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split), including the **observed** collation of the source database, which that section requires to equal the pinned literal; and, for **every** other file in the directory including `schema.json`, its **relative path, byte length and `SHA-256` digest as lowercase hexadecimal**. The manifest is the last file written, so a manifest that exists describes a complete extract |
| **How every later mode takes it** | By the switch **`--extract <extract-id-or-path>`**. A bare `<extract-id>` resolves under the invocation's own `--report-dir`; an absolute or relative path names the directory directly, which is what lets a pipeline stage consume an extract another stage produced. `extract` is the only mode that does **not** accept it — it produces one — and `seed` is the only other, for the reason below |
| **Verification, before any work** | Every mode that takes `--extract` **recomputes the `SHA-256` of every file the manifest lists, and compares byte length and digest, before it opens a connection to the target.** A missing file, an extra file in `data/`, a length mismatch or a digest mismatch is a **precondition failure**: the mode exits `2`, names the offending relative path and both digests — the recorded one and the recomputed one — and **does nothing else**. It does not repair, re-extract or continue with a warning. This is the property that makes "the same extract" checkable rather than assumed |
| **What `load` leaves behind** | The **journal rows** in the target database, written transactionally per group as specified above, and the **derived** `<report-dir>/load-receipt.<scope>.json` beside them. The journal is the record of what was committed; the receipt is a projection of it for readers without a connection. A re-run and a `reconcile` both read the **journal**, and both exit `2` when its `extract-id` or manifest digest for that scope disagrees with the extract they were given |
| **`seed` is deliberately exempt** | It consumes no extract: it writes catalog reference data from `Data/SeedData.cs` behind the three gates of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks), and it is not part of the source-to-target handoff at all (section [5.2](#52-the-seed-is-not-the-data-migration) is the reason). Passing `--extract` to `seed` exits `2` — an unrecognized combination is refused rather than ignored, on the same principle as an unrecognized mode |

**One invocation form, used identically by the tests and by the release pipeline — because two forms
are two artifacts again.** The form is stated here once and every site in this document that invokes the
tool uses it verbatim:

```text
dotnet <published-tool>/MigrateData.dll <mode> [--extract <extract-id-or-path>]
    [--scope catalog|identity] [--model-overrides <file>] --report-dir <dir>
```

**The grammar, exhaustively, per mode — because a switch's legality stated in prose beside the mode it
belongs to is a rule two readers will read two ways.** These four switches are the whole of the command
line; there is no fifth, and an unrecognized switch exits `2` rather than being ignored. **`R`** is
required — absent, the mode exits `2` and writes nothing. **`O`** is legal and optional, and the mode
states what its absence means. **`F`** is forbidden — present, the mode exits `2`, rather than accepting
it with a warning:

| Mode | `--extract` | `--scope` | `--model-overrides` | `--report-dir` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `extract` | **F** — it produces one | **F** | **F** | **R** |
| `schema-diff` | **R** | **F** — it compares the whole extracted record | **O** — absent, no adjustment is applied and the report records that no override was supplied | **R** |
| `load` | **R** | **R** | **F** — no override may influence a write | **R** |
| `reconcile` | **R** | **R** | **F** | **R** |
| `dry-run` | **R** | **R** | **O** — as `schema-diff`, so a rehearsal can rehearse an overridden diff | **R** |
| `seed` | **F** — it consumes no extract | **F** | **F** | **R** |

Two columns are worth reading twice. **`--model-overrides` is legal on exactly two modes and forbidden on
the three that write**, which is what makes section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s "no override can ever
influence a write" bound mechanical rather than a promise; and where it **is** supplied, the report records
the file's path and its `SHA-256`, so a `pass` obtained under an override can never be mistaken for a
`pass` obtained without one. **`--scope` is required on the three modes that act on one store at a time
and forbidden on the three that do not**, and its absence is `2` rather than a default for the reason the
scope table above gives.

Seven properties of that form are requirements, not conventions:

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **`<published-tool>` is a path the caller produced and captured** | The caller publishes `tools/migrate-data` and holds the resulting output directory path; the invocation names `MigrateData.dll` inside it. There is no globally installed tool, no `PATH` entry and no shell wrapper, so **the artifact the tests run and the artifact the pipeline runs are the same published output** — which is the whole claim of this subsection. The form is also **cross-platform by construction**: the same command line runs on the Windows agent that captures the baseline and the Linux agent that runs the target half (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)) |
| **`<mode>` is exactly one of the six above**, as a single positional argument | An unrecognized mode exits `2` — it could not run — rather than defaulting to anything. There is no default mode: an invocation with no mode exits `2` |
| **No connection string and no secret is ever an argument** | Both datasets' connections, and any credential in them, arrive through **named environment variables scoped to the single invocation**: `MIGRATEDATA_SOURCE_CONNECTION` and `MIGRATEDATA_TARGET_CONNECTION`. An argument is visible in a process listing and is recorded by shell and pipeline history, which is the same reasoning section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) applies to the administrator password. A connection supplied as an argument is **refused** rather than accepted-and-warned |
| **The report destination is a caller-supplied directory switch**, `--report-dir <dir>` | Absent, the tool exits `2` and writes nothing: there is no default location, because a default is how a PII-bearing report ends up somewhere nobody is looking. The caller owns the directory, its access restriction and its retention — for the suite, that is the per-run artifact directory of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) |
| **`--extract <extract-id-or-path>` is mandatory for `schema-diff`, `load`, `reconcile` and `dry-run`**, forbidden for `extract`, and forbidden for `seed` | Absent on a mode that requires it, the tool exits `2` and writes nothing — it does **not** search the report directory for "the latest" extract, because "the latest" is precisely the ambiguity the identifier removes. Present on `extract` or `seed`, it also exits `2`. Every invocation in this document that names one of the four consuming modes carries the switch, and the handoff contract above states what the value denotes and what is verified before the mode proceeds |
| **`--scope catalog\|identity` is mandatory for `load`, `reconcile` and `dry-run`** and forbidden for the other three | Per the scope table above: absent, exit `2` and write nothing; an unrecognized value, exit `2`; present on `extract`, `schema-diff` or `seed`, exit `2`. **Every invocation of those three modes anywhere in this document carries it**, and a row whose assertion spans both stores invokes the mode twice, `catalog` first |
| **The exit code is captured and asserted by the caller** | `0`, `1` and `2` per the contract below. A caller that reads the report but not the exit code cannot distinguish a `fail` verdict from a mode that never ran, which is the distinction the two codes exist to draw |

**`dotnet run --project tools/migrate-data -- <mode>` is a developer convenience and nothing more.** It
is stated so that a developer is not left inventing a form, and it is explicitly **not** the form the
tests or the pipeline use: it builds, it resolves the project rather than a published output, and a
build in the middle of a migration invocation is the failure-classification problem section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) keeps out of the runbook.

**Why the reports are machine-readable, stated because it is the property that makes section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s migration rows possible at all.** A human-readable log can only be
asserted against by string matching, which breaks on wording. A structured report — verdict, per-object
differences, per-table counts, per-order totals, per-provider counts — is something a test asserts on by
**field**, which is what every other row in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) does. The report is
also the release record: it is the evidence the acceptance criteria of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9 were met, and it passes the
redactor of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) before it is retained,
because per-order totals and per-account comparisons are computed over PII.

**The exit-code contract, because a pipeline gate is an exit code.**

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The mode completed and its verdict is `pass` |
| `1` | The mode completed and its verdict is `fail`. The **complete** set of conditions that produce it, so that no other condition may: an unexplained schema difference (`schema-diff`); a duplicate normalized **user name** (`load --scope identity`, per section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) — a duplicate normalized **email** is a notice and exits `0`); a per-table row-count mismatch or a per-order total mismatch (`reconcile --scope catalog`); an Identity count mismatch, a per-provider linked-login count mismatch, or a missing administrator membership (`reconcile --scope identity`); a failed check reported by `dry-run`. **A data-affecting mode that exits `1` has written nothing**, and the post-failure state is pinned rather than described: every target table's row count and column values are exactly as they were before the invocation, no migration-history row was added, **no journal row and no receipt was written**, and the source copy is byte-identical. That is what makes a failed gate safe to retry |
| `2` | The mode could not run **or could not complete**: a precondition was absent — no `--extract` on a mode that requires it, **no `--scope` on a mode that requires it**, an extract directory that does not exist, **an extract whose manifest digests do not verify**, a journal naming a different extract for that scope, no `pass` verdict for the named `extract-id`, an unreachable database, insufficient rights, a forbidden switch supplied (per the grammar table above), an unrecognized or absent mode, no `--report-dir` — or the environment withdrew mid-run. Distinguished from `1` deliberately, so a pipeline and a test can tell "the migration says no" from "the migration could not look" — the same distinction section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) draws between an assertion failure and a setup failure. **A `2` raised after the load has begun is the interruption case, and it does not carry the "wrote nothing" guarantee that `1` carries**: the groups already committed remain, the interrupted group is wholly absent, and the **journal** is current by construction — which is the state the transaction boundary above defines and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 64 asserts. `1` is a refusal before any write; `2` may be either a refusal before any write or a stop part-way, and **the journal** is what tells the two apart |

**Idempotence is per operation, not per run** — the same rule
section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) applies to provisioning, and
for the same reason. `load` re-run **for the same scope** after a partial failure inserts only rows absent
from the target, matched on the preserved key values of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5, so a run interrupted between the
album load and the order load is **repaired** by a re-run rather than duplicating what it already wrote.
Idempotence is per scope as well as per operation: re-running `catalog` neither writes nor requires
anything in the Identity store, and vice versa.
`extract`, `schema-diff`, `reconcile` and `dry-run` are naturally repeatable because none writes to
either dataset. `seed` is idempotent on the same rule as `load`: it inserts only catalog rows absent
from the target, matched on the same key values, so a re-run after an interruption completes the set
rather than duplicating it.

**And the resume is keyed on the journal, not on the receipt and not on inspection of the target.** A
re-run of `load` for a scope reads `dbo.MigrationLoadJournal` filtered to that scope, and three cases
follow, all mechanical: **no journal rows for the scope** — the run starts from that scope's first group,
because nothing was committed; **journal rows whose `extract-id` and manifest digest match the extract this
invocation was given** — the run resumes after the last group they name; **journal rows naming a different
`extract-id` or a different manifest digest** — the run exits `2` and writes nothing, because completing one
extract's load with another extract's rows produces a target that reconciles against neither. Keying on the
journal rather than on "which tables look populated" is what makes the resume deterministic: a target row
count can be explained by a prior load, by a seed, or by a partially applied group, and the journal
distinguishes them by record rather than by inference. **The derived receipt is never consulted for this
decision** — a resume that trusted a file would be trusting the one artifact that can disagree with the
database, which is precisely the crash window section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 64 exercises.

**Two failure classes, distinguished, because the two statements above would otherwise read as a
contradiction.** A **verdict** failure is a check the artifact completed and refused on — the enumerated
set in the exit-code table's `1` row — and it exits `1` having written nothing and left no journal row and
no receipt, which is the guarantee that table states. An **interruption** is the artifact ceasing to run
mid-write: a crash, a cancellation, a lost connection. An interruption **can** leave a partially loaded
target, and that is the case idempotence exists for: the journal names the groups that committed, and the
re-run inserts only what is absent. So "a failed mode wrote nothing" and "a re-run repairs a partial load" are statements about
different events, and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) rows 53, 56 and 59 assert the first while
row 64 asserts the second.

**The load's transaction boundary, stated because "a partially loaded target" is meaningless without
it.** `load` commits **one transaction per entity group, in the dependency order** section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 fixes — under `--scope catalog`:
genres and artists; then albums; then carts; then **each order together with its own detail rows**; and
under `--scope identity`: the accounts, then the roles, then the role assignments and linked logins. Each
group's transaction writes its own **journal row** in that same transaction, so the row and the rows it
describes commit or roll back together and the journal can never claim a group that is not there. **The
derived receipt is written after the commit**, outside that transaction, which is why it is a projection
rather than the record.

Three consequences, and they are what row 64 asserts:

- **An order and its details are never separated.** They share one transaction because
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 6 reconciles each order's `Total`
  against the sum of its detail rows: an order committed without its details is not a partial load, it is
  a wrong financial figure that reconciliation would report as a mismatch rather than as an interruption.
- **An interruption leaves whole groups, never half a group.** The committed groups are complete, the
  interrupted group is wholly absent, and the journal names the last group that completed. That is
  the state a re-run reads, and it is why the re-run's repair is a resumption rather than a diff of the
  entire dataset. **The derived receipt may be one group behind the journal** — that is the ordinary
  consequence of writing it after the commit, and it changes nothing, because nothing reads it to decide.
- **A single whole-run transaction is deliberately rejected.** It would hold locks across the whole load
  and, more importantly, would make partial progress *unrecoverable* rather than *repairable* — every
  interruption would restart from nothing. Run-level safety does not need it: the rollback position below
  is that the target is discarded, so all-or-nothing at the run level is already guaranteed by a means
  that costs nothing.

**Rollback is a mode's absence, not a mode.** Section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9 and section
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) define rollback as: the
source is unmodified, the legacy application is redeployable, the target database is discarded. The
artifact's contribution is to **make that position true at every point** — it never writes to the source
in any mode, it retains the source Identity tables until `reconcile` returns `pass`, and its failure
codes guarantee that a failed data-affecting mode left no partial state to reverse. So there is
deliberately **no `rollback` mode**: a rollback command implies the artifact could undo a write, and the
design's whole safety argument is that the write it would undo cannot have happened.

**And the tests invoke this artifact.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s migration rows drive
`tools/migrate-data` in the same modes the release drives it, against the disposable database of section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two, and assert on the machine-readable
verdicts and on the database state afterwards. That is the point of specifying it as an artifact: the
migration the pipeline runs, the migration CI runs and the migration the tests exercise are **one
versioned, source-controlled thing**, so a green suite is evidence about the release rather than about a
rehearsal of it.

**Plan-correction record — the frozen plan's future application map does not list this artifact.**

Recorded in the form section [9.3](#93-two-plan-correction-records-for-the-plan-owner) uses, and for the
same reason: the plan is frozen, nothing here edits it, and a needed artifact absent from its map must be
notified rather than added silently.

| Aspect | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The omission** | The plan's §0.4.1 future application map enumerates every target artifact and **does not include a data-migration executable**. `tools/provision-admin` is mapped; `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` is mapped; the migration folders `Data/Migrations/Catalog/**` and `Data/Migrations/Identity/**` are mapped — and those create **empty tables**, which is precisely the point section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) opens with |
| **Why an implementation is required rather than optional** | The plan's own §0.3.2 specifies the migration as a sequence of obligations — authoritative extraction, a generated-schema diff that **must pass before any data is loaded**, a dependency-ordered load, per-table and per-order reconciliation, PII protection, a stated rollback position — and its §0.11.2 makes the schema-and-data migration a named acceptance criterion of *this* deliverable. An obligation that must be **enforced** at release time and **exercised** by the suite has to be a thing; the map lists no thing |
| **Cause** | The map was written from the *application's* file inventory, where a release-time console tool that is not deployed with the application does not naturally appear. `tools/provision-admin` is in the map because section 0.3.2 names it as a file; the migration steps are named as **steps**, so no file was derived from them |
| **What is being asked** | That the plan's next revision add `tools/migrate-data/MigrateData.csproj`, `tools/migrate-data/Program.cs` and its `packages.lock.json` to the §0.4.1 map, as CREATE / net-new, alongside `tools/provision-admin` — **and that both tool projects be mapped with the reference direction stated**: each takes a `ProjectReference` on `src/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj`, because each must compile against the two contexts, `ApplicationUser`, both migration sets and the composition that registers them, and neither is included in the web application's publish output. The direction is one-way: **the web application references neither tool**, so nothing a tool contains can reach a deployed request path. [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the resulting map rows |
| **Disposition** | **Recorded, and the work is specified here rather than deferred.** [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) is where the target artifact set is mapped, and [04 §12.1](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) states that the set is *governed rather than invented* — so **04 maps this file**, and this record is the notification that authorizes it to. Nothing in this document's own design turns on the map's wording: the artifact is specified above in full, and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s rows exercise it either way. What the record prevents is the artifact arriving in the implementation as an unexplained addition to a governed map |

---

#### 5.5.1 Published-credential accounts are neutralized before the load, not after the cutover

**Carrying every hash verbatim is right for every account but one class, and for that class it is a
credential compromise the migration would perform on purpose.** The seeded administrator's password is
**committed to this repository in cleartext** at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17] and restated
in the tracked per-edition documentation ([09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding). Its
hash sits in the committed credential store
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/aspnet-MvcMusicStore-20131025034205.mdf: binary artifact, tracked —
`git ls-files 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/*'`; the `AspNetUsers.PasswordHash` column it holds is
evidenced by the printable-string probe qualified above, not by a line], and that account holds the
`Administrator` role — the only thing standing between an anonymous caller
and album create, edit and delete
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12]. So a migration that carries the hash
faithfully produces, in a hosted environment, **an administrator account whose password anyone with
read access to this repository already has**. Removing the two `appSettings` keys (section
[10.3](#103-what-this-retires)) does not touch it: the keys were only the *source* of the credential, and
the credential itself now lives in the store.

**The mechanism: replace the hash, keep the shape.** For each account in the neutralization set the
load writes a `PasswordHash` computed by the target's `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` over a
**32-byte cryptographically random value generated in the migration process, never persisted, never
logged and discarded when the row is written**. Nobody — including the operator running the migration —
holds a value that satisfies it, and the account is repaired by the operator command of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — run **with
`--rotate-credential`**, which is one of the exactly two runs that pass that switch — before the
environment is opened.

**Why a random-value hash and not the two more obvious alternatives**, both of which look stronger and
are worse here:

- **Not a null `PasswordHash`.** It works — `UserManager.CheckPasswordAsync` returns failure for a null
  stored hash without invoking the hasher — and it breaks two things this document has already
  committed to. It makes the account's real work *cheaper* than a real verification, leaning on the
  fixed-work service of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) to pad every attempt
  against it, and doing so pointlessly: the padding exists for populations the port cannot avoid, not as
  licence to create another one. And it would **manufacture the one account shape this migration is
  specified to refuse**: a null or empty `PasswordHash` is the external-only condition on which section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) **halts the load
  and writes nothing**, so the neutralization step would produce exactly the row the same migration
  rejects. It would also flip `HasPasswordAsync` to false for an account that is not external-only,
  sending its `Manage` view down the set-password branch that section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) keeps reachable **for genuinely external-only accounts
  and no others** — so the branch would stop meaning what it says, and the migration's own halt condition
  would stop identifying what it is for.
- **Not a permanent lockout** (`LockoutEnd` far in the future). `SignInManager` evaluates lockout
  **before** verifying the password, so a locked account performs no derivation at all and depends
  entirely on the fixed-work top-up of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) to look like
  anything else; and its `AccountLockedOut` outcome is a distinct value in the `AUTH-1002` event of
  [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md), which would let anyone watching the log stream identify the
  account by name. Lockout is for runtime accounting, not for retiring a credential.

A random-value hash costs exactly what every other verification costs, produces the ordinary
`InvalidCredentials` outcome, and leaves `HasPasswordAsync` true, so nothing else in this document
changes.

**Who is in the set, determined by rule rather than by a name.** The set is *every source account whose
password is derivable from tracked repository content*, and the migration's pre-load census must
enumerate it rather than assume it is a single row. It provably contains the seeded administrator
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17].

**Exactly one account is *named* by tracked repository content, and an earlier form of this paragraph
claimed a second.** That form carried "the second seeded account named in the repository's own
documentation" as a standing candidate. **No such account exists**, and the claim is withdrawn rather
than softened, because a candidate nobody can locate is not evidence — it is an instruction to look for
something that is not there. The repository tracks three README files, and only one of them names a
credential at all:

```
git grep -l -iE 'DefaultAdminPassword|Password' -- README.md src/MVC4/README.md src/MVC5/README.md
# -> src/MVC5/README.md          (the only tracked README naming a credential at all)
git grep -c -iE 'password'       -- README.md src/MVC4/README.md src/MVC5/README.md
# -> src/MVC5/README.md:2        (two lines, both the same single account)
```

Both matching lines name **the same single account's** password — the bullet under that file's *Default
Administrator Account* heading, and the `DefaultAdminPassword` configuration key the same section quotes
immediately below it — and the user name bullet alongside them names `Administrator`
[src/MVC5/README.md:75-84]. One account, named twice; not two accounts.

**The rule still governs, and it is not discharged by that census**, because documentation is not the
only derivation path: a source account whose stored hash happens to verify a published value is a member
whether or not any file names it. So membership is decided by **testing**, not by reading: for every
source account, the pre-load census verifies each published value against that account's stored hash
using the configured `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` — an offline, read-only check against the
extracted source rows that issues no sign-in, touches no lockout counter and writes nothing — and every
account for which any published value verifies is a member. Where a hash cannot be evaluated at all, the
account is neutralized anyway, because a needless password reset costs one user one reset and a missed one
leaves a live published credential. The census is a step of the migration, its output is recorded with the
reconciliation report, and **the published values themselves appear in no deliverable** — they are cited
by location, here and everywhere else in this set, which is also why the two commands above are written
in their `-l` and `-c` forms rather than printing the matching lines.

**Ordering: neutralization happens in the load, before the store is reachable.** It is not a
post-cutover clean-up task and not a runbook item to be caught up on later. The row is written already
neutralized, so **no window exists in which the hosted store holds the published hash** — which is the
property a "reset it after go-live" step cannot offer, and the reason this is specified in the migration
rather than in [06 §11](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s runbook.

**Reconciliation and rollback.**

- Account count, role count and role-assignment count compared **before and after**.
- **The administrator's role membership asserted specifically**, by name, not merely counted — it is
  the one assignment whose loss makes the entire administration surface unreachable, which is exactly
  the failure MVC 3 ships as a shipped state ([09 §5.2](09-security-assessment.md)).
- A per-account comparison of username and hash between source and target — **with the neutralization
  set carrying the inverse assertion**. For an ordinary account, source hash equals target hash; for a
  neutralized account, the target hash must **differ** from the source hash and must not equal the hash
  of any published value. Stating this explicitly matters because the general form of the rule, applied
  uniformly, would make a correct migration **fail** reconciliation and invite someone to "fix" it by
  restoring the compromised hash.
- **A negative verification assertion, per environment, before it is reachable — and it is deliberately
  *not* a failed sign-in.** For every account in the neutralization set the gate reads that account's
  stored `PasswordHash` with a read-only query and calls
  `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>.VerifyHashedPassword(user, storedHash, publishedValue)`, requiring
  **`PasswordVerificationResult.Failed`** for every published value. It is the same hasher the
  application verifies with, so a `Failed` result is the same fact a refused sign-in would establish —
  and it establishes it **without issuing a request, without a lockout counter and without writing
  anything**: the gate additionally records `AccessFailedCount` and `LockoutEnd` for each account
  **before and after** and asserts both **unchanged**.

  **A repeated failed `POST /Account/Login` must not be used as this gate**, and an earlier form of this
  bullet made it one. The policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) sets
  `Lockout.MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5` with a fifteen-minute window and the sign-in path of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 3 passes `lockoutOnFailure: true`, so a probe that
  posts a wrong password **increments the counter on the one account that holds the `Administrator`
  role**. Five of them lock it out — and this gate is specified to run *per environment*, so the
  arithmetic is not hypothetical: a re-run, a retried pipeline stage or an operator repeating the check
  by hand locks the only administrator out of a freshly cut-over environment, at the moment the runbook
  most needs to sign in. There is also nothing to reset it: a standing probe has no owner and no
  post-condition, which is exactly why it is replaced rather than merely paired with a reset.

  **If an environment's own policy insists on an end-to-end attempt** — because a refused HTTP request
  is what an auditor will accept — it is permitted under three conditions and no fewer, all recorded in
  the runbook log: **exactly one** attempt per account, never a series and never a timing sample;
  immediately followed by `await userManager.ResetAccessFailedCountAsync(user)` and
  `await userManager.SetLockoutEndDateAsync(user, null)`; and both **asserted afterwards** —
  `AccessFailedCount == 0` and `LockoutEnd == null` — so a reset that silently failed is a gate failure
  rather than a latent lockout. The end-to-end assertion in its unrestricted form, including its timing
  companion, belongs to the suite's **disposable fixture database**, where the accounts are fixture
  accounts and the reset discipline of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) already governs sampling.

  This is still the check that tests the property people actually care about — the others test that a
  field changed — and it is the gate condition [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) attaches to the Identity
  migration and [06 §11](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) repeats per environment. The published
  value is supplied to it by reading the legacy `Web.config` in the build source, so satisfying the gate
  never requires writing the value into a document, a test file or a pipeline variable. **Coverage row
  75** asserts it.
- **Source tables retained until reconciliation passes.** They are the rollback position, and they are
  dropped only as a separate, later step under the security remediation that
  [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md) sequences. Note the consequence for rollback, stated so it is not
  discovered during one: **rolling back to the source store restores the published credential**, because
  the source rows are untouched by design. **There is exactly one acceptable response, and accepting the
  exposure for the rollback's duration is not it.** The legacy account's credential is neutralized **in
  the legacy store** — before the interim Windows option of
  [06 §5.8](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is ever exposed, and before any rollback returns the
  legacy application to service — and the negative-authentication check is run against the legacy host
  too, per [06 §11.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and
  [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md). [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) criterion 6 owns
  the requirement and states why an earlier reading of this bullet was wrong: criterion 2 requires the
  committed value to authenticate in **no** environment, and the legacy application during a rollback is
  an environment. Neutralizing the source store does not weaken the rollback position — the rows, the
  orders and the account all remain; only the published password stops working.

### 5.8 Roles, role assignments, claims and external logins — the other four tables

Section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) specifies the user
table. **The user table is not the whole migration**, and the omission that matters most is the role
one: the entire administration surface is reachable only through
`[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12],
so a role row or an assignment row that does not arrive takes administration with it — and it does so
**silently**, as a 403 rather than an error.

**`AspNetRoles` — four target columns, two source columns.**

| Target column | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| `Id` | Carried from the source, on the same convenience grounds as the user id in section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) |
| `Name` | **Carried exactly. This is an invariant, for the same reason usernames are:** the authorization attribute compares a **string** — `"Administrator"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12] — so a renamed role denies every administrator without failing anywhere |
| `NormalizedName` | Computed by the target's normalizer, **after** the collision check below |
| `ConcurrencyStamp` | Generated fresh per row |

**Role-name collisions stop the migration; they are never merged.** Two role names differing only in
case normalize to one value and violate the unique index — the same mechanism as the username collision
of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration), and the same
resolution: enumerate, compute, **abort and report**. Merging is specifically forbidden here rather than
merely undesirable, because merging two roles grants every member of each the access of the other,
which is a privilege escalation performed by a data-migration script.

**`AspNetUserRoles` — carried row for row.** The pair (`UserId`, `RoleId`) is the whole row in both
schemas, so the mapping is an identity mapping once the two id sets are carried. The reconciliation is
in section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration): counts before
and after, **plus the administrator's membership asserted by name** rather than counted.

**Each assignment this table loads is an audited privilege grant, not a silent row copy.** The migration
emits **one `AUTHZ-3001` per assignment**, which makes it the **second** of that class's two producers
([09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)) — the provisioning command of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) being the first. The outcome
value, the actor rule and the field list are 09's; section
[6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) states the
arithmetic and why no HTTP request produces this class. Without those records the target's audit trail
would begin with every existing administrator's access already granted and nothing recording when or by
what.

**`AspNetUserClaims` — expected empty, and "expected" is verified rather than assumed.** No application
code writes a claim: `git grep -n 'AddClaim' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore'` returns **no matches**. The
migration therefore **counts the source rows and stops if the count is not zero**, reporting them. It
does not carry them silently and it does not drop them silently — a claim row that exists without any
code to create it is an authorization fact placed there by something outside the application, and both
"keep" and "discard" are decisions a person must take.

**`AspNetUserLogins` — the one table whose disposition is a product decision, because of what it
implies about passwords.** The external-login surface is **retained** and re-expressed against the
framework's own mechanism (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), and the source can
genuinely hold rows here: `UserManager.AddLoginAsync` is called at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:252] and [:284]. The rule is two-part:

- **The rows are carried, and the one column with no source value gets a defined origin.** The target's
  login table adds `ProviderDisplayName` to the 1.0 shape; it is **carried as the provider name** where
  a row exists, which is what the retained removal list renders today
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:11]. `LoginProvider`,
  `ProviderKey` and `UserId` are carried verbatim, the last of them re-linked by the preserved id of
  section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration). Carrying them is
  what makes the retained surface's own behaviour preserved rather than merely present: a migrated
  account's registered logins are listed and removable after cutover exactly as before it.
- **The migration still stops before writing anything if any source account has a null or empty
  `PasswordHash`.** Such an account is external-only: it has never had a local password, and **no
  external provider is registered in the target** (section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), exactly as none is registered today, so it would be
  **unable to sign in** until one is. That is a user-facing loss, not a migration detail, so the
  migration reports the affected accounts and halts. The available responses — issue password resets, or
  register a provider for those accounts — are both approval decisions and belong to
  [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s risk register once the count is known. It is also the condition
  that keeps the set-password branch of section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) reachable rather than dead.

**`AspNetRoleClaims` and `AspNetUserTokens` are net-new tables in the target schema.** They have no
source counterpart, are created empty by the Identity migration set, and nothing is loaded into them.
Stated so that a reviewer comparing table lists does not read their emptiness as a lost dataset.

**Acceptance for this section**, as the coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage):
after the load, `RoleManager.RoleExistsAsync("Administrator")` is true, the migrated administrator is in
that role by `UserManager.IsInRoleAsync`, a **non**-administrator is not, and the role and assignment
counts match the source.

---
