## 6. Authentication policy is decided, not inherited

Cookie authentication is configured today with **exactly two values** — an authentication type
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16] and a login path [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:17], inside the options object
at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18] — plus the external sign-in cookie [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20]. Nothing else is set anywhere. **The policy is
therefore not absent: it is in force on every request and it is whatever the framework's defaults
happen to be.** [09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md) owns that finding (F-09-02) and assigns this
document the duty of setting each value explicitly.

**The principle: hardening is welcome; hardening that arrives as an unannounced framework default is a
change nobody approved.** The target's defaults are mostly better than the source's. That is not a
licence to leave them implicit — an unstated value cannot be reviewed, cannot be approved, and
silently changes again on the next framework upgrade. **Every row below is set explicitly in
`Program.cs`, and every row is labelled.**

**What the table covers.** The authentication cookie and the Identity policy around it — the rows
naming an unqualified `Cookie.*` property are that cookie's — plus the `Secure` policy of the
**session** and **anti-forgery** cookies, which belong here because they are the same class of
decision, are set in the same composition root, and are asserted together by the deployment checks of
section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). Those two are the values most easily left
implicit: unlike the authentication cookie, neither has a counterpart setting in the source to prompt a
decision, and both of their framework defaults are `CookieSecurePolicy.None`. This section is the
contract [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and
[11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) cite for all three cookies.

### 6.1 The policy table, every row labelled

Every value below is the value written into `Program.cs`. **No row says "set explicitly" in place of a
value**; where a value is the same as the framework's, it is written out anyway, because an unstated
value cannot be reviewed and changes silently on the next upgrade. Options-object names are given so
each row maps to one assignment.

| Policy | Today | Target value | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password minimum length | `UserManager` default; no `PasswordValidator` assigned anywhere in the edition | `IdentityOptions.Password.RequiredLength = 8` | **Deliberate hardening** — above every Identity default, source or target |
| Password complexity | `UserManager` defaults | `RequireDigit = true`, `RequireLowercase = true`, `RequireUppercase = true`, `RequireNonAlphanumeric = true`, `RequiredUniqueChars = 1` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Allowed user-name characters | **Letters and digits only.** Identity 1.0 validates user names through `UserValidator<TUser>`, whose `AllowOnlyAlphanumericUserNames` defaults to `true`, and **no `UserValidator` and no `PasswordValidator` is assigned anywhere in the edition** (command in [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility)) — so that default is the effective policy | `User.AllowedUserNameCharacters = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"` — the same 62 characters, written out, **and** the Identity data migration reports any source user name containing a character outside the set before the load (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)) | **Preserved**, and this row is the reason the option cannot be left unset: the *target* framework's default set additionally allows `-`, `.`, `_`, `@` and `+`, so inheriting it would **widen** who may register — a new class of accepted user name, on the one anonymous write surface, with no approval behind it and no user-visible symptom until a name nobody expected exists. Widening the set is available as a separate decision with its own owner; this port does not take it, and a widening would have to move this option **and** the provisioning command's pre-store check of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) in one change, because that command validates its `--user-name` against **this** set and not against the framework default. The coverage assertion requires both halves for the registration surface and the coverage assertion requires the command's side |
| Account lockout enabled | **No lockout exists** — sign-in is a single `FindAsync` call with no attempt counter, no delay and no lockout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:60], and the failure path only adds a message and redisplays [:68] | `Lockout.AllowedForNewUsers = true`, and password verification goes through `SignInManager.CheckPasswordSignInAsync(user, password, lockoutOnFailure: true)` — step 3 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — so failures are actually counted | **Deliberate hardening** — the highest-value row in the table. [09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md) F-09-03 rates it High. The `lockoutOnFailure` argument is part of the row: enabling lockout without it counts nothing |
| Lockout threshold and duration | n/a | `Lockout.MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5`, `Lockout.DefaultLockoutTimeSpan = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15)` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Account confirmation required for sign-in | Identity 1.0 default; **no confirmation flow is implemented** and no email is sent | `SignIn.RequireConfirmedAccount = false` and `SignIn.RequireConfirmedEmail = false` | **Preserved** — deliberately, with the reason recorded: requiring it would lock out every migrated account, since `EmailConfirmed` is `false` for all of them (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)) and many hold no email at all. The one row where the hardening is the wrong call |
| Unique email required | Identity 1.0 default | `User.RequireUniqueEmail = false` | **Preserved.** The source may hold accounts with no email; enforcing uniqueness at migration time would fail the load |
| Authentication cookie name | Katana's default: its `.AspNet.` prefix plus the authentication type at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16], giving `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie`; no name is set anywhere | `Cookie.Name = ".MvcMusicStore.Auth"` | **Deliberate change.** A name distinct from the legacy one means a legacy ticket is never even offered to the new handler, which is what makes the expiry middleware of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) safe |
| Cookie lifetime | `CookieAuthenticationOptions` default, unset [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18] | `ExpireTimeSpan = TimeSpan.FromDays(14)` | **Preserved** — the same fourteen days the unset source option gave, now written down |
| Sliding expiration | Middleware default, unset | `SlidingExpiration = true` | **Preserved**, stated |
| Persistent cookie ("remember me") | The flag is honoured at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] with the middleware's own duration | The capability is **preserved**: the checkbox value is passed as `isPersistent` to `SignInManager.SignInAsync(user, isPersistent)` — step 6 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — and a persistent cookie's lifetime is the same `ExpireTimeSpan` of fourteen days | **Preserved**, with the duration now stated |
| Cookie `Secure` attribute | Katana default `SameAsRequest`, which over plain HTTP means **not secure** ([09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md), [11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)) | `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Cookie `HttpOnly` | Middleware default (on) | `Cookie.HttpOnly = true` | **Preserved**, stated |
| Cookie `SameSite` | **Not an option in the source middleware at all** | `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax` — preserves top-level navigation to the site while blocking cross-site sub-requests | **Deliberate hardening**. `Strict` is not chosen: it would break inbound links from external pages into authenticated views |
| Login path | `/Account/Login` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:17] | `LoginPath = "/Account/Login"` | **Preserved** |
| Logout path | No such option in the source middleware; sign-out is the `LogOff` POST at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:302] | `LogoutPath = "/Account/LogOff"` | **Preserved** — the same path, now declared to the handler |
| Access-denied path | Not configured — the source redirects to login for both the unauthenticated and the forbidden case | `AccessDeniedPath = "/Home/Error/403"`, which is the status-code error action of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types); the action sets **403** on the response, so a forbidden request ends as a 403 rather than a 200 | **Deliberate hardening**, minor: an authenticated non-administrator gets a denial rather than a login form. The path is not a net-new view — it reuses the error action the pipeline already requires |
| Return-URL parameter | Katana default; the login view round-trips it through `ViewBag.ReturnUrl` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:47] | `ReturnUrlParameter = "ReturnUrl"` | **Preserved.** The name is part of the URL surface: changing it would silently drop every return URL |
| Security-stamp validation | **None.** The source sets no cookie `Provider`, so no stamp is revalidated after sign-in and a password change or a role change does not invalidate an issued ticket | `SecurityStampValidatorOptions.ValidationInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)` — the framework wires the validator through `AddIdentity`; this row is its interval | **Deliberate hardening (net-new).** It is also why section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) requires a stamp for every migrated account: a null stamp with validation on signs the user straight back out |
| Session cookie name | No `<sessionState>` element is declared in any edition ([11 §3.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the absence and its command), so the platform default `ASP.NET_SessionId` applies | `SessionOptions.Cookie.Name = ".MvcMusicStore.Session"` | **Deliberate change** — a different mechanism with a different name; nothing reads the old name |
| Session idle timeout | Platform default, in force by that same absence | `SessionOptions.IdleTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20)` | **Preserved** — twenty minutes, which is what the undeclared default gives today |
| Session cookie attributes | n/a | `Cookie.HttpOnly = true`, `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always`, `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax`, `Cookie.IsEssential = true` | **Deliberate hardening.** `IsEssential` is the load-bearing one: the cart identity lives in this cookie (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)), so a future consent policy must not be able to suppress it |
| Antiforgery cookie attributes | Ten views emit `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` — `git grep -c 'AntiForgeryToken' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views'` lists ten files at one occurrence each — and each emission pairs the field with the `System.Web` anti-forgery **cookie**, whose `secure` attribute in that framework comes from `<httpCookies requireSSL="true"/>`. **No `<httpCookies>` element is declared in any application configuration file** — `git grep -l -i 'httpCookies' -- 'src/**/*.config' 'src/**/*.Config'` returns nothing — so the source cookie is offered over plain HTTP | `AntiforgeryOptions.Cookie.Name = ".MvcMusicStore.Antiforgery"`, `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always`, `Cookie.HttpOnly = true`, `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Strict`, `Cookie.IsEssential = true`, `Cookie.Path = "/"`, and `HeaderName = "RequestVerificationToken"` for the scripted transport of section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form) | **Deliberate hardening**, and **`SecurePolicy` is the row's reason for existing**: the framework's default for *this* cookie is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, not `Always` — it is the one cookie in this table whose default would leave it marked non-secure while the authentication and session cookies are marked `Always`, so leaving it unstated produces a mixed cookie posture that no review would notice. `SameSite = Strict` is stated rather than inherited and is safe for this cookie specifically: a cross-site top-level navigation that does not carry it simply causes a fresh cookie-and-token pair to be issued with the rendered form, and every request that must *validate* a token is a same-site `POST` from that form. `IsEssential = true` keeps a consent policy from suppressing the cookie and thereby refusing every write in the application. `Path = "/"` is written out because the framework's builder derives the path from the request path base, which is not a value this document leaves implicit |
| External-login surface | Scaffolded and **entirely disabled** — all four provider registrations commented out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35] — plus the external sign-in cookie [:20] | **Retained and re-expressed.** The actions, the views and the removal list are mapped onto the framework's own external-authentication flow, and `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme` — registered by `AddIdentity` — replaces the Katana external sign-in cookie [:20]. **`AuthenticationOptions` gains no provider registration**: the four commented-out ones are not re-created, so the surface is configured-off exactly as it is today. Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) records the mapping and the resolution of `ChallengeResult` in section [13](#13-resolution-register--all-22-blockers-of-deliverable-12) | **Preserved** — reachability is unchanged in both directions: no external handshake is possible before or after, and enabling one remains a provider registration rather than a code change. The dormant surface's standing as deployed attack surface is [09 §6.11](09-security-assessment.md)'s finding and retention does not reduce it, which is why **registering a provider is a separate decision owned by Security** rather than something this document assumes |
| Data-protection key store | **None declared** — no `machineKey` in any edition, so key identity is a property of the host rather than of the deployment: it cannot be assumed shared across hosts, inventoried, rotated deliberately or isolated per environment ([11 §3.2.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the per-host detail) | `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>().SetApplicationName(<the required `DataProtection:ApplicationName` value>)`, with the key table created by the `AddDataProtectionKeys` migration — the decision and its four parts are in section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). **Location, protection at rest, rotation and slot isolation remain [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s** | **Deliberate hardening** |

Two rows deserve a sentence beyond the table. **The confirmation and unique-email rows are the two
places where this document declines a hardening**, and both declines are consequences of the Identity
data migration rather than of taste — which is why they are recorded here with their reason instead of
being quietly omitted. And **the `SameSite` row has no "today" value at all** to be preserved or
hardened relative to, because the source middleware has no such option; it is stated as hardening
because the resulting behaviour is stricter than the absence.

**The labels have an owner, and it is the reason they are labels rather than prose.** Every row marked
**deliberate hardening** or **deliberate change** — **thirteen** of the twenty-five — requires
**Security's** approval before implementation, and the two rows marked *preserved by decision* rather
than by inheritance (confirmation and unique email) require it too, because declining a hardening is as
much a security decision as taking one. The remaining **ten** ordinary **preserved** rows need no
approval: they state, rather than change, today's effective behaviour — `13 + 2 + 10 = 25`. Section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) carries the whole set as approved delta 10 with the same
owner, so the approver sees one entry rather than twenty-five, and
[09](09-security-assessment.md) — which owns the finding this table answers — is the reviewer of record
for it. **Where a target value differs from the framework default it is marked as such in the row**
rather than left to inference; the **six** rows where that matters most are the two password rows, the two
lockout rows, the security-stamp interval and the antiforgery cookie's `SecurePolicy`, all of which are
stricter than the framework's own default for the same setting and none of which it will produce on its
own.

### 6.2 The sign-out surface

Sign-out today is a POST with anti-forgery validation
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:300-306], posted by a form in the shared login
partial [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:4-14]. **That is preserved
exactly** — a POST, token-validated, from a form. It is called out because MVC 3 ships a `GET`
sign-out ([09 §5.4](09-security-assessment.md)) and a reader comparing editions could conclude the
verb needs changing here. It does not.

One change is mechanical: the link at [:12] invokes
`javascript:document.getElementById('logoutForm').submit()`, which an inline-script Content Security
Policy would block. Since the port adds security response headers where the source has none
([11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)), the trigger becomes an ordinary submit button styled as
a link, and the `javascript:` URL is removed.

**The other change is not cosmetic: sign-out clears the session's cart key.** `LogOff` today signs the
identity out and redirects [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:302-306] and
**touches the session slot not at all**, so the value the sign-in path wrote there — the user's own name
[:39] — outlives the ticket. `GetCartId` returns whatever the slot already holds
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] without re-checking who is asking, so every
subsequent **anonymous** request in that session still resolves to the signed-out user's cart and can
read it, add to it and remove from it. On a shared browser that is the next person.

The target's sign-out therefore calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` **before** the redirect, as the
third rule of the isolation set in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model). Two properties
matter and are worth stating so the change is not read as data loss:

- **Nothing is deleted.** The rows keep the user name as their cart id, so the same cart reappears the
  next time that account signs in — which is the source's own behaviour for a signed-in cart
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167].
- **The next anonymous read starts a new anonymous cart.** With the slot empty, the target's anonymous
  branch issues a fresh `anon:`-prefixed key and its protected session marker together, where the source
  issues a bare GUID [:172-175], so the following visitor gets their own empty cart rather than somebody
  else's full one.

It is approved delta 20 of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), because an anonymous
visitor who used to see the previous user's cart items no longer does, and **The coverage assertion requires it.

### 6.3 Session and cart identity

The cart key lives in session, keyed by a constant
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], and is reached two different ways: through
`HttpContextBase.Session` inside `GetCartId` [:161-180] — read at [:163], written at [:167] for a
signed-in user and at [:175] for an anonymous one, read again at [:179] — and through the MVC
`Controller.Session` property [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39].

**Session in the target is opt-in and in-memory by default.** So two registrations are required
rather than optional: `AddSession` over a **distributed cache**, and `UseSession` in the pipeline
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)). Omitting them does not fail to compile — it
produces a cart that empties itself unpredictably.

Three specifics:

- **The cache is SQL-backed, and the registration is named rather than implied.** The call is
  **`AddDistributedSqlServerCache`** (item 6 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)),
  which registers the SQL Server implementation of `IDistributedCache` (*Distributed caching in ASP.NET
  Core*, .NET 8), sharing the one database of section
  [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). Its **table is provisioned by
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)** — `dbo.SessionCache`, created by
  `dotnet sql-cache create` — and created **first** in the ordering of section
  [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), because a cache whose table does not exist fails on the
  first session write rather than at start.

  | Option | Value here | Note |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `ConnectionString` | The validated `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` | Read from the validated options type of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), so the cache cannot reach a database the five connection checks never saw |
  | `SchemaName`, `TableName` | **`dbo`**, **`SessionCache`** | Literals. [06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states that these two are deliberately not configuration-supplied |
  | `ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval` | **Left at its default of 30 minutes** | The minimum the provider accepts is 5 minutes (`SqlServerCacheOptions.ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval`, API reference, .NET 8). Lowering it buys nothing here: it changes only how promptly dead rows are *removed*, not whether a dead entry can be *read* |
  | `DefaultSlidingExpiration` | **Not relied on.** Session's own `IdleTimeout` of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) is what governs a session's lifetime, and the session middleware sets each entry's sliding expiration from it | Stated so that two timeouts are not read as one, and so nobody tunes the cache option expecting the session to follow |

  **Expiry is enforced on read and cleaned up opportunistically, and those are two different things.** An
  entry past its expiry is **never returned** — the provider's read path filters on the expiry column, so
  correctness does not depend on the deletion pass having run. The deletion pass itself is triggered **by
  cache operations** rather than by a background timer of its own, and runs at most once per
  `ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval`. Two consequences follow and both are stated because they surface as
  puzzling observations rather than as failures: a replica taking **no** traffic performs no cleanup at
  all, and expired rows are therefore expected to be present in `dbo.SessionCache` between passes. That is
  the normal state of a healthy table, not evidence of a leak — and it is a further reason
  [06 §6.7.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s restore step empties the table outright instead of
  trying to age its contents.

- **The order is written down because the dependency is invisible at the call site.** `AddSession`'s store
  resolves `IDistributedCache`, so the cache must be the one registered — and **when a service type is
  registered more than once, resolving a single instance yields the last registration** (*Dependency
  injection in .NET*, .NET 8). So the rule is absolute rather than stylistic: **`AddDistributedSqlServerCache`
  is the only `IDistributedCache` registration in the composition**, and neither
  `AddDistributedMemoryCache` nor any other cache registration appears anywhere — not in a Development
  branch, and not in the test fixture, whose substitution rule (section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)) overrides configuration rather than
  re-registering services precisely so that this cannot happen. A memory-backed cache would pass every
  single-replica test and lose carts the moment a second replica existed, which is the failure this
  ordering makes unavailable. The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) resolves
  `IDistributedCache` and asserts the implementation type, then round-trips a session value through a
  second host sharing the same table.
- **The session key constant is preserved** and both access paths converge on one: the service of
  section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) owns cart-id
  resolution, and `AccountController` stops writing session directly — it calls the service, which is
  also what makes the cross-store sequence of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)
  expressible in one place.
- **Session cookie attributes are set explicitly**, on the same principle as section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled): secure, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, and marked
  essential so that it is not suppressed by consent gating.

[11 §3.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the statefulness assessment, including the precise
point that instance affinity permits multiple instances **today** while foreclosing *resilient*
scale-out. This document's contribution is the mechanism: distributed session plus the persisted key
ring of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), after which affinity is no longer
load-bearing.

---

### 6.4 The account surface — authorization map, redirect safety and error paths

`AccountController` is the one file with no line-for-line successor (section
[9](#9-a-namespace-substitution-table-is-not-a-transformation-plan)), so three things it currently gets
right or nearly right have to be **re-established deliberately** rather than assumed to survive a
rewrite: who may reach each action, where a return URL may point, and what the user is told when
something fails.

**The authorization map, action by action.** The source protects the whole controller and opens
individual actions: `[Authorize]` on the class
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:15] with eight `[AllowAnonymous]` attributes
[:44], [:54], [:78], [:87], [:198], [:208], [:263], [:310]. **The class-level `[Authorize]` is
preserved, so the target remains deny-by-default**, and **all eight opt-outs survive**, because the
external-login surface the other four belong to is retained rather than removed (section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). One action leaves the routable surface without
becoming anonymous, and the table states why:

| Source action | Source attributes | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Login` GET [:45] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [:44] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`** |
| `Login` POST [:56] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [:54], `[HttpPost]`, `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:55] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`.** The token attribute is redundant under the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) and is dropped rather than duplicated |
| `Register` GET [:79] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [:78] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`** |
| `Register` POST [:89] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [:87], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:88] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`**, token from the global filter |
| `Manage` GET [:131] and POST [:148] | Class-level `[Authorize]` only | **Kept, authorized**, and the POST keeps **both** branches: change-password when the account has a local password [:153-166] and set-password when it does not [:168-189]. The second branch stays reachable because external-only accounts survive the migration (section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)) |
| `LogOff` POST [:302] | Class-level `[Authorize]` | **Kept, authorized**, and it stays a POST (section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)) |
| `ExternalLogin` [:200], `ExternalLoginCallback` [:209], `ExternalLoginConfirmation` [:265], `ExternalLoginFailure` [:311] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [:198], [:208], [:263], [:310] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`** — the callback and the confirmation must be reachable before a local identity exists, which is what the opt-out is for. Their bodies are re-expressed against the framework's external-authentication API (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)); the attributes are unchanged |
| `Disassociate` [:114], `LinkLogin` [:237], `LinkLoginCallback` [:245] | Class-level `[Authorize]` | **Kept, authorized.** `LinkLogin`'s source XSRF binding through `ChallengeResult`'s `XsrfKey` [:336] becomes `AuthenticationProperties` carrying the user id, set by `SignInManager.ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties` and — the half that is load-bearing rather than incidental — **compared against the current principal's user id in the callback before any login row is added**, per the `LinkLoginCallback` row of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). Authorization on this pair means "some authenticated caller"; the binding is what makes it mean "**this** caller" |
| `RemoveAccountList` [:317] | Class-level `[Authorize]`, plus `[ChildActionOnly]` [:316] | **Kept as rendering, removed as a route.** It becomes `RemoveAccountListViewComponent` (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), and a view component is not routable at all, so it carries no authorization attribute of its own and cannot be reached by URL; its protection is the authorized `Manage` view that invokes it. `/Account/RemoveAccountList` therefore must not resolve — The coverage assertion requires it |

**The rule that makes this checkable rather than a list to trust: the target controller carries
`[Authorize]` at the class and `[AllowAnonymous]` on exactly eight actions — the two `Login`, the two
`Register`, and the four external-login actions `ExternalLogin`, `ExternalLoginCallback`,
`ExternalLoginConfirmation` and `ExternalLoginFailure`.** Anything else anonymous is a defect, and so is
any route resolving to `RemoveAccountList`, which is a view component rather than an action. Coverage row
51 asserts both by probing every account route unauthenticated.

**Input bounds — every account input carries a schema-aligned maximum, and rejection happens before any
Identity call and before any database round trip.**

The source's account models are bounded inconsistently, and the gap is on the unauthenticated surface.
`LoginViewModel.UserName` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:33-35] and
`RegisterViewModel.UserName` [:48-50] carry `[Required]` and **no length constraint of any kind**;
`RegisterViewModel.Password` [:52-53] is bounded at 100 characters while `LoginViewModel.Password`
[:37-40] and `ManageUserViewModel.OldPassword` [:14-17] are **unbounded**. So a syntactically valid
username of arbitrary length binds, passes validation, and travels all the way to
`UserManager.CreateAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:94] and the store
insert behind it — where the only thing that stops it is the column. In the target that surfaces as a raw
`DbUpdateException` from an insert, **on a path an anonymous caller can reach at will** (CWE-20), which
means a 500, a stack trace in the log per attempt, and a provider message that has no business being
anywhere near a response. The same input is also what step 2a of section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) hands to a key-derivation function, whose cost scales with
the candidate's length. Kestrel's request-size limit is not a substitute: a megabyte-long username is
comfortably inside it.

**The maxima, with the column each one matches.** They are added to the adapted
`Models/AccountViewModels.cs` (section [9.2](#92-the-four-groups), Group D) as ordinary `[StringLength]`
annotations, so a violation is a **field validation message on a redisplayed form** — the same outcome as
any other invalid model — and never an error page.

| Member | Maximum | What it is aligned to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UserName` on the login model and on the registration model | **256** | `AspNetUsers.UserName` and `AspNetUsers.NormalizedUserName`, which ASP.NET Core Identity's own model configuration declares as `nvarchar(256)`. Both sides of the surface carry the same bound: a longer value cannot match a stored row on the login path and cannot be stored on the registration path, so accepting it buys nothing |
| `Password` and `ConfirmPassword` on the registration model, and `NewPassword`/`ConfirmPassword` on the change-password model | **100** | **Preserved** from the source's own annotations [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:52-53] and [:19-20]. The minimum is not set here — length policy is the `RequiredLength` row of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) |
| `Password` on the login model, and `OldPassword` on the change-password model | **100** | The **consistency fix**: the source leaves both unbounded [:37-40], [:14-17]. Bounding a *verification* input at the *creation* maximum is safe here because every password that can exist was created either through the registration form, bounded at 100 [:52-53], or by the operator command of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties), which applies the same credential policy (the coverage assertion) — the shipped seeded credential [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:17] is 27 characters. No reachable account can hold a password this bound would refuse |

**Two properties this has to have, and both follow from where the check runs.** DataAnnotations
validation completes during model binding, before the action body runs, so an overlength submission is
refused by the `ModelState` gate — step 1 of section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) on the login path, and its counterpart on the registration
path — **before `FindByNameAsync`, before step 2a's key derivation, before `CreateAsync`, and before any
query or insert**. And the redisplayed form encodes what it echoes, as Razor does by default, so the
submitted value cannot be reflected as markup. **And nothing about the attempt is logged raw**, on either
path. A rejected **registration** is the `ACCT-2001` event of
[09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) at its `ValidationFailed` outcome, which permits a
`ValidationFailureCategory` code and explicitly not the submitted values. A rejected **login** never
reaches a credential check, so it is **not** an `AUTH-1002` event at all — that event's outcome values
cover resolved, unresolved and locked-out credential attempts and none of them describes a request that
failed binding — and it is recorded, if at all, as an ordinary request-level diagnostic under
[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) carrying no submitted value. In neither case is a store or
provider exception recorded, because neither path reaches one. **The coverage assertion requires all four
parts** — no write, bounded work, encoded output, no raw record.

**And the change is recorded rather than slipped in.** Today an overlength username passes validation and
fails at the store; in the target it is refused with a field message on a redisplayed form. Nobody is
worse off, but the outcome of a request an anonymous caller can issue is **observably different**, and a
difference of that kind is an approved delta in this document or it is nothing. It is carried by
**approved delta 10** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), whose subject is precisely
the account policy this document sets explicitly instead of inheriting, and whose owner is **Security** —
the same constituency that owns the maxima themselves.

**Abuse limits — because lockout bounds one account and nothing else.** The lockout policy of section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is real hardening over a source that has neither lockout
nor throttling ([09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md)), and it is **per account**: it constrains attempts
against a *named* account and says nothing about attempts against names that do not exist. That gap is
wider in the target than in the source, and the reason is this document's own doing:

- **Every attempt now costs a full key derivation, by design.** Step 2a of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) spends the target cost on an unknown username precisely so
  that the response time discloses nothing. A caller cycling fabricated user names therefore buys the
  most expensive operation the application performs, at one request each, and no lockout counter is even
  incremented — there is no account to increment. Uniform cost is the right decision and it makes an
  explicit request limit a **precondition** rather than an extra.
- **Every attempt also writes a record.** The `AUTH-1002`/`AccountNotFound` record is emitted at
  `Warning` ([09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)), so the same cycle is a log-volume amplifier: it
  costs the attacker one request and costs the platform an ingested, retained, alert-evaluated record.
- **Neither cost is bounded by anything else in this document.** Request-size limits bound one request's
  bytes, the model maxima above bound one request's fields, and the anti-forgery policy of section
  [7.1](#71-the-policy) bounds cross-site submission — none of the three bounds *how many* requests one
  caller may make.

The response is the rate-limiting composition of **stage 1 item 14 and stage 2 item 11** in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order): a per-partition limiter on the three credential endpoints, an
aggregate limiter over the same endpoints that a distributed flood cannot evade by spreading, and a
general limiter for everything else — **all three chained into one global limiter**, because two named
endpoint policies cannot both apply to one action and the per-source and aggregate credential bounds must
both apply to all three. Three properties belong here rather than there, because they are about behaviour
rather than composition:

- **A refused request is refused *before* the work.** The limiter runs at stage 2 item 11, ahead of the
  endpoint, so a rejected attempt performs **no** `FindByNameAsync`, **no** key derivation and **no**
  credential check — and consequently emits **no** `AUTH-1002` record of any outcome, because no
  credential attempt happened. It emits the single `Information` record stage 1 item 14 specifies. That is the
  amplification closed in both directions at once.
- **Refusal is not lockout, and cannot be used as one.** The partition for an anonymous caller is their
  own client address, never the submitted user name, so nothing an anonymous caller does can ration or
  lock an account belonging to somebody else. A signed-in caller is partitioned by their Identity
  `UserId`, so they are not rationed by whoever shares their egress address either.
- **The residual trade is stated and owned.** Many customers behind one address share an anonymous
  partition, so a large shared-egress population could see 429s on the sign-in form under genuine load.
  It is bounded deliberately: the limits are configuration, not constants; the window is fixed with no
  queue, so `Retry-After` is an accurate, short, self-service wait rather than an opaque failure; and the
  aggregate limiter's ceiling is set high enough that it never engages on real traffic. **429 on these
  endpoints is approved delta 22** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), owned by
  **Security and product** — Security because it is a control, Product because a refused sign-in is a
  user-visible outcome the source never produces. **The coverage assertion requires the aggregate bound against
  a flood arranged so that no per-source bound can fire first, and **The coverage assertion requires the
  per-source bound from a single address partition — the two together are what prove the chain composes rather
  than one limiter masking the other.

**Redirect safety — a preserved control that must not be lost in the rewrite.** The source is already
careful: `RedirectToLocal` [:382-392] tests `Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)` [:384] and falls back to the
home page [:390]. The target preserves the control and states it per site, because an open redirect
(CWE-601) is exactly the kind of protection a wholesale rewrite drops without noticing:

- **`Login` POST** tests the value itself and falls back:
  `if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(returnUrl) && Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)) { return Redirect(returnUrl); }`
  followed by `return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");`. **A non-local, empty or missing return URL
  therefore ends at the home page with a `302`, which is exactly what the source does** — `Url.IsLocalUrl`
  [:384] with the home-page fallback [:390].
- **`LocalRedirect(returnUrl)` is rejected for this site, and the reason is not stylistic.**
  `LocalRedirect` **throws** on a non-local URL. The throw is not caught in the handler, so it reaches the
  exception-handling middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and the
  response to an attacker-supplied return URL is a **500 with a logged server fault** — a behaviour
  change from the source's `302` to Home, a self-inflicted error-rate signal on a public unauthenticated
  path, and a test hazard: "does not redirect off-site" is satisfied by a 500, so a suite asserting only
  that would pass an implementation that turns a hostile link into an unhandled exception. The explicit
  test plus fallback keeps the source's behaviour and leaves nothing for a `catch` to interpret.
- **`Login` GET** validates the incoming `returnUrl` with the same `Url.IsLocalUrl` test **before putting
  it in the model**, and drops it — rendering the form with no return URL — when it fails. The POST
  validates again, so this is belt-and-braces — but an unvalidated value rendered into the form is an
  attacker-controlled link on a page the user trusts, which is worth preventing on the way in as well as
  on the way out.
- **The cookie handler's own round-trip** uses `ReturnUrlParameter` and `LoginPath` from section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) and is validated by the framework.
- **Three other target actions take a return URL**, because the external-login surface is retained
  (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)): `ExternalLogin`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:200], `ExternalLoginCallback` [:209] and
  `ExternalLoginConfirmation` [:265]. **Each applies the same explicit `Url.IsLocalUrl` test and the same
  home-page fallback**, stated as a rule rather than left to the framework, because the callback's return
  URL survives a round trip through `AuthenticationProperties` and comes back from outside the
  application — the one case where an unvalidated value would be most tempting to trust. `LinkLogin`
  [:237] and `LinkLoginCallback` [:245] take no return URL: they redirect to `Manage` unconditionally,
  with or without a message [:250], [:255], [:257], which is preserved.

The coverage assertion posts a **malicious absolute return URL** to `Login` and asserts the exact outcome —
status `302` to `/`, and **not** a 500 — rather than the weaker "does not redirect off-site".

**Error paths, one per flow, with the disclosure rule stated.**

| Flow | Failure | Target behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Login` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay with the field errors. Preserved from [:58], [:73] |
| `Login` POST | Unknown user, wrong password, or `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` returning not-succeeded for any reason **including lockout** | **One generic message — `"Invalid username or password."`, the source's own wording [:68] — for every one of those cases**, with the same status, the same view and the same model state. Preserved deliberately: a distinct "account locked" or "no such user" message is friendlier and **discloses whether an account exists**. Two things make the uniformity real rather than nominal. **(a) The unknown-user case reaches this branch through step 2a of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)**, and the locked-out and legacy-hash cases through step 3's top-up — the fixed-work service specified there — so all four populations cost what the most expensive real verification costs and the *response time* discloses nothing either. A bare early return would leave an enumeration oracle behind an identical page, and so would a single dummy derivation, because this store holds two hash formats at once and a lockout derives nothing. **(b) The distinction goes to the log and nowhere else**, as the `AUTH-1002` event of [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) at one of its three outcome values — **`AccountNotFound`, `InvalidCredentials` or `AccountLockedOut`, emitted at `Warning`**, named here exactly as that catalog names them because a paraphrase is not an identifier and an implementation cannot be checked against one. Its actor rule — the Identity `UserId` where the account resolves and the bounded literal plus keyed pseudonym where it does not — severity and permitted field list are **09's and are not restated here**. The submitted username is never written, per [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) |
| `Login` POST | Cart migration failed after retries | Sign-in **succeeds** with a non-blocking notice (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) |
| `Register` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay with field errors. Preserved from [:91] |
| `Register` POST | `CreateAsync` returns a failed `IdentityResult` — a duplicate username, or a password failing the policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) | **Each `IdentityError` is added to `ModelState` and rendered in the validation summary**, which is what `AddErrors` [:356-362] does today and is preserved. Identity's own duplicate-username error text is user-facing here, and that is accepted: a registration form must say the name is taken, and it discloses nothing the form does not already reveal by refusing the name |
| `Manage` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay. Preserved from [:155] |
| `Manage` POST | `ChangePasswordAsync` returns a failed `IdentityResult` — wrong current password, or a new password failing the policy | Errors mapped into `ModelState` as above, form redisplayed, **nothing changed**. Preserved from [:157-165] |
| `Manage` POST | Success | `RedirectToAction("Manage", new { Message = ManageMessageId.ChangePasswordSuccess })`, rendering *"Your password has been changed."* — preserved from [:160] and [:134] |
| `Manage` GET | Status-message surface | **All four `ManageMessageId` members are kept** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:374-380] — `ChangePasswordSuccess`, `SetPasswordSuccess`, `RemoveLoginSuccess` and `Error` — with their exact source wording [:134-137], because all four flows are retained (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). `ViewBag.HasLocalPassword` [:139] and the `HasPassword()` helper [:364] are kept too, the helper re-expressed as `UserManager.HasPasswordAsync(user)`: the set-password branch is reachable exactly when a migrated account has no local password, which section [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) counts before the load rather than assuming away |

**The account surface's event emission, stated with the catalog's own vocabulary — because two of these
classes are one call apart and an implementation that emits only the obvious one loses the signal that
matters.** [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns the identifiers, actors, outcomes, severities and
field lists; what this document owns is **where in the flow each one is emitted**, and that is the part
no catalog can supply.

| Event | Emitted where | The precision that matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH-1001`, `Success` | Immediately after step 6 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) issues the cookie | After, not before: an event recording a sign-in that then failed to issue a cookie is a false record of an authenticated session |
| `AUTH-1002`, `AccountNotFound` | The step 2a branch — a null result from `FindByNameAsync`, **after** the fixed-cost derivation has been spent | Actor is the literal **`anonymous`** — one of the exactly two actor values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits, the other being the Identity `UserId` — plus a `SubjectPseudonym` **built under [06 §8.4.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s key and label grammar, which that section solely owns**, never the submitted name and never a pseudonym in the actor position. Emitting before the derivation would move the record earlier in the request for this population only, which is a timing signal in the log stream even when the response is uniform |
| `AUTH-1002`, `InvalidCredentials` | Step 3 returning not-succeeded with `IsLockedOut` false | |
| `AUTH-1002`, `AccountLockedOut` | Step 3 returning `IsLockedOut` true | This records **an attempt against a locked account**, which is a different fact from the account becoming locked |
| `AUTH-1003`, `LockedOut` | **Additionally**, on the one attempt that *causes* the lockout | This is the class an implementation drops. `CheckPasswordSignInAsync(..., lockoutOnFailure: true)` returns `IsLockedOut` **both** when the account was already locked and when this very failure crossed the threshold, so the two are indistinguishable from the result alone. **The emission point is therefore not the controller at all**: the transition happens inside Identity's own `AccessFailedAsync`, which increments the failure count and sets `LockoutEnd` in one call, and a before-and-after read either side of step 3 is **not atomic** — two failures arriving together can each observe "not locked before, locked after" and emit two records for one transition, or both observe "already locked" and emit none. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is an override of the virtual `UserManager<ApplicationUser>.AccessFailedAsync` that captures the state, calls `base`, and emits only where the returned `IdentityResult` succeeded *and* the account was unlocked before and locked after. That document owns the artifact, its registration and its at-least-once delivery semantics — the override narrows the window but does not close it, so the contract is **at least one** physical record per transition, each carrying the state-derived de-duplication key `{UserId}\|{LockoutEndUtc:o}` and collapsing to exactly one **logical** event at the reader, and **exactly-once physical delivery is not claimed anywhere**. What belongs here is that the record accompanies the same attempt's `AUTH-1002`/`AccountLockedOut`, that its cardinality is the one the coverage assertion requires, and that **no controller-side reading of lockout state is part of this flow**. Emitting only `AUTH-1002` loses the moment a threshold was crossed, which is the one event a brute-force alert is built on; emitting `AUTH-1003` on every subsequent attempt inflates it into noise and makes the alert useless in the other direction |
| `AUTH-1004`, `Success` | The sign-out action of section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface), after the cookie is expired | |
| `ACCT-2001` at `Success`, `DuplicateUserName` and `ValidationFailed` | R2 of the registration sequence, at each `IdentityResult` branch, and at the `ModelState` gate for a bound-length rejection | The two failure outcomes carry the `anonymous` actor and `none` target sentinels [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) names, because no account exists to identify |
| `ACCT-2002`, `ACCT-2003` | The change-password action's success and its two failure branches | `ACCT-2002` also carries `RehashedOnSignIn` where the write was step 3's migration rehash rather than a user action — and **that case has a different emission point**, because the rehash happens *inside* `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` and the caller sees only a sign-in result. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is **two artifacts, not one**, and that distinction is load-bearing. The first is a decorating `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` — `RehashObservingPasswordHasher` — recording the framework's rehash verdict into a **scoped, per-request signal**, scoped rather than static precisely so two concurrent sign-ins cannot see each other's. That artifact **observes and never emits**, because `PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded` is *advice returned before persistence is attempted*, and `CheckPasswordAsync` then performs the update and **discards its `IdentityResult`** — so a store write that fails leaves the signal set, and a hasher-driven emission would assert a rehash that never persisted. The second artifact is the emitter: the `AuditingUserManager` subclass overriding the protected virtual `UpdateUserAsync(ApplicationUser)`, emitting `ACCT-2002` at `Success` with `RehashedOnSignIn = true` **only** where the returned `IdentityResult.Succeeded` is true, **and** the scoped signal is set, **and** the request is not a user-initiated credential change. Where the update fails, **no `ACCT-2002` is written at all** and a distinct `credential-rehash` diagnostic goes to the ordinary channel instead — deliberately not a seventeenth event class. Where the signal is not set, no `ACCT-2002` is emitted, because a sign-in is not a password change. The coverage assertion forces the failed update |

**A negative test per flow** — The coverage assertions: a bad-credentials login asserting the generic
message **and** that the response distinguishes an unknown user from a wrong password neither in content
nor in timing, **and that the right event class and outcome reached the log in each case**; a registration
whose password fails the policy asserting the error is rendered and no account is created; and a
change-password with the wrong current password asserting the stored hash is unchanged. **Rows 65 and 66
cover the two input contracts above** — the schema-aligned maxima, and the allowed user-name character
set.

### 6.5 The remaining event classes — where each is emitted, and the producer arithmetic

[09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) defines **sixteen** event classes and
[09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) assigns each one a producer. **Thirteen are produced by the
ported web application and three are not**, and both halves of that arithmetic have consequences this
document has to carry: section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)'s
table places only **seven** of the thirteen — the four `AUTH-` classes and the three `ACCT-` classes, all
of them on the account surface — and the remaining six sit in sections that specify a *contract* rather
than an event. An emission requirement that no section states is an emission requirement that ships
missing, and it ships missing invisibly, because a contract with no record still returns the right status
code.

| Event | Emitted where | The precision that matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTHZ-3003`, `Denied` | **Inside pipeline item 12** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) — `UseAuthorization()` — and nowhere else | **The one class with no site in application code.** A denial is decided by the authorization middleware and **never reaches the action**, so no controller body and no action filter observes it, and the `[Authorize]` attributes of sections [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) and [8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) have nothing to hook. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is a custom `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` that **holds the framework's own handler and always delegates to it, on every path**. That delegation is the whole safety property: a handler that emits its record and then produces the response itself has silently redefined every denial's status, its redirect to the login path and its access-denied behaviour, while intending only to add a log line |
| `ADMIN-4001` at `Success` and `ValidationFailed` | The **create contract** of section [8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) — at step 5's redirect, and at both refusals: step 1's `ModelState` redisplay and step 2's foreign-key redisplay | The target on `ValidationFailed` is 09's `none` sentinel, not an `AlbumId`: nothing was inserted, so no key was allocated to name. A posted `AlbumId` is **not** a target either — it was never bound (approved delta 23) |
| `ADMIN-4002` at `Success`, `NotFound` and `ValidationFailed` | The **edit contract** of the same section — step 5's redirect; step 3's `NotFound`; and **three** refusals under `ValidationFailed`: step 1's `ModelState` redisplay, step 2's foreign-key redisplay, and **step 0's route/body id mismatch** | Step 0 is the branch an implementation forgets, because it answers `400` before the action has loaded anything — and an unlogged `400` is indistinguishable from a client that never called. The record names **which properties changed and never their values** ([09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) row 12), which is load-bearing here rather than generic: one of the five is `Price` |
| `ADMIN-4003` at `Success` and `NotFound` | The `DeleteConfirmed` action — **census site F5** in section [4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census): `Success` once the removal is saved, `NotFound` on the null branch that site adds | `Warning`, not `Information`, per 09 — deletion is the one administration operation with no undo, and the severity is not this document's to soften |
| `ORDER-5001`, `Success` | Section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) **step 9**, after the step 3 wrapper's commit has returned and `AcceptAllChanges()` has run — the commit is the execution strategy's, not step 8's | After the commit, never before it, for the same reason `AUTH-1001` follows the cookie: an order event emitted inside the transaction records a placement that a rollback then unmakes, and the record cannot be withdrawn |
| `ORDER-5002` at `ValidationFailed`, `EmptyCart` and `PersistenceFailed` | The same section's refusals and its failure table — `ValidationFailed` for step 0's submission-token rejection, step 1's `ModelState` redisplay and step 2's promo-code no-match; `EmptyCart` for step 4; `PersistenceFailed` for every classifier row that redisplays or renders the generic error page | **Two rows of that table deliberately emit nothing.** `Cancelled` is a client disconnect rather than a failed placement, and `DuplicateSubmission` is a reconciled replay that redirects to an order which already exists and was already recorded at `ORDER-5001`. Both already write their own diagnostic record, and counting either as a failed placement puts a false failure in front of whoever reads this class. The record carries a failure **category**, never the provider text — the same rule as section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s sanitized record, because this is the request whose body is a name, an address, a telephone number and an email address |

**The three the ported application cannot produce — and why a gate demanding sixteen from it fails.**

- **`PROV-6001`** — the provisioning command, one record per operation, section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4.
- **`AUTHZ-3002`** — that command's **revoke mode only**, property 3a. Nothing in the web application
  withdraws a role.
- **`AUTHZ-3001`** — **two producers.** The command's membership operation, at `Success` and only where
  the membership was actually added; and the Identity data migration of section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables), one record per
  role assignment it loads — at `Success` for an assignment it creates and at `AlreadyHeld` for one the
  target already held, which is the outcome value 09 reserves for that producer.

Thirteen plus those three is sixteen. **No HTTP request can produce any of the three**, because nothing in
the ported application grants or revokes a role membership — so a coverage gate that demanded all sixteen
classes from the application's surface would be failed by a correct implementation, and each of the three
is verified at its own producer instead: The coverage assertions at the command, and section
[5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s reconciliation at
the migration. **The coverage assertion requires the thirteen**, class by class, at the surface that produces
them.

## 7. Anti-forgery — three separate problems

### 7.1 The policy

**Global automatic validation.** `AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` is registered as a global
filter, so **every request whose method is not `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` or `TRACE` is validated by
default** — those four are the exact set the attribute exempts, and it "works identically to the
`ValidateAntiForgeryToken` attribute, except that it doesn't require tokens for requests" using them
(*Prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF/CSRF) attacks in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8), which is why the
application's `GET` endpoints appear on no list below. Opt-outs are explicit,
individually justified and reviewable. This is the slot vacated by
`FilterConfig.RegisterGlobalFilters` (section
[2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate)).

Opt-in-per-action is rejected for a reason visible in the repository: the source uses opt-in, and it
covers **one controller of the four that need it**. A policy whose failure mode is "someone forgot an
attribute" has already failed here once.

**The opt-out list has exactly two endpoints, it is published here, and it is closed.** "Explicit and
individually justified" is a list or it is nothing, so the list is the contract: two endpoints, each with
the property that justifies it, and a third requires editing this table.

| Endpoint | Metadata that opts it out | Why the global filter cannot govern it | Why exempting it is safe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /Home/Error` — and the same action under every verb | `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]` on the action | Stage 3 of the pipeline re-executes a failed request **preserving its method** (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so a missing page requested by `POST` re-enters as a **tokenless `POST`**. Validated, it would answer 400 where the caller asked a question whose answer is 404 | It is **rendering-only and changes no state** — the contract in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) makes that a requirement of the endpoint rather than an observation about it. A CSRF attack on an endpoint that writes nothing achieves nothing |
| `POST /csp-report` — the CSP violation collector of [06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) | `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]` on the action | The caller is **the browser's reporting machinery, not a page of this application**: it posts with no anti-forgery token and no form, its response is ignored entirely, and it can arrive with no session at all. Validated, **every violation report would be rejected with a 400** and the report-only phase would collect nothing while appearing to work | It **writes nothing to the application database** and returns `204` with no body ([06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), so there is no state for a forged request to change. Its abuse surface is bounded by size, rate, cardinality and origin checks that are all [06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and are not restated here |

**Both are declared as MVC actions, and that is a decision rather than an incidental.** The collector
could equally be a route handler mapped with `MapPost`, but a route handler sits **outside** the MVC
filter pipeline entirely, so it would be exempt from the global filter **by construction rather than by
declaration** — indistinguishable, in a review, from an endpoint someone forgot to protect. Declaring it
as an action keeps every non-`GET` endpoint in the application under one policy with exactly two visible
exceptions.

**The opt-out is a declared filter, which is why this list is auditable rather than aspirational.**
`[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]` overrides the global filter for the action it decorates (*Prevent Cross-Site
Request Forgery (XSRF/CSRF) attacks in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). The mechanism is a **filter**:
`IgnoreAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` implements `IFilterMetadata`, `IOrderedFilter` and
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ViewFeatures.IAntiforgeryPolicy` (API reference, ASP.NET Core 8), and the
attribute declared on the action is the more specific of the two policies in play. Two properties follow.
The exemption is **discoverable from the action inventory** —
`IActionDescriptorCollectionProvider.ActionDescriptors` returns every action, and each descriptor's
`FilterDescriptors` is "the set of filters associated with this action" (API reference, ASP.NET Core 8) —
so a test can enumerate them and assert that exactly these two actions carry the attribute: coverage row
38 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is that assertion. And a third exemption cannot be added
quietly: adding one means an attribute *and* a row here, and the enumeration test fails on the attribute
alone.

**One near-miss named, because a test written against the wrong surface would report the wrong fact about
a correctly configured application.** .NET 8 also carries
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery.IAntiforgeryMetadata` with a `RequiresValidation` flag, which is the
**minimal-API** surface — the metadata `DisableAntiforgery()` attaches to a route handler.
`IgnoreAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` does **not** implement it (API reference, ASP.NET Core 8), so an audit
looking for that interface would find **zero** exempt endpoints in an application whose two exemptions are
correctly declared. The audit therefore enumerates filter descriptors, and it does **not** read
`ActionDescriptor.EndpointMetadata`, which the same reference marks as "meant for infrastructure and
should not be used by application code". This is the second reason the collector is declared as an MVC
action rather than a `MapPost` handler: one inventory, one mechanism, two visible exceptions.

**No other endpoint opts out**, including the health endpoints of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — they are `GET`, which
the global filter does not validate in the first place, so they need no exemption and are not on this
list. The pipeline exemption those three paths *do* carry is a different mechanism about a different
middleware (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), stages 5 and 6), and conflating the two
is how an anti-forgery hole gets justified by a transport decision.

**The emission/validation asymmetry is why the filter is required and not merely tidy.**
`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` appears **10** times across MVC 5's views
(`git grep -o -E '@Html\.AntiForgeryToken\(\)' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml' | wc -l` → `10`). In the target,
**emission becomes automatic** — form tag helpers emit the field without a helper call, so all ten
calls simply disappear. **Validation does not become automatic.** Removing the ten emission calls while
assuming validation came along is the exact shape of a silent regression: every form still carries a
token and nothing checks it.

Adopting the global policy exposes three problems a namespace-level port would miss. Each gets a named
resolution.

### 7.2 Problem one — coverage today is partial

There are **13** POST actions in the migration source and **8** of them validate.

| Controller | POST actions | Validated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AccountController` | 8 — attributes at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:53], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:86], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:112], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:146], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:197], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:235], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:262], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:300] | **8** — `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:55], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:88], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:113], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:147], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:199], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:236], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:264], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:301] |
| `StoreManagerController` | **3** — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:53] Create, [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:86] Edit, [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116] `DeleteConfirmed` | **0** |
| `ShoppingCartController` | 1 — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:54] `RemoveFromCart` | **0** |
| `CheckoutController` | 1 — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:25] `AddressAndPayment` | **0** |

**Five state-changing POST actions are unprotected**: three administration writes, cart removal, and
the checkout write — the one that creates an order.

**A census trap, stated because getting it wrong understates the work.** `grep -c '\[HttpPost\]'`
against `StoreManagerController.cs` returns **2**, not 3, because its third POST is declared
`[HttpPost, ActionName("Delete")]` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116]
— a combined attribute list the literal pattern misses.
**The real count is 3.** The correct census matches on the attribute *prefix*, and it must also
tolerate the UTF-8 byte-order mark that all 27 source files carry (section
[9.1](#91-the-census-and-how-to-count-it)). The reproducing commands for both the naive and the correct
form are in [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**Resolution: the global filter covers all five, plus every future non-`GET` endpoint, with no
per-action attribute.** Adopting it needs no code change at four of the five sites — only at the
fifth, which is the AJAX post of section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form).
The eight existing `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` attributes are removed as redundant, which is safe
**only because** the global filter is registered; the two changes are one change and must not be split
across commits.

### 7.3 Problem two — one state-changing action is a `GET`, which no policy can cover

`AddToCart` is declared with **no verb attribute**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:33] and it **mutates**: it loads the
album [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:37-38], resolves the cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:41], adds the item [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:43], calls `SaveChanges` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:45] and redirects
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:48]. The comment above it even documents it as `GET: /ShoppingCart/AddToCart/5` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:31].

**No anti-forgery policy can protect a state-changing `GET`**, because a `GET` is issued by any image
tag, link or prefetch without a token and without the user's intent. This is not a coverage gap to
close with a filter; it is a verb that is wrong. [09 §6.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns it as a
finding across all three editions.

**Resolution: convert it to a token-protected `POST`.**

- The action gains an explicit `[HttpPost]`, and the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy)
  validates it with no further attribute.
- **Its call site changes from a link to a posting form.**
  `@Html.ActionLink("Add to cart", "AddToCart", "ShoppingCart", new { id = Model.AlbumId }, "")`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:28-29] becomes a form posting to the same path,
  with the album id as a route value and a submit control styled to match today's appearance. The
  surrounding `<p class="btn btn-default">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:26] is restructured accordingly — a `btn` class on a
  paragraph wrapping a link is Bootstrap 3-era markup that section
  [8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump) revisits anyway.
- **The response behaviour is preserved**: a redirect to the cart index
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:48], so the post-redirect-get
  pattern the page already follows is unchanged.

**This is a deliberate, approval-owned interface delta. The path is unchanged; the verb is not.** Any
external bookmark, link or automation targeting `/ShoppingCart/AddToCart/5` **stops working** — it
will render the cart page or a 405 rather than adding an item. There is no way to have both: a
bookmarkable URL that adds to a cart *is* the vulnerability. It is listed among the approved deltas of
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) with **Security** as its approval owner, and
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires the new verb to be tested and the old one to be
asserted **not** to mutate.

### 7.4 Problem three — cart removal posts without a form

The cart page removes an item with
`$.post(PostToUrl, { "id": recordToDelete }, ...)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17]. The trigger is a plain anchor carrying
`data-id` and `data-url` attributes [:74-75], read at [:12-13]. **There is no surrounding form.**

So the global policy of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) would **reject every cart removal**: no form
means no tag helper, no tag helper means no emitted token, and no token means a rejected POST. This is
the one site where adopting the policy requires client-side work, and it is the reason the policy has
to be adopted deliberately rather than switched on.

**The transport is form-urlencoded, not JSON.** No `contentType` and no `JSON.stringify` is specified,
so jQuery serializes the object as a form body — jQuery's default. That matters because it means a
hidden form field **would** work; the transport does not force the answer, so the answer is a choice
and is recorded as one.

**The selected contract is the `RequestVerificationToken` request header.**

- **Server side, one call:** `builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(...)` — stage 1 item 10 of section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), which carries the full option set. Of it, `HeaderName =
  "RequestVerificationToken"` is what this sub-section needs: the string is stated once, in
  configuration, rather than assumed to be a default, because **there is no default header name** and
  with `HeaderName` left null the header is never consulted at all. **The same call configures the
  antiforgery cookie**, and that is not incidental to this transport: the header carries the *token*, the
  cookie carries its other half, and a `HeaderName`-only configuration leaves that cookie on
  `CookieSecurePolicy.None` while every other cookie in the application is `Always` — so the scripted
  removal path would be the one surface transmitting a non-secure cookie. The values are the antiforgery
  row of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled).
- **Emission, named API:** **`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()`**, called once in
  `Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml` **outside any form**. The helper exists in the target and does two
  things independent of any form: it issues the antiforgery **cookie** on the response and renders
  `<input name="__RequestVerificationToken" type="hidden" value="…">` into the document. That default
  field name is `AntiforgeryOptions.FormFieldName` and is **not** overridden. The field is never posted
  as a field — it is a carrier the script reads.
- **The selector the script reads, exactly:**
  `document.querySelector('input[name="__RequestVerificationToken"]').value`, evaluated **at post
  time** rather than captured at page load, so a token re-rendered by any other interaction on the page
  is still the one sent.
- **How an external script file obtains it.** The removal script moves out of the view and into
  `wwwroot/js/shopping-cart.js`, because the security response headers of section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 2 make an inline `<script>` block a policy
  violation. Being external changes nothing about token access: the file is loaded by a `<script src>`
  in the same document, so the same `querySelector` above reaches the same hidden input. **No token is
  baked into the script file, and no token endpoint is added** — a script served with a token in it
  would be cacheable with one user's token in it.
- **The request, both halves matching:**
  `$.ajax({ url: postToUrl, method: 'POST', data: { id: recordToDelete }, headers: { 'RequestVerificationToken': token } })`.
  The `headers` key is the same literal as `AntiforgeryOptions.HeaderName`; a mismatch between the two
  is a 400 on every removal and is exactly why both sides are written out here. The body stays
  form-urlencoded `id=…`, preserving the source's transport [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17].
- **Why this composes correctly with a form-urlencoded body.** The token store reads the **header
  first** when `HeaderName` is set and falls back to the form field only when the header is absent, so a
  body that carries `id` and no `__RequestVerificationToken` field validates on the header alone. No
  ordering assumption or duplicate emission is required.
- **Why the header rather than a body field:** it keeps the token out of the request body, so it
  applies uniformly to **any** future scripted endpoint regardless of that endpoint's content type. A
  body field only works for form-urlencoded and multipart bodies, and would have to be reinvented the
  first time an endpoint posts JSON.

**Three tests, not one** (the coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)): a token
**freshly rendered by the cart page and sent in the header** removes the item and returns the expected
payload — which is the row that proves the emission point, the selector and the two header names all
agree; a **missing** header is rejected and the cart is **unchanged**; a **structurally valid but
mismatched** token — one issued for a different session — is rejected and the cart is **unchanged**.
The last two must assert on the data, not only on the status code — a rejection that still mutated
would pass a status-only assertion.

The response side of this same endpoint has its own, independent problem; it is section
[8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy).
