inherits the hazard above, because a redisplayed view *does* use the shared layout and the layout's two
view components query the catalog on every render. So the outcome cannot be chosen per `catch` clause in
each handler: two handlers stating it independently is how one of them ends up redisplaying a failure
whose cause is that the database cannot be reached. There is therefore **one** classifier, stated once
here, and section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)'s failure table and section
[8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target)'s write paths consume
it rather than restating it.

**Its input is the exception *chain*, not the exception.** This is the half a per-handler rule gets
wrong: a connectivity failure raised inside `SaveChangesAsync` does not arrive as a bare `SqlException` —
EF Core wraps it in a `DbUpdateException` — so a rule written against `SqlException` never fires on the
path where it matters, while a rule written against `DbUpdateException` alone catches the wrapper and
redisplays a page that cannot render. The classifier therefore walks the whole `InnerException` chain and
classifies on the innermost provider exception; **the wrapper never changes the class**, and a bare
provider exception and a wrapped one classify identically.

| Class | Recognized by | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DuplicateSubmission` | A unique-constraint violation naming the `SubmissionId` index, bare or wrapped | **Neither a redisplay nor an error page.** The other submission won; the handler re-reads by key and username and redirects to the winning order, per step 1a of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |
| `Concurrency` | `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate below |
| `Rejected` | Any error the **server itself produced** having accepted the command — a foreign-key, check or unique violation other than the one above, a permission refusal, a deadlock victim | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate. The store demonstrably answered, so the layout's queries can run |
| `DataIntegrity` | An inconsistency the **application** detected with no provider exception at all — the missing-album case of census site F6, section [4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate |
| `Unavailable` | The store could not be reached, or did not answer: a provider exception raised **while opening the connection** (no command was ever sent), a connection-level failure, or a timeout with no server response — again, bare or wrapped | **Never redisplayed.** Rethrown to the exception-handling middleware and answered by the layout-free generic page above. Redisplaying here is the recursion this section exists to prevent |
| `Cancelled` | `OperationCanceledException` whose token is the request's | Recorded and rethrown; **no response is composed at all**, per the cancellation row of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |

**Anything the classifier does not recognize is not caught.** It reaches the middleware and is answered
by the generic page, which is the correct default: an unclassified fault is one nobody has reasoned
about, and inventing a redisplay for it is how an unrenderable page gets served.

**The render gate, and why it is a probe rather than an error-number list.** Every redisplay-eligible
class is gated on one bounded question — *can the redisplay actually render?* — answered by a single
`await db.Database.CanConnectAsync(ct)` on a fresh connection under a **two-second** linked timeout — long
enough to answer on a healthy store, short enough that a customer waiting on a failed submission is not
made to wait twice — and it runs on the failure path only. **False, or the probe itself timing out or
throwing, re-classifies the failure as `Unavailable`** and it is rethrown. Two reasons this is the
criterion rather than matching provider error numbers: a number list is precisely the hand-maintained
transient-set that section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) refuses for retry classification,
and it fails silently when the provider adds a code; and the provider's own `IsTransient` flag conflates a
deadlock, where the server answered and a redisplay is fine, with a connection failure, where it is not.
The gate is skipped as unnecessary for a provider exception raised before any connection was established,
which is `Unavailable` with certainty and needs no round trip to confirm.

**And the gate is allowed to be wrong in one direction, because the fallback is safe.** If the probe
succeeds and the redisplay then faults anyway, that exception reaches the middleware and the **layout-free**
error view answers it. The cost is one wasted render, not a loop — which holds only because the error view
declares `Layout = null` in the view itself, as the table above requires.

Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) the coverage assertions require the recursion properties from both ends — with
the database stopped, a request to any page yields **exactly one** generic 500 with no recursion and no
second exception in the log, and the same with a view component made to throw while the database is up —
and **The coverage assertion requires the classifier itself, on the pair that distinguishes it from a per-handler rule: a
server-rejected write redisplays, and a connectivity failure **wrapped in `DbUpdateException`** does not.

**The action reads neither `IExceptionHandlerPathFeature` nor the exception.** It does not need to,
because the recording happened before it ran — in the `IExceptionHandler` of stage 1 item 13 (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), specified below — and nothing about the exception may reach
the response. Not reading it is what makes it impossible to leak by accident: there is no exception
object in scope in the action or the view. **It is also why the recording cannot live in the action**, and
that is the whole reason the handler component exists rather than being an implementation detail.

**The status codes, per path.**

| Path | Response status | How it gets there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unhandled exception, outside Development | **500** | `UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error")` sets 500 and re-executes with no route value, so `id` is null and the action confirms 500 |
| Unhandled exception, Development | 500 with the developer exception page | The other branch of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 3; this action is not involved |
| `NotFound()` from any of the six census sites of section [4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **404**, with the generic view | `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-executes `/Home/Error/404` |
| A wrong verb against a mapped action | **405**, with the generic view | Same mechanism |
| An authenticated non-administrator reaching `/StoreManager/**` | **403**, with the generic view | The cookie handler redirects to `AccessDeniedPath`, and the action sets 403 |
| An unauthenticated request to an authorized action | **302** to `/Account/Login` | Unchanged from the source; the error view is not involved |

**Both mechanisms re-execute with the *original* request method, and that has consequences beyond the
status code.** `UseExceptionHandler` and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-run the pipeline against
the configured path while preserving the method, so a **`POST`** that faults — a checkout submission, an
administration write, a sign-in — arrives at this action as a **`POST` to `/Home/Error`**. Three
requirements follow, and the first is the one an otherwise-correct implementation misses:

- **The action is exempt from the global anti-forgery filter**, `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]`, recorded with
  its justification as the **first of the two entries** in the opt-out register of section
  [7.1](#71-the-policy) — the `/csp-report` endpoint being the second.
  Without it the filter validates the re-executed `POST`, and a fault page becomes a bare `400` — either
  because the original request body has already been consumed, or, where the original fault *was* an
  anti-forgery failure, because the re-executed request carries the same invalid token and fails again.
- **The action must not require `[HttpGet]`, and must not be reached by a route that does.** One action,
  no verb constraint, both paths.
- **It reads no form value and no body**, which is what makes the exemption safe rather than merely
  convenient: the only input it accepts is the `int?` route segment, clamped above.

**Neither error path ever returns 200.** That is the concrete defect being fixed on the surfaces that
really do return one — the ownership check of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s
`Complete` discussion below, and the access-denied path — where a crawler indexes the page, a monitor
records it as success and a client script cannot distinguish it from content. For an **unhandled
exception** the 500 is *preserved* rather than introduced, since `RemoteOnly` already produces one for a
remote caller; approved delta 12 owns the change that is real there, and delta 18 is scoped to the two
surfaces above. **The statement holds for a directly requested error URL too, and only because of the
clamp above** — without it `/Home/Error/200` is a 200 with an error page in it, which would make this rule
false by the shortest possible route.

**What is logged, and by what — under the policy [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns.**

**The writer is a named component, because the mechanism chosen for the response cannot produce this
record.** `app.UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error")` re-executes a path; it renders a response and writes
the framework's own diagnostic, and it enriches nothing. The action it re-executes deliberately reads no
exception feature (above). **So with those two alone, the record specified below is written by
nobody** — which is a promise a document can make and an implementation can quietly fail to keep, since
the response looks correct either way. The record is therefore written by
`ErrorRecordExceptionHandler : IExceptionHandler`, registered as stage 1 item 13 of section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order):

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **When it runs** | Inside `UseExceptionHandler`'s middleware, on the unhandled-exception path only, **before** the `/Home/Error` re-execution. That is the second reason it is not in the action: the action runs *after* re-execution, and it deliberately reads no exception feature, so by then it has nothing to record from. Running early is necessary but **not** sufficient to recover the failing request's identity, for the reason in the next row |
| **Where the original request's identity comes from** | Running before the re-execution does **not** mean the `HttpContext` still describes the failing request. `ExceptionHandlerOptions.ExceptionHandlingPath` is "the path used when executing the exception handler", and the middleware **assigns it to `HttpContext.Request.Path` and clears the selected endpoint and the route values before it invokes any `IExceptionHandler`** — so a handler that reads `context.Request.Path` records `/Home/Error` for every fault, and reads a null endpoint and an empty route-value dictionary. Three sources, therefore, and each is chosen because it is the only correct one: the **path** and the **endpoint** come from `IExceptionHandlerFeature` (`Path`, `Endpoint`), whose own summary describes it as carrying "the error of the original request"; the **method** comes from `HttpContext.Request.Method`, which the middleware does not rewrite and which **no feature exposes** — neither exception-handling feature has a method member, so a design that expected one would have nowhere to read it from; and the **user** comes from `HttpContext.User`, likewise untouched. The feature's fourth member, `RouteValues`, is the request's other lost value and is deliberately **not** recorded, for the reason the *Never recorded* row gives. **`IExceptionHandlerFeature`, not `IExceptionHandlerPathFeature`** — the middleware registers one object under both feature keys, so the richer interface costs nothing, while the narrower one, which is the one most examples reach for, exposes only `Path` and cannot supply the endpoint at all |
| **What it returns** | **`false`**, always. `false` means *recorded, not handled*: the middleware proceeds to its configured path and the generic response is produced by the action, unchanged. It never writes a body, never sets a status code and never suppresses the exception |
| **Permitted content** | The **original** request method and path, each from the source named in the row above — the method from `Request.Method`, the path from the feature; the failing **endpoint's display name**, also from the feature, which names code — the controller and action — in the same sense the stack trace does; the response status code; the **trace identifier the response shows** — `Activity.Current?.Id ?? HttpContext.TraceIdentifier`, the same expression the model uses, so the record and the user's screenshot join up; the exception **type name** as `exception.GetType().FullName` **together with the type-name chain of its inner exceptions, types only** — required by the shape this record is, and an earlier form of this row named only the outermost type; the **stack trace as its own string field**, `exception.StackTrace`; a **failure category** from the closed set of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract); and a **pseudonymous actor**. Those fields are assembled by the handler and passed as **values**; the `Exception` **object itself is never handed to the logger**, for the mechanical reason below the table. **The exception *message* is not in this set** |
| **Which record shape this is, and the one thing this document needs from its owner** | It is [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s record shape **`R2`** — the sole exception signal in the system — and the four fields that register lists are all present above: the type name with its inner chain, the stack trace, the failure category, and `R1`'s trace identifier. **Four of the fields above are not in that list, and this document does not treat that as licence to add them to a closed shape.** The original request **method**, the original request **path**, the failing **endpoint's display name** and the **response status code** are what make a recorded fault attributable to a surface at all — without them an operator has a type, a stack and a trace identifier for a request whose path the middleware has already overwritten with `/Home/Error`, which is the specific defect the row above this one exists to prevent. They are therefore stated here as a **consumer requirement on `R2`**: that register is the owner and the fields belong in its list, either as members of `R2` or as a distinct shape it admits for the error path. Until it carries them, this row and that register disagree, and **the register governs the field list** — this document does not resolve it by widening a list it does not own |
| **The actor** | The Identity `UserId` — `User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)` — where the request was authenticated, and the literal **`anonymous`** for a request carrying no authenticated identity. **Those are the exactly two values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits in an application record's actor position**, and that table is the owner of the pair rather than this row. **Never the login name**, never an email, never a client address, never a submitted form value — and **never a `SubjectPseudonym`**, which that table classes as a *subject* field and not an actor. The target-side `none` and `rejected` sentinels and the pseudonym mechanism itself are [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s and are not redefined here |
| **Never recorded** | The request body, any query-string value, **the route values** — offered by the feature as `RouteValues`, and excluded because a route value is caller-supplied text arriving on the same footing as a query-string value, so admitting it would carve an exception into the rule immediately above it — cookie values, anti-forgery tokens, the session id, and the address and contact fields of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract). A 500 raised inside the checkout write path is the case that rule exists for |
| **Severity, sink, retention** | The severity, the collection mechanism, the sink and the retention are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. This document states the **content and the writer**, not the plumbing |

**The exception message is excluded, and the reason is that a provider message is not the
application's text.** [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s log-privacy policy forbids the nine
address and contact fields, the raw login name and the promo-code value from reaching the sink at all —
and it forbids them **wherever** they appear, including inside a message the application did not compose.
A `SqlException` names the constraint and frequently the offending value; `DbUpdateException` wraps it and
its `InnerException.Message` carries the provider text verbatim; a `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` names
the entity and key. So "log the exception message" and "never log an order's address" are not two
independent rules that happen to coexist — the first defeats the second, silently, on exactly the write
paths where personal data is present. Four consequences, and the first three apply to every `ILogger`
call in the port rather than only to this handler:

- **Log the exception `GetType().FullName`, not `Message`.** The type plus the failure category plus the
  trace identifier identifies the fault for an operator; the message adds provider text nobody has
  reviewed.
- **The application logs a sanitized record and never passes the `Exception` object to the logger.** This
  is the rule that is easiest to state incorrectly, and stating it incorrectly reopens the whole channel:
  `ILogger`'s exception parameter is **not** a stack-trace field. Every logger provider renders that
  argument by calling `ToString()` on it, and `Exception.ToString()` is the type name, **the `Message`**,
  the stack trace and the same three for **every** `InnerException` in the chain. So
  `logger.LogError(exception, "…")` writes the provider text this rule exists to keep out, whatever the
  message template omits — and it does so as one opaque blob a sink-side redaction rule cannot act on
  field by field. **The stack trace is permitted** because it names code rather than data, and it is
  therefore captured **explicitly, as a string field**: the handler reads `exception.StackTrace`,
  `exception.GetType().FullName` and the mapped failure category, and passes those three plus the trace
  identifier as named values. Nothing else about the exception object crosses into the record.
- **`InnerException.Message` is never recorded.** Section
  [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)'s failure table is amended accordingly: where
  it says the inner exception is logged, what is logged is the inner exception's **type** and the mapped
  failure category. A message worth an operator's attention that genuinely needs provider text is
  obtained from the platform's own SQL diagnostics, which live under database access control rather than
  in the application log.
- **The channels that log exceptions on the application's behalf are suppressed, not trusted, and the
  list is closed rather than illustrative.** The rule above governs what *this application's* code
  writes, and it is not sufficient on its own: several framework components log unhandled and store
  exceptions **themselves**, and each of them passes the exception object — which is the `ToString()`
  expansion above, provider message included. So the port's logging configuration closes them explicitly,
  in `appsettings` per environment, by **category and minimum level**. **The levels are not this
  document's to choose: they are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s controls 1 and 5, and
  the table below is the `appsettings` expression of them, reproduced so an implementer configuring
  `Program.cs` and `appsettings` has the values at hand and not so that a second authority exists.** Where
  a level here and a level there ever disagree, 06 governs. Two mechanical facts explain the shape: `None`
  rather than `Warning` appears wherever a channel writes its exception-carrying entries at `Error`, which
  no minimum-level threshold short of `None` suppresses; and **this enumeration is not the closure.** 06
  control 5 states explicitly that a list of framework categories cannot be proven complete, so the closure
  is its redaction test and the coverage assertion here — asserted against the **entire** captured stream rather
  than against these categories — and a channel missing from this table fails that row rather than passing
  unnoticed.

  | Category | Level outside Development | What it would otherwise disclose | What carries the diagnostic instead |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `Default` | `Warning` | — | The baseline 06 control 1 sets, stated here because leaving it at the framework default is what makes every row below a partial measure |
  | The application's own `MvcMusicStore` category | `Information` | — | Its records are the closed record of this section and the event classes of section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic), all sanitized at the producer |
  | The reserved security-event category ([06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names it) | `Information`, **pinned explicitly** | — | Nothing: this is the one pin whose purpose is that a later tightening of `Default` cannot silently drop an audit record |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` — the parent | `Warning` | At `Information` its command sub-category records the executed SQL for **every** query, which is the largest single source of application data in a log | The sub-category is pinned harder below; the parent pin is what stops the rest of the EF tree from reaching `Information` |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery` | `Warning` | Token-validation diagnostics; at `Information` and below it narrates each validation | The closed record for a genuine failure; the 400 the filter returns for a rejected token needs no log line of its own |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics` | **`None`** | The unhandled exception object for every 500, `ToString()`-expanded with every inner exception's message — **and** the developer-exception-page middleware in the same category, which is why 06 pins the parent rather than the handler sub-category alone | This section's closed record, written by `ErrorRecordExceptionHandler` before the re-execution |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.Diagnostics` | **`None`** | The same exception object on any path where no handler is reached — the case the entry above does **not** cover | The same closed record; the request-level timing and status it also emits are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s platform telemetry |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel` | **`None`** | `ApplicationError` and connection-level failures at `Error`, each carrying the exception object, including faults raised after the response has started — which the exception handler cannot intercept | The closed record for application faults, and the platform front end's own connection telemetry ([06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) for transport failures |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Update` | **`None`** | `DbUpdateException` and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` objects, whose inner provider text names the constraint and frequently the offending value | The closed record's failure category, drawn from the closed set of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Query` | **`None`** | Query-execution failures with the provider exception attached | The same closed record. **This row is beyond 06 control 5's enumeration and is deliberately retained**: control 5 states that no enumeration of framework categories is provably complete, so pinning one it does not name is never a conflict with it |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` | **`None`** | Both of its levels are channels, not one: `Information` echoes command text with parameter placeholders, and `Error` carries the failing command **and** the exception | The closed record, plus the platform's SQL diagnostics, which live under database access control rather than in the application log |
  | `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks` | **`None`** | The health-check service logs each failed result **with the result's `Exception`** — which is why stage 1 item 11 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) replaces `AddDbContextCheck<T>`, whose result carries one. A probe failure is the one fault that recurs every few seconds, so an open channel here is the highest-volume disclosure in the application | The one sanitized `Warning` the custom check writes itself, carrying [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 6's six fields — the endpoint literal, the failure category, the exception type name and inner type-name chain, the stack trace as a string, the elapsed milliseconds, and the trace identifier — and never the exception object. That is control 4's four-field general fault shape plus the two a probe record has and an arbitrary fault does not |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc` | `Warning` | Model-binding and filter diagnostics; it writes no application fault the closed record does not already own | Held at `Warning` rather than closed, because nothing at or above it carries an exception object |
  | `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` | **`None`** | Provider-level connection, retry and command diagnostics. **An earlier form of this table held it at `Warning`** on the reasoning that the provider's exception text reaches the log only through the EF categories above — which is not a property the provider guarantees, and 06 control 5 names this category among those pinned to `None`. It is closed, and the reasoning above is withdrawn | The closed record for application faults; connection-level and pool behaviour is read from the platform's own SQL diagnostics, under database access control |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` | **`None`** | Key-ring records carrying key material and key identifiers, and unprotect failures with the exception attached — which is the channel every protected cart marker, antiforgery token and authentication cookie failure would surface through | Nothing from this channel is needed: a key-ring fault is a hard startup or request failure the closed record already carries, and the key-ring's own operational counters are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies` | **`None`** | Cookie decryption and validation failures with the exception attached, which occur in bulk at cutover when every legacy ticket is undecryptable (section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)) | The sign-in and sign-out event classes of section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic), which record the outcome without the ticket |

  `EnableSensitiveDataLogging` and `EnableDetailedErrors` are **never** enabled outside Development, since
  either one reintroduces parameter values into whatever channels remain open.

  With those closed, the record of this section is the **only** application-scoped record of a fault,
  which is what makes the coverage assertion's "appears nowhere in the captured output" assertion satisfiable
  rather than aspirational — it is asserted against the whole captured stream, so a framework channel left
  open fails it. **[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the sinks**, and the same rule
  therefore has a second half this document states and 06 enforces: a retained sink that collects
  exception detail automatically — a platform auto-instrumentation channel, a provider-level trace, an
  unfiltered standard-output capture — reopens exactly what this table closes, so no retained sink may
  carry framework-supplied exception detail. The coverage assertions require it from the application side
  by injecting a uniquely marked provider fault and requiring the marker in **no** retained sink.

**The coverage assertion requires the record field by field**, including the fields that must be absent, and
**The coverage assertion injects a forbidden value into a real provider fault** — a unique-index violation whose
message contains a customer's email — and asserts that value appears nowhere in the captured output,
with **every category captured at `Trace`** so the framework channels above are in scope of the
assertion rather than outside it. Row 73 additionally asserts the two mechanisms: that the application's
record carries no `ToString()`-shaped expansion of the exception, and that the suppressed categories emit
nothing. That test is the one that distinguishes a stated policy from an enforced one, because every
other redaction test exercises text the application itself composed. **The coverage assertion runs the same
injection against the other exception-producing surface** — a marked provider fault raised by the
readiness probe rather than by a write path — because the health-check channel fires on a timer rather
than on a user action, so it is the one channel a request-driven test never reaches.

**What the response may disclose.** The two generic headings [:7-8], preserved verbatim, plus the trace
identifier. **No exception type, no message, no stack trace, no query text and no configuration value**
in any environment other than Development, where the developer exception page handles it instead
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)).

**The view's own user-facing text is preserved.** Only its model and its plumbing change.

**The coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)** assert this contract:
the response shape on the exception path, status preservation through re-execution, the 403 at the
access-denied path, the status clamp on a client-supplied code, and the closed record itself.

**(1b) The other caller of the error view — `Checkout.Complete`, which must stop using it.**

`Complete` renders the error view **directly** as the answer to a failed ownership check:
`storeDB.Orders.Any(o => o.OrderId == id && o.Username == User.Identity.Name)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73], and on false
`return View("Error")` [:81]. Two things are wrong with that in the target, and only one of them is the
model type:

- It answers **200**. A request for an order that is not yours succeeds, as far as any client can tell.
- It is a controller rendering the error view as content, which the error contract above does not cover
  — the middleware never sees it, nothing is logged, and no trace identifier is produced.

**Resolution: the branch returns `NotFound()`, and the status is 404 rather than 403.** The choice is
deliberate. A 403 would assert *this order exists and is not yours*, which turns the action into an
existence oracle for other customers' order ids — the same disclosure the cart-scoped lookup at census
site S3 closes (section
[4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census)). A 404 answers **both** the
non-existent-order and the not-your-order case identically, which is also what the source already does
behaviourally: `Any(...)` is false in both cases and both reach [:81]. So the merge is preserved and
only the status is corrected. The class-level `[Authorize]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:8] still sends an anonymous caller to the
login page, unchanged.

**One wording correction that belongs with this, because the capability is routinely overstated.**
`Complete` is the **only** order-reading surface in the application: it shows **one order, to its owner,
by id**. There is no order list, no order index and no order-history page anywhere in the migration
source — `git ls-files 'src/MVC5/*/Views/Checkout/*'` returns exactly two files,
`AddressAndPayment.cshtml` and `Complete.cshtml`, and the `View("Error")` at [:81] resolves to the
*shared* view above rather than to one of its own. Statements about preserving "the user's own orders"
mean exactly this one owner-scoped confirmation page, and the port owes nothing more.

**Do not attribute MVC 4's exception disclosure to this view.** MVC 4's disclosure is in its
*controller* — `ModelState.AddModelError("", e)` passing the exception object rather than a string
[src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:211-213], which
[09 §4.15](09-security-assessment.md) owns — and MVC 5's error view discloses nothing at all. This view
is rewritten for exactly one reason: its model type is gone.

**(2) `Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml` — two separate problems in one file.**

- `Request.IsAuthenticated` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:2] does not exist
  on the target's request type. **Resolution:** an explicit, null-handled identity check —
  `User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated == true` — because both `User` and `Identity` are reference-typed in
  the target and an unauthenticated request can present a non-null principal with a null name.
- `User.Identity.GetUserName()` [:10] is an extension method from the Identity 1.0 namespace imported
  at [:1]. **Resolution:** the namespace import is updated and the call becomes a direct read of the
  identity name, which is what the extension returned. The rendered text — `"Hello " + name + "!"` —
  is preserved exactly.

**Both signed-in and signed-out rendering need tests**, because the file's **entire structure** is a
conditional on the first of those two problems [:2-22]: the signed-in branch renders the sign-out form
and the manage link [:4-14], the signed-out branch renders register and log-in links [:18-21]. A
null-handling mistake does not error — it silently renders the wrong branch, and a suite that only
exercises one of them cannot tell.

**(3) `Views/Account/Manage.cshtml` — namespace import plus a rewritten call site.**
`@using Microsoft.AspNet.Identity;` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Manage.cshtml:2] becomes the
target's Identity namespace. Its `@Html.Action("RemoveAccountList")` [:22] becomes a **view-component
invocation** per section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components), and the surrounding
`<section id="externalLogins">` block [:21-24] is **kept** — the surface is mapped rather than removed,
per the decision below. Its `@Scripts.Render` [:28] is rewritten per section
[8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler).

**(4) `Views/Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml` — namespace import plus an identity read.**
`@using Microsoft.AspNet.Identity` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml:1]
becomes the target's Identity namespace, and `@User.Identity.GetUserName()` [:4] becomes a direct
identity-name read, as in (2). Its `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` [:8] disappears into automatic emission
(section [7.1](#71-the-policy)).

**(5) `Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml` — and `UserLoginInfo` is *not* renamed.**
`@model ICollection<Microsoft.AspNet.Identity.UserLoginInfo>`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:1]. **The type name survives** — the
target's Identity keeps `UserLoginInfo` under its own namespace — so this looks like a one-word
namespace edit and is not: **the type's shape and the API that produces it both differ**, so the change
is a namespace update **plus** adaptation of how the collection is obtained (today
`UserManager.GetLogins(User.Identity.GetUserId())`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:319], in the target
`UserManager.GetLoginsAsync(user)` returning `IList<UserLoginInfo>`) and of what the view reads from each
element (`account.LoginProvider` [:11], `account.ProviderKey` [:20]).

**The view is not deleted: it becomes the third view component's `Default.cshtml`**
(`src/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Components/RemoveAccountList/Default.cshtml`, section
[8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), which is also where `ViewBag.ShowRemoveButton` [:13]
becomes a typed model property. The adaptation above is therefore work this port does, not a hypothetical
it avoids.

**The external-login decision, made and recorded here.** [12 §7.3](12-migration-blockers.md) records
this as 05's choice: map `ChallengeResult` onto the framework's external-challenge flow, or **remove the
disabled external-login surface entirely**. **It is mapped.** Three reasons, in the order that decides
it:

- **The authoritative artifact list already requires the surface's rendering component.**
  [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) names
  `src/MvcMusicStore/ViewComponents/RemoveAccountListViewComponent.cs` and its `Default.cshtml` as
  created artifacts, sourced from MVC 5's third `[ChildActionOnly]` action — and that component exists
  for one purpose, rendering an account's registered external logins. Deleting the surface while creating
  its component would be a self-contradiction; deleting both would leave one of MVC 5's three child
  actions with no successor, which is the one outcome
  [12 F-12-23](12-migration-blockers.md#f-12-23--mvc-child-actions) does not permit. The choice 05 holds
  is over the *challenge* flow, not over whether the management surface exists, and taking the mapping
  option settles both consistently.
- **Removal costs a capability for a set of accounts the migration cannot rule out in advance — and
  retention does not restore it.** An account with a null or empty `PasswordHash` has never had a local
  password, and only an external login can create one. Section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) already halts the
  Identity load if any such account exists, precisely because removing the surface would leave it unable
  to sign in. **Mapping the surface does not remove that halt condition and must not be presented as
  reducing its severity** — which an earlier form of this bullet claimed, and which is wrong for a simple
  reason: the retained code is **dormant**, no provider is registered in the target exactly as none is
  registered today, so an external-only account has nothing to sign in *with* whether the surface exists
  in mapped form or not. What retention actually buys is narrower and is worth stating precisely: the
  moment a provider **is** registered the account becomes usable with **no further code written**, and
  the `Manage` set-password branch stays reachable so a linked account can acquire a local password. What
  it does not buy is a sign-in for an account with no available linked provider. So section
  [5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)'s halt stands
  unchanged and the risk stays **open** in [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s register until one of
  the two named responses is approved — a registered provider, or a local password-reset route for the
  affected accounts — neither of which this decision assumes or supplies.
- **Mapping is smaller than the source makes it look, because the framework supplies the mechanism.**
  What has to be written is a properties object, a `Challenge`, and a callback that reads the returned
  login info. What it replaces is 27 lines of hand-rolled challenge plumbing
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:394-420] plus an XSRF constant and an
  authentication-manager property. The flow is dormant either way — all four provider registrations are
  commented out with empty credentials [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35],
  [:24-25], [:28-29], [:32-33] — and **it stays dormant in the target**: retention re-expresses the
  surface, it does not enable it. The dormant surface's standing as deployed attack surface is
  [09 §6.11](09-security-assessment.md)'s finding and [08 §9.3](08-technical-debt-register.md)'s dead
  scaffolding, and it is unchanged by this decision, which is why **enabling a provider remains a
  separate decision owned by Security** rather than a consequence of mapping.

**What mapping requires**, so that the scope is explicit and nothing is left half-mapped. Every item the
removal option would have deleted is listed with the form it takes instead:

| Source construct | Target form |
| --- | --- |
| `ChallengeResult` nested class [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:394-420] and its `ExecuteResult(ControllerContext)` override [:411] | **Deleted and replaced by framework calls** — `SignInManager.ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties(provider, redirectUrl, userId)` to build the properties, then the controller's own `Challenge(properties, provider)`. No custom action-result type exists in the target |
| `IAuthenticationManager` property [:338-344] | **Deleted.** `SignInManager<ApplicationUser>` and `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` are constructor-injected (section [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces)) and carry the whole flow |
| `XsrfKey` constant [:336] and the `UserId` the source threads through it | **Deleted as a constant.** The user id travels in `AuthenticationProperties`, set by `ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties`'s `userId` argument and re-read from the callback's `ExternalLoginInfo.AuthenticationProperties` |
| `ExternalLogin` POST [:200] | **Kept.** Builds the properties and challenges the requested provider |
| `ExternalLoginCallback` GET [:208-209] | **Kept, and its rendering preserved exactly.** `SignInManager.GetExternalLoginInfoAsync()` then `ExternalLoginSignInAsync`; where no local account is linked it **renders the confirmation view directly** — `return View("ExternalLoginConfirmation", …)` [:229] — rather than redirecting to a `GET` action, because there is no such action to redirect to |
| `ExternalLoginConfirmation` **POST only** [:262-265] and the `ExternalLoginConfirmationViewModel` it binds | **Kept, adapted.** `UserManager.CreateAsync` followed by `AddLoginAsync` with the info from the callback. **The verb is POST and nothing else** — `[HttpPost]` [:262], `[AllowAnonymous]` [:263], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:264] — and an earlier form of this row said "GET/POST", which is a `GET` the source does not have. Inventing one would add an anonymous route that renders an account-creation form from no posted state, and it is the shape a reader assumes from the redirect-to-confirmation pattern the source deliberately does not use |
| `ExternalLoginFailure` GET [:311] and its view | **Kept unchanged** apart from the mechanical view work of section [8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) |
| `LinkLogin` POST [:237] | **Kept.** The same challenge with the signed-in user's id in the properties, which is what the source's `XsrfKey` was for |
| `LinkLoginCallback` GET [:245] | **Kept, and its XSRF binding kept with it — this is the one row in this table where dropping a source argument is exploitable.** The call is `await signInManager.GetExternalLoginInfoAsync(expectedXsrf: userManager.GetUserId(User))`, and **only** a non-null result reaches `UserManager.AddLoginAsync`. The source already does exactly this — `GetExternalLoginInfoAsync(XsrfKey, User.Identity.GetUserId())` [:247] — and the framework's overload compares its argument against the `XsrfId` item that `ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties` wrote at challenge time, returning **null** on absence or mismatch. **Writing `GetExternalLoginInfoAsync()` with no argument compiles, works in manual testing, and silently removes the check**: the correlation cookie proves only that *some* challenge from this application produced this callback, not that **this** signed-in principal issued it, so a victim who follows a link-completion URL prepared under an attacker's challenge would have the **attacker's** external identity attached to their own account — a permanent, unprompted alternative sign-in path into it. A null result redirects to `Manage` with the source's `Error` message [:255], adds no login row, and is recorded once as an authorization failure |
| `Disassociate` POST [:114] | **Kept.** `UserManager.RemoveLoginAsync(user, loginProvider, providerKey)` replaces the source's `RemoveLoginAsync(userId, new UserLoginInfo(...))` [:117], redirecting with `RemoveLoginSuccess` or `Error` exactly as today [:116-126] |
| `RemoveAccountList` `[ChildActionOnly]` [:316-322] | **The third view component** of section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components). Counted separately because it is a child-action declaration rather than a route, and it is the one item whose **route** disappears while its rendering does not |
| External sign-in cookie registration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20] | **Replaced by `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme`**, registered by `AddIdentity` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) |
| The four commented-out provider registrations [:23-35] | **Not re-created.** No `AddGoogle`, `AddFacebook`, `AddMicrosoftAccount` or `AddTwitter` call appears in `Program.cs`, and no provider package is pinned ([04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)) |
| All **nine** views under `Views/Account/` | **All kept.** `_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml` moves to the component's `Default.cshtml`; `_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml`, `ExternalLoginConfirmation.cshtml`, `ExternalLoginFailure.cshtml` and `_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml` port with the namespace and helper changes of sections [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and [8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role); the `<section id="externalLogins">` block of `Manage.cshtml` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Manage.cshtml:21-24] is kept |

**The verb and anti-forgery posture of all seven retained actions, enumerated, because one row of the
table above got a verb wrong and nothing in the document would have caught it.** A mapping table names
what each construct becomes; it does not state the request contract, and a wrong verb is invisible until
a route answers a method it should not. Every retained action is therefore listed with the source
attributes it actually carries and the target posture it takes. **No action gains a verb it does not have
in the source, and none loses one.**

| Action | Source verb and attributes | Target verb | Target anti-forgery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ExternalLogin` | **POST** — `[HttpPost]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:197], `[AllowAnonymous]` [:198], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:199] | **POST**, anonymous | **Validated**, by the global `AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` of section [7.1](#71-the-policy); no per-action attribute is written, and none is needed |
| `ExternalLoginCallback` | **GET** — `[AllowAnonymous]` [:208], no verb attribute and no token attribute [:209] | **GET**, anonymous | **Not validated, and must not be.** The request arrives from the provider and carries no token of this application's; what protects it is the `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme` correlation cookie the framework issues at challenge time and validates on return. The global filter validates non-`GET` requests only, so no opt-out register entry is required |
| `ExternalLoginConfirmation` | **POST only** — `[HttpPost]` [:262], `[AllowAnonymous]` [:263], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:264] | **POST only** | **Validated**, by the global filter. The form is the one the callback rendered directly at [:229], so the token is emitted by that view's form tag helper |
| `ExternalLoginFailure` | **GET** — `[AllowAnonymous]` [:310], no verb attribute [:311] | **GET**, anonymous | Not applicable — a `GET` that reads nothing and writes nothing |
| `LinkLogin` | **POST** — `[HttpPost]` [:235], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:236], authorized by the class-level `[Authorize]` [:15] | **POST**, `[Authorize]` | **Validated**, by the global filter |
| `LinkLoginCallback` | **GET** — no verb attribute and no token attribute [:245], authorized by the class-level `[Authorize]` [:15] | **GET**, `[Authorize]` | **Not validated** — the same provider round-trip as the sign-in callback, and the same reason. What stands in its place is the correlation cookie **and** the principal binding the source performs at [:247], which this document's contract requires and does not treat as optional |
| `Disassociate` | **POST** — `[HttpPost]` [:112], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [:113], authorized by the class-level `[Authorize]` [:15] | **POST**, `[Authorize]` | **Validated**, by the global filter |

Four of the seven are anonymous and three are authorized, which is the split **The coverage assertion counts
from the other direction when it probes every account route unauthenticated.

**`_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml` stays reachable, and that is the point of the second reason above.** It
exists **only** for accounts with no local password. The `ViewBag.HasLocalPassword` conditional
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Manage.cshtml:12-19] therefore keeps **both** branches — the
change-password partial [:14] and the set-password branch [:18] — and the `Manage` POST keeps both of its
own (section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)). Whether
any such account exists is answered by the migrated data, not assumed: section
[5.6](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) counts them and halts
before writing if there are any, so the count is known before cutover either way.

**What a dormant provider list renders is preserved behaviour, not an error, and it is the assertion that
proves the surface is configured-off rather than broken.** The source partial enumerates the registered
providers and, when the list is empty, renders an explanatory paragraph instead of a form
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml:5-13]. In the target the
enumeration is `SignInManager.GetExternalAuthenticationSchemesAsync()`, which with no provider registered
returns empty, so the same explanatory branch renders and **no provider button and no posting form is
emitted**. Two consequences are stated because a reader will ask:

- **`ExternalLogin` and `LinkLogin` are unreachable from the UI**, since the form that posts to them is
  not rendered. A hand-crafted POST naming an unregistered scheme must **not** reach `Challenge` — which
  throws for a scheme with no registered handler and would surface as the generic 500 of item (1) above.
  The actions therefore validate the requested provider against
  `GetExternalAuthenticationSchemesAsync()` **before** challenging and redirect to
  `ExternalLoginFailure` when it is absent, which is the retained view built for exactly that outcome.
- **Enabling a provider later is additive and scoped**: a registration call, its pinned package, its
  secrets in configuration, and its tests. Nothing in the surface changes, which is what mapping bought.
  Section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) labels the retention **preserved** for that
  reason.

**Route and behaviour tests attach to the retained surface**: the four anonymous external routes and the
three authorized ones resolve and behave as the table above states, `/Account/RemoveAccountList` does
**not** resolve because it is a component rather than an action, the empty-provider branch renders, and
the sign-in, register, sign-out and manage flows are unaffected. The coverage assertion in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) carries them.

### 8.4 The view disposition, by semantic role

**Twenty-nine views, twenty-nine dispositions, and the disposition is set by what a view *is* — a routed
page, a component's view, a rendered partial, the layout — not by whether its filename begins with an
underscore.** The distinction is not pedantry: `Store/GenreMenu.cshtml` and
`ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml` carry no underscore and are **not** pages — they are the rendered
bodies of the two `[ChildActionOnly]` actions of section
[8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) — while `Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml` carries one and is
rendered into every page. A filename heuristic gets both wrong in opposite directions, and section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) depends on getting them right,
because it is the capture set.

Every view has exactly **one primary disposition** and the arithmetic closes:

| Disposition | Count | Views |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| **Ports unchanged** | 1 | `Views/_ViewStart.cshtml` |
| **Becomes a view component's `Default.cshtml`** | 3 | `Store/GenreMenu.cshtml`, `ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml`, `Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml` — section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) |
| **Per-line rewrite — names a legacy type** | 4 | `Shared/Error.cshtml`, `Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml`, `Account/Manage.cshtml`, `Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml` — section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) items (1)-(4) |
| **Per-line rewrite — no successor for a non-type construct** | 2 | `Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml` (OWIN provider enumeration), `StoreManager/Index.cshtml` (`@helper Truncate`) — section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (6) |
| **Per-line rewrite — the checkout input model** | 1 | `Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml` — sections [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) and [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice), the latter element by element |
| **Ported with the shared mechanical transformations** | 18 | `Account/ExternalLoginConfirmation.cshtml`, `Account/ExternalLoginFailure.cshtml`, `Account/Login.cshtml`, `Account/Register.cshtml`, `Account/_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml`, `Checkout/Complete.cshtml`, `Home/About.cshtml`, `Home/Contact.cshtml`, `Home/Index.cshtml`, `Shared/_Layout.cshtml`, `ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml`, `Store/Browse.cshtml`, `Store/Details.cshtml`, `Store/Index.cshtml`, `StoreManager/Create.cshtml`, `StoreManager/Delete.cshtml`, `StoreManager/Details.cshtml`, `StoreManager/Edit.cshtml` |
| **Total** | **29** | 1 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 18 = 29 |

**Two notes the table needs, because both are available to be misread.**

- **The AAP's five legacy-type views are all present and none is double-counted.** Four are rewritten
  **in place** and appear in row three; the fifth, `Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml`, appears in row
  two because it relocates under its view component — its legacy-type problem is resolved *there*, at its
  new path, and section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (5) specifies it. Adding it
  to row three as well would make the total 30.
- **"Mechanical" means no legacy type and no missing successor. It does not mean small.** Several views
  in row six carry substantial per-view work: `Shared/_Layout.cshtml` is the entire navbar migration of
  section [8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump) plus the
  script and style tags of section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler); `ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml`
  is the script externalization of section
  [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script) and the table semantics of section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements); `StoreManager/Details.cshtml` restructures
  a removed Bootstrap component. What they share is that a **compiler** finds the mistakes, which the
  rows above it cannot rely on.

The four shared mechanical transformations, which every ported view takes:
`@Html.Partial` becomes the `<partial>` tag helper at **5** call sites
(`git grep -o '@Html.Partial' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml' | wc -l` → `5`), `@Url.Content` remains valid at
its **4** call sites (→ `4`), `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` disappears into automatic emission at its 10
call sites (section [7.1](#71-the-policy)), and the bundling helpers are rewritten per section
[8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler). Form and input helpers are source-compatible; tag
helpers are the target convention and are adopted where a form is being touched anyway — which,
because of the anti-forgery change, is every form (**12** `Html.BeginForm` sites,
`git grep -o 'Html.BeginForm' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml' | wc -l` → `12`).

**One asymmetry makes this less safe than it sounds, and it cuts in the port's favour.** These 29 views
have **never been compile-checked**: `MvcBuildViews` is `false`, so no view is compiled at build time
today ([10 §12.3](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md), [08 §8.1](08-technical-debt-register.md)).
The target compiles Razor views as part of the build. So type errors that are invisible today —
including the removed model type in (1) above — become **build** errors, discovered for free rather
than at first request. The consequence for this plan is that the view port needs no separate
type-checking pass; it needs a build.

### 8.5 The Bootstrap upgrade is markup work, not a version bump

[04 §9.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins the target Bootstrap version. **The markup work is
this document's**, and it is not optional: **upgrading the package without touching the markup changes
the rendered page.**

Bootstrap 3 navbar classes are pervasive in the shared layout, and several were renamed or removed
after Bootstrap 3:

| Class | Location |
| --- | --- |
| `navbar navbar-inverse navbar-fixed-top` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:12] |
| `navbar-header` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:14] |
| `navbar-toggle` (with three `icon-bar` spans at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:16], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:17], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:18]) | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15] |
| `navbar-brand` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:20] |
| `navbar-collapse collapse` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:22] |
| `nav navbar-nav` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:23] |
| `navbar navbar-fixed-bottom navbar-default text-center` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:35] |
| `nav navbar-nav navbar-right` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:8], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:18] |
| `form-horizontal`, `col-md-*`, `control-label`, `form-group`, `btn btn-default` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml:6], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml:12-35] and the other form views |
| `table`, `table-striped` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:6], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:47] |

**Resolution: a visual-preservation port.** Every affected class name is mapped old-to-new, the
collapse mechanism's data attributes are updated to the target library's form, the horizontal-form
grid is re-expressed in the target's grid utilities, and **acceptance is defined as the rendered layout
matching the Bootstrap 3 baseline captured *before* the port.** The baseline capture and the review are
scoped in section [12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual); they are
deliberately **not** claimed by the automated suite.

**Glyphicons are removed rather than replaced with an icon library.** They were dropped from Bootstrap
after 3. Use is decorative and confined to **exactly two views** — verified:

```text
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:5:  <span class="glyphicon glyphicon glyphicon-shopping-cart"></span>
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:27:            <span class="glyphicon glyphicon-shopping-cart"></span>
```

**Neither is the shared layout** — a natural assumption, since the cart badge renders *into* the
layout, but the markup lives in the cart-summary partial rather than in `_Layout.cshtml`. The two spans
are removed; the adjacent text and link in each view are preserved, so both controls keep their label
and their behaviour and lose only the pictogram. (The cart-summary span also carries the `glyphicon`
class twice [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:5], which is worth nothing except as a sign that nobody has looked at this markup in a
long time.)

**Removing them adds no dependency, no acquisition mechanism and no licence question**, which is
precisely the argument for removal over substitution at this scale. It is an **approved visual delta**
(section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)), not an unnoticed regression. **If a stakeholder
wants icons retained, that is a scoped decision with its own pinned source and its own licence
review — this document does not assume one.**

#### 8.5.1 The breakpoint, and the two viewports

**Target navbar expansion: `navbar-expand-md`.** The source navbar has no expansion class at all,
because Bootstrap 3 hard-codes one collapse boundary: the toggle is hidden at `min-width: 768px`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4235-4239], so the navbar is collapsed below 768px and
expanded at 768px and above. The target library makes the boundary explicit and its `md` tier begins at
768px, so **`navbar-expand-md` reproduces the source boundary exactly**. `navbar-expand-lg` — the value
the target's own templates default to — would move the boundary to 992px and leave the navbar collapsed
across a 224-pixel band where it is expanded today. That is a visible regression from a copied default,
and naming the class here is what prevents it.

**Baseline and comparison viewports, by dimension:**

| Viewport | Dimensions | Why this one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Narrow | **375 x 812** | Below the 768px boundary, so the navbar is **collapsed** and the toggle is rendered. Also below the source's `sm` tier and below the target's `md`, so in **both** scales only the infix-free column widths apply — `col-xs-4` today, `col-4` after the port ([8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)) |
| Wide | **1280 x 800** | Above every boundary either scale places below 1400px, so in the source `col-sm-*`, `col-md-*` and `col-lg-*` are all active at once and in the target `col-md-*`, `col-lg-*` and `col-xl-*` are, with the narrowest-declared tier winning in each. The expanded navbar, both album grids and the horizontal forms are therefore all exercised in one capture |

Both are stated as exact dimensions because "one wide and one narrow" is not reproducible, and section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) computes its capture count from them.

**Two endpoint viewports are the right basis for comparing appearance and the wrong basis for verifying
tier behaviour, and section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) therefore carries a second, separate
pass.** 375px and 1280px sit inside the first and last intervals of both scales, so neither can observe
what happens in the intervals between — and the tier remapping of
[8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) is precisely a set of claims about interval
boundaries. The **breakpoint-boundary verification pass** of section 12.5 brackets every boundary in both
scales; the two viewports above remain the basis for the whole-page appearance comparison and are not
widened to do the boundary pass's job.

**One consequence of the wide viewport that is pinned rather than merely checked.** Bootstrap 3's
`.container` is capped at 750px, 970px and 1170px at its three breakpoints
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:927-930], [:1081-1084], [:1244-1247]; the target's caps
differ in value and its ladder has **five** steps to the source's three, adding one below 768px and one at
1400px. At 1280px wide the page's outer container would therefore resolve to a **different maximum width**
after the upgrade even with identical markup. Because that is not something a reviewer can be asked to
accept or reject, section
[8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) **group 1a pins all three source
caps at the source's own three boundaries and neutralizes the target's other two**, and the reviewer's job
at the wide viewport is to confirm the pinned 1170px rather than to discover a number. It is
compounded by an application-level oddity: `container` is applied to the album `<li>` elements
themselves [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:13],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:13], nested inside a `row`, so each grid cell carries
a capped-width block. The markup is **preserved as-is** — changing it would be a redesign — but both
album grids are checked at both viewports for exactly this reason.

**The two per-view results, written out, because these are the two elements where four column tokens meet
on one `class` attribute:**

```html
<!-- src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:13 and
     src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:13, source: -->
<li class="col-lg-2 col-md-2 col-sm-2 col-xs-4 container">
<!-- target: -->
<li class="col-xl-2 col-lg-2 col-md-2 col-4 container">
```

The `container` token stays on the `<li>` — it is the application-level oddity
[8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports) records, and removing it would be a redesign.

**The remapping rule, and the arithmetic behind it.** Bootstrap 3 has **four** tiers and the target has
**six**, and only two boundaries coincide:

| Source tier | Source boundary, from the committed stylesheet | Target tier at the same boundary | Target's own tiers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `xs` | none — `col-xs-*` widths are declared unconditionally [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:879-925] | the **infix-free** column, which also carries none | — |
| `sm` | `min-width: 768px` [:927] | **`md`**, which begins at 768px | `xs` <576, `sm` ≥576 |
| `md` | `min-width: 992px` [:1081] | **`lg`**, which begins at 992px | `md` ≥768, `lg` ≥992 |
| `lg` | `min-width: 1200px` [:1244] | **`xl`**, which begins at 1200px | `xl` ≥1200, `xxl` ≥1400 |

So the rule is **`xs` → infix-free, `sm` → `md`, `md` → `lg`, `lg` → `xl`**, and the target's `sm`
(≥576px) and `xxl` (≥1400px) tiers are **not used by this port at all** — there is no source tier at
either boundary, and introducing one would create a reflow the source does not have.

**What carrying a name across unchanged would actually have done**, stated concretely because "the
breakpoints differ" understates it. `col-sm-2` left as `col-sm-2` would begin applying at **576px**
instead of 768px, so the album grid would go from three tiles per row to **six** across the whole
576-767px band — the six-up grid is 2 of 12 columns, and nothing in the source produces it below 768px.
`col-md-2` and `col-md-10` left unchanged in the horizontal forms would begin applying at **768px**
instead of 992px, so every one of the seven forms would break into its two-column label-beside-control
layout **224 pixels early**, in a band where the source still stacks the label above the control. Both are
regressions a class-name diff cannot see, and both are why every column token above carries a target.

**`navbar-expand-md` is already correct and is explicitly exempt from the rule above.** It is **not** a
carried-across source infix — Bootstrap 3 has no expansion class at all, and its collapse boundary is
hard-coded at `min-width: 768px` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4235-4239]. The `md` in
`navbar-expand-md` was chosen directly against the **target's** scale, whose `md` begins at 768px, so it
is already an equal-pixel match ([8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports) states the same
reasoning from the other direction). A reader applying the `md` → `lg` rule mechanically to it would
produce `navbar-expand-lg` and reintroduce exactly the 224-pixel collapsed band that section warns about.
**Do not remap it.**

**Forms — 5 tokens.** This is the group where a class rename is not enough, because the target has no
horizontal-form component at all.

| Source token | Target | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `form-horizontal` | **Removed with no replacement class.** The horizontal layout is expressed structurally instead: `row` on the group and `col-form-label` on the label | **7 sites, in two shapes.** Five are an `@class` on the form itself — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/ExternalLoginConfirmation.cshtml:8], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Login.cshtml:11], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Register.cshtml:8], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml:6], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml:8] — and two are a wrapper `<div>` *inside* a form: [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Create.cshtml:13], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Edit.cshtml:13]. **The second shape leaves an empty wrapper `<div>` once the class is removed**, which is retained rather than unwrapped — deleting an element changes the DOM the reviewer is comparing, and it costs nothing to keep |

**`text-error` is a Bootstrap *2* class that never existed in Bootstrap 3**, so the heading it is applied
to renders **unstyled today** — the stylesheet the application actually ships defines `.text-danger`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:440] and has **no** `text-error` rule at all
(`Select-String -Path src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css -Pattern text-error` → 0 matches).
Correcting it therefore makes that one
heading render in the danger colour where today it renders in the body colour: a **visible change on one
page**.

**Because it is visible, it is an approved delta and not a silent correction.** It is **delta 15** of
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), owner **Product**, and it is on the reviewer's
checklist as an expected difference on `Account/ExternalLoginFailure` rather than as a defect to raise.
Treating it as a mere latent-defect correction — the earlier reading — would have left the reviewer with
a red heading nobody had approved, which is the same failure mode section 11.5 exists to prevent, whatever
the change's origin. The alternative disposition, **dropping the class** so the heading keeps rendering in
the body colour exactly as it does today, is genuinely available and needs no approval at all; it is
**rejected** because it preserves an accident and leaves a failure heading indistinguishable from body
text. Product owns that choice, and the delta row is where it is recorded.
