No stylesheet rule matches either token (`git grep -n 'editor-label\|editor-field' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content'` → no match), so the *class names* carry no appearance — but the two `<div>` elements they sit on do, because a block wrapper is what puts the label on its own line above the control. The hand-written pair at [:23], [:26] mirrors the naming of the framework's built-in object template, which is what `@Html.EditorForModel()` [:17] renders the nine shipping fields through, so the same stacked wrapper shape surrounds **every** field on this page and not only the promo code. Section [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice) therefore keeps the wrappers and adds **no** field chrome: `mb-3`, `form-label` and `form-control` are **not** applied, because each would change what the page renders today — `mb-3` inserts `1rem` of space between groups that currently have none, and `form-control` replaces an unstyled browser control with the library's bordered, rounded, `34px` box. This is the **stacked** structure, not the `row` / `col-form-label` pair the horizontal forms get: the checkout form carries neither `form-horizontal` nor `form-group` (`git grep -c form-group -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml'` → no match) |
| `RemoveLink` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:74] | **Retained as a script hook**, and it moves onto a `<button>` per section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements). The externalized script of section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script) selects on it |

`14 + 5 + 11 + 5 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 5 = 56`.

#### 8.5.3 Non-class markup that changes with the library

Four changes are not class substitutions and would be missed by a search-and-replace over `class`
attributes:

- **The collapse plugin's data attributes are namespaced.** `data-toggle="collapse"` and
  `data-target=".navbar-collapse"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15] become
  `data-bs-toggle="collapse"` and `data-bs-target="#navbarMain"`, and `data-toggle="dropdown"`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/GenreMenu.cshtml:4] becomes `data-bs-toggle="dropdown"`. **A
  missed prefix fails silently**: the markup renders, the button is clickable, and nothing happens.
- **The collapse target becomes an id rather than a class selector, and the id is fixed here as
  `navbarMain`.** The source targets `.navbar-collapse` — a *class* selector that happens to match one
  element — and a class selector cannot supply an accessible name-and-state relationship, because
  `aria-controls` takes an **id reference** and nothing else. So the collapse element gains
  `id="navbarMain"` and the toggler references it three times over: as the plugin's target, as
  `aria-controls`, and implicitly through the `aria-expanded` state the plugin maintains on the toggler.
  The id is stated as a literal rather than left to the implementer because two of those three
  references must agree exactly, and section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) item **a1** asserts them in the rendered
  response. **The literal target markup** — this replaces the toggler at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15-19] and the collapse wrapper at [:22], and it
  is the markup section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) **a1** and coverage
  The coverage assertion assert against:

  ```html
  <button class="navbar-toggler" type="button"
          data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#navbarMain"
          aria-controls="navbarMain" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle navigation">
    <span class="navbar-toggler-icon"></span>
  </button>
  <div class="collapse navbar-collapse" id="navbarMain">
  ```

  `aria-expanded="false"` is the **initial** value; the plugin flips it on toggle, and that flipping is
  what makes the attribute worth emitting rather than decorative. `aria-label="Toggle navigation"` is
  net-new: the source toggler's only content is three empty `<span class="icon-bar">` elements
  [:16-18], so it has **no accessible name at all** today — the label is what gives it one, and it is
  additive markup rather than a visual change.
- **The toggler's three bars become one icon element**, as the token table records and the literal
  markup above shows.
- **The caret element is deleted, not reclassed** — `<b class="caret"></b>`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/GenreMenu.cshtml:4] leaves no element behind, and the empty
  divider `<li>` [:14] is replaced by an `<li>` wrapping an `<hr>`.

#### 8.5.4 Glyphicons are removed rather than replaced

**Glyphicons are removed rather than replaced with an icon library.** They were dropped from Bootstrap
after 3. Use is decorative and confined to **exactly two views** — verified:

```text
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:5:  <span class="glyphicon glyphicon glyphicon-shopping-cart"></span>
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:27:            <span class="glyphicon glyphicon-shopping-cart"></span>
```

**Neither is the shared layout** — a natural assumption, since the cart badge renders *into* the
layout, but the markup lives in the cart-summary partial rather than in `_Layout.cshtml`. The two spans
are removed; the adjacent text and link in each view are preserved, so both controls keep their label
and their behaviour and lose only the pictogram. (The cart-summary span also carries the `glyphicon`
class twice [:5], which is worth nothing except as a sign that nobody has looked at this markup in a
long time.)

**Removing them adds no dependency, no acquisition mechanism and no licence question**, which is
precisely the argument for removal over substitution at this scale. It is an **approved visual delta**
(section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)), not an unnoticed regression. **If a stakeholder
wants icons retained, that is a scoped decision with its own pinned source and its own licence
review — this document does not assume one.**

#### 8.5.5 `Content/Site.css` — the named change list

The application's own stylesheet is **86 lines and eighteen qualified rule blocks**, and three of them are coupled to the
library being replaced. It relocates to `wwwroot/css/site.css` (section
[8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)), which is also what settles the casing mismatch at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/BundleConfig.cs:28]. Every rule has a stated disposition — "review the
CSS" is not one of them, and neither is "adjust where needed": each row below states **retained
unchanged**, **retained with a rewritten selector**, or **removed**, and where a selector is rewritten
the target selector is written out.

**Eighteen blocks, and the table's twelve rows account for all of them**, because four rows carry more
than one block:

```text
(Get-Content src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css | Select-String -Pattern '\{').Count   # -> 18
```

`body` 1 + `.body-content` 1 + `input, select, textarea` 1 + the six validation blocks 6 +
`ul#album-list li` 1 + the two `img` blocks 2 + the `a` block 1 + the `a:hover` block 1 +
`.navbar-inverse, .navbar-inverse .navbar-brand` 1 + `.navbar-inverse .navbar-text` 1 +
`.navbar-inverse .navbar-nav > li > a` 1 + `.jumbotron` 1 = **18**.

| Rule | Lines | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `body { padding-top: 50px; padding-bottom: 20px }` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:1-4] | **Re-measured, not copied.** The 50px exists solely to clear the fixed-top navbar, and it matches Bootstrap 3's `.navbar { min-height: 50px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4025-4028] exactly. The target's navbar has different intrinsic padding and line-height, so **the value is set from a measurement of the rendered target navbar at each viewport** — including the collapsed navbar at 375px, where an expanded menu pushes content further. No replacement number is invented here; the measurement is the acceptance step in [8.5.6](#856-acceptance). `padding-bottom: 20px` clears the fixed-bottom footer and is re-measured on the same basis. **Section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) pins the navbar's own constituent metrics** — its minimum height, its vertical padding and the brand's padding and line-height — to the source values, so the measurement is expected to confirm 50px rather than to discover a new number; if it does not, **the offset follows the measurement**, not the other way round |
| `.body-content { padding-left: 15px; padding-right: 15px }` | [:7-10] | **Retained unchanged**, selector included. Application-owned; the class is preserved per [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens), so nothing about the rule needs to move |
| `input, select, textarea { max-width: 280px }` | [:13-17] | **Retained, and checked at both viewports.** It is an unqualified element selector that overrides `form-control`'s full-width behaviour on **every** input in the application, including the ones inside the restructured `row form-group` groups. At 375px the column is already narrower than 280px so the cap is inert; at 1280px it is what makes the form fields short rather than column-wide. Preserving that appearance is the point, so the rule stays and the reviewer confirms it still bites |
| The six validation rules — `.field-validation-error`, `.field-validation-valid`, `input.input-validation-error`, `input[type="checkbox"].input-validation-error`, `.validation-summary-errors`, `.validation-summary-valid` | [:20-42] | **All retained, unchanged and still correct.** The pinned unobtrusive-validation successor ([04 §9.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)) emits the same five class names, so these rules keep working. Stated explicitly because they look like framework leftovers and are not: deleting them silently removes every client-side error style in the application. `#b94a48` is the colour being preserved |
| `ul#album-list li { height: 160px }` | [:47-49] | **Retained unchanged**, selector included. Fixes the album tile height in both grids, and it is the reason the grids do not reflow when the library's own line-height changes |
| `ul#album-list li img:hover { box-shadow … }` and `ul#album-list li img { box-shadow …; border: none; padding: 0 }` | [:51-53] and [:55-59] | **Both retained unchanged**, selectors and values included. Two blocks, not one: the `:hover` block [:51-53] carrying `box-shadow: 1px 1px 7px #777`, and the base block [:55-59] carrying `box-shadow: 1px 1px 5px #999`, `border: none` and `padding: 0`. Neither selector names a library class, so neither is affected by the upgrade |
| `ul#album-list li a, ul#album-details li a { text-decoration: none }` | [:61-63] | **Retained unchanged**, and it acquires a companion rather than an edit. **What it does and does not do is stated precisely, because the opposite is easy to assume**: it removes the *underline* from those anchors, and it does **not** leave a keyboard user without an indication. The library's global `a:focus { outline: thin dotted #333; outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color; outline-offset: -2px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:348-352] still applies to them, and nothing in the application stylesheet cancels it — the album rule below is `:hover` only and declares no `outline` property at all [:65-70] — so **a focused album link shows the platform focus ring today**. Section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) item **d1** therefore **restates** that indication rather than creating one, by **adding** a rule and not by deleting this one. The `ul#album-details` half of the selector matches nothing — `album-details` is a `<div>`, not a `<ul>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:13] — and is **carried across as-is**, because correcting a dead selector would change the detail page's appearance |
| `ul#album-list li a:hover { background: none; text-shadow …; color: #363430 }` | [:65-70] | **Retained unchanged**, and it is the source of the values the added rule reuses. **It is a `:hover` rule and nothing more** — it sets `background`, the two `text-shadow` properties and `color` [:66-69] and declares **no `outline`**, so it neither supplies nor suppresses the focus ring of the row above. The companion required by [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) **d1** is written out here so it is not left to interpretation: `ul#album-list li a:focus-visible { background: none; text-shadow: 1px 1px 2px #bbb; color: #363430; }` — the same declarations this `:hover` rule carries [:66], [:68], [:69], so a keyboard user gets exactly the indication a mouse user gets and no new visual vocabulary is introduced. The `-webkit-text-shadow` prefix [:67] is **not** reproduced in the new rule: it is a legacy prefix for browsers outside the target matrix ([06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the matrix), while the unprefixed property [:68] is what every browser in it honours. The existing rule keeps its prefix, untouched. **This CSS is additive, but the behaviour it completes is not net-new**: the focus ring already exists [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:348-352], group 2 of [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) preserves its presentation, and the selector narrowing that goes with it is **approved delta 19** of [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) rather than an entry in the additions register |
| `.navbar-inverse, .navbar-inverse .navbar-brand { color: #ddd }` | [:72-74] | **Retained with a rewritten selector.** `navbar-inverse` does not exist in the target; the element carries `navbar navbar-dark bg-dark` instead ([8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)), so the target selector is written out as `.navbar-dark, .navbar-dark .navbar-brand { color: #ddd; }` — the same declaration, re-anchored on the class the element actually has. `#ddd` is the value being preserved, and it is preserved literally rather than replaced by the library's own `rgba` brand colour, which is what makes this a rewrite and not a deletion. **The reviewer compares against the `#222222` Bootstrap 3 navbar background** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4503-4505] rather than against the target's default dark background, and `bg-dark`'s own value is checked against it at both viewports — see [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) |
| `.navbar-inverse .navbar-text { color: #ddd }` | [:76-78] | **Deleted.** Doubly dead: the selector's outer class is gone, and **no view in the application uses `navbar-text`** (`git grep -n navbar-text -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'` → no matches). Deleting it changes nothing that renders |
| `.navbar-inverse .navbar-nav > li > a { color: #ddd }` | [:80-82] | **Retained with a rewritten selector**, on the same basis as [:72-74], and the rewrite is structural as well as nominal: the target's nav anchors carry `nav-link` and the library styles them through `.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link`, so a `> li > a` child combinator loses to it on specificity even with the outer class corrected. Target selector, written out: `.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link { color: #ddd; }`. Same declaration, same `#ddd`, matched against the class the anchor actually carries |
| `.jumbotron { background-color: transparent }` | [:84-86] | **Folded into the retained class.** `jumbotron` is gone from the library but is **retained as an application-owned class** ([8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)), so this rule's *intent* — a transparent showcase band rather than a grey panel — is carried by the single `.jumbotron` declaration block of [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) group 8, which sets `background-color: transparent` and never `#eeeeee`. This separate rule is therefore deleted as redundant rather than as dead |

#### 8.5.6 Acceptance

**The rendered layout matches the Bootstrap 3 baseline captured before the port, at both stated
viewports, except for the approved deltas of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) and the approval-owned additions of section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions)**. **The expected-difference set is enumerated once, in section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual)**, classified by what the reviewer is
asked to do with each entry; it is cited here rather than restated, so the two cannot drift apart. Four of
those entries originate in this section: deltas **15**, **16**, **19** and **20** are the library-default
differences that section
[8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) resolves as approved
changes rather than as preserved appearance — the last two of them partially, since delta 19 preserves the
ring's values and narrows only the selector, and delta 20 changes the checkbox control while the wrapper
and the label around it are pinned.

Ten checks are named individually because they are the ones a class-by-class diff cannot establish:

- The **body offset** clears the target navbar at 375px and at 1280px, with no content hidden behind it
  and no visible gap ([8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list), first row).
- The **outer container width** at 1280px, and the album-tile widths in both grids at both viewports
  ([8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports)).
- The **navbar collapses below 768px and is expanded at and above it**, matching the source boundary, with
  the toggler operable and the genre dropdown opening in both states.
- The **form field widths** still reflect the 280px cap at 1280px
  ([8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list), third row).
- The **navbar's rendered height** at both viewports, against the 50px the source composes from
  `.navbar { min-height: 50px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4025-4031] and the brand's
  `15px + 20px + 15px` [:4194-4199] — the check that decides the body offset above
  ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses)).
- The **sampled colours** of the four values a class mapping cannot carry: the dark navbar's background
  against `#222222` [:4503-4506], the table cell border against `#dddddd` [:1421-1431], the stripe
  against `#f9f9f9` [:1482-1485], and the list-group item border against `#dddddd` [:5255-5262]
  ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses)).
- **Which edge carries each rule, not only its colour** — the horizontal rule sits above every table cell
  and above every list-group item boundary with no doubled line, and the rule under the header row is the
  heavier one. Colour sampling passes even when every rule has moved a row, which is why the edge is a
  check of its own ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) groups 4 and
  5).
- **Links are undecorated at rest and underlined on hover, and the two controls that became `<button>`
  elements are indistinguishable from the links they replace** — no box, no border, no shifted baseline,
  and the same hover behaviour as their neighbours. The sign-out control specifically matches the `#ddd`
  of the nav links beside it rather than the body link colour
  ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) groups 2 and 10).
- **The footer's two lines are stacked and centred, not side by side** — the check that the `navbar` class
  came off that element, since a flex row is what its presence produces
  ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) group 13).
- **The genre menu in its open state**: the hovered item is white on the link blue, the open toggle sits
  on the darkened panel, and the menu's top corners are square against the navbar
  ([8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) groups 6 and 11).

The review procedure, the capture set and the sign-off artifact are section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual)'s;
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries it as a task.

#### 8.5.7 Library default differences that no class mapping expresses

Section [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) maps class *names*. It cannot
express the other half of a major-version upgrade: a difference where the **same** class, or no class at
all, renders differently because the library's own base values changed. Those differences are invisible
to a class-by-class diff, they appear on **every** page rather than on the one being edited, and they are
exactly what a reviewer would otherwise record as an unexplained regression. Each one below is therefore
resolved in one of two ways and never left open:

- **Preserved** — with the `wwwroot/css/site.css` declaration that preserves it **written out** in the
  block below. The value in the declaration is the Bootstrap 3 value measured from the committed
  stylesheet, which is the baseline the review compares against.
- **An approved change** — with its number and its named owner in section
  [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).

**Why the preservation mechanism is application CSS rather than build variables.** The successor is
acquired as **pre-built CSS** and committed, not compiled from source
([8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler), with the manifest and the pins owned by
[04 §9.6](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so there is no variable layer to set these values in. They
are set as overrides in the application's own stylesheet, which the layout links **after** the library's
([8.1.3](#813-the-rendered-tags-and-every-bundle-path-they-replace), rows one and two of the element
table) — that ordering is what makes the overrides win, and it is why the two `<link>` elements are
stated in a fixed order rather than as a pair.

| Difference | Bootstrap 3 baseline, from the committed stylesheet | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Base typography** — font stack, size, line-height and body colour, which set the metrics of every block of text on every page | `"Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif`, `14px`, `1.428571429`, `#333333` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:313-319] | **Preserved** — the four declarations in group 1 below. The port does **not** rescale the root font size to achieve this: the successor sizes its components in `rem` against the root element, so moving the root would move every library padding, margin and border-radius at once — a far larger change than the one being prevented. The root stays where the successor puts it, `body` is pinned here, and the handful of components that carry their own `rem` type scale are pinned individually in group 3 |
| **The grid gutter and the container's side padding — a 30px gutter against the successor's 24px, on every column of every page.** The source states the three halves of one measurement as three fixed values; the successor derives all three from one custom property, so pinning that property is what preserves them together | `.container { padding-right: 15px; padding-left: 15px; margin-right: auto; margin-left: auto }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:759-764]; `.row { margin-right: -15px; margin-left: -15px }` [:786-789]; and every column `padding-right: 15px; padding-left: 15px` under the full column selector list [:811-863] | **Preserved** — group 1a, by setting `--bs-gutter-x: 30px` and writing the container padding explicitly. The successor's default is `1.5rem`, which is **24px**, so leaving it alone narrows every gutter by 6px and every container's side padding by 3px — the album tiles move, the horizontal-form columns move, and the body content shifts 3px inward on all 29 views at once. The custom property is set on **both** `.container` and `.row` rather than on one of them: custom properties inherit, so a `.row` inside a `.container` would pick it up, but the two album grids are **not** the same shape — `<ul class="row list-unstyled">` on the home page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:10] carries `row` and `<ul id="album-list" class="list-unstyled">` on the browse page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:10] does **not**, so the browse tiles are columns with no row ancestor and inherit the property from the `container` class each `<li>` carries instead |
| **The container's three width caps, against the successor's five-step ladder.** This is the difference section [8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports) records at the wide viewport, resolved here rather than left for the reviewer to discover | `max-width: 750px` at `min-width: 768px` [:927-930], `970px` at `992px` [:1081-1084], `1170px` at `1200px` [:1244-1247] — and **no cap at all below 768px**, where `.container` is fluid | **Preserved** — group 1a, which pins the three source values at the source's own three boundaries and neutralizes the successor's two extra steps: its cap at `min-width: 576px` is cancelled with `max-width: none`, restoring the source's fluid band across 576-767px, and its cap at `min-width: 1400px` is overridden with the same `1170px` so no fourth cap appears where the source has three. Both neutralizing rules are written even though source order alone would win, because a reader must be able to see that the two extra steps were considered rather than missed |
| **`.row` changes layout model — the successor's row is a flex container where the source's is a block with floated columns.** The class name is identical, so a class diff sees nothing, and the consequence differs on each of the three surfaces that carry it | `.row` is a block element with a `:before`/`:after` clearfix [:786-809] and its columns are floated [:865-877]; there is no flex property anywhere in the source's grid | **Preserved — one surface needs a declaration, the other two are unaffected, and the reason each is unaffected is stated rather than assumed.** The jumbotron's showcase row is `<div class="row text-center">` wrapping a bare `<img>` with **no column class** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:6-8]: `text-align: center` centres an inline image inside a block, but a flex item is placed by `justify-content`, which defaults to `flex-start`, so the home page's first image would move from centred to left-aligned. Group 1a **preserves** it with `justify-content: center` scoped to `.jumbotron .row`. **The home page's album grid needs no declaration**, because the one difference flex could produce there — a wrapped line starting below the tallest tile of the line above rather than below the tile directly above — requires tiles of unequal height, and the application fixes every tile at one height: `ul#album-list li { height: 160px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:47-49], retained unchanged ([8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list)). Equal-height items wrap identically under both models. The tiles also carry no background and no border, so a stretched flex item and a floated block are indistinguishable. **The browse grid's `<ul>` carries no `row` at all** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:10], so no layout model changes on it |
| **Vertical rhythm between form groups — `15px` in the source, and the successor has no `form-group` class to carry it** | `.form-group { margin-bottom: 15px }` [:1755-1757], plus `.form-horizontal .form-group { margin-right: -15px; margin-left: -15px }` [:1969-1972], which is the row behaviour the target gets from `row` | **Preserved** — group 1a, and the mapping in [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) is written to make it possible: `form-group` becomes **`row form-group`**, retaining the source class name as an application-owned class, rather than `row mb-3`. `mb-3` is **rejected on measurement**: it is `1rem`, which against the pinned `14px` body is **16px**, one pixel more than the source on each of the **29** groups — and it carries `!important`, so a `.row.mb-3` override would have to carry `!important` too, to restore a value the library never needed to be told. Retaining the class name follows the same pattern as `jumbotron` and `dl-horizontal` in groups 8 and 9: a name the successor has dropped, defined once in the application's own stylesheet |

**The complete set of preserving declarations.** This is the whole of what section 8.5 adds to
`wwwroot/css/site.css` beyond the rules section
[8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list) carries across, and it is written out in full so that
no part of it is left to interpretation:

```css
/* Group 1 — base typography, preserving the source's body metrics. */
body {
  font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #333333;
}

/* Group 1a — grid geometry: the 30px gutter, the container's 15px side padding, the
   three container caps at the source's own three boundaries, and the two successor
   steps that have no source counterpart. The custom property is set on both
   .container and .row because the browse-page album grid has no row ancestor and
   inherits it from the `container` class on each <li> instead. */
.container,
.row {
  --bs-gutter-x: 30px;
}

.container {
  padding-right: 15px;
  padding-left: 15px;
  margin-right: auto;
  margin-left: auto;
}

/* The source has no cap below 768px; the successor introduces one at 576px. */
@media (min-width: 576px) {
  .container {
    max-width: none;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 750px;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 992px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 970px;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 1200px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 1170px;
  }
}

/* The successor's fifth step. Source order alone would already win here; the rule is
   written so that the step is visibly accounted for rather than silently outranked. */
@media (min-width: 1400px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 1170px;
  }
}

/* The showcase image is a bare <img> in a row with no column class, centred today by
   text-align. A flex item is placed by justify-content, so the alignment is restated.
   Scoped to the jumbotron: no other row in the application centres its children. */
.jumbotron .row {
  justify-content: center;
}

/* No rule is written for the album grid's line behaviour, and the reason is a measured
   fact rather than a judgement: a wrapped flex line starts below the tallest tile of
   the line above, which can only differ from float behaviour when tile heights differ,
   and Site.css:47-49 fixes every tile at height: 160px. Equal-height items wrap
   identically under both models. The tiles also carry no background and no border, so a
   stretched flex item is indistinguishable from a floated one. */

/* Vertical rhythm between form groups: 15px, retained under the source's own class
   name because the successor dropped it. `mb-3` is 1rem — 16px against the pinned
   14px body — and carries !important, so it is not used. */
.form-group {
  margin-bottom: 15px;
}

/* Group 1b — the heading scale, on the elements and on the six type utilities. The
   utilities are pinned because section 8.9 item a4 holds the catalog's rendered sizes
   with class="h3" and class="h5" while correcting the heading outline. */
h1,
h2,
h3,
h4,
h5,
h6,
.h1,
.h2,
.h3,
.h4,
.h5,
.h6 {
  font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  line-height: 1.1;
}

h1,
h2,
h3 {
  margin-top: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h4,
h5,
h6 {
  margin-top: 10px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h1,
.h1 {
  font-size: 36px;
}

h2,
.h2 {
  font-size: 30px;
}

h3,
.h3 {
  font-size: 24px;
}

h4,
.h4 {
  font-size: 18px;
}

h5,
.h5 {
  font-size: 14px;
}

h6,
.h6 {
  font-size: 12px;
}

/* Group 1c — the three contextual colour utilities. !important matches the
   successor's own utilities, which carry it; without it the override loses. */
.text-danger {
  color: #b94a48 !important;
}

.text-success {
  color: #468847 !important;
}

.text-info {
  color: #3a87ad !important;
}

/* Group 1d — block-level text metrics: 24 paragraphs, 7 lists, 10 rules, 2 address
   blocks and 1 small element. The hr rule draws the hairline above the footer on
   every page. */
p {
  margin: 0 0 10px;
}

ul,
ol {
  margin-top: 0;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

ul ul,
ol ul,
ul ol,
ol ol {
  margin-bottom: 0;
}

.list-unstyled {
  padding-left: 0;
  list-style: none;
}

hr {
  margin-top: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-top: 1px solid #eeeeee;
}

small {
  font-size: 85%;
}

address {
  display: block;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  font-style: normal;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

/* Group 1e — the two form elements around a control. `float: none` is written because
   the successor floats its legend and the source does not; the bottom border is the
   hairline under each of the checkout's two legends. The label weight reaches the
   checkout's labels, which are not col-form-label. */
legend {
  display: block;
  float: none;
  width: 100%;
  padding: 0;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  font-size: 21px;
  line-height: inherit;
  color: #333333;
  border: 0;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #e5e5e5;
}

label {
  display: inline-block;
  margin-bottom: 5px;
  font-weight: bold;
}

/* The source declares this colour through four vendor-prefixed selectors; one standard
   selector covers every browser in the target matrix. The successor's accompanying
   `opacity: 1` is left in place, which is what makes the colour render as declared. */
.form-control::placeholder {
  color: #999999;
}

/* Group 2 — link colour, resting decoration and the focus ring. Both decoration halves are required: the
   successor underlines links at rest and drops the underline on hover, which is the
   inverse of the source, on every link in the application. */
a {
  color: #428bca;
  text-decoration: none;
}

a:hover,
a:focus {
  color: #2a6496;
  text-decoration: underline;
}

/* The source's own focus ring, preserved rather than dropped: this is the indication
   every link in the application has today (bootstrap.css:348-352). Both `outline`
   declarations are kept in the source's order — the keyword form wins in the engines
   that recognise it, the `thin dotted #333` form is the fallback for the rest. */
a:focus {
  outline: thin dotted #333;
  outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color;
  outline-offset: -2px;
}

/* Approved delta 19 (section 11.5): the ring is narrowed to keyboard focus. `:focus`
   matches a pointer click as well, so the source draws the ring after a mouse click
   too; suppressing it for pointer interaction is a visible change to an existing
   behaviour and is owned as such. This is the one rule in this stylesheet permitted
   to remove a focus ring, and section 8.9 item d2 states the exception explicitly. */
a:focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 0;
}

/* Group 3 — control geometry, type scale and all three input states, so the button
   and input boxes neither move nor change appearance on focus or when disabled. */
.btn {
  padding: 6px 12px;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

.form-control {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: 34px;
  padding: 6px 12px;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #555555;
  vertical-align: middle;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid #cccccc;
  border-radius: 4px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.075);
  transition: border-color ease-in-out 0.15s, box-shadow ease-in-out 0.15s;
}

.form-control:focus {
  border-color: #66afe9;
  outline: 0;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.075), 0 0 8px rgba(102, 175, 233, 0.6);
}

.form-control[disabled],
.form-control[readonly],
fieldset[disabled] .form-control {
  cursor: not-allowed;
  background-color: #eeeeee;
}

/* Not optional: with height pinned at 34px above and no exception here, the
   checkout's address textarea collapses to a single line. */
textarea.form-control {
  height: auto;
}

/* The `input, select, textarea { max-width: 280px }` cap of Content/Site.css:13-17 is
   carried across unchanged by 8.5.5 and is deliberately not restated here. It composes
   with `width: 100%` above: the control fills its column until 280px and then stops,
   which is exactly today's rendering. */

/* Group 4 — table metrics, border structure and palette, for all three tables. The
   source rules the TOP edge of every cell and the successor rules the bottom, so the
   edges are set explicitly rather than only recoloured. */
.table {
  --bs-table-bg: transparent;
  --bs-table-striped-bg: #f9f9f9;
  --bs-table-border-color: #dddddd;
  width: 100%;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.table > :not(caption) > * > * {
  padding: 8px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  vertical-align: top;
  border-top: 1px solid #dddddd;
  border-bottom-width: 0;
}

.table > thead > tr > th {
  vertical-align: bottom;
  border-bottom: 2px solid #dddddd;
}

.table > thead:first-child > tr:first-child > th {
  border-top-width: 0;
}

/* The stripe is left to the successor's own mechanism, driven by the custom property
   set above, rather than fought with a competing background rule. */

/* Group 5 — the genre list on the store index. The -1px bottom margin is the
   mechanism that collapses adjacent 1px borders into one rule; without it every
   adjacent pair of genres shows a doubled 2px line. */
.list-group {
  padding-left: 0;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.list-group-item {
  position: relative;
  display: block;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  margin-bottom: -1px;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid #dddddd;
  border-radius: 0;
}

.list-group-item:first-child {
  border-top-left-radius: 4px;
  border-top-right-radius: 4px;
}

.list-group-item:last-child {
  margin-bottom: 0;
  border-bottom-right-radius: 4px;
  border-bottom-left-radius: 4px;
}

/* The successor collapses adjacent borders by removing the top one, through a
   two-class selector that outranks the single-class `border` above. Left alone, every
   genre after the first loses its top rule and the -1px margin pulls its opaque
   background over the rule above it, so no line renders between rows at all. No state
   rule is written: the source's own hover, focus and active rules match nothing here
   (the anchor is inside the <li>, and no item is active), and `list-group-item-action`
   is deliberately not applied. */
.list-group-item + .list-group-item {
  border-top-width: 1px;
}

/* Group 6 — navbar height arithmetic (15 + 20 + 15 = 50) and both backgrounds.
   The !important matches the successor's background utilities, which carry it. */
.navbar {
  min-height: 50px;
  padding-top: 0;
  padding-bottom: 0;
}

.navbar-brand {
  padding: 15px 15px;
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 20px;
}

.navbar-nav .nav-link {
  padding: 10px 15px;
  line-height: 20px;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-nav .nav-link {
    padding-top: 15px;
    padding-bottom: 15px;
  }
}

.navbar.bg-dark {
  background-color: #222222 !important;
}

/* Scoped to the footer element rather than to .navbar, because the footer no longer
   carries that class — see group 13. It is the only bg-light consumer in the
   application. */
footer.bg-light {
  background-color: #f8f8f8 !important;
}

/* Navbar states. The resting #ddd comes from the rewritten Site.css selectors of
   section 8.5.5; everything below is the library's, and is lost with the class the
   library keyed it on. The hover underline is group 2's `a:hover` and needs no rule
   here — it is the successor's `.nav-link { text-decoration: none }` that loses, on
   specificity. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-brand:hover,
.navbar-dark .navbar-brand:focus,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link:hover,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link:focus {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* The genre toggle while its menu is open: the successor whitens the text and drops
   the panel behind it, so the darkened toggle disappears. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .show > .nav-link,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.show {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #080808;
}

/* States no view applies today, pinned so the class behaviour matches the source. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.active {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #080808;
}

.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.disabled {
  color: #444444;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* The collapsed panel's divider and inset highlight, visible only below 768px. The
   media query reproduces the source's own neutralization above that width. */
.navbar-collapse {
  border-top: 1px solid #101010;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-collapse {
    border-top: 0;
    box-shadow: none;
  }
}

/* The toggler's box. Its glyph is delta 5's, not this group's. */
.navbar-toggler {
  padding: 9px 10px;
  margin-top: 8px;
  margin-right: 15px;
  margin-bottom: 8px;
  background-color: transparent;
  border: 1px solid #333333;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

.navbar-toggler:hover,
.navbar-toggler:focus {
  background-color: #333333;
}

/* Group 7 — the horizontal form layout `form-horizontal` used to supply. The ported
   markup carries `col-form-label` on each of the 21 labels inside the seven horizontal
   shapes; the alignment stays inside the source's own breakpoint so the narrow
   viewport keeps its stacked, left-aligned labels. */
.col-form-label {
  padding-top: 7px;
  padding-bottom: 0;
  margin-top: 0;
  margin-bottom: 0;
  font-weight: bold;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .col-form-label {
    text-align: right;
  }
}

/* Group 8 — the showcase band. `jumbotron` is gone from the library and retained as an
   application-owned class with the markup unchanged. Content/Site.css's transparent
   background folds in here as the background-color declaration. */
.jumbotron {
  padding: 30px;
  margin-bottom: 30px;
  font-size: 21px;
  font-weight: 200;
  line-height: 2.1428571435;
  color: inherit;
  background-color: transparent;
}

.jumbotron h1 {
  line-height: 1;
  color: inherit;
}

.jumbotron p {
  line-height: 1.4;
}

.container .jumbotron {
  border-radius: 6px;
}

@media screen and (min-width: 768px) {
  .jumbotron {
    padding-top: 48px;
    padding-bottom: 48px;
  }

  .container .jumbotron {
    padding-right: 60px;
    padding-left: 60px;
  }

  .jumbotron h1 {
    font-size: 63px;
  }
}

/* Group 9 — the horizontal description list on the administration detail page,
   retained as an application-owned class with the markup unchanged. The geometry stays
   inside the source's own breakpoint so the narrow viewport keeps term-above-definition.
   `margin-bottom: 0` on the definitions cancels a bottom margin the successor's base
   `dd` carries and the source's does not. */
.dl-horizontal {
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.dl-horizontal dt,
.dl-horizontal dd {
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

.dl-horizontal dt {
  font-weight: bold;
}

.dl-horizontal dd {
  margin-bottom: 0;
  margin-left: 0;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .dl-horizontal dt {
    float: left;
    width: 160px;
    overflow: hidden;
    clear: left;
    text-align: right;
    text-overflow: ellipsis;
    white-space: nowrap;
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd {
    margin-left: 180px;
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd::before,
  .dl-horizontal dd::after {
    display: table;
    content: " ";
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd::after {
    clear: both;
  }
}

/* Group 10 — the two controls that become <button> elements under items a6 and a7 of
   section 8.9 but must keep rendering as the inline links they are today. The
   appearance reset is required because `background: none` alone does not remove the
   platform button chrome on every engine. Applied as
   `<button type="button" class="RemoveLink link-button">` on cart removal, keeping
   RemoveLink for the script's selector, and `<button type="submit" class="link-button">`
   on sign-out. */
.link-button {
  padding: 0;
  font: inherit;
  line-height: inherit;
  color: #428bca;
  text-align: inherit;
  text-decoration: none;
  cursor: pointer;
  background: none;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 0;
  -webkit-appearance: none;
  appearance: none;
}

.link-button:hover,
.link-button:focus {
  color: #2a6496;
  text-decoration: underline;
  background: none;
}

/* One generic rule cannot serve both consumers. The rule above is the cart-removal
   control's, in a table cell, where the body link colour is correct. The sign-out
   control sits between #ddd nav links, so it takes their colour and their box instead;
   only the properties that differ are restated, so the appearance reset, the pointer
   cursor and the hover underline still come from the base rule. Scoped by ancestry
   rather than by an extra class, so it holds whether or not the button also carries
   nav-link. */
.navbar-nav .link-button {
  display: block;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  line-height: 20px;
  color: #ddd;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-nav .link-button {
    padding-top: 15px;
    padding-bottom: 15px;
  }
}

.navbar-nav .link-button:hover,
.navbar-nav .link-button:focus {
  color: #ffffff;
}

/* Group 11 — the genre dropdown. Hover is white on the link blue rather than the
   successor's pale grey, and item padding differs on both axes. The library's own two
   focus suppressions — `outline: 0` on the active item and on .dropdown-toggle:focus —
   are deliberately not reproduced; section 8.9 item d2 exists to remove them. */
.dropdown-menu {
  padding: 5px 0;
  margin: 2px 0 0;
  font-size: 14px;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
  border-radius: 4px;
  box-shadow: 0 6px 12px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.175);
}

/* Flattened against the navbar it hangs from, as the source flattens it. */
.navbar-nav .dropdown-menu {
  margin-top: 0;
  border-top-left-radius: 0;
  border-top-right-radius: 0;
}

.dropdown-item {
  display: block;
  padding: 3px 20px;
  font-weight: normal;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #333333;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

.dropdown-item:hover,
.dropdown-item:focus,
.dropdown-item.active,
.dropdown-item:active {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #428bca;
}

.dropdown-item.disabled,
.dropdown-item:disabled {
  color: #999999;
  cursor: not-allowed;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* Group 12 — the Remember-me control's wrapper and label. The control's own rendering
   is approved delta 20 and is not pinned here. The label's weight is the declaration
   that would otherwise be silently wrong: group 1e pins `label { font-weight: bold }`
   from the source's base rule, and the source overrides it to normal for this label. */
.form-check {
  display: block;
  min-height: 20px;
  padding-left: 20px;
  margin-top: 10px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
  vertical-align: middle;
}

  float: left;
  margin-left: -20px;
}

.form-check-label {

  font-weight: normal;

/* Group 13 — the footer, which drops the `navbar` class because the successor's navbar
   is a flex container and this element's two children are blocks. `fixed-bottom`
   supplies the positioning and `bg-light` the background (group 6); the declarations
   below are the ones `.navbar` and `.navbar-fixed-bottom` used to supply. */
footer.fixed-bottom {
  min-height: 50px;
  margin-bottom: 0;
  border-width: 0 0 1px;
  border-style: solid;
  border-color: #e7e7e7;
}
```

**One acceptance rule governs all twenty-five preserved rows — the twenty-seven rows above less the two
numbered approved changes, deltas 15 and 16 — and it is about the criterion rather than the mechanism.**
Two of the twenty-five carry a **partial** exception rather than being wholly preserved, and each is split
in a stated place. The resting-link-decoration row preserves the focus ring's three values and narrows
only its selector, which is **approved delta 19**. The checkbox row preserves the wrapper's and the
label's every metric and hands only the control's own rendering to **approved delta 20**. In both cases
the preserved values are held to the criterion below while the named change is held to section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) instead. A successor may apply a property through a mechanism a plain declaration does not override
— a per-component custom property, or a utility carrying `!important`, as `bg-dark` and `bg-light` do.
Where that happens, the **same value** is set through whichever mechanism the pinned build honours. What
does not move is the acceptance criterion: **the measured rendered value against the Bootstrap 3 value
cited in the row**, sampled at both viewports of
[8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports) and recorded on the sign-off artifact of section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual). A row is satisfied by the measurement
matching, never by the declaration having been written.

### 8.6 View serving and `_ViewImports`

`Views/Web.config` carries two unrelated constructs and they have opposite fates.

**The `BlockViewHandler` mapping ends, and needs no replacement.**
`<remove name="BlockViewHandler"/>` followed by
`<add name="BlockViewHandler" path="*" verb="*" preCondition="integratedMode" type="System.Web.HttpNotFoundHandler" />`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:31-32] exists to stop `.cshtml` files under `Views/` being
requested directly. **The target does not serve content-root `.cshtml` files at all**, so the behaviour
the handler enforces is the default rather than something to configure. `preCondition="integratedMode"`
is meaningless outside IIS in any case.

**The namespace registration has a direct successor: `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`.** Six namespaces are
imported into every view today [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:14-21]. **Three survive and
three are dead:**

| Namespace | Line | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `System.Web.Mvc` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:15] | **Survives, remapped** to the target's MVC namespace |
| `System.Web.Mvc.Ajax` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:16] | **Dead.** The unobtrusive-Ajax helper family does not exist in the target, and **no view uses it** — there is no `@Ajax.` call anywhere in MVC 5's views |
| `System.Web.Mvc.Html` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:17] | **Dead** as a namespace. The `Html` helpers it contained are reached through the view's own `Html` property in the target and need no import |
| `System.Web.Optimization` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:18] | **Dead entirely** — the package has no successor (section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)) |
| `System.Web.Routing` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:19] | **Survives, remapped** to the target's routing namespace — retained only if a ported view actually references a routing type; **verify during the port and drop it if none does**, rather than carrying an unused import forward |
| `MvcMusicStore` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:20] | **Survives** as the application root namespace, and `MvcMusicStore.Models` is added alongside it, since every strongly-typed view names a model under it — for example [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:1] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:1] |

`_ViewImports.cshtml` additionally registers the framework's tag helpers, which the source has no
equivalent of and which sections [7.1](#71-the-policy) and
[8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler) both depend on. The Razor host and page-base-type
registration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:12-13] and the `configSections` group that declares them [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:4-9] **end**: the
configuration section does not exist in the target and the base type is a framework concern rather
than an application one. `Views/_ViewStart.cshtml` ports unchanged.

The redundant `webpages:Enabled` key [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:26] ends with the rest of the Web Pages surface (section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)).

### 8.7 The JSON contract — annotate one model, not the policy

The cart-removal endpoint returns a view model with five **PascalCase** properties — `Message`,
`CartTotal`, `CartCount`, `ItemCount`, `DeleteId`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/ViewModels/ShoppingCartRemoveViewModel.cs:5-9] — populated at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:73-81] and returned as
`return Json(results)` [:83].

The page's JavaScript reads **exactly those PascalCase names** — **five distinct properties across seven
reads**: `data.ItemCount` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:21], `data.DeleteId`
[:22], `data.DeleteId` and `data.ItemCount` again on the same line [:24], `data.CartTotal` [:27],
`data.Message` [:28] and `data.CartCount` [:29]. Line 24 carries **two** of the seven, which is why the
read count exceeds the property count by two rather than by one:
`$('#item-count-' + data.DeleteId).text(data.ItemCount);` selects by one property and writes the other.
[12 F-12-16](12-migration-blockers.md) states the same five and seven.

**The target's default web serializer camel-cases property names, and the failure is silent.** After
the port the request still succeeds, the response is still 200, the JSON is still well-formed — and
every one of those reads evaluates to `undefined`. The row does not fade out [:22], the count does not
update [:24], the total does not change [:27], the message stays empty [:28] and the header badge stops
tracking [:29]. **No error occurs, so nothing is logged.**

**One of those seven reads has a second problem this section does not own.** `data.CartCount` [:29] is
written to an element **no view emits**, and the quantity it carries is not the quantity the server
renders — so fixing the property name alone leaves that read working and still landing nowhere. The
element, the rendered format and the single count definition are specified in section
[8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract), and the **payload is unchanged by that
decision**: its five property names and their meanings are preserved exactly as this section requires,
and the alignment happens on the component's side. Nothing is added to the response.

**Get the attribution right, because the wrong attribution produces the wrong fix.** The serializer
producing PascalCase today is `JavaScriptSerializer`, by way of MVC 5's `JsonResult` — **not**
Newtonsoft.Json, which is pinned as a package but never called from application source.
[12 F-12-16](12-migration-blockers.md) establishes both facts with its command; this document does not
re-derive them. The consequence is that **removing Newtonsoft.Json is the removal of an unused
dependency, not a serializer replacement** ([04 §8.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns that
outcome).

**Resolution: annotate that one response model with explicit JSON property names. Do not change the
application-wide serializer policy.** [12 §7.3](12-migration-blockers.md) records the choice as 05's;
it is taken this way for three reasons:

1. **The affected surface is exactly one endpoint and one model.** There is one `Json(...)` return in
   the entire migration source, at [:83].
2. **A global PascalCase policy would be a decision about every future endpoint**, taken to
   accommodate one 2013-era script — precisely the kind of application-wide default that section
   [6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited) argues against inheriting silently.
3. **The annotation is local, visible and self-documenting**: a reader of the model sees why the names
   are pinned, whereas a serializer option in `Program.cs` is invisible from the model and from the
   script.

The alternative of changing the JavaScript to read camelCase was considered and **not** taken: it
would work, but it changes the client and the server contract at once for no gain, and the annotation
keeps the wire format byte-identical to the baseline — which is what lets the same assertion run
against both runtimes in section [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage).

**The test asserts on property names and values, not merely on a 200** (section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)) — a status-only assertion is exactly what this failure passes.

### 8.8 The checkout input model — ten properties, not nine

`TryUpdateModel(order)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:29] is applied to an
`Order` constructed one line earlier [:28], inside a POST action whose parameter is a raw
`FormCollection` [:26]. What makes the call safe today is a **separate** construct: a class-level
attribute on the entity,
`[Bind(Include = "FirstName,LastName,Address,City,State,PostalCode,Country,Phone,Email")]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8]. That include list is the **entire** over-posting control at
checkout ([09 §6.4](09-security-assessment.md) owns the consequence), and both halves have to move
together.

**Both halves fail to compile in the target.** Only the asynchronous overload,
`TryUpdateModelAsync`, exists — so [:29] does not compile — and `[Bind(Include = ...)]` is superseded
by explicit binding models, so the attribute at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] has no target either.

**Resolution: `Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs`, carrying TEN properties.** Nine is the number written
down in the repository and **ten is the number the action actually reads**:

- **Nine** from the `[Bind]` include list [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8]: `FirstName`,
  `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`, `Phone`, `Email`. Each carries its
  existing DataAnnotations attributes across verbatim — `[Required]`, `[StringLength]`,
  `[DisplayName]`, `[DataType]` and the email `[RegularExpression]` [:20-61] — so client and server
  validation messages are preserved.
- **The tenth is `PromoCode`**, which the action reads **separately, straight out of the raw form**:
  `values["PromoCode"]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33], compared
  case-insensitively [:33-34] against `const string PromoCode = "FREE"` [:12]. It is not on the
  `[Bind]` list because it is not bound at all.

**Two of the ten are unbounded in the source, and the input model closes both** — because "copied across
verbatim" is only safe where an attribute exists to copy. Eight of the nine address properties carry a
`[StringLength]`; **`Email` does not** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61], carrying only
`[Required]`, `[DisplayName]`, `[RegularExpression]` and `[DataType]`, and `PromoCode` carries nothing at
all because it is never a bound property. So today an arbitrarily long email address and an arbitrarily
long promo code both reach the action, the email reaches the insert, and the only ceiling on either is
the request-body limit — which is the framework's 30 MB default (section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)).

| Property | Bound on the input model | Why that value, and what it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Email` | `[StringLength(254)]`, alongside the existing `[Required]`, `[RegularExpression]` and `[DataType]` copied from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61] | 254 is the longest address an SMTP path can carry, so it rejects nothing a real customer can own. **The bound is on the input model and the column keeps the source's width** — EF 6's convention for a `string` with no `MaxLength` gives `nvarchar(max)`, and the baseline model therefore declares **no `HasMaxLength` on `Order.Email`**, so the initial migration reproduces the extracted type and the diff gate of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 reports nothing at all. **An earlier form of this row narrowed the column to `nvarchar(256)` and recorded the narrowing as a "deliberate schema difference" annotated on that gate; both halves of that are withdrawn**, because step 3 admits **no** annotated exception — an intended target-state change has to ship as a named post-load migration, as the `datetime2` change of section [8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) does — and no such migration is warranted here: the enforced ceiling is the validation attribute, which refuses an overlength value at step 1 of section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) **before** any read or write, so a narrower column would add a second ceiling behind the one that already stops the request and would buy nothing. **Two consequences, stated because they are what the narrowing would have changed:** the load carries the pre-existing population through unaltered, so a source `Order.Email` longer than 254 characters is **neither truncated nor a load failure** — it is historical order data the target displays and never rewrites; and the 254 bound governs every address the *target* accepts, which is the population a stored-width limit could have protected. Narrowing the column is available as a separate decision with its own named post-load migration and an overlength precheck over the loaded rows; this port does not take it, and the closed post-load set of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) therefore stays at three groups |
| `PromoCode` | `[StringLength(16)]` and `[RegularExpression("^[A-Za-z0-9]*$")]`, optional | The only value with any meaning is the four-character constant at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:12], so the bound is generous by an order of magnitude and still refuses everything a promo field is abused for — long payloads, control characters, markup and injection probes. The pattern is stated as a **whitelist** rather than as an escape rule. **Nothing changes about the outcome a customer sees:** a value that fails either attribute redisplays the form with a field message, which is the same branch the no-match promo code takes under approved delta 16, and the value is **still never persisted** — see the paragraph below |

Both bounds are enforced at step 1 of section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract), before the cart is read and before the
transaction opens, so an oversized value produces **no** read, **no** write and — under the
permitted-content rule of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — **no** log record
carrying it. Together with the per-endpoint request and form limits of section
[8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) they are recorded as approved delta 21 in
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), because an overlength email that used to place an
order now does not. **The coverage assertion requires the pair.

**`PromoCode` belongs on the input model and NOT on the `Order` entity.** `Order` has no such property
and must not gain one: its surface is fourteen properties — the nine bound ones, four suppressed with
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` (`OrderId` [:11-12], `OrderDate` [:14-15], `Username` [:17-18], `Total`
[:63-64]) and the `OrderDetails` navigation [:66]. Persisting `PromoCode` would store a **transient form
value** as a column, and would appear in the schema diff of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) as a difference — which that section's
step 3 admits under no annotation at all, so it would fail the gate rather than be explained away.

**Ten remains ten: the submission key is neither a bound property of this model nor a transient value.**
Section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) adds a server-generated
`submissionToken` hidden field and a `SubmissionId` column on `Orders`, and neither belongs here:

- **It is not on `CheckoutInputModel`**, but is a separate `[FromForm] string?` action parameter carrying
  the protected token that section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) specifies. This model
  exists to carry exactly what the source action read, which is what makes "ten, not nine" a checkable
  claim against [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] and
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33]; folding a net-new mechanism into it would
  make the count a coincidence. It travels the same way the anti-forgery token does — a hidden field the
  server emits and the handler reads, outside the domain input.
- **It *is* persisted on `Order`, and that does not contradict the paragraph above.** The objection to
  persisting `PromoCode` is that it is transient — its value has no meaning once the promo branch has been
  evaluated. The submission key is the opposite: **durability is its entire function**, because the thing
  it protects against is the loss of a commit acknowledgement, and only a committed row can answer that
  question. Its arrival is sequenced so the schema diff still holds — a second migration after the
  baseline, per section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract).

**Why a nine-property model is the dangerous near-miss.** It compiles, binds and persists correctly —
and **silently loses promo-code handling**. The order-completion branch [:38-55] is guarded by the
promo-code comparison [:33-34], so with the value never bound the comparison always fails and **every
checkout returns to the form** at [:36] with no error message and no log entry. **Test valid, invalid
and missing promo-code values** (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)).

Two further changes in the same action:

- **`Order.cs` loses `using System.Web.Mvc`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:4], which exists
  purely to reference that attribute, along with the attribute itself. A model-layer file with an MVC
  dependency is why this port is not confined to `Controllers/`.
- **The bare `catch` is replaced**, and the whole write path around it is specified as one ordered
  contract in section [8.10](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) — including the
  per-exception-type branches, what may and may not appear in a log record, and the assertion that no
  row is written on any failure path. `catch { return View(order); }`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62] has **no exception variable**: it
  discards the exception, redisplays the view and records nothing, wrapping the entire order
  transaction [:31-62] ([08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt).

**The checkout path is the one most exposed to the lifetime change, and must be re-verified
explicitly.** It adds the order, resolves the cart, writes order details, empties the cart and calls
`SaveChanges` in one sequence [:44-51] — and it already passes **its own** context into `GetCart` [:47],
so it is *not* an instance of the multi-context problem. What it is exposed to is the change from a
controller-lifetime context to a request-scoped one across a five-step write: the required verification
is that all of order, order details and cart-emptying commit together, and that a failure part-way
leaves **none** of them. The **account cart-migration path** [:30-40] must be re-verified for the same
reason, against the sequence of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

### 8.11 The administration input models — the entity stops being a binding target

Checkout is not the only place an entity is bound from the request. **Administration binds the `Album`
entity directly, with no include list at all**, and that is the one over-posting exposure in the
repository with no control whatsoever:
`public ActionResult Create(Album album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:54]
and `public ActionResult Edit(Album album)` [:87].
[09](09-security-assessment.md) F-09-27 records the finding and **hands the resolution to this
document**; this section is that resolution.

**What the binder will accept today, property by property.** `Album` declares six scalars and three
navigations [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:7-33]:

| Property | Intended to be posted? | What the source does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AlbumId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:10] | **No** on create | `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` [:8] suppresses it in *scaffolded views*; it does **not** stop the model binder. A create post naming `AlbumId` sets it |
| `Title` [:18], `Price` [:24], `AlbumArtUrl` [:28] | Yes | Bound, with their validation attributes [:16-17, :20-23, :26-27] |
| `GenreId` [:12], `ArtistId` [:14] | Yes | Bound, and **not validated against existing rows** — the referential check is left to the database |
| `Genre` [:30], `Artist` [:31] | **No** | Bound as object graphs. A post carrying `Genre.Name` yields a populated `Genre` instance hanging off the album, and `db.Albums.Add(album)` [:58] cascades that instance into the change tracker as a **new genre row** |
| `OrderDetails` [:32] | **No** | A collection of order-detail rows, bindable by index and cascaded on `Add` the same way |

**And `Edit` is worse than `Create` in a way that is easy to miss.** `db.Entry(album).State = EntityState.Modified`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:91] applied to a **detached** instance
marks **every scalar** as modified, so any scalar the post omits is written as its CLR default — an
omitted `AlbumArtUrl` becomes `NULL`, an omitted `Price` becomes `0`. The POST action also takes **no
`id` parameter**: the identity of the row being edited comes entirely from the request body, so the
route id displayed in the URL is decorative.

**Resolution: two input models, and the `Album` entity is never a binding target again.** Both live in
`Binding/`, beside `Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs` — the same pattern, applied to the one other action
pair that binds an entity. No new folder, no new project and no new package.

| Type | Properties | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Binding/AlbumCreateInputModel.cs` | `Title`, `Price`, `AlbumArtUrl`, `GenreId`, `ArtistId` | **Five properties, and no `AlbumId`** — the store assigns the key. The validation attributes are copied across from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:16-27] verbatim, so client-side and server-side messages are preserved exactly |
| `Binding/AlbumEditInputModel.cs` | **`int? AlbumId`**, plus the same five | `AlbumId` is present **deliberately**, not by oversight: the edit form round-trips it in a hidden field [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Edit.cshtml:17], so on this model it is the request's **identity** rather than an over-post. What the action does with it is step 0 of the edit contract below — require it to be present and equal to the route id, and refuse anything else. Two sources of identity that can disagree is a defect whether or not it is exploitable. **It is declared `int?` rather than `int`, and that is a contract rather than a style choice** — the reason is below the edit table, because step 0 cannot otherwise mean what it says |

**Create and edit are not one contract, and treating them as one is how this resolution goes wrong.**
They differ in exactly the property that matters. On **create** the key is **absent from the model and
assigned by the store**, so a posted `AlbumId` must have no effect. On **edit** the key is **required**,
and it arrives from two places that have to agree. A single "the models reject `AlbumId`" rule would be
wrong on the edit side — it would reject the form the application itself renders — and a single "the
models carry `AlbumId`" rule would be wrong on the create side. So each action is specified as its own
ordered contract, and the two shared rules are stated once as **R3** and **R4** below.

**`POST /StoreManager/Create`** —
`[HttpPost] public async Task<IActionResult> Create(AlbumCreateInputModel input, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`:

| Step | What happens | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The `ModelState` gate, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:56] | Both select lists repopulated (R4) and the form redisplayed, as at [:63-65]. Nothing written |
| 2 | `GenreId` and `ArtistId` validated against existing rows (R3) | Model error against that field, select lists repopulated, form redisplayed. Nothing written |
| 3 | A **new** `Album` is constructed and exactly the five permitted properties are assigned to it. `Genre`, `Artist` and `OrderDetails` are never assigned; `AlbumId` is never assigned | — |
| 4 | `Albums.Add(...)`, then `SaveChangesAsync` | The persistence-failure classifier of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| 5 | Redirect to `Index`, preserved from [:60] | — |

**A posted `AlbumId` on create is not rejected — it is never bound**, because the model has no such
property and an unmatched form key is ignored without a model error. The observable consequence, which is
what the coverage assertion requires, is that the created row's key is the one **the store** assigned rather than
the one posted. That is what the source *intends* and the opposite of what it does:
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:8] suppresses the field in the
scaffolded view, and `Create.cshtml` accordingly renders only the five
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Create.cshtml:51-54] — but the binder is not governed by the
view, so today a hand-crafted post sets the key.

**`POST /StoreManager/Edit/{id}`** —
`[HttpPost] public async Task<IActionResult> Edit([FromRoute] int id, AlbumEditInputModel input, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`:

| Step | What happens | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | **The two identities are compared before anything else**, as `input.AlbumId.HasValue && input.AlbumId.Value == id` — one expression, evaluated on the nullable property, with presence tested before value | **`BadRequest()`** for anything else — absent, unparseable, or a different value — with **no album loaded, no select list built and no column written** in any table. The empty 400 is re-executed into the generic error page by the status-code middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), so the caller gets a page rather than a blank body, and it is **not** the form |
| 1 | The `ModelState` gate, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:89] | Select lists repopulated (R4) and the form redisplayed, as at [:95-97]. The stored album is unchanged **in every column** |
| 2 | `GenreId` and `ArtistId` validated against existing rows (R3) | As create's step 2 |
| 3 | The row is loaded **tracked**: `FirstOrDefaultAsync(a => a.AlbumId == id)` — census site F3 in section [4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **`NotFound()`**, nothing written |
| 4 | The five permitted fields are applied **presence-aware** — the table below. **`Entry(...).State = Modified` is not used** | — |
| 5 | `SaveChangesAsync`, then redirect to `Index`, preserved from [:93] | The classifier of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |

**Step 0 runs ahead of the `ModelState` gate, and that order is part of the contract.** Behind the gate,
a body whose `AlbumId` is absent or unparseable has already failed validation, so the same request would
be answered with a **200 and a redisplayed form** — reporting a tampered identity as a field message on a
page that invites a retry. Ahead of it, that request is a flat 400 that never reads or writes the store.
The route id is the authority either way: it is the value the administrator sees and the value the URL's
own semantics imply. **The source has no such check at all** — its POST takes no `id` parameter
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:87], so the row it edits is whichever one
the **body** names and the id in the URL is decorative.

**Why the property is `int?`, and why an `int` would make step 0 unable to keep its own promise.** Step 0
says `input.AlbumId` "must be present", and **presence is not representable on a non-nullable `int`**. The
model binder gives an `int` property the type's default for both of the cases step 0 is supposed to refuse:
a key absent from the body binds `0`, and a key present but unparseable — `AlbumId=abc` — also binds `0`,
adding a `ModelState` error the gate at step 1 would see and step 0 runs ahead of. So on an `int`, three
different requests arrive at step 0 as the identical value `0`: the absent one, the unparseable one, and a
body that genuinely posted the literal `0`. The comparison then answers correctly only by accident — it
refuses them because a stored `AlbumId` is never `0`, so `0 != id` for every real route id — and the
accident fails in one specific case: `POST /StoreManager/Edit/0` with an absent or unparseable body
compares `0 == 0`, **passes step 0**, and reaches step 3, which is the one place this contract promised
nothing would be loaded. Nothing is written even then, because step 3's lookup returns `null` and answers
`NotFound()` — so the consequence is a `404` where the contract specifies a `400`, and a store read where
it specifies none. That is a small effect with a specific cause, and the cause is a type that cannot
express absence.

`int?` removes the conflation instead of compensating for it. Absent binds `null`; unparseable binds
`null` with a `ModelState` error nobody consults, because step 0 has already refused it; and a posted
literal `0` binds `0`, which is a **value** and is refused by the comparison rather than by the presence
test — the two failures stay distinct even though both answer `400`. The route id needs no lower-bound
check of its own: with presence handled, a route id of `0` and a body of `0` agree at step 0 and are
refused at step 3 as an album that does not exist, which is the correct answer for that URL. Coverage row
90 asserts all four cases, the literal `0` included, for exactly this reason.

**Presence-aware application (step 4), and why the obvious version of it is wrong.** "Load the row and
assign the five properties" is the natural way to state step 4 and it silently reintroduces the defect
the step exists to close. Four of the five fields are guarded by validation and so can never reach step 4
absent: `Title` and `Price` carry `[Required]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:16,20], and
`GenreId` and `ArtistId` are non-nullable value types, whose absence the framework reports as a missing
required value — all four fail step 1 and redisplay. **`AlbumArtUrl` is the exception, and it is the only
one:** it carries `[StringLength(1024)]` and no `[Required]` [:26-27], so an absent key binds to `null`,
passes validation, and an unconditional assignment writes `NULL` over a stored value nobody asked to
remove. That is the same erasure as `Entry(...).State = Modified`, reached from the other direction.

| Case | What the request carries | What is applied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Omission** | the key `AlbumArtUrl` is **absent** from the form | **Nothing.** The stored column keeps the value it has |
| **Explicit clear** | the key is **present and empty** — what the rendered form posts when an administrator empties the box | **`NULL`.** `ConvertEmptyStringToNull` is the framework default in the source and in the target alike, so an empty text input binds to `null` and the clear is honoured |
| **New value** | the key is present and non-empty | The bound value, after `[StringLength(1024)]` |

**Presence is read from the request, never inferred from the bound value**, because the first two cases
produce the identical CLR `null` and only the request distinguishes them: the action tests
`Request.Form.ContainsKey(nameof(AlbumEditInputModel.AlbumArtUrl))`. **The ordinary path is untouched by
this rule** — `Edit.cshtml` renders the field on every load
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Edit.cshtml:52-55], so a browser post always carries the key
