and always lands in one of the two lower rows. The rule exists for the hand-crafted post, which is the
only thing that can produce the top row.

**The two shared rules.**

- **R3 — `GenreId` and `ArtistId` are validated against existing rows before the write:**
  `AnyAsync(g => g.GenreId == input.GenreId)` and the artist equivalent. A value with no matching row adds
  a model error **against that field** and redisplays the form. The source defers this to the database,
  where it surfaces as a `DbUpdateException` — classified as `Rejected` by section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — rather than as a validation message next to the
  offending dropdown.
- **R4 — the select lists are repopulated on every failure path**, preserving the source's behaviour at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:63-64] and [:95-96]. In the target they
  are properties on a view model rather than `ViewBag` entries, for the reason in section
  [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) — a typed member cannot be misspelled at
  the call site — but **the rendered form and its messages are unchanged**.

**Nested over-post graphs are a separate case with a separate test, because they fail for a different
reason from a scalar over-post.** `Genre`, `Artist` and `OrderDetails` are absent from **both** models, so
`Genre.Name` and `OrderDetails[0].Quantity` bind to nothing — and, independently, neither action ever
calls `Add` on a graph: create constructs the entity and assigns scalars, edit mutates a tracked row. Both
halves are load-bearing, because binding is not the mechanism the source's exposure actually runs through:
it is `db.Albums.Add(album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:58] cascading
whatever the binder attached into the change tracker as **new rows**. The assertion is therefore on **row
counts in `Genres`, `Artists` and `OrderDetails`** before and after, not on the response — a rejected
graph and a silently inserted one answer with the same redirect.

**Nothing changes for an administrator using the form**: the same fields, the same validation messages,
the same redirect. **Five things change for a hand-crafted post**, and each is recorded as its own
approved delta in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — with its own reason and its own
approval owner — rather than presented as an internal fix: the key can no longer be set on create
(**delta 23**); a route/body id mismatch answers 400 where the source edits whichever row the body named
(**delta 24**); a nonexistent `GenreId` or `ArtistId` redisplays the form where the source reaches the
database (**delta 25**); an omitted `AlbumArtUrl` leaves the column alone where the source blanks it
(**delta 26**); and a posted `Genre`, `Artist` or `OrderDetails` graph inserts nothing where the source
cascades new rows (**delta 27**). **The coverage assertions in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) assert each of these**: row 39 the create-side over-post, row 40 the
omission, row 41 the foreign keys, row 90 the id authority, row 91 the clear-versus-omit pair and row 92
the nested graphs.

### 8.12 The checkout write path — one ordered contract

Section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) settles what the checkout action
*binds*. This section settles what it *does*, step by step, because the source's write path spans two
files, has no validation gate, computes a total from two different reads of the same price, copies a
foreign key that does not exist yet, and wraps the whole of it in a `catch` with no exception variable.
**Every branch below is stated; an omitted branch here is an order that either fails silently or
persists something wrong.**

**Target signature.**
`[HttpPost] [RequestSizeLimit(16 * 1024)] [RequestFormLimits(ValueCountLimit = 32, KeyLengthLimit = 128, ValueLengthLimit = 4096, MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0)] public async Task<IActionResult> AddressAndPayment(CheckoutInputModel input, [FromForm(Name = "submissionToken")] string? submissionToken, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`.
The class-level `[Authorize]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:8] is preserved
as-is; anti-forgery validation arrives from the global filter of section
[7.1](#71-the-policy) rather than from an attribute on the action. The `FormCollection` parameter
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:26] and the `TryUpdateModel` call [:29]
both disappear. `submissionToken` carries the **submission key** specified immediately below; it is a
separate parameter rather than a property of the input model, for the reason section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) gives.

**The two size limits are part of the signature rather than a footnote — and they are two different
limits, with two different failure statuses, which a single "oversized input is refused" sentence gets
wrong.** The framework's defaults are a 30 MB request body and a form body sized for file upload; the
verified `FormOptions` defaults are `ValueCountLimit` **1,024**, `KeyLengthLimit` **2,048** and
`ValueLengthLimit` **4,194,304**. This endpoint's whole payload is ten short fields, an anti-forgery token
and a submission token — under 2 KB in practice — so both are tightened, and the two tightenings behave
differently:

| Limit | Set here by | Framework default | What a violation produces |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Request body size**, bytes on the wire | `[RequestSizeLimit(16 * 1024)]` | 30 MB | The server refuses the body and the request answers **413**, before form parsing and before model binding. This is the only limit on this endpoint that produces 413 |
| **Form shape** — `ValueCountLimit = 32`, `KeyLengthLimit = 128`, `ValueLengthLimit = 4096`, `MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0` | `[RequestFormLimits(...)]` | 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,194,304 / 128 MB | The **form parser** throws `InvalidDataException` the first time the body is read. That read happens inside the **global anti-forgery filter**, which touches `Request.Form` before model binding, so the request answers **400** — not 413, and **not** a field-level validation message, because no model was ever bound |

The form limits bound the shape as well as the total, because a single 4 MB field and thirty thousand
empty ones are both accepted under a byte ceiling alone, and both cost model binding, validation and — if
the values were echoed or recorded — logging. `MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0` refuses multipart bodies
outright: this form posts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and has no file input, so multipart is only
ever a probe.

**`ValueLengthLimit = 4096` is a deliberate tightening by three orders of magnitude, and it draws a second
boundary that acceptance tests have to respect.** It sits far above every legitimate field — the longest
is the 254-character `Email` bound of section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) — and far below anything worth calling a
payload. So a field of, say, five thousand characters is a **parser**-boundary case that answers 400 with
no field message, while a field of three hundred characters is a **model**-boundary case that answers 200
with a field message from its `[StringLength]`. Both behaviours are correct and neither substitutes for
the other: a suite that submits five thousand characters and expects a validation message is asserting an
outcome the parser precludes, and one that only ever submits five thousand characters never exercises the
DataAnnotations bounds at all. The coverage assertion requires the two boundaries separately for that reason.

Either refusal is a change from the source, which accepts such a request and answers 200; both are
covered by **approved delta 21** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — 413 for the
byte ceiling, 400 for the form shape — and in both cases no bound value, no cart read and no log record
carrying a payload exists. The same discipline is **not** applied to the account POSTs: they carry no
`[RequestFormLimits]`, so the framework's 4,194,304-character default applies and even a
hundred-thousand-character user name parses and reaches model validation, which is exactly why their
bounds are model-level by design (section
[6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)) and why coverage
The coverage assertion requires a validation message and 200 there rather than a refusal.

**The submission key, and the reason this path needs one: a throwing commit does not mean nothing was
committed.** The obvious reading of step 8 below — the transaction threw, therefore nothing persisted —
is true of a failed `SaveChangesAsync` and **false of a failed `CommitAsync`**. A commit that reached
the server, succeeded there, and whose acknowledgement was then lost to a dropped connection, a
cancelled token or a request timeout raises an exception that is **indistinguishable** from one raised by
a commit that never happened. The client sees the redisplayed form of the failure table, does the only
thing a customer does with a redisplayed checkout form, and **submits again — creating a second real
order for one purchase.** Nothing in the transaction, the retry policy or the catch list can tell the two
apart, because the information needed to tell them apart never arrived. So the write is made
**idempotent** instead, keyed on something durable:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Generation** | The **server** generates the key — `Guid.NewGuid()` — in the `GET` action, which today returns a bare `View()` with no model [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:17-20] and in the target passes it to the view for a hidden field. It is never taken from a client-supplied value, on a fresh render or on any other |
| **Binding — the key travels as a protected token, not as a bare GUID** | A bare `Guid?` on the wire is **client-chosen state**, and a mechanism keyed on client-chosen state is not a control: a caller can mint one, omit one, or post one that was issued to somebody else. So the hidden field carries a **data-protection protected token** whose payload is the GUID, the **user name it was issued to** and its issue time; the handler unprotects it to obtain the GUID. A token that cannot be unprotected has been tampered with or was produced by a different key ring; a token whose user name is not the authenticated caller's was issued to somebody else; a token older than **24 hours** (absolute, no sliding renewal) belongs to a form nobody is still filling in. **None of the three is accepted**, and none of them requires server-side state to detect — which is what lets the check run on a replica that never rendered the form |
| **Stability across redisplays** | Every redisplay of the form — the `ModelState` failure of step 1, the promo-code no-match of step 2, the empty-cart rejection of step 4 and every row of the failure table — re-renders **the same token that arrived**, so the idempotency window is not closed at the exact moment a customer is most likely to resubmit. A **fresh** token is minted only where there was no valid one to re-render: the `GET` action, and the step-0 rejection below |
| **Persistence** | A nullable `SubmissionId` column on `Orders`, set in step 5 from the unprotected key. **`NULL` is permitted for exactly one reason and one population: rows loaded from the legacy store, which have no key because the source has no such concept.** It is **not** a permitted state for an order the target creates — step 0 rejects a submission with no valid key before any cart work, so there is no path on which the target inserts a `NULL` here. Stating it the other way round is what makes the mechanism bypassable: "a submission that arrives without a key still has to be able to place an order" is precisely the sentence an attacker, and an ordinary double-click, both rely on |
| **The constraint** | A **unique index on `SubmissionId`, filtered to `WHERE [SubmissionId] IS NOT NULL`.** The filter is not optional: SQL Server's unique index treats two `NULL`s as equal, so an unfiltered one would reject the second migrated order. This index is what makes the guarantee a database guarantee rather than an application convention, and it is the only thing that holds under two concurrent submissions of the same key |
| **Schema sequencing** | The column and its index are **net-new target state and therefore arrive in a second catalog migration**, applied after the baseline migration and after the domain data load. They are deliberately **not** in the initial migration, because that migration must match the extracted source schema exactly or the generated-schema diff of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) fails — and it should fail on a real discrepancy, not on this one |
| **Reconciliation on retry** | Step 1a below. A submission whose key already names an order belonging to this caller is **not written again**: it is redirected to that order's confirmation, which is the outcome the customer was owed by the attempt that was lost |
| **The concurrent race** | Two submissions of the same key that overlap cannot both be reconciled by a lookup, because neither has committed when the other reads. One insert wins and the other violates the unique index. That branch is in the failure table below, and it resolves the same way step 1a does — look the key up, redirect to the order that won — rather than as a user-facing error |
| **Rejection, and where it happens** | **Step 0**, ahead of everything: a submission with no token, an unprotectable one, one issued to another user name, or one past its 24-hour lifetime **re-renders the checkout form with a fresh token and one generic model error** — *"Your checkout form has expired. Please review your details and submit again."* — and **reads no cart row, opens no transaction and writes nothing**. The status is 200 and the submitted address values are re-rendered so the customer does not retype them. Two things this is **not**: it is not an anti-forgery control — the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) has already validated that token, and this one answers a different question — and it is not a security boundary around the order itself, which is `[Authorize]` plus the username predicate of step 1a. It is the guarantee that **every** order the target writes carries a server-issued key, which is what the unique index then makes enforceable |

This is an addition to the source's behaviour with no source analogue: the source has no retry path at
all, since its bare `catch` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62] redisplays
the form and records nothing. It is recorded under approved delta 16 in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), whose subject is already this action's write discipline.
**The coverage assertion requires it against the exact failure it exists for** — a commit that succeeds on the
server with the acknowledgement lost — and the coverage assertion requires the cancellation route into the same
condition.

| Step | Contract | Why it is where it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | **Submission-token validation, before `ModelState` and before anything else in the method body.** Unprotect `submissionToken`; require that it unprotects, that its user name equals `User.Identity!.Name`, and that its issue time is within 24 hours. **Any failure re-renders the form with a fresh token and the generic expiry message, reading no cart row and writing nothing.** On success the unprotected `Guid` is what steps 1a and 5 use | **A key that is only validated later is not a key.** Placed after step 1 it would be skipped for any submission that also failed validation — so a caller could drive unlimited order attempts by posting a deliberately invalid model with no token and fixing the model on the attempt that counts. Placed after step 1a it would let a fabricated GUID be used as a lookup predicate. It is also the cheapest check on the path: no database round trip, so a crafted request costs one unprotect and stops |
| 1 | **`if (!ModelState.IsValid) { return View(input); }` — before any read or write.** Nothing is written on this path | The source **discards** the result of `TryUpdateModel` [:29] and no `ModelState.IsValid` check appears anywhere in the controller, so an order failing its own `[Required]` and `[StringLength]` attributes [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] is **persisted** whenever the promo code matches. Adding the gate is a behaviour change and is approved delta 16 in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) |
| 1a | **Replay reconciliation, before anything else touches the cart.** With the key step 0 produced, `await db.Orders.SingleOrDefaultAsync(o => o.SubmissionId == submissionKey && o.Username == User.Identity!.Name, cancellationToken)`. **A match returns `RedirectToAction("Complete", new { id = order.OrderId })` and writes nothing.** No match continues. The key is never null here, because step 0 has already refused that case. The lookup is filtered by username as well as by key so that even a key obtained some other way cannot reveal, or redirect to, another customer's order — it behaves exactly as if no such key existed | **This step's position is the whole of its correctness.** It has to be before step 4, because a first attempt that committed **has already emptied the cart** — so a retry that reached step 4 would be rejected as an empty cart, and the customer would be told their cart is empty while an order they cannot see sits in the database. It is placed before step 2 as well, so a retry short-circuits regardless of any later branch. It reads and does not write, so it costs one indexed lookup on the normal path |
| 2 | **Promo-code evaluation, three named branches.** `string.Equals(input.PromoCode, PromoCode, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` against `const string PromoCode = "FREE"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:12] — the comparison and the constant are preserved exactly, and the constant stays a compile-time constant rather than becoming configuration. **Match → continue. No match → redisplay with a model error against `PromoCode`, nothing written. Absent (null or empty) → the same branch as no match, deliberately** | The source's comparison [:33-34] redisplays with **no message** [:36], which is why an invalid code looks like a broken form. Missing and invalid must be the *same* stated branch because a nine-property input model makes "missing" the only reachable outcome (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)) — the trap that section exists to close |
| 3 | **Enter the retrying execution strategy's transaction wrapper, which is what opens the transaction — and the submission key is verified *inside* it. The wrapper is entered *after* steps 4 to 7 have run, and its delegate contains step 8 and nothing else.** `var strategy = db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy();` then `await strategy.ExecuteInTransactionAsync(operation: async ct => { if (await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(o => o.SubmissionId == submissionKey && o.Username == userName, ct)) { replayObserved = true; return; } /* step 8 only — no construction, no re-read of the cart */ }, verifySucceeded: async ct => await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(o => o.SubmissionId == submissionKey && o.Username == userName, ct), cancellationToken);` then, if `replayObserved`, the redirect of step 1a; otherwise `db.ChangeTracker.AcceptAllChanges();`. **`BeginTransactionAsync` is not called here and must not be**, for the reason stated immediately after this table, and **the replay boundary is where it is for the reason stated immediately after that** | The path performs one read and three logical writes (order, details, cart emptying). A single `SaveChangesAsync` is already atomic, but that atomicity is then a property of *how many save calls happen to exist*. An explicit transaction makes it a stated property that survives a later edit, and it is what the rollback assertion in the coverage assertion tests against. The wrapper is what makes that transaction **compatible with the catalog context's `EnableRetryOnFailure`** and what supplies the commit-unknown decision procedure the submission key was introduced for. **The key is checked in three distinct places and none of them is redundant:** step 1a checks it *before* the request does anything, outside any transaction, and answers a customer's resubmission; this in-operation check runs *inside* the wrapper's transaction on **every** attempt including every replay, so a replay can never insert a second order even where `verifySucceeded` was not consulted; and `verifySucceeded` answers the one question neither read can, namely whether a commit whose acknowledgement was lost had in fact committed. The filtered unique index of the submission-key table above is the fourth and final guard, refusing a second row at the store rather than trusting any of the three reads |
| 4 | **Read the cart rows** through `ShoppingCartService`, with the album eagerly loaded (lazy-loading site a6, section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)). **This step and steps 5 to 7 run once, before the wrapper of step 3 is entered** — they are listed after it because they are what the wrapper's single save sends, not because they execute inside it. **An empty cart is rejected**: a model error, nothing written, and the wrapper is never entered | The source iterates zero items, sets `Total = 0` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:151] and **persists a zero-total order with no lines**. That is a junk row a customer can create by resubmitting the form after a successful checkout; rejecting it is part of approved delta 16 |
| 5 | **Construct the order.** `Username = User.Identity!.Name` — the username invariant of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration), preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:40]; `OrderDate = DateTime.UtcNow` per section [8.11](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display); the nine address properties copied from the input model; and **`SubmissionId = submissionKey`** — the key step 0 unprotected, never a value read straight off the wire — which is what this row will be reconciled against if its commit is ever indeterminate. **`Total` is not set here and is never bound** | `Total` is computed in step 6 from the rows actually billed. It carries `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] and is absent from the input model, so no request can influence it — The coverage assertion |
| 6 | **Build the order details through the principal's navigation collection.** For each cart row: load the album (**census site F6** — missing album is a data-integrity failure, section [4.9](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census)), construct `new OrderDetail { AlbumId = …, UnitPrice = album.Price, Quantity = item.Count }` **with no `OrderId` assignment**, and add it to `order.OrderDetails`. Then `order.Total` is the sum of `UnitPrice * Quantity` over those same rows | **This is the fixup defect, and it is the one place a line-for-line port breaks silently.** The source sets `OrderId = order.OrderId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:139] at a point where the store has generated no key, so the value copied is `0`; EF 6 still associates the rows because the added principal is tracked under that same default key value and the generated key is propagated at insert. **EF Core tracks an added principal under a temporary key value, so a dependent whose `OrderId` is `0` is associated with nothing and the insert fails the foreign-key constraint.** Expressing the relationship through the navigation is correct on either runtime and does not depend on knowing which. `Order.OrderDetails` is a plain `List<OrderDetail>` with no initializer [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:66], so it must be instantiated. Computing `Total` from the **same** `album.Price` used for `UnitPrice` also removes the source's two-reads-of-one-value shape — unit price from the loaded album [:140] but the total from the lazy navigation [:145] — which can disagree under concurrent price edits |
| 7 | **Empty the cart** — the rows **read at step 4** are marked `Deleted` on the tracked graph, and the deletion is sent by step 8 inside the wrapper's transaction alongside the inserts. **The set deleted is exactly the set billed, because there is no re-read between step 4 and step 8 and that is deliberate.** So a row that a concurrent request inserts into the same cart after step 4 is **neither billed nor deleted**: it is still in the cart when the customer reaches the confirmation page, and their next visit to `/ShoppingCart` shows it, at its original `RecordId`, `Count` and `DateCreated`. **That is a difference from the source, in the safer direction**, and it is recorded under **approved delta 16** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) rather than as a new delta, for the reason opposite | **An earlier form of this row said the target "preserved, not fixed" the source's race — "a row added between step 4 and step 7 is removed without being billed" — and the algorithm above cannot produce that outcome**, so the claim is withdrawn: step 7 marks the step-4 graph `Deleted`, the concurrent row was never in that graph, and nothing else deletes it. The source behaves differently and worse: `EmptyCart` **re-queries** the cart at deletion time [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:87-96] after `CreateOrder` has already read the lines it bills [:129], so it deletes whatever is there when it runs and a concurrently added row is **destroyed without being billed**. Reproducing that would mean re-reading `Carts` between step 4 and step 8 and deleting whatever came back — writing a data-loss race in on purpose, and inside a transaction, where it would be *reliable* rather than occasional. **Not taken.** The outcome the stated algorithm produces is the one a customer would choose, it needs no extra work, and it belongs to the same rewritten write path, the same section and the same approval owners as delta 16 — which is why it is a clause of that row rather than a twenty-eighth delta. The coverage assertion requires both halves: the billed total covers exactly the step-4 rows, and the surviving row is untouched |
| 8 | **One `await db.SaveChangesAsync(acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false, ct)`, and nothing else — the commit is the wrapper's.** The `false` is required rather than stylistic: accepting the tracked changes at the end of the save would leave the change tracker believing the entities are persisted, so a replay driven by step 3's strategy would find nothing to re-send and commit an empty transaction. The tracked state is accepted **after** `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` returns, by the `AcceptAllChanges()` call in step 3. A throwing `SaveChangesAsync` leaves the wrapper's transaction uncommitted, so **no order, no order detail and no cart deletion is persisted**. A failure during the **commit** the wrapper performs is **indeterminate** — the server may have committed and lost the acknowledgement — and is **not** claimed to have persisted nothing; `verifySucceeded` is what decides it | The coverage assertion requires the determinate half: after a failure induced **inside `SaveChangesAsync`**, the order table, the order-detail table and the cart are all identical to their pre-request state. The coverage assertion requires the indeterminate half, and the coverage assertions require the replay and non-transient paths. Distinguishing the determinate case from the indeterminate one is the point — treating a failed commit as proof of rollback is what turns one lost acknowledgement into two orders |
| 9 | **`RedirectToAction("Complete", new { id = order.OrderId })`** — the generated key, available after step 8 | Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54]. The confirmation number a customer is shown is that key, which is why section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 forbids renumbering orders during migration |

**Why the transaction is the execution strategy's and not the caller's — this is a throw, not a
preference.** The catalog context is registered with `EnableRetryOnFailure` (section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)), and under a retrying execution strategy EF Core
**refuses** a user-initiated transaction: `BeginTransactionAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException`,
because the strategy cannot replay an operation whose transaction boundary it does not own — a retry
would re-run part of the work inside a transaction the caller had already begun or disposed. So the
`await using var transaction = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(...)` shape is not merely
suboptimal here; it fails on the first checkout submission, in every environment, at run time. The
cart-migration path in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) already wraps its transaction
in the strategy for the same reason, and this path now matches it rather than contradicting it.

**Where the replay boundary falls, and why the order graph is built outside it.**
`ExecuteInTransactionAsync` replays its `operation` delegate on a transient failure, and it replays it
against the **same `DbContext` and the same change tracker** — the strategy resets the connection and the
transaction, never the tracker. Step 8's `acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false` is what makes a replay able to
re-send the work, and it is also what makes the delegate's *contents* consequential: whatever the first
attempt added is **still `Added`** when the second attempt begins. So a delegate that **constructs** the
order graph accumulates rather than repeats. After a failed attempt the tracker already holds one `Added`
`Order` with its `OrderDetail` children and one `Deleted` `Cart` row per cart row read; a replay running
steps 5 to 7 again builds a **second** graph and re-marks the same cart rows; and the replay's single
`SaveChangesAsync` then sends **two** order inserts. Both carry the same `SubmissionId`, so the filtered
unique index of the submission-key table above refuses the second — turning a recoverable transient
failure into a **non-transient unique-index violation** that the strategy does not retry, that the
failure branch answers as a persistence error, and that costs the customer the order it was trying to
save. Were that index ever absent, the same replay would commit **two orders for one submission**, which
is the exact outcome the submission key was introduced to make impossible.

The rule therefore has two parts, and both are asserted rather than trusted:

- **Construction happens once, outside the replayable region.** Steps 4 through 7 run before
  `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` is called. The operation delegate contains **only** the in-operation
  submission-key guard of step 3 and step 8's single save: it creates no entity, mutates no entity, reads
  no cart row and computes no total, so its body is identical on every attempt **by construction** rather
  than by care. Placing the cart read outside the wrapper's transaction changes nothing about what is
  billed, because the read-then-empty race is already the preserved source behaviour recorded in step 7,
  and the three logical writes remain in one transaction — which is what atomicity here actually means.
- **The tracker state at the head of every attempt is a named invariant.** On entering the wrapper the
  tracker holds exactly one `Added` `Order`, exactly one `Added` `OrderDetail` per billed cart row and
  exactly one `Deleted` `Cart` row per cart row read — and it holds **that same set** at the head of every
  replay, because nothing between attempts adds to it and `acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false` prevents a
  successful-but-uncommitted save from emptying it. `db.ChangeTracker.AcceptAllChanges()` is called once,
  after the wrapper returns successfully, and that is the only point at which the invariant is permitted
  to change. **`db.ChangeTracker.Clear()` must not be called inside this delegate** — it would discard
  precisely the work the replay exists to re-send. That is the mirror image of the cart-migration
  delegate's requirement in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), where the delegate owns
  **no** tracked state and clearing is the safeguard; the two rules differ because the two delegates hold
  opposite kinds of state, and confusing them breaks whichever one borrows the other's rule.

**The coverage assertion's fourth companion assertion is what enforces this**, by observing the tracker's
contents at the head of every attempt and observing that the delegate constructs nothing.

**What `verifySucceeded` is for, and why this path has something to give it.** After a **retriable**
failure, the strategy cannot tell whether the transaction committed: the failure may have arrived before
the commit, or after a commit whose acknowledgement was lost. `verifySucceeded` is the application's
answer to that question, and it must be a read the application can trust:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **The check** | `await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(o => o.SubmissionId == submissionKey && o.Username == userName, ct)`. `AsNoTracking` is required: the failed attempt's entities are still tracked, and a tracking query could answer from the change tracker rather than from the store |
| **Why it is sound** | The submission key is unique per submission and carried on the order row under a filtered unique index, so the presence of a row bearing this key **is** the fact that this submission committed. Nothing else in the write has that property — the order id is generated by the insert, so it is unknown to a caller whose commit outcome is unknown, and a match on customer, total and timestamp would misidentify a genuine second order |
| **Outcome true** | The strategy stops retrying and returns as a success. The handler proceeds to step 9's redirect, which re-reads the order by key exactly as step 1a does |
| **Outcome false** | The strategy replays the whole operation — including, at its head, the in-operation submission-key re-read of step 3, which runs inside the fresh transaction and abandons the attempt if a row with this key has appeared meanwhile. Because step 8 deferred accepting the tracked changes, a replay that passes that guard re-sends the same inserts and the same deletions in the fresh transaction |
| **Non-transient failures** | Are not the strategy's business at all: it does not classify them as retriable, so it does not call `verifySucceeded` and does not replay. They propagate to the failure table below and are answered there. **The coverage assertion requires that a unique-index violation is answered once rather than attempted four times |
| **Cancellation** | Not a transient failure. The request token is passed to `ExecuteInTransactionAsync`, to the operation and to `verifySucceeded`, and a cancelled operation is not replayed — the convention of section [4.10](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once) |

**The coverage assertion drives a transient provider error at three points — inside `SaveChangesAsync`, during
the commit with the commit having failed, and during the commit with the commit having **succeeded** — and
asserts exactly one order in all three, which is the assertion that fails if `verifySucceeded` is omitted
or reads through the change tracker.

**The failure branches, replacing `catch { return View(order); }`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62].** The source's bare `catch` has no
exception variable: it discards the exception, redisplays an empty-looking form and records nothing
([08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt). The target catches by type:

The **classes are the persistence-failure classifier's**, defined once in section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and not re-derived here: the exception chain is walked to
its innermost provider exception, so a bare `SqlException` and one wrapped in `DbUpdateException` reach the
same row, and every redisplay row is subject to that section's render gate — which re-classifies the
failure as `Unavailable` where the store cannot be reached, so **no row in this table redisplays a page
that cannot render**.

| Class (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) | Caught here as | Response | Log | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `DuplicateSubmission` | A unique-constraint violation naming the `SubmissionId` index, bare or wrapped | **Not a user-facing failure.** The other submission of this key won the race and its order exists, so this one re-reads by key and username exactly as step 1a does and returns `RedirectToAction("Complete", new { id = … })`. If — and only if — that re-read finds nothing, the case falls through to `Rejected` rather than looping | `Information`, category `duplicate-submission`, with the winning `OrderId`. A concurrent double-submit is a customer double-clicking, not a fault | Row 70 |
| `Concurrency` | `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` | The form is redisplayed with one generic model error — *"We could not complete your order. Please try again."* — and nothing is persisted | `Error`, failure category `concurrency` | Row 42 |
| `Rejected` | A server-produced rejection of the command — foreign-key, check or other unique violation, permission refusal, deadlock victim — bare or wrapped | Same user-facing outcome as `Concurrency` | `Error`, failure category `persistence`. The innermost exception's **type** and the failure category are recorded — **not its message**, and the exception object is **not** passed to the logger, per section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types); nothing is surfaced in the response | Row 85 |
| `DataIntegrity` | The missing-album case of census site F6 | Same user-facing outcome | `Error`, failure category `missing-album`, with the cart record id and album id | Row 44 |
| `Unavailable` | A provider exception raised while opening the connection, a connection-level failure or an unanswered timeout — bare or wrapped — **or** any of the three rows above whose render gate found the store unreachable | **Not redisplayed.** Rethrown, so the exception-handling middleware answers with the layout-free generic 500 and a trace identifier | `Error`, failure category `database`, written by the `IExceptionHandler` of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) rather than twice | Row 85, and rows 71 to 72 for the recursion properties |
| `Cancelled` | `OperationCanceledException`, **caught only under the filter `when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)`** | **Not an error, and not an outcome.** No model error, no view, no status code — the catch body records the cancellation and then **`throw;`**, which is the only terminal behaviour available to it. Returning `View(input)` would write a response to a client that has gone and would report a *validation* shape for work that never completed; returning a status code would report an outcome nobody is listening for; and returning nothing does not compile in an `async Task<IActionResult>` method. Rethrowing hands the request back to the framework, which abandons the response for a cancelled request rather than inventing one, so **no 500 and no error page is produced**. The `await using` transaction is disposed on the way out, uncommitted — see the state note below, which is where the commit-time case is settled. An `OperationCanceledException` whose token is *not* the request token fails the filter, is **not** caught here, and travels on as the genuine fault it is | `Information`, category `cancelled`. Recorded before the rethrow, with the permitted fields below and nothing else | Row 69 |
| Unclassified | Anything the classifier does not recognize | **Not caught.** It reaches the exception-handling middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), which answers 500 with the generic view and a trace identifier | The closed record of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), written by its `IExceptionHandler` | Rows 56, 68 |

**The state each failure leaves behind, cancellation included — three cases, not one.** The coverage assertion
asserts all three.

- **Cancelled or failed before `SaveChangesAsync` completes** — steps 4 to 7. The in-flight command is
  aborted and the transaction is disposed without committing: **nothing persisted**, and the cart still
  holds every row it held.
- **Cancelled or failed after `SaveChangesAsync` but before the wrapper's commit completes.** The same
  outcome: an uncommitted transaction is rolled back by the server when the connection is released, so
  the order, the order details and the cart deletions all disappear together. This is the property step
  3's transaction wrapper exists to make stated rather than incidental.
- **Cancelled or failed *during* the wrapper's commit** — the one case where the client's outcome and the
  database's can differ, and it is not specific to cancellation: a dropped connection produces it too.
  A commit that reached the server and succeeded there, but whose acknowledgement never arrived, leaves
  **an order that exists** behind an exception that looks identical to one that changed nothing. Nothing
  in the transaction, the cancellation convention or the catch list can distinguish the two, so this path
  does not try to. It is settled by the **submission key** specified at the head of this section, in two
  places that do not overlap: **inside** the request, by step 3's `verifySucceeded`, where the failure was
  retriable and the strategy is deciding whether to replay; and **across** requests, by step 1a, where the
  customer resubmits. The honest statement is that a failing commit means *indeterminate*, never *nothing
  persisted* — and the two mechanisms above are what make *indeterminate* actionable rather than merely
  admitted.

**What the log record may contain, and what it may not.**
[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the log-privacy policy and this path is its most
sensitive consumer, because the request body is a name, a postal address, a phone number and an email
address. Applying that policy here:

- **Permitted, and the list is 06's and closed — it is that document's record shape `R3` and nothing
  else.** [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes the order record at **six** fields over
  its envelope `R1`: the `OrderId` once assigned, the **line-item count**, the **order total**, the
  **outcome**, a failure **category** rather than a message and present only on a failure, and
  **`PromoCodeApplied`, a boolean**. This document emits exactly those six and **adds none** — a seventh
  field is a defect by that register's own rule, and an omitted one is an incomplete record, which is why
  the boolean is emitted on every order record rather than only when a code was supplied. The boolean's
  form is not a choice here either: [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s never-logged table
  forbids the promo code's *value*, so a recorded fact of *application* has exactly one admissible shape.
  The **trace identifier** is present because it is an `R1` envelope field attached to every application
  record, including the failed-rehash diagnostic of [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md); it is not an
  order-specific field, it is not counted among the six, and it is not this document's to add or withhold.
  The **submission key is deliberately not logged**: the duplicate-submission case is identified by the
  `OrderId` of the order the reconciliation of step 1a matched, which is already permitted, so nothing is
  lost by keeping the closed list closed.
- **The level is `R1`'s and follows the outcome** — `Information` on success and `Error` on failure, per
  [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R3` row, under the application's own
  `MvcMusicStore` category. It is stated because a single fixed level would make a failed checkout
  indistinguishable from a successful one at the sink's filter.
- **The actor is the Identity `UserId`** — the GUID, `User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)` —
  **never the login name**, even though `User.Identity.Name` is what the order row itself stores. That is
  one of the **exactly two** actor values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits an
  application record to carry; the other, the literal **`anonymous`**, cannot arise here because the
  checkout write path is reachable only by an authenticated principal (section
  [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)), and a
  `SubjectPseudonym` is a *subject* field rather than an actor and never appears in this position.
- **Never logged:** `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`,
  `Phone`, `Email`, the promo-code value, the session id, any cookie value and any anti-forgery token.
  This is why the `DbUpdateException` row above logs the inner exception's type rather than the entity values
  that caused it: a constraint-violation message can carry a column value.

### 8.13 Timestamp semantics — UTC in the database, converted for display

The migration source writes **local server time** in both places it writes a timestamp:
`order.OrderDate = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:41] and
`DateCreated = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:49]. Neither value carries
an offset, and `DateTime.Kind` is not persisted, so **the stored rows record a wall-clock reading whose
zone is a property of the machine that wrote them** and is documented nowhere.

**This is a decision the port cannot avoid, because the meaning of the identical line of code changes
underneath it.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) selects a Linux App Service host, whose
process time zone is UTC unless configured otherwise. Porting `DateTime.Now` verbatim therefore yields
UTC values in the same column that already holds local ones, with no marker distinguishing them — a
silent, permanent mixed-zone column. **The decision:**

| Part | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| **Storage** | **UTC.** Both writes become `DateTime.UtcNow`, and both columns end as `datetime2` — EF Core's default mapping for `DateTime` on SQL Server. **The type change does not reach the schema baseline, and it is not annotated onto the diff.** Section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 admits **zero** differences and no annotation, so where extraction (step 1) shows `datetime`, the baseline model maps `datetime` explicitly and the widening ships afterwards as the named `AlterTimestampColumnTypes` migration in that section's third held-back group — after the load and after reconciliation, before traffic admission. Where extraction shows the columns are already `datetime2`, the baseline maps `datetime2` and no alteration migration exists. Either way the diff gate compares a baseline that reproduces the source exactly |
| **Migration** | The domain-data load takes a **required `LegacySourceTimeZone` parameter** — a time-zone identifier resolvable by `TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById` — and converts every legacy `Order.OrderDate` and `Cart.DateCreated` from that zone to UTC as it loads. **It fails closed**: if the parameter is absent, unresolvable, or if any source value is an *invalid* local time in that zone (a reading inside a spring-forward gap, which indicates the wrong zone was supplied), the load **stops before writing any row**. An *ambiguous* value (inside a fall-back overlap) is resolved with the **standard-time** offset and recorded per row in the migration log, because one hour of ambiguity on an order timestamp is tolerable and a silent guess is not |
| **Display** | UTC is converted to a configured presentation zone at render time, `Display:TimeZone` in configuration, **defaulting to `UTC`**. Stated for completeness and for the acceptance test below: **no view in the migration source renders either value** — `git grep -n 'OrderDate\|DateCreated' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore'` returns four matches, all of them the two writes and the two property declarations, and none of them a `.cshtml` file. So this rule governs the migration equivalence check and any later display, not an existing page |
| **New writes after cutover** | Are UTC by construction, so the column is single-zoned from the first row written by the target |

**Acceptance**, as the coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage): a newly created
order's `OrderDate` and a newly created cart row's `DateCreated` are both UTC within a tolerance of the
test clock; a migration run with no `LegacySourceTimeZone` writes **nothing**; and for a migrated legacy
order, the stored UTC value converted back to the supplied source zone equals the wall-clock value the
source row held. Approved delta 17 in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) records the
change, with **Data owner and Product** as approval owner — the data owner because it rewrites stored
values, Product because the zone a timestamp is understood in is a user-facing decision.

---

#### 8.8.1 The view rewrite — why changing only `@model` renders `PromoCode` twice

**Designing the input model is half of this change. The view that posts to it is the other half, and it
is the half where a duplicate control appears silently.**
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml` is declared
`@model MvcMusicStore.Models.Order` [:1] and renders the whole Shipping fieldset [:14-18] with a
**single** call — `@Html.EditorForModel()` [:17]. The tenth field is written by hand in the Payment
fieldset [:19-29]: `@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [:24] and `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [:27], each inside
a `div` [:23], [:26].

**What that single call renders today is nine editors, and the reason is an attribute rather than
anything in the view.** `Order` exposes fourteen members. Four are suppressed with
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` — `OrderId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:11-12], `OrderDate`
[:14-15], `Username` [:17-18] and `Total` [:63-64] — and `OrderDetails` [:66] is a collection the object
template skips. Nine remain, which is why one untyped call happens to render exactly the nine that
`[Bind]` [:8] also permits. Two independent attribute-driven mechanisms agree by coincidence, and
neither is visible in the view.

**Point `@model` at the ten-property input model and leave `EditorForModel()` in place, and `PromoCode`
renders twice.** It is an ordinary string with no `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]`, so the object template emits
an editor for it — `name="PromoCode"`, `id="PromoCode"` — **inside the Shipping fieldset**, while the
hand-written control [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27] emits a second
input with the same name and the same id. Three consequences, none of which produces an error at build
time:

- **A duplicate `id`.** Invalid HTML, and a `for` attribute can no longer identify one control — so the
  label association this rewrite is supposed to fix (section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b2) cannot be established at all.
- **Two form entries under one key.** The form value provider surfaces both and a simple string target
  receives them combined rather than either one alone. Whatever the exact combining rule, the bound
  value is not `FREE`, so the comparison
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-34] fails and **every checkout returns to
  the form** — the same end state as the nine-property near-miss above, reached by the opposite mistake.
- **One concept labelled twice, in two fieldsets**, one of them headed "Shipping Information"
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:15].

**Decision: `EditorForModel()` is replaced by the nine shipping fields rendered explicitly, and
`PromoCode` is rendered exactly once, in the Payment fieldset.** Element by element — every bare
locator in the table below is a line of
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml`:

| Current element | Target |
| --- | --- |
| `@model MvcMusicStore.Models.Order` [:1] | `@model MvcMusicStore.Binding.CheckoutInputModel` |
| `@Html.EditorForModel()` [:17] | **Nine explicit fields** in the `[Bind]`-list order [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] — `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`, `Phone`, `Email` — each a `<label asp-for>`, an `<input asp-for>` and a `<span asp-validation-for>` |
| `@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [:24] | `<label asp-for="PromoCode">`, whose `for` is derived from the same expression as the input's `id`, fixing the association defect of section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b2 |
| `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [:27] | `<input asp-for="PromoCode">` plus a `<span asp-validation-for="PromoCode">` the field has never had, rendered **only here** |
| `<div class="editor-label">` [:23], `<div class="editor-field">` [:26] | **Retained, and repeated around each of the nine explicit fields**, because that is the wrapper shape `@Html.EditorForModel()` [:17] puts around every field today. **No stylesheet in the application defines either** — `git grep -n 'editor-label\|editor-field' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content'` returns no match — so the class names carry no appearance and are kept for continuity with the generated markup they replace; what carries the appearance is the `<div>` block formatting, which is exactly what must not change ([8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)) |
| No validation summary at all | `<div asp-validation-summary="ModelOnly">` — see below |
| `@Scripts.Render("~/bundles/jqueryval")` [:8] | The two validation `<script>` elements of section [8.1.3](#813-the-rendered-tags-and-every-bundle-path-they-replace), in the required order |
| `@using (Html.BeginForm())` [:11], `<input type="submit">` [:31] | Unchanged in shape. The form tag helper emits the anti-forgery token automatically, replacing nothing the view declares today — this view has no `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()`, which is why the checkout write is one of the five unprotected POST actions section [7.2](#72-problem-one--coverage-today-is-partial) counts |

**The rejected alternative, and why.** An editor template for `CheckoutInputModel` that excludes
`PromoCode` — or `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` on the property — would also render nine fields, and it is
rejected: it would leave the view's rendered field set governed by an invisible attribute on a class in
another file, which is precisely the arrangement that makes the current view fragile. Explicit fields
put the nine, their order and their per-field markup where a reviewer of the port can see them, and they
are what section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b1-b5 attach to.
`EditorForModel()` over the new type is rejected outright, for the duplicate above.

**The field structure is stacked, not horizontal, because that is what this form is today.** This is the
one form in the application that carries no form class —
`Html.BeginForm()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:11] with no
attributes, against the seven `form-horizontal` shapes section
[8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) inventories — and the object template
stacks the label above the field inside two block wrappers. **The target reproduces that shape rather
than re-expressing it in the successor's form utilities**, and the three utilities a Bootstrap 5 port
reaches for by reflex are each rejected for a measured reason: `mb-3` would insert `1rem` between
groups that have **no** vertical gap today, `form-label` would add `0.5rem` under each label where the
source adds none, and `form-control` would replace an unstyled browser control with the library's
`34px`, bordered, rounded box — a visible change on nine fields plus the promo code. The wrappers are
kept, no field class is added, and the fields therefore keep the one constraint that *does* shape them
today, `input, select, textarea { max-width: 280px }`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:13-17], retained by section
[8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list):

```razor
<div class="editor-label">
    <label asp-for="FirstName"></label>
</div>
<div class="editor-field">
    <input asp-for="FirstName" />
    <span asp-validation-for="FirstName"></span>
</div>
```

**The validation span carries no colour class either, and does not need one.** The validation tag
helper emits the same `field-validation-valid` and `field-validation-error` class names the current
markup relies on, and section [8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list) retains the six
`Content/Site.css` rules that style them — including the `#b94a48` the error message renders in
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:20-22], with the valid state hidden outright by
`.field-validation-valid { display: none }` [:24-26]. Adding `text-danger` would set the same colour a
second time through a utility carrying `!important`, so the retained rule would no longer be what
governs the message — and the reviewer's colour check in section
[8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) would be measuring the wrong
declaration. The submit control likewise stays unclassed, exactly as it
is today [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:31].

The nine `[Required]`, `[StringLength]`, `[DisplayName]`, `[DataType]` and `[RegularExpression]`
annotations move to the input model verbatim (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)), so each label renders the same text it
renders today — `First Name`, `Last Name`, `Postal Code` and `Email Address` come from `[DisplayName]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:21], [:26], [:43], [:57] and the other five from the property
names — and each field keeps its current client-side rules. The email message's existing wording,
`"Email is is not valid."` [:59], is carried across **as written**: correcting the doubled word is a
user-visible content change, which belongs to Product rather than to the port.

**The validation summary is `ModelOnly`, chosen from the application's own convention.** The view has
none today — `git grep -n ValidationSummary -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'` matches seven views and **not this
one**, so a model-level failure currently renders no message anywhere on the checkout page. Of those
seven, five use the model-level-only overload and two the all-errors overload, so `ModelOnly` is the
majority convention and it avoids duplicating messages that already render beside their field. It is
also where the two model-level errors land: the promo-code rejection and the message the replaced
`catch` adds (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)).

**Both redisplay paths return the input model.** `View(order)` appears twice — the promo-code rejection
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:36] and the bare `catch` [:61] — and both must
pass the **input model** instance in the target, not an `Order`. The type has to match `@model`, and
`Order` has no `PromoCode` property to redisplay. One consequence is worth naming because it is an
**addition rather than a change**, registered as **A15** in section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions): today the nine shipping values do repopulate on redisplay, because they
are bound onto the `Order` the view is handed, while the promo-code box re-renders **empty** — nothing
binds `PromoCode`, so neither model state nor the model can supply it to
`@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27]. After
the rewrite it is a bound property and repopulates with the rest. Nothing that works today stops
working.

**In the action, explicit mapping replaces `TryUpdateModel`.** The nine input-model properties are
assigned onto a new `Order`; `Username` and `OrderDate` stay server-set
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:40-41]; `Total` continues to be written by
`cart.CreateOrder(order)` [:48]; and `PromoCode` is read from the input model instead of
`values["PromoCode"]` [:33] and **never persisted**. That mapping — not an attribute — is the
over-posting control in the target, which is the point section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) makes about both halves moving
together.

Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) carries the assertions this rewrite has to satisfy: one control
named `PromoCode` and one only, a label whose `for` resolves to it, the nine fields with their display
names and validation messages, valid / invalid / missing promo-code behaviour, and a redisplay that
retains what the user typed.

### 8.9 Accessibility and interaction-state requirements

**Scope, stated before the list, because the boundary matters.** Every item below is a **static,
checkable requirement on the ported markup**, derived from a named defect or gap in the source. Two
things this section deliberately does **not** do:

- **It does not claim conformance to any accessibility standard.** Conformance cannot be established
  from source: it needs a running application, assistive technology and a contrast tool. The claim this
  section supports is "these requirements are met", and conformance is asserted — if at all — only after
  the **manual accessibility review** that [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries as a task,
  which is separate from the appearance review of section
  [12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) because screenshots cannot verify
  keyboard operation, focus order, announcement or contrast.
- **It does not authorize a redesign.** Where a requirement would change appearance, the change is
  named and bounded: a heading's semantic level changes while its rendered size is held with a type
  utility, a link becomes a button styled to look the same. The no-redesign boundary of section
  [1.2](#12-what-this-document-is-not) holds.

Most of these are **net-new**, because the source has essentially none of them. That is the finding, not
a criticism of the requirement list — and because they are net-new they are **approval-owned rather than
free**: they are rows in the additions register of section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions), with a named owner, and none of them is described in this document
as an improvement that needs no decision.

**Which register each item lands on, stated exhaustively so that "most" is not doing work a count should
do.** There are **22** numbered requirements below — `a1`-`a7` plus `a5b` (8), `b1`-`b5` (5), `c1`-`c5`
(5) and `d1`-`d4` (4) — and each one lands in exactly one of three places:

- **Sixteen are net-new and carried by the additions register** — `a1`, `a2`, `a3`, `a4`, `a5`, `a5b`,
  `a6`, `b2`, `b3`, `b4`, `b5`, `c1`, `c2`, `c3`, `c4`, `c5`. They resolve to **thirteen** rows of
  section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions), because three of those rows each cover a pair:
  `a1`+`a2`, `a5`+`a5b` and `b3`+`b4`.
- **Two change an existing behaviour and are therefore approved deltas, not additions** — `a7` is
  **delta 13** (the sign-out control), and `d1` is **delta 19** (the focus ring's presentation preserved
  and its selector narrowed), both in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).
- **Four are on neither register, by kind rather than by omission** — `b1` records a behaviour the source
  **already has** and the port preserves; `d2` is a **prohibition** on the port's own stylesheet; and
  `d3` and `d4` are **measurements** that record ratios against stated thresholds. None of the four is a
  change, so none needs an approver.

**16 + 2 + 4 = 22**, so every requirement is accounted for exactly once and no item is left as an
unowned improvement.

**Structure and semantics.**

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a1 | **The navbar toggle gets an accessible name and announces its state.** `aria-controls` naming the collapse element's id (the id introduced in section [8.5.3](#853-non-class-markup-that-changes-with-the-library)), `aria-expanded` maintained by the collapse plugin, and an explicit `aria-label` — "Toggle navigation" | `<button type="button" class="navbar-toggle" data-toggle="collapse" data-target=".navbar-collapse">` with three unlabelled `<span>` bars and **no accessible name and no state attribute at all** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15-18] |
| a2 | **The genre dropdown is operable from the keyboard and announces its state, and its `href` stays a real destination.** `aria-expanded` managed by the plugin, `dropdown-item` on the menu anchors, and `<hr class="dropdown-divider">` in place of an empty `<li class="divider">` — an empty list item announced as a list item with no content. **The toggle keeps `href="@Url.Action("Store")"` and therefore does *not* take `role="button"`**: the source anchor is a working link to the store index that *also* opens the menu, so it is a link that behaves like one, and re-describing it as a button would misannounce a real navigation and discard the no-JavaScript fallback. That fallback is the reason the decision goes this way rather than the other: with scripting unavailable or the plugin failing to load, the anchor still reaches the catalog, whereas `href="#"` plus `role="button"` would leave the genre navigation with no destination at all. Section [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)'s `dropdown-toggle` row is corrected to match — no `role="button"` is added | `<a href="@Url.Action("Store")" class="dropdown-toggle" data-toggle="dropdown">Store <b class="caret"></b></a>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/GenreMenu.cshtml:4] — **a real link, not `href="#"`** — menu at [:5], empty divider at [:14] |
| a3 | **The showcase image gets an image alternative.** Either a meaningful `alt` describing the promotion, or `alt=""` if it is decided to be purely decorative. **The decision is recorded with its reason**, because an omitted `alt` and a deliberately empty one are indistinguishable in markup and opposite in meaning | `<img src="~/Images/home-showcase.png" />` — **no `alt` attribute** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:7]. The album images already carry one [:15], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:17], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:10], so this is the outlier rather than the pattern |
| a4 | **The catalog page gets a top-level heading and a coherent level sequence.** The page heading becomes `<h1>` and album titles take the next level, with the **rendered size held by a type utility** (`class="h3"` on the `<h1>`, `class="h5"` on the album heading). **That preserves the appearance only because the utilities themselves are pinned**, and the dependency is stated rather than assumed: the successor's `h3` and `h5` are not the source's, so an unpinned `class="h3"` would hold a *different* size and this item would silently resize the page heading it is supposed to leave alone. Group **1b** of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) declares `.h3` at `24px` and `.h5` at `14px`, the values the source's `<h3>` and `<h5>` render at today [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:522-525], [:532-535], which is what makes the substitution size-neutral. The misapplied form class is **dropped** rather than translated (section [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)) | `<h3>` page heading [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:6] with **no `<h1>` anywhere on the page**, jumping to `<h5 class="control-label">` per album [:19] |
| a5 | **All three data tables get an accessible name and explicit structure**, and **two different defects are being fixed**, so the treatment differs by table. For the two tables that *have* header cells: a `<caption>` or `aria-label`, `<thead>` around the header row, `<tbody>` around the data rows, `scope="col"` on every header cell, and a name for the empty action-column header rather than a blank. For the third — see the row below, because it has no header cells at all and its treatment is deliberately narrower | The cart table is `<table id="cart-summary" class="table table-striped">` with a bare `<tr>` of `<th>` elements, **no `<thead>`, no `<tbody>`, no `scope`, no caption**, and an empty `<th></th>` for the remove column [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:47-59]. The administration table is the same shape [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Index.cshtml:24-25] |
| a5b | **The Registered Logins table gets an accessible name and keeps its headerless shape.** The name is supplied by pointing `aria-labelledby` at the visible `<h4>Registered Logins</h4>` that already sits immediately above it, given an `id` for the purpose — reusing the heading rather than inventing a `<caption>`, so the table's name has one source of truth and the rendering does not change by a pixel. **It does not gain a header row, and that is a decision rather than an omission**: the table has *no* `<th>` anywhere, so there are no mismarked headers to correct, and every way of adding column context is visible — a `<thead>` adds a row of height and a border, `<th scope="row">` on the provider cell renders it bold, and a `visually-hidden` header row still occupies its row box. Changing the rendering of a retained surface would need an approved delta under section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), and the accessible name plus the per-button `title` already present [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:21] carry the meaning at zero visual cost. If a stakeholder later prefers visible column headers, that is a scoped addition with its own approval owner, exactly as the disabled-control option in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (5) is | `<table class="table">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:6] with a `<tbody>` [:7] and **no `<thead>`, no header row, no `<th>` of any kind and no caption** — two columns, the provider name [:11] and the removal control [:12-29]. It is easy to miss because the whole table is inside `@if (Model.Count > 0)` [:3] and because section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (5) relocates it into a view component; **it is retained, so it is in scope** |
| a6 | **Cart removal becomes a semantic control.** `<button type="button" class="RemoveLink link-button">` carrying the same `data-id` / `data-url` attributes, so the externalized script of section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script) selects it unchanged. A button is keyboard-operable and announced as a control by default; the label text is unchanged, and `link-button` — group 10 of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) — keeps it **rendering** as the inline link it is today, which is why this is an addition and not a visual delta | `<a href="#" class="RemoveLink" data-id="…" data-url="…">Remove from cart</a>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:74-77] — **a link that performs a state change and navigates nowhere**, reachable by keyboard only as a link to `#` |
| a7 | **The sign-out control becomes a submit control** | Already **approved delta 13** (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)), owned by section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface). Cross-referenced here rather than restated, because the accessibility benefit is a consequence of a decision taken elsewhere |

**Labels, errors and validation.**

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| b1 | **Every field's label is programmatically associated with its control.** In the ported forms this follows from `<label asp-for>` plus `asp-for` on the input, which derive the same name | 22 `control-label` sites, all of which do associate today via the typed helpers |
| b2 | **The promo-code label association is fixed.** `<label asp-for="PromoCode">` and `<input asp-for="PromoCode">` in section [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice)'s rewrite derive the same identifier, so the association exists for the first time | **`@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:24] emits a `for` derived from the string `"Promo Code"`, while `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [:27] emits `id="PromoCode"`.** The space guarantees the two values differ, so **there is no label association on this field today.** It is therefore an **addition rather than a change** — nothing that works today stops working, because nothing works today — and it is registered as **A10** in section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) rather than left as an unowned improvement |
| b3 | **Field errors are associated with their fields.** `aria-describedby` on the input referencing its validation-message element | Validation messages render adjacent to their inputs with **no programmatic association** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Login.cshtml:21], [:28] and the other form views |
| b4 | **Invalid inputs are marked invalid.** `aria-invalid="true"` set on inputs that fail validation, and removed when they pass. **This is net-new**: unobtrusive validation adds `input-validation-error` as a *class* [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:28-30] and sets **no ARIA state**, so the invalid condition is conveyed by colour alone today | the six validation rules [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:20-42] |
| b5 | **The checkout form gains a validation summary**, which it does not have today (section [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice)), placed so that it precedes the fields it describes | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:11-31] |

**The cart interaction — announcement, pending, failure and focus.** This is the one interactive surface
in the application, and it currently has none of the four.

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| c1 | **The status message is announced.** `role="status" aria-live="polite"` on the message container, with the cart count either updated inside that region or itself announced | `<div id="update-message"></div>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44-45] is written by script [:28] with **nothing announced**; the cart count is written to `#cart-status` [:29] — an element **no view emits**, which section [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract) supplies |
| c2 | **A pending state exists.** The control is disabled and carries `aria-busy="true"` while the request is in flight, and is re-enabled on completion — success or failure. **Net-new**: the source's handler has no pending state, so a double-click posts twice | `$.post(…)` [:17-31] with a success callback and nothing else |
| c3 | **Failure is handled and announced.** A visible error message in the live region of c1 on a failed or rejected request, and the row left unchanged. **Net-new, and the most consequential item in this table**: the source handler has **no failure path at all** — no `.fail`, no `error` callback, no status check — so a rejected removal (including one rejected by the anti-forgery validation of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems)) is **completely silent** and the user believes the item was removed | [:17-31] |
| c4 | **Focus is managed across the removal, to one deterministic destination.** The removed row is faded out while focus sits on the control inside it, so focus is destroyed with the row and lands on `<body>`. **The destination is the status container of c1, and it is made focusable to be one**: `<div id="update-message">` gains `tabindex="-1"` alongside c1's `role="status" aria-live="polite"`, and the script moves focus to it **in the `fadeOut` completion callback**, after the row is gone. `tabindex="-1"` is not optional decoration — **without it a `.focus()` call on a `<div>` does nothing at all**, focus stays on `<body>`, and the code reads as if it managed focus while doing nothing, which is the same silent failure the source already has. **There is no branch for the last row**: the container sits outside the table [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44-45] and is present whether or not any row remains, which is exactly why it is chosen over "the next actionable element" — that alternative needs a fallback for the emptied table and moves focus to a control whose position shifts under the user. One interaction between c1 and c4 is resolved rather than left open: if the interaction-state pass finds the message announced **twice** — once by the live region and once as the newly focused element's name — the remedy is to move focus **before** writing the message text, so the live region announces the change once; the pass records which ordering was used | `$('#row-' + data.DeleteId).fadeOut('slow')` [:22], with no focus handling of any kind, and `<div id="update-message">` [:44-45] carrying **no `tabindex`**, so it cannot receive focus even if a port called `.focus()` on it |
| c5 | **Animation respects a reduced-motion preference.** The fade is suppressed under `prefers-reduced-motion` | [:22] |

**Focus visibility and colour — checked, never asserted.**

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| d1 | **The focus indication on album links is restated and narrowed — it is not created.** Three things together: the source's own ring is **preserved** by group 2 of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses); its selector is **narrowed** to keyboard focus, which is **approved delta 19** (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)); and album links additionally get an explicit `:focus-visible` rule carrying the same shadow the source gives on `:hover`, so the focused state on those anchors reads the way the hovered state does. The underline-suppressing rule is **retained**, not deleted (section [8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list)). **Because this changes an existing behaviour rather than adding one, it sits on the deltas register and not on the additions register** — an earlier reading of this item had it the other way round | `ul#album-list li a, ul#album-details li a { text-decoration: none }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:61-63] removes the underline, and the shadow appears on `:hover` only [:65-70]. **A focused album link is nonetheless indicated today**: the library's global `a:focus { outline: thin dotted #333; outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color; outline-offset: -2px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:348-352] applies to it, and neither of the two application rules above declares an `outline` property, so nothing cancels it |
