## 10. Administrator provisioning becomes an operator command

### 10.1 What it is today

`private async void CreateAdminUser()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] runs at
application startup, called from `ConfigureApp` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18]. It reads two app settings [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24], hard-codes
the role name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:25], hand-builds a context, a user manager and a role manager [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29], creates the
role if absent [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:32-36], and creates the user if absent [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:38-44]. MVC 4 does the equivalent through
SimpleMembership [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:21-37].

Three properties of that make it the wrong shape rather than merely the wrong place:

- **`async void`.** An unhandled exception in an `async void` method has nowhere to propagate, so a
  provisioning failure at startup is **unobservable** — the application starts, appears healthy, and has
  no administrator ([09 §3.6](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding).
- **A plaintext credential in source control** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17], read on every
  start ([09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns it; [08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) rates
  it).
- **Partial idempotence.** See property 3 below.

### 10.2 The target: `tools/provision-admin`, and five required properties

A separate console project, `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj` and its `Program.cs`. Five
properties are **required**, not implied — each is a design constraint whose absence would reproduce a
defect the source has.

**One project, four verbs — stated here because this section is where a reader arrives looking for the
tool.** The mapped project is the **only** operator console project in the target
([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), and it carries four verbs: **`admin`**, the administrator
provisioning this section specifies; **`load-catalog`** and **`load-identity`**, the two data phases of
section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract); and **`seed`**, the
non-production seeding of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks). Section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) states why one project rather than
four. The division of labour inside this section follows from that: **properties 1, 1b, 3, 4 and 5 below
are the `admin` verb's**, while **properties 1a, 2 and 2a are the machinery all four verbs share** — the
host they build, the registration surface they reach across the `ProjectReference`, the principal and
connection channel they use, and the environment assertion every one of them makes before doing any work.
Where a load or seeding verb differs, the difference is stated in its own section and not here.

**1. The secret does not arrive on the command line.** A password passed as an argument is visible in
process listings to any user on the host and is recorded by shell history and by pipeline logs, which
would move the credential from one durable store to three. It is supplied either through an
**environment variable scoped to the single invocation**, or by **interactive prompt with terminal echo
disabled**. **The release process uses the environment-variable channel**, injected by the pipeline from
the platform secret store for that one step and not persisted to any file; the interactive prompt is
the path for an operator running the command by hand outside a pipeline. Both are implemented; the
command refuses to read a password from an argument at all, so the unsafe channel is not merely
discouraged.

**The three inputs, by name, because "supplied through the environment" is not an input contract.**

| Input | Channel | Exact name | Validated, before anything is written |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password | Environment variable scoped to the single invocation, **or** an echo-disabled prompt when the variable is absent and a terminal is attached | **`MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`** | Present and non-empty; then by **Identity's own password validators**, which is property 2's consequence rather than a second rule — so the policy of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) applies without being restated here |
| Target username | Command-line switch | **`--username`**, mapped to the configuration key `ProvisionAdmin:Username` | Present, non-whitespace, at most 256 characters, and **every character present in `Identity:UserAllowedUserNameCharacters`** (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). A username that violates the set can be created and then never updated, which is the defect section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) refuses to create during the load and this command refuses to create by hand |
| Role name | Command-line switch, **no default** | **`--role`**, mapped to `ProvisionAdmin:Role` | Present, non-whitespace, and **equal to `Administrator`** — the literal the authorization attribute names [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12]. Any other value provisions a role that authorizes nothing, which is [09 §5.2](09-security-assessment.md)'s MVC 3 failure reached by a different route |

**Why the username and role travel on the command line while the password cannot.** The two arguments
are *not* secrets, and their appearing in the pipeline's own record of the step is the point: the audit
record of property 4 and the pipeline log then agree on who was provisioned, without the tool having to
be trusted to report it. The password's channel is chosen by the opposite reasoning in the paragraph
above. **The absence of a default on `--role` is deliberate**: the source hard-codes the role name
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:25], and a default here would recreate that
invisibility — an operator who has to type the role is an operator who has read what they are granting.

**The two switches are mapped, not accepted raw.** This tool is the **only** host in the plan that
registers the command-line provider at all — the site is built parameterless precisely so that it does not
(section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)) — and here the provider is registered last and
outranks every other source, so a bare
`--username` would add a top-level configuration key named `username`. The tool therefore supplies an
explicit switch mapping — `--username` to `ProvisionAdmin:Username`, `--role` to `ProvisionAdmin:Role` —
and binds the pair to a validated `ProvisionAdminOptions` under the same `ValidateOnStart` mechanism as
every other options type. One property follows: the switches land in a section **no other part of this
contract defines**, so no argument can shadow a real key.

**1b. A switch mapping does not reject anything, so the tool rejects before the host is built.** This is
the property a mapping is most often assumed to provide and provably does not, which is why it is a
numbered requirement rather than a remark. **Verified against the provider on the pinned band, with the
mapping above in place:**

| What is passed | What the command-line provider does with it |
| --- | --- |
| `--username admin --role Administrator` | Binds the two mapped keys. The intended case |
| `--rolel Administrator` — one character wrong | Binds a **top-level key named `rolel`**. No error, no warning. `ProvisionAdmin:Role` is simply absent, and the only reason the run stops at all is that `[Required]` on that member happens to catch it |
| `--phase catalog` — a switch that used to exist | Binds a top-level key named `phase`. Nothing reads it, nothing reports it, and the run proceeds as though the argument had not been typed |
| `/role Administrator` | Maps to `ProvisionAdmin:Role` — the forward-slash form goes through the **same** mapping, so one switch has two accepted spellings unless something forbids the second |
| `-x 1` | **Silently dropped.** No key, no exception |
| A bare positional `load-catalog` | **Ignored entirely** — no key of any kind. A verb therefore cannot be read from configuration at all |
| `--batch` with no value after it | **Ignored entirely.** The missing value is not an error; the key simply does not appear |
| `--resume --batch 500` — a valueless flag before another switch | Binds **`resume` = `--batch`**, and `--batch` is consumed as that value, so the batch size is **never set**. A flag taking no value is not expressible in this provider at all |
| `--role A --role B` | Binds **`B`**. Last wins, and the first value is discarded silently |

So the failure mode is precise: **an unknown switch enters configuration outside every bound section**,
where `ValidateOnStart` cannot see it — it validates the members of the options types this contract
defines, and a stray top-level key is a member of none of them. A typo in an operator invocation then
looks like success, and the switch it was meant to be is missing.

**The rule: `args` is pre-parsed against a closed table before `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder` is
called.** The pre-parse is the tool's own code, not a configuration feature, and it is the same code for
every verb:

1. **`args[0]` must be one of `admin`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity`, `seed`.** Absent or unrecognised
   is a failure — and it has to be checked here rather than in options validation, because the
   bare-positional row above establishes that a positional argument never reaches configuration.
2. **Every remaining token must appear in that verb's exact accepted set**, and the sets are closed:
   `admin` accepts `--username` and `--role`; `load-catalog` and `load-identity` accept `--batch` and
   `--resume`; `seed` accepts nothing. A token outside the set fails, whether it is a near-miss of an
   accepted switch, a switch belonging to a different verb, or a switch this document has never defined.
3. **Only the `--switch` spelling is accepted.** The `/switch` form is rejected even where it would map
   correctly, because two spellings of one input make an audit of what was actually run harder for no
   gain; and no single-dash short form is defined at all, so every `-x` is rejected rather than dropped.
4. **Every value-taking switch must be followed by a value**, and one given none fails. The provider
   ignores it instead, so without this rule `--username` with a missing name produces the same outcome as
   not passing it at all.
5. **`--resume` is a flag, and the pre-parse is the only thing that may see it.** The
   `--resume --batch 500` row above is
   why: a valueless flag cannot be expressed by this provider, and passed through it would eat the next
   switch as its value. So the pre-parse recognises `--resume`, records the intent, and **removes it from
   the tokens handed on** — it is never a configuration key, and section
   [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) already treats it as a statement of
   intent rather than a bound value.
6. **A repeated switch fails.** The provider's own behaviour is last-wins, which silently discards the
   first value; for an argument that names the account being granted an administrator role, that is not a
   behaviour to inherit.
7. **The failure is exit 2 — the invalid-inputs class of section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — naming
   the rejected token and listing the accepted set for that verb**, and it happens **before the host is built** — so nothing is read, no connection is opened and
   nothing is written. The non-zero exit contract of section [10.3](#103-what-this-retires) is the same
   one; this is an additional way to reach it, not a second convention.

Only the surviving tokens, with the verb removed, are handed to the host builder together with **that
verb's** switch mapping — so the mapped keys are the only keys the command line can contribute, and the
mapping's real job is naming, not filtering.

**`MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is deliberately not a key in this contract, and the reason is worth being
precise about.** Every environment variable is visible to `IConfiguration` — that is what the
environment-variable provider does — so the honest claim is not that the value is unreachable but that
**it belongs to no bound options type and no section this document defines**. Nothing enumerates
configuration into a log, the value is read once into a local, and it is passed straight to
`UserManager.CreateAsync`. It also carries no `__` separator, so it cannot be mistaken for a member of
any section above.

**Where the pipeline is concerned, one obligation is not the tool's to enforce and is stated as a
requirement on the release rather than as a hope.** The variable carrying the password **is registered as
a secret in the CI provider**, so the provider masks it in every log line the step produces, and it is
**scoped to that single step** rather than defined for the job. Whichever provider is selected —
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) owns that gate — the masking and the scoping are entry conditions for
the provisioning step, and the identity the step runs under is
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. A pipeline that emits the password once has published it to
whatever retains that log, and no property of the tool can undo it.

**1a. The invocation, the principal and the connection channel — because a command whose execution is
undescribed is a design, not an operation.**

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| The invocation | `provision-admin admin --username <name> --role Administrator`, with `MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` set for that one invocation and nothing else on the command line. It runs **once per environment**, after step 3 of the order in section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and after the Identity data migration of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) where one is being performed — an administrator created before the load would be an account the load then has to reconcile against a source that never contained it |
| The principal | **Never the application's runtime managed identity.** The runtime identity belongs to the site and is reachable only from inside it, so an invocation outside the site cannot present it and should not want to: the write is being made by a pipeline step or a person, and the audit record of property 4 is only worth keeping if the principal in it is the one that acted. The release-step identity and its grants are [06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; this document requires only that the principal is **not** the runtime one and that it holds write access to the Identity tables and nothing wider |
| The connection channel | Through the **same** configuration contract as the site's — `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection`, supplied by the pipeline's configuration channel for the release-job invocation that [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) makes the normal path, or by an invocation-scoped environment variable in the operator session that section records as the exception, and **never as a command-line argument** (properties 1 and the precedence rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). Because property 2 reaches the application's own registration surface, section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s connection-string validation applies unchanged: a string carrying an inline credential, or an unresolved `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` literal, fails the command before it opens a connection |
| How it authenticates | Token-based Microsoft Entra authentication, not a SQL login — and in **exactly one** mode rather than whichever one the host can satisfy. The connection carries `Authentication="Active Directory Managed Identity"` (equivalently `Active Directory MSI`) with the **deployment** principal's client ID in `User Id`, and `Authentication="Active Directory Workload Identity"` as the single permitted fallback where the pipeline's identity is federated — the one flow [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) selects for every release-side operation, and mode **M3** of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is what validates it here. **`Active Directory Default` is not used**, and an earlier version of this row specified it: it "acquire[s] a token by passing `DefaultAzureCredential`" (*Using Microsoft Entra authentication with Microsoft.Data.SqlClient*), which resolves whichever of several credential sources the host happens to offer — so the identity that wrote an administrator account would be decided by the agent's ambient state rather than declared, and [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) prohibits it on the release path for that reason. Which principal actually connected is then asserted at the database by `USER_NAME()`, assertion 3 below, so the mode is named *and* confirmed. One version-sensitive fact, stated so a package bump does not quietly break it: from **Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 7.0** the Entra modes require the separate `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.Extensions.Azure` package (same source), so a provider move past the pin [04 §5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) carries has to re-check this row |

**Assertions before the first write, and there are four.** The command is short, which is exactly why it
is worth refusing to run it against the wrong database:

1. **The environment assertion of property 2a** — both variables pinned and the resolved name checked.
2. **The options validation of property 2, run explicitly, because building the host does not run it.**
   `ValidateOnStart` does not validate during `Build()`: it registers an `IStartupValidator` that the
   **host's start** invokes — "`ValidateOnStart` … validation is performed when the host starts"
   (*Options pattern in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8; `OptionsBuilderExtensions.ValidateOnStart`), and the
   validator is resolved and called inside `Host.StartAsync`. A console command that calls `Build()` and
   then goes straight to work therefore resolves and uses operational services **before any validation has
   happened** — which is precisely the failure mode this assertion list exists to prevent, and an earlier
   version of this row asserted the opposite. The command therefore does one of two things and states
   which: it **resolves `IStartupValidator` from the built host and calls `Validate()` itself**, as the
   very first statement after `Build()` and before any scope is created, any `DbContext` is resolved or
   any connection is opened. `Validate()` throws an aggregated `OptionsValidationException` on failure,
   which becomes the non-zero exit below. **`RunAsync` is deliberately not used**: this is a one-shot
   command, not a service, and starting a host would also start any hosted service registered in the
   shared half — which today is none, and which a future addition to section
   [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) could silently make one. Calling the validator directly
   keeps the tool's container a strict subset in behaviour as well as in registration.
3. **The target is the intended database, asserted the same way.** The server on the **control plane** —
   `properties.fullyQualifiedDomainName` read from the resource and compared case-insensitively against the
   expected server, which must carry the `database.windows.net` suffix — and then `DB_NAME()` and
   `USER_NAME()` asserted **in session** against their expected values. That is section
   [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) assertion 1, which is in turn
   [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, rather than a third copy of the same idea. An
   administrator provisioned into a neighbouring environment's database is a real credential in a place
   nobody is looking. `@@SERVERNAME` is recorded in the evidence line and gates nothing, for the reason
   [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) gives.
4. **Every migration the deployed Identity assembly defines is present in
   `__EFMigrationsHistory_Identity`.** Containment, not equality — the semantics section
   [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) fixes and for the same
   reason. Without it, a run against a half-applied Identity schema fails inside `CreateAsync` with a
   provider-level column error, which is a diagnostic message about the wrong subject.

Each failure is an exit **4** (section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation)) naming the assertion and the two
compared values, **before** the first write.

**2. Identity hashes the password — the command builds a host and resolves the managers from the
container.** "The same Identity configuration as the web application" is not a resemblance to be
maintained by hand; it is **the same method call**. The command:

1. builds a **plain host** — `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args)`, not a web host: no server, no
   middleware pipeline and no endpoint, because it serves no request;
2. calls **`Program.AddMusicStoreServices(builder.Services, builder.Configuration)`** — the single
   registration surface specified in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), reached across
   the `ProjectReference` edge and the `public partial class Program` declaration that
   [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns;
2a. registers **`IHostRoleSignal` as `HostRole.Operator`** — one `AddSingleton`, immediately after step 2
   and before step 3, because step 3 is what consumes it. It is deliberately **not** inside
   `AddMusicStoreServices` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so each root declares
   what it is; and it is what makes the validator apply **M3** rather than the web host's **M1** to this
   invocation's connection string (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). Omitting it does
   not fall back to a default — step 3 fails, naming `Configuration:HostRole`;
3. builds the host and, **as the very next statement**, resolves `IStartupValidator` and calls
   `Validate()` — assertion 2 above, and a numbered step of its own precisely because it is **not** a side
   effect of `Build()`;
4. opens a scope, and resolves `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` and the role manager from it;
5. calls their create methods, and returns the failure's allocated exit code — **3** where the store
   refused the identity, **6** where an operation reported an unusable result (the allocation of section
   [10.2](#exit-code-allocation), whose observability rationale is section
   [10.3](#103-what-this-retires)'s).

**Three properties follow from step 2 rather than being separately promised.** The command gets the
**same password hasher**, so the hash it writes is the one the application validates. It gets the **same
validated options** (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)), so a missing or invalid
required key fails the command **before** it touches the database — by way of step 3's explicit
`Validate()` call rather than by way of `Build()`, which is the distinction assertion 2 turns on — and the
password is checked against the
**same** policy the web application enforces (section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) — a provisioned administrator cannot bypass the complexity
rules. And there is **exactly one registration implementation**: a second copy inside the tool is what
would let its password policy, its context configuration or its hasher drift from the application's,
silently, in the direction nobody tests.

**2a. The environment is pinned on *both* variables and then asserted, because the tool is a generic
host and the generic host does not read the variable everyone reaches for.** This is a correctness
property of every non-web invocation in this document, not a nicety, and it is stated here once because
`tools/provision-admin` is the invocation that makes the distinction unavoidable.

Three verified facts force the shape:

- **The generic host's environment comes from `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT`, not `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`.**
  `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(String[])` builds its host configuration from **`DOTNET_`-prefixed**
  environment variables (API reference, .NET 8). `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` reads the
  `ASPNETCORE_`-prefixed set. So a release step that pins only `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` pins the site and
  **not** this tool.
- **For a host built by either of the two builders above, an unset environment is `Production`, not
  Development.** "If the `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT` and `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` environment variables aren't
  set, the Production environment is the default environment" (*Use multiple environments in ASP.NET
  Core*, .NET 8). So the risk for this tool is not an accidental Development default, it is an accidental
  *Production* one — which is why the guard of section
  [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) cannot rest on an environment name and why
  this assertion exists at all. **The design-time `dotnet ef` path is a different host with a different
  default**, which is why it is not covered by this rule and why it pins the environment explicitly
  instead — either on the two variables or through the argument-forwarding form EF Core's design-time
  documentation describes (*Design-time DbContext Creation*, EF Core). **The invocation itself is not
  restated here**: every design-time command and every option on it is
  [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, its environment pin is
  [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, and the release-time execution is
  [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. Between the two rules **no invocation in this plan
  relies on a default at all**, which is the property that matters and is why neither default needs to be
  argued about.
- **The documented precedence between the two variables is not something to rely on.** The same
  Microsoft page states it in both directions in different paragraphs. A contract that depends on which
  paragraph is current is a contract that changes meaning on a doc revision, so this one **does not
  depend on precedence at all**.

**The rule, for every invocation this document specifies that is not the running site — and it is an
equality against a third value, not a pin to a literal.** The three names below are all read from the
environment; none of them is written into a step, and none of them is `Production` by default:

1. **Both `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` and `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT` are set, and neither is left to a default.**
   Both, because one of them governs whichever host type the invocation happens to build, and setting both
   removes the need to know which. Never neither, because the default is `Production` and a defaulted
   `Production` is indistinguishable from an intended one.
2. **They hold the same value**, and a disagreement fails rather than being resolved by precedence.
   Disagreement means the operator believed one thing and one of the two hosts believed another, and there
   is no safe way to guess which.
3. **That value equals the invocation's own `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT`** — the name of the environment being
   acted on, declared once per pipeline environment and **read rather than written** by the step. The
   variable and its per-environment value set are
   [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
   states the same comparison for the design-time invocations, so the build side, the release side and the
   in-process assertion are one rule rather than three similar ones. **`EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` being absent
   is itself a failure**: a comparison against nothing is not a check, and defaulting it to `Production`
   would recreate exactly the blanket pin the next paragraph rejects.
4. **The invocation then reads the resolved `IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName` and fails, before any other
   work, if it is not that value.** This is the assertion that survives a doc revision, a platform default
   and a mistyped variable name alike: it checks the value the framework actually resolved rather than the
   input that was supposed to produce it.
5. **Every one of those failures is an exit 4 — the expected-value refusal class of section
   [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — naming the two variable values, `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT`
   and the resolved name**, and nothing is written. Four values in one line are what make the diagnosis
   immediate, and none of them is a configuration value, so the message echoes nothing sensitive.

**Why the rule is an equality and not "always `Production`", stated because the blanket version is the
tempting one and it is wrong in both directions.** A rule pinned to the literal `Production` would be
**unusable** for every operation against a non-production deployment — those invocations resolve to that
deployment's own name — and it would be **actively wrong** for seeding, which has no legitimate production
execution at all. A rule an invocation cannot obey is a rule that stops being applied anywhere, which is
how a guard becomes decoration. So the expected value is per invocation:

| Invocation | Its `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| This provisioning command's `admin` verb; both data-load verbs (sections [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) and [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)); the migration and bundle generation [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns; the bundle run in the release step | **The name of the environment being acted on** — `Production` when the target is the production deployment, and that deployment's own name otherwise. Never inferred, never defaulted, and never a literal written into the step | These run **against** the environment they name, including production, so the equality is how the invocation and the target are made to agree. [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declares which value each environment carries, including the fact that the production site's staging slot carries `Production` like the slot it swaps into |
| The `seed` verb (section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)) | **The target's explicit non-production environment name — and it can never be `Production`.** The invocation additionally fails if the resolved name **is** `Production`, whatever `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` says | Seeding writes ~780 catalog rows and has no legitimate production execution. It **never appears in a production release path**, so no invocation of it has a production expected value — and the extra check exists so that a mis-declared variable cannot create one |

**That is a distinction of expected value, not of mechanism.** Every invocation in both rows pins both
variables, reads `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` and asserts the resolved name; what differs is what it asserts
*to*. And the seeding row's
assertion is the **first** of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s three
checks, not a fourth one — which is why that section says in its own words that check 1 is necessary and
not sufficient: an environment name pinned by the same operator who mistyped the connection string proves
nothing on its own, and checks 2 and 3 are what bind the decision to the database.

**Where the other halves live.** [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the same pinning for
the **design-time** invocations — migration generation and bundle generation — and
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns it for the **release step** that runs the bundles, the
seeding command and this command. This document owns the in-process assertion, which is the half that
holds even when a release definition forgets a variable.

**Direct SQL is explicitly not an acceptable substitute**, because it cannot produce a valid Identity
password hash: the hash format, iteration count and salt handling are the hasher's, and a hand-written
`INSERT` produces a row that exists and cannot sign in. That is also the reason the tool resolves the
managers from a container rather than constructing them — the hasher, the validators and the normalizer
are what the container supplies, and hand-building them is how the source arrived at three objects
assembled by hand [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29].

**2b. The content root is set explicitly, and the published console carries no configuration file at
all.** These two go together: a host that reads optional JSON files needs a defined place to look for
them, and the cleanest way to make that place irrelevant is to ship nothing there.

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Content root | Set **explicitly** to `AppContext.BaseDirectory` through `HostApplicationBuilderSettings.ContentRootPath` (API reference, .NET 8), passed to `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder`. It is not left to a default and it is **never** the process's current directory: a release step's working directory is whatever the agent chose, so an implicit content root is the one input to this command that varies between two invocations that look identical in the pipeline definition |
| Configuration files | **None ship.** The published output contains no `appsettings.json` and no `appsettings.{Environment}.json`. The builder registers both as **optional** sources, so their absence is not a failure — and setting the content root to the deployed folder is what guarantees the absence is real rather than a stray file in a working directory being picked up |
| Why no file | Every value the tool needs is declared **once per environment** in the pipeline's environment definition (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)), and a committed file inside the tool would be a second home for values that document says have one. It would also be the obvious place for somebody to put a connection string |
| How configuration arrives | **Invocation-scoped environment variables in the double-underscore form**, rendered into the step by that same environment definition. The tool's container is a strict subset of the web host's, but the *options* it binds are not a subset: step 1 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) binds **every** options type of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), so the invocation must supply **every unconditionally required member of every one of them** — not merely the connection string, the `Identity` policy and `DataProtection__ApplicationDiscriminator`, but the `Expected:*`, `Antiforgery`, `Session` and `Site` members too |
| Why that cost is accepted | It is the price of the single registration surface above, and the alternative is worse: a tool-only options subset would mean two definitions of "the required configuration", and the one no deployment runs is the one that drifts. The cost is also **bounded and loud** — the values are the same declaration the site's platform settings come from, and a missing one fails at step 3's `Validate()` with the member named, before any connection is opened |
| What must not be supplied | `Site__*` values that differ from the site's, and anything resembling a *second* environment's declaration. The tool reads these members and acts on none of them; supplying a divergent value would make the environment definition self-inconsistent for no gain |

**3. Idempotence is per operation, not overall.** Three checks, evaluated **independently**: create the
user only if absent, create the role only if absent, add the membership only if absent.

**The evidence that this matters is a difference between the two editions.** MVC 4 checks all three
independently — `WebSecurity.UserExists` [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:29],
`Roles.RoleExists` [:32] and `Roles.IsUserInRole` [:35] — whereas **MVC 5 adds the membership only
inside the user-creation branch**: `AddToRoleAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:43]
sits inside `if (user == null)` [:39-44]. So if a prior MVC 5 run created the user and then failed
before the membership was added, **every subsequent run skips it** — the user exists, so the branch is
not entered, and the account never gets the role. The administration surface is then permanently
unreachable and nothing reports why. The target repairs such a run rather than skipping it, which is
the whole point of checking the three independently.

**Restart after a partial failure is therefore the same command again, with two boundaries stated so
"idempotent" is not read as "does whatever is needed".** A run interrupted at any point leaves each of
the three operations either done or not done — none of them is partial in itself — so re-running with the
same three inputs completes exactly the ones outstanding and exits zero with an audit record saying which
(property 4). The boundaries: the command **never deletes or demotes** anything, and it **never modifies
an existing account** — in particular it does **not** reset the password of a user that already exists, so
a re-run cannot silently rotate a credential and a forgotten administrator password is a different
operation than this one. Both properties mean the worst outcome of an unnecessary re-run is that nothing
happens.

**4. The audit record has exactly one destination, exactly one instance per invocation, and no secret in
it.** Content first: **actor, timestamp, target username, role name, and the outcome of each of the three
operations separately**, so "role already existed, membership added" is distinguishable from "nothing to
do". **The password is never serialised, never echoed, and never included in an exception message** — the
rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s never-record list, applied here to the one
process that holds the secret. This is net-new: the repository has no audit logging of any kind
([09 §3.13](09-security-assessment.md)).

**Its owner is the immutable blob container, and the workspace is not a destination.** An earlier version
of this property said the record was "written through `ILogger` to the application's configured sink and
retained under the platform's log-retention policy", and that is wrong twice over.
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is the authority and states both corrections: this command
runs on a build agent, so **no console-log collection applies to it at all** — there is no captured
container stream and no agent — and its record's **single owner is that document's append-only container
under a 365-day time-based immutability policy**, reached by the pipeline capturing the command's output
and uploading it. [06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) draws the same conclusion from the
other side: `AdminProvisioned` is the one mandatory record that "does not travel this channel at all", and
no alert, gate or audit query is written against a workspace table for it. So **an operator querying the
workspace for this event finds nothing, by design**, and this document must not describe a sink that would
imply otherwise.

**The serialisation is deterministic and separate from diagnostic logging, and the reason is a hard one
rather than a stylistic one.**

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| How it is produced | By a **dedicated serialiser over a dedicated record type** — one `System.Text.Json` call with fixed options: not indented, invariant culture, UTC timestamps in round-trip `"O"` form, and an explicit property order — writing **one** line to standard output. **It is not an `ILogger` call.** The record type's shape is fixed by the parity row below rather than chosen: the fields this tool contributes — `eventName`, `actor`, `outcome`, `rejectedCheck`, the target username and role, and the three per-operation results — sit **inside a nested `State` object**, exactly where the pipeline of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) puts them, and the top level carries only the formatter's own `Timestamp`, `EventId`, `LogLevel`, `Category` and `Message` |
| Why not `ILogger` | **Because the record has to survive a failure that happens before the host exists.** The pre-parse rejection of property 1b, the missing-actor check below, the environment assertion of property 2a and the validation of assertion 2 all fail **before** any logger can be resolved, and every one of them is an invocation that must leave an audit record. A logging call cannot emit on those paths; a static serialiser can, and does |
| The second reason | An `ILogger` record's field set is a function of four formatter options and one level filter (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)): its own fields sit under `State`, its `Timestamp` exists only because `TimestampFormat` is set, and its emission depends on a category level. An audit blob read years later must not depend on any of that. The serialiser removes all five dependencies |
| Shape parity, so nothing has to be re-learned to read it — **and it is what fixes the selector below** | The emitted object is **field-for-field and nesting-for-nesting what the formatter of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) would have produced for the same record**, carrying **`State.eventName = "AdminProvisioned"`** on [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s schema — **nested, not top level**. That is not a preference: `AddJsonConsole` writes every log-state property inside `State`, section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) states in as many words that "a top-level `eventName`" is one of the three fields a query "will look for at the top level and not find", and parity means the serialiser matches that placement. An earlier version of this row wrote the field as a top-level `eventName` while claiming parity with a formatter that nests it — a contradiction whose consequence was concrete rather than cosmetic: **the selector below, keyed on the top-level name, would have matched zero lines on every invocation**, so the "exactly one match" rule would have failed every run and the promised single immutable upload would never have happened. So [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s statement that "the record's shape is identical wherever it is read" holds exactly; what this row refines is that the *producer* is a serialiser rather than the logging pipeline, which is what makes the shape independent of configuration |
| What diagnostic logging still does | The tool's ordinary progress and error records go through `ILogger` as before, and **none of them is the audit record**. They may be filtered, sampled by nothing, and lost without consequence. The audit record is the one line that may not be |

**How the actor reaches the record — transported, not asserted.** A process cannot vouch for who invoked
it, so the field is not something the tool determines:

- The actor arrives as an **invocation-scoped environment variable rendered by the pipeline from its own
  authenticated trigger** — the channel of property 2b, and the same declaration mechanism as every other
  value the tool reads. It is **never** read from the operating-system user, never defaulted, and never
  typed into a prompt on the pipeline path.
- **An absent, empty or whitespace-only actor value fails the invocation before any work**, alongside the
  assertions of property 2 — because a provisioning record whose actor is blank is not an audit record, and
  filling it in with whatever the process can see about itself is worse than failing. The check is a
  presence-and-shape check only: non-empty after trimming, and **not equal to the sentinel below**, so the
  channel cannot be used to forge the one value that means "there was none".
- **What the record carries when the actor itself is what is missing**, because the rejection still owes an
  audit record and an empty field would contradict the rule immediately above. The `actor` field carries
  the **reserved literal `(unavailable)`** — parenthesised precisely so it cannot collide with any identity
  the pipeline renders — and `rejectedCheck` carries `actor-missing`. Two consequences make the sentinel
  safe rather than a hole: it is legal **only** in a record whose `outcome` is `rejected` **and** whose
  `rejectedCheck` is `actor-missing`, so a record carrying it in any other combination is itself a finding;
  and no work was attempted, so the record documents an invocation that changed nothing rather than an
  unattributed change.
- **The field is a copy for readability; the authority is elsewhere.** The blob is written into the
  immutable container **by the pipeline's deployment identity**, and the pipeline's own run record carries
  the authenticated trigger independently
  ([06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) hops 2 to 4). So the record is **corroborated by two
  artifacts the command cannot write**, and a tampered or mis-set actor field is detectable by comparing
  them rather than being taken on trust.

**Every path emits exactly one record, and that includes the paths that fail.**

The four rows are ordered by **how far the invocation got**, and the boundary that matters is drawn where
the host is *built* rather than where it is *started* — an earlier version of this table put startup
validation on the pre-host side, which is wrong: validation is the explicit `IStartupValidator.Validate()`
call of assertion 2, and that call happens **after** `Build()` returns.

| Path | What is emitted |
| --- | --- |
| Success | One record, `outcome` naming each of the three operations' results |
| Failure **after work has begun** — a create that fails, a database error, an assertion of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) that a live target contradicts | One record, with the failing step named and the same three per-operation outcomes as far as they got. No exception text, no connection string, no password: the sanitised fields of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) |
| Failure **after the host is built but before any work** — the environment assertion of property 2a, and the configuration validation of assertion 2, both of which run between `Build()` and the first scope | One record, `outcome = rejected`, naming the check and — for a validation failure — each member the aggregated result named. A logger **is** resolvable on this path, and the record is emitted by the serialiser regardless, because one producer for the audit record is the property being kept and a second producer chosen by how far the process got would be indistinguishable from a missing record when one of the two is broken |
| Failure **before any host is built** — an unrecognised, duplicated or valueless switch, a missing verb, two verbs, a missing actor | One record, `outcome = rejected`, naming the check that rejected it. This is the path the serialiser **exists** for: there is no container, no configuration binding and no logger, so a logging call could not emit here at all |
| The **manual** path — an operator session, which [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records as the exception rather than an equal alternative | The **same** single record on standard output, and the operator is responsible for capturing it, running the **same `jq` selection** as the pipeline and uploading the selected line with the same `az storage blob upload --auth-mode login --overwrite false` invocation the row below specifies, supplying their own identity as the actor. Stated with its weakness rather than as an equivalent: a human-supplied actor value is not corroborated by a pipeline trigger, so this path's record is weaker evidence and the invocation is recorded as an exception in the run record |

**How the one line is found, because it shares standard output with ordinary diagnostic records.** The
tool's progress and error records go to the same stream, so "capture the output and upload it" is not
specific enough to be implementable. The rule is a selection with a count:

- The pipeline reads the captured standard output **line by line**, parses each line that is a complete
  JSON object, and selects those whose **`State.eventName` is exactly `AdminProvisioned`** — the **nested**
  path, for the reason the parity row above gives, and expressed once so no consumer has to reconstruct it:

  ```bash
  # $CAPTURE is the command's captured standard output, which also carries the
  # tool's diagnostic records. -R reads each line as raw text and 'fromjson?'
  # drops the lines that are not JSON instead of aborting on them; 'objects'
  # drops any JSON value that is not an object, so the path is only applied to
  # something it can be applied to. --exit-status makes an empty result non-zero.
  jq -Rc --exit-status \
    'fromjson? | objects | select(.State.eventName == "AdminProvisioned")' \
    "$CAPTURE" > "$AUDIT_LINE"
  test "$(wc -l < "$AUDIT_LINE")" -eq 1
  ```

  `jq` is not a new dependency: [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) pins it on the release
  agent image and asserts `jq --version` at provisioning, precisely so a readback that captures JSON has
  something to assert with. The serialiser writes its object on a single line, and `AdminProvisioned` is
  one named event in [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s closed schema which **no other
  record in this tool may carry** — so the predicate is exact rather than heuristic. A selector written
  against a top-level
  `eventName` matches **nothing**, for the reason the parity row states; that is the one mistake this
  subsection is written to prevent.
- **Exactly one match is required.** Zero matches and two or more matches are **both** failures of the
  provisioning step, reported distinctly: zero means the tool exited without discharging its audit
  obligation, and more than one means something emits the event name that should not, which invalidates
  "one record per invocation" more quietly than an absence would. Neither is resolved by picking a line.
  The two are distinguishable in the block above without any extra reporting code, which is why it is
  written that way: **zero fails at the `jq` line**, because `--exit-status` returns non-zero when the
  filter produced no output, and **two fails at the `test` line**, because the count is not 1. So the
  failing line names which of the two happened.
- **The selected line is uploaded verbatim** — the exact bytes, not a re-serialisation — which is what makes
  the byte-for-byte read-back below a meaningful comparison rather than a comparison of two renderings.
- Lines that are not JSON, and JSON objects carrying any other event name, are **left in the diagnostic
  capture and never uploaded to the audit container**, so the container holds provisioning records and
  nothing else.

**Uploaded and verified, because an audit copy nobody checked is an assumption.** The selected line — the
exact bytes, `$AUDIT_LINE` above — is uploaded to the immutable container, then **read back and compared
byte-for-byte with what the command emitted**, and the read-back copy is re-tested against the **same**
`State.eventName` predicate, so the artifact in the container is verified to be the record rather than
merely to be a file of the right length:

```bash
set -euo pipefail

AUDIT_BLOB="adminprovisioned-$INVOCATION_ID.json"

az storage blob upload \
  --account-name "$AUDIT_ACCOUNT" \
  --container-name "$AUDIT_CONTAINER" \
  --name "$AUDIT_BLOB" \
  --file "$AUDIT_LINE" \
  --auth-mode login \
  --overwrite false

az storage blob download \
  --account-name "$AUDIT_ACCOUNT" \
  --container-name "$AUDIT_CONTAINER" \
  --name "$AUDIT_BLOB" \
  --file "$AUDIT_READBACK" \
  --auth-mode login

cmp -- "$AUDIT_LINE" "$AUDIT_READBACK"
jq -Rc --exit-status \
  'fromjson? | objects | select(.State.eventName == "AdminProvisioned")' \
  "$AUDIT_READBACK" > /dev/null
```

A missing or mismatched blob is a **failed provisioning step** even where the
provisioning itself succeeded — the account exists and the audit obligation does not, which is a state that
must be visible immediately rather than discovered at a review. **An invocation with no verified record is
itself a finding**, which is the property that makes "one record per invocation" checkable. `--overwrite
false` on the upload is what makes the immutable container's own guarantee assertable from this side too:
a second invocation cannot reuse the name, because the name carries the invocation id.

**Coverage rows O5 to O9 of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes)** exercise this: one
record on each of the four paths, exactly one, the actor carried through, the rejected path emitting
without a host, and the secret absent from every one of them.

<a id="exit-code-allocation"></a>

**The exit codes, allocated here — because "distinct numeric codes" is not a contract anybody can
implement, test or branch on.** Every failure path in this section and in section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) is specified as "a non-zero exit", and
coverage row **O9** required those codes to be "documented, distinct" while no document allocated a single
value. Three consumers need the actual numbers: the implementation, which has to return one; the tests,
which assert on one; and the release pipeline, which branches on one. So the allocation is made **once,
here**, and every one of those three cites it rather than choosing.

| Code | Class | What returns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | **Success** | The verb completed. For `admin`, all three operations reached a terminal state — created or already present. For the load verbs, the phase completed and its reconciliation passed |
| **2** | **The invocation's inputs are invalid** | The closed pre-parse of property 1b — an unrecognised switch, a switch spelled for another verb, a value-taking switch with nothing after it, a repeated switch, a missing verb, two verbs; and the startup validation of assertion 2 — any of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s five connection checks, a missing required member, or the absent `IHostRoleSignal` registration. Both are "what you passed me cannot be acted on", they both happen before any work, and a pipeline's response to both is the same: fix the invocation, do not retry it |
| **3** | **Authentication or authorization failed** | Token acquisition for the deployment identity failed, the login was refused, or a statement was refused for want of a grant — the `SET IDENTITY_INSERT` and DDL rights of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) among them. Separated from **2** because the invocation was *right* and the identity was not, which is a different fix and often a different owner |
| **4** | **An expected value did not match, so the run refused** | The environment assertion of property 2a; the `EXPECTED_*` comparisons; the target assertions of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) — the control-plane fully qualified server name, `DB_NAME()` and `USER_NAME()`; and the three-check seeding guard of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks). Every one of these is "you are pointed at something other than what you declared", and **nothing had been written** when it fired |
| **5** | **A precondition was not met, or a lock was not acquired** | `sp_getapplock` not granted within its wait; the session cache table or a migration history table absent when a step requires it; a load run finding rows already present and **not** given `--resume`. The distinction from **4** is that nothing is *mismatched* — the world is simply not yet in the state this step requires, which frequently makes the right response to wait and retry |
| **6** | **Data or verification failed** | The per-table row counts and per-order totals of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) step 6 not matching, and any other check the tool performs on data it has just written. The operation ran and its result is **not trustworthy**, which is the one class that must never be retried blindly. **The shell steps' verifications are not this code** — the transfer block's `sha256sum --check` and the audit read-back's `cmp` return **their own** statuses per the third property below; they belong to the same *class* for the pipeline's branching, and the pipeline classifies them by **which step failed** rather than by translating a status |
| **7** | **Partial completion, and a human has to decide** | The one case section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) reserves for a person: rows in the target whose keys are **not** in the source, so the target is not a partially loaded copy of this source. Also a load that committed some phases and then failed in a way the checkpoint records but no rule resolves. Distinct from **6** because there is nothing to re-run — the next action is a decision, not a command |

Three properties of the allocation, stated because each one is a decision:

- **`1` is deliberately unallocated.** It is what a runtime-terminated process and most shell built-ins
  produce, so giving it a meaning of its own would make an unhandled failure indistinguishable from a
  classified one. A `1` from this tool means "it fell over", and that is worth being able to tell apart.
- **The allocation is by *class*, not by individual check** — which is why two checks share **2** and four
  share **4**. A pipeline branches on the class; the **specific** check is named in the output and in the
  audit record's `rejectedCheck`, where a human reads it. Coverage row **O9** asserts the class per path
  and the named check in the output, rather than a unique integer per check, which is the form that is
  actually stable across future checks being added.
- **Exit statuses from other commands are passed through unchanged and are not part of this allocation.**
  The `az`, `sha256sum`, `cmp` and `jq` invocations in this document's shell blocks return their own
  statuses; the blocks re-raise them rather than translating them, because a translated status loses the
  tool's own diagnosis. This allocation governs `provision-admin` and nothing else — in particular it does
  **not** govern `dotnet sql-cache`, whose own `0`/`1`/`2` contract and the release actions for each are
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, and whose `1` deliberately carries two meanings that
  that section resolves with a post-condition rather than with a code.

**5. It is not deployed with the web application.** A separate project, not referenced by the web
project and not included in its publish output, run from the release pipeline or an operator session.
**The `ProjectReference` of property 2 points from the tool to the web application and never the
reverse**, so sharing the registration surface does not put the tool into the deployed site — the
structural consequence is [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s and is not restated here.
**The credential leaves configuration entirely** — no `appsettings` key, no environment variable on the
web application, and nothing for a compromised web process to read.

### 10.3 What this retires

The `async void` method [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] and its call [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18]; the
three hand-built objects [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29]; the two `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` reads [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24] and the
`using System.Configuration;` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:7] that supports them; and the two committed credential keys
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17]. **Failure becomes observable** — a non-zero exit code and a
log record from a command someone ran, rather than silence inside a start-up path.

Provisioning moves out of the application and into an operator action, which is an **approved delta**
with **Security and operations** as its approval owners (section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)). The user-visible consequence is that a freshly deployed
environment has no administrator until the command is run, which the deployment runbook of
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) must include as a step.

## 11. The cutover decision

### 11.1 The decision

**A single cutover, not a strangler fig.** The ported application replaces the legacy application in
one switch, during a planned window, with a rollback plan.

This is a **decision**, not a comparison, and it is stated once. [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)
sequences around it. **A reappearance of this question as an unresolved comparison anywhere in the
deliverable set is a defect**, not a nuance — the incremental path appears below only as a conditional
alternative with named trigger conditions.

### 11.2 Why

MvcMusicStore is **one deployable unit** with six controllers and roughly **2,097 non-blank lines** of
C# in the migration source — the **sizing metric** of [08 §2.1](08-technical-debt-register.md), non-blank
lines excluding assembly metadata, which is the method [08 §4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) uses
for that figure and the only method under which it should be read. It has:

- **no independently deployable module** — one project, no `ProjectReference`, no areas, and one
  conventional route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:16-20] serving the whole URL
  surface;
- **no route family migratable in isolation.** The layout renders the cart summary and the genre menu
  on **every** page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:25-26], and the cart identity
  lives in session [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180], so migrating any route
  drags session and identity across the boundary with it;
- **no traffic profile that makes a partial cutover safer** than a whole one — there is no measured
  load, no SLA and no observability to measure one with ([11 §3.8](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)).

The strangler path would require a second host, adapters on both sides, shared session across the
boundary and authentication continuity across it — real, permanent-feeling complexity, built and then
discarded, in exchange for a granularity this application cannot use.

### 11.3 What single cutover does not buy

It does not remove the need for the pre-port test suite; it increases it, because there is no
route-by-route soak period in which a regression surfaces on a fraction of traffic. Section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) is the compensating control, and it is why tests
precede the port rather than accompanying it.

### 11.4 Two accepted costs

Both follow from facts already established, and both are accepted **deliberately here** rather than
discovered on the day.

**Cost one — every signed-in user is signed out at cutover.**

Katana cookie authentication tickets are protected by the old application's key material, and the new
application has a different key ring; there is no shared key material in the repository to bridge them
(no `machineKey` in any edition — [11 §3.2](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). **The tickets are
unreadable by the new runtime.** The adapters' remote-authentication mechanism exists precisely to
avoid this and is not in play under a single cutover.

The response is **operational, not technical**:

- **Expire the legacy authentication cookie at the new application's first request**, so no browser
  retries an undecryptable ticket and then presents an ambiguous state. This is a deliberate deletion
  of the old cookie by name, not a reliance on the framework ignoring it.
- **Notify users ahead of the window.**
- **Accept re-authentication as the cost.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states it in the
  cutover runbook.

**Cost two — anonymous carts do not survive, even though their rows do.**

An anonymous cart's identity lives **only** in in-process session: a `Guid.NewGuid()` written to
session and never sent to the client as anything else
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180], specifically [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:175]. When the old
process stops, **the browser-to-GUID link is lost**, so the `Cart` rows become **orphaned regardless of
whether they are migrated** — nothing can ever look them up again.

**Signed-in carts are unaffected**, because their key is the login name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167], which the Identity data
migration preserves as its invariant (sections
[4.4](#44-what-the-cart-is-coupled-to--and-what-it-is-not) and
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)).

The response:

- **Schedule cutover in a low-traffic window** and **drain the legacy application** before switching, so
  the number of live anonymous sessions at the moment of the switch is as close to zero as scheduling
  can make it.
- **Migrate the `Cart` rows anyway.** No data is destroyed, and the orphaned rows can then be reported
  and cleaned up on a stated schedule afterwards rather than silently vanishing.
- **Building a session-bridging mechanism is explicitly rejected as disproportionate** — it would mean
  standing up shared session state between two frameworks in order to preserve anonymous shopping
  carts on a store whose checkout requires authentication anyway
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:8].

**Both costs, plus the maintenance window and the drain step, belong in the rollback plan — because a
cutover that must be reversed produces the same two effects in the other direction.** Reverting signs
everyone out again, and anonymous carts created on the new application are lost on the way back. The
rollback plan must therefore state: the window, the drain, the legacy redeployment, the unmodified
source database as the data position (section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)), the second forced re-authentication,
and the second anonymous-cart loss. A rollback that is written as if it were free is a rollback nobody
will be willing to execute at 2am.

### 11.5 The full set of approved deltas

Behaviour preservation is the baseline: a visitor can browse genres and albums, view album detail, add
to and remove from a cart, see a cart count and summary, register, sign in and out, place an order with
promo-code handling, view their own orders, and — as an administrator — create, edit and delete albums.
Every one of those outcomes is preserved.

**The table below is everything that deliberately changes.** Its purpose is to let validation
distinguish **a preserved contract from an approved change**, rather than treating every difference as
a regression — and equally to stop an approved change being used to excuse a real one.

| # | Approved delta | Why | Section | Approval owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Preserving that would be preserving data loss; distinguishing the two changes **what is stored** for an existing request shape, so it is recorded rather than absorbed. `AlbumArtUrl` is the only field the rule can reach, the other four being guarded by `[Required]` or by being non-nullable value types | [8.9](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) | **Data owner and engineering** |
