Everything **not** in that table is a preserved contract, and a difference in it is a regression.

**Two changes this section is specifically asked about and deliberately does *not* record as deltas, with
the reasoning stated rather than left as an omission.** The table claims completeness, so a reader must be
able to tell an item that was considered and excluded from one that was forgotten.

- **Cart-mutation retry and idempotence is a *preserved* contract, not a delta.** Section
  [4.11](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 4 withdraws the
  earlier accepted over-count exposure and replaces it with a durable operation ledger. With that ledger a
  replayed mutation is a **no-op returning the committed result**, so the committed effect of one
  submission is **exactly one application** — which is precisely what the source does when no fault occurs
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:34-58]. The behaviour a visitor can observe is therefore
  unchanged, and promoting it to a delta row would misreport a defect *closed* as a contract *altered*.
  What **is** recorded is delta 20, which covers the different case: the mutation that cannot be applied at
  all.
- **An unhandled exception becoming a 404 is a defect resolution, not a change of contract.** This covers
  the three `NotFound()` conversions of section
  [13](#13-resolution-register--all-22-blockers-of-deliverable-12) and the genre zero-match 404 of section
  [4.12](#414-the-duplicate-genre-browse-contract). Nothing documented ever said the application returns a
  500 for an unknown album id or an unknown genre name; [08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns
  those as recorded debt, and closing debt is not an approved delta. It is also why **branch (a) of the
  Genre contract carries no delta row at all**.

### 11.6 The incremental path — a conditional alternative

The incremental path is **available and not selected**. It becomes the right answer only if one of the
following holds — stated as **operational conditions**, not as durations, because a duration is
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s to state:

- **The application must remain continuously available throughout the port, with no maintenance window
  available at any point.** Single cutover requires a window; if none can be obtained, the decision
  changes.
- **The Identity migration must be proven against live production traffic before it is committed.** The
  incremental path lets one host remain the authentication authority while the other is exercised.
- **A risk policy requires route-by-route isolation with independent rollback per route.**

Two facts make it genuinely available rather than theoretical: **MVC 5 targets the framework version
recorded at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj:16]**, which
clears the System.Web adapters' framework floor, and the reverse proxy supports the target framework.
[04 §7.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the conditional package pins for both, and this
document names no version.

**If it is selected, sign-in continuity is provided by the adapters' remote authentication** —
delegating authentication to the .NET Framework application so that **one host remains the single
authority** for the duration of the port. That is chosen over cookie-format interoperability, which
would require matching cookie names, authentication schemes, application names and key rings across two
frameworks and would fail silently and intermittently when any one of the four drifted. Remote
authentication has one authority and one failure mode.

Selecting it also **removes cost one and cost two of section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)** and adds
its own: two hosts to operate, two deployment pipelines, an adapter surface on both sides, and a
proxy hop on every request for the duration. That trade is the reason it is the alternative rather than
the plan.

---

### 11.7 Approval-owned additions

**Why this register exists as well as section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).** That table
records deliberate **changes to an existing** user-perceptible behaviour or interface. It is not the whole
approval surface, because the port also **adds** behaviour that no source behaviour corresponds to — a
validation summary where there is none, a pending state where there is none, a failure path where there is
none — and an addition cannot be recorded as a change to something that does not exist. Calling those
"improvements" and leaving them out of the approval accounting is the defect this section closes: an
improvement is still a decision, it is still visible to a user or to assistive technology, and somebody
still has to own it.

**This table is exhaustive for its category.** Every deliberate net-new user-perceptible or
assistive-technology behaviour the port introduces is a row here. The rows carry their specifying section
rather than restating its design, so the requirement has one owner and this register stays a register.

| # | Addition | Why it exists | Specified in | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | **A validation summary on the checkout form** | The form has no summary today, so a model-level failure — the promo-code rejection and the message the replaced bare `catch` adds — renders **nowhere at all** on the page | [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice), item **b5** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Product** |
| A2 | **A pending state on cart removal** — the control is disabled and carries `aria-busy="true"` while the request is in flight, and is re-enabled on completion either way | The source handler has no pending state at all, so a double-click posts twice | item **c2** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements), [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script) | **Product** |
| A3 | **A failure path on cart removal, with a visible and announced message**, leaving the row unchanged | The source handler has **no failure path** — no `.fail`, no `error` callback, no status check — so a rejected removal is completely silent and the user believes the item was removed | item **c3** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Product** |
| A4 | **Deterministic focus restoration after a removal** — focus moves to the status container, made focusable with `tabindex="-1"`, in the fade-out completion callback | Today the removed row is faded out while focus sits on the control inside it, so focus is destroyed with the row and lands on `<body>` | item **c4** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Product** |
| A5 | **The removal animation is suppressed under `prefers-reduced-motion`** | The source fade honours no motion preference | item **c5** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Product** |
| A6 | **A live status region** — `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"` on the message container the script writes | The container exists and is written to, and **nothing is announced** | item **c1** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements), [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract) | **Product** |
| A7 | **Accessible names and expanded state on the two disclosure controls** — an `aria-label` and `aria-controls` on the navbar toggle, and `aria-expanded` maintained on both it and the genre dropdown toggle | The navbar toggle is three unlabelled `<span>` bars with no accessible name and no state attribute; neither control announces whether it is open | items **a1** and **a2** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Engineering** |
| A8 | **Accessible names and explicit structure on the three data tables** — a name for each, plus `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `scope="col"` on the two that have header cells, and a name for the previously blank action-column header | None of the three carries a name; two have a bare header row with no `<thead>`, no `<tbody>` and no `scope`; the Registered Logins table has no header cells at all and deliberately keeps that shape | items **a5** and **a5b** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Engineering** |
| A9 | **An image alternative on the showcase image** — either meaningful text or a deliberate `alt=""`, with the choice recorded | The element carries **no** `alt` attribute, and an omitted one is indistinguishable in markup from a deliberately empty one while meaning the opposite | item **a3** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Product** |
| A10 | **A working programmatic label association on the promo-code field** | The label's `for` is derived from the string `"Promo Code"` while the input's id is `PromoCode`, so **there is no association today** | item **b2** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements), [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice) | **Engineering** |
| A11 | **Field errors associated with their fields, and invalid inputs marked invalid** — `aria-describedby` on each input referencing its message element, and `aria-invalid` set and cleared | Messages render adjacent to their inputs with no programmatic association, and the invalid condition is conveyed by **colour alone** | items **b3** and **b4** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Engineering** |
| A12 | **A top-level heading and a coherent heading outline on the catalog page**, with the rendered sizes held by type utilities | The page has **no `<h1>` anywhere** and jumps from `<h3>` to `<h5>` | item **a4** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | **Engineering** |
| A13 | **Cart removal becomes a semantic control** — `<button type="button" class="RemoveLink link-button">` retaining `data-id` and `data-url` | A link that performs a state change and navigates nowhere is reachable by keyboard only as a link to `#` and is announced as a link. **Its rendering is preserved by the declarations of [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses)**, so this is a markup addition and not a visual delta; a visible difference here is a regression against those declarations | item **a6** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements), [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) | **Engineering** |
| A14 | **A health endpoint at a new URL** | There is no health endpoint today, and a hosted deployment needs one. It is listed here rather than left implicit because it is a **new URL the platform requests**, which is the one non-visual addition with an externally reachable surface | [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) | **Engineering and operations** |
| A15 | **The promo-code value repopulates when the checkout form is redisplayed** after a failed submission, as the nine shipping values already do | Nothing binds `PromoCode` today, so neither model state nor the model can supply it and the box re-renders **empty** while every field beside it keeps its value. Once it is a property on the input model it repopulates with the rest — a visible change on the redisplay path, so it is owned rather than absorbed | [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice) | **Product** |

**Where the boundary between the two registers falls, stated so the pair is closed.** A deliberate
difference in an **existing** user-perceptible behaviour belongs in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas); a deliberate **net-new** user-perceptible or
assistive-technology behaviour belongs here. A difference in an existing behaviour that appears in neither
register is a **regression**. Changes with no user-perceptible surface at all — a namespace substitution, a
registration moving into `Program.cs`, the cart handler moving from an inline block into a served file — are
in neither register by design, and they are owned by the sections that specify them rather than by an
approver.

**Both registers are consumed together, and neither is a subset of the other.** [07 §7.1](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s
visual review takes the visible rows of both; [07 §7.2](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s sign-off counts
both and states the two counts **separately**; [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s accessibility
review takes the assistive-technology rows of this one. [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) W1's approval
gate covers both, because approving one and not the other would leave half the deliberate difference
unapproved.

## 12. The test suite: architecture and coverage

### 12.1 Why tests precede the port

**The repository contains no test of any kind.** Two independent searches confirm it:

```bash
git ls-files | grep -ic test                                                          # -> 0
git grep -l -E "TestClass|\[Fact\]|\[Theory\]|xunit|NUnit|MSTest" -- '*.cs' '*.csproj' '*.config'   # -> 0
```

([08 §7.3](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns this as debt.) So **nothing that exists today would
detect a behaviour change** — and section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy),
section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) and the **eight silent of the nine**
blockers of [12 §4](12-migration-blockers.md) are precisely the kind that produce a 200 response and a
wrong outcome. The ninth, F-12-01, is the group's one loud entry and is not of that kind.

Combined with the single-cutover decision (section [11.3](#113-what-single-cutover-does-not-buy)), which
gives no partial-traffic soak period, **the suite is the only control that stands between this port and
a silent regression. It is written before the port, against the legacy application, so that it
characterizes the baseline rather than the result.** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) places it;
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries the absent baseline as a risk.

### 12.2 The architecture: HTTP-level black box

**The suite asserts over HTTP** — status codes, redirect targets, JSON payloads and selected rendered
content — **not on internal types.** That is not a preference; it is the property that lets **one suite
run against two different runtimes**. A test that references `System.Web.Mvc.ActionResult` can only run
against the source; a test that issues `GET /Store/Details/1` and asserts on the response runs against
both, and comparing the two runs is the entire value.

**Two test projects, not one, and the reason is a build-order fact rather than a taste for structure.**
The baseline characterization is authored and run **before the target web project exists** — that is what
"tests precede the port" means, and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W4 runs to completion before the
port workstream opens. A single test project that referenced the web application could not compile until
the port existed, so the baseline half could not be written first, and the whole sequencing argument of
section [12.1](#121-why-tests-precede-the-port) would collapse into "write the tests alongside the port".
The graph is therefore:

| Project | References | Hosts | Owns | Runs from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj` — `net8.0` | **No reference to the web application**, and none to any of its types. Its only input is the fixture-owned context defined below — a base address, an HTTP client and an `IStoreObserver` | Nothing. It drives an **already-running** host over HTTP | The shared `Contracts/**` **abstract** contract classes; the **legacy** concrete derivations that bind them to the baseline fixture; the `IStoreObserver` abstraction and its legacy implementation; `LegacyBaselineFixture.cs`; the standalone sweep class of section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety); and the **deployed-only** fixture and its concrete class, which reference no application type | [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s **W4**, before the target web project exists. It compiles and runs against the legacy application alone |
| `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Tests.csproj` — `net8.0` | **Both** `src/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj` and `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj` | The ported application **in process**, through `CoreApplicationFixture.cs` | The target-only rows; the **target** concrete derivations of every shared contract; the target `IStoreObserver` implementation; and the wiring that hands the in-process context to the contracts it consumes | The port workstream, once the web project exists |

- `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Contracts/**` — the per-surface assertions of section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage), each an **abstract class** parameterized by the fixture-owned context
  below, so **the same assertion body runs against either host**.
- `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Legacy/**` — the **concrete** legacy derivations, one sealed class per
  abstract contract, each binding its base to `LegacyBaselineFixture`.
- `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/LegacyBaselineFixture.cs` — deploys, starts and drives the **MVC 5**
  application over HTTP and captures normalized responses (section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one).
- `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Core/**` — the **concrete** target derivations, one sealed class per abstract
  contract, each binding its base to `CoreApplicationFixture`.
- `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/CoreApplicationFixture.cs` — hosts the ported application in-process against a
  disposable database (section
  [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)).

**Contracts are written once and consumed twice — and a project reference alone does not achieve that.**
The reference direction is one-way: the target project depends on the contracts project, the contracts
project depends on nothing of the application's. But **the runner discovers tests only in the assembly it
is asked to run**, and a `ProjectReference` does not make the referenced assembly's `[Fact]` methods part
of the referencing assembly's test run — the referenced assembly is a dependency, not a second test
assembly the run enumerates. A design that stopped at the reference would execute every shared assertion
**exactly once**, against whichever fixture the contracts assembly bound them to, and the target half
would report a green run with **no shared coverage at all**. That failure is silent: nothing errors, the
case count is simply lower than the reader believes. So the composition is stated as a mechanism, in
three parts.

**1. Every shared contract is an `abstract class` in the contracts project, and it holds the test
methods.** `abstract class StoreBrowseContract`, `abstract class CartContract`,
`abstract class CheckoutContract`, `abstract class IdentityContract`, `abstract class AdministrationContract`,
`abstract class ErrorAndHealthContract` — one per surface of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage), each
carrying that surface's `[Fact]` and `[Theory]` methods and **no** fixture construction of its own. Its
dependencies arrive as the injected context of part 2. An abstract class is not itself discovered — the
runner will not attempt to instantiate it — so the contracts assembly contributes no phantom cases.

**2. Each runnable assembly declares its own concrete `sealed` classes deriving from those bases.**
`sealed class LegacyStoreBrowseTests : StoreBrowseContract` is declared in the contracts project and bound
to `LegacyBaselineFixture`; `sealed class CoreStoreBrowseTests : StoreBrowseContract` is declared in
`src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` and bound to `CoreApplicationFixture`. The property this rests on, stated
because it is the whole reason the topology works: **an inherited `[Fact]` method on a class *declared in
the assembly being run* is discovered and executed.** The runner enumerates the types in the run
assembly, walks each type's inherited members, and produces one test case per `[Fact]` it finds —
including the ones the base class in a referenced assembly declares. The derived class supplies the
fixture binding and nothing else; **no contract body is duplicated**, because the method that runs is the
base's. A copy of an assertion in each project is the failure mode this split exists to prevent: two
copies drift, and a drifted pair reports its own drift as a behaviour difference.

**3. The context the contracts receive is fixture-owned and runtime-neutral.** A contract that asserted
"no row was written" through a `DbContext` would be a target-only contract, because the legacy runtime has
no such type and the ported model is a target artifact. But a large share of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s oracles **are** database outcomes — row counts unchanged, a cart's rows
reassigned, an order's detail rows and total, an Identity membership present. Those are only expressible
in a shared contract if the observation itself is abstracted, so it is:

| Member of the injected context | What it supplies | Why the contract cannot own it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BaseAddress` | The absolute `https` base the fixture is serving on | One fixture produces it by starting a Windows-hosted application on a per-run port, the other by hosting in process. Section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) points 4 and 5 |
| `CreateClient()` and `CreateCookielessClient()` | The two clients of section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 4, on identical redirect and cookie policy on both sides, **constructed per test** (section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)) | The policy must be identical across the two runtimes or a difference in the client is read as a difference in the application |
| `Observer` — an **`IStoreObserver`** | Read-only state observation, as the DTO surface immediately below. **No write member of any kind**, and no `IStoreSetup` — section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3c states why the writes are on a surface the contracts cannot see | The two stores are reached by different connection strings, under different principals, with different catalog names, and in the legacy case through files the fixture copied |
| `Deltas` | The approved-delta ledger of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) as data, so a contract can assert "expected difference" rather than "regression" | The ledger is one list; a contract that carried its own copy would let the two halves disagree about what is approved |

**`IStoreObserver` — read-only, and narrow on purpose.** It is deliberately a narrow read-only
projection rather than a data-access abstraction, because a general one would grow into a second ORM and
would let a contract assert on schema shape it has no business knowing. **Every member returns state and
none mutates**; the suite's writes — the manifest load, the per-test reset, a row's pre-state, a fault
injection — belong to the separate `IStoreSetup` interface of section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3c, which is a member of the
fixture and **not** of this injected context, so no contract body can reach a write at all. The members
below are the ones the shared contracts use; section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3c adds the further read
projections the data-migration and seeding rows need, and the two lists together are the whole surface:

| Member | Returns | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GetTableRowCountsAsync()` | A DTO of row counts keyed by logical table name — the six catalog tables, the Identity tables, the session cache table and the key table — using **logical** names the observer maps to physical ones, so a contract never names a physical table | Every zero-write assertion; rows 13, 16, 24, 31, 41, 54 and the token negatives |
| `GetCartAsync(string cartKey)` | A DTO listing that cart's rows: album key, quantity, date created; and the row count | Rows 4, 5, 19, 35, 36, 38 |
| `GetOrderAsync(int orderId)` | A DTO carrying the order's owner name, its total, and its detail rows with album key, quantity and unit price | Rows 10, 31, 55 |
| `GetLatestOrderForAsync(string userName)` | The same DTO for the most recent order of a named account, or absent | Rows 10, 14 |
| `GetIdentityAccountAsync(string userName)` | A DTO carrying the account's user name, normalized user name, email, normalized email, the stamp fields' presence, lockout and confirmation flags, and its **role assignments** by role name | Rows 18, 56, 57, 63, 65; the quiescence poll of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) |
| `GetRoleNamesAsync()` | The role names present | Rows 57, 65 |
| `RowExistsAsync(LogicalTable table, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object?> key)` | Whether a row with that logical key exists | Rows 16, 39, 40, 41, 66 |
| `GetDataProtectionKeyCountAsync()` | The number of persisted key-ring rows | Rows 25, 42, 43 |

**Two implementations, both through the SQL client [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins.**
`LegacyStoreObserver` reads the **copied** attached stores of section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one — never the tracked files — and
maps the logical names onto the Identity 1.0 and EF 6 physical schema; `TargetStoreObserver` reads the
provisioned target database under the **owner** principal of section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a and maps them onto the
ported schema. Both are plain parameterized SQL over that client. **Neither the contracts nor their
derivations reference EF Core, a `DbContext`, a migration type, or any provider-specific type**, which is
what keeps the contracts assembly compilable before the port exists (the whole point of the two-project
split) and what stops a database oracle from being satisfied by the same model the application under test
is using.

**4. Every type in this topology is declared `public`, and it is a mechanical requirement rather than a
convention.** A top-level C# type with no access modifier is **`internal`**, and internal defeats this
design in two independent places, either of which is enough to make the suite report a green run with
missing coverage:

| What breaks under `internal` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Cross-assembly derivation** | `CoreStoreBrowseTests` is declared in `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` and derives from `StoreBrowseContract`, declared in `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests`. An internal base type is not visible outside its own assembly, so the target half would not compile at all — and the tempting repair, an `InternalsVisibleTo` attribute, would make the contracts assembly's internals visible wholesale to keep one inheritance legal |
| **Test discovery** | The selected framework discovers **public** test classes. A concrete derivation left internal is silently not enumerated: nothing errors, the assembly's case count is simply lower than the reader believes — which is the same silent-undercount failure mode part 3 exists to prevent, arriving by a different route |

So the following are **`public`**, without exception, and this document states it rather than leaving it to
whoever types the first file: every `abstract` contract base; every concrete `sealed` derivation in both
assemblies; both fixtures and the deployed-only fixture below; `IStoreObserver`, its two implementations
and **every DTO type its members return**, since a public member cannot expose a less accessible return
type; the setup API of section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) and its implementations; the
standalone sweep class of section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety); and every
collection-definition class below. Nothing in the suite is `internal`, so no `InternalsVisibleTo` attribute
appears anywhere in it. [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) maps the files; the visibility is
this document's requirement on their contents.

**5. Each surface group has a collection-definition class, declared once *per assembly*, and each concrete
carries the matching `[Collection]`.** The grouping is section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)'s — catalog, cart, checkout, administration,
account and Identity, seeding, continuity, operational, data migration — and it is what makes "one fixture
instance and one database per surface group" a fact the runner enforces rather than a convention:

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The definition class** | `[CollectionDefinition("<the group's name>")] public class <Group>Collection : ICollectionFixture<TFixture>` — an **empty** class whose only purpose is to carry the attribute and the interface. It declares no members and holds no state, so it cannot become a second home for shared mutable state |
| **`TFixture` differs by assembly, which is why the class is declared twice** | A collection definition is scoped to **its own test assembly**: a definition in the contracts assembly does not name collections for the target assembly. So the contracts assembly declares `public class Legacy<Group>Collection : ICollectionFixture<LegacyBaselineFixture>` for each group, and `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` declares `public class Core<Group>Collection : ICollectionFixture<CoreApplicationFixture>` for each group, with correspondingly distinct collection names. Two definitions, one grouping |
| **Each concrete carries `[Collection("…")]`** | `[Collection("Legacy catalog")] public sealed class LegacyStoreBrowseTests : StoreBrowseContract` and `[Collection("Core catalog")] public sealed class CoreStoreBrowseTests : StoreBrowseContract`. A concrete with **no** `[Collection]` is its own implicit collection, which would give it its own fixture instance and its own database — the opposite of the grouping, and invisible until someone counts provisioned databases |
| **`ICollectionFixture<T>` is what gives one instance per collection** | The runner constructs **one** `TFixture` per collection, before the collection's first test, and disposes it after the last. That is exactly the provisioning unit section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) requires, and it is why the reset is a per-test call on that shared instance rather than a per-test construction of it |
| **The fixture instance reaches the contract through the concrete's constructor** | The concrete takes `TFixture` as a constructor parameter — the runner supplies it — and passes the runtime-neutral context of part 3 to the abstract base. The base never names a fixture type, which is what keeps one assertion body runnable against both |
| **A row that needs its own database gets its own collection** | Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 24 requires an empty, freshly provisioned database, and row 25 `25c` requires a host whose database lacks the Identity schema (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)). Each is therefore its **own** collection with its own definition class and its own fixture instance, rather than an exception inside a shared one — the grouping is the isolation mechanism, so an exception to it has to be expressed as a group |

**The deployed-only binding — section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 47 needs a runnable context, and
neither fixture above can supply one.** Row 47 asserts against a **deployed** instance: it has no
in-process host to start and no database to provision, and it must not acquire either, since a deployed
smoke check that provisioned a database would be asserting about something other than the deployment. It
is also the whole of `Category=Deployed` (section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)), so it cannot borrow another category's
fixture. The binding is therefore its own, and it lives in the **contracts** project, because it references
no application type:

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **`public sealed class DeployedEndpointFixture`** | In `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/`. **Runtime-neutral**: it starts nothing and provisions nothing. It **consumes** a base address from configuration — the deployed instance's — and fails as a `SETUP` failure with the configuration key named when that value is absent, so "nobody set the address" is never reported as "the deployment is unhealthy" |
| **Its client policy is its own, and redirects are not followed** | It constructs the client with **automatic redirect following disabled**, because row 47's assertion **is** the redirect: a client that followed it would observe the redirected response and could never assert the status code or the `Location` value. The two clients of section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 4 belong to the two hosted fixtures and are not reused here |
| **No `IStoreObserver`, no setup API, no reset** | It exposes neither, so no assertion bound to it can reach a database even by accident. There is nothing to reset between its tests because it writes nothing |
| **`[CollectionDefinition("Deployed")] public class DeployedCollection : ICollectionFixture<DeployedEndpointFixture>`, and `[Collection("Deployed")] public sealed class DeployedEndpointTests`** | The concrete is `public` and `sealed` like every other, holds row 47's cases directly rather than deriving from a shared contract — the legacy application has no equivalent deployed surface to characterize — and is the **only** class carrying the `Deployed` trait |
| **Who runs it** | [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s deployment verification stage, which selects `Category=Deployed` and gets exactly this class. Section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s **Stage C** is where the invocation is written, and it invokes **this** project rather than the target one for the discovery reason that subsection states; the effort is [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s |
| **The map row** | [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) maps `DeployedEndpointFixture.cs` and `DeployedEndpointTests.cs` under the contracts project, alongside the artifacts the plan-correction record below already asks it to map |

**Two supporting requirements, because without them the architecture above is not executable.**

- **HTML is parsed, not scanned.** Every row of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) that asserts an
  element's identity, an attribute's value or a form's structure — the `id`-located elements of section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), the rendered forms of rows 4, 21, 22 and
  40, the asset references of row 23 — is asserted against a **parsed HTML5 document queried by CSS
  selector**, using **AngleSharp**. Regular-expression or substring scanning of the response body is
  **not acceptable** for those rows: it cannot distinguish an attribute from text that resembles one,
  it silently passes when markup nests differently, and it is the mechanism that turns a real regression
  into a green run. [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the pin and its verification; what this
  document owns is the requirement and which rows it binds. Rows that assert only a status code, a header
  or a JSON property need no parser.
- **Parallelism is off, declaratively, in both projects.** Each project carries its own
  `xunit.runner.json` with **`parallelizeTestCollections: false`**, copied to the output directory.
  Section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) explains why — the fixture provisions
  and drops real databases and, in the legacy half, binds a port — and this is where the setting lives, so
  that the policy is a committed file rather than a convention a runner flag could contradict.

**Plan-correction record — the frozen plan's future application map carries one test project, not this
graph.**

Recorded in the form section [9.3](#93-two-plan-correction-records-for-the-plan-owner) uses, for the same
reason: the plan is frozen, nothing here edits it, and an artifact the design needs but the map omits is
notified rather than added silently.

| Aspect | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The omission** | The plan's §0.4.1 future application map lists `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Tests.csproj` with `LegacyBaselineFixture.cs`, `CoreApplicationFixture.cs` and `Contracts/**` **inside that one project**. It lists no second test project and no `xunit.runner.json` |
| **Why the second project is required rather than tidier** | The plan's own §0.3.1 requires the suite to be authored **before** the port and to characterize the legacy application, and its §0.11.2 makes the pre-port baseline an acceptance criterion. A project referencing `src/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj` cannot compile before that project exists, so a single-project graph makes the plan's own sequencing unbuildable. The split changes no coverage and no assertion — it changes only which assembly the shared assertions live in |
| **Why the runner files are required** | Section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) forbids collection-level parallelism because the fixtures own databases and, in the legacy half, a port. xUnit's default is to parallelize collections, so the prohibition is only real if a committed configuration file states it |
| **What is being asked** | That the plan's next revision map `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj` with `Contracts/**`, `LegacyBaselineFixture.cs`, the per-group collection-definition classes and the deployed-only `DeployedEndpointFixture.cs` and `DeployedEndpointTests.cs`; retain `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Tests.csproj` with `CoreApplicationFixture.cs`, its own per-group collection-definition classes and the target-only cases; record the reference direction in the table above; and add one `xunit.runner.json` per test project — all CREATE / net-new |
| **Disposition** | **Recorded, and the design is specified here rather than deferred.** [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the target artifact map and states that the set is governed rather than invented, so **04 maps these files** and this record is the notification that authorizes it to. Test-framework and parser pins are [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s; this document names no version |

**One suite, authored once — and it lands in two places, because half of it has nothing to run
against until the port exists.** This is stated here rather than left to the reader to infer, because
reading section [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) as a single pre-port deliverable
produces a circular requirement: the target fixture would have to be working before the target
application it hosts had been written.

| Half | What it is | When it lands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **(a) The legacy-facing baseline** | The shared contract assertions, `LegacyBaselineFixture`, the two-database legacy reset (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one), the normalization rules (problem three) and the enumerated approved deltas — **run against the running MVC 5 application** | **Complete and green before the port.** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W4 places it and states its exit criteria; this document does not restate them |
| **(b) The target-facing half** | `CoreApplicationFixture`, the disposable engine it provisions (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two), the in-process host wiring of section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring), and every assertion run against the **ported** application | **With the port.** It exercises a target artifact, so it cannot exist earlier; [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W7 carries it as an exit criterion |

**Nothing in section [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) requires the target fixture to
exist before the target application does.** Where a subsection below specifies target-side machinery —
the host wiring of section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring), the provisioning and teardown of sections [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) and [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety), the
`Category=Target` half of the runbook in section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) — it is specifying half (b), and the
sequencing consequence is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to enforce. What is **not** deferred is
the *specification*: both halves are designed here, in full, before either is built, because half (a)'s
assertions are the ones half (b) re-points at a second runtime and a contract invented twice is two
contracts.

**The two fixtures share the assertions and nothing else.** They are not two implementations of one
abstraction: one drives an out-of-process application over the network, the other hosts an application
in-process (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)). What crosses between them is an abstract `Contracts/**` class parameterized by the
fixture-owned context above — base address, clients, `IStoreObserver`, delta ledger — which is exactly
what the black-box choice above buys.

### 12.3 Three problems that must be handled explicitly

**Problem one — the legacy baseline needs BOTH databases, not one.** MVC 5 has a catalog store **and** a
separate Identity store, and both are file-attached from `App_Data`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13]. The directory holds exactly four files — two `.mdf`/`.ldf`
pairs (`git ls-files 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/*'`). So a deterministic reset **restores both
pairs** and reattaches them before each run. A fixture that resets only the catalog pair produces a
credential store that accumulates state across runs, and the sign-in assertions then pass or fail
depending on run order.

Two constraints on that reset: it operates on **copies outside the checkout**, because attaching the
tracked files causes the engine to write to them and dirty the working tree; and the Identity database
carries a fixed catalog name in its connection string [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12], so **concurrent fixtures must rename it**
or they collide inside one shared engine instance.

**And the fixture owns the legacy deployment, rather than assuming somebody has one running.** A fixture
that reads a base address and hopes an application is listening on it is not a fixture; it is a
prerequisite dressed as one, and its failure mode is a suite that reports the port as broken because a
developer's IIS Express window was closed. `LegacyBaselineFixture` therefore performs the whole
lifecycle, in this order:

1. **Copies the built MVC 5 output** — the `bin` output plus the content tree the application serves — into
   a **private per-run directory outside the repository checkout**, named from the run identifier of
   section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism). Nothing in the checkout is read
   except as a source to copy from, and nothing in the checkout is written: this is what keeps the
   documentation-only constraint of section
   [14.2](#142-what-this-document-creates-nothing-and-what-the-assessment-nonetheless-wrote) true of the
   suite as well as of this document. The **build** that produced that output is not the fixture's job and
   its status is [10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s to report.
2. **Copies both committed store pairs** — all four files under `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13] — into that private directory's own `App_Data`. **The tracked
   `.mdf` and `.ldf` files are never attached**, in any run, on any machine: an attached database is a
   database the engine writes to, and writing to a tracked file dirties the working tree and corrupts the
   next run's baseline. Copy-then-attach is the only permitted shape.
3. **Rewrites the deployed copy's connection strings** — the deployed copy's, never the tracked file's — so
   that two things hold: `|DataDirectory|` resolves to the private copy's `App_Data` rather than to the
   checkout, and the Identity database is attached under a **per-run catalog name**. The second is not
   cosmetic: the committed Identity connection string names a fixed catalog
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12] inside a **shared** LocalDB instance, so two runs on one machine
   collide on that name and the second silently attaches the first's file.
4. **Starts the host itself, on a per-run port, and captures the process id it spawned.** The host is
   **IIS Express**, because the legacy application is declared to the ASP.NET pipeline by a markup file and
   needs a Windows web server ([10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) owns the toolchain and its
   install location). The invocation is a literal, not a description:

   ```text
   iisexpress.exe /path:<private-deploy-dir> /port:<per-run-port> /clr:v4.0 /systray:false
   ```

   `/path` is the private directory step 1 produced, given as an absolute path; `/port` is the port
   allocated for this run and recorded with the run's other owned resources (section
   [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)), so a second run on the same machine neither binds an
   occupied port nor answers the first run's requests; `/clr:v4.0` selects the runtime the application
   targets; `/systray:false` suppresses the tray icon, which is what makes the process usable from a
   non-interactive agent. **This exact form was executed on the assessment host and served the
   application**, which is what makes it a specification rather than a guess.

   **The fixture holds the process id of the process it started, and holds nothing else.** Termination at
   teardown is by **that captured id alone**. Selecting the target by image name is forbidden: a developer
   machine and a shared agent both routinely run other instances of the same host, and a name-matched kill
   takes down a colleague's or a sibling run's application. The captured id is also the only thing the
   teardown of step 7 is authorized to act on, which is the process analogue of the identifier rule
   section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) applies to databases.
5. **Polls a readiness probe with a bounded timeout** — a `GET` of the application root, polled on a fixed
   interval to a stated ceiling, with the first `200` ending the wait. A ceiling breach is a **setup**
   failure naming the probe target and the elapsed time (section
   [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)), not a scenario failure: nothing has been
   asserted yet, and reporting it as a scenario failure is how an environment problem gets filed as a
   regression.
6. **Waits for startup quiescence — and this is a real race, not a precaution.** A `200` from the root
   means the pipeline is serving; it does **not** mean startup has finished writing to the database. The
   legacy application provisions the configured administrator from
   `private async void CreateAdminUser()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21], called
   without `await` from `ConfigureApp` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18]: it is
   fire-and-forget, so it creates the role [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:32-36] and the
   user [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:38-44] at a moment **nothing in the HTTP surface
   reports**, some time after the first request has already been answered. The EF initializer registered at
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:16] is in the same position for the catalog store.

   So the fixture polls **through the `IStoreObserver`** of section
   [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) — not through HTTP, because the condition is a
   database state and no endpoint exposes it — until **both** of these hold, on the same fixed interval and
   bounded ceiling as step 5: the source-provisioned account named by
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16] exists, **and** its assignment to the `Administrator` role
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:25] exists. A ceiling breach here is a setup failure
   for the same reason step 5's is.

   **Only then** does the fixture load the fixture dataset (section
   [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) below) and check its row-count invariants.
   The ordering is the whole point: a fixture that loads before quiescence is loading into a store whose
   row counts are **still moving**, so the invariant check either fails intermittently or passes against a
   count that changes a moment later — and the first assertion that reads a count then fails in a way that
   looks like an application defect. Restated as a rule: **every invariant is checked after the last writer
   the fixture does not control has finished.**
7. **On teardown, in this order**: stops the host **by the process id captured in step 4**, waits for its
   exit, **detaches both databases** from the LocalDB instance — an attached file cannot be deleted, so a
   teardown that skips this leaves the directory undeletable — and deletes the private per-run directory in
   full. Teardown is authorized and audited exactly as every other owned resource is, by section
   [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety), and the private directory is one of the run-owned resources
   its registry records.

**This lifecycle is exercised rather than merely proposed.** During this assessment the deployment steps
above were carried out on a Windows host against the legacy application — deploy a copy outside the
checkout, copy and rename both store pairs, rewrite the deployed copy's connection strings, serve on a
private port with the step 4 invocation, drive it over HTTP, then detach and delete — and the responses
observed that way are the source of the
**observed** legacy oracles marked as such in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage). That is evidence
about **the fixture design**: the mechanics work and the oracles are measured rather than inferred.

**It is not evidence about the build status, and nothing here revises it.** MVC 5's build outcome is
[10 §3.2](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s to state and it states **blocked pending a Windows
verification run** — a *documented* verification against the toolchain that deliverable specifies, with
tool versions, restore source, configuration and result recorded. An ad-hoc execution during an assessment
is not that run and does not stand in for it. So step 1's input remains a prerequisite this suite consumes
and does not own, section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) carries it as the
one outstanding prerequisite of the Windows half, and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) sequences the
dependency.

**Problem two — the Core fixture needs a real SQL Server.** The in-process integration host supplies no
database, and **two** target features require a SQL Server-compatible engine rather than an in-memory
substitute: **migrations** (section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)) and the **SQL-backed
session cache** (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)). An in-memory provider would apply no
migrations and would leave the cart identity untested, which is the mechanism most of the coverage below
depends on.

So the fixture **provisions a disposable SQL Server instance** — a container locally, a throwaway
managed database in CI — and then:

1. creates the session cache table, then applies **both** migration sets in the order of section
   [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) — which is also how the fixture gets the key table,
   because, as section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) decides,
   `ApplicationDbContext` implements `IDataProtectionKeyContext`, and the `DataProtectionKeys` table belongs to the Identity migration set.
   There is therefore **no separate create step** for it here either;
2. loads the **fixture-data manifest** specified below — the single logical dataset **both** fixtures
   load, because a cross-baseline comparison of two applications holding different data compares nothing;
3. **asserts the manifest's own invariants after loading** — the load itself is a fixture that can fail
   silently, and a suite built on an unverified fixture reports the fixture's bugs as the application's;
4. tears the instance down afterwards.

**The fixture-data manifest, stated as exact counts and keys rather than as a description.** "A small set
of migrated users, roles, carts and orders" is not loadable and not assertable: a row that says "the
fixture `Genres` row count" needs that count to be a published number, and section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 24 asserts row counts before and after a refused seeding attempt, which
requires knowing what they were. The manifest is one committed logical description with **fixed integer
keys** and it is the default dataset for every row that does not construct its own.

**It is one file, and the file is named, because two files diverge.** The manifest is
**`src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Fixtures/fixture-data.json`**, tracked in the repository, and
`src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Fixtures/` is **the fixture path** that the rest of this document
refers to — section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s divergence-seam override files live beside it,
under `Fixtures/ModelOverrides/`.

**Why that path and not a repository-root `tests/fixtures/`, stated once and not repeated at each
file.** The fixture content sits **inside the mapped contracts project** ([04
§12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the map rows), which is what makes it reachable at run
time without a path convention: content under the project is declared `CopyToOutputDirectory` and lands
beside the test assembly, so every fixture, every override file and both loaders resolve it relative to
the assembly's own location. A root-level directory would have to be found by walking up from the
output directory to a repository root that does not exist on an agent that only downloaded an artifact
— which is exactly the class of setup failure section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) requires to be distinguishable from an
application regression, and the cheapest way to not have to distinguish it is to not create it. **This
document names the paths; [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) maps them and owns the
copy-to-output declaration.** Both loaders below
**deserialize that same file**; neither embeds a copy of the dataset in code, and neither reads a
per-runtime variant. Stated as a requirement rather than as tidiness: two loaders each holding their own
literals is how a cross-baseline suite ends up comparing two applications over two datasets, and the
comparison then measures the difference between the fixtures. The fingerprint below is what makes the
single-source rule checkable — one file has one hash, and both halves record it.

**Plan-correction record — the frozen plan's map does not carry the fixture manifest.**

| Aspect | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The omission** | The plan's §0.4.1 future application map lists the test project and its fixtures but **no fixture-data file**. It says the Core fixture "load[s] a controlled fixture set with row-count/key invariants" without mapping the artifact that set lives in |
| **Why the file is required rather than tidier** | The plan's §0.3.1 requires **one** logical dataset loaded by **both** fixtures, and its §0.11.2 requires the target run to fail closed when the dataset differs from the one a baseline was captured against. Neither is expressible without a single addressable artifact to hash: a dataset spread across two loaders' source code has no fingerprint, and the fail-closed rule of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) would have nothing to compare |
| **What is being asked** | That the plan's next revision map `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Fixtures/fixture-data.json` — CREATE / net-new — together with the nine divergence-seam override files under `Fixtures/ModelOverrides/`, the seed expectation and the baseline reference under the same `Fixtures/` path, and record that both test projects read them as content copied to output |
| **Disposition** | **Recorded, and the dataset is specified here rather than deferred.** [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the target artifact map, so **04 maps the file**; this record is the notification that authorizes it to. This document states the file's path, contents and invariants and creates nothing |

Names distinct and ASCII, so the `Browse?genre={name}` query needs no escaping to be exercised, and the escaping case is a row of its own rather than an accident of the fixture. **Ten and not three**, for the reason the ranking table below states: the source's genre menu takes **nine** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:51] |

The source-provisioned account's own assignment is **not** removed — see the pre-existing set below — so any count over this table is `1 + the declared pre-existing count` |

**The two rankings the source computes, and the numbers that make them assertable.** This is why the
dataset is the size it is. The source ranks **genres** by the sum of `OrderDetails.Quantity` over each
genre's albums and takes **nine** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52], and it
ranks **albums** by the **count** of their order-detail rows and takes **six**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:18], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:29-32].
A three-genre, six-album fixture cannot express either assertion: nine cannot be taken from three, and a
six-album `Take(6)` returns every album, so the ranking is unobservable and section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) rows 9 and 30 would assert against a set the ordering cannot change. An
earlier revision of this manifest published three and six against rows that demand nine and a boundary,
which was an internal contradiction rather than a small dataset.

| Genre | Name | Total ordered quantity | Rank | Rendered by the menu? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `4` | `Blues` | 24 | 1 | yes |
| `9` | `Country` | 21 | 2 | yes |
| `1` | `Rock` | 18 | 3 | yes |
| `2` | `Jazz` | 16 | 4 | yes |
| `6` | `Metal` | 15 | 5 | yes |
