| `Category=Deployed` | **Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 47, and nothing else** — the transport and HSTS observation at the deployed edge, held by the deployed-only class of section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) | A deployed non-traffic target and its base address. **No database, no engine and no in-process host**, which is why this category is the only one with no infrastructure prerequisite at all | Wherever the release runs, and **out of the `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests` assembly**, because that is where the deployed-only fixture and class are declared and a runner discovers only the assembly it is asked to run. This is the category [06 §12.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s **Verify** stage consumes |

**`Category=Deployed` is narrow, and its boundary is stated because it is easy to widen by accident.**
It covers **row 47 alone** — a single case, which is why the execution totals of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) show `Deployed` as `1`. **The health rows are not in it**, and the reason is
worth stating because "health checks are what you run against a deployment" is the obvious assumption:
row 27's five cases include the **unreachable-database** cases, whose fault is a `DENY CONNECT` the fixture
issues against its own disposable engine (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injection table).
Neither half of that is available against a deployed host — the suite owns no principal there and must not
break one — so row 27 is `Target` alone, and re-pointing it at a deployment would silently reduce it to
its two reachable cases while still reporting as the same row. It specifically does **not** cover the
**three deployment verifications** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order): those are
boundary observations rather than application assertions, section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) already states that none is run by this suite, and
[06 §10.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) carries the two forwarding-dependent ones in its own
gate. Adding them here would give one fact two owners.

**Category assignment is a rule, not a per-row decision.** Every row of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) with a legacy counterpart carries **both** `Baseline` and `Target`; every
row whose behaviour is target-only carries `Target` alone; and **exactly one row, row 47, carries
`Deployed`** — in the singular, and instead of `Target` rather than in addition to it, because its
assertion is on the deployed edge's transport behaviour and there is no in-process equivalent to run. A
mixed row carries `Baseline` and `Target` at the row level and its target-only cases carry `Target`
alone. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) states which rows are which, and its counts are
derived from exactly that rule: 144 `Baseline`, 241 `Target`, 1 `Deployed`, summing to the 386 executions
that section publishes.

**`Category=Sweep` is a fourth trait value and deliberately not a fourth category.** It is carried by
exactly one type — `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Maintenance/OrphanSweepTests.cs`, the concrete
runnable class the always-run cleanup job of point 3 invokes — and by no row of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage). It asserts nothing about either application: it removes leaked resources
under section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s authorization, and it exists as a test class only
because that is the runner the pipeline already has on both agents. It is therefore **excluded from every
count in this document** — the row, case and execution totals of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage), and the three category figures above — and a reader reconciling those
numbers against a runner's own output should expect the sweep class's cases to appear there and nowhere
here. Stating the exclusion in both places is deliberate: a maintenance trait silently folded into a
coverage figure inflates it with work that proves nothing.

**2. The handoff — what crosses from the Windows run to the Linux run.**

**The Windows characterization run's output is an artifact, and the Linux target run consumes that
artifact instead of driving the legacy application itself.** Concretely: a `Category=Baseline` run emits
a **normalized baseline record** — one entry per scenario identifier, carrying the expected value of each
named field in the schema of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1, the `normalized` exclusion list for
that scenario, and the 4.5-quirks-mode note that section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) requires the
capture to record. It passes the redactor before it is written, so it carries pseudonymized usernames and
no masked material, and it is retained for the life of the port under the exemption section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) names. A `Category=Target` run reads it and
compares against it.

| | **Recommended: the redacted artifact** | **Alternative: a hosted Windows baseline service the target run queries** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mechanism** | The Windows run writes the record; the Linux run reads it as an input | A Windows host keeps the legacy application and its LocalDB copies running; the target run calls it per scenario |
| **What the baseline is** | **Immutable and versioned.** A target run six weeks into the port compares against the same characterization, which is exactly the frozen-reference property [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W4 exists to establish | **Live and mutable.** Whatever the legacy application is at the moment of the query, including any change somebody made to it since |
| **Standing commitment** | None. The Windows machine is needed for the capture and for a re-capture, and at no other time | A Windows host, LocalDB and a served legacy application available for the **whole** duration of the port |
| **Exposure** | The record is redacted; the store copies never leave the Windows machine | A network path from the target pipeline to a machine holding an attached **credential store** (section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4), live for months |
| **Failure mode** | A missing or stale record is a **setup** failure naming the record (section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)) — unambiguous | The service being down, slow or mid-restart fails target rows for a reason that is not the port, which is the false-regression class this document keeps eliminating |
| **Its one advantage** | Adding an assertion late requires a re-capture run | Adding an assertion late captures on the next query |
| **Verdict** | **Selected.** Its one cost is a re-capture run, and that cost is largely notional: adding an assertion means learning the legacy application's value for it, which requires exercising the legacy application either way | Rejected on the standing commitment and the exposure, neither of which buys anything the re-capture does not |

**The record carries metadata in two separate namespaces, and only one of them gates.** An immutable
versioned baseline is only worth its immutability if a consumer can tell whether it is the right baseline;
without that, "immutable" degrades into "old", and a target run six weeks into the port compares against a
characterization of something else and reports the discrepancy as a behavioural difference. But the record
also has to carry things a consumer must **not** compare for equality — the agent that captured it, its SDK
patch, its engine image — because those legitimately differ between the Windows capture and the Linux
consumption and gating on them would refuse every run. Conflating the two is what makes a provenance block
either toothless or unusable, so they are two named objects in the record:

**`baselineSource` — immutable provenance of what was characterized. Eleven items, and every one of them
gates.** The count is published because [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) sizes against it and a
namespace whose membership is only enumerated is a namespace two documents can disagree about the size
of: the table below carries **eleven gating items** — `legacyCommit`, `legacyBinarySha256`,
`legacyConfigurationFingerprint`, `suiteSchemaVersion`, `fixtureDatasetFingerprint`, `culture`,
`uiCulture`, `timeZone`, `databaseCollation`, `aliasKeyId` and `lookupNormalizer` — in ten rows, because
`culture` and `uiCulture` share one row and are two items. A
`Category=Target` run **refuses to consume the record** — a `SETUP` failure naming the mismatched item, per
section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1b — when any item disagrees with
the value the current run establishes for it:

| Item | What it pins | How the consuming run establishes its own value | Why a mismatch invalidates the comparison |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `legacyCommit` | The commit of this repository the characterized application was built from | From the committed baseline reference below — **not** from the consuming checkout's own `HEAD`, which has moved because the port is what moved it | The baseline is a statement about a specific source state. Comparing against a record captured from a different commit is comparing against a different application |
| `legacyBinarySha256` | The `SHA-256` of the built legacy assembly that was served | The same committed baseline reference | The commit is not sufficient: a build from the same commit with a different toolchain, configuration or restored package set is a different binary, and [10 §3.2](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) records that the legacy build is not yet verified on a supported toolchain — so the binary that eventually gets built is precisely the thing that must be identified rather than assumed |
| `legacyConfigurationFingerprint` | A digest over the configuration the characterized host ran with, including the 4.5-quirks-mode note above | The same committed baseline reference | Two runs of the same binary under different configuration are two behaviours, and the quirks-mode note is the case this document already knows about |
| `suiteSchemaVersion` | The version of the record format and the field set of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1a | The constant the running suite implements | A record written before a field was added has no value for it. Absent this, that field silently compares as absent-versus-absent and the new assertion is vacuous |
| `fixtureDatasetFingerprint` | The `SHA-256` of the fixture manifest of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) | Recomputed over the manifest file in the consuming checkout | Every expected value in the record is a value *for that dataset*. A record captured against a different dataset is expected values for different rows |
| `culture`, `uiCulture` | The two locale literals pinned below | Read from the consuming process's own effective culture, after the pinning mechanism below has run | They decide currency rendering, decimal separators and date formatting in every exact-text assertion, and the two halves of the handoff run on different operating systems |
| `timeZone` | The literal pinned below | Read from `TimeZoneInfo.Local` in the consuming process | Row 10's `OrderDate` window, row 50 `50b`'s lockout arithmetic, row 51 `51b`'s cookie expiry and row 70's minted timestamps are all time comparisons |
| `databaseCollation` | The literal pinned below | Read from the consuming run's own provisioned database | String ordering and comparison **inside the engine**, which rows 1, 8 and 9 assert an order over |
| `aliasKeyId` | The key identifier of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s alias rule | Derived from the consuming run's configured alias key, by that section's fixed-label construction | A rotated key produces a baseline whose aliases match nothing, so **every** per-account assertion fails as a behavioural difference. This is the item whose absence would produce the largest number of confidently wrong answers |
| `lookupNormalizer` | The **type name and assembly version** of the `ILookupNormalizer` the aliases were canonicalized with | Read from the normalizer the consuming run resolves | A different normalizer merges or splits accounts relative to the baseline, per that section's merge-and-split correction — the failure would present as a per-account mismatch and belong to neither runtime |

**`targetRun` — provenance of the consuming run. No item gates.** Recorded so that a failure can be
diagnosed and never compared for equality: the run identifier; the agent's operating system and version;
the SDK version; the engine's resolved image digest or the managed instance's identifier; the provisioned
database name; the UTC start time; and the resolved `tools/migrate-data` output path. A record consumed on
a different agent than it was captured on is the **normal** case — that is the whole point of the two-stage
split — so an equality check here would fail every run for a reason that is not a difference in behaviour.

**The gating values for the three legacy items come from a committed baseline reference, because a
consuming run cannot compute them.** `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Fixtures/baseline-reference.json`,
tracked in the repository beside the fixture manifest and copied to output with it (section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) states the path rule once), carries
the `legacyCommit`, `legacyBinarySha256` and `legacyConfigurationFingerprint` the port has **accepted** as
its baseline. It is updated in the same change that accepts a re-capture, by the reviewer who accepts it,
which makes accepting a new baseline a reviewable act rather than a side effect of somebody re-running a
job. Without it there is nothing to compare those three items against, and a swapped or silently
re-captured record would be consumed without complaint — the record would be internally consistent and
about the wrong application.

**Fails closed, not warns.** A mismatch in **any** `baselineSource` item is a `SETUP` failure and every
dependent row reports **not run** — it is emphatically **not** a warning next to a comparison that
proceeded anyway, because a proceeding comparison against the wrong baseline produces confident, specific,
wrong answers, and those are worse than no answer. The remedy is always the same and is always available:
re-capture, and update the committed reference in the same change.

**A re-capture is a normal operation, not an incident**, and the runbook below is what makes it cheap:
it is the same command with the same category filter, run on the Windows machine, replacing the record.

**And the record has to actually travel between two machines, which is a mechanism rather than an
assumption.** Stage A runs on a Windows agent and Stage B on a Linux agent; they share no filesystem, so
"Stage B reads it" needs the transfer stated, and a transfer that is not verified is a silent corruption
path — a truncated record consumed as authoritative produces missing expected values, which read as
behavioural differences:

| Step | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **Stage A writes both files** | `<artifacts>/baseline/baseline-record.json`, and beside it `<artifacts>/baseline/baseline-record.json.sha256` containing that file's `SHA-256` as lowercase hexadecimal. The record is written first and the digest second, so a digest that exists describes a complete record — the same ordering rule the extract manifest of section [5.6](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) uses, and for the same reason |
| **Stage A publishes them as one named artifact — and only on a complete, wholly passing capture** | Published as the pipeline artifact **`baseline-record`**, containing both files and nothing else, **if and only if** the capture ran every `Category=Baseline` case and every one of them passed. A capture that failed a case, or that did not reach every case, publishes the **diagnostic** artifact of the row below instead and publishes **no** baseline record — it neither creates one nor replaces an existing one. This is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s rule, not a second one: [06 §12.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) already states that an incomplete capture does not replace a record, and an earlier revision of this subsection published a partial record beside that rule, which is the contradiction this row closes |
| **A failed or incomplete capture publishes a diagnostic artifact instead** | Published as **`baseline-capture-diagnostic`** — a deliberately different artifact name, so that no consuming step can pick it up by looking for `baseline-record`. It carries the per-case status list below, the `SETUP` and `ASSERTION` records of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) for the cases that failed, and **no expected-value record**: it is evidence about the capture, never an input to a comparison. It passes the same redactor and gets the same retention as the record it is not |
| **Completeness is provable by enumeration, and the metadata carries the enumeration** | The record's metadata carries a **`coverage`** object: the suite's expected `Category=Baseline` case identifiers, and for each one its status. Publication requires that list to be complete and every status to be `passed`; Stage B re-checks it before reading a single expected value, and a list that omits a case the consuming suite knows about is a `SETUP` failure naming the missing identifiers. **The digest cannot do this job and is not asked to** — a digest proves that the bytes are the bytes that were written, which is integrity; it says nothing whatever about whether those bytes describe every case, which is completeness. Conflating the two is how a truncated-but-intact capture gets consumed as authoritative. `coverage` is **not** a twelfth `baselineSource` item: it is a precondition of publication and a completeness check, not immutable provenance to be compared for equality, and the gating namespace remains the eleven items above — which is the count [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) reproduces |
| **Stage B downloads it before it starts a host** | Stage B's first action after restore is to download artifact `baseline-record` to a known directory, and to set `Tests:Baseline:RecordPath` to the downloaded record. It does **not** reach across to the Windows agent, mount a share, or fall back to a path from a previous run |
| **Stage B verifies the digest before reading the record** | It recomputes the record's `SHA-256` and compares it to the sidecar. A mismatch, a missing sidecar or a missing record is a `SETUP` failure naming the file and both digests, and **no** `Category=Target` row runs. The verification precedes the `baselineSource` comparison above, because comparing metadata inside a corrupt file is not a check |
| **What the digest does and does not protect** | It detects truncation, partial upload and corruption in transit — the failure modes a two-agent handoff actually produces. It is **not** a signature and is not claimed as one: it travels with the file it describes, so anything that could rewrite both could rewrite both consistently. It is also **not** a completeness proof, per the row above. What protects against a *substituted* baseline is the committed reference above, which lives in the repository rather than in the artifact; what establishes completeness is the enumerated `coverage` list |
| **Retention matches the record's** | The artifact is retained for the life of the port, under the retention and encryption controls of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) — it is a redacted, PII-derived artifact and gets no weaker treatment for being a pipeline artifact ([06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the artifact controls) |

**Culture, time zone and database collation are pinned, in both hosts and both agents.** Several oracles
in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) are exact string comparisons over values whose rendering is
culture-dependent — the album price rendered as currency in rows 1, 2 and 3, the cart total and per-item
prices in row 5, the ordering of genre names and album titles in rows 1, 8 and 9 — and one is a timestamp
comparison, row 10's `OrderDate` window. None of those is decidable across a Windows agent and a Linux
agent unless the inputs are fixed:

**The three literals, published rather than described.** Every one of them is a value, not a policy, because
"an invariant or explicitly named culture" is not something two implementations can agree on:

| What is pinned | The literal |
| --- | --- |
| Culture and UI culture | **`en-US`** |
| Time zone | **`UTC`** |
| Database collation | **`SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS`** |

`en-US` rather than the invariant culture, deliberately: the source's own currency and date rendering is
whatever the legacy Windows host produced, the assertions are exact-text comparisons against **that**, and
the invariant culture renders currency with a non-breaking-space-separated international symbol that no
observed baseline value carries. `SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS` because it is the collation the legacy
LocalDB stores carry, and the ordering assertions compare against orderings those stores produced. That
last one is **verified rather than trusted**: `extract`'s schema record (section
[5.6](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)) includes the source database's collation, and
a value other than the literal above is a `SETUP` failure naming both — so a source store that turns out to
carry a different collation stops the run instead of silently re-ordering every comparison.

**And each is set in a named place, per host and per agent — four places, not a general intention.**

| Where | Culture and UI culture | Time zone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The target host** (in-process, Linux and Windows alike) | Configuration key **`Localization:DefaultCulture`** = `en-US`, consumed by section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 5's `UseRequestLocalization` — single-element supported-culture lists, providers cleared, ahead of routing. That item owns the mechanism and its three properties; what this section owns is the literal. One key, so the fixture and the deployment pin it the same way | The process environment variable **`TZ=UTC`**, set by whatever starts the host — the fixture for a test run, the platform configuration for a deployment ([06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the deployed setting). On Linux the .NET runtime honours `TZ`; on Windows it does not, so the Windows path is the agent row below |
| **The legacy host** (IIS Express, section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one) | `<globalization culture="en-US" uiCulture="en-US" />` inside `<system.web>` of the **deployed copy's** `Web.config`, written by the same rewrite step that rewrites its connection strings. The tracked `Web.config` declares no `<globalization>` element at all and is **not** edited — the rewrite targets the copy, which is why this is expressible under the no-modification constraint | The Windows agent's system time zone, per the agent row below. .NET Framework offers no configuration switch for it |
| **Both test agents** (the `dotnet test` processes) | A `[ModuleInitializer]` method in each test assembly assigns `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture` and `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentUICulture` to `CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("en-US")`. A module initializer runs before the first test in that assembly and applies to every thread that does not set its own culture, which is what makes it cover a parallelized run without a per-test hook | Linux: `TZ=UTC` in the agent environment. Windows: the agent's system zone set to UTC as a documented agent prerequisite ([10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) owns agent prerequisites) |

**Why the host time zone matters and is not a fussy detail:** the source writes local time, not UTC —
`order.OrderDate = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:41] and
`DateCreated = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:49] — and the port preserves
that behaviour, so row 10's "`OrderDate` within the request window" is a comparison between a value the
**host process** produced from its local zone and a window the **agent process** observed from its own. Two
processes in two zones turn a correct write into an off-by-hours failure that looks exactly like a defect.
The fixture therefore does not merely set the zone, it **checks** it, and the check differs by fixture
because the process topology does:

- **The target host shares the agent's process** — `WebApplicationFactory` hosts it in-process (section
  [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)) — so one assertion covers both:
  `TimeZoneInfo.Local` must equal `TimeZoneInfo.Utc`, checked once during fixture bring-up.
- **The legacy host is a separate process** on the same Windows agent, inheriting the agent's system zone,
  and nothing it serves reports a zone. So the fixture **probes it through behaviour it already has**: during
  the readiness step it adds one item to an anonymous cart, reads that row's `DateCreated` — which the
  application wrote with `DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:49] — through the
  `IStoreObserver`, and requires it to fall within the agent's own UTC clock window for that request. The
  probe row is then removed as part of the reset. A divergence of hours is exactly what a mis-set agent zone
  produces, and this is the one observation that catches it.

Either check failing is a `SETUP` failure before any row runs. A pinned value nobody verifies is a pinned
value on the one agent that happened to be configured.

**Collation is applied at creation, to every database without exception.** The fixture's create statement
is literal:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE [<generated-name>] COLLATE SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS;
```

and it is the statement used for **every** database the run brings into existence: each per-collection
target database, the fixture-owned control database of section
[12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) that holds the ownership registry, and **row 24's own** database —
that last one named explicitly because row 24 provisions a database whose *name* must match the seeding
gate's allow-list, and a case that provisions its database by a different path is a case whose ordering
behaviour is a property of the engine default. An engine's default collation differs between a container
image and a managed instance, so leaving it unset makes rows 1, 8 and 9 assert a property of where the run
happened.

The three values are recorded in the baseline record's `baselineSource` namespace above, which is what makes
the pinning **enforced** rather than documented: a record captured under one set and consumed under another
is refused.

**3. The runbook, from a clean checkout — three stages, because the platform split of point 1 makes it
three.** Provider-neutral, and executable as written. **Every command names the solution or project it
acts on**: an unqualified `dotnet restore`, `dotnet build` or `dotnet test` at the repository root
discovers whatever it finds, which changes meaning as the solution grows and silently runs the wrong
assembly's tests. Angle-bracketed tokens are values the operator supplies or captures, and each is
identified where it appears; every other token is literal.

**Stage A — the Windows characterization run.** Emits the normalized baseline record of point 2. It builds
and runs **only the contracts project**, which by section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)'s graph references nothing of the port's, so this stage
is executable before the target web project exists.

**It is written in PowerShell, and that is a correctness requirement rather than a preference.** This stage
runs on a Windows agent, and the shell there is PowerShell: `export VAR=value` sets nothing, a trailing
`\` is not a line continuation, and `$(...)` command substitution is not the same construct. An earlier
revision of this runbook wrote Stage A in Bourne shell, which meant the stage that captures the baseline
could not be executed as written on the only platform that can capture it. Stages B and C stay shell
because they run on Linux. Angle-bracketed tokens are operator-supplied or captured; everything else is
literal.

```powershell
# A0. Prerequisites (see point 5): Windows; the .NET SDK at the band 04 §3 pins; git; LocalDB with the
#     instance the legacy connection strings name; Visual Studio Build Tools (for MSBuild); and the
#     NuGet CLI on PATH. The agent's system time zone is UTC (point 2's locale pinning).
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'   # governs CMDLET errors only - see the next comment
# $ErrorActionPreference does NOT apply to a native executable's exit code: `dotnet`, `nuget` and
# MSBuild return non-zero and PowerShell 5.1 carries straight on to the next line. So EVERY native
# call below is followed by an explicit check. This is correctness, not style: without it a failed
# `nuget restore` reaches MSBuild, and a failed MSBuild reaches `dotnet test`, which then reports a
# missing assembly - a diagnosis that points at the wrong stage entirely.
function Assert-NativeExit([string]$What) {
  if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "SETUP: $What exited $LASTEXITCODE" }
}

# A1. Restore, then build ONLY the contracts test project. Named explicitly: it must not pull in the
#     web application, and at W4 the web application does not exist.
dotnet restore ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj `
  --locked-mode --configfile ./NuGet.config
Assert-NativeExit 'dotnet restore (contracts project)'
dotnet build ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj `
  --no-restore -c Release
Assert-NativeExit 'dotnet build (contracts project)'

# A2. LOCATE MSBuild rather than hardcoding a path, then restore and build the legacy application,
#     whose output the fixture copies (section 12.3 problem one, step 1). Two separate steps: MVC 5
#     commits no `packages` tree, so its HintPaths resolve only after a restore - deliverable 10 owns
#     that finding, and a build attempted without the restore fails on unresolved references rather
#     than on anything about the application.
#     The legacy build's status is deliverable 10's to report (BLOCKED pending a Windows verification
#     run); it is named here, not asserted here.
$vswhere = "${env:ProgramFiles(x86)}\Microsoft Visual Studio\Installer\vswhere.exe"
$msbuild = & $vswhere -latest -products * -requires Microsoft.Component.MSBuild `
  -find 'MSBuild\**\Bin\MSBuild.exe' | Select-Object -First 1
if (-not $msbuild) { throw 'MSBuild not found; see deliverable 10 for the required toolchain.' }

nuget restore ./src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore.sln -ConfigFile ./NuGet.config
Assert-NativeExit 'nuget restore (MVC 5)'
& $msbuild ./src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore.sln /p:Configuration=Release /nologo
Assert-NativeExit 'MSBuild (MVC 5)'

# A3. Point the fixture at that output and at a private per-run root OUTSIDE the checkout. The fixture
#     performs the deployment and OWNS THE HOST PROCESS: it copies the output, copies both store pairs,
#     rewrites the deployed copy's connection strings and its <globalization> element, starts
#     iisexpress.exe by the literal form of section 12.3 problem one step 4 on a per-run port, captures
#     that process id, polls readiness, waits for startup quiescence, and on teardown stops THAT pid,
#     detaches both databases and deletes the directory.
#     THIS STAGE NEITHER STARTS NOR STOPS THE HOST. Two owners of one process is how a stage kills a
#     host a fixture is still using, or leaves one running that nothing will stop.
$env:Tests__Baseline__LegacyBuildOutput = '<legacy-out>'
$env:Tests__Baseline__DeployRoot        = '<a directory outside the repository checkout>'
$env:Tests__Baseline__LocalDbInstance   = '<the LocalDB instance>'
$env:Tests__Baseline__IisExpressPath    = '<absolute path to iisexpress.exe>'
$env:Tests__Baseline__RecordPath        = '<artifacts>/baseline/baseline-record.json'
$env:Tests__Run__ArtifactPath           = '<the per-run artifact directory>'

# A4. Run the characterization. One project, one filter. Its exit code is CAPTURED and deliberately
#     NOT asserted here: A5 needs it, and the step's own pass or fail is the pipeline's to record.
#     This is the one native call in the stage that Assert-NativeExit must not follow.
dotnet test ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj `
  --no-build -c Release --filter Category=Baseline
$baselineExit = $LASTEXITCODE

# A5. Publish EXACTLY ONE artifact, and WHICH ONE depends on A4 - point 2's publication rule, which is
#     06 12.1's rule and not a second one. A COMPLETE, WHOLLY PASSING capture publishes the baseline
#     record and its digest, in that order. A FAILED OR INCOMPLETE capture publishes `baseline-
#     diagnostic` and NO record: it neither creates one nor replaces the one already accepted.
#     A5 IS A SEPARATE ALWAYS-RUN PIPELINE STEP, not a continuation of the script above. $ErrorAction-
#     Preference = 'Stop' means a failed A4 ends that invocation, so an A5 written as its next line
#     would be skipped in exactly the case it exists for. Same agent, same working directory, same
#     $env:Tests__Baseline__RecordPath value - supplied to the step, not inherited from a dead process.
#     $baselineExit is A4's captured exit code, passed in by the pipeline as a literal step input.
$record = $env:Tests__Baseline__RecordPath
$complete = ($baselineExit -eq 0) -and (Test-Path -LiteralPath $record) -and `
  ((Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath $record | ConvertFrom-Json).coverage.cases `
    | Where-Object { $_.status -ne 'passed' } | Measure-Object).Count -eq 0
if ($complete) {
  (Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $record).Hash.ToLowerInvariant() `
    | Set-Content -LiteralPath "$record.sha256" -NoNewline -Encoding ascii
  # Then publish "$record" and "$record.sha256" as pipeline artifact `baseline-record`.
} else {
  # Then publish the per-run artifact directory's SETUP/ASSERTION records - and NOT "$record" - as
  # pipeline artifact `baseline-capture-diagnostic`. A different name is what stops a consumer picking it up.
  Remove-Item -LiteralPath "$record.sha256" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
#     The publish task itself is the selected provider's, and the provider is 03's gate, so it is not
#     named here; what is fixed is which artifact name carries which outcome.
```

**Stage B — the Linux target run.** Consumes the record Stage A wrote. It builds and runs the target test
project, which references both the web application and the contracts project.

```bash
# B0. Prerequisites: Linux; the SDK at the band 04 §3 pins; a container runtime (developer path) or
#     access to the allow-listed managed test server (CI path); and PowerShell (`pwsh`), which the
#     browser installer of B1b is written in - the harness package generates a .ps1 and no shell
#     equivalent, so pwsh is a prerequisite of this stage rather than a preference.

# B0a. EVERY NATIVE COMMAND IN THIS STAGE IS CHECKED, by the shell rather than one line at a time:
#      -e stops on the first non-zero exit, -u makes an unset variable an error instead of an empty
#      string, and -o pipefail is what stops a failure inside a pipeline being masked by the last
#      command in it - which is exactly the shape of B3a. The two places a code must NOT end the
#      stage (B5's `dotnet test`, and cleanup) disable it locally and say so.
#      EVERY BOUND BELOW IS A LITERAL: 5 password attempts, 120 seconds for the engine start, 900 for
#      the browser install, B4's 2-second interval and 120-second ceiling, and the sweep job's 10 and
#      15 minutes. None is computed from another value and none is a retry-until-success.
set -euo pipefail

# B0b. The run identifier is the CALLER's, generated once and handed to every job of the run
#      (section 12.7). This stage does not compose one: an identifier composed here would make the
#      sweep job treat this job's resources as another run's and defer them behind the 24-hour gate.
RUN_ID="${Tests__Run__Id:?SETUP: Tests__Run__Id is unset - see section 12.7}"

# B1. Restore and build the solution, named explicitly.
dotnet restore ./MvcMusicStore.sln --locked-mode --configfile ./NuGet.config
dotnet tool restore --configfile ./NuGet.config   # local-tool restore has no locked mode; 06 §12.1
dotnet build ./MvcMusicStore.sln --no-restore -c Release

# B1b. ACQUIRE THE BROWSER ENGINE for row 28 `28b`. The harness package ships a DRIVER, not a browser
#      (04 §7.7), so this step is a prerequisite of the run and not an optional extra: without it that
#      one case fails on a missing engine, which is a SETUP failure and must not read as a defect in
#      the removal flow. Only Chromium is installed - one engine is the claim (04 §7.7) - and
#      --with-deps is what makes a bare CI image usable. It runs AFTER B1 because the installer the
#      package generates is a build output of the test project.
timeout 900 pwsh ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/bin/Release/net8.0/playwright.ps1 \
  install chromium --with-deps

# B1a. DOWNLOAD the baseline artifact Stage A published, VERIFY its digest, and point the fixture at
#      it. This is the transfer of point 2: the two agents share no filesystem, so nothing here reads
#      across to the Windows machine and nothing falls back to a path from an earlier run.
#      The download itself is the provider's task (03's gate); what is fixed is the destination, the
#      verification, and that it happens BEFORE any host or engine starts.
BASELINE_DIR=./artifacts/baseline            # where artifact `baseline-record` is downloaded to
RECORD="$BASELINE_DIR/baseline-record.json"
EXPECTED=$(cat "$RECORD.sha256")
ACTUAL=$(sha256sum "$RECORD" | cut -d' ' -f1)
if [ "$EXPECTED" != "$ACTUAL" ]; then
  echo "SETUP: baseline record digest mismatch: expected $EXPECTED actual $ACTUAL for $RECORD" >&2
  exit 1                                     # no Category=Target row runs against an unverified record
fi
export Tests__Baseline__RecordPath="$RECORD"

# B2. Publish the data-migration tool and CAPTURE the output path. The migration rows of section 12.4
#     and the release pipeline invoke this same published output, by the single form of section 5.6:
#       dotnet <published-tool>/MigrateData.dll <mode> [--extract <extract-id>] \
#         [--scope catalog|identity] [--model-overrides <file>] --report-dir <run artifacts>
#     Per-mode switch legality is the table in section 5.6 and is exhaustive; the three rules a caller
#     trips first: --extract is MANDATORY for schema-diff, load, reconcile and dry-run and forbidden for
#     extract and seed; --scope is MANDATORY for load, reconcile and dry-run, forbidden for the other
#     three, and has no default and no `both`; --model-overrides is legal ONLY on schema-diff and
#     dry-run, so no override can influence a write. Any violation exits 2 and writes no data. The
#     extract value is the extract-id the fixture's own `extract` invocation emitted; every consuming
#     mode re-verifies the extract manifest's SHA-256 digests and exits 2 on any mismatch (section 5.6).
#     Connections arrive through MIGRATEDATA_SOURCE_CONNECTION and MIGRATEDATA_TARGET_CONNECTION,
#     scoped to the single invocation, never as arguments. Exit codes: 0 pass, 1 ran and refused,
#     2 could not run - captured and asserted by the caller.
dotnet publish ./tools/migrate-data/MigrateData.csproj --no-build -c Release \
  -o ./artifacts/migrate-data
export Tests__Target__MigrateDataPath=./artifacts/migrate-data

# B3. Engine, developer path: start the container by IMMUTABLE DIGEST, with a GENERATED name, and
#     CAPTURE the container id. The digest is the pinned reference recorded in point 5; a tag is not
#     acceptable (see the note below). The name is generated so two runs cannot collide; the id is
#     what teardown deletes by, because a name can be reused by an unrelated container.
#
#     THE PASSWORD IS NOT AN ARGUMENT. It is generated per run into an env-file with owner-only
#     permissions, outside the checkout, and passed by --env-file. A `-e "MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD=$VAR"`
#     form puts the secret in this shell's process listing and in the pipeline's own command log,
#     where it is retained for the log's lifetime - the same reasoning section 5.6 applies to
#     connection strings and section 10 to the administrator password.
#     WHAT --env-file DOES AND DOES NOT BUY, stated so it is not over-claimed: it keeps the value out
#     of the argument vector and out of the command log. It does NOT remove it from the container's own
#     environment, which `docker inspect` will show to anyone who can reach the runtime socket. Access
#     to that socket is therefore itself a control (deliverable 06 owns agent access), and the value is
#     per-run, used by nothing else, and destroyed with the container at B7.
#     In CI the platform's secret injection supplies the same variable and NO FILE IS WRITTEN by this
#     stage at all - which is the stronger path, and the one the CI engine row of point 5 selects.
set +x   # tracing OFF for the block that materialises the password; this stage never sets -x

# B3d. THE IMAGE REFERENCE IS A LITERAL DIGEST, AND ITS SHAPE IS CHECKED BEFORE ANYTHING RUNS. The
#      pipeline supplies the point 5 pin in TESTS_ENGINE_IMAGE; an angle-bracket placeholder left in
#      a command by a copy-paste and a mutable tag are the two ways this goes wrong, and both produce
#      a run whose engine nobody can identify afterwards - the first as a pull failure that reads as
#      a network fault, the second silently, next week, as a different build.
ENGINE_IMAGE="${TESTS_ENGINE_IMAGE:?SETUP: TESTS_ENGINE_IMAGE is unset; supply the point 5 digest}"
case "$ENGINE_IMAGE" in
  mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server@sha256:*) : ;;
  *) echo "SETUP: engine image must be mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server@sha256:<64 hex>" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
printf '%s' "${ENGINE_IMAGE#*@sha256:}" | grep -Eq '^[0-9a-f]{64}$' || {
  echo "SETUP: engine digest is not 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters" >&2; exit 1; }

# B3p. THE PASSWORD IS GENERATED, VALIDATED, AND NEVER ECHOED. Validated because SQL Server enforces
#      its own complexity policy and a rejected password does not fail here: the container starts,
#      exits, and the run reports B4's READINESS TIMEOUT - a symptom that points at the network or
#      the image rather than at the one line that caused it. The bound is a literal 5 attempts,
#      because a generator that cannot satisfy three character classes in five tries is broken and an
#      unbounded loop in a setup step holds an agent forever.
#      NEVER ECHOED means three things exactly: no `echo` of the value; no `set -x` anywhere in this
#      stage, which the `set +x` above asserts; and no `-e MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD=...` argument. Its only
#      sinks are the 0600 env-file and the connection string exported at B3a.
ENGINE_ENVFILE="$(mktemp)"; chmod 600 "$ENGINE_ENVFILE"
ENGINE_PASSWORD=""
for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  ENGINE_PASSWORD="$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9#%*+-' </dev/urandom | head -c 32)"
  if printf '%s' "$ENGINE_PASSWORD" | grep -q '[A-Z]' \
  && printf '%s' "$ENGINE_PASSWORD" | grep -q '[a-z]' \
  && printf '%s' "$ENGINE_PASSWORD" | grep -q '[0-9]'; then break; fi
  ENGINE_PASSWORD=""
done
[ -n "$ENGINE_PASSWORD" ] || {
  echo "SETUP: no policy-conformant engine password in 5 attempts" >&2; exit 1; }
{ echo "ACCEPT_EULA=Y"; echo "MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD=$ENGINE_PASSWORD"; } > "$ENGINE_ENVFILE"

# B3e. Start it. The name derives from the CALLER-GENERATED run id (section 12.7), so two runs cannot
#      collide and the name is attributable; the id is what teardown deletes by.
ENGINE_NAME="mvcmusicstore-tests-sql-$RUN_ID"
ENGINE_ID=$(timeout 120 docker run -d --name "$ENGINE_NAME" -p 0:1433 \
  --env-file "$ENGINE_ENVFILE" "$ENGINE_IMAGE")
export Tests__Target__EngineContainerId="$ENGINE_ID"

# B3t. RECORD OWNERSHIP, THEN INSTALL A TRAP - in that order, because a resource with no record is
#      unauthorizable (section 12.8(a)). For the ENGINE the filesystem record is the authority rather
#      than the convenience copy, for the reason that subsection gives: on this path the control
#      database lives INSIDE this container. It is also the only way B7 and the sweep job reach the
#      captured id and the env-file path at all - both are separate processes and neither can see
#      this shell's variables.
mkdir -p "$Tests__Run__ArtifactPath"
cat > "$Tests__Run__ArtifactPath/owned-engine.json" <<JSON
{"creator":"MvcMusicStore.Tests","runId":"$RUN_ID","agent":"$(hostname)",
 "createdUtc":"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)","containerId":"$ENGINE_ID",
 "image":"$ENGINE_IMAGE","envFile":"$ENGINE_ENVFILE"}
JSON

cleanup_stage_b() {
  status=$?
  trap - EXIT INT TERM                      # so a failure inside cleanup cannot re-enter it
  if [ -n "${ENGINE_ID:-}" ]; then docker rm -f "$ENGINE_ID" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; fi
  if [ -n "${ENGINE_ENVFILE:-}" ]; then
    shred -u "$ENGINE_ENVFILE" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$ENGINE_ENVFILE" || true
  fi
  exit "$status"
}
trap cleanup_stage_b EXIT INT TERM
#      The trap covers the three cases B7 cannot: Ctrl-C at a developer's terminal (INT), a TERM to
#      this shell, and any `set -e` exit from a later line. It is idempotent, so B7 running after it
#      is harmless. It does NOT replace the always-run sweep JOB: a job the platform kills runs no
#      trap either, which is the case that job exists for.

# B3a. CAPTURE THE MAPPED PORT rather than assuming one. `-p 0:1433` asks the runtime to choose a free
#      host port - which is what lets two runs share a machine - so the port is an OUTPUT and must be
#      read back. A connection string built on a hardcoded 1433 fails to connect on the developer path
#      and, worse, may reach a DIFFERENT engine that happens to be listening there.
#      `set -o pipefail` is what makes this line honest: without it a failed `docker port` leaves
#      `head` and `sed` exiting 0 over empty input, and the port is silently empty.
ENGINE_PORT=$(docker port "$ENGINE_ID" 1433/tcp | head -n1 | sed 's/.*://')
[ -n "$ENGINE_PORT" ] || { echo "SETUP: could not read the mapped engine port" >&2; exit 1; }
export Tests__Target__EngineConnectionString="Server=127.0.0.1,$ENGINE_PORT;User ID=sa;\
Password=$ENGINE_PASSWORD;Encrypt=True;TrustServerCertificate=True"
unset ENGINE_PASSWORD
#      `sa` is this path's BOOTSTRAP principal (section 12.8) and carries no database name, as that
#      subsection requires. TrustServerCertificate is accepted HERE ONLY: a disposable container on
#      loopback presents a self-signed certificate, and this is a test engine rather than the
#      application's transport posture, which 06 owns. On the CI path the platform supplies this one
#      variable for the allow-listed managed server and neither B3 nor B3a runs at all.

# B4. Readiness probe against the engine, before any test: open a connection and execute SELECT 1,
#     polled every 2 seconds to a ceiling of 120 seconds. A ceiling breach is a SETUP failure.
#     The fixture performs this; it is named here so the stage's ordering is unambiguous.

# B5. Run the target half. One project, one filter. `set -e` is lifted around it deliberately: B6
#     publishes on success only and B7 must run either way, so the code is CAPTURED and the stage
#     ends on it at B7 rather than here.
set +e
dotnet test ./src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Tests.csproj \
  --no-build -c Release --filter Category=Target
TARGET_EXIT=$?
set -e

# B6. PUBLISH the build outputs Stage C needs, so that its `--no-build` has an input. Stage C runs on a
#     separate agent after a deploy and does not build: it downloads artifact `test-binaries` into the
#     same relative paths and invokes the same command. The artifact carries BOTH test projects' `bin`
#     AND `obj` trees - the contracts project's included, because Stage C runs THAT project - since
#     `--no-build` reads the project's build assets and not only its assembly.
#     Published on success only - there is nothing to deploy, and so nothing for Stage C to observe,
#     if the target half failed.

# B7. Teardown of the stage's own resources, by CAPTURED IDENTIFIER. Configured as an ALWAYS-RUN STEP
#     within this job, so it runs whether B5 passed or failed - including when B5's own watchdog
#     (section 12.7 layer 2) kills the `dotnet test` PROCESS TREE and returns a failure to the job.
#     WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER, stated because the distinction is the whole reason the sweep job exists:
#     if the JOB is cancelled or killed by the platform, no step of it runs, B7 included. The separate
#     always-run sweep job below is the guarantee for that case; B7 is the fast path for every other.
#     The env-file goes with it, secret and all.
#     IT READS THE CAPTURED IDENTIFIERS FROM THE OWNERSHIP RECORD, not from this shell, because as an
#     always-run STEP it is a separate process - and because a teardown that reconstructed an id would
#     be guessing, which section 12.8(c) forbids.
ENGINE_RECORD="$Tests__Run__ArtifactPath/owned-engine.json"
RECORDED_ID=$(sed -n 's/.*"containerId":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$ENGINE_RECORD")
RECORDED_ENVFILE=$(sed -n 's/.*"envFile":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$ENGINE_RECORD")
[ -n "$RECORDED_ID" ] || {
  echo "SETUP: no engine ownership record; the always-run sweep job owns this case" >&2; exit 1; }
docker rm -f "$RECORDED_ID"
[ -z "$RECORDED_ENVFILE" ] || shred -u "$RECORDED_ENVFILE" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$RECORDED_ENVFILE"
exit "${TARGET_EXIT:-0}"                     # the stage's result, preserved through the trap
```

**The orphan sweep is a separate always-run job, not a step inside this one.** Section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) layer 3 is the cleanup guarantee, and a step
placed after `dotnet test` **cannot be** that guarantee: layer 2's watchdog kills the process tree, so a
step in the killed job does not run at all — which is precisely the case the sweep exists for. An earlier
revision of this runbook put the sweep at the end of Stage B and was therefore relying on a command that
the failure mode it addresses prevents from executing. So it is its own job:

| Aspect | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **What runs** | Three commands against the **contracts** project, in order: `dotnet restore ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj --locked-mode --configfile ./NuGet.config`, then `dotnet build … --no-restore -c Release`, then `dotnet test … --no-build -c Release --filter Category=Sweep`. The sweep needs neither the web application nor a target host, and running it from the assembly with fewest dependencies is what lets it run when the port is broken |
| **Why it builds rather than downloading `test-binaries`** | Because that artifact is published by B6 **on success only**, and every case this job exists for is a failure case — so a `--no-build` invocation over a downloaded artifact would fail on a missing assembly in precisely the runs that leaked resources. It also must not depend on any output of the job it is cleaning up after: a job that was killed published nothing. The cost is one restore and one build of a project that references no application code, which is the cheapest thing in this runbook |
| **What `Category=Sweep` denotes** | A **concrete runnable class**, `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Maintenance/OrphanSweepTests.cs`, declared in that assembly and traited `Category=Sweep`. It is a real class with real `[Fact]` methods, discovered like any other — not a filter over nothing. It is a **maintenance invocation and not a fourth coverage category**: it selects no row of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) and appears in no count in this document. Point 1's trait rule above states the same exclusion from the other direction |
| **Where it runs** | A pipeline job **separate from the job that runs Stage B**, configured to execute **always** — on Stage B's success, on its failure, and on its cancellation or watchdog kill. Separate because a job cannot be killed and then clean up after itself, and always-run because the failure cases are the ones with resources left over |
| **What it is authorized to do** | Only what section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) permits, and its deletion authority always comes from **that candidate's own ownership record** — the captured `database_id` and `create_date` re-resolved against the name, or the directory's run-marker — never from the fact that the sweep chose it |
| **The `runId` it is handed, and the two candidate sets that follow** | The job is given **the same `runId` as the Stage B job it follows**, which is what lets it finish that run's cleanup when the job was killed before B7. Records carrying that `runId` are **own-resource deletions with no age gate**; records carrying **any other** `runId` are **orphan candidates** under the **24-hour** gate. One invocation, two sets, partitioned by the identifier — section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s two deletion paths, reached from here. Read as "anything this *process* did not create", the age gate would defer the killed run's own leaked database for a day, which is the leak the job exists to close |
| **Two operational controls, stated as values and explicitly not as a schedule** | The **grace period** the always-run job waits before sweeping: **10 minutes** past the external stage timeout of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) layer 2, so a run that is merely slow to dispose is not swept out from under itself. And the **deadline** by which the sweep itself must finish: **15 minutes**, after which it reports a `SETUP` failure naming the candidates it did not reach, because a sweep that hangs holds an agent and hides the leak it was called to fix. Both are bounds on one invocation; neither is a cadence, and this document schedules nothing — when the job runs is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to place |

**Stage C — the deployed transport and HSTS observation**, after a deploy to a non-traffic target. It
selects section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 47 and nothing else** — not the health rows, which are
`Category=Target` and ran in Stage B, for the reason section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) gives above.

**It runs the *contracts* assembly, not the target one, and that is a consequence of where the class
lives rather than a preference.** The deployed-only fixture and its concrete class are declared in
`src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests` (section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)), because they reference no application type — and a
runner discovers tests only in the assembly it is asked to run, so `--filter Category=Deployed` against
the target project would select **nothing** and report a green stage that observed no deployment. That
failure is silent, which is why the project path is stated here rather than inferred. The stage needs
**no** Windows, no engine and no database: the only prerequisites are the published build assets and the
base address.

```bash
# C0. DOWNLOAD artifact `test-binaries` (published by B6) into the same relative paths it was built at,
#     because this stage does not build and `--no-build` needs the project's build assets present.
#     Without this the command below fails on a missing assembly, which reads as a broken stage rather
#     than as the missing input it is.

export Tests__Deployed__BaseAddress=<the deployed non-traffic base address>
dotnet test ./src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests.csproj \
  --no-build -c Release --filter Category=Deployed
```

**Why `--no-build` on the test commands and a separate build step**: a `dotnet test` that builds reports
a compile error inside the test output, where it reads as a test failure. The classification of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) exists to keep those apart, and the runbook
should not undo it at the shell.

**A re-capture is Stage A again**, unchanged, replacing the record at `Tests__Baseline__RecordPath` — which
is what makes the "adding an assertion late requires a re-capture" cost of point 2 a command rather than a
project.

**Engine acquisition, per audience — and the image is referenced by digest.**

| Audience | Engine | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A developer** | The Microsoft SQL Server 2022 container image, referenced as `mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server@sha256:<digest>` | Started per run by Stage B3 with a **generated** container name and the container **id captured** for teardown; the EULA accepted and a **per-run generated** administrator password supplied through an **owner-only `--env-file` outside the checkout**, never as a `-e` argument and never a committed or shared value, and masked in output by section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s connection-string rule. The **host port is read back** with `docker port` (B3a) rather than assumed, because `-p 0:1433` makes it an output. Requires a container runtime, the one prerequisite beyond the SDK. Removed by `docker rm -f "$ENGINE_ID"` in B7, with the env-file shredded alongside it |
| **CI** | A **throwaway managed database** on the allow-listed test server (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gate 1), created for the run and dropped at teardown | No image, so Stage B3, B3a and the container half of B7 do not apply — the platform's secret injection supplies the connection and no env-file is written — and the fixture's acquisition and deletion gates (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)) operate on the database identifier instead. The server is long-lived and allow-listed; the *databases* are per-collection and disposable, exactly as section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) requires |

**Why a digest and not `:2022-latest`, stated because the tag is the obvious choice and it is the wrong
one.** A moving tag makes the engine an **uncontrolled input**: a servicing update changes collation
defaults, error-message text, transient-error classification and query-plan behaviour, and the suite then
reports a difference the port did not cause — the exact false-regression class this section exists to
eliminate. A digest also makes the baseline record's configuration fingerprint (point 2) meaningful, since
an engine that can change under a fixed fingerprint makes the fingerprint a lie. **The digest is resolved
once, at pin time, and recorded**: the operator runs `docker image inspect` (or `docker buildx imagetools
inspect`) against the tag they intend to adopt, takes the manifest digest, and records it in this
runbook's own pin line, together with the date it was resolved and the tag it corresponded to. Moving to a
newer image is therefore a deliberate edit with a re-run behind it, not something that happens overnight.
**No digest literal is published here**, for the same reason no package version is: this document names no
version (point 1's ownership boundary), and a digest asserted from a machine that could not verify it
would be a fabrication. [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the **CI agent and base
image**; this is the developer-path engine, which that section does not cover.

**The readiness check runs before the first test, and it is trivial by design.** A **connectivity
probe** — open a connection and execute `SELECT 1` — polled **every 2 seconds to a ceiling of 120
seconds**. It is deliberately not a schema or migration check: those are the fixture's own steps and have
their own setup categories, and a readiness probe that fails for a migration reason would misclassify the
failure. Failure to become reachable within the ceiling is setup category (a) of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction), naming the reduced connection target and the
elapsed time.

**4. The configuration keys the fixtures read.** Supplied by environment variables, user secrets or
pipeline variables — the mechanism is the operator's, the names are not. Each has one purpose and no
default that could make a destructive operation possible by omission.

| Key | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Tests:Baseline:LegacyBuildOutput` | The built legacy output Stage A2 produced, which the fixture **copies** (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one, step 1). `Category=Baseline` only |
| `Tests:Baseline:DeployRoot` | The private per-run root, **outside the repository checkout**, into which the fixture deploys that copy and its `App_Data` copies of **both** store pairs (the same directory section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4 governs) |
| `Tests:Baseline:LocalDbInstance` | The LocalDB instance the **copied** store pairs are attached to. The tracked files are never attached |
| `Tests:Baseline:IisExpressPath` | The absolute path to the `iisexpress.exe` the fixture invokes with the literal form of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one step 4. Its install location is [10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s to state; the fixture is given it rather than searching for it, so a machine with two installs cannot silently serve from the wrong one. **There is no key that supplies a base address instead** — the base address is always an output of that step |
| `Tests:Baseline:RecordPath` | Where `Category=Baseline` **writes** and `Category=Target` **reads** the normalized baseline record of point 2 |
| `Tests:Target:EngineConnectionString` | The **BOOTSTRAP** principal's connection to the disposable engine, carrying **no database name**. It is the one externally provisioned credential (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a), and it is what the fixture creates the run's databases and its two run-scoped principals from, in the order section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) fixes. Its secret arrives from the platform secret store and is redacted in every artifact by section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s connection-string rule |
| `Tests:Target:EngineContainerId` | The container id Stage B3 **captured**, for the developer path only. Teardown deletes by this value and never by a container name (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gate 3(c)) |
| `Tests:Target:MigrateDataPath` | The published output path Stage B2 captured, which the migration rows invoke by the single form of section [5.6](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) |
| `Tests:Target:ServerAllowList` | Section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gate 1's allow-list. **No default**, so an unset value refuses rather than permits |
| `Tests:Target:ProductionTargetPatterns` | Section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gate 1's production-shape refusal patterns |
| `Tests:Deployed:BaseAddress` | The deployed non-traffic target's base address. `Category=Deployed` only |
| `Tests:Run:ArtifactPath` | The per-run artifact directory of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) |

**What the fixture writes rather than reads**: the resolved per-run connection string, injected through
in-memory configuration into the application's **single** connection-string key (section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) consolidates the
two legacy entries into one) and bound from there by both contexts and by the distributed cache — which
is section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) override (ii). The
seeding rows likewise **write** the three inputs section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s guard reads — environment name, enable flag
and target database name — through the same mechanism, which is how a gate can be failed one at a time
without a real database being involved (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)).

**The per-collection database-naming rule.** Each collection fixture's database is named
`test_<run-identifier>_<collection>`, where `<run-identifier>` is the UTC-timestamp-plus-random value of
section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) and `<collection>` is the surface
group's short name. Three properties follow, and all three are load-bearing: the name is unique across
concurrent runs, it is **matchable** by section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gate 2's
pattern, and it is readable by a human looking at an engine and wondering what a database is.

**Timeouts, stated so that a hang fails rather than occupies an agent — and stated with what each one
does and does not guarantee.** Three bounds, matching the three layers of section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism):

| Bound | Value | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Per scenario** | **60 seconds**, as the cancellation token every HTTP call, SQL command and child process observes | Generous for an in-process request and short enough that a deadlock is a failure rather than a stall. Because it is **cooperative**, the run stays alive: the scenario fails, disposal is still reached, and the reset of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) still runs |
| **Per run, in-process** | **45 minutes `Category=Target`, 30 minutes `Category=Baseline`, 10 minutes `Category=Deployed`** | On breach the run **stops itself** and reports a **setup** failure naming the last scenario that started, because a suite that never returns has told the reader nothing. This path is cooperative too, so disposal runs |
| **Per stage, external** | The stage timeout of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) layer 2 — the in-process ceiling **plus a stated grace period** — owned by the pipeline stage or the operator's wrapper | On breach the watchdog **kills** the process. **Disposal does not run**, and nothing in this document claims otherwise: the runner cannot deliver an asynchronous disposal callback to a terminated process. Cleanup in this case is Stage B7's post-process sweep, which is why that stage is unconditional |

**5. What the reader installs, and what the suite provisions for itself.** Stated as two lists, because
the boundary is the whole of "can this be run from a clean checkout".

| Installed by the operator | Provisioned by the suite |
| --- | --- |
| The .NET SDK at the band [04 §3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins — a mismatched feature band fails the build, which is the intended behaviour [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records | Both `dotnet-ef` and `dotnet-sql-cache`, restored from the committed tool manifest by Stage B1 — [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the manifest and the pins |
| A container runtime, for the developer path only, and the **resolved image digest** recorded in this runbook's pin line | The disposable database, its schema and its data: the cache table, **both** migration sets in the order of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), the two run-scoped SQL principals BOOTSTRAP creates (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a), and the fixture-data manifest with its seven post-load invariants (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two) |
| For `Category=Baseline` only: Windows, LocalDB, MSBuild, and a **built** legacy application — whose build status [10 §3.2](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) records and this document does not restate. **Serving** it is the fixture's job, not the operator's | The legacy **deployment**: the private per-run directory outside the checkout, the copies of both store pairs, the rewritten connection strings, the per-run port, the readiness poll, and the stop-detach-delete teardown (sections [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring), [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)) |
| The configuration values of point 4, and the **external stage timeout** of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) layer 2 | The per-run identifier, every resource name derived from it, the ownership registry, the orphan sweep and all in-process teardown (sections [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism), [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)) |

**One prerequisite is outstanding rather than satisfiable today, and it is named here because the runbook
above would otherwise read as executable in both halves.** Stage A2 builds the legacy application, and
MVC 5's build status is **blocked pending a Windows verification run**
([10 §3.2](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)). So Stage A is executable **once that verification
succeeds**, and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) is where that dependency is sequenced — its W4 entry gate
is explicit about needing an application that builds *and runs*. This document neither asserts that build
outcome nor works around it, and the fixture-lifecycle evidence recorded in section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) does not alter it.

### 12.11 Coverage limits and the scope-change requests

**A suite that does not state what it fails to cover reads as though it covered everything, which is the
one claim this section exists to prevent.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) publishes 75 rows and
242 cases; the list below is what those 242 cases **do not** establish. Each entry names the gap, why it
is a gap rather than an oversight, and what closing it would take — and where closing it would change
another deliverable's decision, it is raised as a **scope-change request** to the plan owner rather than
absorbed here. **No scope-change request to the plan owner is open** — the one this section previously
carried, browser-executed behaviour of the scripted cart flow, is closed, and the subsection below records
the closure rather than deleting the reasoning, because a gap that disappears without a record reads as a
gap that was never found. **One residual is open and is routed elsewhere**: the functional behaviour of the
three browser engines the automation does not install is an approval decision for
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W1 rather than a change to the plan, and it is stated in the closure
subsection below and carried as entry **8** of the limits table. It is recorded as open, not as settled.

#### The former scope-change request, now closed: browser-executed behaviour of the scripted cart flow

**The request is narrower than it first appears, and the narrowing is deliberate.** Three caller-side
artifacts in this application are HTML or script that a browser consumes: the cart page's removal handler,
the checkout address form, and the linked-login remove form. **Two of the three need no browser**, and are
covered rather than requested: a form is fetched, parsed and submitted over ordinary HTTP with the fields
and token the server actually rendered, which is what rows 4 `4a`, 10, 22 `22i` and 69 do. That closes the
class of defect a hand-built request cannot see — a form rendered with the wrong action, the wrong verb, a
missing token field, or a field the server no longer reads — because the request under test is built *from
the response*. Parsing is AngleSharp's, per section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box). What remains is the one artifact
that is not markup but **behaviour**: script that must execute.

**What was not covered, and what now covers it.** The cart page's removal handler is the application's
only scripted flow [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:7-35]. An earlier revision of
this section recorded the gap and raised a request, naming no mechanism because the dependency set was
another deliverable's to pin. **That hand-off is discharged and the gap is closed**: the mechanism is
`Microsoft.Playwright` driving **Chromium**, pinned with its version, its declaring projects and its
one-engine boundary by [04 §7.7](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md), and the coverage is section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 28 `28b`** — the page loaded and the removal control clicked in the
engine, asserting the `RequestVerificationToken` **request header actually sent**, the JSON response
handled, the four DOM updates applied to the named elements, and **zero** console errors and **zero**
policy-violation reports across the navigation.

The coverage now stands in two layers rather than stopping short of the runtime: rows 5 to 7 drive the
server endpoint directly and assert its status, its JSON shape and its token transport; row 28 `28a`
asserts **statically** that the token is rendered, that the script carries the exact header name
`RequestVerificationToken` and that it names the exact element identifiers the page renders; and `28b`
asserts that the script, loaded and executed, does what `28a` says it is spelled to do.

**Two boundaries the closure does not cross, stated because a closure that overstates itself is worse than
an open gap.**

**One: the automation is one engine and one flow, and the other three engines' *functional* behaviour is
covered by nothing.** [06 §10.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the supported-browser matrix —
four evergreen families — and the coverage this suite provides against it splits three ways rather than
two, which an earlier revision of this paragraph collapsed:

| What | Engines | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Functional behaviour of the one scripted flow** | **Chromium only** | Automated, section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 28 `28b` |
| **Rendered appearance** | Whichever engine the reviewer captures in, per section [12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) | Manual review against a captured baseline, which the plan's §0.11.2 scopes there |
| **Functional behaviour on the other three families** | The remaining three of [06 §10.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s matrix | **Nothing.** Not the automation, which installs one engine; and not the appearance review, which looks at rendering rather than at whether the removal control works |

**That third line is an open residual and this document does not settle it.** It is **not** closed by
`28b`, and it is **not** absorbed by the manual review: a reviewer confirming that the cart page *looks*
right in Safari has not established that its removal handler sends the token header there. Closing it would
mean installing three more engines in Stage B and running `28b` under each, which is a cost
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) sizes and a matrix decision
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) bounds — so the residual is **routed to
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W1 as a mandatory approval decision**, in the same set as every
numbered delta: either the residual is accepted with the narrowed functional scope recorded, or the
automation is extended to the matrix and the effort is admitted. **An undecided residual is unresolved
scope**, which is W1's own standard, and this entry exists so that nobody reads `28b` as evidence about
four engines. Entry **8** of the limits table below carries it in the form this section carries every other
limit.

**Two: the engine binaries are not in the package.** The harness ships a driver and acquires the browser
through its own install step, which is a **prerequisite of any run that selects this case** and is placed
in the runbook by section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split).
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries the effort for both the harness and that acquisition.

**Why the static assertion alone was not equivalent, which is the reason `28b` exists rather than a
tightened `28a`.** A script can satisfy every string-level assertion `28a` makes and still fail at
runtime — a selector that matches nothing on the rendered page, a handler attached before the element
exists, a dependency load order that leaves the library undefined, a policy refusal (which fails
**silently to the server**, as [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records). The failure mode
is precisely the one a text assertion cannot see: the page renders, the removal control does nothing, and
the only evidence is a console error in the user's browser. That is why `28b`'s fourth assertion reads the
browser's **own** console and violation channels rather than only the DOM — a case that asserted the DOM
alone would report "the row did not disappear" for a policy refusal, a script error and a server failure
identically.

**A manual sign-off was explicitly not accepted as the alternative, and that constraint is what the
closure respects.** The approved plan permits a manual review in place of automation for **rendered
appearance** and for nothing else — that is what section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) discharges. Behavioural coverage of a
scripted request is not rendered appearance, so substituting a reviewer clicking the remove link would
have reclassified a behavioural gap as a visual one. The gap is therefore closed by **automation** — one
engine, one flow, four assertions — and the manual review keeps exactly the scope it had.

#### The remaining limits, each with what would close it

| # | What is not covered | Why | What would close it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The fifth DOM update in the source's removal script, `#cart-status` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29] | **No view in the repository renders that identifier**, so the source's fifth update is already a no-op and there is no behaviour to preserve. Row 28 deliberately does not assert it, because asserting an element the application never had would invent a requirement | A product decision: either the identifier is dropped from the ported script, or a status element is added to the cart view and row 28 gains an assertion for it. Either way it is a **port decision**, not a test gap, and it belongs to whoever approves the cart view's markup |
| 2 | **Closed.** The lockout **expiring** — that a locked account can sign in once its 15 minutes have elapsed — is now asserted, by section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 71** | This entry previously recorded the gap and proposed registering the framework's time abstraction so a fixture could advance the clock. **That proposal was wrong on the mechanism**, and the correction is recorded rather than quietly replaced: the lockout decision is taken inside Identity's user manager against the ambient UTC clock, not against a clock this target's framework version lets the composition substitute, so registering a time abstraction would not have moved it — and the alternative it was weighed against, a fifteen-minute wait inside a test, is not a test | Already closed. **Row 71 uses state instead of time**: the fixture writes the account's lockout end to an instant in the past, which *is* the state fifteen minutes of elapsed time produces, and the case is then instant and deterministic.
